name: Volume rendering
head: Volume rendering makes images of data that fill space (a density, a material, a temperature sampled through a region) rather than of surfaces alone.
body: Volume rendering makes images of data that fill space (a density, a material, a temperature sampled through a region) rather than of surfaces alone. This introduction was written by Claude. A volume is a function over 3D space, f(\mathbf{x}), usually known only at samples. The commonest case, and the core of this encyclopedia, is a regular grid: a 3D array of values in which each cell, a voxel, is a small cube. CT and MRI scans, smoke and fluid simulations, cloud textures, Minecraft-style worlds and the occupancy grids of game engines all have this form. A voxel can hold a scalar (density, temperature), a material id, a color, or a single occupancy bit. The same ideas carry over to other sampled fields: hierarchical and adaptive grids that store detail only where it is needed (octrees, VDB, adaptive mesh refinement), unstructured meshes of tetrahedra and other cells, implicit fields such as signed distance functions that are evaluated on demand, and learned fields such as neural radiance fields and 3D Gaussians. Extract a surface, then draw the surface. Choose a level f(\mathbf{x}) = c (an isosurface) or the boundary of the solid voxels, turn it into triangles, and draw them with an ordinary GPU pipeline. Most voxel games and many medical viewers work this way. Render the volume directly. Treat the data as a semi-transparent medium and add up its contribution along each viewing ray. This is direct volume rendering, introduced in its common form by Levoy and by Drebin, Carpenter and Hanrahan. Everything from medical CT viewers to film clouds to neural radiance fields is a variant of it. Along a ray \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\,\mathbf{d} through a medium with extinction coefficient \sigma(t) and emitted color c(t), the color that reaches the eye is C = \int0^{D} T(t)\,\sigma(t)\,c(t)\,dt, \qquad T(t) = \exp\!\Big(-\int0^{t} \sigma(s)\,ds\Big) T is the transmittance: the fraction of light from depth t that survives to the eye. Max surveys this emission–absorption model and its relatives. Renderers approximate the integral by taking samples every \Delta t and compositing them, usually front to back so that a ray can stop as soon as it is nearly opaque (early ray termination): \alphai = 1 - e^{-\sigmai \Delta t}, \qquad C \leftarrow C + T\,\alphai\,ci, \qquad T \leftarrow T\,(1 - \alphai) Classification turns raw data values into \sigma and c, usually through a transfer function: a lookup table from value (and sometimes gradient magnitude) to color and opacity. The same two formulas drive NeRF and Gaussian splatting; only the source of \sigma and c changes. The encyclopedia is a tree. Its root is this page; below it are ten branches, ordered from the data, to the ways of drawing it, to what it is used for. How a volume is held in memory. Dense grids are simple but large, so layouts such as bricking and Morton (Z-order) curves keep neighbouring voxels close in memory. Real volumes are mostly empty or uniform, so sparse structures store only the occupied parts: octrees and sparse voxel octrees, sparse voxel DAGs, which merge identical subtrees (Kämpe, Sintorn and Assarsson), and VDB, the shallow, wide tree used in film production (Museth). The branch also covers value compression, levels of detail, out-of-core streaming of data larger than memory, non-regular meshes, and neural and Gaussian representations. Where volumes come from: voxelization of triangle meshes and point clouds, procedural fields built from noise and distance functions, measurement by CT, MRI, microscopy or seismic surveys, and the output of fluid, fire and astrophysics simulations. Methods that start from the pixels and cast a ray per pixel. Volume ray casting samples the volume along the ray, interpolates (usually trilinearly), classifies and composites. To visit exactly the cells a ray crosses, the 3D DDA of Amanatides and Woo keeps, per axis, the distance to the next cell boundary and always steps across the nearest one; this is the inner loop of most voxel ray tracers. Speedups include empty space skipping and early ray termination (Levoy). For surfaces, isosurface ray casting stops at the first crossing of a level, and sphere tracing (Hart) uses a distance field's value as a safe step size. Methods that walk the volume and project each piece onto the screen. Splatting (Westover) draws each voxel as a small blurred footprint; 3D Gaussian splatting (Kerbl et al.) applies the same idea to millions of fitted Gaussians. Shear-warp (Lacroute and Levoy) shears the volume so that its slices line up with the image. Texture slicing draws many blended, view-aligned polygons and was the classic way to run volume rendering on early GPUs. Cell projection draws unstructured meshes one tetrahedron at a time (Shirley and Tuchman), and Fourier volume rendering computes projections in the frequency domain (Malzbender). Turning a volume into a mesh. Marching Cubes (Lorensen and Cline) looks up triangles for each cell from the signs at its eight corners; dual contouring (Ju et al.) places one vertex per cell and keeps sharp features. Blocky worlds instead emit the visible faces of solid voxels and merge them with greedy meshing. The emission–absorption model above ignores light that scatters inside the medium. Physically based renderers add shadows within the volume, phase functions, and single and multiple scattering, usually solved by Monte Carlo methods such as delta (Woodcock) tracking; Kajiya and Von Herzen gave an early formulation and Novák et al. survey the field. Real-time renderers approximate this with froxel grids (Hillaire) and voxel cone tracing (Crassin et al.). Making a picture that explains the data, not only one that looks right. The core tool is the transfer function; multi-dimensional transfer functions also use gradient magnitude and other derived values to separate materials that share a data value (Kindlmann and Durkin; Kniss, Kindlmann and Hansen). The branch also covers multi-field, vector and tensor data, illustrative and non-photorealistic styles, and interaction such as clipping and focus-plus-context views. Running rendering backwards: given images, find the volume that produced them. Because the volume rendering integral is differentiable, its parameters can be fitted by gradient descent. Neural radiance fields (Mildenhall et al.) fit a network that returns \sigma and c at any point; Plenoxels (Fridovich-Keil et al.) and Instant NGP (Müller et al.) store the parameters in voxels or hash tables to train far faster. Tomographic reconstruction, as in CT, is the classic inverse problem of the same kind (Feldkamp, Davis and Kress). Where the methods are used, linking back to the branches above: voxel engines and games, film production (VDB pipelines, clouds, fire), scientific and medical visualization, GPU, web and parallel renderers, and volumetric displays and holography. The small pieces that volume renderers are built from: ray–box intersection by the slab test (Kay and Kajiya) and other ray–primitive tests, camera models that generate the rays, and parallel GPU primitives such as atomics, prefix sums, sorting and stream compaction. Render a CT scan or a smoke simulation: volume ray casting, then transfer functions and empty space skipping. Build a blocky voxel game: greedy meshing, then the voxel engines in branch 9. Ray trace huge voxel scenes: 3D DDA, sparse voxel octrees, then sparse voxel DAGs. Extract smooth surfaces: Marching Cubes, then dual contouring. Render clouds and fog: light transport in participating media. Reconstruct a scene from photographs: neural radiance fields, then 3D Gaussian splatting. Amanatides, J. and Woo, A. (1987). name: Gradient Computation via Finite Differences
head: Central Difference Gradient, Central-Difference Gradient Operator, FD Gradient, Finite Difference Gradient, Gradient Computation Using Central Differences
body:
Gradient Computation via Finite Differences estimates the spatial gradient vector of a scalar volume field at sample positions or voxel centers to provide surface normals for shading (e.g., Phong shading) and opacity modulation. It sets itself apart from Analytic Gradient Computation by approximating derivatives numerically rather than evaluating basis function derivatives, and from Sobel Operator by using a minimal 6-neighbor stencil which is computationally cheaper but less smooth and less robust to noise. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume V defined on a regular grid with dimensions Nx 	imes Ny 	imes Nz. Output: A gradient field G containing 3D vectors (
ablax, 
ablay, 
ablaz) for each voxel or sample point. Data Structures: Volume Data: Accessible via index (i, j, k) or texture coordinate. For array-based storage, linear index idx = i + j \cdot Nx + k \cdot Nx \cdot Ny. Gradient Storage: Float Array: Interleaved 3-component floats per voxel, size Nx Ny Nz 	imes 3. Normalized Texture: 8-bit signed normalized format (e.g., GLRGBA8SNORM) storing direction in RGB and optionally magnitude in Alpha. Packed Voxel: Union of gradient vector and scalar value in a single structure. Parameters: Step Size (h): Physical distance between voxels along the coordinate axis. Boundary Handling: Clamping to edge voxels, repeating boundary values, or zero-padding. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate over all voxels (i, j, k) in the volume grid. 2. Compute X-component: Calculate the central difference along the X-axis: \deltaX = V(i+1, j, k) - V(i-1, j, k). If physical spacing hx is used: 
ablax =  rac{\deltaX}{2hx}. 3. Compute Y-component: Calculate the central difference along the Y-axis: \deltaY = V(i, j+1, k) - V(i, j-1, k). 
ablay =  rac{\deltaY}{2hy}. 4. Compute Z-component: Calculate the central difference along the Z-axis: \deltaZ = V(i, j, k+1) - V(i, j, k-1). 
ablaz =  rac{\deltaZ}{2hz}. 5. Handle Boundaries: If a neighbor index is out of bounds, substitute the value of the boundary voxel (clamping) or use a one-sided difference. 6. Normalize (Optional): Compute magnitude L = \sqrt{
ablax^2 + 
ablay^2 + 
ablaz^2}. If L > \epsilon (e.g., 10^{-6}), normalize \mathbf{n} =  rac{1}{L}(
ablax, 
ablay, 
ablaz); otherwise set \mathbf{n} = (0,0,0). 7. Encode (Optional): If storing in 8-bit textures, map \mathbf{n} \in [-1, 1] to [0, 1] via enc = \mathbf{n} \cdot 0.5 + 0.5, then quantize to integers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegradient(volume, resolution, physicalspacing=None): """ Computes the gradient field for a scalar volume using central differences. Args: volume: 3D list of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) or flat list. resolution: Tuple (Nx, Ny, Nz). physicalspacing: Tuple (hx, hy, hz). If None, assumes unit spacing. Returns: gradient: 3D list of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, 3) containing gradient vectors. """ Nx, Ny, Nz = resolution gradient = [[[None for in range(Nz)] for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] if physicalspacing is None: hx, hy, hz = 1.0, 1.0, 1.0 else: hx, hy, hz = physicalspacing inv2hx = 0.5 / hx inv2hy = 0.5 / hy inv2hz = 0.5 / hz for k in range(Nz): for j in range(Ny): for i in range(Nx): # X neighbors with boundary clamping iprev = max(i - 1, 0) inext = min(i + 1, Nx - 1) valprevx = volume[iprev][j][k] valnextx = volume[inext][j][k] # Y neighbors with boundary clamping jprev = max(j - 1, 0) jnext = min(j + 1, Ny - 1) valprevy = volume[i][jprev][k] valnexty = volume[i][jnext][k] # Z neighbors with boundary clamping kprev = max(k - 1, 0) knext = min(k + 1, Nz - 1) valprevz = volume[i][j][kprev] valnextz = volume[i][j][knext] # Compute central differences dx = (valnextx - valprevx) inv2hx dy = (valnexty - valprevy) inv2hy dz = (valnextz - valprevz) inv2hz gradient[i][j][k] = [dx, dy, dz] return gradient def normalizegradient(gradient): """ Normalizes gradient vectors in-place. """ Nx, Ny, Nz = len(gradient), len(gradient[0]), len(gradient[0][0]) for k in range(Nz): for j in range(Ny): for i in range(Nx): gx, gy, gz = gradient[i][j][k] mag = (gxgx + gygy + gzgz) 0.5 if mag > 1e-6: gradient[i][j][k] = [gx/mag, gy/mag, gz/mag] else: gradient[i][j][k] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return gradient Computes diffuse lighting for a scalar volume by estimating surface normals from voxel gradients and compositing the lit color into a framebuffer using front-to-back alpha blending. It integrates gradient estimation, lighting application, and compositing into a single per-voxel step rather than storing precomputed gradients separately. A gradient estimation method used in volume rendering to compute the spatial gradient vector for each voxel in a scalar volume. It solves the problem of determining the rate of change of data values to generate opacity functions and shading normals, emphasizing regions of high spatial frequency corresponding to edges. Unlike general edge detection where spatial location is critical, in volume rendering opacity functions are applied uniformly regardless of position, so the goal is to locate boundaries in the data value domain rather than the spatial domain. It is distinguished from its sibling Gradient-based Diffuse Lighting with Alpha Blending by being a fundamental gradient computation primitive rather than a lighting model, and from Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by using separable smoothing weights that make it less sensitive to noise than the Roberts Cross operator. Computes gradient vectors for local shading (BRDF) in volume rendering using analytic derivatives of the basis reconstruction function, avoiding additional samples or ray traversals. It sets itself apart from Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by requiring no additional sample evaluations or ray traversals, relying solely on the data values already loaded for the scalar reconstruction. Computes gradient vectors for volume shading by sampling the 3D texture at positions offset from the current reconstruction sample, thereby avoiding the expensive computation of a separate pre-calculated gradient field. It performs the finite difference approximation implicitly during the ray-casting shading pass rather than storing the result in a dedicated array. It differs from the Sobel Operator by using simple forward/backward offsets along axes rather than a 3x3x3 kernel, and from Jacobian Estimation via Central Differences by relying on specific hardware texture sampling offsets provided by the rendering pipeline context. Estimates the 3x3 Jacobian matrix of a deformation field by computing central differences of the simpleBrush function. It differs from Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by returning the full matrix of partial derivatives rather than a single gradient vector, and from Sobel Operator by using isotropic central differences on the raw function rather than convolution kernels on sampled data. Computes the 3D gradient vector for each voxel in a scalar volume by averaging directional gradients across multiple discrete scalar regions, using a binary neighbor check to detect region boundaries. It builds on Gradient Computation via Finite Differences but replaces continuous interpolation with discrete region membership checks. Computes the mean curvature \kappa = 
abla \cdot ( rac{
abla f}{|
abla f|}) for every active voxel in a scalar volume grid. It differs from sibling methods by calculating this second-order differential quantity directly in a single pass using a BoxStencil, avoiding the creation of intermediate gradient or normal grids. This builds on Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by extending finite difference operations to the divergence of the normalized gradient field. Computes the scalar divergence field 
abla \cdot \mathbf{v} for a 3D vector velocity grid using central finite differences. It solves the problem of quantifying local volume expansion or compression in fluid simulations, which is a prerequisite for pressure projection steps. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Gradient-based Diffuse Lighting with Alpha Blending by its focus on vector field calculus rather than scalar shading, and from Sobel Operator by its specific application to fluid dynamics boundary conditions rather than general edge detection. The Neumann Gradient is a high-quality 3D gradient estimation method for scalar volumes that utilizes a 3x3x3 neighborhood of 26 neighboring voxels to compute nearly isotropic gradient vectors with reduced fringing artifacts. It distinguishes itself from simpler finite difference methods by employing a linear regression framework that yields superior gradient quality, making it suitable for high-fidelity volume rendering systems where visual accuracy outweighs computational cost. A GPU compute shader pass that calculates gradients for all voxels and stores them in a 3D image buffer (rgba8snorm). It computes the gradient vector, calculates its magnitude, applies a magnitude modifier, normalizes the direction, and stores direction in RGB and magnitude in Alpha. A pre-processing step using the Sobel operator (a variant of finite differences) to detect edges. Gradient magnitude modulates voxel opacity to hide homogeneous regions, and direction is used for shading. A variant for adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) or structured grids where offset positions are clamped to the current region's boundaries to avoid expensive ray traversals to find containing regions. This reduces quality at level boundaries where offset sizes change. A method where gradients are precomputed and stored alongside scalar values in a VoxelVertex union. It uses msafeget to return 0.0 for out-of-bounds neighbors, effectively zero-padding boundaries. The gradient is normalized and stored as a vec4 with the scalar value in the w component. Visualizes interfaces between density regions by projecting through gradient magnitude values. The surface normal N is approximated by finite differences, and surface strength is |N|. This allows visualization of diffuse transitions at sub-voxel accuracy. Computes the curl 
abla 	imes \mathbf{F} of a vector grid using central differences with a 6-point stencil. It computes components like curlx = (v[4][3] - v[5][3] - v[6][2] + v[7][2]) \cdot 0.5 and stores the result in a vector grid. Computes the Laplacian 
abla^2 f at every active voxel using a 6-point stencil in index space. It builds on the gradient stencil infrastructure but sums second-order differences. Computes the Euclidean norm |\mathbf{v}| at every active voxel of a vector grid. It iterates over active voxels, computes the norm, and builds a scalar result grid. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, as each voxel requires a constant number of reads and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the gradient field if precomputed. If computed on-the-fly during raycasting, memory overhead is minimal but bandwidth usage increases due to 6 extra texture fetches per sample. Performance: The central difference operator is significantly faster than Sobel or Zucker-Hummel operators because it requires only 6 sampling points instead of 54 for the Zucker-Hummel operator. Strengths: Simple to implement, low computational cost, provides reasonable shading normals for smooth volumes. Limitations: Less smooth than Sobel operators; sensitive to noise in the scalar field; provides a worse description of local surface structure compared to larger kernels. Boundary handling via padding or clamping can introduce visual artifacts similar to trilinear interpolation resampling. In volume rendering, it was popularized for real-time raycasting to enable Phong shading and opacity modulation without precomputing complex derivative fields. It is widely used in systems like VolumePro, which implemented hardware-accelerated gradient estimation using FIFO buffers to pipeline the computation. It is also a standard component in scientific visualization libraries like CGAL for isosurfacing. name: Gradient-based Diffuse Lighting with Alpha Blending
head: Gradient-based Diffuse Lighting
body: This method computes diffuse lighting for a scalar volume by estimating surface normals from voxel gradients and compositing the lit color into a framebuffer using front-to-back alpha blending. It integrates gradient estimation, lighting application, and compositing into a single per-voxel step rather than storing precomputed gradients separately. Inputs: parent: Volume data structure containing: width: Integer width of the volume grid (bounds for x and y dimensions). zSize: Integer depth (z-dimension) of the volume grid. v2: 1D array of voxel values (integers, typically 0-255). transfera: 1D array of 32-bit integers storing alpha values indexed by voxel value. transferrgb: 1D array of 32-bit integers storing RGB values indexed by voxel value. light: 3D vector (light[0], light[1], light[2]) representing the light direction. outa: Accumulated alpha (float, initialized to 0.0). rgb: Accumulated color (array of 3 floats, initialized to 0.0). Outputs: Updated outa: Accumulated alpha. Updated rgb: Accumulated color. Data Structures: Voxel values are accessed via linear indexing using coordinates ida, idb, idc. The memory layout follows v(idc, ida + idb width), implying a linear index of idc (width width) + ida + idb width. Neighbor indices are clamped to valid ranges: lower bounds to 0, ida2 and idb2 to width - 1, and idc2 to zSize - 1. Steps: 1. Gradient Estimation: Calculate the 3D gradient vector \mathbf{g} = (gx, gy, gz) using central differences on the least significant byte (0-255) of voxel values, normalized by 255.0. gx = \frac{V(idc, id{a2}, idb) \ \& \ 0xFF}{255.0} - \frac{V(idc, id{a1}, idb) \ \& \ 0xFF}{255.0} gy = \frac{V(idc, ida, id{b2}) \ \& \ 0xFF}{255.0} - \frac{V(idc, ida, id{b1}) \ \& \ 0xFF}{255.0} gz = \frac{V(id{c2}, ida, idb) \ \& \ 0xFF}{255.0} - \frac{V(id{c1}, ida, idb) \ \& \ 0xFF}{255.0} where V(idc, ida, idb) returns the clamped voxel value. 2. Gradient Normalization: Calculate magnitude |\mathbf{g}| = \sqrt{gx^2 + gy^2 + gz^2}. If |\mathbf{g}| > 0, divide each component by |\mathbf{g}|; otherwise, set all components to 0. 3. Diffuse Lighting Factor: Calculate D = \max(gx lx + gy ly + gz lz, 0). 4. Transfer Function Lookup: Extract alpha: \alpha{src} = \frac{\text{parent.transfer\a}[v] \ \& \ 0x000000FF}{255}. Extract RGB from rgbval = parent.transferrgb[v]: R{src} = \frac{(rgb\val \ \& \ 0x00FF0000) \gg 16}{255.0}, \quad G{src} = \frac{(rgb\val \ \& \ 0x0000FF00) \gg 8}{255.0}, \quad B{src} = \frac{rgb\val \ \& \ 0x000000FF}{255.0}. 5. Lighting Application: Apply diffuse lighting with an ambient term of 0.25, clamped to 1.0: R{lit} = \min(D \cdot R{src} + 0.25 \cdot R{src}, 1.0) G{lit} = \min(D \cdot G{src} + 0.25 \cdot G{src}, 1.0) B{lit} = \min(D \cdot B{src} + 0.25 \cdot B{src}, 1.0). 6. Alpha Blending (Front-to-Back): Composite the lit color: R{out} = (1.0 - \alpha{out}) \cdot R{lit} \cdot \alpha{src} + R{out} G{out} = (1.0 - \alpha{out}) \cdot G{lit} \cdot \alpha{src} + G{out} B{out} = (1.0 - \alpha{out}) \cdot B{lit} \cdot \alpha{src} + B{out}. Update accumulated alpha: \alpha{out} = (1.0 - \alpha{out}) \cdot \alpha{src} + \alpha{out}. 7. Output Packing: Convert final RGB to 8-bit integers and pack into a 32-bit integer with opaque alpha: R{final} = \lfloor R{out} \cdot 255 \rfloor, \quad G{final} = \lfloor G{out} \cdot 255 \rfloor, \quad B{final} = \lfloor B{out} \cdot 255 \rfloor. Pixel = (255 \ll 24) \ | \ (R{final} \ll 16) \ | \ (G{final} \ll 8) \ | \ B{final}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Gradient Estimation gx = getvoxel(ida + 1, idb, idc) - getvoxel(ida - 1, idb, idc) gy = getvoxel(ida, idb + 1, idc) - getvoxel(ida, idb - 1, idc) gz = getvoxel(ida, idb, idc + 1) - getvoxel(ida, idb, idc - 1) # 2. Gradient Normalization gradl = (gx2 + gy2 + gz2)0.5 if gradl > 0: nx, ny, nz = gx / gradl, gy / gradl, gz / gradl else: nx, ny, nz = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # 3. Diffuse Lighting Factor diffuse = max(nx light[0] + ny light[1] + nz light[2], 0) # 4. Transfer Function Lookup currentidx = idc (width height) + ida + idb width currentval = parent.v2[currentidx] aa = (parent.transfera[currentval] & 0x000000FF) / 255 rgbval = parent.transferrgb[currentval] vvred = ((rgbval & 0x00FF0000) >> 16) / 255.0 vvgreen = ((rgbval & 0x0000FF00) >> 8) / 255.0 vvblue = (rgbval & 0x000000FF) / 255.0 # 5. Lighting Application vvred = min(diffuse vvred + 0.25 vvred, 1.0) vvgreen = min(diffuse vvgreen + 0.25 vvgreen, 1.0) vvblue = min(diffuse vvblue + 0.25 vvblue, 1.0) # 6. Alpha Blending rgb[0] = (1.0 - outa) vvred aa + rgb[0] rgb[1] = (1.0 - outa) vvgreen aa + rgb[1] rgb[2] = (1.0 - outa) vvblue aa + rgb[2] outa = (1.0 - outa) aa + outa return outa, rgb Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel for the lighting and blending step, requiring 6 neighbor lookups for gradient estimation and constant-time transfer function access. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per voxel for the current step, plus storage for the transfer functions and volume data. Performance: The method is computationally lightweight per voxel, suitable for CPU-based direct volume rendering as indicated by the source repository. The 6 neighbor lookups and transfer function accesses add overhead compared to simple alpha blending. Strengths: Provides surface-like shading effects without explicit surface extraction and is straightforward to implement. Limitations: Gradient estimation via central differences can be noisy in low-resolution volumes, and boundary clamping may distort normals at edges. name: Sobel Operator
head: Sobel Gradient Estimation, Sobel edge detector, Sobel gradient operator
body: The Sobel Operator is a gradient estimation method used in volume rendering to compute the spatial gradient vector for each voxel in a scalar volume. It solves the problem of determining the rate of change of data values to generate opacity functions and shading normals, emphasizing regions of high spatial frequency corresponding to edges. Unlike general edge detection where spatial location is critical, in volume rendering opacity functions are applied uniformly regardless of position, so the goal is to locate boundaries in the data value domain rather than the spatial domain. It is distinguished from its sibling Gradient-based Diffuse Lighting with Alpha Blending by being a fundamental gradient computation primitive rather than a lighting model, and from Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by using separable smoothing weights that make it less sensitive to noise than the Roberts Cross operator. The method computes the gradient \mathbf{G} = (Gx, Gy, Gz) at a voxel by convolving the local neighborhood with separable kernels that combine differentiation and smoothing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume texture V, the current voxel coordinate (x, y, z), and the voxel size h. Output: A 3D gradient vector \mathbf{G}. Data Structures: Derivative weights k: A 1D array of size 3, k = [-1.0, 0.0, 1.0]. Smoothing weights s: A 1D array of size 3, s = [1.0, 2.0, 1.0]. Gradient accumulator: Three floating-point variables Gx, Gy, Gz, initialized to 0.0. Steps: 1. Determine the voxel size h from the texture properties. 2. Initialize Gx = 0.0, Gy = 0.0, Gz = 0.0. 3. Iterate over the 3 \times 3 \times 3 neighborhood defined by offsets dx, dy, dz \in \{-1, 0, 1\}. 4. For each offset, calculate the spatial offset vector \mathbf{offset} = (dx \cdot h, dy \cdot h, dz \cdot h). 5. Sample the volume data at the offset position: v = V(x + dx, y + dy, z + dz). 6. Calculate the separable weights for each axis based on the current indices ix, iy, iz (mapped from \{-1, 0, 1\} to \{0, 1, 2\}): wx = k[ix] \cdot s[iy] \cdot s[iz] wy = s[ix] \cdot k[iy] \cdot s[iz] wz = s[ix] \cdot s[iy] \cdot k[iz] 7. Accumulate the weighted contributions: Gx \leftarrow Gx + wx \cdot v Gy \leftarrow Gy + wy \cdot v Gz \leftarrow Gz + wz \cdot v 8. Normalize the accumulated gradients by multiplying by \frac{1}{16.0} and a normalization constant NORM. 9. Return \mathbf{G} = (Gx, Gy, Gz) \cdot NORM. Formulas: The separable weight calculation effectively implements the convolution with the Sobel kernels. For a 2D slice, the horizontal gradient E(H) and vertical gradient E(V) are computed as: E(H) = (a0 + 2a1 + a2) - (a4 + 2a5 + a6) E(V) = (a2 + 2a3 + a4) - (a0 + 2a7 + a6) Where a0 \dots a7 are the pixel intensities in the 3 \times 3 window arranged around the current pixel. The diagonal kernels are defined as: E(DL) = (a1 + 2a2 + a3) - (a7 + 2a6 + a5) E(DR) = (a1 + 2a0 + a7) - (a3 + 2a4 + a5) Parameters: NORM: Not given in the sources. applies a multiplication by NORM after the 1/16.0 scaling but does not define its value. Isotropy: The operator aims for uniform response in all directions. Localization: Good precision in edge positioning. Signal-to-Noise: High resistance to noise due to smoothing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sobelgradient(volumetexture, coord, voxelsize): """ Computes the 3D gradient at coord using the Sobel operator. Args: volumetexture: Object with method sampledata(offset) returning scalar value. coord: Tuple (x, y, z) of the current voxel. voxelsize: Float scalar h. Returns: Tuple (Gx, Gy, Gz) representing the gradient vector. """ # Derivative weights k = [-1, 0, 1] # Smoothing weights s = [1, 2, 1] Gx = 0.0 Gy = 0.0 Gz = 0.0 # Loop over the 3x3x3 neighborhood for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: # Map index -1,0,1 to array index 0,1,2 idxx = dx + 1 idxy = dy + 1 idxz = dz + 1 # Calculate spatial offset offsetx = dx voxelsize offsety = dy voxelsize offsetz = dz voxelsize # Sample data at offset # Boundary conditions (e.g., clamping, mirroring, zero-padding) # must be handled by sampledata if coord is near the volume edge. v = volumetexture.sampledata(coord + (offsetx, offsety, offsetz)) # Calculate separable weights # k = [-1.0, 0.0, 1.0], s = [1.0, 2.0, 1.0] kx = -1.0 if idxx == 0 else (1.0 if idxx == 2 else 0.0) ky = -1.0 if idxy == 0 else (1.0 if idxy == 2 else 0.0) kz = -1.0 if idxz == 0 else (1.0 if idxz == 2 else 0.0) sx = 1.0 if idxx == 0 or idxx == 2 else 2.0 sy = 1.0 if idxy == 0 or idxy == 2 else 2.0 sz = 1.0 if idxz == 0 or idxz == 2 else 2.0 wx = kx sy sz wy = sx ky sz wz = sx sy kz # Accumulate Gx += wx v Gy += wy v Gz += wz v # Normalize # Source specifies division by 16.0 and multiplication by NORM. # NORM value not given in the sources. NORM = 1.0 # Placeholder for implementation-specific normalization scale = 1.0 / 16.0 NORM return (Gx scale, Gy scale, Gz scale) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overflow: Output values can overflow the maximum allowed pixel value for image types with small integer ranges (e.g., 8-bit). The standard practice is to clamp overflowing pixels to the maximum allowed value, or use a larger pixel value range. Edge Width: Natural edges often result in output lines several pixels wide due to the smoothing effect of the Sobel operator. Boundary Conditions: The method requires sampling neighbors. If the voxel is on the boundary of the volume, sampling must be handled (e.g., clamping, mirroring, or zero-padding). Approximates the Euclidean norm of the gradient vector using a linear combination of the maximum gradient component and the perpendicular component to avoid square root calculations. Choose this when performance is critical and exact magnitude is not required. It builds on the Sobel Operator by extracting the scalar magnitude. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel, as it involves a fixed 3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27 sample convolution. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per voxel for the gradient vector. Performance: The Sobel operator is slower to compute than the Roberts Cross operator. Strengths: Less sensitive to noise than Roberts Cross or simple central differences due to the smoothing component. Produces considerably higher output values for similar edges, aiding in thresholding. Good localization and signal-to-noise characteristics. Limitations: Slower than Roberts Cross. Edges may be wider than 1 pixel due to smoothing. Potential for overflow in fixed-point integer representations. When to use: When noise reduction is important and a good balance between edge localization and smoothness is required for opacity function generation or shading. When not to use: When maximum computational speed is the only constraint (use Roberts Cross) or when exact edge width is critical without post-processing. The Sobel operator is an efficient edge detecting operator used for gradient measurement in volume rendering, specifically for opacity function generation and shading. It is a 2-D spatial gradient measurement operator that emphasizes regions of high spatial frequency corresponding to edges. In the context of volume rendering, it is used to locate boundaries in the data value domain rather than the spatial domain, as opacity functions are applied uniformly. It is one of several edge detection kernels, alongside Prewitt, Kirsch, and Robinson, which calculate the 1st derivative. name: Sobel Gradient Magnitude Approximation
head: Euclidian normal approximation, K-value approximation
body: This method approximates the Euclidean norm of a gradient vector using a linear combination of the maximum gradient component and the perpendicular component to avoid square root calculations. It builds on Sobel Operator by extracting the scalar magnitude required for subsequent processing steps. Inputs: Gradient components: x (the larger absolute gradient component) and y (the smaller absolute gradient component). Threshold T: A value to determine if the gradient represents an edge. Outputs: Approximated gradient magnitude A. Binary edge mask based on thresholding. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values derived from Sobel kernel convolutions. No complex data structures are required beyond the input components x and y. Steps: 1. Identify Components: Determine the absolute values of the gradient components in the primary direction (x) and the perpendicular direction (y), ensuring x \ge y. 2. Apply Approximation Formula: Calculate the magnitude A using the linear approximation A = x + K y. 3. Thresholding: If the calculated magnitude A exceeds a specified threshold T, classify the pixel as an edge. 4. Assignment: Assign a foreground value (255) to edge pixels and a background value (0) to non-edge pixels. Formula Details: The exact Euclidean magnitude is A(\theta) = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}. The approximation assumes the gradient direction \theta falls within a specific range relative to the grid axes, specifically 0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{4} where x > y. The error percentage E(\theta, K) of this approximation relative to the true Euclidean norm is E(\theta, K) = 100 \left( \frac{\tan \theta}{\tan \theta + K} + K - 1 \right). This formula assumes normalized components or derives from the geometric relationship where the error depends on the angle \theta and the constant K. Parameters: K: The optimal value for K is 1/4 (0.25). This value minimizes the maximum error for both the 0–22.5° range (associated with four Sobel operators) and the 0–45° range (associated with two Sobel operators). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sobelgradientmagnitudeapprox(xabs, yabs, k=0.25, threshold=None): # Ensure x is the larger component if xabs < yabs: xabs, yabs = yabs, xabs # Calculate approximation magnitude = xabs + k yabs # Thresholding and assignment if threshold is not None: if magnitude > threshold: return 255 else: return 0 return magnitude Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The formula assumes x \ge y. If the components are equal, the error is maximized for the given K. Degenerate Input: If both x and y are zero, the magnitude is zero. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel/voxel. Gradient Magnitude Modulation is a post-processing step that uses the computed gradient magnitude to modulate sample opacity and illumination values. It emphasizes surface boundaries by increasing opacity and brightness where gradients are high, while de-emphasizing homogeneous regions and noise where gradients are small. It differs from the underlying Sobel Gradient Magnitude Approximation by adding a lookup-based mapping and the final multiplication step, rather than just computing the raw magnitude value. Choose this when you need to enhance surface detail in volume rendering. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel/voxel. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: Significantly faster than exact Euclidean norm calculation on hardware without dedicated square root units or when integer arithmetic is preferred. Strengths: Low computational cost, simple implementation, isotropic response when combined with appropriate Sobel kernels. Limitations: Approximate nature introduces error that varies with the gradient angle, though K=1/4 minimizes the peak error. When to use: Real-time volume rendering, hardware implementations, or scenarios where square root operations are prohibitively expensive. When not to use: Applications requiring high-precision gradient magnitudes for scientific visualization where error bounds are strict. The method originates from early volume rendering systems, specifically the Shear-warp factorization approach. It was developed to optimize the computation of gradient magnitudes for edge detection and shading in real-time visualization. The specific choice of K=1/4 was derived from error analysis to balance accuracy across different gradient orientations. name: Gradient Magnitude Modulation
head: Gradient Magnitude Approximation, Gradient Magnitude Illumination Modulation, Gradient Magnitude Opacity Modulation
body: Gradient Magnitude Modulation is a post-processing step in volume rendering that uses the computed gradient magnitude to modulate sample opacity and illumination values. It emphasizes surface boundaries by increasing opacity and brightness where gradients are high, while de-emphasizing homogeneous regions and noise where gradients are small. It differs from the underlying Sobel Gradient Magnitude Approximation by adding a lookup-based mapping and the final multiplication step, rather than just computing the raw magnitude value. Inputs: Gradient magnitude approximation M, an 8-bit approximation in the range [0, 2^{20}] derived from the previous stage. Current sample opacity \alpha and illumination I (diffuse/specular). Three control registers: Gmimd (Gradient Magnitude Illumination Modulation for diffuse), Gmims (for specular), and Gmom (Gradient Magnitude Opacity Modulation). Gradient Magnitude Lookup Table (GmLUT). Outputs: Modulated opacity \alpha' and illumination I'. Modulation value m \in [0, 1]. Data Structures: GmLUT: A table of eight entries specifying points of a piece-wise linear function at equal intervals along the gradient magnitude axis. The output values of the table entries represent the modulation factor. Steps: 1. Compute Squared Magnitude: Calculate the sum of the squares of the gradient components (gx, gy, gz). Each component has signed 8-bit precision in the range [-127, 127]. S = gx^2 + gy^2 + gz^2 2. Approximate Square Root: Use a Newton-Raphson iteration to compute the square root of S, resulting in the 8-bit approximation M in the range [0, 2^{20}]. 3. Map to Lookup Index: Map the magnitude M into the range [0, 255] using the piece-wise linear function defined by GmLUT. Since GmLUT has 8 entries at equal intervals, the input domain [0, 2^{20}] is divided into 7 segments. The index i for the table is determined by scaling M to [0, 255] and identifying the segment. 4. Interpolate Modulation Value: Perform linear interpolation between the two nearest table values in GmLUT to compute the 8-bit repeating-fraction modulation value m. This value represents a float in the range [0, 1]. 5. Apply Modulation: If Gmom is enabled, compute \alpha' = \alpha \times m. If Gmimd is enabled, compute I'{diffuse} = I{diffuse} \times m. If Gmims is enabled, compute I'{specular} = I{specular} \times m. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientmagnitudemodulation(gx, gy, gz, alpha, Idiffuse, Ispecular, Gmimd, Gmims, Gmom, GmLUT): """ gx, gy, gz: signed 8-bit integers representing gradient components in [-127, 127]. alpha: current sample opacity. Idiffuse, Ispecular: current illumination values. Gmimd, Gmims, Gmom: boolean flags enabling modulation for diffuse, specular, and opacity respectively. GmLUT: list of 8 floats representing the piece-wise linear function values. Returns: modulatedalpha, modulatedIdiffuse, modulatedIspecular """ # Step 1: Compute squared magnitude S = gxgx + gygy + gzgz # Step 2: Newton-Raphson square root approximation # Result M is an 8-bit approximation in range [0, 2^20] x = S / 2.0 if S > 0 else 0.0 for in range(4): if x == 0: break x = 0.5 (x + S / x) M = x # Step 3 & 4: Map M to [0, 255] and interpolate using GmLUT # GmLUT has 8 entries at equal intervals along the gradient magnitude axis. maxmag = 220 numentries = 8 step = maxmag / (numentries - 1) idx = int(M / step) idx = min(idx, numentries - 2) # Clamp to valid interpolation pair frac = (M - idx step) / step vallow = GmLUT[idx] valhigh = GmLUT[idx + 1] # Linear interpolation yields the 8-bit repeating-fraction value in [0, 1] m = vallow + frac (valhigh - vallow) m = max(0.0, min(1.0, m)) # Step 5: Apply modulation modalpha = alpha modIdiffuse = Idiffuse modIspecular = Ispecular if Gmom: modalpha = alpha m if Gmimd: modIdiffuse = Idiffuse m if Gmims: modIspecular = Ispecular m return modalpha, modIdiffuse, modIspecular Parameters: GmLUT: 8-entry table defining the piece-wise linear mapping. Gmimd, Gmims, Gmom: Boolean registers enabling the modulation. Edge Cases: Zero gradient: Results in m=0 (if LUT maps 0 to 0) or the base LUT value, effectively removing the sample from view if opacity is modulated. Noise: Small gradients in noisy data result in low modulation values, reducing visual impact. Time Complexity: Constant time per sample, involving a few arithmetic operations and a table lookup/interpolation. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the GmLUT (8 entries) and 3 control registers. Strengths: Effectively emphasizes surface boundaries and reduces noise artifacts by attenuating samples with small gradients. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the gradient magnitude approximation; incorrect LUT configuration can lead to over- or under-emphasis of features. When to use: When surface definition is critical and noise reduction is desired. Gradient Magnitude Modulation is part of the VolumePro real-time ray-casting system. It was introduced in the VolumePro architecture to provide flexible control over surface appearance and noise handling. The method builds on the Sobel Gradient Magnitude Approximation to provide a computationally efficient way to modulate rendering parameters. name: Analytic Gradient Computation
head: Analytic Basis Gradients, Analytic Derivatives of Basis Reconstruction
body: Analytic Gradient Computation computes gradient vectors for local shading (BRDF) in volume rendering using analytic derivatives of the basis reconstruction function, avoiding additional samples or ray traversals. It sets itself apart from Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by requiring no additional sample evaluations or ray traversals, relying solely on the data values already loaded for the scalar reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The scalar volume data values Cv and basis function parameters (cell width Cw, control point coordinates Cp) used for the current sample evaluation at position p. Output: The gradient vector \nabla B(p) = [\frac{\partial B}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial B}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial B}{\partial z}]. Data Structures: The method operates on the same buffers used for scalar reconstruction. No additional storage is required for gradient samples. The gradient is computed per sample point during ray traversal. Formulas: The gradient of the reconstructed scalar field B(p) is derived from the quotient rule applied to the basis reconstruction equation. For the x-component: \frac{\partial B(p)}{\partial x} = \frac{\sumC \hat{H}C(p) \sumC \frac{\partial \hat{H}C(p)}{\partial x} Cv - \sumC \hat{H}C(p) Cv \sumC \frac{\partial \hat{H}C(p)}{\partial x}}{(\sumC \hat{H}C(p))^2} The partial derivative of the individual basis function component \hat{H}C(p) with respect to x is: \frac{\partial \hat{H}C(p)}{\partial x} = \hat{h}\left(\frac{|C{py} - py|}{Cw}\right) \hat{h}\left(\frac{|C{pz} - pz|}{Cw}\right) \chi(x) \frac{1}{Cw} Where: \hat{h}(\cdot) is the 1D basis function component. Cw is the cell width. C{py}, C{pz} are the y and z coordinates of the control point C. \chi(t) is the sign function defined as: \chi(t) = \begin{cases} -1, & \text{if } C{pt} - pt \geq 0 \\ 1, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} In the context of \frac{\partial B}{\partial x}, the argument t corresponds to the x-dimension relative to the control point, i.e., C{px} - px. The source text explicitly writes \chi(x) in the derivative formula but defines \chi(t) with a generic argument. The sign depends on the relative position of the sample point to the control point in the dimension being differentiated. Steps: 1. For each contributing control point C, evaluate the 1D basis function \hat{h} for the absolute normalized distances in all three dimensions: hx = \hat{h}(|C{px} - px|/Cw), hy = \hat{h}(|C{py} - py|/Cw), hz = \hat{h}(|C{pz} - pz|/Cw). 2. Compute the basis function value \hat{H}C(p) = hx hy hz and accumulate SH = \sum \hat{H}C(p) and S{Hv} = \sum \hat{H}C(p) Cv. 3. Compute the partial derivative \frac{\partial \hat{H}C(p)}{\partial x} using hy, hz, and \chi(C{px} - px), then accumulate S{dHx} = \sum \frac{\partial \hat{H}C(p)}{\partial x} and S{dHx\v} = \sum \frac{\partial \hat{H}C(p)}{\partial x} Cv. Repeat for y and z dimensions to get S{dHy}, S{dHy\v}, S{dHz}, S{dHz\v}. 4. Compute the final gradient component using the quotient rule: \frac{\partial B}{\partial x} = \frac{SH S{dHx\v} - S{Hv} S{dHx}}{SH^2}. Repeat for y and z. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeanalyticgradient(p, controlpoints, Cw, basisfunch): sumH = 0.0 sumHv = 0.0 sumdHx = 0.0 sumdHxv = 0.0 sumdHy = 0.0 sumdHyv = 0.0 sumdHz = 0.0 sumdHzv = 0.0 for C in controlpoints: dx = C.px - p.x dy = C.py - p.y dz = C.pz - p.z hx = basisfunch(abs(dx) / Cw) hy = basisfunch(abs(dy) / Cw) hz = basisfunch(abs(dz) / Cw) HC = hx hy hz sumH += HC sumHv += HC C.v chix = -1 if dx >= 0 else 1 chiy = -1 if dy >= 0 else 1 chiz = -1 if dz >= 0 else 1 dHCx = hy hz chix (1.0 / Cw) sumdHx += dHCx sumdHxv += dHCx C.v dHCy = hx hz chiy (1.0 / Cw) sumdHy += dHCy sumdHyv += dHCy C.v dHCz = hx hy chiz (1.0 / Cw) sumdHz += dHCz sumdHzv += dHCz C.v if sumH == 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) dHdx = (sumH sumdHxv - sumHv sumdHx) / (sumH sumH) dHdy = (sumH sumdHyv - sumHv sumdHy) / (sumH sumH) dHdz = (sumH sumdHzv - sumHv sumdHz) / (sumH sumH) return (dHdx, dHdy, dHdz) Parameters: Cw: Cell width. Typical values depend on the grid resolution and level of detail. Basis function \hat{h}: Typically a cubic B-spline or similar smooth function. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Analytic gradients are not continuously differentiable, leading to shading artifacts at cell and level boundaries. Division by zero if \sum \hat{H}C(p) = 0; guard against this. Precision issues near cell boundaries where the sign function \chi changes. Computes exact gradient vectors for local shading by evaluating analytic derivatives of the underlying box-spline basis function. It sets itself apart from this method by specifically exploiting the symmetry and structure of Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) box-spluses to reuse the 19 samples already fetched for scalar evaluation, whereas finite difference methods require six additional full spline evaluations. Choose it when rendering FCC-structured data to maximize sample reuse. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, same as scalar evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per sample for gradient components. Performance: Much faster than both central difference variants, which require 6 additional basis reconstruction samples and ray traversals. Quality: Provides superior quality to clamped central differences. May be slightly worse than accurate central differences due to discontinuities in the derivative at boundaries, but the trade-off favors speed. When to use: When performance is critical and the discontinuities at cell boundaries are acceptable or mitigated by other means. Default in the ExaBricks renderer. When not to use: When continuous gradients are strictly required and performance is not a constraint. Originated in the context of ray tracing structured AMR data using ExaBricks. The method was introduced to enable efficient local shading with BRDFs without the prohibitive cost of additional samples required by finite difference methods. It leverages the mathematical structure of the basis reconstruction function to provide analytic derivatives. Ray Tracing Structured AMR Data Using ExaBricks, https://www.sci.utah.edu/~wald/Publications/2020/exabrick/exabrick.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Analytic Gradient Computation via Box-Spline Derivatives
head: Derivative Spline Evaluation, Exact Gradient for FCC
body: This method computes exact gradient vectors for local shading in volume rendering by evaluating analytic derivatives of the underlying box-spline basis function, avoiding the inaccuracies and extra memory bandwidth of finite differences. It sets itself apart from Analytic Gradient Computation by specifically exploiting the symmetry and structure of Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) box-splines to reuse the 19 samples already fetched for scalar evaluation, whereas finite difference methods require six additional full spline evaluations. Inputs: Volume data V defined on an FCC grid. Evaluation point x in continuous space. The set of direction vectors \Xi{\text{fcc}} defining the FCC box-spline M{\text{fcc}}. Outputs: Gradient vector \nabla(V M{\text{fcc}})(x). Data Structures: The scalar value is computed as s(x) = V M{\text{fcc}}(x). The gradient is computed using three directional derivatives d{110}, d{101}, d{011} along vectors \xi{110}, \xi{101}, \xi{011}. Derivative kernels M\xi are defined as sums of two box-splines. Due to symmetry, only the BB-coefficients for M{110} are explicitly stored/computed; others are derived via permutation. M{110} requires handling three polynomial piece types: \tau0, \tau2, \tau4. Steps: 1. Fetch Samples: Retrieve the 19 voxel values V required for the evaluation of the FCC box-spline M{\text{fcc}} at point x. These samples cover the support of M{\text{fcc}}. The support of each derivative kernel M\xi is a subset of the support of M{\text{fcc}}, so no additional texture fetches are needed. 2. Compute Directional Derivatives: Calculate the three directional derivatives d\xi = V M\xi for \xi \in \{\xi{110}, \xi{101}, \xi{011}\}. The directional derivative of the spline s = V M{\text{fcc}} along \xi is given by D\xi(V M{\text{fcc}}) = V M\xi. The kernel M\xi is defined as M\xi(x) = 2M{\Xi{\text{rec}} \setminus \{\xi\}}(x + \xic) - 2M{\Xi{\text{rec}} \setminus \{\xi\}}(x + \xic - \xi), where \Xi{\text{rec}} is the set of directions for the reconstructed spline, and \xic is a centering vector. Evaluate M\xi using the de Casteljau algorithm. Since M\xi is quadratic, this is computationally efficient. For M{110}, determine the polynomial piece type (\tau0, \tau2, \text{or } \tau4) based on the local grid position. Apply the corresponding precomputed BB-coefficients for that piece type to the fetched samples. Use permutational symmetries to compute M{101} and M{011} from the coefficients of M{110}. 3. Reconstruct Gradient: Combine the directional derivatives to form the Cartesian gradient vector: \nabla(V M{\text{fcc}}) = \frac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} d{110} + d{101} - d{011} \\ d{110} + d{011} - d{101} \\ d{101} + d{011} - d{110} \end{bmatrix} where d\xi = V M\xi. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeanalyticgradientfcc(V, x, gridinfo): # Map continuous point x to the 19 FCC grid indices covering the support of Mfcc. indices = maptofccsupport(x, gridinfo) samples = [V[idx] for idx in indices] # Determine polynomial piece type for M110 based on local fractional coordinates. # Not given in the sources. piecetype = getpolynomialpiecetype(x, gridinfo) # Retrieve BB-coefficients for M110 from Table 1 in based on piecetype. # Not given in the sources. coeffs110 = getbbcoefficientsM110(piecetype) # Evaluate d110 = V M110 using the dot product of samples and coefficients. d110 = sum(s c for s, c in zip(samples, coeffs110)) # Evaluate d101 and d011 using permutational symmetries of M110. # Not given in the sources. coeffs101 = permutecoefficients(coeffs110, '101') coeffs011 = permutecoefficients(coeffs110, '011') d101 = sum(s c for s, c in zip(samples, coeffs101)) d011 = sum(s c for s, c in zip(samples, coeffs011)) # Reconstruct Cartesian gradient vector. gradient = ( (d110 + d101 - d011) / 2.0, (d110 + d011 - d101) / 2.0, (d101 + d011 - d110) / 2.0) return gradient Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Finite difference methods suffer from rounding errors if the offset \delta is too small, or poor approximation if \delta is too large. The analytic method avoids this entirely. Polynomial Piece Identification: Correctly identifying the polynomial piece type (\tau0, \tau2, \tau4) is critical for using the correct BB-coefficients. Support Mismatch: While the support of M\xi is a subset of M{\text{fcc}}, care must be taken to align the coefficients with the correct fetched samples. This variant uses the analytic gradient to compute normal vectors for isosurface rendering. It is preferred over finite difference normals because it always yields accurate results regardless of step size, whereas finite difference normals are sensitive to offset selection (too small causes rounding errors, too large causes approximation errors). It offers a speed-up of 1.2x to 1.3x on standard datasets (MRI-Head, VisMale, CT-Head) due to lower data fetch overhead. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is dominated by the evaluation of the quadratic derivative kernels using the de Casteljau algorithm. Memory complexity is identical to scalar evaluation as it reuses the same 19 samples. Measured Performance: The analytic method is faster than finite difference because it avoids six additional spline evaluations. Speed-ups observed: MRI-Head 1.3x, VisMale 1.3x, CT-Head 1.2x, Carp 1.0x. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Exact gradients, lower memory bandwidth usage than finite differences, superior isosurface quality. Limitations: Requires precomputed BB-coefficients for derivative kernels and polynomial piece types. The method is specific to FCC box-spluses. When to Use: Use when high-quality normals are required for shading or isosurface rendering and performance is a concern. Do not use if the volume data is not represented by FCC box-spluses. This method was introduced by Minho Kim and Jürgen Peters in their 2012 paper "GPU Isosurface Raycasting of FCC Datasets". It addresses the limitations of finite difference gradient estimation in the context of FCC grid volume rendering, leveraging the mathematical properties of box-spluses to provide exact derivatives. GPU Isosurface Raycasting of FCC Datasets, https://minho-kim-uos.github.io/papers/kim12gpu.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Gradient Estimation from Samples
head: Gradient-based Volume Shading, Multi-Volume Ray Casting Gradient Estimation and Shading, vtkGPUMultiVolumeRayCastMapper shading logic
body: This method computes gradient vectors for volume shading by sampling the 3D texture at positions offset from the current reconstruction sample, thereby avoiding the expensive computation of a separate pre-calculated gradient field. It performs the finite difference approximation implicitly during the ray-casting shading pass rather than storing the result in a dedicated array. It differs from the Sobel Operator by using simple forward/backward offsets along axes rather than a 3x3x3 kernel, and from Jacobian Estimation via Central Differences by relying on specific hardware texture sampling offsets provided by the rendering pipeline context. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current sample position in texture coordinates (posX[volNumber-1]), the 3D volume texture (dataSetTexture), color mapping texture (colorTexture), light source parameters (position, attenuation, spot cutoff/exponent/direction), material parameters (shininess), and transformation matrices (eyeToTexture4, transposeTextureToEye). Output: A vec4 final color value for the sample. Data Structures: dataSetTexture: Array of sampler3D objects. Index volNumber accesses the texture for the current volume. colorTexture: Array of sampler1D objects. Max size is 4 on Apple platforms and 5 otherwise. xvec, yvec, zvec: Vectors defining the sampling offsets for the gradient components. cellScale: Scalar scaling factor for coordinate conversion. transposeTextureToEye: Matrix for transforming normals from texture space to eye space. Steps: 1. Gradient Sampling (Forward): Compute the gradient vector g1 by sampling the volume data at positions offset by xvec, yvec, and zvec from the current sample position posX[volNumber-1]. g1.x = \text{texture3D}(dataSetTexture[volNumber], posX[volNumber-1] + xvec[volNumber]).x g1.y = \text{texture3D}(dataSetTexture[volNumber], posX[volNumber-1] + yvec[volNumber]).x g1.z = \text{texture3D}(dataSetTexture[volNumber], posX[volNumber-1] + zvec[volNumber]).x 2. Gradient Sampling (Backward): Compute the gradient vector g2 by sampling the volume data at positions offset by the negative of xvec, yvec, and zvec. g2.x = \text{texture3D}(dataSetTexture[volNumber], posX[volNumber-1] - xvec[volNumber]).x g2.y = \text{texture3D}(dataSetTexture[volNumber], posX[volNumber-1] - yvec[volNumber]).x g2.z = \text{texture3D}(dataSetTexture[volNumber], posX[volNumber-1] - zvec[volNumber]).x 3. Scale Gradient: Convert the gradient from texture coordinates to eye coordinates by scaling g2 with cellScale. g2 = g2 \times cellScale 4. Normalize and Transform Gradient: Calculate length: L = \text{length}(g2). If L > 0.0: Normalize: g2{norm} = \text{normalize}(g2). Transform to eye space: g2 = \text{transposeTextureToEye} \times g2{norm}. Else: Set g2 = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0). 5. Initialize Color: Set finalColor to (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0). 6. Light Direction Calculation: If the light is positional (glLightSource[0].position.w != 0.0): Transform vertex position hPos to texture coordinates: tmp = eyeToTexture4 \times hPos. Convert to eye coordinates: ldir = tmp.xyz / tmp.w. Calculate light direction: ldir = lightPos - ldir. Calculate squared distance: sqrDistance = \text{dot}(ldir, ldir). Normalize: ldir = \text{normalize}(ldir). Calculate half vector: h = \text{normalize}(ldir + wReverseRayDir). Else (directional light): ldir is derived directly from the light source direction (implementation detail: typically glLightSource[0].position.xyz normalized). sqrDistance = 0.0 (or irrelevant). h = \text{normalize}(ldir + wReverseRayDir). 7. Attenuation: If positional: att = \frac{1.0}{C + L\sqrt{sqrDistance} + Q \cdot sqrDistance} Where C, L, Q are glLightSource[0].constantAttenuation, linearAttenuation, and quadraticAttenuation respectively. Else: att = 1.0. 8. Spot Illumination: If glLightSource[0].spotCutoff == 180.0: spot = 1.0. Else: coef = -\text{dot}(ldir, gl\LightSource[0].spotDirection). If coef \ge gl\LightSource[0].spotCosCutoff: spot = coef^{gl\LightSource[0].spotExponent}. Else: spot = 0.0. 9. Shading Calculation: If spot > 0.0: Calculate dot products: nDotL = \text{dot}(g2, ldir). nDotH = \text{dot}(g2, h). Two-sided shading: If nDotL < 0.0, negate nDotL. If nDotH < 0.0, negate nDotH. Ambient: finalColor += gl\FrontLightProduct[0].ambient. Diffuse: If nDotL > 0.0: finalColor += (gl\FrontLightProduct[0].diffuse \times nDotL) \times color. Where color is obtained from colorFromValue(volNumber, value). Specular: shininessFactor = nDotH^{gl\FrontMaterial.shininess}. finalColor += gl\FrontLightProduct[0].specular \times shininessFactor. Apply Light Factors: finalColor = att \times spot. Scene Ambient: finalColor += gl\FrontLightModelProduct.sceneColor \times color. 10. Clamping: finalColor = \text{clamp}(finalColor, clampMin, clampMax). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shadevolumesample(volnumber, value, postexture, hpos, lightsource, frontmaterial, eyetotexture, transposetexturetoeye, cellscale, xvec, yvec, zvec, clampmin, clampmax, wreverseraydir, isonecomponent, volumedata, colortexture): """ Computes the shaded color for a volume sample using gradient estimation from samples. """ # 1. Sample Gradient Components (Forward) g1x = volumedata[volnumber].sample(postexture + xvec[volnumber]) g1y = volumedata[volnumber].sample(postexture + yvec[volnumber]) g1z = volumedata[volnumber].sample(postexture + zvec[volnumber]) # 2. Sample Gradient Components (Backward) g2x = volumedata[volnumber].sample(postexture - xvec[volnumber]) g2y = volumedata[volnumber].sample(postexture - yvec[volnumber]) g2z = volumedata[volnumber].sample(postexture - zvec[volnumber]) # 3. Construct and Scale Gradient g2 = vec3(g2x, g2y, g2z) cellscale[volnumber] # 4. Normalize and Transform Gradient normallength = length(g2) if normallength > 0.0: g2normalized = normalize(g2) # Transform to eye coordinates g2 = transposetexturetoeye[volnumber] @ g2normalized else: g2 = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 5. Initialize Final Color finalcolor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 6. Light Direction and Properties lightpos = lightsource.position ispositional = lightpos.w != 0.0 if ispositional: # Transform vertex position to texture coords then to eye coords tmp = eyetotexture[volnumber] @ hpos ldir = tmp.xyz / tmp.w ldir = lightpos.xyz - ldir sqrdistance = dot(ldir, ldir) ldir = normalize(ldir) else: # Directional light ldir = normalize(lightpos.xyz) sqrdistance = 0.0 # Half vector calculation h = normalize(ldir + wreverseraydir) # 7. Attenuation att = 1.0 if ispositional: c = lightsource.constantattenuation l = lightsource.linearattenuation q = lightsource.quadraticattenuation att = 1.0 / (c + l sqrt(sqrdistance) + q sqrdistance) # 8. Spot Illumination spot = 1.0 if lightsource.spotcutoff != 180.0: coef = -dot(ldir, lightsource.spotdirection) if coef >= lightsource.spotcoscutoff: spot = pow(coef, lightsource.spotexponent) else: spot = 0.0 # 9. Shading if spot > 0.0: # Get color from value color = getcolorfromvalue(volnumber, value, isonecomponent, colortexture) nDotL = dot(g2, ldir) nDotH = dot(g2, h) # Two-sided shading if nDotL < 0.0: nDotL = -nDotL if nDotH < 0.0: nDotH = -nDotH # Ambient finalcolor += lightsource.frontambient # Diffuse if nDotL > 0.0: finalcolor += lightsource.frontdiffuse nDotL color # Specular shininessfactor = pow(nDotH, frontmaterial.shininess) finalcolor += lightsource.frontspecular shininessfactor # Apply attenuation and spot finalcolor = att spot # Scene Ambient finalcolor += lightsource.sceneambient color # 10. Clamping finalcolor = clamp(finalcolor, clampmin, clampmax) return finalcolor def getcolorfromvalue(volnumber, value, isonecomponent, colortexture): """ Converts the raw volume value to a color. Handles 1-component (uses color map) and 4-component (uses RGBA directly) datasets. """ if isonecomponent: scalar = value.x return colortexture[volnumber].sample(scalar) else: # Four-component dataset return vec4(value.x, value.y, value.z, 1.0) Parameters: clampMin, clampMax: Float values defining the lower and upper bounds for clamping the final color to prevent black spots. cellScale: Scalar used to scale the gradient vector from texture coordinates to eye coordinates. transposeTextureToEye: Matrix used to transform the normalized gradient from texture space to eye coordinates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Black Spots: Occur if the final color is not clamped or if negative dot products are not handled for two-sided shading. The algorithm mitigates this by negating nDotL and nDotH if negative and clamping the result. Zero Gradient: If the gradient length is zero, the normal is set to (0,0,0), resulting in no diffuse/specular contribution (only ambient). Texture Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Focuses on combining gradient-based diffuse lighting with alpha blending for transparency. Choose when transparency is required. Uses a 3x3x3 kernel for gradient estimation. Choose when higher accuracy or smoother gradients are needed at the cost of more samples. Computes the Jacobian matrix. Choose when deformation or anisotropic scaling is involved. Averages gradients over regions. Choose when noise reduction is prioritized over sharp feature preservation. Computes mean curvature grids for surface rendering. Choose when curvature-based shading is required. Computes divergence grids for vector field visualization. Choose when analyzing flow fields is required. Pre-computes a shading volume (SHADING) from the CT density volume (CT) by calculating the surface normal via central finite differences and applying a diffuse lighting model. This avoids per-ray normal computation during rendering. Iterate over the volume grid for z from 1 to SLCS-2, y from 1 to ROWS-2, and x from 1 to COLS-2, skipping boundary layers. Compute partial derivatives using central differences: dx = \frac{CT[z][y][x+1] - CT[z][y][x-1]}{2.0}, dy = \frac{CT[z][y+1][x] - CT[z][y-1][x]}{2.0}, dz = \frac{CT[z+1][y][x] - CT[z-1][y][x]}{2.0}. Compute gradient magnitude: D = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2}. Compute normalized normal vector N = (dx/D, dy/D, dz/D) and diffuse shading value: S = Ip \cdot kd \cdot (N \cdot \hat{L}), where \hat{L} is the normalized light direction. Store as unsigned char. If gradient magnitude D is less than epsilon (7.25), set shading to 0 to avoid division by zero or noise amplification in flat regions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Efficient for interactive visualization on GPU workstations, as it avoids pre-computing and storing large gradient fields. Strengths: Low memory footprint, simple implementation, suitable for adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) data where gradient fields might be complex to pre-calculate. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Interactive volume rendering where memory is constrained or data is adaptive (AMR). When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method was described in the context of ray tracing structured AMR (Adaptive Mesh Refinement) data using ExaBricks. It was introduced to support high-quality cell interpolation and interactive visualization on individual GPU workstations for highly complex models. The implementation details are found in the VTK source code for vtkOpenGLGPUMultiVolumeRayCastMapper. bozorgi/VTKMultiVolumeRayCaster, https://github.com/bozorgi/VTKMultiVolumeRayCaster, fetched 2026-10-26 PDF Ray Tracing Structured AMR Data Using ExaBricks, https://www.sci.utah.edu/~wald/Publications/2020/exabrick/exabrick.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 kkhese/Volume-Rendering, https://github.com/kkhese/Volume-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Jacobian Estimation via Central Differences
head: Central Difference Jacobian, Finite Difference Jacobian
body: Estimates the 3x3 Jacobian matrix of a deformation field by computing central differences of the simpleBrush function. It differs from Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by returning the full matrix of partial derivatives rather than a single gradient vector, and from Sobel Operator by using isotropic central differences on the raw function rather than convolution kernels on sampled data. Inputs and outputs: Input: A position vector pos and a force/deformation parameter force passed to the deformation function simpleBrush. Output: A 3x3 matrix J where columns are the partial derivatives with respect to x, y, z. Data structures: mat3: A 3x3 matrix stored as three column vectors gradx, grady, gradz. vec3: 3D vectors for positions and differences. Parameters: EPSILON: The step size for finite differences. Steps: 1. Define the difference vectors along each axis: diff\x = (\epsilon, 0, 0) diff\y = (0, \epsilon, 0) diff\z = (0, 0, \epsilon) 2. Compute the partial derivative with respect to x by evaluating the deformation function at pos + diff\x and pos - diff\x: grad\x = \frac{simpleBrush(pos + diff\x, force) - simpleBrush(pos - diff\x, force)}{2 \cdot \epsilon} 3. Compute the partial derivative with respect to y: grad\y = \frac{simpleBrush(pos + diff\y, force) - simpleBrush(pos - diff\y, force)}{2 \cdot \epsilon} 4. Compute the partial derivative with respect to z: grad\z = \frac{simpleBrush(pos + diff\z, force) - simpleBrush(pos - diff\z, force)}{2 \cdot \epsilon} 5. Construct and return the Jacobian matrix J using these vectors as columns: J = \begin{bmatrix} | & | & | \\ grad\x & grad\y & grad\z \\ | & | & | \end{bmatrix} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def truediv(self, scalar): return vec3(self.x / scalar, self.y / scalar, self.z / scalar) class mat3: def init(self, c1, c2, c3): self.c1, self.c2, self.c3 = c1, c2, c3 def simpleBrush(pos, force): # Computes the 3D displacement vector for a given position and force parameter. # Implementation is external to this method. return vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def estimatejacobian(pos, force, epsilon): diffx = vec3(epsilon, 0.0, 0.0) diffy = vec3(0.0, epsilon, 0.0) diffz = vec3(0.0, 0.0, epsilon) dispplusx = simpleBrush(pos + diffx, force) dispminusx = simpleBrush(pos - diffx, force) dispplusy = simpleBrush(pos + diffy, force) dispminusy = simpleBrush(pos - diffy, force) dispplusz = simpleBrush(pos + diffz, force) dispminusz = simpleBrush(pos - diffz, force) gradx = (dispplusx - dispminusx) / (2.0 epsilon) grady = (dispplusy - dispminusy) / (2.0 epsilon) gradz = (dispplusz - dispminusz) / (2.0 epsilon) return mat3(gradx, grady, gradz) Edge cases and pitfalls: If EPSILON is too small, numerical precision errors may dominate the subtraction. If EPSILON is too large, the approximation deviates from the true derivative due to non-linearity. Boundary conditions for simpleBrush must handle positions outside the valid domain. Evaluates the derivative for the ODE solver by normalizing the inverse Jacobian times the direction vector w. It is chosen when a normalized direction is required for integration steps. The formula is: \text{result} = \text{normalize}(\text{inverse}(J) \cdot w) where J is the Jacobian estimated by the parent method. Time complexity: O(1) per evaluation, requiring 6 calls to simpleBrush. Memory complexity: O(1), storing only temporary vectors and the resulting matrix. Strengths: Simple to implement; isotropic accuracy for small steps. Limitations: Requires the deformation function to be differentiable; sensitive to step size choice. When to use: When the full deformation gradient is needed for physics or ray marching adjustments. When not to use: When the function is not smooth or when performance is critical and approximate gradients suffice. Not given in the sources. tink-expo/ntsl-graphics, https://github.com/tink-expo/ntsl-graphics, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Jacobian Normalization for ODE Step
head: Normalize Inverse Jacobian Step, ODE Evaluation
body: This method computes the normalized direction vector for an Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) solver by applying the inverse of an estimated Jacobian matrix to a base direction vector. It differs from raw Jacobian estimation by performing the matrix inversion and vector normalization required for stable stepping. Inputs: pos: The current 3D position in the volume. w: The base direction vector for the ODE step. force: A parameter passed to the Jacobian estimator. Outputs: stepdir: The normalized direction vector for the next ODE step. Data Structures: The Jacobian matrix J is a 3 \times 3 matrix estimated by the parent method Jacobian Estimation via Central Differences. J^{-1} is the inverse of this matrix. Steps: 1. Estimate the Jacobian matrix J at pos using estimateJacobian(pos, force). 2. Compute the inverse J^{-1}. 3. Multiply the inverse Jacobian by the direction vector: v = J^{-1} w. 4. Normalize v to obtain stepdir. Formula: step\dir = \text{normalize}\left( J^{-1} \cdot w \right) Where J = \text{estimateJacobian}(pos, force). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def estimatejacobiancentraldifferences(pos, force): # Not given in the sources; parent method handles this return [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] def jacobiannormalizationodestep(pos, w, force): J = estimatejacobiancentraldifferences(pos, force) det = (J[0][0](J[1][1]J[2][2] - J[1][2]J[2][1]) - J[0][1](J[1][0]J[2][2] - J[1][2]J[2][0]) + J[0][2](J[1][0]J[2][1] - J[1][1]J[2][0])) if abs(det) < 1e-8: return w # Fallback for singular Jacobian invdet = 1.0 / det Jinv = [ [(J[1][1]J[2][2] - J[1][2]J[2][1])invdet, (J[0][2]J[2][1] - J[0][1]J[2][2])invdet, (J[0][1]J[1][2] - J[0][2]J[1][1])invdet], [(J[1][2]J[2][0] - J[1][0]J[2][2])invdet, (J[0][0]J[2][2] - J[0][2]J[2][0])invdet, (J[0][2]J[1][0] - J[0][0]J[1][2])invdet], [(J[1][0]J[2][1] - J[1][1]J[2][0])invdet, (J[0][1]J[2][0] - J[0][0]J[2][1])invdet, (J[0][0]J[1][1] - J[0][1]J[1][0])invdet] ] v = [ Jinv[0][0]w[0] + Jinv[0][1]w[1] + Jinv[0][2]w[2], Jinv[1][0]w[0] + Jinv[1][1]w[1] + Jinv[1][2]w[2], Jinv[2][0]w[0] + Jinv[2][1]w[1] + Jinv[2][2]w[2] ] normv = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 if normv < 1e-8: return w # Fallback for zero vector return [v[0]/normv, v[1]/normv, v[2]/normv] Parameters: force: Passed to the Jacobian estimator. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Singular Jacobian: If \det(J) = 0, the inverse does not exist. A fallback to the unnormalized direction or identity step is required. Zero Vector: If J^{-1} w results in a zero vector, normalization fails. A fallback to the original direction w is required. Computes a 3x3 Jacobian matrix for a batch of 3D points to facilitate coordinate space transformations or derivative propagation in rendering pipelines. It differs from general numerical Jacobian estimation by using a closed-form analytical derivation based on the input vector's components and Euclidean norm, rather than finite differences. name: Jacobian Computation for Coordinate Transformation
body: Computes a 3×3 Jacobian matrix for a batch of 3D points to facilitate coordinate space transformations or derivative propagation in rendering pipelines. It differs from general numerical Jacobian estimation by using a closed-form analytical derivation based on the input vector's components and Euclidean norm, rather than finite differences. Inputs: A tensor a of shape (N, 3) containing N 3D points (ax, ay, az). Outputs: A tensor J of shape (N, 9) containing the Jacobian elements in row-major order, or (N, 3, 3) if reshaped. Data Structures: a: Float tensor, shape (N, 3). r: Float tensor, shape (N,), representing the inverse Euclidean norm. J: Float tensor, shape (N, 9) or (N, 3, 3). Parameters: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Extract components ax, ay, az from a. 2. Compute the inverse Euclidean norm: r = 1 / \sqrt{ax^2 + ay^2 + az^2}. 3. Construct the 9 elements of the Jacobian matrix J according to the formula below. Formula: The Jacobian matrix J is defined as: J = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{az} & 0 & -\frac{ax}{az^2} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{az} & -\frac{ay}{az^2} \\ ax \cdot r & ay \cdot r & az \cdot r \end{bmatrix} where r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{ax^2 + ay^2 + az^2}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computejacobian(a: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes the Jacobian matrix for coordinate transformation. Args: a: Tensor of shape (N, 3) with coordinates (x, y, z). Returns: Tensor of shape (N, 9) with Jacobian elements in row-major order. """ # Unpack coordinates ax = a[:, 0] ay = a[:, 1] az = a[:, 2] # Compute inverse Euclidean norm r = 1 / sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) r = torch.rsqrt(ax2 + ay2 + az2) # Compute terms involving az # Note: Division by zero if az == 0 results in Inf/NaN invaz = 1.0 / az invazsq = invaz invaz # Construct the 9 elements in row-major order # Row 0 j00 = invaz j01 = torch.zeroslike(ax) j02 = -ax invazsq # Row 1 j10 = torch.zeroslike(ax) j11 = invaz j12 = -ay invazsq # Row 2 j20 = ax r j21 = ay r j22 = az r # Stack into (N, 9) J = torch.stack([j00, j01, j02, j10, j11, j12, j20, j21, j22], dim=1) return J Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If any point has az = 0, the terms 1/az and 1/az^2 will produce Inf or NaN. The source code does not explicitly clamp or mask these cases. Implementers must ensure az \neq 0 or add a small epsilon to the denominator. Computes directional derivatives of a neural network's output with respect to input coordinates using the Jacobian. It constructs two orthogonal normal vectors n1 = (ny, -nx, 0) and n2 = \text{cross}(n, n1) relative to a primary normal n, then multiplies the Jacobian by these normalized vectors to get directional derivatives. It also provides a numerical baseline using central finite differences with \epsilon = 10^{-5}, computing J[:, i] = (\text{network}(posh)[:,:3] - \text{network}(negh)[:,:3]) / (2\epsilon) where posh and negh are points perturbed by \pm \epsilon along axis i. Time Complexity: O(N) for N points, involving basic arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the output Jacobian tensor. Strengths: Analytical computation is significantly faster than numerical finite differences. Limitations: Singularities at az = 0 require external handling. Not suitable for general coordinate systems where az might be zero. This method is used to transform derivatives between coordinate spaces, likely for gradient propagation during optimization.
