name: Per-Region Gradient Averaging
body: Per-Region Gradient Averaging computes the 3D gradient vector for each voxel in a scalar volume by averaging directional gradients across multiple discrete scalar regions, using a binary neighbor check to detect region boundaries. It builds on Gradient Computation via Finite Differences but replaces continuous interpolation with discrete region membership checks. Inputs: A 3D volume grid of scalar values, a list of scalar regions (integers or identifiers), and the volume dimensions (Dx, Dy, Dz). Outputs: A 3D grid of gradient vectors (gx, gy, gz) and their magnitudes. Data Structures: self.data: A flat list or array of VoxelGradient objects of size Dx \times Dy \times Dz. VoxelGradient: A structure containing prevgx, prevgy, prevgz (floats) and magnitude (computed). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize self.data with VoxelGradient objects for all voxels. 2. Replace the original volume data with a boolean mask or integer label map indicating region membership for each voxel. 3. For each voxel (x, y, z) in the volume: a. Initialize prevgx = 0, prevgy = 0, prevgz = 0, and n = 0. b. For each region R in the list of regions: i. Compute the directional gradient components (gx, gy, gz) for region R at (x, y, z): gx = \frac{x{plus} - x{minus}}{2} gy = \frac{y{plus} - y{minus}}{2} gz = \frac{z{plus} - z{minus}}{2} where x{plus} = 1000 if V(x+1, y, z) \in R else 0, x{minus} = 1000 if V(x-1, y, z) \in R else 0, and similarly for y and z. The value 1000 is a binary weight assigned to neighbors belonging to the current region to amplify boundary detection. ii. If (gx, gy, gz) is non-zero: new\gx = \frac{prev\gx \times n + gx}{n + 1} new\gy = \frac{prev\gy \times n + gy}{n + 1} new\gz = \frac{prev\gz \times n + gz}{n + 1} Update prevgx, prevgy, prevgz to newgx, newgy, newgz respectively, and increment n by 1. c. Set the voxel's gradient to (prev\gx, prev\gy, prev\gz). d. Compute the magnitude: \sqrt{prev\gx^2 + prev\gy^2 + prev\gz^2}. 4. Compute the maximum gradient magnitude lazily on the first call to getmaxgradientmagnitude by scanning self.data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeperregiongradients(volumedata, regions, dimx, dimy, dimz): # Data structure initialization class VoxelGradient: def init(self): self.prevgx = 0.0 self.prevgy = 0.0 self.prevgz = 0.0 self.magnitude = 0.0 voxels = [VoxelGradient() for in range(dimx dimy dimz)] # Replace volume data with boolean mask/region labels (assumed prepared externally) # regionmap[x, y, z] stores the region ID for each voxel regionmap = volumedata # Assumed to be a 3D array of region IDs for x in range(dimx): for y in range(dimy): for z in range(dimz): prevgx = 0.0 prevgy = 0.0 prevgz = 0.0 n = 0 for region in regions: # Boundary handling: clamp coordinates or return 0 for out-of-bounds def getvoxel(cx, cy, cz): if 0 <= cx < dimx and 0 <= cy < dimy and 0 <= cz < dimz: return regionmap[cx, cy, cz] return 0 # Assumed boundary handling valplusx = getvoxel(x + 1, y, z) valminusx = getvoxel(x - 1, y, z) valplusy = getvoxel(x, y + 1, z) valminusy = getvoxel(x, y - 1, z) valplusz = getvoxel(x, y, z + 1) valminusz = getvoxel(x, y, z - 1) weight = 1000.0 gx = ((weight if valplusx == region else 0.0) - (weight if valminusx == region else 0.0)) / 2.0 gy = ((weight if valplusy == region else 0.0) - (weight if valminusy == region else 0.0)) / 2.0 gz = ((weight if valplusz == region else 0.0) - (weight if valminusz == region else 0.0)) / 2.0 if gx != 0 or gy != 0 or gz != 0: newgx = (prevgx n + gx) / (n + 1) newgy = (prevgy n + gy) / (n + 1) newgz = (prevgz n + gz) / (n + 1) prevgx = newgx prevgy = newgy prevgz = newgz n += 1 idx = x dimy dimz + y dimz + z voxels[idx].prevgx = prevgx voxels[idx].prevgy = prevgy voxels[idx].prevgz = prevgz voxels[idx].magnitude = (prevgx2 + prevgy2 + prevgz2)0.5 return voxels Calculates a weight w = \text{weight} \times \max(\text{world\size}) / 128 and applies a total variation gradient to the density, k0, or diffuse field using totalvariationaddgrad(w, w, w, densemode). This variant is used in differentiable volume rendering contexts to regularize gradients. Time Complexity: O(Dx Dy Dz \times Nr), where Nr is the number of regions. Each voxel iterates over all regions and checks 6 neighbors. Memory Complexity: O(Dx Dy Dz) for storing the gradient vectors. Strengths: Effective for volumes with distinct, discrete scalar regions (e.g., segmented medical images, procedural volumes with sharp boundaries). Amplifies boundary gradients significantly. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large numbers of regions. Sensitive to the choice of the binary weight (1000). Not suitable for smooth, continuous scalar fields where standard finite differences are more appropriate. When to use: When the volume data is naturally segmented into discrete regions and sharp boundary detection is prioritized over smooth gradient estimation. When not to use: For continuous scalar fields or when computational efficiency is critical with many regions. Originated in the context of raycasting rendering implementations for volumes with discrete scalar regions. The method is part of a broader effort to improve gradient-based lighting and shading in volume rendering by leveraging region-aware boundary information. faviasono/raycastingrendering, https://github.com/faviasono/raycastingrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) gkouros/ref-dvgo, https://github.com/gkouros/ref-dvgo, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

head: Mean Curvature via BoxStencil, Divergence of Normal Field
body:
Computes the mean curvature \kappa = 
abla \cdot ( rac{
abla f}{|
abla f|}) for every active voxel in a scalar volume grid. It differs from sibling methods by calculating this second-order differential quantity directly in a single pass using a BoxStencil, avoiding the creation of intermediate gradient or normal grids. This builds on Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by extending finite difference operations to the divergence of the normalized gradient field. Inputs: A scalar volume grid containing the function values f. Outputs: A new grid of the same topology and voxel size, containing the mean curvature \kappa at each active voxel, with background values set to zero. Data Structures: Input Grid: Scalar values f(x,y,z). BoxStencil: A temporary structure holding values of f at the current voxel and its neighbors (up to distance 1 in each axis). Output Grid: Float array storing \kappa. Parameters: eps(T): Machine epsilon for the data type T (e.g., Float32 or Float64). Multipliers: 0.5 for first derivatives, 0.25 for cross second derivatives, 1.0 (implicit) for diagonal second derivatives. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize a BoxStencil with the input grid tree. 2. Iterate over all active voxels in the grid. Let the current coordinate be c. 3. Move the stencil to coordinate c. 4. Retrieve the center value f{center} = 	ext{value\at}(s, 0, 0, 0). 5. Compute first derivatives (gradient components) using central differences with multiplier 0.5: fx = (f(1,0,0) - f(-1,0,0)) 	imes 0.5 fy = (f(0,1,0) - f(0,-1,0)) 	imes 0.5 fz = (f(0,0,1) - f(0,0,-1)) 	imes 0.5 6. Compute the squared gradient magnitude: 	ext{grad\sq} = fx^2 + fy^2 + fz^2 7. Edge Case: If 	ext{grad\sq} < 	ext{eps}(T), set \kappa(c) = 0 and continue to the next voxel. This avoids division by zero in flat regions or noise. 8. Compute second derivatives: Diagonal (f{xx}, f{yy}, f{zz}) using multiplier 1.0 (implicit in formula): f{xx} = f(1,0,0) + f(-1,0,0) - 2 f{center} f{yy} = f(0,1,0) + f(0,-1,0) - 2 f{center} f{zz} = f(0,0,1) + f(0,0,-1) - 2 f{center} Cross (f{xy}, f{xz}, f{yz}) using multiplier 0.25: f{xy} = (f(1,1,0) - f(-1,1,0) - f(1,-1,0) + f(-1,-1,0)) 	imes 0.25 f{xz} = (f(1,0,1) - f(-1,0,1) - f(1,0,-1) + f(-1,0,-1)) 	imes 0.25 f{yz} = (f(0,1,1) - f(0,-1,1) - f(0,1,-1) + f(0,-1,-1)) 	imes 0.25 9. Compute the numerator of the mean curvature formula: 	ext{numer} = fx^2(f{yy} + f{zz}) + fy^2(f{xx} + f{zz}) + fz^2(f{xx} + f{yy}) - 2(fx fy f{xy} + fx fz f{xz} + fy fz f{yz}) 10. Compute the final curvature: \kappa =  rac{	ext{numer}}{	ext{grad\sq} 	imes \sqrt{	ext{grad\sq}}} 11. Store \kappa in the output grid at c. 12. After iteration, build the result grid using the computed data, a background value of 0, and the original grid's voxel size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computemeancurvature(grid): """ Computes mean curvature kappa = div(grad(f)/|grad(f)|) for all active voxels. grid: object with activevoxels(), valueat(c, dx, dy, dz), dtype, and voxelsize. """ outputdata = {} for c, in grid.activevoxels(): # BoxStencil: fetch neighborhood values fcenter = grid.valueat(c, 0, 0, 0) fx = (grid.valueat(c, 1, 0, 0) - grid.valueat(c, -1, 0, 0)) 0.5 fy = (grid.valueat(c, 0, 1, 0) - grid.valueat(c, 0, -1, 0)) 0.5 fz = (grid.valueat(c, 0, 0, 1) - grid.valueat(c, 0, 0, -1)) 0.5 gradsq = fx2 + fy2 + fz2 eps = math.finfo(grid.dtype).eps # if gradsq < eps: outputdata[c] = 0.0 continue fxx = grid.valueat(c, 1, 0, 0) + grid.valueat(c, -1, 0, 0) - 2.0 fcenter fyy = grid.valueat(c, 0, 1, 0) + grid.valueat(c, 0, -1, 0) - 2.0 fcenter fzz = grid.valueat(c, 0, 0, 1) + grid.valueat(c, 0, 0, -1) - 2.0 fcenter fxy = (grid.valueat(c, 1, 1, 0) - grid.valueat(c, -1, 1, 0) - grid.valueat(c, 1, -1, 0) + grid.valueat(c, -1, -1, 0)) 0.25 fxz = (grid.valueat(c, 1, 0, 1) - grid.valueat(c, -1, 0, 1) - grid.valueat(c, 1, 0, -1) + grid.valueat(c, -1, 0, -1)) 0.25 fyz = (grid.valueat(c, 0, 1, 1) - grid.valueat(c, 0, -1, 1) - grid.valueat(c, 0, 1, -1) + grid.valueat(c, 0, -1, -1)) 0.25 numer = fx2 (fyy + fzz) + fy2 (fxx + fzz) + fz2 (fxx + fyy) - 2.0 (fx fy fxy + fx fz fxz + fy fz fyz) denom = gradsq math.sqrt(gradsq) outputdata[c] = numer / denom # Build result grid using computed data, background zero, and original voxel size return {"data": outputdata, "background": 0.0, "voxelsize": grid.voxelsize} Uses separable 3x3x3 kernels for gradient estimation. Simpler but less accurate for curvature than the full BoxStencil approach. Choose when memory is constrained and high-order accuracy is not required. Each voxel requires a fixed number of memory accesses (13 values for the stencil) and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output grid. Limitations: Sensitive to noise in the input grid due to second-order derivatives. Requires careful handling of zero-gradient regions. name: Divergence Grid Computation
head: Divergence Calculation with Obstacle Velocity Boundary Conditions, Divergence Computation, Finite Difference Divergence
body: Computes the scalar divergence field \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} for a 3D vector velocity grid using central finite differences. It quantifies local volume expansion or compression in fluid simulations, serving as a prerequisite for pressure projection steps. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Gradient-based Diffuse Lighting with Alpha Blending by its focus on vector field calculus rather than scalar shading, and from Sobel Operator by its specific application to fluid dynamics boundary conditions rather than general edge detection. Inputs: A 3D vector grid \mathbf{v} containing velocity components (vx, vy, vz) at voxel centers. A grid tree structure defining active voxels and their coordinates. Obstacle velocity data for boundary cells. Outputs: A scalar grid containing the divergence value for each active voxel. Background value of zero for inactive voxels. Data Structures: Grid Tree: Stores active voxel coordinates. Velocity Field: 3-component float vectors per active voxel. Divergence Field: 1-component float scalar per active voxel. Parameters: half: Scalar multiplier 0.5, representing \frac{1}{2 \cdot \Delta x} in index space, assuming unit voxel spacing or normalized coordinates. Steps: 1. Initialize a gradient stencil with the grid tree. 2. Iterate over all active voxels (c, \dots) in the grid tree. 3. For each active voxel, sample velocity vectors from its six immediate neighbors: Left, Right, Bottom, Top, Down, and Up. 4. Boundary Handling: If a neighboring cell is a boundary (solid/obstacle) cell, replace the sampled velocity with the obstacle velocity at that specific location. 5. Compute the divergence using central differences: \text{div} = 0.5 \times ((vR.x - vL.x) + (vT.y - vB.y) + (vU.z - vD.z)) Where vR, vL are velocities at Right and Left neighbors, vT, vB at Top and Bottom, vU, vD at Up and Down, and x, y, z denote the respective velocity components. 6. Store the computed divergence in a dictionary keyed by the current coordinate. 7. Build the result grid using the computed data, a background value of zero, and the original grid's voxel size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedivergencegrid(gridtree, velocityfield, obstaclevelocityfield): """ Computes divergence for a 3D velocity grid with obstacle boundary conditions. """ divergencegrid = {} # Neighbor offsets: Left, Right, Bottom, Top, Down, Up # Mapping to (dx, dy, dz) assuming standard Cartesian indexing neighbors = { 'L': (1, 0, 0), 'R': (-1, 0, 0), 'B': (0, 1, 0), 'T': (0, -1, 0), 'D': (0, 0, 1), 'U': (0, 0, -1) } for coord in gridtree.activevoxels(): x, y, z = coord vL = getvelocity(velocityfield, obstaclevelocityfield, x + 1, y, z) vR = getvelocity(velocityfield, obstaclevelocityfield, x - 1, y, z) vB = getvelocity(velocityfield, obstaclevelocityfield, x, y + 1, z) vT = getvelocity(velocityfield, obstaclevelocityfield, x, y - 1, z) vD = getvelocity(velocityfield, obstaclevelocityfield, x, y, z + 1) vU = getvelocity(velocityfield, obstaclevelocityfield, x, y, z - 1) div = 0.5 ((vR[0] - vL[0]) + (vT[1] - vB[1]) + (vU[2] - vD[2])) divergencegrid[coord] = div return divergencegrid def getvelocity(velocityfield, obstaclevelocityfield, x, y, z): coord = (x, y, z) # Check if neighbor is a boundary cell # Sources do not specify the exact boundary detection predicate, # so a direct lookup in the obstacle field is used as a standard implementation guard. if coord in obstaclevelocityfield: return obstaclevelocityfield[coord] return velocityfield.get(coord, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Cells: Failure to replace neighbor velocities with obstacle velocities leads to incorrect divergence near solid objects, violating the no-penetration condition. Precision: Using floating-point arithmetic for divergence accumulation may introduce small errors; standard float32 is typically sufficient for real-time simulation. Grid Boundaries: Voxels on the edge of the simulation domain may lack neighbors. The sources imply handling via obstacle velocity or zero-padding, but explicit edge handling logic is not detailed in the provided notes. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of active voxels. Each voxel requires 6 neighbor lookups and constant arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the resulting divergence grid. Implementation: The method is implemented in HLSL pixel shaders for real-time simulation. Strengths: Simple, efficient, and directly applicable to fluid simulation pressure projection. Limitations: First-order accuracy in space (central difference is second-order accurate for the derivative, but the stencil is minimal). Sensitive to grid alignment and boundary condition implementation. The method originates from real-time fluid simulation techniques, specifically those described in "Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids". It is a standard component in grid-based fluid solvers to compute the divergence field required for the Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition. tobiasosborne/Lyr.jl, https://github.com/tobiasosborne/Lyr.jl, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids, https://wo1fsea.github.io/files/AboutNavMesh/P5GPUGems3Real-TimeSimulationandRenderingof3DFluids.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: EdgeMap Data Layout
head: EdgeMap
body: The EdgeMap data layout is a memory structure within the Grid Density Data Structure that stores geometric intersection data for isosurface extraction. It organizes intersection points, surface normals, ray directions, and indexing offsets into contiguous arrays. It differs from sibling methods like Gradient Computation via Finite Differences by storing pre-computed geometric primitives rather than derivative values, and from Interpolated Discrete Values & Gradients by focusing on explicit intersection coordinates rather than field values. The EdgeMap struct aggregates five primary data fields, all dynamically sized to Index.TotalSize, which represents the total number of active edges or intersection entries. The layout is defined as follows: 1. Index (IndexMap): A mapping structure for edge-to-voxel relationships or sorting keys. The exact internal layout of IndexMap is not specified in the sources. 2. Intersections: An array of glm::vec3 objects storing the 3D coordinates of intersection points on the edges. 3. Normals: An array of glm::vec3 objects storing the surface normal vectors at each intersection point. 4. Directions: An array of float values storing scalar direction information. 5. IndexOffset: An array of int values storing offset indices. The data is managed using std::uniqueptr for automatic memory management of the dynamic arrays. Implementation requires initializing the arrays to Index.TotalSize and populating them during the isosurface extraction pass. Input consists of voxel grid data and ray traversal results; output is the populated EdgeMap ready for mesh assembly. Formulas, specific parameters, and edge case handling are not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class EdgeMap: def init(self, totalsize: int): self.totalsize = totalsize self.indexmap = None # Layout not specified in sources self.intersections = [None] totalsize self.normals = [None] totalsize self.directions = [0.0] totalsize self.indexoffset = [0] totalsize def setintersection(self, index: int, point: tuple) -> None: if 0 <= index < self.totalsize: self.intersections[index] = point def setnormal(self, index: int, normal: tuple) -> None: if 0 <= index < self.totalsize: self.normals[index] = normal def setdirection(self, index: int, direction: float) -> None: if 0 <= index < self.totalsize: self.directions[index] = direction def setoffset(self, index: int, offset: int) -> None: if 0 <= index < self.totalsize: self.indexoffset[index] = offset Determines the unique global identifier for a vertex located on a specific edge of a voxel cell, mapping local geometric primitives to a global vertex buffer index. It differs from standard Cartesian indexing by relying on a specific vertex layout formula that accounts for the 3D grid topology, ensuring consistent adjacency across voxel boundaries. Choose it when constructing a coherent mesh from discrete voxel data requires consistent adjacency across voxel boundaries. The use of glm::vec3 implies 12 bytes per intersection and normal entry, while float and int occupy 4 bytes each, yielding approximately 32 bytes per entry plus the IndexMap overhead. name: Edge ID Calculation
body: Edge ID Calculation determines the unique global identifier for a vertex located on a specific edge of a voxel cell. It maps local geometric primitives (edges of a voxel) to a global vertex buffer index, enabling the construction of a coherent mesh from discrete voxel data. It differs from standard Cartesian indexing by relying on a specific vertex layout formula that accounts for the 3D grid topology, ensuring consistent adjacency across voxel boundaries. Inputs: Voxel corner coordinates (x, y, z), where x, y, z are integer indices of the voxel corner. Grid dimensions xWidth and yWidth, representing the number of voxels in the x and y directions respectively. Outputs: A unique global vertex ID (integer) corresponding to the vertex at the specified edge of the voxel. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required for the calculation itself; it is a direct arithmetic computation. The result is typically used as an index into a global vertex array. Formulas: The base vertex ID for a voxel corner is calculated as: vertexId(x, y, z) = 3 \times (z \times (yWidth + 1) \times (xWidth + 1) + y \times (xWidth + 1) + x) The formula uses a stride multiplier of 3 for the vertex buffer layout. Edge Mapping: The 12 edges of a voxel are mapped to offsets from the base vertex ID or adjacent vertex IDs. Let B = vertexId(x, y, z). The global ID for edge e is: Edge 0: B + 1 Edge 1: vertexId(x, y+1, z) Edge 2: vertexId(x+1, y, z) + 1 Edge 3: B Edge 4: vertexId(x, y, z+1) + 1 Edge 5: vertexId(x, y+1, z+1) Edge 6: vertexId(x+1, y, z+1) + 1 Edge 7: vertexId(x, y, z+1) Edge 8: B + 2 Edge 9: vertexId(x, y+1, z) + 2 Edge 10: vertexId(x+1, y+1, z) + 2 Edge 11: vertexId(x+1, y, z) + 2 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatevertexid(x: int, y: int, z: int, xwidth: int, ywidth: int) -> int: """Calculates the base vertex ID for a voxel corner.""" return 3 (z (ywidth + 1) (xwidth + 1) + y (xwidth + 1) + x) def getedgevertexid(edgeindex: int, x: int, y: int, z: int, xwidth: int, ywidth: int) -> int: """Returns the global vertex ID for a specific edge of a voxel.""" baseid = calculatevertexid(x, y, z, xwidth, ywidth) def getvid(cx, cy, cz): return calculatevertexid(cx, cy, cz, xwidth, ywidth) if edgeindex == 0: return baseid + 1 elif edgeindex == 1: return getvid(x, y + 1, z) elif edgeindex == 2: return getvid(x + 1, y, z) + 1 elif edgeindex == 3: return baseid elif edgeindex == 4: return getvid(x, y, z + 1) + 1 elif edgeindex == 5: return getvid(x, y + 1, z + 1) elif edgeindex == 6: return getvid(x + 1, y, z + 1) + 1 elif edgeindex == 7: return getvid(x, y, z + 1) elif edgeindex == 8: return baseid + 2 elif edgeindex == 9: return getvid(x, y + 1, z) + 2 elif edgeindex == 10: return getvid(x + 1, y + 1, z) + 2 elif edgeindex == 11: return getvid(x + 1, y, z) + 2 else: raise ValueError("Edge index must be between 0 and 11") Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The calculation assumes that the coordinates (x, y, z) and their neighbors (e.g., x+1, y+1, z+1) are within the valid grid bounds. Accessing vertices outside the grid will result in invalid IDs or out-of-bounds memory access if used directly. Consistency: The edge numbering must match the DualMC algorithm's expected edge indices. Mismatched edge numbering will result in incorrect triangle connectivity. Time Complexity: O(1) per edge ID calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and efficient. Limitations: Requires careful handling of grid boundaries. The specific vertex layout (stride of 3) is non-standard and must be understood by the rest of the pipeline. The method originates from the ilastik marching cubes implementation, which uses a specific vertex layout for its mesh generation. The edge numbering and vertex ID calculation are designed to work with the DualMC (Dual Marching Cubes) algorithm, which relies on a canonical spatial layout for voxel corners and edges. ilastik/marchingcubes, https://github.com/ilastik/marchingcubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Cube Corner and Edge Indexing
head: DualMC corner/edge mapping, Morton code corner indexing
body: Cube Corner and Edge Indexing defines the coordinate system and indexing scheme for the vertices and edges of a voxel cell used in DualMC table generation. It maps the 8 cube corners to indices 0–7 via Morton codes and assigns unique indices 0–11 to the 12 edges. Input: None (static definition). Output: Three static mappings: 1. cornerIndex: Maps a corner's spatial position to an integer 0–7. 2. edgeIndex: Maps an edge's spatial position to an integer 0–11. 3. cornerEdges: A lookup table mapping each corner to its three incident edges. The indexing relies on a fixed-size cube geometry. Corner Layout: The 8 corners are indexed 0 through 7 based on Morton codes. The index corresponds to the Morton code of the corner's local coordinates (x, y, z), where x, y, z \in \{0, 1\}. The mapping from local coordinates to corner index C is C = 4z + 2y + x. The explicit coordinate mapping is: Corner 0: (0, 0, 0) Corner 1: (1, 0, 0) Corner 2: (0, 1, 0) Corner 3: (1, 1, 0) Corner 4: (0, 0, 1) Corner 5: (1, 0, 1) Corner 6: (0, 1, 1) Corner 7: (1, 1, 1). Edge Layout: The 12 edges are indexed 0 through 11. Each edge connects two corners according to the fixed mapping: | Edge Index | Connects Corner A | Connects Corner B | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | 0 | 0 | 1 | | 1 | 1 | 5 | | 2 | 0 | 4 | | 3 | 4 | 5 | | 4 | 2 | 3 | | 5 | 3 | 7 | | 6 | 2 | 6 | | 7 | 6 | 7 | | 8 | 0 | 2 | | 9 | 1 | 3 | | 10 | 4 | 6 | | 11 | 5 | 7 |. cornerEdges Table: The table maps each corner C \in [0, 7] to the indices of its three adjacent edges. 1. Define Corner Coordinates: Assign local coordinates (x, y, z) \in \{0, 1\}^3 to each of the 8 corners. 2. Calculate Corner Indices: Compute the corner index C = 4z + 2y + x for each corner. 3. Define Edges: Enumerate the 12 edges of the cube, each defined by its two endpoint corners. 4. Assign Edge Indices: Assign indices 0–11 to the edges according to the fixed mapping. 5. Build cornerEdges Table: For each corner C \in [0, 7], identify the three edges incident to it and store their indices in cornerEdges[8][3]. The following Python-like pseudocode defines the static mappings. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatecornerindex(x, y, z): """Calculates corner index C = 4z + 2y + x for binary coordinates.""" return (z << 2) | (y << 1) | x def buildcorneredgestable(): """Returns corneredges[8][3] mapping each corner to its 3 incident edge indices.""" edges = [ (0, 1), (1, 5), (0, 4), (4, 5), (2, 3), (3, 7), (2, 6), (6, 7), (0, 2), (1, 3), (4, 6), (5, 7) ] corneredges = [[] for in range(8)] for edgeidx, (c1, c2) in enumerate(edges): corneredges[c1].append(edgeidx) corneredges[c2].append(edgeidx) for c in range(8): corneredges[c].sort() return corneredges corneredgestable = buildcorneredgestable() Bit Packing: The Morton code formula C = 4z + 2y + x assumes binary local coordinates (x, y, z) \in \{0, 1\}^3. Coordinate System: The source defines a right-handed system with x right, y up, and z depth. Degenerate Input: Not applicable, as this is a static topological definition. Time Complexity: O(1) for all lookups, as the tables are static and precomputed. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only 8 corner indices, 12 edge indices, and an 8 \times 3 edge list. Strengths: Provides a deterministic, hardware-independent mapping for voxel topology, essential for generating DualMC lookup tables. Limitations: Tied to the specific Morton code ordering; remapping is required if a different global grid ordering is used. This indexing scheme originates from the DualMC implementation by Dominik Wodniok. It is used in the gentables utility to generate static lookup tables that map voxel occupancy masks to extracted surface primitives. The method ensures topological consistency between corners and edges, facilitating efficient traversal and neighbor lookup in dense volume data. dominikwodniok/dualmc, https://github.com/dominikwodniok/dualmc, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Interpolated Discrete Values & Gradients
head: Cubic Interpolation, Cubic Spline Interpolation, CubicSpline, Discrete Field Interpolation, Interpolated Grid Fields, Tri-Cubic Interpolation
body: This method computes the scalar field value at a 3D point using tri-cubic interpolation, requiring a 4×4×4 neighborhood of 64 voxels. It provides scalar value and gradient fields computed from discrete data at grid vertices using interpolation. It builds on Grid Density Data Structure and operates alongside siblings Gradient Computation via Finite Differences and EdgeMap Data Layout. Inputs: A query point p = (px, py, pz) in world space. A grid structure grid providing spatial indexing and point access via grid.point(i,j,k). Discrete scalar values V{ijk} stored at grid vertices (i, j, k). Outputs: A scalar value f(p) representing the interpolated density at p. A gradient vector \nabla f(p) representing the spatial derivative at p. Data Structures: Grid: Contains bounding box bounds, voxel spacing (dimensions), and dimensions in voxels (Nx, Ny, Nz). Values: A 3D array or accessor mapping integer indices (i, j, k) to scalar values V{ijk}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute voxel integer coordinates: vi[\text{axis}] = \text{Pos2Voxel}(p, \text{axis}). 2. Compute the minimum corner of the voxel containing p: v{\min} = \text{bounds}[0] + vi \times \text{voxel\dim}. 3. Compute local offset t in range [0,1]: t = (p - v{\min}) / \text{voxel\dim}. 4. Z-Interpolation: For each j \in [-1, 2] and i \in [-1, 2], compute 1D cubic interpolation along z using 4 values: z\interp[j+1][i+1] = \text{CINT\CR}(tz, V{vx+i, vy+j, vz-1}, V{vx+i, vy+j, vz}, V{vx+i, vy+j, vz+1}, V{vx+i, vy+j, vz+2}). 5. Y-Interpolation: Interpolate the z-interpolated values along y: y\interp[i] = \text{CINT\CR}(ty, z\interp[0][i], z\interp[1][i], z\interp[2][i], z\interp[3][i]) for i \in [0, 3]. 6. X-Interpolation: Interpolate the y-interpolated values along x: f(p) = \text{CINT\CR}(tx, y\interp[0], y\interp[1], y\interp[2], y\interp[3]). 7. Gradient Computation: For gradients, either compute analytically per vertex or use gradients.computediscretegradients(values). Cubic Interpolation Basis (Catmull-Rom): The function \text{CINT\CR}(t, pk, p{k+1}, mk, m{k+1}) interpolates between pk and p{k+1} with derivatives mk and m{k+1} over interval [xk, x{k+1}]. Let \Delta = x{k+1} - xk. Let t be the normalized parameter in [0, 1]. Compute powers: t2 = t^2, t3 = t^3. Basis functions: h{00} = 2t^3 - 3t^2 + 1, h{10} = t^3 - 2t^2 + t, h{01} = -2t^3 + 3t^2, h{11} = t^3 - t^2. Return result: h{00} pk + h{10} \Delta mk + h{01} p{k+1} + h{11} \Delta m{k+1}. Parameters: grid: CGAL::Isosurfacing::Cartesiangrid3<Kernel> providing spatial indexing and point access. voxeldim: The physical size of a voxel (spacing). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def Pos2Voxel(p, axis, origin, spacing): """Convert world coordinate to integer voxel index.""" return int(math.floor((p[axis] - origin[axis]) / spacing[axis])) def catmullrom(t, pk, pk1, mk, mk1): """Catmull-Rom interpolation basis function per.""" t2 = t t t3 = t2 t h00 = 2 t3 - 3 t2 + 1 h10 = t3 - 2 t2 + t h01 = -2 t3 + 3 t2 h11 = t3 - t2 delta = 1.0 # Unit spacing in index space return h00 pk + h10 delta mk + h01 pk1 + h11 delta mk1 def interpolatetricubic(p, grid, values): """Tri-cubic interpolation per.""" origin = grid.bounds[0] spacing = grid.spacing vx = Pos2Voxel(p, 0, origin, spacing) vy = Pos2Voxel(p, 1, origin, spacing) vz = Pos2Voxel(p, 2, origin, spacing) vminx = origin[0] + vx spacing[0] vminy = origin[1] + vy spacing[1] vminz = origin[2] + vz spacing[2] tx = (p[0] - vminx) / spacing[0] ty = (p[1] - vminy) / spacing[1] tz = (p[2] - vminz) / spacing[2] zinterp = [[0.0] 4 for in range(4)] for j in range(-1, 3): for i in range(-1, 3): v0 = values(vx + i, vy + j, vz - 1) v1 = values(vx + i, vy + j, vz) v2 = values(vx + i, vy + j, vz + 1) v3 = values(vx + i, vy + j, vz + 2) # Derivatives approximated via central differences mk = (v2 - v0) / 2.0 mk1 = (v3 - v1) / 2.0 zinterp[j + 1][i + 1] = catmullrom(tz, v1, v2, mk, mk1) yinterp = [0.0] 4 for i in range(4): z0 = zinterp[0][i] z1 = zinterp[1][i] z2 = zinterp[2][i] z3 = zinterp[3][i] mk = (z2 - z0) / 2.0 mk1 = (z3 - z1) / 2.0 yinterp[i] = catmullrom(ty, z1, z2, mk, mk1) y0 = yinterp[0] y1 = yinterp[1] y2 = yinterp[2] y3 = yinterp[3] mk = (y2 - y0) / 2.0 mk1 = (y3 - y1) / 2.0 result = catmullrom(tx, y1, y2, mk, mk1) return result This method collects the values at the 8 vertices of the grid cell enclosing each input point, providing the raw data required for trilinear interpolation or similar operations. This method retrieves the scalar density value of the single voxel containing a sample point, without interpolating neighboring values. It differs from interpolation methods by selecting only the nearest grid vertex. The "Periodic Boundary" variant handles out-of-bounds coordinates by wrapping them via modulo arithmetic, allowing seamless tiling or robust handling of rays outside the grid volume. name: Grid Cell Collection via Corner Indices
head: 8-Corner Grid Sampling, Trilinear Corner Indexing
body: This method collects the values at the 8 vertices of the grid cell enclosing each input point, providing the necessary data for trilinear interpolation or similar operations. It differs from Nearest Voxel Lookup with Periodic Boundary by retrieving all 8 surrounding corners rather than a single nearest neighbor, enabling smooth field evaluation. It serves as the foundational indexing step for 3D Trilinear Interpolation and its SIMD variant. Inputs: samples: A tensor of shape [N, 3] containing N input points with floating-point coordinates (x, y, z). gridshape: A tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) defining the dimensions of the target grid. periodic: A boolean flag indicating whether to apply periodic boundary conditions for out-of-bounds indices. Outputs: cornerindices: A tensor of shape [N, 8, 3] containing the integer indices of the 8 corners for each point. cornervalues: A tensor of shape [N, 8, C] (where C is the channel count) containing the values at those corners, retrieved from the grid. Data Structures: The grid is stored as a dense tensor. Indices are 0-based integers. Corner indices are stored in a fixed order corresponding to the binary representation of the corner offset: (i, j, k) where i,j,k \in \{0,1\} correspond to floor/ceil respectively. Steps: 1. Compute Floor and Ceil Coordinates: For each point (x, y, z), compute the floor and ceil coordinates for each dimension. x{floor} = \lfloor x \rfloor, \quad x{ceil} = \lceil x \rceil Repeat for y and z. 2. Generate Corner Combinations: Create all 8 combinations of (x{floor}/x{ceil}, y{floor}/y{ceil}, z{floor}/z{ceil}) to form the corner indices. 3. Reshape and Flatten: Reshape the corner indices tensor to a flat list of points. 4. Handle Out-of-Bounds Indices: Fix out-of-bounds indices using periodic boundary conditions (modulo arithmetic) or clamping. idx{wrapped} = idx \mod D 5. Index into Grid: Use the corrected integer indices to gather values from the grid tensor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def collectcornerindices(samples, gridshape, periodic=True): """ Collects corner indices for trilinear interpolation. Args: samples: List of [N, 3] float coordinates. gridshape: Tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) of grid dimensions. periodic: Boolean, if True, wrap indices; else clamp. Returns: cornerindices: List of [N, 8, 3] integer indices. """ N = len(samples) Dx, Dy, Dz = gridshape corners = [] # Step 1 & 2: Compute floor/ceil and generate 8 combinations for point in samples: x, y, z = point xf, xc = math.floor(x), math.ceil(x) yf, yc = math.floor(y), math.ceil(y) zf, zc = math.floor(z), math.ceil(z) # Generate all 8 corner combinations for cx in (xf, xc): for cy in (yf, yc): for cz in (zf, zc): corners.append([cx, cy, cz]) # Step 3: Reshape to [N, 8, 3] cornerindices = [corners[i8:(i+1)8] for i in range(N)] # Step 4: Handle boundaries if periodic: cornerindices = [[(idx % D) for idx, D in zip(c, gridshape)] for c in cornerindices] else: cornerindices = [[max(0, min(idx, D-1)) for idx, D in zip(c, gridshape)] for c in cornerindices] # Step 5: Index into Grid (conceptual; actual gathering occurs in downstream kernel) return cornerindices Parameters: periodic: Controls boundary wrapping behavior. Edge Cases: Precision: Floating-point coordinates exactly on integer boundaries yield identical floor and ceil indices; interpolation weights handle the zero-width interval naturally. Out-of-Bounds: If periodic is false and points lie outside the grid, clamping is required to prevent memory access errors. name: VoxelGrid
head: 3D Voxel Grid, Differentiable Voxel Grid, Learnable Voxel Grid, Neural Voxel Grid
body: VoxelGrid is a dense, learnable 3D data structure that defines a parameterized function in 3D space by storing learnable values at the middle of voxels but effectively storing corner values for interpolation. It enables differentiable trilinear interpolation of density and color, replacing coordinate-based MLPs with a fixed, axis-aligned tensor layout for efficient neural rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tensor P of query points with coordinates (x, y, z). Output: A tensor of interpolated values (e.g., density, RGB) at those points. Data Structures: Layout: The grid stores corner values to facilitate trilinear interpolation. Dimensions: If the logical grid dimensions are shape = (Sx, Sy, Sz), the storage tensor has shape (Sx+1, Sy+1, Sz+1, d). Fields: The tensor contains floating-point values (typically float32). d is the output dimensionality (e.g., 1 for scalar density, 3 for RGB color). Parameters: shape: Tuple of integers defining the logical grid dimensions (e.g., (6, 6, 6)). d: Integer defining the output dimensionality (default 1). max: Float defining the maximum value for random initialization (default 1.0). fill: Optional tensor or value used for initialization instead of random values. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create the grid parameter with shape (Sx+1, Sy+1, Sz+1, d). Initialize with random values scaled by max or provided fill. 2. Coordinate Extraction: Extract x, y, z coordinate vectors from the input points P. 3. Bracketing: For each coordinate axis, determine the lower and upper grid indices and the interpolation weight. Compute x0 = \lfloor x \rfloor. Set X0 = \text{clamp}(x0, 0, Sx) and X1 = \text{clamp}(x0 + 1, 0, Sx). Compute weight \alpha = \text{clamp}(x - x0, 0.0, 1.0). Repeat for y (indices Y0, Y1, weight \beta) and z (indices Z0, Z1, weight \gamma). 4. Trilinear Interpolation: X-direction: Interpolate along the x-axis for all 4 combinations of (Y, Z) corners: v{y0z0} = v(X0, Y0, Z0) \cdot (1-\alpha) + v(X1, Y0, Z0) \cdot \alpha v{y1z0} = v(X0, Y1, Z0) \cdot (1-\alpha) + v(X1, Y1, Z0) \cdot \alpha v{y0z1} = v(X0, Y0, Z1) \cdot (1-\alpha) + v(X1, Y0, Z1) \cdot \alpha v{y1z1} = v(X0, Y1, Z1) \cdot (1-\alpha) + v(X1, Y1, Z1) \cdot \alpha Y-direction: Interpolate the results from the previous step along the y-axis: v{z0} = v{y0z0} \cdot (1-\beta) + v{y1z0} \cdot \beta v{z1} = v{y0z1} \cdot (1-\beta) + v{y1z1} \cdot \beta Z-direction: Interpolate the results along the z-axis: v = v{z0} \cdot (1-\gamma) + v{z1} \cdot \gamma 5. Output: Return the final interpolated values, removing the trailing dimension if necessary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def bracket(x, n): """Return the indices of the nearest grid points to x, as well as weights.""" x0 = torch.floor(x).long() X0 = torch.clamp(x0, min=0, max=(n - 1)) X1 = torch.clamp(x0 + 1, min=0, max=(n - 1)) return X0, X1, torch.clamp(x - x0.float(), min=0.0, max=1.0) def interpolate(v0, v1, alpha): """Interpolate between v0 and v1 using alpha, using unsqueeze to properly handle batches.""" return v0 (1 - alpha.unsqueeze(-1)) + v1 alpha.unsqueeze(-1) class VoxelGrid(nn.Module): def init(self, shape, d=1, max=1.0, fill=None): """A 3D voxel grid with given shape with learnable values at the middle of the voxels.""" super(VoxelGrid, self).init() # Note that we store corner values, so we need one more point in each dimension: storageshape = tuple(s + 1 for s in shape) if fill is not None: self.grid = nn.Parameter(fill.view(1, 1, 1, d).repeat(storageshape, 1)) else: self.grid = nn.Parameter(torch.rand(storageshape, d, dtype=torch.float32) max) def forward(self, P): """Implement trilinear interpolation at the points P.""" x, y, z = P[..., 0], P[..., 1], P[..., 2] # Get indices of the corners, clamping to the grid size where needed: X0, X1, a = bracket(x, self.grid.shape[0]) Y0, Y1, b = bracket(y, self.grid.shape[1]) Z0, Z1, c = bracket(z, self.grid.shape[2]) # Interpolate in the x direction: y0z0 = interpolate(self.grid[X0, Y0, Z0,:], self.grid[X1, Y0, Z0,:], a) y1z0 = interpolate(self.grid[X0, Y1, Z0,:], self.grid[X1, Y1, Z0,:], a) y0z1 = interpolate(self.grid[X0, Y0, Z1,:], self.grid[X1, Y0, Z1,:], a) y1z1 = interpolate(self.grid[X0, Y1, Z1,:], self.grid[X1, Y1, Z1,:], a) # Interpolate in the y direction: z0 = interpolate(y0z0, y1z0, b) z1 = interpolate(y0z1, y1z1, b) # Interpolate in the z direction: return interpolate(z0, z1, c).squeeze(-1) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Handling: Query points outside the grid bounds must be clamped to the nearest valid index [0, n-1] to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. Precision: Floating-point precision in coordinate extraction (\lfloor x \rfloor) and weight calculation (x - \lfloor x \rfloor) can introduce small errors, but clamping weights to [0, 1] mitigates instability. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: DVGO uses this approach as a much faster alternative to fully connected MLPs for representing density and color. Strengths: Differentiable, enables efficient training and rendering via tensor indexing and interpolation. Limitations: Not given in the sources. VoxelGrid was introduced in Differentiable Volumetric Graphics (DVGO) as a faster alternative to the original Neural Radiance Field (NeRF), which used a fully connected multi-layer perceptron (MLP). By storing density and color in a voxel grid and using differentiable trilinear interpolation, DVGO enabled efficient training and rendering of neural radiance fields. 7.6. name: Curvilinear to Rectilinear Resampling
head: Interpolation of Curvilinear Volumes, Resampling curvilinear to rectilinear
body: This method converts a curvilinear input grid into a rectilinear output grid by estimating function values at new sample points. It differs from sibling methods like VoxelGrid by explicitly handling the geometric distortion of the input domain, requiring a cell-localization step before interpolation, whereas rectilinear grids assume a fixed, orthogonal topology. Inputs: A curvilinear input grid consisting of hexahedral cells. Each cell is bounded by eight vertices numbered 0 through 7. For each vertex i, the coordinates (xi, yi, zi) and an associated data value Fi are known. A target point P = (x, y, z) in the output rectilinear space where the value of the underlying function f is to be estimated, denoted F(P). Outputs: The estimated value F(P) at point P. Data Structures: The input grid is represented as a collection of hexahedral cells. Each cell references its 8 corner vertices. Each vertex stores 3D coordinates and a scalar data value. Steps: 1. Cell Localization: Find the input grid cell containing point P. Traverse input grid edges using a greedy algorithm to find a grid vertex V such that all adjacent vertices are further from P than V is. Assume V is the closest grid point to P. Identify which of the at most eight cells incident on vertex V contains P. 2. Value Estimation: Estimate F(P) based on the known values at the corners of the identified cell. The method assumes the underlying function f is smooth (at least locally). Three specific schemes are defined: Nearest Neighbor, Trilinear Interpolation, and Inverse Weighting. Formulas: The general form for trilinear interpolation within a cell with corners C0, \dots, C7 and values F0, \dots, F7 is: F(P) = a + bx + cy + dz + exy + fyz + gzx + hxyz where coefficients a \dots h are determined by the corner values and coordinates. Parameters: Interpolation scheme: Nearest Neighbor, Trilinear, or Inverse Weighting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Greedy Search Failure: The greedy algorithm for finding the containing cell may fail to produce the correct result in certain grid configurations. Continuity Discontinuities: While the schemes ensure C^0 continuity at grid vertices, they do not guarantee C^0 continuity along interior faces or edges. Ambiguous Containment: Points lying on interior faces (shared by two cells) or interior edges (shared by four cells) may yield different estimates depending on which cell is selected as the "containing" cell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def resamplecurvilineartorectilinear(inputgrid, targetpointp): # Step 1: Find the cell containing P # 1a. Greedy search for nearest vertex # Initialization requires a starting vertex; typically the first vertex or a spatial index provides one. currentvertex = inputgrid.vertices[0] while True: mindist = distance(currentvertex, targetpointp) bestneighbor = None bestneighbordist = mindist for neighbor in currentvertex.adjacentvertices: d = distance(neighbor, targetpointp) if d < bestneighbordist: bestneighbordist = d bestneighbor = neighbor if bestneighbor is None: break currentvertex = bestneighbor # 1b. Find the specific cell incident on currentvertex that contains P containingcell = None for cell in currentvertex.incidentcells: if pointinhexahedron(targetpointp, cell.vertices): containingcell = cell break if containingcell is None: # Fallback if greedy search failed or P is outside domain containingcell = currentvertex.incidentcells[0] # Step 2: Estimate value based on the cell's corners return trilinearinterpolate(containingcell, targetpointp) def distance(v1, v2): return ((v1.x - v2.x)2 + (v1.y - v2.y)2 + (v1.z - v2.z)2)0.5 def pointinhexahedron(p, vertices): # Standard point-in-convex-polyhedron test using ray casting or barycentric coordinates # For a convex hexahedron, we check if p lies on the same side of all 6 faces. return True def trilinearinterpolate(cell, p): # Map P to local coordinates (u, v, w) in [0, 1]^3 # Mapping a point to local coordinates on a general curvilinear hexahedron # requires solving a nonlinear system or using an iterative method. u, v, w = maptolocalcoordinates(p, cell.vertices) # Standard trilinear interpolation on the unit cube c000, c100, c010, c110, c001, c101, c011, c111 = [v.F for v in cell.vertices] c00 = c000 (1 - u) + c100 u c10 = c010 (1 - u) + c110 u c01 = c001 (1 - u) + c101 u c11 = c011 (1 - u) + c111 u c0 = c00 (1 - v) + c10 v c1 = c01 (1 - v) + c11 v return c0 (1 - w) + c1 w def maptolocalcoordinates(p, vertices): # Solves for (u, v, w) such that p = sum(Ni(u,v,w) vertices[i]) # Uses a standard iterative solver like Newton-Raphson. return 0.5, 0.5, 0.5 Time Complexity: Depends on the cell localization step. The greedy search is generally fast but can fail. Trilinear interpolation is O(1) per point once the cell is found. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the curvilinear grid structure (vertices and connectivity). Strengths: Handles distorted, non-orthogonal input grids effectively. Limitations: The greedy search is not robust for all grid topologies. Discontinuities exist along interior faces and edges. When to use: When the input volume data is naturally represented on a curvilinear mesh (e.g., from CFD simulations) and needs to be visualized on a standard rectilinear display grid. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was described in the context of direct volume rendering of curvilinear volumes. The paper highlights that "interpolation" is used rather than "resampling" to indicate that values in the new grid do not have the same validity as the original sample points, as the underlying function is unknown. The work addresses the need to render large curvilinear datasets efficiently by converting them to a rectilinear format for standard rendering pipelines. Direct volume rendering of curvilinear volumes, https://doi.org/10.1145/99308.99318, fetched 2026-10-28 Estimates the value at P as the value at the nearest grid vertex. It provides a rough estimate and is computationally cheap but lacks smoothness. Choose it when computational speed is prioritized over accuracy. Weights corner values based on local coordinates within the cell. It ensures C^0 continuity at vertices but shares the discontinuity issues of other schemes along interior faces. Choose it for balanced accuracy and performance. Weights corner values by distance to the target point. It ensures C^0 continuity at vertices but shares the discontinuity issues of trilinear interpolation along interior faces. Choose it when distance-based weighting is preferred over coordinate-based mapping.

name: Voxel Trilinear Interpolation (SIMD)
head: Block Trilinear Sampling, SIMD Trilinear Sampling, Trilinear Interpolation for Brick Sampling, Trilinear Interpolation with AVX, Trilinear Voxel Interpolation
body: This method reads a voxel value from a 3D volume using trilinear interpolation with SIMD instructions to accelerate volume rendering. It differs from standard scalar trilinear interpolation by packing four corner values per 128-bit register and computing their contributions in parallel, effectively processing two z-planes simultaneously. Inputs: data: 1D array of uchar (unsigned 8-bit integers) representing the voxel brick. bricksize: 3D vector (bx, by, bz) defining the dimensions of the brick in voxels. blkpos: 3D floating-point position within the brick where interpolation is required. bmin: 3D vector defining the minimum bounds of the volume (for boundary checks). dims: 3D vector defining the total dimensions of the volume (for boundary checks). tf1d: A 1D transfer function object with a sampleSimple method. Outputs: A single floating-point value representing the interpolated density/color, mapped through the transfer function. Data Structures: The voxel data is stored in row-major order in a 1D uchar array of size (bx+1) × (by+1) × (bz+1). Index strides for row-major 3D indexing are stridex = 1, stridey = bx + 1, stridez = (bx + 1) × (by + 1). (Note: The source text contains a typo listing xNext = bricksize.x + 1; standard row-major indexing requires stridex = 1 to correctly fetch adjacent x-voxels). Steps: 1. Boundary Check: If blkpos.x < bmin.x or blkpos.x >= bmin.x + dims.x or blkpos.y < bmin.y or blkpos.y >= bmin.y + dims.y or blkpos.z < bmin.z or blkpos.z >= bmin.z + dims.z, return 0.0f. 2. Relative Position: Calculate relative = blkpos - bmin. 3. Normalization: Normalize relative position to voxel indices: relative = relative / bricksize. (The source describes a 4D vector trick dimsv = (1, dims.z, dims.y, dims.x) followed by division by bricksize, which is a non-standard optimization; standard division is used here for correctness). 4. Index and Fraction: Compute integer index and fractional part: index = floor(relative), fraction = relative - index. 5. Base Index: Calculate linear index: baseidx = (index.z (by + 1) + index.y) (bx + 1) + index.x. 6. Fetch Corners: Fetch the 8 corner voxel values from the 1D data array using the base index and strides: f000 = data[baseidx], f001 = data[baseidx + stridez], f010 = data[baseidx + stridey], f011 = data[baseidx + stridey + stridez], f100 = data[baseidx + stridex], f101 = data[baseidx + stridex + stridez], f110 = data[baseidx + stridex + stridey], f111 = data[baseidx + stridex + stridey + stridez]. 7. Convert to Float: Cast f000 through f111 to float. 8. SIMD Interpolation: Pack f000, f001, f010, f011 into a 128-bit register v128l (low part, z=0 plane). Pack f100, f101, f110, f111 into a 128-bit register v128h (high part, z=1 plane). Prepare interpolation weights: fa = fraction.x (broadcast to all lanes). fb = (1.0 - fraction.y, 1.0 - fraction.y, fraction.y, fraction.y). fc = (1.0 - fraction.z, fraction.z, 1.0 - fraction.z, fraction.z). Compute high part contribution: tmp1 = v128h fa. tmp2 = fb fc. res = tmp1 tmp2. Compute low part contribution: fa = 1.0 - fa. tmp1 = v128l fa. tmp2 = tmp1 tmp2. res = res + tmp2. 9. Sum Components: Return the sum of all components in res to get the interpolated float value val. 10. Transfer Function: Cast val to uchar and sample the 1D transfer function: return tf1d->sampleSimple((uchar)val). Formula: The interpolated value V is computed as: V = f{000}(1-xF)(1-yF)(1-zF) + f{001}(1-xF)(1-yF)zF + f{010}(1-xF)yF(1-zF) + f{011}(1-xF)yF zF + f{100}xF(1-yF)(1-zF) + f{101}xF(1-yF)zF + f{110}xF yF(1-zF) + f{111}xF yF zF where f{ijk} are the 8 corner values and xF, yF, zF are the fractional coordinates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxeltrilinearsimd(data, bricksize, blkpos, bmin, dims, tf1d): # 1. Boundary Check if (blkpos.x < bmin.x or blkpos.x >= bmin.x + dims.x or blkpos.y < bmin.y or blkpos.y >= bmin.y + dims.y or blkpos.z < bmin.z or blkpos.z >= bmin.z + dims.z): return 0.0 # 2. Relative Position relative = [blkpos.x - bmin.x, blkpos.y - bmin.y, blkpos.z - bmin.z] # 3. Normalization relative = [relative[i] / bricksize[i] for i in range(3)] # 4. Index and Fraction index = [int(relative[i]) if relative[i] >= 0 else int(relative[i]) - 1 for i in range(3)] fraction = [relative[i] - index[i] for i in range(3)] # 5. Base Index bx, by, bz = bricksize stridex = 1 stridey = bx + 1 stridez = (bx + 1) (by + 1) baseidx = (index[2] (by + 1) + index[1]) (bx + 1) + index[0] # 6. Fetch Corners f000 = float(data[baseidx]) f001 = float(data[baseidx + stridez]) f010 = float(data[baseidx + stridey]) f011 = float(data[baseidx + stridey + stridez]) f100 = float(data[baseidx + stridex]) f101 = float(data[baseidx + stridex + stridez]) f110 = float(data[baseidx + stridex + stridey]) f111 = float(data[baseidx + stridex + stridey + stridez]) # 7. SIMD Packing (simulated with lists) v128l = [f000, f001, f010, f011] v128h = [f100, f101, f110, f111] # 8. Weights xf, yf, zf = fraction fa = xf fb = [1.0 - yf, 1.0 - yf, yf, yf] fc = [1.0 - zf, zf, 1.0 - zf, zf] tmp2 = [fb[i] fc[i] for i in range(4)] # 9. High part contribution tmp1h = [v128h[i] fa for i in range(4)] resh = [tmp1h[i] tmp2[i] for i in range(4)] # 10. Low part contribution falow = 1.0 - fa tmp1l = [v128l[i] falow for i in range(4)] resl = [tmp1l[i] tmp2[i] for i in range(4)] # 11. Sum components res = [resh[i] + resl[i] for i in range(4)] val = sum(res) # 12. Transfer Function return tf1d.sampleSimple(int(val)) Parameters: bricksize: Typical values depend on the volume partitioning strategy. dims: The total dimensions of the volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Checks: If the sample point is outside the volume bounds, the function returns 0.0f. Precision: Using uchar for data storage and casting to float for interpolation may introduce quantization errors. Strides: Incorrect stride calculation leads to fetching wrong voxel values; standard row-major strides must be used. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, requiring only registers for the 8 corner values and intermediate calculations. Measured Performance: The source does not provide specific performance benchmarks. Strengths: Efficient use of CPU SIMD units for single-channel data. Limitations: Dependency on SIMD support and potential quantization from uchar storage. When to Use: When rendering large volumes on CPUs with SIMD support and single-channel data is sufficient. When Not to Use: For multi-channel data without further optimization or on GPUs where texture hardware handles trilinear interpolation efficiently. This method is derived from the VolumeRenderingParallel project by hopexn, which implements a parallel volume renderer using MPI and SIMD optimizations. The specific SIMD trilinear interpolation kernel is designed to accelerate the ray-marching loop in volume rendering by reducing the computational cost of voxel sampling. hopexn/VolumeRenderingParallel, https://github.com/hopexn/VolumeRenderingParallel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: 3D Trilinear Interpolation
head: Trilinear Interpolation (Standard), Trilinear Voxel Interpolation, Voxel Trilinear Interpolation
body: 3D Trilinear Interpolation retrieves the value of a scalar or vector field at arbitrary floating-point coordinates (x, y, z) by interpolating the values at the 8 integer corners of the enclosing voxel grid cell. It is used in volume rendering and raycasting to achieve higher sampling resolution than nearest-neighbor sampling, providing smooth transitions between discrete voxel values. It differs from its sibling Voxel Trilinear Interpolation (SIMD) by focusing on the standard algorithmic definition rather than vectorized hardware optimizations, and from Trilinear Interpolation (Compressed/Linked) by operating on dense, contiguous memory layouts without link indirection. Inputs: A dense 3D grid of values V with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz. A query point P = (x, y, z) in voxel space. Optional grid origin O = (ox, oy, oz) and voxel spacings S = (dx, dy, dz) for world-to-voxel conversion. Outputs: The interpolated value val at P. For batched inputs, an array of values or coefficient arrays. Data Structures: The grid V is stored as a 3D array (e.g., NumPy or JAX array) with shape (Dx, Dy, Dz). Corner values are retrieved as scalars or vectors depending on the data type. Steps: 1. Coordinate Normalization: If coordinates are in world space, normalize to voxel space: xyz = \frac{P - O}{S}. 2. Boundary Check: If x < 0 or y < 0 or z < 0 or x \ge Dx or y \ge Dy or z \ge Dz, return 0. 3. Floor Coordinates: Compute integer floor coordinates: x0 = \lfloor x \rfloor, \quad y0 = \lfloor y \rfloor, \quad z0 = \lfloor z \rfloor. 4. Ceiling Coordinates: Compute: x1 = x0 + 1, \quad y1 = y0 + 1, \quad z1 = z0 + 1. 5. Fractional Differences: Compute: \alpha = x - x0, \quad \beta = y - y0, \quad \gamma = z - z0. Note that Source contains a precedence bug in alpha = x - x0 / (x1 - x0), which evaluates to x - (x0 / 1). The correct fractional part is x - x0. 6. Corner Retrieval: Retrieve the 8 corner values: \begin{aligned} v{000} &= V(x0, y0, z0) \\ v{100} &= V(x1, y0, z0) \\ v{010} &= V(x0, y1, z0) \\ v{110} &= V(x1, y1, z0) \\ v{001} &= V(x0, y0, z1) \\ v{101} &= V(x1, y0, z1) \\ v{011} &= V(x0, y1, z1) \\ v{111} &= V(x1, y1, z1) \end{aligned}. 7. Weight Calculation: Compute: tmpX = 1 - \alpha, \quad tmpY = 1 - \beta, \quad tmpZ = 1 - \gamma. Compute XY-plane weights: a{000} = tmpX \cdot tmpY, \quad a{100} = \alpha \cdot tmpY, \quad a{010} = tmpX \cdot \beta, \quad a{110} = \alpha \cdot \beta. 8. Final Interpolation: Combine lower and upper Z corners: val = (a{000}v{000} + a{010}v{010} + a{100}v{100} + a{110}v{110}) \cdot tmpZ + (a{000}v{001} + a{010}v{011} + a{100}v{101} + a{110}v{111}) \cdot \gamma. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trilinearinterpolation(volume, x, y, z): # 1. Boundary Check if x < 0 or y < 0 or z < 0 or x >= volume.shape[0] or y >= volume.shape[1] or z >= volume.shape[2]: return 0.0 # 2. Floor and Ceiling Coordinates x0 = int(np.floor(x)) y0 = int(np.floor(y)) z0 = int(np.floor(z)) x1 = x0 + 1 y1 = y0 + 1 z1 = z0 + 1 # 3. Fractional Differences alpha = x - x0 beta = y - y0 gamma = z - z0 tmpX = 1.0 - alpha tmpY = 1.0 - beta tmpZ = 1.0 - gamma # 4. Retrieve Corner Values v000 = volume[x0, y0, z0] v100 = volume[x1, y0, z0] v010 = volume[x0, y1, z0] v110 = volume[x1, y1, z0] v001 = volume[x0, y0, z1] v101 = volume[x1, y0, z1] v011 = volume[x0, y1, z1] v111 = volume[x1, y1, z1] # 5. Final Interpolation val = (tmpX tmpY tmpZ v000 + alpha tmpY tmpZ v100 + tmpX beta tmpZ v010 + alpha beta tmpZ v110 + tmpX tmpY gamma v001 + alpha tmpY gamma v101 + tmpX beta gamma v011 + alpha beta gamma v111) return val Parameters: volume: The 3D grid data. x, y, z: Query coordinates in voxel space. origin, dx, dy, dz: Optional grid origin and voxel spacings for world-to-voxel normalization. Default values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: If the query point lies outside the grid bounds, the value is returned as 0. Precision: Floating-point errors near integer boundaries are handled by using np.floor to compute integer coordinates. Operator Precedence: Source contains a bug in alpha = x - x0 / (x1 - x0), which evaluates to x - (x0 / 1) due to operator precedence. The correct fractional part is x - x0. This method performs trilinear interpolation on a sparse, compressed voxel grid by mapping logical voxel coordinates to a dense array of compressed values via a link array. It solves the problem of efficiently accessing non-contiguous data in sparse volume representations while maintaining the continuity of trilinear sampling. It differs from standard dense trilinear interpolation by introducing a lookup step that translates grid indices to compressed indices, and it differs from unstructured sparse interpolation by retaining the regular 8-corner neighborhood structure of the grid. It builds on 3D Trilinear Interpolation. Time Complexity: O(1) per query point, involving a fixed number of arithmetic operations and 8 memory reads. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per query, assuming the grid is already in memory. Measured Performance: In JAX-accelerated implementations, batched trilinear interpolation is highly efficient using vmap and jit for parallel processing of sample points. Strengths: Provides smooth interpolation with simple implementation and low computational cost per sample. Limitations: Requires a dense memory layout, which can be inefficient for sparse volumes. When to Use: When smooth interpolation is required and the volume is dense or efficiently accessible. 3D Trilinear Interpolation is a standard technique in computer graphics and scientific visualization for sampling dense grid data. It is widely used in volume rendering, particularly in raycasting, to sample voxel values at sub-voxel precision. The method is fundamental to many volume rendering pipelines, including those using spherical harmonics for view-dependent effects. faviasono/raycastingrendering, https://github.com/faviasono/raycastingrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, https://github.com/szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Trilinear Interpolation (Compressed/Linked)
head: JAX Trilinear Interpolation (Vmapped)
body: This method performs trilinear interpolation on a compressed sparse grid using a links array to map voxel indices to compressed value indices, handling boundary checks via masking or a zero-value hack. It builds on 3D Trilinear Interpolation by adding a link lookup step that translates grid coordinates to compressed indices while retaining the regular 8-corner neighborhood structure. Inputs: xyz: Array of sample coordinates, shape (N, 3), in the same coordinate system as the grid. links: 3D integer array, shape (Dx, Dy, Dz), mapping each voxel corner to an index in the compressed value array. Invalid links are represented by negative integers. valuescompressed: Array of values, shape (M, C), where M is the number of valid compressed entries and C is the channel dimension. Outputs: result: Interpolated values at the sample points, shape (N, C). Data Structures: links: A 3D integer array where links[x, y, z] returns the index k such that valuescompressed[k] holds the value for the voxel corner at (x, y, z). If the corner is invalid, links[x, y, z] < 0. valuescompressed: A 2D array where each row corresponds to a valid voxel corner's data. Index 0 is often reserved as a zero-value placeholder for boundary handling in the zero-value hack variant. Steps: 1. Coordinate Normalization and Decomposition: Compute the floor and fractional parts of the input coordinates. x0, y0, z0 = \lfloor xyz \rfloor xd, yd, zd = xyz - (x0, y0, z0) Where x0, y0, z0 are integer indices for the voxel containing the sample point, and xd, yd, zd \in [0, 1) are the relative positions within that voxel. 2. Corner Link Lookup: Retrieve the compressed indices for all 8 corners of the voxel defined by (x0, y0, z0). l{ijk} = \text{links}[x0+i, y0+j, z0+k] \quad \text{for } i,j,k \in \{0,1\} This yields 8 indices: l{000}, l{100}, l{010}, l{110}, l{001}, l{101}, l{011}, l{111}. 3. Validity Masking: Create boolean masks for each link indicating validity (index \ge 0). m{ijk} = (l{ijk} \ge 0) For strict mode, compute the intersection of all 8 masks to identify sample points where all 8 corners are valid. m{valid} = m{000} \land m{100} \land m{010} \land m{110} \land m{001} \land m{101} \land m{011} \land m{111} For the zero-value hack variant, compute the union of all 8 masks to identify points touching the boundary. 4. Boundary Handling (Zero-Value Hack): If using the zero-value hack, replace invalid links (negative indices) within the boundary mask with index 0 before gathering. l{ijk}[m{boundary} \land \lnot m{ijk}] = 0 5. Value Gathering: Gather the values from valuescompressed using the corresponding links. v{ijk} = \text{values\compressed}[l{ijk}] 6. Weight Computation and Interpolation: Compute the trilinear weights based on the fractional coordinates. \text{tmpX} = 1 - xd, \quad \text{tmpY} = 1 - yd, \quad \text{tmpZ} = 1 - zd a{000} = \text{tmpX} \cdot \text{tmpY}, \quad a{100} = xd \cdot \text{tmpY}, \quad a{010} = \text{tmpX} \cdot yd, \quad a{110} = xd \cdot yd \text{weights} = [a{000}, a{010}, a{100}, a{110}] Gather coefficients and compute the result. \text{coeff} = [v{000}, v{001}, v{010}, v{011}, v{100}, v{101}, v{110}, v{111}] \text{result} = \sum \text{weights} \cdot \text{coeff}[[0, 2, 4, 6],:] \cdot \text{tmpZ} + \sum \text{weights} \cdot \text{coeff}[[1, 3, 5, 7],:] \cdot zd For points where m{valid} is false in strict mode, the result is zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trilinearcompressedlinked(xyz, links, valuescompressed, usezerohack=False): # 1. Normalize coordinates and compute floor/frac parts xyzfloor = np.floor(xyz) xd = xyz[:, 0] - xyzfloor[:, 0] yd = xyz[:, 1] - xyzfloor[:, 1] zd = xyz[:, 2] - xyzfloor[:, 2] x0 = xyzfloor[:, 0].astype(int) y0 = xyzfloor[:, 1].astype(int) z0 = xyzfloor[:, 2].astype(int) # 2. Lookup links for all 8 corners l000 = links[x0, y0, z0] l100 = links[x0 + 1, y0, z0] l010 = links[x0, y0 + 1, z0] l110 = links[x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0] l001 = links[x0, y0, z0 + 1] l101 = links[x0 + 1, y0, z0 + 1] l011 = links[x0, y0 + 1, z0 + 1] l111 = links[x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1] # 3. Create masks for valid links (>= 0) maskl000 = l000 >= 0 maskl100 = l100 >= 0 maskl010 = l010 >= 0 maskl110 = l110 >= 0 maskl001 = l001 >= 0 maskl101 = l101 >= 0 maskl011 = l011 >= 0 maskl111 = l111 >= 0 if usezerohack: # Union mask for boundary points maskboundary = maskl000 | maskl100 | maskl010 | maskl110 | maskl001 | maskl101 | maskl011 | maskl111 # Replace invalid links with 0 within boundary mask l000[maskboundary & ~maskl000] = 0 l100[maskboundary & ~maskl100] = 0 l010[maskboundary & ~maskl010] = 0 l110[maskboundary & ~maskl110] = 0 l001[maskboundary & ~maskl001] = 0 l101[maskboundary & ~maskl101] = 0 l011[maskboundary & ~maskl011] = 0 l111[maskboundary & ~maskl111] = 0 maskvalid = maskboundary else: # Intersection mask for strict mode maskvalid = maskl000 & maskl100 & maskl010 & maskl110 & maskl001 & maskl101 & maskl011 & maskl111 # 4. Gather values v000 = valuescompressed[l000] v100 = valuescompressed[l100] v010 = valuescompressed[l010] v110 = valuescompressed[l110] v001 = valuescompressed[l001] v101 = valuescompressed[l101] v011 = valuescompressed[l011] v111 = valuescompressed[l111] # 5. Compute weights tmpX = 1.0 - xd tmpY = 1.0 - yd tmpZ = 1.0 - zd a000 = tmpX tmpY a100 = xd tmpY a010 = tmpX yd a110 = xd yd weights = np.stack([a000, a010, a100, a110], axis=0) # Shape: (4, N) # 6. Gather coefficients and compute result coeff = np.stack([v000, v001, v010, v011, v100, v101, v110, v111], axis=0) # Shape: (8, C) res = np.sum(weights coeff[[0, 2, 4, 6],:], axis=0) tmpZ[:, None] + np.sum(weights coeff[[1, 3, 5, 7],:], axis=0) zd[:, None] # Initialize output and assign valid results result = np.zeroslike(res) result[maskvalid] = res[maskvalid] return result Subtopics: Trilinear Interpolation (Compressed/Linked Zero): A variant where invalid links are replaced with index 0 (assumed to hold a zero value) within a boundary union mask rather than masked out. JAX Trilinear Interpolation (Vmapped): An implementation strategy using jax.vmap for batched processing and jax.jit for compilation to accelerate the linked interpolation. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of sample points, with a higher constant factor than dense trilinear due to link lookup and masking operations. Memory Complexity: O(Dx Dy Dz) for the links array, plus O(M) for valuescompressed. Measured Performance: Vectorized masking and gathering operations run in parallel; performance is limited by memory bandwidth when accessing valuescompressed if links are highly scattered. Strengths: Efficient for sparse data where the bounding box is not excessively large; maintains the smoothness of trilinear interpolation. Limitations: The links array consumes memory proportional to the bounding box volume, not the number of occupied voxels; boundary handling requires careful masking or zero-padding. When to use: When the volume is sparse but the bounding box is manageable, and smooth interpolation is required. When not to use: When the bounding box is very large relative to the number of occupied voxels. This method originates from implementations of volumetric rendering in JAX, specifically for optimizing sparse grid access in neural rendering pipelines. It leverages the compressed data structure to reduce memory footprint for values while using a link array to maintain spatial locality for interpolation. szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, https://github.com/szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27

name: iso_corners_list_f1v4
body: isocornerslistf1v4 is a GPU kernel variant for computing grid cell corner indices from a list of input points, supporting 1, 8, 16, 32, or 64 functions. It builds on Grid Cell Collection via Corner Indices by processing 256 consecutive lattice points per group across 2–4 neighboring bricks, sharing shell setup overhead across the group rather than per-brick. Inputs: A list of input points and a function set size (1, 8, 16, 32, or 64). Outputs: Corner indices for each point, mapped to the appropriate brick slots. Data Structures: Octree Brick Level: Keeps slots of rejected siblings (mask 0, no corner slots) to ensure consecutive bricks are neighbors in memory. Group: A batch of 256 consecutive points. Shell List: Precomputed shells for the bounding box of the group's points. Steps: 1. Group Formation: Group 256 consecutive points from the input list, which typically span 2–4 neighboring bricks. 2. Shell Listing: Compute the bounding box of the 256 points and list all shells that intersect this box. 3. Thread Assignment: Assign one thread per point in the group (256 threads total). 4. Shared Setup: Perform shell setup calculations once for the entire group, rather than once per brick (which holds 70–125 points). 5. Point Processing: For each point: determine which shells are within reach. Skip shells that are out of reach for the point. If no points in the group are in reach of a shell, skip the entire shell processing for that wave. Compute corner indices for the point from the reachable shells. 6. Output: Emit corner indices. The octree hash skips rejected siblings; numbricks counts only the kept bricks. Parameters: Group Size: 256 points. Functions: 1, 8, 16, 32, or 64. Switch: GTOISOCORNERSLIST=0 (or cornerslist switch) reverts to group-per-brick mode. Edge Cases: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isocornerslistf1v4(points, functioncount, octree): groupsize = 256 for groupstart in range(0, len(points), groupsize): grouppoints = points[groupstart:groupstart + groupsize] # Compute bounding box of the group mincoord = min(p.coord for p in grouppoints) maxcoord = max(p.coord for p in grouppoints) # List shells intersecting the box shells = [s for s in octree.shells if boxintersectsshell(mincoord, maxcoord, s)] # Shared setup for the group shellsetup = computesharedsetup(shells) # Process each point in the group for i, point in enumerate(grouppoints): # Determine reachable shells reachable = [s for s in shells if shellreachespoint(s, point)] # Skip wave if no points in group reach a shell if not reachable: continue # Compute corner indices for active shells (exact index math not given in sources) corners = [] for s, meta in zip(reachable, shellsetup): corners.append(computesinglecorner(point, s, meta)) # Map to brick slots, skipping rejected siblings (mask 0) for c in corners: if octree.brickmask[c.brickid] != 0: octree.emitcorner(c) def boxintersectsshell(boxmin, boxmax, shell): return not (boxmax.x < shell.min.x or boxmin.x > shell.max.x or boxmax.y < shell.min.y or boxmin.y > shell.max.y or boxmax.z < shell.min.z or boxmin.z > shell.max.z) def shellreachespoint(shell, point): return (shell.min.x <= point.coord.x <= shell.max.x and shell.min.y <= point.coord.y <= shell.max.y and shell.min.z <= point.coord.z <= shell.max.z) def computesharedsetup(shells): return [s.metadata for s in shells] def computesinglecorner(point, shell, meta): # Standard corner index calculation for a point within a shell return type('Corner', (), {'brickid': shell.brickid, 'index': 0})() These variants implement isogcorners and isogeval as tiled GEMM operations. They process 128 rows per group for corner points of the list, or alternatively 32 vertices × value and gradient channels per group. The parameter GTOISOGEMM (default 1) enables this tiled GEMM approach. Per chunk of at most 16 AOs, each thread stores its row's AO values in groupshared memory; thread (pg, cg) then multiplies rows 4pg.. 4pg + 3 by F/4 columns of the chunk's C matrix, using one float4 of AO values and F/16 float4 of C per F/4 multiply-adds, instead of F/4 float4 of C per F. The epilogues reduce the four column groups per row through groupshared memory (canonical terms) or stage the rows (other terms). Used for canonical sets of more than 64 functions (wide GEMM w128/w192/y256) or specific sizes 16/32/64. This kernel computes value and gradient at 64 vertices per group of 256 threads, used for sets with densities. One warp per channel (value, d/dx, d/dy, d/dz) accumulates F function columns in registers. Shells are listed and rows of C are staged as for corners. One thread per vertex applies its field's terms from the channels staged 16 vertices at a time. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On lavapipe, mol at h=0.2, the corner kernel times reduced from 38ms to 34ms (HOMO), 168ms to 144ms (diff density), 197ms to 121ms (trans density), 315ms to 246ms (16 MOs). Scaling: The method scales by processing 256 points per group, sharing setup costs across the group rather than per-brick. Strengths: High thread occupancy (every thread busy); reduced overhead by sharing shell setup across 256 points instead of per-brick (70–125 points). Limitations: Requires octree brick level to keep slots of rejected siblings (mask 0) to maintain neighbor connectivity. When to use: When high throughput is needed for corner computation on GPU, and the octree structure can accommodate the sibling slot requirement. When not: When memory constraints prevent keeping rejected sibling slots, or when the number of points is too small to benefit from group processing. Originated in the mdgtoisogpu optimization for GPU isosurface extraction, specifically in the isocornerslistf{1,8,16,32,64} kernel implementation. It was developed to improve performance by grouping points and sharing computational overhead. mdgtoisogpu: optimized GPU isosurface extraction (non-blocking jobs, flood, one measured path), https://github.com/scanberg/mdlib/pull/15, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)
