name: VDB Volume Rendering with OpenVDB/NanoVDB
head: OpenVDB/NanoVDB rendering, NanoVDB encoding, OpenVDB structure
body: This method enables GPU volume rendering of large, sparse volumetric datasets by combining offline fixed-rate lossy compression on the CPU (using OpenVDB) with fast, low-overhead on-the-fly decompression and sampling on the GPU (using NanoVDB). It solves the problem of rendering volumes that exceed single-GPU memory capacity by significantly reducing the memory footprint while maintaining random access patterns suitable for incoherent workloads like path tracing. Unlike hierarchical space-skipping approaches which show diminishing returns with RGBA transfer functions, this method typically employs a uniform majorant grid for traversal acceleration to facilitate direct comparison with dense texture rendering. The method consists of two phases: CPU-side compression/conversion and GPU-side rendering. Input: A dense volumetric dataset (e.g., structured regular grid) and a user-defined quality parameter q \in [0, 1]. Output: A NanoVDB structure in GPU memory, supporting nearest-neighbor and trilinear interpolation sampling. The standard OpenVDB structure uses a hierarchical layout with three levels of internal nodes and leaf voxels. Index Space: 4096^3 (1 \ll 12). Node5 (Top): Span 32^3 (1 \ll 5). Node4 (Middle): Span 16^3 (1 \ll 4). Node3 (Bottom): Span 8^3 (1 \ll 3). Brick Size: 32 \times 32 \times 32 voxels for the standard {3,4,5} layout. Note: Some implementations (e.g., Evolve) use 8^3 bricks for the leaf data storage. NanoVDB creates a linear, pointer-free layout optimized for GPU access. The structure on GPU memory is defined as: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct Volume { constants: Vec<VolumeConstants>, // Translation, scale, AABB (unique per animation frame) nodes5: Vec<Node5>, nodes4: Vec<Node4>, nodes3: Vec<Node3>, voxeldata: VoxelData, // 3D texture buffer } Node Layout: Each node (Node5, Node4, Node3) contains: childpointer: u32: Points to the start of N\CHILDREN child nodes. tilevalue: f32: Value for homogeneous regions. minvalue: f32, maxvalue: f32, meanvalue: f32: Statistical bounds. childmask: [u32; N\CHILDREN / 32]: Bitmask indicating validity of child nodes. Voxel Data: Stored in a 3D texture buffer. Layout: Voxels are stored in bricks of 8^3. Packing: Each 4 values in the Z direction are stored as RGBA components of a texel. Compression: BC7 block compression is applied to the 3D texture, resulting in 2 bits per voxel. The fixed-rate encoding algorithm achieves target compression ratios by encoding homogeneous blocks as nearly empty and voxelizing non-empty regions. 1. Background Value Identification: Compute a histogram of the input volume's values. The most frequent value is assumed to be the background value B. 2. Bricking: Divide the volume conceptually into bricks sized to match the leaf node dimensions (e.g., 32 \times 32 \times 32). 3. Brick Analysis: For each brick, compute the minimum and maximum voxel values [lo, hi]. 4. Brick Sorting: Sort bricks in ascending order of distance to B (most similar first). Three metrics are defined: f1 = \min(|lo - B|, |hi - B|) (closest point-in-range) f2 = \max(|lo - B|, |hi - B|) (farthest point-in-range) f3 = |(lo + hi)/2 - B| (median distance) Evaluation suggests f2 and 32 \times 32 \times 32 brick size generally yield better quality. 5. Voxel Activation: Determine the target number of bricks to activate based on quality q. Iterate through the sorted list starting from the brick least similar to the background (end of list). Activate all voxels in the current brick by setting their original values. Continue until the target number of bricks is processed. Voxels in non-selected bricks remain inactive (implicitly background). 6. Finalization: Prune the resulting OpenVDB tree for memory optimization. 1. Conversion: Convert the compressed OpenVDB structure to NanoVDB. This creates a linear, pointer-free layout. Copy this block to GPU memory. 2. Traversal Acceleration: Use a uniform majorant grid for traversal acceleration. Hierarchical traversal was found to offer diminishing returns for this representation. 3. On-the-Fly Decompression: During rendering, GPU threads sample the volume using NanoVDB accessor and sampler functions. These functions handle tree traversal and voxel value retrieval directly on the GPU. Supported sampling: Nearest-neighbor and trilinear interpolation. If a sample location falls into an inactive region, the background value B is returned. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def compressvolume(volume, W, H, D, quality): # 1. Background Value Identification histogram = computehistogram(volume) # Standard histogram computation backgroundidx = argmax(histogram) # Standard argmax B = volume.valueat(backgroundidx) # 2. Bricking bricksize = 32 numbricksx = math.ceil(W / bricksize) numbricksy = math.ceil(H / bricksize) numbricksz = math.ceil(D / bricksize) numbricks = numbricksx numbricksy numbricksz # 3. Brick Analysis brickranges = [] for i in range(numbricks): lo = i bricksize hi = (i + 1) bricksize brickranges.append((lo, hi)) # 4. Brick Sorting (using f2 metric, ascending distance -> most similar first) def similarity(brickrange): lo, hi = brickrange return max(abs(lo - B), abs(hi - B)) sortedbricks = sorted(enumerate(brickranges), key=lambda x: similarity(x[1])) # 5. Voxel Activation openvdbtree = createemptyopenvdbtree() # Standard OpenVDB tree creation # Activate extreme corners explicitly to preserve world bounds openvdbtree.set((0, 0, 0), volume.valueat((0, 0, 0))) openvdbtree.set((W-1, H-1, D-1), volume.valueat((W-1, H-1, D-1))) brickstoactivate = int(numbricks quality) bricksactive = 0 # Iterate from the end (least similar to background) for idx, brickrange in reversed(sortedbricks): if bricksactive >= brickstoactivate: break for voxel in getvoxelsinbrick(brickrange): # Iterate over 3D voxel coordinates in brick openvdbtree.set(voxel, volume.valueat(voxel)) bricksactive += 1 # 6. Finalization prunetree(openvdbtree) # Standard OpenVDB pruning return openvdbtree def rendervdb(nanovdbptr, ray, uniformgrid): # 1. Traversal Acceleration cell = uniformgrid.findcell(ray.origin) # Standard uniform grid lookup # 2. On-the-Fly Decompression # NanoVDB accessor handles tree traversal and sampling # If sample falls in inactive region, returns background value B value = nanovdbptr.sample(ray.position) # Standard NanoVDB accessor call return value Compression Rates: 1:8, 1:4, 1:2, 1:1. 1:1 means zero percent targeted reduction (lossless activation of non-empty voxels). Quality: A user-defined parameter between 0 and 1 that controls the compression rate. It determines the percentage of bricks to fully activate. NanoVDB Overhead: Modest, approximately 10% for large datasets compared to raw data size. Lossless Compression: At 1:1 rate, the algorithm only activates voxels not considered empty, resulting in an actual size lower than the original even if target reduction is zero. High Compression: High compression rates may lead to missing features if the transfer function highlights regions deemed 'background' and thus deactivated during compression, resulting in block artifacts. Corner Voxels: The extreme (minimum and maximum) corners of the VDB must be explicitly activated even if they match the background value. If not, OpenVDB excludes them, causing the VDB tree's aspect ratio (world bound size) to differ from the original volume. Tile Activation: Activating a whole tile on a level higher than leaf node level 0 (using addTile) sets all voxels in that tile to the same value, providing no additional compression benefit from hierarchical encoding. Animation: Each animation frame has a unique Node5 vector. Switching frames changes only the starting point of structure traversal. Time Complexity: Rendering performance is competitive with hardware-accelerated 3D texture sampling. Memory Complexity: Significant memory savings compared to dense textures. For the Galaxy dataset (108 GB raw), VDB achieves 14 GB at 1:8 rate. NanoVDB overhead is ~10% for large datasets. Measured Performance: Galaxy dataset: VDB achieves 34.8 FPS on 1 GPU vs 18.6 FPS for dense textures on 3 GPUs. Aneurism dataset: VDB achieves 55.8 FPS on 1 GPU vs 75.9 FPS for dense textures on 1 GPU. WDAS dataset: VDB achieves 24.2 FPS on 1 GPU vs 25.4 FPS for dense textures on 1 GPU. Scaling: Enables rendering of datasets requiring multiple GPUs uncompressed on a single GPU. Strengths: Low memory footprint, random access suitable for path tracing, competitive performance with dense textures. Limitations: Block artifacts at high compression; hierarchical traversal offers diminishing returns. Origin: The method was proposed by Stefan Zellmann, Milan Jaros, Jefferson Amstutz, and Ingo Wald in 2025. Development: It integrates OpenVDB for CPU-side compression and NanoVDB for GPU-side rendering, integrated into the Barney ray tracer using the ANARI API. Usage: Used for scientific visualization of large, sparse volumetric data. name: Bottom-up SVO to DAG Reduction
head: SVO to DAG reduction, SVO to DAG transformation, SVO to Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) Reduction, Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) to Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) Reduction, Sparse Voxel DAG Reduction, Reducing a Sparse Voxel Tree to a DAG, SVO reduction
body: Bottom-up SVO to DAG Reduction is a method for compressing a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) into a Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG) by merging identical subtrees into shared nodes. While an SVO efficiently encodes empty regions of space, it stores redundant copies of identical non-empty geometry, leading to high memory consumption at high resolutions. This method solves that problem by generalizing the tree structure to a DAG, allowing multiple parent nodes to share pointers to the same child instance, thereby encoding identical regions of space efficiently. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Compact pointer tree or OpenVDB (VDB) by focusing on topological redundancy (identical geometry) rather than just spatial sparsity or pointer compression, achieving lossless compression without decompression overhead during traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) representing a 3D voxel grid. The SVO may be too large to fit in memory entirely. Output: A minimal Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) representing the same geometry with minimal node count. Data Structures: SVO Node: Defined by a traversal path from the root. Contains a childmask and pointers to children. DAG Node Layout: childmask: 8-bit integer encoding the existence of child pointers (bit i is 1 if child i exists, 0 otherwise). pointers: Array of pointers stored consecutively in memory immediately after the mask. Only pointers to non-empty children are stored. Size: Between 8 and 36 bytes per node, depending on the number of children (1 to 8). Indirection Table: A table mapping each original node's position in a level to its position in the compacted (unique) list of that level. Algorithm Steps: The reduction is performed iteratively from the leaves up to the root. The algorithm is guaranteed to find the smallest possible DAG within L iterations, where L is the maximum level of the octree. 1. Initialization: If the SVO is too large to fit in memory, construct the top L-10 levels top-down using triangle/cube intersection tests. For each leaf node in this top tree, construct a subtree to the maximum depth using a CPU-assisted algorithm (e.g., depth-peeling). Reduce each subtree to a DAG independently before inserting it into the top tree, creating a partially reduced DAG. 2. Leaf Reduction: Leaf nodes are uniquely defined by their childmasks (describing 8 voxels). There are at most 2^8 = 256 unique leaf nodes. Identify all unique leaf nodes. Update child-pointers in the level above the leaves to reference these new unique leaf instances. 3. Iterative Level Reduction: For each level l from the leaves up to the root: Identify all nodes at level l. Two nodes are identical if they have the same childmask AND identical pointers to their children. Sorting: Sort the nodes of level l using their child-pointers (and childmask) as a key. A 256-bit key is used (8 pointers \times 32 bits, or optimized for lower levels). Optimization: For the two lowest levels (where the majority of nodes reside), store subtrees of resolution 4^3 without pointers in a 64-bit integer to improve sorting performance. Compaction: Compact the sorted list to contain only unique nodes. Identical nodes become adjacent in the sorted list. Indirection: Maintain a table of indirections. For each original node, store its position in the compacted list. Pointer Update: Update the child-pointers of nodes in level l-1 using the indirection table to point to the unique instances in level l. Repeat until the root level is processed. 4. Finalization: Apply the reduction one last time to the top-SVO (if sub-DAGs were used) to generate the final DAG. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reducesvotodag(svolevels): """ Reduces a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) to a minimal DAG. Input: svolevels is a list of lists, where svolevels[l] contains all nodes at level l. Level 0 is the root, Level L is the leaves. Output: The root node of the resulting DAG. """ numlevels = len(svolevels) # Process from leaves (highest level) up to the root (level 0) for level in range(numlevels - 1, -1, -1): nodes = svolevels[level] # Step 1: Sort nodes to group identical ones together # Key is the combination of childmask and child pointers # In practice, a parallel sort like tbb::parallelsort is used sortednodes = sorted(nodes, key=lambda n: (n.childmask, tuple(n.pointers))) # Step 2: Compact unique nodes and build indirection map uniquenodes = [] indirectionmap = {} # Maps original node ID to index in uniquenodes uniqueindex = 0 currentunique = None for node in sortednodes: # Check if current node is identical to the last added unique node if currentunique is None or (node.childmask == currentunique.childmask and node.pointers == currentunique.pointers): currentunique = node uniquenodes.append(node) indirectionmap[node.id] = uniqueindex uniqueindex += 1 else: # Node is a duplicate, map to the existing unique node indirectionmap[node.id] = uniqueindex - 1 # Step 3: Update pointers in the level above if level > 0: parentlevelnodes = svolevels[level - 1] for parentnode in parentlevelnodes: # Update each child pointer to point to the unique instance for childidx in range(8): if parentnode.childmask & (1 << childidx): childid = parentnode.pointers[childidx] newuniqueindex = indirectionmap[childid] # Update pointer to reference the unique node's ID/address parentnode.pointers[childidx] = uniquenodes[newuniqueindex].id # Replace the current level with the unique nodes for the next iteration svolevels[level] = uniquenodes return svolevels[0] Parameters: Max Level (L): The depth of the octree. The algorithm runs in O(L) iterations. Resolution: Demonstrated at 128K^3 (131,072^3) voxel grids. Sub-DAG Threshold: For resolutions over 1K^3, generate sub-DAGs of that size first to manage memory. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Constraints: The complete SVO may be orders of magnitude larger than the final DAG. The method must support streaming or chunk-based processing (constructing sub-DAGs) to handle scenes that do not fit in RAM or on disk. Attribute Compression: The method focuses on geometry (visibility). It does not compress material or reflectance properties (color, normal). Decoupling attributes is handled by Voxel Attribute Decoupling. Precision: Pointer indirection must be exact to preserve geometry. The resulting data structure. It shares identical subtrees, enabling lossless compression and efficient traversal without decompression. Choose this when memory footprint is critical and geometry has high redundancy. A technique to separate attributes from geometry. Use this in conjunction with SVO to DAG reduction to compress attributes independently, as the base reduction method does not handle material properties. Time Complexity: The reduction is guaranteed to find the minimal DAG within L iterations. The dominant operation is sorting, which is O(N \log N) per level, where N is the number of nodes at that level. Parallel sorting (e.g., tbb::parallelsort) is used on CPU. GPU parallelization is suggested using parallel prefix sums for compaction. Memory Complexity: The final DAG requires significantly less memory than the SVO. In the EPICTTADEL scene (128K^3, 19 billion voxels), the DAG requires 945MB, while the SVO requires 5.1GB (excluding pointers). Node count reduction is 1-3 orders of magnitude. Measured Performance: Reduction Time: On an Intel Core i7 3930K, reducing a 1K^3 SVO takes ~33ms, and an 8K^3 SVO takes ~4.5s. Traversal: On an NVIDIA GTX680, traversal speeds for the EPICTTADEL scene are 170 MRays/sec for ambient occlusion and 240 MRays/sec for shadows. Strengths: Lossless compression; no decompression overhead during traversal; handles extremely high resolutions (>1K^3) that would otherwise exceed memory limits; effective on irregular data. Limitations: Does not compress material properties; requires significant memory during construction if not using sub-DAGs; sorting large keys (256-bit) can be costly. When to Use: Ray tracing hard/soft shadows, ambient occlusion, and primary rays in high-resolution scenes with redundant geometry. When Not to Use: Scenes with no geometric redundancy; dynamic scenes requiring real-time compression (the method is static). The method was introduced by Viktor Kampe, Erik Sintorn, and Ulf Assarsson from Chalmers University of Technology in the paper "High Resolution Sparse Voxel DAGs". It builds on earlier work by Webber and Dillencourt [1989] on quadtrees and Parker et al. [2003] on 3D voxel data, but distinguishes itself by decoupling voxel content from geometry, allowing successful compression of irregular data. The bottom-up approach was chosen over top-down recursive testing for its efficiency. It is used primarily for GPU ray tracing of visibility queries in extremely high-resolution voxel grids. name: Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG)
head: Sparse Voxel DAG
body: A Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG) is a hierarchical data structure for representing 3D voxelized scenes that reduces memory footprint by identifying and merging identical subtrees, allowing multiple parent nodes to share the same child node instance. Unlike a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) which only encodes empty regions efficiently, the SVDAG additionally encodes identical regions of space by sharing pointers to identical subtrees. This allows for lossless compression without decompression overhead during traversal, making it suitable for real-time rendering and interactive editing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary voxel grid R of size N^3 voxels, where N \ge 2 and N = 2^m. The grid contains active (filled) and passive (empty) voxels. Output: A root node of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) representing the voxel grid, where identical subvolumes are merged into shared nodes. Data Structures: The SVDAG consists of two node types: Internal Nodes (INODE) and Leaf Nodes (LNODE). 1. Internal Node (INODE): Child Node Mask (CHNM): An 8-bit field where each bit is a Header Tag (HT) corresponding to one of the 8 potential children (octants). If HT = 0: The subDAG is homogenously filled with passive voxels (pruned); no pointer is needed. If HT = 1: At least one voxel is active; a child node pointer is present. Reserved Bits (p): Concatenated after CHNM for alignment. Pointers (PTS): An array of 1 to 8 pointers (PT), each r bits long, pointing to child nodes. The order of pointers corresponds to the linearization order (e.g., Morton order). Layout: CHNM (8 bits) + p (reserved) + PTS (variable). Standard alignment uses p=24 and r=32, ensuring 32-bit alignment. 2. Leaf Node (LNODE): Represents a homogeneous subvolume (all passive or all active) or the base resolution. Algorithm (Bottom-Up Reduction): The construction transforms an SVO into a DAG by searching for common subtrees and referencing only unique instances, proceeding from leaves upward. 1. Root Construction: If N=2, the root is a leaf node. If N>2, the root is an internal node. 2. Recursive Build: For a given grid section: a. Check if the section is homogeneous (all voxels identical) or if the base resolution is reached. b. If homogeneous/passive: Create a Leaf Node (LNODE). If active, it represents the filled volume; if passive, it is pruned. c. If not homogeneous: Create an Internal Node (INODE). d. For each of the 8 octants: i. Extract the sub-grid. ii. Recursively build the child node. iii. If the child is a leaf representing passive voxels, set the corresponding HT in CHNM to 0 and do not add a pointer to PTS. iv. If the child is active, set HT to 1 and add the pointer to PTS. 3. Common Subtree Merging (CSM): a. Generate a unique key for the current subtree configuration (e.g., based on child pointers and structure). b. Check a cache of existing nodes. If a node with the same key exists, return the existing node's pointer instead of creating a new one. c. If not in cache, insert the new node into the cache and return its pointer. 4. Propagation: Merging opportunities propagate from leaf nodes upward. Identical subtrees at any level are merged into a single instance, and all parents point to this single instance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class VoxelNode: isleaf: bool value: int # 0 for passive, 1 for active children: list[VoxelNode] # 8 elements, None if leaf chnm: int # 8-bit header tag mask pts: list[VoxelNode] # pointers to active children def getoctant(grid: list[list[list[int]]], octantidx: int, size: int) -> list[list[list[int]]]: half = size // 2 x0 = (octantidx & 1) half y0 = (octantidx & 2) half // 2 z0 = (octantidx & 4) half // 4 return [[[grid[z0+z][y0+y][x0+x] for x in range(half)] for y in range(half)] for z in range(half)] def ishomogeneous(grid: list[list[list[int]]]) -> bool: val = grid[0][0][0] for z in grid: for y in z: for x in y: if x != val: return False return True def builddag(grid: list[list[list[int]]], depth: int, size: int, cache: dict) -> VoxelNode: # Generate unique key from grid content key = str(tuple(grid[z][y][x] for z in range(size) for y in range(size) for x in range(size))) if key in cache: return cache[key] node = VoxelNode() if depth == 0 or ishomogeneous(grid): node.isleaf = True node.value = grid[0][0][0] node.children = [None]8 node.chnm = 0 node.pts = [] else: node.isleaf = False node.children = [None]8 node.chnm = 0 node.pts = [] newsize = size // 2 for i in range(8): octant = getoctant(grid, i, newsize) child = builddag(octant, depth - 1, newsize, cache) node.children[i] = child if child.isleaf and child.value == 0: pass # HT=0, pruned else: node.chnm |= (1 << i) node.pts.append(child) cache[key] = node return node def traceray(node: VoxelNode, origin: list[float], direction: list[float], bounds: list[float]) -> tuple[int, int, int]: # Standard SVDAG ray traversal # 1. Compute ray-box intersection with current node bounds # 2. If no intersection, return None # 3. If leaf: return voxel coordinates if active, else None # 4. If internal: iterate i in 0..7 # if (node.chnm >> i) & 1: # res = traceray(node.pts[i], origin, direction, childbounds[i]) # if res: return res # 5. Return None pass Parameters: N: Grid dimension size, N \ge 2, N=2^m. p: Reserved bits for alignment. Typical value: 24 bits (for 32-bit alignment). r: Length of child node pointer. Typical value: 32 bits (for 32-bit alignment). gridDepth: Maximum recursion depth. Default 4 (implies 16^3 base, but typically scaled to higher resolutions like 128K^3 via depth 16-17). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Attributes: Adding extra bits of information (e.g., color) to leaf nodes reduces the number of identical elements, abolishing compression because previously identical leaves become unique. Memory Layout: Identical pointers exist because nodes can have multiple parents. Rearranging nodes could potentially share pointers and amortize their cost, but this is an open issue. Key Generation: The caching mechanism relies on a unique key for subtree content. Incorrect key generation leads to failure to merge identical subtrees. SSVDAG is a compact, lossless volume representation that merges subtrees identical through reflective symmetries (planar reflections along principal grid axes) and employs variable bit-rate encoding for child pointers to minimize memory footprint while maintaining GPU-friendly traversal performance. It differs from its parent Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG) by recognizing geometric similarity via transformations rather than requiring exact node identity, and from Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAG (SSVDAG) by explicitly detailing the binary layout and tagged pointer encoding [1349-ssvdag-node-layout-and-tagged-pointer-encoding.md]. The PSVDAG–SVDAG Conversion Algorithm transforms a Pointerless Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (PSVDAG) into a Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG). While PSVDAGs use variable-length Labels/Callers and intermittent binary encoding to save space, SVDAGs use constant-length 32-bit pointers and uninterrupted binary sequences to enable efficient rendering and editing. This conversion replaces the pointerless structure with a pointer-based one, allowing for Child Subtree Merging (CSM) and random access, at the cost of increased memory usage (inflation factor 3.01x–3.70x). Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The DAG consumes 8 to 36 bytes per node. It reduces total memory consumption by up to 38x compared to ESVO and up to 26x compared to a minimal pointer-less SVO. Node Reduction: In the CRYSPONZA scene, a 576x reduction in node count was achieved. In the HAIRBALL scene, a 28x reduction was achieved despite lacking obvious regularities. Build Time: Building the DAG for CRYSPONZA at 512^3 takes 8.4ms total (1.9ms sorting). At 8K^3, it takes 4.5s total (0.6s sorting). For HAIRBALL at 8K^3, it takes 40.6s total (4.5s sorting). Measured Performance: In the EPICCITADEL scene voxelized to 128K^3 resolution, the SVDAG stores 19 billion voxels in 945MB of GPU memory. An SVO would require 5.1GB (excluding pointers). On an NVIDIA GTX680, ray tracing in the sparse voxel DAG achieves 170 MRays/sec for ambient occlusion and 240 MRays/sec for shadows. The new encoding (Modisett & Billeter) reduces geometric data size by 13%-18% compared to the original SVDAG. The new encoding improves rendering time by around 10%-12% for static models and by up to 20%-25% for editable voxel models. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: No decompression overhead; efficient traversal; handles extremely high resolutions (up to 128K^3) in real-time. Limitations: Higher memory usage per node compared to pointerless structures due to pointers. Adding attributes to leaves destroys compression benefits. High Resolution Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graphs (SVDAGs) were proposed in 2013 by Kämpe, Sintorn, and Assarsson. The method was introduced to address the limitations of Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) and Efficient Sparse Voxel Octrees (ESVOs) by exploiting geometric similarity (identical subtrees) in addition to sparsity (empty regions). It allows for the storage and rendering of voxel geometry at resolutions as high as (128k)^3 in real time. name: Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAG (SSVDAG)
body: SSVDAG is a compact, lossless volume representation that merges subtrees identical through reflective symmetries (planar reflections along principal grid axes) and employs variable bit-rate encoding for child pointers to minimize memory footprint while maintaining GPU-friendly traversal performance. It differs from its parent Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG) by recognizing geometric similarity via transformations rather than requiring exact node identity, and from its child article by explicitly detailing the binary layout and tagged pointer encoding [1349-ssvdag-node-layout-and-tagged-pointer-encoding.md]. Inputs: A Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) or an existing SVDAG. Outputs: A Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAG (SSVDAG) stored in a compressed binary format. Data Structures: 1. Indexing Structure: Contains the maximum level L and three 32-bit offsets indicating the start of each level in the inner level array. 2. Inner Node Header: A 16-bit header containing a 2-bit code for each of the 8 potential children. Tag 00: Reserved for null pointers (not stored). Tag 01: Child pointer is 16 bits. Tag 10: Child pointer is 32 bits. Tag 11: Child pointer is 32 bits. 3. Child Pointer Formats: Tag 01 (16 bits): Leftmost 3 bits encode the transformation T (reflection codes). Remaining 13 bits encode the offset in number of level-words from the beginning of the next level. A level-word is 2 bytes for an inner level and 8 bytes for the leaf level. This allows encoding reflections and references to nodes in the first 2^{14} bytes of an inner level or first 2^{16} bytes of the leaf level. Tag 10/11 (32 bits): Leftmost 3 bits encode the transformation T. Remaining 29 bits encode the lowest 29 bits of the offset. The highest bit of the offset is stored in the header or a subsequent byte. Algorithm Steps: The construction is a bottom-up external-memory process that reduces an SVO to a minimal SSVDAG by alternating phases at each level, starting from the finest level L-1 up to the root at level 0. 1. Leaf Grouping (Coarsening): The construction graph is coarsened by one level. 4^3 grids are encoded as simple grids in a single array of bricks, each occupying 64 bits. This is done by grouping the 2^3 leaves from the bottom-up process into 4^3 inner nodes at level L-2 without performing new matches. 2. Leaf Node Clustering: Each small voxel grid G of size 2^3 is represented by a binary number B(G) by concatenating occupancy bits. The canonical representation G^? is defined as G^? = T{x,y,z}(G) where T{x,y,z} = \arg \max{T{x,y,z}} B(T{x,y,z}(G)). This is the reflection with the largest integer value. Two leaf nodes are similar if their canonical representations are identical. A precomputed table of 256 entries maps all possible 2^3 voxel combinations to the canonical transformation and the unique canonical representation (one of 46 possible ones). 3. Inner Node Clustering: Inner nodes n1 and n2 are merged if they represent the same subtrees under a transformation T. First, sort inner nodes by the lexicographically sorted set of child pointers. During a streaming pass, verify similarity: for every tagged pointer (tag, p) of n1, it must map to (T(tag), p) in n2 if p is not invariant to T, or to (T(tag) \neg T(tag), p) if p is invariant. Repeat for all 8 reflection combinations, stopping at the first match. Replace pointers to the clustered nodes in the immediately higher level with tagged pointers to the single representative, where the tag encodes the specific transformation required to recover the original subtree. 4. Frequency-based Pointer Compaction: Nodes at each level are reordered by reference count (most referenced first). Pointers are replaced by offsets from the beginning of the level array. The number of bits for each offset is chosen as the smallest available in the encoded format (16-bit or 32-bit). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildssvdag(svolevels): # svolevels: list of lists of Node objects. # Node has:.children (list of 8 tuples (tag, ptr)),.refcount,.parent,.parentidx L = len(svolevels) - 1 processed = [set() for in range(L + 1)] # Precomputed table for 2^3 leaf grids: maps 256 occupancy patterns to (canonicalrep, transformbits) LEAFTABLE = buildleafcanonicaltable() for level in range(L - 1, -1, -1): nodes = svolevels[level] representatives = [] for i, node in enumerate(nodes): if i in processed[level]: continue cluster = [node] processed[level].add(i) transforms = [0] for j in range(i + 1, len(nodes)): if j in processed[level]: continue other = nodes[j] T = findsymmetrymatch(cluster[0], other) if T is not None: cluster.append(other) processed[level].add(j) transforms.append(T) representatives.append((cluster[0], transforms)) # Update parent pointers for merged nodes for k, other in enumerate(cluster[1:], start=1): T = transforms[k] other.parent.children[other.parentidx] = (T, cluster[0]) # Frequency-based compaction representatives.sort(key=lambda x: x[0].refcount, reverse=True) for offset, (rep,) in enumerate(representatives): rep.offset = offset rep.header = encodeheader(rep.children) rep.pointers = encodepointers(rep.children, offset) svolevels[level] = [rep for rep, in representatives] # Leaf coarsening: group 2^3 leaves into 4^3 bricks (64 bits each) bricks = [] leafnodes = svolevels[L-1] for i in range(0, len(leafnodes), 8): brickdata = packleafbrick(leafnodes[i:i+8]) bricks.append(brickdata) return buildindex(svolevels), bricks def findsymmetrymatch(n1, n2): # Check 8 reflections. Returns transform bits or None. for Tbits in range(8): match = True for i in range(8): tag1, ptr1 = n1.children[i] tag2, ptr2 = n2.children[i] mappedtag = applyreflectiontag(tag1, Tbits) if ptr1 != ptr2: if not isinvariant(ptr1, Tbits): match = False break else: if mappedtag != tag2: match = False break if match: return Tbits return None def applyreflectiontag(tag, Tbits): # Standard octree child index permutation under axis reflections # Tags are 2-bit codes representing child indices 0-7 return tag # Actual permutation depends on specific child indexing scheme def isinvariant(ptr, Tbits): # Checks if the subtree pointed to by ptr is symmetric under T return ptr.issymmetricunder(Tbits) def encodeheader(children): header = 0 for i in range(8): tag, ptr = children[i] if ptr is None: code = 0 else: offset = ptr.offset if offset < (1 << 13): code = 1 else: code = 2 header |= (code << (2 i)) return header def encodepointers(children, baseoffset): packed = [] for i in range(8): tag, ptr = children[i] if ptr is None: continue offset = ptr.offset - baseoffset T = ptr.tag if offset < (1 << 13): # 16-bit format: 3 bits T, 13 bits offset val = (T << 13) | offset packed.append(val & 0xFFFF) else: # 32-bit format: 3 bits T, 29 bits offset val = (T << 29) | (offset & 0x1FFFFFFF) packed.append(val & 0xFFFFFFFF) return packed def buildleafcanonicaltable(): # Returns dict mapping 256 occupancy patterns to (canonicalrep, transformbits) # Uses precomputed 2^3 voxel reflection table return {} def packleafbrick(leaves): # Packs 8 leaves into a 64-bit brick return 0 def buildindex(svolevels): # Returns indexing structure with max level L and 3 offsets return {} Parameters: Symmetry Transforms: Planar reflections along the main grid directions (X, Y, Z). Leaf Size for Construction: 2^3 voxels. Transformation Encoding: 3 bits corresponding to reflections along the X, Y, and Z axes. The transformation T{x,y,z} is its own inverse: T{x,y,z}^{-1} = T{x,y,z}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invariant Pointers: When checking similarity, if a child pointer p is invariant to the transformation T, the tag mapping logic differs from non-invariant pointers. The source specifies mapping to (T(tag) \neg T(tag), p) if invariant, requiring careful implementation of the invariant check. Precision: The method relies on exact bitwise comparison of canonical representations for leaves and exact pointer matching for inner nodes. Defines the binary layout of inner nodes, replacing fixed-size child pointers with variable-length tagged pointers (2 or 4 bytes) that embed transformation codes, solving the memory overhead problem of standard SVDAGs where all pointers are fixed at 4 bytes. Compression: In the PowerPlant scene (64K^3 resolution, ~6 billion non-empty voxels), SSVDAG stores data in <86MB (0.123 bits/voxel), compared to 16.2GB for SVO (without pointers) and 167MB for SVDAG. Performance: Real-time GPU in-core visualization with shading and shadows is achieved for the full Boeing 777 model at sub-millimetric precision. The tracing overhead for SSVDAG compared to standard SVO/SVDAG is less than 15%. Memory Distribution: In the Powerplant dataset, the most common 10% of nodes account for nearly 90% of references at level 14 and nearly 50% at level 11, justifying the frequency-based pointer compaction. Strengths: High compression ratio for scenes with reflective symmetry; transparent to standard ray-casting algorithms; GPU-friendly traversal. Limitations: Construction is complex and requires external-memory processing; limited to reflective symmetries (other similarity transforms not supported). SSVDAG was introduced by Alberto Jaspe Villanueva, Fabio Marton, and Enrico Gobbetti from CRS4 in 2016. It extends the concept of Sparse Voxel DAGs (SVDAGs) by incorporating symmetry-aware merging, building on prior work in DAG compression for SVOs. name: SSVDAG Node Layout and Tagged Pointer Encoding
head: Compact representation, Tagged pointer encoding
body: This method defines the binary layout of inner nodes in a Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAG (SSVDAG) to minimize memory footprint while supporting GPU-friendly traversal. It replaces fixed-size child pointers with variable-length tagged pointers (2 or 4 bytes) that embed transformation codes, solving the memory overhead problem of standard SVDAGs where all pointers are fixed at 4 bytes. It differs from its parent Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAG (SSVDAG) by explicitly detailing the bit-packing scheme for these pointers and the associated traversal state management. Input: A voxelized scene represented as a Sparse Voxel DAG with symmetry-aware compression. Output: A memory layout for inner nodes where child pointers are encoded as variable-length tagged pointers, and a traversal algorithm that maintains a cumulative transformation status. Each inner node begins with a 16-bit header. This header contains 8 entries, each 2 bits wide, corresponding to the 8 potential children in octant order. Tag 00: Null pointer. No child data follows. Tag 01: 16-bit child pointer. Tag 10: 32-bit child pointer. Tag 11: 32-bit child pointer. Child pointers are stored immediately after the header. The size and format depend on the header tag. 1. 16-bit Pointer (Tag 01) Size: 2 bytes (16 bits). Layout: Bits [15:13]: Transformation code (3 bits). Bits [12:0]: Offset in number of level-words (13 bits). Addressing: For inner levels: Level-word size is 2 bytes. Max addressable offset is 2^{13} \times 2 = 2^{14} bytes (16 KB). For leaf levels: Level-word size is 8 bytes. Max addressable offset is 2^{13} \times 8 = 2^{16} bytes (64 KB). 2. 32-bit Pointers (Tags 10 and 11) Size: 4 bytes (32 bits). Layout: Bits [31:29]: Transformation code (3 bits). Bits [28:0]: Lowest 29 bits of the offset. The highest bit of the full offset (bit 29) is not stored in the pointer; it is reconstructed from the least significant bit of the 2-bit header tag for that child. If Tag is 10 (binary 10), the header's LSB is 0, so the offset high bit is 0. If Tag is 11 (binary 11), the header's LSB is 1, so the offset high bit is 1. Addressing: For inner levels: Max addressable offset > 2 GB. For leaf levels: Max addressable offset > 8 GB. During ray traversal, a 3-bit Transformation Status variable is maintained. Initialization: 0. Update: When descending to a child, XOR the current status with the 3-bit transformation code extracted from the child's pointer. Restoration: The status must be pushed to a stack along with the current node index to allow restoration upon backtracking. Application: This status indicates which reflections must be applied to indices when accessing child pointers in inner nodes or voxel contents in leaf nodes. Accessing the i-th child requires computing the byte offset within the node's data stream. Unlike SVDAG, where pointers are either 0 or 4 bytes, SSVDAG pointers are 0, 2, or 4 bytes. 1. Read the 16-bit header. 2. Extract the 2-bit tag for child i. 3. Compute the byte offset from the start of the child pointer array: \text{Offset} = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} \text{Size}(\text{Tag}j) Where \text{Size}(\text{Tag}j) is 0 if \text{Tag}j = 00, 2 if \text{Tag}j = 01, and 4 if \text{Tag}j \in \{10, 11\}. 4. Read the pointer data at this offset. 5. Extract the transformation code from the top 3 bits. 6. Decode the offset based on the pointer size (see formulas below). 16-bit Pointer Offset Decoding: Let P{16} be the 16-bit integer value of the pointer. \text{Transform} = P{16} \gg 13 \text{WordOffset} = P{16} \ \& \ 0x1FFF \text{ByteOffset} = \text{WordOffset} \times \text{LevelWordSize} Where \text{LevelWordSize} = 2 for inner levels, 8 for leaf levels. 32-bit Pointer Offset Decoding: Let P{32} be the 32-bit integer value of the pointer. \text{Transform} = P{32} \gg 29 \text{LowOffset} = P{32} \ \& \ 0x1FFFFFFF \text{HighBit} = (\text{HeaderTag} \ \& \ 1) \text{FullOffset} = (\text{HighBit} \ll 29) \ | \ \text{LowOffset} \text{ByteOffset} = \text{FullOffset} \times \text{LevelWordSize} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decodechildpointer(header16bit, childindex, levelwordsize, buffer): """ Decodes the child pointer for a specific child index in an SSVDAG inner node. buffer: list of bytes containing the node data starting immediately after the header. """ # Extract the 2-bit tag for the specific child tag = (header16bit >> (childindex 2)) & 0x3 if tag == 0x0: # Null pointer return (0, None) # Calculate byte offset within the child pointer array # Sum sizes of all previous children byteoffsetinarray = 0 for j in range(childindex): prevtag = (header16bit >> (j 2)) & 0x3 if prevtag == 0x0: byteoffsetinarray += 0 elif prevtag == 0x1: byteoffsetinarray += 2 else: # 0x2 or 0x3 byteoffsetinarray += 4 # Read pointer data based on size if tag == 0x1: # 16-bit pointer ptrval = (buffer[byteoffsetinarray] << 8) | buffer[byteoffsetinarray + 1] transformcode = ptrval >> 13 wordoffset = ptrval & 0x1FFF byteoffset = wordoffset levelwordsize return (transformcode, byteoffset) else: # 32-bit pointer (tags 0x2 or 0x3) ptrval = (buffer[byteoffsetinarray] << 24) | (buffer[byteoffsetinarray + 1] << 16) | (buffer[byteoffsetinarray + 2] << 8) | buffer[byteoffsetinarray + 3] transformcode = ptrval >> 29 lowoffset = ptrval & 0x1FFFFFFF # Determine high bit from header tag headertaglowbit = tag & 0x1 highbit = headertaglowbit << 29 fulloffset = highbit | lowoffset byteoffset = fulloffset levelwordsize return (transformcode, byteoffset) def traversessvdagray(rayorigin, raydirection, nodebuffer, levelwordsize, leveloffsets): """ Demonstrates traversal logic with transformation status management. """ # Stack for backtracking stack = [] # Current transformation status currenttransform = 0 # Start at root (index 0) currentnodeidx = 0 currentlevel = 0 # Track current tree level for offset lookup while True: # Read node header header = (nodebuffer[currentnodeidx] << 8) | nodebuffer[currentnodeidx + 1] # Compute childidx from ray-node intersection logic childidx = None if childidx is None: # No intersection with this node's children, backtrack if not stack: break # Ray escaped # Restore state prevnodeidx, prevtransform = stack.pop() currentnodeidx = prevnodeidx currenttransform = prevtransform continue # Decode child pointer # Buffer for child pointers starts after the header bytes. childbuffer = nodebuffer[currentnodeidx + 2:] transformcode, childbyteoffset = decodechildpointer(header, childidx, levelwordsize, childbuffer) # Update transformation status # XOR with the pointer's reflection tag newtransform = currenttransform ^ transformcode # Push current state to stack for backtracking stack.append((currentnodeidx, currenttransform)) # Move to child # Absolute child address requires adding the level start offset from leveloffsets. currentnodeidx = leveloffsets[currentlevel] + childbyteoffset currenttransform = newtransform Variable Size Access: Accessing the i-th child requires summing the sizes of all preceding pointers [0, i-1]. This differs from SVDAG, which only had sizes 0 and 4. This computation must be performed in the shader, typically via a manually unrolled loop. Precision: The 13-bit offset in 16-bit pointers limits addressing to the first 16 KB of inner levels and 64 KB of leaf levels. If a node is located beyond this range, it must use a 32-bit pointer (Tag 10 or 11). Transformation Accumulation: The transformation status is cumulative. It must be XOR-ed with each pointer's transformation code as the traversal descends. It must be saved to the stack to be restored upon backtracking. Memory Footprint: Significantly reduced compared to fixed-pointer SVDAGs. Null children consume 0 bytes, common children consume 2 bytes, and rare/distant children consume 4 bytes. Complexity: Time: Traversal requires computing variable offsets via a loop for each child access. Space: Inner node headers are fixed at 16 bits. Child data is variable. Performance: Designed for GPU efficiency. The variable-length encoding allows compact storage, improving cache utilization. The transformation status is a simple 3-bit integer, minimizing register pressure. Limitations: The 16-bit pointer is limited to small offsets. Large scenes may require more 32-bit pointers, reducing the compression benefit. The SSVDAG node layout was introduced by Kämpe et al. in 2016 as an extension of the Sparse Voxel DAG (SVDAG). The original SVDAG used fixed 4-byte pointers. The SSVDAG method was developed to further reduce memory consumption by exploiting the fact that many child pointers are null or point to nearby nodes, allowing for variable-length encoding. It also integrates symmetry-aware compression, storing transformation codes directly in the pointers. SSVDAGs: Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAGs - CRS4, https://www.crs4.it/vic/data/papers/i3d2016-symmetry-dags.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: PSVDAG–SVDAG Conversion Algorithm
head: Hierarchical Data Structure conversion, PSVDAG to SVDAG conversion, PSVDAG to SVDAG transformation, Pointerless Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph to Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph conversion
body: The PSVDAG–SVDAG Conversion Algorithm transforms a Pointerless Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (PSVDAG) into a Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG). While PSVDAGs use variable-length Labels/Callers and intermittent binary encoding to minimize storage, SVDAGs use constant-length 32-bit pointers and uninterrupted binary sequences to enable efficient rendering and editing. This conversion replaces the pointerless structure with a pointer-based one, allowing for Child Subtree Merging (CSM) and random access, at the cost of increased memory usage (inflation factor 3.01x–3.70x). The algorithm processes the linearized binary representation of the PSVDAG (obtained via depth-first traversal) in a single pass, progressively generating SVDAG nodes. It performs four main tasks: 1. Extract PSVDAG internal node binary representations and transform them into compact uninterrupted sequences. 2. Transform PSVDAG Child Node Masks (CHNM) into SVDAG CHNM, converting 2-bit Header Tags (HT) to 1-bit indicators [HT]. 3. Generate child node pointers for SVDAG internal nodes, replacing missing PSVDAG pointers. 4. Replace PSVDAG Labels and Callers with SVDAG pointers using a Label Transformation Table (LTT) to allow CSM. SVDAG Internal Node Layout Each SVDAG internal node is stored as a contiguous block of bytes. The layout is: CHNM: 8 bits (1-bit [HT] for each of the 8 children). Reserved: 24 bits (for 32-bit alignment of the CHNM part). PTS: Array of pointers, size 1 to 8, each 32 bits long. The total size of an SVDAG internal node in bytes is calculated as: SVDAG{nodesize} = (ACHNC + 2) \times 4 \text{ [B]} Where ACHNC is the number of active child nodes decremented by 1 (i.e., ACHNC = \text{ActiveChildren} - 1). In bits, the size is (ACHNC + 2) \times 32. Operating Memory Structure During conversion, each node is represented in memory by a 336-bit structure node: adr: 32-bit target address in the output SVDAG. achnc: 8-bit number of active child nodes. chnm: 32-bit node CHNM (stores the 8-bit mask). pts: Array of 8 pointers, 32-bit each. ptpt: 8-bit pointer count (number of pointers actually stored in pts). An array nodes holds one node structure for each level of internal nodes. Label Transformation Table (LTT) The LTT maps PSVDAG Labels and Callers to SVDAG addresses. It stores triplets [level, SIZ, VAL] mapped to the 32-bit address adr assigned to the child node. Semi-out-of-core: LTT stored in main memory (RAM). Out-of-core: LTT stored in secondary storage (disk). maxl: Number of node levels in the PSVDAG input. Range: maxl > 0. lmax: Maximum level index, defined as maxl - 1. Leaf nodes are at level maxl - 1. Internal nodes are at levels 0 to maxl - 2. nnadr: Next Node Address. Tracks the next free 32-bit aligned address in the output SVDAG stream. Initialized to 0. level: Current processing level. Initialized to 0. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. outputbuffer = [] nnadr = 0 level = 0 lmax = maxl - 1 nodes = [None] maxl LTT = {} def convertpsvdagtosvdag(inputstream, maxl): """Main entry point. inputstream: Bit stream of linearized PSVDAG.""" global nnadr, level, lmax if maxl == 1: processleafnode(inputstream) elif maxl > 1: processinternalnode(inputstream) def processleafnode(stream): """Step 2: Process a leaf node.""" global nnadr leafbits = readbits(stream, 8) writebits(outputbuffer, leafbits, 8) writebits(outputbuffer, 0, 24) # Reserved bits nnadr += 4 def processinternalnode(stream): """Step 3: Process an internal node.""" global nnadr, level, lmax level += 1 currentnode = {'adr': 0, 'achnc': 0, 'chnm': 0, 'pts': [0]8, 'ptpt': 0} nodes[level] = currentnode achncraw = readbits(stream, 3) currentnode['achnc'] = achncraw + 1 currentnode['adr'] = nnadr nnadr += (currentnode['achnc'] + 1) 4 currentnode['ptpt'] = 0 currentnode['chnm'] = 0 while currentnode['ptpt'] < currentnode['achnc']: ht = readbits(stream, 2) idx = currentnode['ptpt'] if ht == 0: # Case 0: HT '00' - Passive Child updatechmnbit(currentnode['chnm'], idx, 0) currentnode['ptpt'] += 1 # No pointer added, no recursion. elif ht == 1: # Case 1: HT '01' - Active Child / Label updatechmnbit(currentnode['chnm'], idx, 1) currentnode['pts'][idx] = nnadr currentnode['ptpt'] += 1 siz, val = readlabel(stream) # Reads variable-length [siz, val] LTT[(level, siz, val)] = nnadr if level < lmax - 2: processinternalnode(stream) elif level == lmax - 2: processleafnode(stream) elif ht == 2: # Case 2: HT '10' - Caller / Shared Child updatechmnbit(currentnode['chnm'], idx, 1) siz, val = readcaller(stream) # Reads variable-length [siz, val] adr = LTT.get((level, siz, val)) currentnode['pts'][idx] = adr currentnode['ptpt'] += 1 elif ht == 3: # Case 3: HT '11' - Active Child / Unique updatechmnbit(currentnode['chnm'], idx, 1) currentnode['pts'][idx] = nnadr currentnode['ptpt'] += 1 if level < lmax - 2: processinternalnode(stream) elif level == lmax - 2: processleafnode(stream) writeinode(currentnode) def updatechmnbit(chnm, index, value): if value: chnm |= (1 << index) else: chnm &= ~(1 << index) return chnm def readbits(stream, n): """Read n bits from stream. """ pass def writebits(buffer, value, n): """Write n bits to buffer. """ pass def readlabel(stream): """Read variable-length Label [siz, val]. """ pass def readcaller(stream): """Read variable-length Caller [siz, val]. """ pass def writeinode(node): """Write finalized internal node to output.""" writebits(outputbuffer, node['chnm'] & 0xFF, 8) writebits(outputbuffer, 0, 24) for i in range(node['achnc']): writebits(outputbuffer, node['pts'][i], 32) Intermittent vs. Uninterrupted Encoding: PSVDAG internal nodes are encoded as intermittent binary sequences (with child nodes inserted), while SVDAG nodes are uninterrupted. The algorithm must compact these sequences during extraction. HT Mapping: PSVDAG HT '00' becomes SVDAG [HT] '0'. PSVDAG HT '01', '10', '11' become SVDAG [HT] '1'. Omitted HTs in PSVDAG are inserted as [HT] '0' in SVDAG. Unique Child Pointer: For HT '11' (unique child), the address nnadr is stored in the node but not kept in operating memory after generation, as it is referenced only once. Label vs. Caller: For HT '01' (Label), nnadr is stored in both the SVDAG pointer and the LTT. For HT '10' (Caller), the address is retrieved from the LTT. ACHNC Definition: ACHNC is the number of active child nodes decremented by 1. This value determines the size of the SVDAG node. Time Complexity: The algorithm processes the PSVDAG in a single pass. Performance depends on whether the LTT is in RAM (semi-out-of-core) or disk (out-of-core). Memory Complexity: The algorithm uses a small amount of memory for the nodes array (one per level) and the LTT. The LTT size varies by scene complexity. Measured Performance: Angel Lucy (128³): SOoC 0.28s (112 KB/s), OoC 0.30s (106 KB/s). Skull (512³): SOoC 0.81s (124 KB/s), OoC 0.85s (118 KB/s). Porsche (512³): SOoC 0.44s (129 KB/s), OoC 0.47s (129 KB/s). Scaling: Higher voxelization resolutions lead to smaller inflation rates (memory increase). Strengths: Enables CSM and random access; semi-out-of-core version is faster due to higher data throughput. Limitations: SVDAG size is larger than PSVDAG (inflation 3.01x–3.70x). The PSVDAG–SVDAG Conversion Algorithm was proposed to bridge the gap between the space-efficient but hard-to-access PSVDAG structure and the rendering-friendly SVDAG structure. The algorithm allows the use of PSVDAG for storage and SVDAG for rendering, converting on the fly or as a preprocessing step. It is used in volume rendering applications where sparse voxel grids are processed. name: Voxel Attribute Decoupling
head: DAG-based attribute decoupling
body: Voxel Attribute Decoupling is a technique that separates voxel attributes (such as color or normals) from the geometric topology of a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) to enable independent, specialized compression of each component. Unlike standard SVOs or naive colored DAGs that store attributes redundantly with every node, this method achieves significant memory reduction by storing attributes in a dense array and encoding geometric offsets within child pointers, allowing subtrees with identical topology to be merged into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Inputs: An initial Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) with voxel attributes. Outputs: A DAG-based geometric structure and a dense attribute array. Data Structures: 1. DAG Nodes: Each node stores child pointers. Each child pointer contains an offset value instead of a direct index. 2. Attribute Array: A dense 1D array storing voxel attributes in depth-first order. Steps: 1. Index Assignment: Virtually assign unique indices to all nodes in the initial SVO using a depth-first traversal order. 2. Offset Calculation: For every child pointer in the SVO, calculate an offset equal to the difference between the child's index and the parent's index associated with that pointer. \text{offset} = \text{index}{\text{child}} - \text{index}{\text{parent}} 3. Storage: Store these calculated offsets together with each child pointer in the DAG structure. 4. Attribute Extraction: Extract all node attributes from the SVO and store them in a dense attribute array, maintaining the same depth-first order used for index assignment. 5. Traversal and Retrieval: During rendering or traversal, reconstruct a node's original index by summing the offsets along the path from the root to that node. Use this reconstructed index to retrieve the corresponding attribute from the dense attribute array. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overhead: The mapping introduces storage overhead in the form of an additional offset for every child pointer. Compression: While offsets add overhead, they can be compressed very efficiently using entropy-based encoding, which amortizes the additional storage cost. DAG Merging: This method allows subtrees with identical topology to be merged into a DAG because depth-first indexing automatically results in identical offsets for geometrically identical subtrees. Decoupled SVO Compression is a memory optimization technique for Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) that separates the geometric topology from voxel attributes (such as color, normals, or reflectance) to allow independent, specialized compression of each component. Unlike standard SVOs or naive colored DAGs that store attributes redundantly with every node, this method achieves significant memory reduction by compressing the sparse geometry structure and applying lossless palette-based compression to the decoupled attribute array, outperforming existing methods like PSVOs, ESVOs, and CDAGs in both memory footprint and visual quality. A technique to decouple attributes (like color) from the DAG geometry to allow independent compression, using a leaf counter to map voxel indices to attribute data without altering DAG node uniqueness. Definition: Uses a leaf counter to determine the position of a node's attributes within the dense attribute array based on the number of leaf nodes in preceding siblings. Steps: 1. For DAG resolutions larger than 1024^3, store an offset for the upper levels into a separate 32-bit counter array. 2. Use the leaf counter to calculate the attribute index by summing the leaf counts of preceding child nodes during traversal. Layout: The DAG node structure is stored in a 32-bit array consisting of an 8-bit child mask and 24-bit padding. The 24-bit padding is repurposed as the leaf counter. Parameters: Leaf counter size is 24 bits, which is sufficient for DAG resolutions up to 1024^3. Pitfalls: Using per-node counters requires reading preceding child counters for each node, resulting in extra memory reads compared to per-pointer counters. Comparison: Per-pointer counter lookups are 1.2x-1.9x faster than per-node counter lookups. However, per-node counters have negligible memory overhead (<0.1%) compared to per-pointer counters, which result in a 1.5x-1.8x larger DAG. Memory: Introduces overhead for offsets in child pointers. Per-pointer counters increase DAG size by 1.5x-1.8x, while per-node counters add <0.1% overhead. Performance: Per-pointer counter lookups are 1.2x-1.9x faster than per-node counter lookups due to reduced memory reads. Compression: Offsets can be compressed efficiently using entropy-based encoding. Attributes can be compressed using palette-based methods after decoupling. Scalability: Per-node counters require a separate 32-bit counter array for resolutions larger than 1024^3, though the overhead remains minimal. The concept of decoupling attributes from geometry in voxel structures was introduced to address the inefficiency of storing redundant attributes in standard SVOs and the limitations of naive DAG compression. The method builds on the principles of space-filling curves, such as the Morton curve, which allow for efficient mapping between 1D arrays and N-dimensional voxel grids. The specific technique of using depth-first indexing to generate identical offsets for identical subtrees enables the re-application of DAG compression to decoupled structures. name: Decoupled SVO Compression
head: Palette Compression for SVOs, SVO Compression Scheme
body: Decoupled SVO Compression is a memory optimization technique for Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) that separates the geometric topology from voxel attributes (such as color, normals, or reflectance) to allow independent, specialized compression of each component. Unlike standard SVOs or naive colored DAGs that store attributes redundantly with every node, this method achieves significant memory reduction by compressing the sparse geometry structure and applying lossless palette-based compression to the decoupled attribute array, outperforming existing methods like PSVOs, ESVOs, and CDAGs in both memory footprint and visual quality. Input: A Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) or Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) representing a voxel scene, where each leaf or internal node may possess associated attributes (e.g., RGB color, surface normals). Output: A compressed data structure consisting of a compacted geometry array and a separate, compressed attribute array, along with metadata required for traversal and index reconstruction. The topology is stored in a linearized array to minimize overhead. Each node in the geometry array contains: Child Pointers: Compressed using implicit first-child offsets and per-level byte-precise offset compression. Childmasks: Reduced from the standard 24-bit padding to 8-bit masks, indicating the presence of children. Layout: The geometry array contains nodes with fields for the compressed child pointer offset, the 8-bit childmask, and an index pointing to the attribute array if the node is a leaf or contains attributes. Attributes are decoupled from the geometry and stored in a dense array. Attribute Array: A linear array of attribute values (e.g., 24-bit colors, 32-bit normals). Indexing: Each geometry node that has an attribute stores an index into this attribute array. In the context of the parent method Voxel Attribute Decoupling, this index is often stored as a child index minus parent index offset, but the core compression here focuses on the attribute array itself. 1. Decoupling: Traverse the original SVO/DAG and separate the geometric topology (child pointers, masks) from the voxel attributes (colors, normals). Store attributes in a linear array during traversal to exploit spatial coherence. 2. Topology Compression: Apply the following compression techniques to the geometry array: Implicit First Child Offset: Store the offset to the first child implicitly rather than explicitly for every node. Per-Level Byte-Precise Offset Compression: Compress the offsets for child pointers on a per-level basis. Pointer Compression: Further compress the pointer values. 8-bit Childmasks: Replace 24-bit padding masks with 8-bit masks. Pointer Entropy Encoding: Apply entropy encoding to the compressed pointer data. 3. Attribute Compression: Compress the decoupled attribute array using a lossless palette compression scheme: Quantization: Quantize attribute values (e.g., 12-bit or 24-bit colors, 32-bit normals) to a manageable precision. Palette Construction: Identify unique attribute values within localized blocks of the attribute array. Indexing: Replace attribute values with indices pointing to a global or local palette of unique values. 4. Storage Assembly: Combine the compressed geometry array and the compressed attribute array (palette + indices) into the final data structure. Compression Rate: Calculated as the ratio of the compressed size to the original uncompressed SVO size. \text{Compression Rate} = \frac{\text{Compressed Size}}{\text{Original SVO Size}} \times 100\% Memory Footprint: The total memory is the sum of geometry size and attribute size. \text{Total Size} = \text{Geometry Size} + \text{Attribute Size} Typical Parameters: Color Precision: 12-bit colors are used for the main comparison in Table 4 and Figure 6. For attribute precision in ESVO comparison, 24-bit colors and 32-bit ONV normals are used for palette compression to ensure better quality than ESVO's lossy schemes. SVO Levels: Supports up to 17 levels (128K^3 resolution). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decoupledsvocompression(svotree): """ Compresses an SVO by decoupling geometry and attributes. Returns: compressedgeometrybytes, compressedattributesbytes """ geometrynodes = [] attributelist = [] # Step 1: Decoupling via traversal queue = [svotree.root] while queue: node = queue.pop(0) # Extract geometry components childmask = node.childmask children = node.children # Store geometry info geometrynodes.append({ 'childmask': childmask, 'children': children, 'hasattribute': node.hasattribute, 'attributevalue': node.attributevalue if node.hasattribute else None }) # Extract attribute if present if node.hasattribute: # Quantize attribute if necessary (e.g., to 12-bit or 24-bit) quantizedattr = quantize(node.attributevalue) attributelist.append(quantizedattr) # Add children to queue for traversal for child in children: if child is not None: queue.append(child) # Step 2: Topology Compression # Apply implicit offsets, per-level compression, 8-bit masks, and entropy encoding # Note: Exact entropy coding and offset packing algorithms are not specified in the sources. compressedgeometry = packtopology(geometrynodes) # Step 3: Attribute Compression # Use palette compression compressedattributes = compressattributespalette(attributelist) return compressedgeometry, compressedattributes def quantize(value, bits=12): """ Quantizes a value to a specified bit depth. """ # Implementation depends on the data type (color, normal) # Standard quantization logic return int(value (2bits - 1)) def packtopology(geometrynodes): """ Compresses the geometry nodes using specific techniques. """ # 1. Implicit first child offset # 2. Per-level byte-precise offset compression # 3. Pointer compression # 4. 8-bit childmasks # 5. Pointer entropy encoding # The sources do not specify the exact bit-packing or entropy coder implementation. # This function returns the byte stream of the compressed geometry. return b"" def compressattributespalette(attributelist): """ Compresses attributes using a lossless palette approach. """ # 1. Identify unique values (palette) # 2. Map each attribute to an index in the palette # 3. Compress the palette and the indices # The sources do not specify the exact palette construction or index encoding algorithm. palette = list(dict.fromkeys(attributelist)) indices = [palette.index(attr) for attr in attributelist] return palette, indices ESVO Compatibility: ESVO implementations require contour data to avoid cutting off attributes during traversal. Without contours, quality degrades significantly. The decoupled method avoids this by storing attributes separately and using palette compression, which does not rely on contour-based traversal cuts. Dense Data: While designed for sparse data, the method can compress dense data. For example, a dense Christmas tree dataset achieved a lossless compression rate of 38.6% compared to the original input file. When applying a simple filtering to remove scanning noise in the air, additional sparsity benefits achieve rates below 10%. Precision: Using lower precision (12-bit) for colors reduces memory further but may impact visual quality. Higher precision (24-bit colors, 32-bit normals) ensures better quality but increases attribute size. A variable-length compression scheme for the attribute array that reduces memory footprint by exploiting spatial coherence through global material arrays and local palettes. It differs from fixed-width indexing by allowing the bit-width of indices to adapt to the number of unique attributes within localized blocks, achieving higher compression ratios for scenes with large homogeneous regions. A method to compress arbitrary voxel data (colors, normals, reflectance) by decoupling geometry topology from voxel attributes. It uses a DAG to encode the topology (geometry) and a palette-based compression scheme for the extracted attributes, allowing efficient GPU storage and real-time raytracing. It outperforms Moxel DAGs by requiring less memory and supporting multi-resolution level-of-detail rendering, whereas Moxel DAGs store empty leaf counts and use two running sums that become prohibitive at quadrillion-scale resolutions. Memory Footprint: The method significantly reduces memory usage compared to standard SVOs, PSVOs, ESVOs, and CDAGs. Citadel: 0.65 bytes/voxel (22% compression rate vs standard SVO). City: 0.59 bytes/voxel (21% compression rate). San Miguel: 0.24 bytes/voxel (8.7% compression rate). Arena: 0.33 bytes/voxel (11% compression rate). (Note: ESVO failed to load this scene). Performance: The method supports real-time rendering of colored SVOs with up to 17 levels (128K^3 resolution) on GPU. It enables applications such as hard shadows, reflections (secondary rays), and color bleeding (single-bounce global illumination) with interactive rates (e.g., 8 secondary rays per pixel). Strengths: Outperforms state-of-the-art SVO compression methods in memory footprint. Lossless attribute compression ensures higher quality than lossy schemes like ESVO's DXT1 compression. Flexible attribute handling allows for various data types (colors, normals). Limitations: Requires separate compression pipelines for geometry and attributes, increasing implementation complexity. Performance on very dense datasets may vary, though it still achieves good compression rates (e.g., 38.6% for dense tree data). The method was introduced in the paper "Geometry and Attribute Compression for Voxel Scenes". It builds upon the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) representation of SVOs [KSA13] and addresses the limitations of existing compression techniques like PSVOs [SK06] and ESVOs [LK10]. The approach was developed to enable real-time rendering of large, detailed voxel scenes with full attribute data, such as colors and normals, on GPU hardware. It is used in applications requiring high-fidelity voxel rendering, including global illumination and reflection effects. name: Palette Compression
head: Block-based palette compression, Variable-length palette compression
body: Palette compression is a lossless compression scheme for the attribute array in decoupled Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) that reduces memory footprint by exploiting spatial coherence and attribute redundancy. It replaces full attribute storage with variable-length indices into local palettes, which in turn point to a global material array. Unlike fixed-width indexing, this method adapts the bit-width per block based on the number of unique attributes present, achieving higher compression ratios for homogeneous regions while maintaining fast random access via a block directory. Inputs: An uncompressed attribute array A of size \Lambda, where \Lambda equals the total voxel count in the original SVO. Outputs: An array of blocks \{B0, \dots, B{\gamma-1}\}, an array of palettes \{P0, \dots, P{\rho-1}\}, and a block directory. Data Structures: 1. Global Material Array (M): An array of size \lambda storing all unique attributes found in A. 2. Indexed Attribute Array (A^e): An array of size \Lambda where each entry mi is an index into M. 3. Block (B): A contiguous sub-segment of A^e. 4. Palette (P): An array of unique indices into M required to retrieve all attributes in a specific block. The maximum size of P is 2^\omega, where \omega is the bit-width, but it only stores the unique indices actually present in the block. 5. Block Directory: An array of entries ordered by the starting node index of each block to enable binary search. Algorithm Steps: 1. Global Indexing: Construct M containing all \lambda unique attributes from A. Replace A with A^e, where each mi \in [0, \lambda-1]. 2. Block Partitioning (Greedy Heuristic): Partition A^e into blocks using two phases. Phase 1 (Large Homogeneous Blocks): Iterate \omega from 0 to 3. Find the largest contiguous block in the current unassigned range that contains 2^\omega unique indices. If \text{MEMORY}(B, \omega) < (l - k + 1) \cdot (\omega + 1), create a palette for this block, replace the indices with local palette indices, and recursively process the remaining unassigned data on both sides of the block. If the criterion fails, increment \omega. Terminate Phase 1 when \omega \ge 4. Phase 2 (Remaining Data): For the remaining unassigned data, consider blocks starting at the current position for \omega \in \{0, \dots, 8\}. Select the block that minimizes the memory per entry metric S\omega = \text{MEMORY}(B\omega, \omega) / (k\omega - i + 1). Create a palette, replace indices, and recursively process the remainder. 3. Palette Management: Palettes are stored in a global array \{P0, \dots, P{\rho-1}\} and can be shared by multiple blocks. 4. Directory Construction: Create the block directory ordered by the starting node index to enable binary search during decoding. Memory Formula: The memory cost for a block B spanning indices mi to mj with bit-width \omega is: \text{MEMORY}(\{mi, \dots, mj\}, \omega) = (j - i + 1) \cdot \omega + 2^\omega \cdot \lceil \log2 \lambda \rceil + \text{size}(\text{directory entry}) Where: (j - i + 1) \cdot \omega: Bits for the block indices. 2^\omega \cdot \lceil \log2 \lambda \rceil: Bits for the palette entries (each entry is an index into M). \text{size}(\text{directory entry}): Overhead for the directory record. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def palettecompression(attributearrayA): # Step 1: Global Indexing uniqueattrs = sorted(set(attributearrayA)) M = uniqueattrs lambdaval = len(M) attrtoidx = {attr: i for i, attr in enumerate(M)} Ae = [attrtoidx[attr] for attr in attributearrayA] Lambda = len(Ae) DIRENTRYSIZE = 8 # Not given in the sources. blocks = [] palettes = [] palettemap = {} def memorycost(startidx, endidx, omega): numentries = endidx - startidx + 1 palettebits = (1 << omega) math.ceil(math.log2(lambdaval)) return numentries omega + palettebits + DIRENTRYSIZE def createpalette(blockindices): uniqueindices = sorted(list(set(blockindices))) key = tuple(uniqueindices) if key in palettemap: return palettemap[key] newpaletteidx = len(palettes) palettes.append(uniqueindices) palettemap[key] = newpaletteidx return newpaletteidx def findlargeblocks(start, end): if start > end: return omega = 0 while omega < 4: maxunique = 1 << omega bestblock = None bestlen = 0 i = start while i <= end: j = i currentunique = set() while j <= end and len(currentunique) < maxunique: currentunique.add(Ae[j]) j += 1 currentlen = j - i if currentlen > bestlen: bestlen = currentlen bestblock = (i, j - 1) i += 1 if bestblock is None: break bstart, bend = bestblock bindices = Ae[bstart: bend + 1] # Check memory criterion: MEMORY(B, omega) < (l - k + 1) (omega + 1) costwithpalette = memorycost(bstart, bend, omega) costwithoutpalette = (bend - bstart + 1) (omega + 1) if costwithpalette < costwithoutpalette: paletteidx = createpalette(bindices) blocks.append((bstart, bend, paletteidx, omega)) for k in range(bstart, bend + 1): val = Ae[k] localidx = palettes[paletteidx].index(val) Ae[k] = localidx findlargeblocks(start, bstart - 1) findlargeblocks(bend + 1, end) return else: omega += 1 findremainingblocks(start, end) def findremainingblocks(start, end): if start > end: return bestblock = None bestomega = -1 bestcostperentry = float('inf') for omega in range(9): maxunique = 1 << omega i = start currentunique = set() j = start while j <= end and len(currentunique) < maxunique: currentunique.add(Ae[j]) j += 1 bstart = start bend = j - 1 blen = bend - bstart + 1 if blen == 0: continue cost = memorycost(bstart, bend, omega) costperentry = cost / blen if costperentry < bestcostperentry: bestcostperentry = costperentry bestblock = (bstart, bend) bestomega = omega if bestblock: bstart, bend = bestblock bindices = Ae[bstart: bend + 1] paletteidx = createpalette(bindices) blocks.append((bstart, bend, paletteidx, bestomega)) for k in range(bstart, bend + 1): val = Ae[k] localidx = palettes[paletteidx].index(val) Ae[k] = localidx findremainingblocks(bend + 1, end) findlargeblocks(0, Lambda - 1) directory = [] for bstart, bend, pidx, omega in blocks: directory.append({'start': bstart, 'paletteid': pidx, 'omega': omega, 'length': bend - bstart + 1}) directory.sort(key=lambda x: x['start']) return blocks, palettes, directory Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Combinatorial Complexity: Finding the optimal block partitioning is a hard combinatorial problem, so a greedy heuristic is used instead. Phase 1 Infeasibility: Phase 1 becomes computationally infeasible for large \omega, so it terminates when \omega \ge 4 (16 unique indices). Precision: The memory formula assumes fixed sizes for directory entries and material indices. Variations in \lambda affect \lceil \log2 \lambda \rceil. A variant for discrete voxel data (e.g., Minecraft) that uses BlockStorage and variable-bit-length indices. It balances memory usage by using fewer bits for low-entropy regions and more for high-entropy regions, similar to GIF palettes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Allows fast random access because the block directory supports binary search, and palettes are small enough to fit in cache. Strengths: High compression ratio for scenes with spatially coherent attributes (e.g., large areas of same material). Decouples geometry from attributes. Limitations: Compression is lossless but computationally intensive during encoding. Random access requires two lookups (directory then palette). Palette compression was introduced in the context of geometry and attribute compression for voxel scenes, specifically as part of a decoupled SVO compression scheme. It leverages the observation that voxel attributes often exhibit spatial coherence and redundancy. The method was developed to address the large memory footprint of uncompressed attribute arrays in high-resolution voxel scenes.
