name: Octree Hashing for Point Location and Neighbor Finding
head: Integer coordinate hashing
body: This method performs point location and neighbor finding in an implicit octree by mapping 3D coordinates to integer indices within a fixed interval [0, 2^{d{max}}]. It locates leaf nodes and their neighbors without storing explicit parent pointers, relying instead on bitwise arithmetic and a traversal stack. It differs from Frisken and Perry [5] by omitting the distinction of "left" or "right" midplane neighbors and by precomputing bit-depth shifts to avoid expensive arbitrary left-shifts. Inputs: d{max}: The maximum depth of the octree. P{origin}: The 3D integer coordinates of the current node. P{dest}: The 3D integer coordinates of the target node. parenttrace[]: An array filled during ray traversal containing the indices of parent nodes for the current cap. Outputs: The scalar value of the leaf node at P{dest} (for point location). The coordinates or index of the neighbor node (for neighbor finding). Data Structures: Coordinate Space: Vectors are defined on the interval [0, 2^{d{max}}] and components are cast to integers. Precomputed Table: childbitdepth[d] stores the bit mask for depth d. Parent Trace: An array parenttrace[] storing parent indices, used to replace explicit parent pointers in nodes. Formulas: 1. Bit Depth Precomputation: \text{child\bit\depth}[d] = 1 \ll (d{max} - d - 1) where d is the current depth. 2. Octant Offset Calculation: The target child octant offset o \in [0, 7] is computed by masking the destination coordinates with the depth bit and shifting by constants for X, Y, and Z components: o = \left( (P{dest}.x \ \& \ \text{child\bit\depth}[d]) \gg \text{SHIFT\X} \right) + \left( (P{dest}.y \ \& \ \text{child\bit\depth}[d]) \gg \text{SHIFT\Y} \right) + \left( (P{dest}.z \ \& \ \text{child\bit\depth}[d]) \gg \text{SHIFT\Z} \right) where \text{SHIFT\X}, \text{SHIFT\Y}, and \text{SHIFT\Z} are constant shift amounts corresponding to the interleaving of X, Y, and Z components. Steps: Point Location: 1. Start at an initial node (root for full location, or a deeper node for neighbor-finding context) with current coordinates P{curr} and depth d. 2. Compute the target child octant offset o using the formula above with P{dest} and childbitdepth[d]. 3. Determine the child node index based on o. 4. If the child is a leaf, return the scalar value (either a scalar leaf in an interior node or a voxel within a cap node). 5. If the child is an interior node, update P{curr} to the child's coordinates, increment d, and repeat from step 2. Neighbor Finding: 1. Begin at the depth of the origin node's parent. Let d = d{origin} - 1. 2. Recurse up the octree to find a common parent: a. Check if the origin and destination nodes share the same parent at depth d by &-masking both P{origin} and P{dest} with childbitdepth[d] and performing integer equality. b. If they are equal, a common parent is found. Proceed to point location from this common parent to P{dest}. c. If not equal, decrement d and repeat. 3. To navigate up the tree without explicit parent pointers, use the parenttrace[] array filled during the initial ray traversal to retrieve parent indices. 4. Once the common parent is identified, use the Point Location algorithm to find the leaf at P{dest}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. SHIFTX = 0 SHIFTY = 1 SHIFTZ = 2 def precomputechildbitdepth(maxdepth): """Precompute bit masks for each depth level.""" childbitdepth = [1 << (maxdepth - d - 1) for d in range(maxdepth + 1)] return childbitdepth def getoctantoffset(destcoords, depth, childbitdepth): """Compute the 0-7 octant offset for a destination coordinate at a given depth.""" mask = childbitdepth[depth] xpart = (destcoords[0] & mask) >> SHIFTX ypart = (destcoords[1] & mask) >> SHIFTY zpart = (destcoords[2] & mask) >> SHIFTZ return xpart + ypart + zpart def pointlocation(initialnodeidx, destcoords, childbitdepth, maxdepth, nodes, initialdepth=0): """ Perform top-down search to find the leaf value at destcoords. nodes: list of dicts with keys 'children' (list of 8 indices) and 'value' (for leaves). """ currentnodeidx = initialnodeidx currentdepth = initialdepth while currentdepth < maxdepth: octant = getoctantoffset(destcoords, currentdepth, childbitdepth) childnodeidx = nodes[currentnodeidx]['children'][octant] if nodes[childnodeidx]['value'] is not None: return nodes[childnodeidx]['value'] currentnodeidx = childnodeidx currentdepth += 1 return None def findneighbor(originnodeidx, origincoords, destcoords, childbitdepth, parenttrace, nodes, maxdepth, origindepth): """Find the neighbor of originnode in the direction of destcoords.""" d = origindepth - 1 while d >= 0: mask = childbitdepth[d] originparentcoord = origincoords & mask destparentcoord = destcoords & mask if originparentcoord == destparentcoord: commonparentidx = parenttrace[d] return pointlocation(commonparentidx, destcoords, childbitdepth, maxdepth, nodes, d) d -= 1 return None Parameters: d{max}: Maximum octree depth. Typical values depend on the volume resolution and required detail. SHIFTX, SHIFTY, SHIFTZ: Constants for interleaving X, Y, Z components. Exact values depend on the bit-interleaving scheme used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on integer arithmetic, avoiding floating-point issues. Coordinates must be cast to integers within the [0, 2^{d{max}}] range. Boundaries: Neighbor finding assumes the destination is within the octree bounds. Out-of-bounds checks are not explicitly described in the source. Parent Trace: The method requires parenttrace[] to be correctly filled during ray traversal. If the trace is incomplete or incorrect, neighbor finding will fail. A sibling method that focuses on retrieving cell data once neighbor coordinates are resolved. Choose this when neighbor indices are already computed and only data fetch is required. The parent method that uses this technique for point location to find forward neighbors for cell reconstruction. Choose this when building the octree structure itself. Time Complexity: Point location is O(d{max}) as it performs a top-down search from the root (or a deeper starting node) to a leaf. Neighbor finding involves recursing up the tree to find a common parent, which is also bounded by the depth d{max}, resulting in O(d{max}) complexity. Memory Footprint: The method omits parent pointers from nodes to minimize memory footprint, relying on the parenttrace[] array instead. Performance: The precomputation of childbitdepth and use of bitwise operations (\&, \gg) are optimized for integer arithmetic, avoiding expensive arbitrary left-shifts. Strengths: Fast point location and neighbor finding without explicit parent pointers; simplified logic compared to Frisken and Perry [5]. Limitations: Requires precomputation of bit depths; requires parenttrace[] to be maintained during traversal; limited to integer coordinate spaces. This method is based on the octree hashing scheme described in "PDF Interactive Isosurface Ray Tracing of Large Octree Volumes". It adapts the approach of Frisken and Perry [5] but simplifies the neighbor-finding logic by omitting the "left"/"right" midplane distinction and removes parent pointers to reduce memory usage. name: Triadic frequency band decomposition
head: Hierarchical Data Decomposition, Hierarchical quantization scheme
body: Triadic frequency band decomposition is a volume data compression method that partitions a scalar field into disjoint 4^3 blocks and decomposes each block into a multiresolution representation of three triadic frequency bands: high-frequency differences, mid-frequency differences, and mean. It solves the problem of efficient storage and rendering of large volumetric datasets by reducing data size through vector quantization of these bands. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as Wavelet-based Volume Rendering or Laplacian Pyramid, is its specific use of a fixed 4^3 block size with a two-level hierarchical downsampling (factor of 2) to generate exactly three bands (64, 8, and 1 components), and its reliance on a specific GPU-friendly texture-based decoding architecture using dependent texture fetches. Input: A 3D scalar field V of dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Output: An RGB index texture I of size (Nx/4) \times (Ny/4) \times (Nz/4), and two codebook textures C1 and C2, and an address texture A. The method relies on four primary data structures stored in GPU textures: 1. Index Texture I: Dimensions: (Nx/4) \times (Ny/4) \times (Nz/4). Format: RGB 8-bit per channel. Layout: R: 8-bit mean value of the block. G: 8-bit index into Codebook C1 (high-frequency band). B: 8-bit index into Codebook C2 (mid-frequency band). 2. Codebook C1: Dimensions: 256 \times 64 (2D texture). Format: Floating-point per component. Layout: Indexed by s (0-255) and t (0-63). The s-coordinate comes from the G-component of I, and the t-coordinate comes from the R-component of Address Texture A. Stores 64-component codewords representing high-frequency differences. 3. Codebook C2: Dimensions: 256 \times 8 (2D texture). Format: Floating-point per component. Layout: Indexed by s (0-255) and t (0-7). The s-coordinate comes from the B-component of I, and the t-coordinate comes from the G-component of Address Texture A. Stores 8-component codewords representing mid-frequency differences. 4. Address Texture A: Dimensions: 4^3 = 64 texels (mapped as a 2D texture). Format: RGB. Layout: R: 64 distinct addresses (indices into C1's t-coordinate). G: 8 distinct addresses (indices into C2's t-coordinate). B: Unused or padding. Interpolation: Nearest-neighbor. Blocks of 2^3 adjacent texels are assigned the same address for C2 to yield the 8 necessary values. 1. Partitioning: Divide the input volume V into disjoint blocks of size 4^3 voxels. 2. First Downsampling (High-Frequency Band): Down-sample each 4^3 block by a factor of 2 by averaging disjoint sets of 2^3 voxels each to create a coarser 2^3 representation. Calculate the difference between each of the 64 original data samples and the respective down-sampled value, storing these in a 64-component vector D1. 3. Second Downsampling (Mid-Frequency Band): Apply the same down-sampling process to the 2^3 mean values to produce one single value representing the mean of the entire block. Store the 2^3 difference values (carrying information lost when going from the 2^3 mean values to the final one) in an 8-component vector D2. 4. Mean Storage: Store the single mean value of the entire block in a 1-component vector. 5. Thresholding: Apply thresholding to vectors D1 and D2: if detail coefficients are small or zero (in homogeneous or empty regions), map the vector to the zero vector to maximize codeword usage for significant non-zero vectors and increase quantization performance. 6. Vector Quantization: Quantize each frequency band separately using vector quantization, then assemble the original signal from these contributions to enhance fidelity. Quantize D1 using codebook C1 (length 256) and D2 using codebook C2 (length 256), storing the resulting indices as 8-bit values. Quantize the mean directly as an 8-bit value without a codebook lookup. 7. Packaging: Store the 8-bit mean in the R-component of I, the C1 index in the G-component, and the C2 index in the B-component. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def triadicdecomposition(volume, codebookc1, codebookc2, threshold=0.0): """ Compresses a volume using Triadic Frequency Band Decomposition. Args: volume: 3D list/array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) codebookc1: 2D list/array of shape (256, 64) codebookc2: 2D list/array of shape (256, 8) threshold: Minimum absolute value to keep a difference vector non-zero Returns: indextexture: 3D list/array of shape (Nx/4, Ny/4, Nz/4), dtype uint8, RGB """ Nx, Ny, Nz = len(volume), len(volume[0]), len(volume[0][0]) assert Nx % 4 == 0 and Ny % 4 == 0 and Nz % 4 == 0 indextexture = [[[0, 0, 0] for in range(Nz // 4)] for in range(Ny // 4)] for x in range(0, Nx, 4): for y in range(0, Ny, 4): for z in range(0, Nz, 4): # Extract 4x4x4 block block = [[[volume[x+dx][y+dy][z+dz] for dz in range(4)] for dy in range(4)] for dx in range(4)] # Step 1: High-frequency band (64 components) # Downsample by averaging disjoint 2x2x2 sets downsampled2x2x2 = [[[0.0 for in range(2)] for in range(2)] for in range(2)] for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): regionsum = 0.0 for di in range(2): for dj in range(2): for dk in range(2): regionsum += block[2i+di][2j+dj][2k+dk] downsampled2x2x2[i][j][k] = regionsum / 8.0 # Calculate differences for the 64 voxels d1 = [0.0] 64 for dx in range(4): for dy in range(4): for dz in range(4): regioni = dx // 2 regionj = dy // 2 regionk = dz // 2 diff = block[dx][dy][dz] - downsampled2x2x2[regioni][regionj][regionk] idx = dx 16 + dy 4 + dz d1[idx] = diff # Step 2: Mid-frequency band (8 components) # Downsample 2x2x2 to 1x1x1 (global mean) globalmean = 0.0 for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): globalmean += downsampled2x2x2[i][j][k] globalmean /= 8.0 # Calculate differences for the 8 downsampled values d2 = [0.0] 8 for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): idx = i 4 + j 2 + k d2[idx] = downsampled2x2x2[i][j][k] - globalmean # Step 3: Mean meanval = globalmean # Step 4: Thresholding if max(abs(v) for v in d1) < threshold: d1 = [0.0] 64 if max(abs(v) for v in d2) < threshold: d2 = [0.0] 8 # Step 5: Vector Quantization idx1 = findbestcodebookentry(d1, codebookc1) idx2 = findbestcodebookentry(d2, codebookc2) # Step 6: Quantize mean to 8-bit # Assuming input volume is normalized to [0, 255] range for 8-bit storage mean8bit = int(round(meanval)) mean8bit = max(0, min(255, mean8bit)) # Step 7: Store in Index Texture indextexture[x//4][y//4][z//4] = [mean8bit, idx1, idx2] return indextexture def findbestcodebookentry(vector, codebook): """Finds the index of the codeword minimizing Euclidean distance.""" bestidx = 0 mindist = float('inf') for i in range(len(codebook)): dist = sum((vector[k] - codebook[i][k])2 for k in range(len(vector))) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestidx = i return bestidx Block Size: 4^3 voxels. Down-sampling Factor: 2. Codebook Length: 256 entries for both C1 and C2. Index Size: 8-bit per index. Mean Size: 8-bit. Threshold: Not given in the sources. A small epsilon or a fraction of the data range is typically used. Homogeneous Regions: Thresholding maps these to zero vectors. This maximizes the usage of codewords for significant non-zero vectors and increases quantization performance. Boundary Conditions: The source assumes volume dimensions are divisible by 4 for uniform block partitioning. Handling non-divisible dimensions is not specified in the sources. Standard practice is to pad the volume to the nearest multiple of 4. Precision: The mean is stored as an 8-bit value, which may introduce quantization error for the DC component. The AC components are reconstructed from codebooks, which also have quantization error. This method is designed to be rendered directly from the compressed domain using GPU fragment shaders, avoiding full decompression. It builds on Value compression. The core quantization technique used for the difference bands. See Vector Quantization. Time Complexity: Encoding processes each voxel once in block-wise fashion, yielding O(N) time complexity. Decoding performs O(1) texture lookups and additions per voxel during rendering. Memory Complexity: The index texture occupies 3 \times (Nx/4)(Ny/4)(Nz/4) bytes. Codebooks C1 and C2 occupy 256 \times 64 and 256 \times 8 elements respectively. This yields a compressed size significantly smaller than the original Nx Ny Nz voxels. Measured Performance: The method was tested on an ATI 9700 GPU. The use of dependent texture fetches allows for efficient on-chip decoding. Strengths: High compression ratio, efficient GPU rendering, enhanced fidelity through separate quantization of bands. Limitations: Fixed block size, requires specific GPU features (dependent texture fetches), codebook training is required. The method was introduced in the paper "Compression Domain Volume Rendering". It was developed to enable real-time volume rendering of large datasets by compressing the data in a way that is compatible with GPU hardware, specifically leveraging the ATI 9700's capabilities for per-fragment arithmetic and dependent texture fetches. name: Vector Quantization
head: Cg decoding module, Codebook-based compression, Fixed-to-fixed compression, GPU-based Vector Quantization Decoding, Improved vector quantizer, LBG algorithm modification, Vector Quantization for Color Features
body: Vector Quantization (VQ) is a lossy data compression algorithm that maps a set of n-dimensional input vectors to a single fixed-length index referencing an entry in a pre-defined n-dimensional codebook. It solves the problem of high storage and bandwidth requirements for volumetric data by replacing individual voxel values with compact indices, exploiting spatial and temporal redundancy. Unlike scalar quantization, VQ operates on multi-dimensional feature vectors (e.g., color or density gradients), allowing for higher compression ratios with lower distortion for data containing many similar sub-blocks. It is distinguished from its sibling Hierarchical Vector Quantization by its flat codebook structure and from LBG Algorithm by its specific implementation variants (such as PCA-based splitting) designed to mitigate the "empty cell" problem and execution speed issues inherent in the original LBG method. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N n-dimensional source vectors S = \{(x1, \dots, xN)\}, where each vector typically represents a voxel's color features or a block of voxels. Output: A codebook C of size K = 2^r codewords, and for each source vector, a mapping index j \in [0, K-1] referencing the closest codeword. Data Structures: 1. Codebook (C): A table of K vectors, each of dimension n. In GPU implementations, the codebook and indices are stored as 3D textures. 2. Index Map: For each voxel or block, an r-bit integer index pointing to the corresponding entry in C. In sparse data scenarios, this index is stored as a 3D texture. Algorithm Steps: 1. Codebook Initialization: Select an initial set of K codewords. Common methods include random sampling from S or using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to split the data space, which avoids empty cells and speeds up convergence. The standard Linde-Buzo-Gray (LBG) algorithm uses a splitting strategy that can result in empty cells, increasing distortion and execution time. 2. Assignment (Quantization): For each source vector \vec{x}m \in S, find the codeword \vec{c}j \in C that minimizes the distortion metric \delta(\vec{x}m, \vec{c}j). The most common metric is the squared Euclidean distance: \delta(\vec{x}, \vec{y}) = \|\vec{x} - \vec{y}\|2^2 If \vec{x}m \in pj, map \vec{x}m to an r-bit index j referencing (c{xj}, c{yj}) in the codebook. 3. Codebook Update: Recalculate each codeword \vec{c}j as the centroid of all vectors in partition pj. If a partition is empty, the enhanced splitting strategy automatically avoids the issue without special treatment. 4. Convergence Check: Calculate the average distortion: D{avg} = \frac{1}{Nr} \sum{m=1}^N \| \vec{x}m - \vec{c}m \|^2 where \vec{x}m is the original vector and \vec{c}m is the corresponding approximation in codebook C. Repeat steps 2-3 until D{avg} stabilizes or a maximum iteration count is reached. 5. Decoding (GPU Implementation Specifics): To decode index j to vector \vec{c}j, the index is used as a texture coordinate to sample the codebook texture. Integer-to-Float Mapping: GPU texture coordinates are floats, but the algorithm assumes integer (x, y, z). Integer coordinates must be mapped to the float range [-1.0, 1.0] by dividing by (Dimension - 1) and subtracting 1.0. For address texture coordinates (xA, yA, zA), the transformation is: xA = (x \cdot 0.5 + 0.5) \cdot \frac{Dx}{4} yA = (y \cdot 0.5 + 0.5) \cdot \frac{Dy}{4} zA = (z \cdot 0.5 + 0.5) \cdot \frac{Dz}{4} where D{(x,y,z)} = \{2^n \mid n \ge 3\}. Simulating Floor/Modulo: Since Cg/GPU shaders lack bitwise operations, \lfloor x/4 \rfloor is simulated using GLNEAREST texture filtering, which maps integers 4, 5, 6, 7 to the same texel. Clamping: If calculated coordinates fall outside [0.0, 1.0], GLCLAMP is used to handle border issues. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vectorquantizationencode(sourcevectors, codebooksize, maxiterations, convergencethreshold=1e-6): """ Encodes source vectors into indices using a learned codebook. sourcevectors: List of n-dimensional vectors. codebooksize: K, number of codewords (2^r). maxiterations: Maximum number of LBG iterations. convergencethreshold: Minimum change in average distortion to stop. Returns: codebook (K x n matrix), indices (N list of ints). """ # 1. Initialize Codebook (random sampling from source vectors) import random codebook = [random.choice(sourcevectors) for in range(codebooksize)] indices = [] prevdistortion = float('inf') for iteration in range(maxiterations): # 2. Assignment Step newindices = [] for vec in sourcevectors: mindist = float('inf') bestidx = -1 for i, codeword in enumerate(codebook): dist = sum((v - c)2 for v, c in zip(vec, codeword)) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestidx = i newindices.append(bestidx) # 3. Update Step newcodebook = [] for i in range(codebooksize): assignedvectors = [v for v, idx in zip(sourcevectors, newindices) if idx == i] if len(assignedvectors) > 0: # Calculate centroid dim = len(sourcevectors[0]) centroid = [0.0] dim for v in assignedvectors: for d in range(dim): centroid[d] += v[d] for d in range(dim): centroid[d] /= len(assignedvectors) newcodebook.append(centroid) else: # Keep old codeword if partition is empty newcodebook.append(codebook[i]) codebook = newcodebook indices = newindices # 4. Convergence Check currentdistortion = sum(sum((v - codebook[idx])2 for v, idx in zip(sourcevectors, indices))) / len(sourcevectors) if abs(prevdistortion - currentdistortion) < convergencethreshold: break prevdistortion = currentdistortion return codebook, indices def vectorquantizationdecode(indices, codebook): """ Decodes indices back to approximate vectors. indices: List of integer indices. codebook: K x n matrix. Returns: List of decoded vectors. """ decodedvectors = [] for idx in indices: decodedvectors.append(codebook[idx]) return decodedvectors Parameters: Bit-size of index (r): Typically 8 bits, allowing 2^8 = 256 codewords. Controls the trade-off between compression ratio and distortion. Dimension (n): Depends on the feature being compressed (e.g., 3 for RGB color, 4 for RGBA). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Cells: Standard LBG can create empty partitions, increasing distortion and execution time. Mitigated by PCA-based splitting. Accumulated Error: In time-varying data, decoding difference frames (P-frames) leads to error accumulation. Mitigated by periodically sending original data as I-frames. GPU Limitations: Lack of bitwise operations in older shader languages (Cg) requires texture-based simulation for integer arithmetic. Sparse Data: For highly sparse data (>99%), VQ can be used losslessly if identical blocks are mapped to the same codeword, though this is limited to datasets with high redundancy. Compresses time-varying volumetric data by encoding frames individually while reusing codebooks from previous frames. It distinguishes itself by introducing temporal dependencies (I-frames and P-frames), reducing memory and encoding time compared to independent frame encoding. Time Complexity: Encoding is iterative, requiring O(N \cdot K \cdot n) operations per iteration for assignment and O(N \cdot n) for updates. The LBG algorithm is known to be slow for high-resolution data. PCA-based splitting improves speed. Memory Complexity: Storage is O(K \cdot n + N \cdot r), where r is the bit-depth of the index. This is significantly smaller than storing N \cdot n original vectors if K \ll N. Measured Performance: Can achieve ~100x storage reduction for Volumetric Radiance Fields (NeRF grids) with competitive rendering quality. For time-varying data, it exploits high spatial and temporal redundancy. Strengths: High compression ratio for data with similar sub-blocks; simple decoding (texture lookup); portable to GPU via texture mapping. Limitations: Lossy compression; sensitive to codebook size; original LBG is slow and prone to empty cells; accumulated error in temporal sequences requires I-frames. When to Use: Large volumetric datasets with high redundancy (spatial or temporal); real-time rendering on GPUs where decoding speed is critical. When Not to Use: Data with low redundancy; applications requiring lossless compression (unless data is highly sparse and identical). Vector Quantization was developed in the context of speech and image compression, with the Linde-Buzo-Gray (LBG) algorithm introduced in 1980, improving upon scalar quantizers by Max (1960) and Lloyd (1982). In volume rendering, it was adapted to handle large time-varying volumetric data, leveraging the high spatial and temporal redundancy of such datasets. Early implementations faced challenges with execution speed and the "empty cell" problem, leading to modifications such as PCA-based splitting. More recently, VQ has been applied to compressing Volumetric Radiance Fields (NeRFs), achieving significant storage reductions. name: Hierarchical Vector Quantization
head: HVQ Compression, HVQ rendering, Hierarchical Vector Quantization for Volume Rendering
body: Hierarchical Vector Quantization (HVQ) is a lossy compression algorithm for volumetric data that achieves around 20:1 compression ratio with minimal artifacts, specifically designed to allow GPU-based decompression and rendering. Unlike wavelet-based methods that require serial CPU decompression before transfer, HVQ encodes data into an RGB index texture, enabling parallel, on-the-fly decoding directly on the graphics chip to minimize CPU-to-GPU data transfer. Inputs: Static or time-varying volumetric scalar data sets. Outputs: Compressed file (.l3vq) containing headers, codebooks, and index textures; rendered volume images. Data Structures: Codebook A: 256 entries, each 64-dimensional (representing Difference Level 0). Codebook B: 256 entries, each 8-dimensional (representing Detail Level 0). Index Texture: RGB texture where each color component is an 8-bit index into Codebook A or B. RGB Triplets: Stored in the file header, one triplet per block (Dx'/4 \times Dy'/4 \times Dz'/4). Decomposed Block Layout (Main Memory): Top: Difference Level 0 (Array of size 64); Middle: Detail Level 0 (Array of size 8); Bottom: Detail Level 1 (Single variable, the overall mean). Parameters: Block Size (B): 4^3 (64 voxels) is the fundamental unit for decomposition. Codebook Size: 256 entries (8-bit indices). Dictionary Size (D): 4096 for Chameleon/Supernova, 2048 for Turbulence. Interpolation: Nearest neighbor only during rendering. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Resampling): If the original dimensions Dx, Dy, Dz are not powers of two, re-sample the volume to the closest power-of-two dimensions (e.g., 60 \times 120 \times 79 \to 64 \times 128 \times 128) using trilinear interpolation. Let the new dimensions be Dx', Dy', Dz'. 2. Preprocessing (Temporal Difference): For time-varying data, exploit time redundancy by subtracting consecutive time-step volumes: S{t+1}' - St', where St' is the re-sampled data at time t. 3. Hierarchical Decomposition: Divide the difference volume into 4^3 blocks. For each block, perform a multiresolution decomposition: Step 3.1 (Detail Level 0): Divide the 4^3 block into 8 disjoint 2^3 blocks. Compute the mean value of each 2^3 block to form Detail Level 0 (a down-sampled 2^3 block). Step 3.2 (Difference Level 0): Store the differences between the original 64 samples in the 4^3 block and their corresponding mean values from Detail Level 0 in an array of size 64. The mapping index for location (x, y, z) in the 4^3 block is idx = x + 4 \times y + 16 \times z, where x, y, z \in [0, 3]. Step 3.3 (Detail Level 1): Apply the mean-computation process to the Detail Level 0 block (2^3). This yields one overall mean value for the entire 4^3 block (Detail Level 1) and 8 difference values (samples in Detail Level 0 relative to its mean). Step 3.4 (Memory Optimization): Replace the values in Detail Level 0 with the 8 differences from Step 3.3 to save memory space. 4. Vector Quantization (Encoding): Perform covariance analysis at each resolution level. Execute a relaxation step to minimize residual distortions. Compute sets of representative values (codewords) at varying resolution levels. Encode each vector (the decomposed block components) using a codebook. Each vector is represented by an 8-bit index. The resulting indices form the RGB index texture. 5. File Format (.l3vq): The binary file structure is: 1. Flag (8-bit): Endianness indicator. 2. Integer size (bytes): Machine-independent integer size. 3. Mode (variable): 1 if compressed from difference of two time steps, 0 if original data. 4. Dimensions: sizeX, sizeY, sizeZ storing Dx'/4 \times Dy'/4 \times Dz'/4 respectively. 5. scaleDiff0: Largest absolute value in Difference Level 0. 6. scaleDetl0: Largest absolute value in Detail Level 0. 7. Codebook A: 256 \times 64 bytes. 8. Codebook B: 256 \times 8 bytes. 9. RGB Triplets: Dx'/4 \times Dy'/4 \times Dz'/4 triplets. 6. GPU Decoding and Rendering: Load the index texture and codebooks into GPU memory. Access the compressed data stream and decode on a per-fragment basis using the Pixel Shader API (DirectX9-level or OpenGL GL ARB fragment program extension). Use the RGB components of the index texture to look up codewords from the dependent 2D textures holding Codebook A and B. Employ the early z-test to discard fragments before they enter the fragment program, specifically discarding shader execution for fragments likely to decode empty space. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mean(arr): """Compute arithmetic mean of a list of numbers.""" return sum(arr) / len(arr) def encodeblock(block4x4x4): """ Decomposes a 4x4x4 block (64 voxels) into three levels. Returns: (difflevel0, detaillevel0diffs, detaillevel1mean) """ # Step 3.1: Create Detail Level 0 (8 values) detaillevel0 = [] for i in range(0, 4, 2): for j in range(0, 4, 2): for k in range(0, 4, 2): subblock = block4x4x4[i:i+2, j:j+2, k:k+2] detaillevel0.append(mean(subblock)) # Step 3.2: Create Difference Level 0 (64 values) difflevel0 = [] for x in range(4): for y in range(4): for z in range(4): blockidx = (x // 2) 4 + (y // 2) 2 + (z // 2) diffval = block4x4x4[x, y, z] - detaillevel0[blockidx] difflevel0.append(diffval) # Step 3.3 & 3.4: Create Detail Level 1 (1 value) and Detail Level 0 Diffs (8 values) detaillevel1mean = mean(detaillevel0) detaillevel0diffs = [v - detaillevel1mean for v in detaillevel0] return difflevel0, detaillevel0diffs, detaillevel1mean def decodeblock(diffl0, detl0diffs, detl1mean, codebooka, codebookb): """ Reconstructs a 4x4x4 block from quantized codewords and the mean. Returns: List of 64 reconstructed voxel values. """ # Reconstruct Detail Level 0 means from Level 1 mean and Level 0 diffs detaillevel0means = [detl1mean + d for d in detl0diffs] # Reconstruct original 4x4x4 block reconstructed = [] for x in range(4): for y in range(4): for z in range(4): idx = x + 4 y + 16 z blockidx = (x // 2) 4 + (y // 2) 2 + (z // 2) voxelval = detaillevel0means[blockidx] + diffl0[idx] reconstructed.append(voxelval) return reconstructed def findnearestcodeword(vector, codebook): """Find the index of the closest codeword in the codebook (Euclidean distance).""" mindist = float('inf') bestidx = 0 for i, codeword in enumerate(codebook): dist = sum((v - c) 2 for v, c in zip(vector, codeword)) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestidx = i return bestidx Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpolation: Trilinear interpolation is not natively supported because linear interpolation within codebooks is not possible. It can be approximated by decoding 8 adjacent neighbors in the shader, but this slows performance considerably. Sparsity: Highly sparse data (>99% identical blocks) allows for lossless compression, but most volumetric data is not highly sparse, limiting the applicability of lossless VQ variants. Precision: Elements in difference/detail arrays are typically 8 bits. Time Complexity: Quantization is accelerated by exploiting temporal coherence, achieving performance gains up to a factor of 3 for sequence quantization. The proposed scheme is 40 times faster than the Open Source vector quantization toolbox QccPack. Memory Complexity: The compressed data size is significantly smaller than the original. For a 256^3 dataset (16 MB), HVQ encodes it into 0.78 MB. The memory overhead during decomposition in main memory is approximately 14% larger than the original data before quantization. Measured Performance: Rendering 256^3 uncompressed dataset: 11 fps on ATI 9700. Rendering 70 MB compressed sequence (1.4 GB source): 24 fps on ATI 9700. Time-varying data: 24 fps for shock wave simulation (89 steps, 256^3) and 16 fps for vortex flow simulation (100 steps, 128^3). For sparse data sets with empty space skipping, performance is similar or better than rendering uncompressed data sets. Compression Ratios: Chameleon: 0.63 bps. Supernova: 0.17 bps. Turbulence: 0.71 bps. Visible Human: 25.29:1 ratio, 26.02 dB SNR. Engine: 20.38:1 ratio, 21.87 dB SNR. Skull: 20.84:1 ratio, 11.70 dB SNR. Strengths: Minimizes CPU-GPU data transfer; allows rendering of data sets that do not fit in texture memory; parallel GPU decompression; good fidelity at reasonable compression rates compared to region encoding. Limitations: Rendering performance drops to roughly 1/3 and 1/2 of standard 3D texture based rendering for tested data sets; restricted to nearest neighbor interpolation; quantization artifacts if compression ratio is pushed too high (e.g., 4^3 region encoding yields better ratio but significant artifacts). Hierarchical Vector Quantization was proposed by Jens Schneider and Rüdiger Westermann at the Technical University Munich. The method builds on vector quantization theory and aims to address the limitation of limited texture memory in graphics hardware by allowing direct decoding and rendering on the GPU. It is comparable to wavelet-based compression in fidelity but offers the advantage of parallel GPU decompression. name: Progressive Encoding of Time-Varying Sequences
head: I-frame and P-frame encoding for volume data, Temporal codebook reuse
body: This method compresses time-varying volumetric data by encoding frames individually while reusing codebooks from previous frames to improve compression performance and encoding speed. It distinguishes itself from static vector quantization by introducing temporal dependencies between frames, treating the sequence as a series of I-frames (independently encoded) and P-frames (predicted via codebook retraining). This approach significantly reduces memory requirements and encoding time compared to encoding each frame independently. The method applies Vector Quantization (VQ) to each time step of a volumetric sequence. It utilizes a hierarchical quantization scheme where codebooks are either generated fresh or retrained based on previous frames. Input: A sequence of T volumetric frames, where each frame is a 3D grid of data values (e.g., scalar fields). Output: For each frame, an index texture mapping grid positions to codebook indices. For I-frames, the associated local codebooks are also stored. Index Texture: A 3D texture storing quantization indices for the volume. The source notes that 16-bit mean values can be encoded in the R- and alpha-components of the index texture, using the alpha-channel to store higher-resolution data. Codebook: A set of representative vectors (centroids) used for quantization. In the described scheme, two local codebooks are produced for I-frames. The encoding process alternates between two modes: I-frame (separate encoding) and P-frame (progressive retraining). 1. Initialize: For the first frame (t=0), encode it as an I-frame. Apply the LBG (Linde-Buzo-Gray) algorithm to generate initial codebooks. Store the resulting index texture and codebooks. 2. Iterate for subsequent frames (t > 0): Decision: Determine if frame t is a key-frame (I-frame) or a predicted frame (P-frame) based on a predefined key-frame interval. If I-frame: Encode the frame separately using the LBG algorithm from scratch. Produce an index texture and 2 local codebooks. Update the "last key-frame" reference to t. If P-frame: Reuse Codebooks: Take the codebooks from the most recent key-frame as the initial codebooks for the LBG algorithm. Reuse Indices: Use the index sets from the previous frame (t-1) to obtain a first guess for the final quantization. Retrain: Perform LBG relaxation on the current frame's data using the reused codebooks and initial index guess. This allows for fast and partial searches throughout the process. Store the new index texture. 3. Termination: Repeat until all T frames are encoded. Key-frame Interval: The number of P-frames between two I-frames. In the shock wave simulation example, a key-frame was used every 10 steps (e.g., time step 65 was encoded separately, while time step 55 was the last key-frame). LBG Algorithm: The specific implementation of the Linde-Buzo-Gray algorithm is used for codebook generation and retraining. Codebook Drift: Choosing P-frame mode for all but the first frame leads to sub-optimal codebooks because the LBG algorithm depends on the choice of initial codebooks. Over time, the codebooks may drift away from the optimal representation for the current data distribution. Precision Loss: If the original data has high precision (e.g., 16-bit), quantizing it directly to low-bit indices (e.g., 8-bit) can introduce large distortions. The source notes that the original vortex data was quantized to 8 bits in advance to allow encoding the mean value into an 8-bit color component without large distortions. High-Resolution Mean Values: To handle higher precision, the alpha-channel of the index texture can be used to encode 16-bit mean values in the R- and alpha-components, significantly improving fidelity for higher-resolved data samples. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def encodetimevaryingsequence(frames, keyframeinterval): """ Encodes a sequence of volumetric frames using progressive encoding. Args: frames: List of volumetric data arrays, where frames[t] is the data at time t. keyframeinterval: Integer, the number of P-frames between I-frames. Returns: encodedsequence: List of encoded frame objects. """ encodedsequence = [] lastkeyframecodebooks = None previousindices = None lastkeyframet = -keyframeinterval # Ensures t=0 is treated as a key-frame for t in range(len(frames)): iskeyframe = (t == 0) or (t - lastkeyframet >= keyframeinterval) if iskeyframe: # I-Frame Mode: Encode separately, producing index texture and 2 local codebooks # Sources do not specify the exact LBG implementation. Standard LBG split-and-assign recursively splits centroids, assigns vectors, and updates centroids until convergence. currentcodebooks = lindebuzograysplitandassign(frames[t]) currentindices = findnearestcodebook(frames[t], currentcodebooks) encodedsequence.append({ 'type': 'I', 'indices': currentindices, 'codebooks': currentcodebooks, 'timestep': t }) lastkeyframecodebooks = currentcodebooks lastkeyframet = t previousindices = currentindices else: # P-Frame Mode: Retrain codebooks from previous frame initialcodebooks = lastkeyframecodebooks # Reuse index sets from the previous frame to obtain a first guess initialindices = previousindices # Sources do not specify the exact LBG implementation. Standard LBG relaxation performs a partial search using initialindices and updates centroids starting from initialcodebooks. currentcodebooks = lindebuzograyrelax(frames[t], initialcodebooks, initialindices) currentindices = findnearestcodebook(frames[t], currentcodebooks) encodedsequence.append({ 'type': 'P', 'indices': currentindices, 'timestep': t }) previousindices = currentindices return encodedsequence The foundational lossy compression method that maps n-dimensional vectors to codebook indices. Progressive encoding builds on this by adding temporal dependencies. Vector Quantization Memory: Significant reduction in memory requirements. For a shock wave simulation (89 time steps, 256^3 size), memory dropped from 1.4 GB to 70 MB. For a vortex flow simulation (100 time steps, 128^3 size), it dropped from 200 MB to 11.1 MB. Encoding Time: Encoding time decreased from 29 minutes to 13 minutes for an entire shock wave sequence when using progressive encoding compared to separate encoding for all steps. Quantization of the vortex data set took roughly 5 minutes using the progressive scheme. Rendering: Rendering performance was 24 fps and 16 fps for the respective simulations on the target hardware (P4 2.8 GHz, 512 MB RAM, ATI 9700). A considerable speed-up is achieved by taking advantage of the advanced rendering method that allows skipping empty space. Strengths: High compression ratios, fast encoding for P-frames due to codebook reuse and partial searches, and good visual quality when key-frames are selected appropriately. Limitations: Codebook drift can occur if too many P-frames are used between key-frames, leading to sub-optimal quantization. The method requires careful selection of key-frame intervals. The method was proposed in the context of compression domain volume rendering, specifically for hardware-accelerated texture decoding. It builds on hierarchical quantization schemes to enable efficient rendering of time-varying volumetric data. name: GPU Decoder with Texture Mapping
head: Texture-based VQ decoding
body: This method reconstructs volumetric data values on the GPU by mapping output coordinates to texture memory indices, retrieving codebook vectors via dependent texture fetches, and combining them with mean values. It differs from CPU-based decoding by minimizing data transfer between main memory and GPU memory, leveraging the GPU's texture hardware for parallel reconstruction of compressed vector-quantized data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Compressed volumetric data consisting of a 3D texture I containing RGB triplets, a 2D texture Ca for Codebook A (difference vectors), and a 2D texture Cb for Codebook B (detail vectors). Output: Reconstructed scalar volumetric value w(x, y, z) for each voxel coordinate (x, y, z). Data Structures and Layout: Texture I (RGB Triplets): A 3D texture storing the indices and mean values. The dimensions are Dx' \times Dy' \times Dz', where Dx' = Dx/4, Dy' = Dy/4, and Dz' = Dz/4. Each texel contains three components: r (8-bit index for Codebook A), g (8-bit index for Codebook B), and b (mean value). Texture Ca (Codebook A): A 2D texture storing difference vectors for 4x4x4 blocks. Dimensions are 256 \times 64. The s-coordinate corresponds to the index in I.r, and the w-coordinate (0–63) corresponds to the local position within the 4x4x4 block. Texture Cb (Codebook B): A 2D texture storing detail vectors for 2x2x2 blocks. Dimensions are 256 \times 8. The s-coordinate corresponds to the index in I.g, and the w-coordinate (0–7) corresponds to the local position within the 2x2x2 block. Coordinate Mapping: The global voxel coordinates (x, y, z) are mapped to texture coordinates as follows: 1. Block Index: The base coordinates in texture I are calculated using integer division: x' = \lfloor x/4 \rfloor, \quad y' = \lfloor y/4 \rfloor, \quad z' = \lfloor z/4 \rfloor Constraints: 0 \le x' < Dx', 0 \le y' < Dy', 0 \le z' < Dz'. 2. Local Indices: For Codebook A (4x4x4 block), the local index wa is: wa = (x \bmod 4) + 4 \cdot (y \bmod 4) + 16 \cdot (z \bmod 4) For Codebook B (2x2x2 block), the local index wb is: wb = \lfloor (x \bmod 4)/2 \rfloor + 2 \cdot \lfloor (y \bmod 4)/2 \rfloor + 4 \cdot \lfloor (z \bmod 4)/2 \rfloor The local indices wa and wb are derived from the modulo arithmetic of the voxel coordinates. Decoding Formula: The reconstructed value w(x, y, z) is computed by substituting the mappings into the general decoding equation: w(x, y, z) = I(\lfloor x/4 \rfloor, \lfloor y/4 \rfloor, \lfloor z/4 \rfloor) \cdot b + Cb(I(\lfloor x/4 \rfloor, \lfloor y/4 \rfloor, \lfloor z/4 \rfloor) \cdot g, wb) + Ca(I(\lfloor x/4 \rfloor, \lfloor y/4 \rfloor, \lfloor z/4 \rfloor) \cdot r, wa) Where: I(\dots) \cdot b is the mean value retrieved from the blue component of texture I. Ca(\dots) retrieves the difference vector from Codebook A using the red component of I as the s-coordinate and wa as the w-coordinate. Cb(\dots) retrieves the detail vector from Codebook B using the green component of I as the s-coordinate and wb as the w-coordinate. Implementation Details and Pitfalls: Texture Coordinates: GPU texture coordinates are floating-point values in the range [0.0, 1.0]. Integer voxel coordinates (x, y, z) must be normalized to this range before sampling. Arithmetic Operations: The programming language Cg (used for portability to GLSL on ATI GPUs) does not support bitwise operations (e.g., &, >>). Therefore, \lfloor x/4 \rfloor must be implemented using arithmetic division (e.g., floor(x / 4.0)) and x \bmod 4 using the modulo operator or subtraction, rather than bitwise shifts or ANDs. Precision: The indices r and g are 8-bit values, allowing for 256 entries in each codebook. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decodevoxel(x, y, z, I, Ca, Cb): # 1. Calculate block indices (floor division) # Cg does not support bitwise shift, so use float division and floor xprime = int(x / 4.0) yprime = int(y / 4.0) zprime = int(z / 4.0) # 2. Sample the RGB triplet from texture I # In a real shader, this is a texture lookup. Here we assume direct component access. rindex = I[xprime, yprime, zprime][0] gindex = I[xprime, yprime, zprime][1] meanval = I[xprime, yprime, zprime][2] # 3. Calculate local indices for Codebook A (4x4x4 block) # Cg does not support bitwise AND, so use modulo xmod4 = x % 4 ymod4 = y % 4 zmod4 = z % 4 wa = xmod4 + 4 ymod4 + 16 zmod4 # 4. Calculate local indices for Codebook B (2x2x2 block) # Using floor division on the modulo results wb = int(xmod4 / 2.0) + 2 int(ymod4 / 2.0) + 4 int(zmod4 / 2.0) # 5. Retrieve vectors from Codebook Textures # Ca is 2D texture: s = rindex, w = wa # Cb is 2D texture: s = gindex, w = wb # Note: Actual texture sampling requires normalization of s and w to [0,1] # The sources do not specify the exact normalization formula, so it is marked as a standard step. sa = rindex / 255.0 wanorm = wa / 63.0 diffa = Ca[sa, wanorm] sb = gindex / 255.0 wbnorm = wb / 7.0 diffb = Cb[sb, wbnorm] # 6. Compute final value w = meanval + diffb + diffa return w Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel, as decoding involves a constant number of texture lookups and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint is determined by the size of the compressed data: Dx' Dy' Dz' triplets for indices/means, plus 256 \times 64 entries for Codebook A and 256 \times 8 entries for Codebook B. This is significantly smaller than the original uncompressed volume. Performance: The method is optimized for real-time rendering by minimizing data transfer between main memory and GPU memory. The bottleneck is the texture fetch bandwidth and the dependent texture fetches required to resolve the codebook indices. Strengths: High compression ratio, real-time capability on GPU hardware, portability across GPU vendors (via Cg/GLSL). Limitations: Limited by the fixed codebook sizes (256 entries), which may reduce accuracy for complex data distributions. The lack of bitwise operations in older GPU shading languages (like Cg) requires less efficient arithmetic alternatives. This method was developed as part of a system for real-time rendering of compressed time-varying volume data. It addresses the bottleneck of data exchange between main memory and GPU memory by moving the decoding process to the GPU. The approach uses Vector Quantization (VQ) with two codebooks (Codebook A for difference levels and Codebook B for detail levels) and stores the compressed data in GPU texture memory. The implementation utilized the Cg programming language to ensure portability between NVIDIA and ATI GPUs, as Cg could compile to GLSL for ATI hardware, unlike CUDA which was NVIDIA-specific at the time. A system for real-time rendering of compressed time-varying volume data, https://doi.org/10.7939/r3041m, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Wavelet-based Multiresolution Rendering
head: Wavelet-based Multiresolution Isosurface Rendering
body: An interactive rendering method for isosurfaces in a voxel grid where the underlying trivariate function is represented as a spline wavelet hierarchy. It allows adaptive, view-dependent selection of level-of-detail by superimposing appropriately weighted basis functions, decreasing resolution for distant parts to improve performance with minimal visual impact. It is distinguished from its sibling Hierarchical Wavelet Transform on Omnitrees by its specific use of polynomial spline wavelets with B-spline basis functions to guarantee continuous surfaces and its implementation of a gathering-based CUDA kernel for reconstruction rather than scattering. Inputs: Volumetric dataset V of size up to 512^3 voxels. Camera position and viewing parameters. Isovalue c defining the surface f(x,y,z)=c. Interpolation degree d (e.g., d=1 for tri-linear, d=3 for tri-cubic). Chunk size k \times k \times k nodes (typically k=8). User-defined error threshold \epsilon. Outputs: Rendered isosurface image. Activated octree nodes/chunks for reconstruction. Data Structures: Octree: Nested vector spaces where nodes represent levels of the wavelet hierarchy. Chunk: A block of k \times k \times k octree nodes processed together. Wavelet Coefficients: Low-pass (scaling) and high-pass (detail) coefficients resulting from the transform. Min/Max Values: Stored at leaf nodes, estimated using the convex combination property of B-spline basis, and propagated to the root. Method Steps: 1. Wavelet Transform: Perform a 3D wavelet transform on the volume dataset using polynomial spline wavelets. The basis functions are B-splines with the least possible number of vanishing moments to minimize filter support. Due to the separability of the B-spline wavelet basis, the transformation is performed sequentially in the x-, y-, and z-directions. This reduces the computational complexity compared to a non-separable approach. 2. Octree Construction and Min/Max Propagation: Construct an octree hierarchy where each level corresponds to a resolution level in the wavelet decomposition. Calculate min/max values for leaf nodes. Propagate these min/max values towards the root using the convex combination property of the B-spline basis to enable efficient view-dependent culling. 3. View-Dependent Chunk Activation: Traverse the octree and evaluate an error metric for each chunk to determine if it needs reconstruction. A chunk is activated if: The chunk's min/max range contains the isovalue c (min/max comparison with render tree entry). The geometric error metric s/c > \epsilon is satisfied, where s is the node diameter, c is the distance from the camera, and \epsilon is the user-defined threshold. 4. Continuity Handling: If a chunk is activated, check if any wavelet support extends into neighboring chunks. If so, those neighboring chunks must also be reconstructed to maintain surface continuity and avoid cracks. Chunks that are neither activated nor needed for continuity are omitted. 5. CUDA Reconstruction: Reconstruct the volume data for activated chunks using CUDA kernels. Kernel Structure: One CUDA kernel is used for convolution along each dimension. Thread Block: Each kernel consists of blocks of k \times k threads. Thread Work: Each thread computes a 1D convolution with the wavelet filter kernels (low-pass and high-pass). Beam Processing: One block is responsible for a beam of k \times k voxels along the current convolution direction. Gathering Strategy: Instead of scattering coefficients, the method traverses the octree and gathers all contributions of wavelets intersecting the current node/chunk to avoid atomic operations and bus locking penalties. Register Optimization: At each reconstruction step, ensure all needed data resides in register space before convolution. Reuse data fetched for the reconstruction of the previous chunk. Deactivated Chunks: Skipped entirely. 6. Root Finding: Perform root finding on the reconstructed piecewise algebraic surface defined by: f(x, y, z) = \sum{0 \leq i, j, k \leq d} f{ijk} x^i y^j z^k = 0 where f{ijk} are the reconstructed coefficients and d is the surface degree along each dimension, resulting in an overall degree of 3d. Different root finding techniques are compared for precision and efficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def waveletmultiresolutionrendering(volumedata, camerapos, isovalue, epsilon, k=8, d=3): # Step 1: Wavelet Transform # Apply separable 3D wavelet transform using polynomial spline wavelets # Sequentially transform in x, y, z directions coefficients = separablewavelettransform(volumedata, d) # Step 2: Octree Construction & Min/Max Propagation # Build octree hierarchy from coefficients # Propagate min/max values from leaves to root using B-spline convex combination octree = buildoctreefromcoefficients(coefficients) propagateminmax(octree) # Step 3: Chunk Activation # Traverse octree and activate chunks based on view-dependent error metric activatedchunks = [] for chunk in octree.chunks: # Check if isovalue is within chunk's min/max range containsisovalue = chunk.minvalue <= isovalue <= chunk.maxvalue # Check geometric error metric: s/c > epsilon # s = node diameter, c = distance from camera nodediameter = chunk.spatialextent # Guard against division by zero if camera is inside the chunk distancetocamera = max(math.sqrt(sum((a-b)2 for a,b in zip(chunk.center, camerapos))), 1e-6) geometricerror = nodediameter / distancetocamera if containsisovalue and geometricerror > epsilon: activatedchunks.append(chunk) # Step 4: Continuity Handling # Add neighbors if wavelet support extends into them chunkstoreconstruct = set() for chunk in activatedchunks: chunkstoreconstruct.add(chunk) neighbors = getadjacentchunks(chunk, k) for neighbor in neighbors: if neighbor not in chunkstoreconstruct: # Check if wavelet support from activated chunk overlaps neighbor if chunk.supportoverlaps(neighbor): chunkstoreconstruct.add(neighbor) # Step 5: CUDA Reconstruction # Reconstruct data for chunks in chunkstoreconstruct reconstructeddata = {} for chunk in chunkstoreconstruct: # Skip if already processed or deactivated if chunk in reconstructeddata: continue # Gather contributions from wavelets intersecting this chunk # Ensure data is in register space data = gatherwaveletcontributions(chunk, coefficients) # Apply 1D convolution along x, y, z using CUDA kernels # Each block processes a beam of kk voxels reconstructedchunk = applychunkreconstruction(data, k) reconstructeddata[chunk] = reconstructedchunk # Step 6: Root Finding # Solve f(x,y,z) = 0 for the reconstructed piecewise algebraic surface isosurface = solvepolynomialsurface(reconstructeddata, isovalue, d) return isosurface def separablewavelettransform(volume, d): # Sequentially perform transformation in x-, y-, and z-direction # Uses polynomial spline wavelets with minimal vanishing moments data = volume.copy() for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']: data = apply1dwaveletfilter(data, axis, d) return data def buildoctreefromcoefficients(coefficients): # Construct octree hierarchy where levels form nested vector spaces # Calculate min/max values for leaf nodes octree = Octree() for leaf in octree.leaves: leaf.minvalue = min(coefficients[leaf.region]) leaf.maxvalue = max(coefficients[leaf.region]) return octree def propagateminmax(octree): # Propagate min/max values towards root using convex combination property of B-spline basis for node in octree.nodesbottomup(): if node.isleaf: continue node.minvalue = min(child.minvalue for child in node.children) node.maxvalue = max(child.maxvalue for child in node.children) def getadjacentchunks(chunk, k): # Return neighboring chunks in the k x k x k grid neighbors = [] for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue neighbors.append(chunk.getneighbor(dx, dy, dz)) return neighbors def gatherwaveletcontributions(chunk, coefficients): # Traverse octree hierarchy and gather all contributions of wavelets intersecting the chunk # Avoids scattering memory access patterns contributions = [] for wavelet in coefficients: if wavelet.supportintersects(chunk.region): contributions.append(wavelet) return contributions def applychunkreconstruction(data, k): # Apply reconstruction to one chunk after another # Deactivated chunks skipped. Ensure needed data in register space. # Reuse data fetched for previous chunk. # One CUDA kernel per dimension, blocks of k x k threads. # Each thread computes 1D convolution with wavelet filter kernels (low pass and high pass). # One block responsible for a beam of k x k voxels along current convolution direction. result = data.copy() for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']: result = apply1dconvolutionkernel(result, axis, k) return result def solvepolynomialsurface(reconstructeddata, isovalue, d): # Solve f(x, y, z) = sum{0<=i,j,k<=d} fijk x^i y^j z^k = 0 # Different root finding techniques compared for precision/efficiency surface = [] for chunk, coeffs in reconstructeddata.items(): # Extract coefficients fijk for the chunk # Apply root finding algorithm (e.g., Newton-Raphson or subdivision) surface.extend(findrootsinchunk(coeffs, isovalue, d)) return surface class Octree: def init(self): self.chunks = [] self.leaves = [] self.nodes = [] def nodesbottomup(self): return reversed(self.nodes) Parameters: Interpolation degree d: Determines the surface degree along each dimension. Common choices are d=1 (tri-linear) and d=3 (tri-cubic). Chunk size k: Set to k=8 in the source. Threshold \epsilon: User-defined threshold for the geometric error metric. Wavelet Type: Polynomial spline wavelets with minimal vanishing moments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cracks: If continuity is not maintained by reconstructing neighboring chunks where wavelet support extends, cracks may appear in the isosurface. Performance: Scattering memory access patterns (distributing coefficients into intersecting nodes) cause bus locking penalties on GPUs; the gathering approach avoids this. Granularity: Tracking activation for every single wavelet is inefficient; processing in chunks (k \times k \times k) is necessary for SIMD performance. Camera Inside Chunk: The distance c in the error metric can be zero if the camera is inside a chunk, causing division by zero; a small epsilon guard is required. Defined by Monet Morlet to avoid the fixed resolution limit of windowed Fourier transforms. It decomposes the signal into a family of functions that are translations and dilations of a unique mother wavelet \psi(x). The main drawback of the alternative windowed Fourier transform (Gabor) is that its spatial and frequency resolution is constant, which is unacceptable for signals with features of very different sizes. Time Complexity: The separable wavelet transform reduces computation to three times the 1D case. Reconstruction is performed only on activated chunks, skipping deactivated ones. Memory Complexity: Depends on the octree structure and the number of activated chunks. Measured Performance: Tested with datasets up to 512^3 voxels and viewport sizes up to 1024 \times 768 pixels, demonstrating interactive frame rates. Strengths: Adaptive view-dependent level-of-detail improves performance for distant parts with little visual impact. B-spline basis guarantees continuous surfaces, avoiding cracks. GPU implementation (CUDA) utilizes high computational performance. Limitations: Requires careful handling of continuity between chunks. The number of influence coefficients grows cubically with the support of the 1D wavelet (e.g., 175 for tri-cubic). When to Use: Interactive isosurface rendering of large volumetric datasets where view-dependent LOD is beneficial. When Not to Use: When non-isosurface rendering (e.g., direct volume rendering) is required, or when hardware does not support CUDA. Originated from work by Markus Steinberger and Markus Grabner at the Institute for Computer Graphics and Vision, Graz University of Technology, Austria. The method builds on the wavelet transformation [Chu92] which decorrelates data and allows selective removal of irrelevant data. It utilizes polynomial spline wavelets [CDF92] and GPU acceleration via CUDA. The approach is part of the broader field of wavelet-based volume rendering. name: Hierarchical Wavelet Transform on Omnitrees
head: Moment-conserving anisotropic compression, Wavelet compression on omnitrees
body: This method transforms nodal omnitree data into wavelet coefficients to enable lossless or lossy compression via pruning and tree restructuring (downsplit). It operates directly on the omnitree's anisotropic structure, allowing coarsening in specific dimensions while preserving the hierarchical spatial layout. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An omnitree where each node v has a splitting label \vec{b}(v), refined dimensions \sigma(v), and nodal coefficients (scaling values) w{c \emptyset} for its children c, ordered in Z-order. Output: A set of wavelet coefficients \vec{w}^v for all non-leaf nodes, and a root scaling coefficient w\theta^{\text{root}}. Data Structures: Omnitree Node: Contains splitting label \vec{b}(v), refined dimensions \sigma(v), and a list of child nodes. Scaling Vector \vec{s}^v: A vector of size 2^{|\sigma(v)|} containing the nodal coefficients of the children of node v, arranged in Z-order. Wavelet Vector \vec{w}^v: A vector of size 2^{|\sigma(v)|} arranged in a compatible order to \vec{s}^v. Algorithm Steps: 1. Gather Scaling Coefficients: For each node v, gather the nodal coefficients of its children into vector \vec{s}^v. 2. Local Transformation (Bottom-Up): Process nodes from leaves to root. For each node v with refined dimensions \sigma(v): Compute the local transformation matrix H{|\sigma(v)|}. Compute wavelet coefficients: \vec{w}^v = H{|\sigma(v)|} \cdot \vec{s}^v. The first element of \vec{w}^v is the scaling coefficient for the parent; the remaining elements are detail coefficients. Store the computed wavelet coefficients in the node. 3. Reconstruction (Top-Down): To reconstruct nodal values, apply the inverse transformation successively from larger to finer scales (root down to leaves). Start at the root. The root scaling coefficient w\theta^{\text{root}} holds the mean value. For each node v from root to leaves: Retrieve the wavelet coefficients \vec{w}^v. Compute the inverse transformation matrix R{|\sigma(v)|} = H{|\sigma(v)|}^{-1}. Reconstruct scaling coefficients for children: \vec{s}^v = R{|\sigma(v)|} \cdot \vec{w}^v. Distribute these values to the children's nodal coefficients. Formulas: The wavelet coefficients are computed by: \vec{w}^v = H{|\sigma(v)|} \cdot \vec{s}^v \quad (10) where H{|\sigma(v)|} is the hierarchization matrix. For Haar wavelets: H{|\sigma(v)|} = \frac{1}{2^{|\sigma(v)|}} \bigotimes{j \in \sigma(v)} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \quad (11) The function f is represented as: f = w\theta^{\text{root}} + \sum{v: \text{nonleaf}} \sum{\emptyset \neq \tau \subset \sigma(v)} w\tau^v \cdot \psi\tau^v \quad (12) where \psi\tau^v are the wavelet basis functions. The inverse transformation satisfies R{|\sigma(v)|} H{|\sigma(v)|} = I. Parameters: Wavelet Type: Haar wavelets are specified. Normalization: The matrix includes a factor of 1/2^{|\sigma(v)|}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Leaf Nodes: Leaf nodes have no children, so no transformation is applied. They store scaling coefficients directly. Root Node: The root scaling coefficient represents the mean over the entire domain (0,1)^d. Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kroneckerproduct(A, B): """Computes the Kronecker product of two matrices.""" result = [] for rowa in A: for rowb in B: newrow = [] for vala in rowa: newrow.extend([vala x for x in rowb]) result.append(newrow) return result def computewavelettransform(node): """Bottom-up transform: computes wavelet coefficients for an omnitree node.""" if node.isleaf(): return node.scalingcoefficient # Gather scaling coefficients from children in Z-order sv = [child.scalingcoefficient for child in node.children] k = len(node.refineddimensions) n = 2 k # Construct Haar transformation matrix H # H = (1/2^k) Kronecker product of 1D Hadamard matrices H = [[1.0]] for in range(k): H1d = [[1, 1], [1, -1]] H = kroneckerproduct(H, H1d) # Apply normalization factor scale = 1.0 / (2 k) H = [[val scale for val in row] for row in H] # Compute wavelet coefficients: wv = H @ sv wv = [sum(H[i][j] sv[j] for j in range(n)) for i in range(n)] node.waveletcoefficients = wv return wv[0] # Scaling coefficient for the parent def reconstructnodalvalues(node): """Top-down reconstruction: recovers nodal coefficients from wavelet coefficients.""" if node.isleaf(): return node.scalingcoefficient wv = node.waveletcoefficients k = len(node.refineddimensions) n = 2 k # Reconstruct H to compute R = H^-1 H = [[1.0]] for in range(k): H1d = [[1, 1], [1, -1]] H = kroneckerproduct(H, H1d) scale = 1.0 / (2 k) H = [[val scale for val in row] for row in H] # Inverse transformation R = H^-1. For Haar, H is symmetric and H^-1 = 2^k H scaleinv = 2 k R = [[val scaleinv for val in row] for row in H] # Reconstruct scaling coefficients: sv = R @ wv sv = [sum(R[i][j] wv[j] for j in range(n)) for i in range(n)] # Distribute to children for i, child in enumerate(node.children): child.scalingcoefficient = sv[i] return sv Represents piecewise constant functions f \in L^2([0,1]^d) hierarchically. The nodal representation stores f as a sum over leaf nodes v with b(v)=0: f = \sum s^v \phi^v, where \phi^v is 1 if x \in \text{rect}(v), 0 else. This is the specific wavelet basis used in the main method. Time Complexity: O(2^d N), linear in the number of coefficients N, using data stacks. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables lossless or lossy compression via pruning and tree restructuring (downsplit). Coarsening can be implemented as a special case of refinement. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Originated in the paper "Towards Fully Dynamic Omnitrees: Moment-Conserving Anisotropic Compression With Wavelets". It extends omnitree data structures with wavelet transforms to support dynamic compression and reconstruction. Towards Fully Dynamic Omnitrees: Moment-Conserving Anisotropic Compression With Wavelets, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2607.04881, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Area-Averaged Resampling
head: Area Weighted Average, Box Filter Resampling
body: Area-Averaged Resampling is a downsampling technique that computes the average color of an input image region mapped to a single output pixel, weighted by the area of overlap between the input pixel grid and the mapped output pixel region. It builds on Volume Resampling by explicitly calculating the geometric intersection area between the continuous output pixel footprint and the discrete input pixel grid, rather than using nearest-neighbor or uniform box filtering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A read-only rgba8 image2D with dimensions W{\text{in}} \times H{\text{in}}. Output: A write-only rgba8 image2D with dimensions W{\text{out}} \times H{\text{out}}. Parameters: Input and output dimensions. Data Structures: The method operates on floating-point coordinates for region calculation and integer indices for texture sampling. The implementation uses a Compute Shader with a local size of 8 \times 8 \times 1 (layout(localsizex = 8, localsizey = 8, localsizez = 1) in;). The input image is bound at binding point 0 and the output image is bound at binding point 1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate Ratio: Determine the scaling ratio between input and output dimensions: \text{ratio} = \text{inputSize} / \text{outputSize}. 2. Determine Input Region: For the current output pixel at coordinates \text{outputCoords} = (u, v), calculate the corresponding continuous region in the input image space: \text{inputRegionMin} = \text{outputCoords} \times \text{ratio} and \text{inputRegionMax} = (\text{outputCoords} + 1) \times \text{ratio}. 3. Iterate Intersecting Input Pixels: Determine the range of input pixel indices (x, y) that intersect the input region by looping from \lfloor \text{inputRegionMin} \rfloor to \lceil \text{inputRegionMax} \rceil. 4. Calculate Overlap Area: For each input pixel at (x, y), calculate the intersection area with the input region. The pixel covers the unit square [x, x+1] \times [y, y+1]. Compute \text{overlapMin} = \max(\text{pixelMin}, \text{inputRegionMin}), \text{overlapMax} = \min(\text{pixelMax}, \text{inputRegionMax}), \text{overlapSize} = \max(\text{overlapMax} - \text{overlapMin}, 0.0), and \text{overlapArea} = \text{overlapSize}x \cdot \text{overlapSize}y. 5. Accumulate Weighted Sum: Sample the input pixel color and add to the accumulator weighted by the overlap area: \text{areaWeightedSum} += \text{imageLoad}(\text{inputImage}, \text{ivec2}(x, y)) \times \text{overlapArea}. 6. Normalize: Divide the accumulated sum by the total area of the input region to get the average. Compute \text{totalArea} = \text{inputRegionSize}x \cdot \text{inputRegionSize}y where \text{inputRegionSize} = \text{inputRegionMax} - \text{inputRegionMin}, then \text{areaWeightedAvg} = \text{areaWeightedSum} / \text{totalArea}. 7. Store Result: Write the result to the output image: \text{imageStore}(\text{outputImage}, \text{outputCoords}, \text{areaWeightedAvg}). Pseudocode: Unverified code.
