name: Octree-based Level of Detail and Culling
head: CPU Culling, LoD, CPU Frustum Culling, CPU-based Octree LOD & Frustum Culling, Distance-based LoD
body: This method reduces the rendering load of large point clouds by traversing a pre-built octree on the CPU to perform frustum culling and view-dependent sampling before uploading data to the GPU. It sets itself apart from GPU-based culling techniques by aggregating point data into cached averages at internal octree nodes, allowing the CPU to decide exactly which subset of points to render based on distance thresholds. Input: An octree structure built from a point cloud, where each node contains a bounding volume and a cached average point representing all points in its subtree. The current Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix and camera eye position. Output: A list of aggregated points (positions and colors) suitable for upload to a Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) for rendering as GLPOINTS. Octree Node: Contains a bitmask activeOctants indicating which of the 8 children exist, a bounding region region (with center() and testAgainstFrustum() methods), and a cached averagepoint (position and color). PointModel: A structure containing position and color data, used to define the layout for the VBO. maxDepth: Maximum recursion depth for the LOD traversal, typically 15. worldsize: The diagonal length of the point cloud's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB), calculated as glm::length(pc.aabb.max() - pc.aabb.min()). cpuCulling: Boolean flag to enable/disable CPU-side aggregation and frustum culling. Default: false. cpuCullingEveryFrame: Boolean flag to recompute culling every frame. Default: false. 1. Preparation (Load Time): Compute worldsize from the point cloud's AABB diagonal. Build the octree. For each node, compute and cache the average position and color of all points in its subtree. 2. Traversal (Per Frame): If cpuCulling is disabled, skip this method. Start recursive traversal at the root node at depth 15 with the current MVP matrix and eye position. For each node, iterate through its 8 potential children (index i from 0 to 7): Check if the child is active: if (!(node->activeOctants & (1 << i))) continue;. Perform frustum culling: if (!node->children[i]->region.testAgainstFrustum(mvp)) continue;. Calculate distance from the child's center to the eye: dist = glm::length(node->children[i]->region.center() - eye). Determine the target emission depth for this child based on distance thresholds relative to worldsize: If dist > worldsize / 2: set target depth to 9. If worldsize / 4 < dist < worldsize / 2: set target depth to 10. Otherwise (dist <= worldsize / 4): set target depth to 15. Recurse into the child with the new target depth. Base Case (Emission): If the current traversal depth matches the target depth for the current node, emit the node's cached averagepoint to the output list and stop recursing into this branch. 3. Rendering: Upload the emitted aggregated points to a VBO using the byte size of PointModel. If the point list is empty (due to aggressive culling), return early from the draw call to prevent drawing invalid buffers. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def norm(v): """Compute Euclidean length of a 3D vector.""" return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 def traverseoctree(node, currentdepth, targetdepth, mvp, eye, worldsize, outputpoints): """ Recursively traverse the octree to cull and sample points. Args: node: The current octree node. currentdepth: The current absolute depth in the octree (starts at 15). targetdepth: The absolute depth at which to emit points for this subtree. mvp: The Model-View-Projection matrix. eye: The camera eye position. worldsize: The diagonal length of the point cloud AABB. outputpoints: List to append aggregated points to. """ # Base case: If we have reached the target depth for this branch, emit the cached average point. if currentdepth == targetdepth: outputpoints.append(node.averagepoint) return # Guard against over-traversal if target depth is shallower than current if currentdepth < targetdepth: return # Iterate through all 8 possible children for i in range(8): # Check if this child exists using the bitmask if not (node.activeoctants & (1 << i)): continue child = node.children[i] # Frustum culling: Skip if the child's bounding region is outside the view frustum if not child.region.testagainstfrustum(mvp): continue # Calculate distance from child center to eye dist = norm(child.region.center() - eye) # Determine the new target depth for the child based on distance thresholds if dist > worldsize / 2: newtargetdepth = 9 elif worldsize / 4 < dist < worldsize / 2: newtargetdepth = 10 else: newtargetdepth = 15 # Recurse with the new target depth, decrementing current depth by 1 traverseoctree(child, currentdepth - 1, newtargetdepth, mvp, eye, worldsize, outputpoints) def renderpointcloudoctreelod(scene, mvp, eye): """ Main entry point for octree-based LOD and culling. """ if not scene.renderingparams.cpuculling: return [] worldsize = norm(scene.pc.aabb.max - scene.pc.aabb.min) outputpoints = [] # Start traversal at max depth (15) traverseoctree(scene.octree.root, 15, 15, mvp, eye, worldsize, outputpoints) # Edge case: Empty list after culling if not outputpoints: return [] # Upload to VBO using sizeof(PointModel) stride stride = 24 # sizeof(PointModel) as defined in the source vbo = allocatevbo(outputpoints, stride) gldrawpoints(vbo) return outputpoints def allocatevbo(points, stride): """Allocate GPU memory and upload point data.""" buffer = creategpubuffer(size=len(points) stride) uploaddata(buffer, points, stride) return buffer def gldrawpoints(vbo): """Issue a draw call for the uploaded point data.""" bindvbo(vbo) drawarray(mode=GLPOINTS, count=len(vbo.data)) Empty Output: If all nodes are culled by the frustum or distance thresholds, the output list may be empty. The draw function must check for this and return early to avoid rendering invalid buffers. Precision: Distance calculations and frustum tests should use sufficient precision to avoid jittering or incorrect culling, especially near threshold boundaries. What it is: The process of testing octree node bounding volumes against the camera's view frustum to skip subtrees that are not visible. Differentiation: Unlike GPU culling, this happens on the CPU before data transfer, reducing bandwidth usage. When to choose: When bandwidth to the GPU is a bottleneck or when the scene has large empty regions. Link: CPU Frustum Culling What it is: A technique to select the level of detail (depth) of the octree traversal based on the distance of the node from the camera. Differentiation: Uses fixed distance thresholds relative to the world size to determine sampling density, rather than screen-space error metrics. When to choose: When a simple, predictable reduction in point count is sufficient and screen-space error is not critical. Link: Distance-based LOD Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not: Not given in the sources. This method is described in the context of a point cloud rendering engine using OpenGL and ImGui. It is part of a pipeline that includes voxelization and octree construction for point clouds. The specific implementation details, including the depth thresholds (9, 10, 15) and the use of cached averages, are derived from the arminkz/PointCloudRendering repository. arminkz/PointCloudRendering, https://github.com/arminkz/PointCloudRendering, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Octree Data Structure
head: CGAL::Octree, CGAL::Orthtree, RFVoxelOctree, RFVoxelOctreeNode, Voxel Octree Data Structure
body: The octree partitions 3D space into a hierarchical grid of voxels to organize point cloud data for volume rendering and surface extraction. It recursively subdivides space into eight octants, distinguishing it from flat voxel grids. Inputs: A set of 3D points (point cloud) and a bounding volume defining the spatial extent. Outputs: A tree structure where internal nodes represent partially filled space, leaf nodes represent occupied voxels, and empty leaf nodes retain a surface distance metric. Two primary implementations are cited: the RFVoxelOctree and CGAL::Orthtree. RFVoxelOctreeNode Layout: mpkChildren[8]: Array of 8 pointers to child nodes. mkBuildAabb: Axis-aligned bounding box in build space. mkWorldAabb: Axis-aligned bounding box in world space. meNodeType: Enum indicating state: NTINTERNAL, NTEMPTYLEAF, or NTLEAF. mfDistanceToSurface: Double-precision distance to the nearest surface (for empty leaves). RFVoxelOctree Layout: mpkRoot: Pointer to the root node. mkDataDimension: 3D integer vector defining the grid dimensions. mkOctreeOrigin: 3D double vector for the octree origin. mfVoxelSize: Physical size of a single voxel unit (default 1.0f). muiOctreeDim: Total dimension of the cubic voxel grid. Depth is derived as \log2(m\uiOctreeDim). muiOctreeDepth: Calculated depth. muiNumberOfNodes, muiNumberOfLeafs, muiNumberOfEmptyLeafs, muiNumberOfInternalNodes: Counters for statistics. CGAL::Orthtree Definition: Defined as CGAL::Orthtree< Orthtreetraitspoint< GeomTraits, PointRange, PointMap, cubicnodes, 3 > >. This template specialization uses cubic nodes in 3 dimensions. 1. Initialization: Define the bounding box and point range. Set mfVoxelSize (default 1.0f) and muiOctreeDim. 2. Construction: Recursively subdivide the bounding volume into 8 octants. CGAL supports specific refinement splitters, such as Refineoneeighth or Refinearoundisovalue, to control refinement density around the isosurface. 3. Leaf Classification: Leaf nodes represent occupied voxels. Empty leaf nodes represent empty space but retain mfDistanceToSurface for potential surface extraction. 4. Traversal: Supports iteration over leaf nodes via CGAL::Orthtrees::Leavestraversal. 5. Output: Nodes can be dumped to polylines via octree.dumptopolylines(oo) or used for Marching Cubes (MC), Topologically Correct Marching Cubes (TMC), or Dual Contouring (DC). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from math import log2 from enum import Enum class NodeType(Enum): NTINTERNAL = 0 NTEMPTYLEAF = 1 NTLEAF = 2 class RFAABB3i: def init(self, minval, maxval): self.min = minval self.max = maxval class RFAABB3d: def init(self, minval, maxval): self.min = minval self.max = maxval class RFVector3i: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z class RFVector3d: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z class RFVoxelOctreeNode: def init(self): self.mpkChildren = [None] 8 self.mkBuildAabb = RFAABB3i((0, 0, 0), (1, 1, 1)) self.mkWorldAabb = RFAABB3d((0.0, 0.0, 0.0), (1.0, 1.0, 1.0)) self.meNodeType = NodeType.NTINTERNAL self.mfDistanceToSurface = 0.0 class RFVoxelOctree: def init(self, origin, voxelsize, dim): self.mpkRoot = RFVoxelOctreeNode() self.mkDataDimension = RFVector3i(dim, dim, dim) self.mkOctreeOrigin = RFVector3d(origin) self.mfVoxelSize = voxelsize self.muiOctreeDim = dim self.muiOctreeDepth = int(log2(dim)) self.muiNumberOfNodes = 1 self.muiNumberOfLeafs = 0 self.muiNumberOfEmptyLeafs = 0 self.muiNumberOfInternalNodes = 0 def insertpoint(self, point): # Not given in the sources. pass mfVoxelSize: Physical size of a voxel. Default: 1.0f. muiOctreeDim: Total dimension of the voxel grid. Depth = \log2(m\uiOctreeDim). isovalue: Threshold for isosurfacing (e.g., 0.3 in CGAL examples). Cracks: If nodes are split with uniform size around the surface but varying depths exist around the isosurface, cracks (boundaries) will appear in the resulting mesh. Refinement Strategy: Dense refinement around the isosurface ensures a manifold surface, whereas arbitrary refinement can lead to non-manifold surfaces. Precision: CGAL examples use oo.precision(17) for output polylines. The parent method describing the hierarchical subdivision process. A sibling method using the octree for rendering optimization rather than spatial indexing for surface extraction. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Integrates with CGAL isosurfacing algorithms (MC, TMC, DC). Limitations: Varying depths can cause mesh cracks if not handled by adaptive refinement strategies. When to use: When organizing point clouds for surface extraction or spatial queries requiring hierarchical access. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The CGAL::Orthtree implementation originated from the 2022 Google Summer of Code, contributed by Julian Stahl, mentored by Daniel Zint and Pierre Alliez. It provides first implementations of Marching Cubes, Topologically Correct Marching Cubes, and Dual Contouring using octrees. itsyouyi/Voxelizer, https://github.com/itsyouyi/Voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) 3D Isosurfacing, https://doc.cgal.org/latest/Isosurfacing3/index.html, fetched 2026-10-29

name: VoxelGrid from Mesh (Ray Method)
head: CUDA Mesh Voxelizer, Mesh to Particle Cloud Conversion, Raycasting-based Voxelization, X-ray Voxelization
body: This method converts a 3D triangle mesh into a discrete voxel grid by casting rays from voxel centers to determine occupancy. It distinguishes itself from rasterization-based siblings by relying on geometric intersection tests rather than screen-space projection, allowing it to robustly handle arbitrary mesh orientations and generate solid volumes or signed distance fields (SDFs). It solves the problem of converting continuous surface representations into discrete volumetric data suitable for volume rendering or 3D printing. Inputs: A triangle mesh (OBJ or STL format) and a resolution parameter (voxel spacing or grid dimension). Outputs: A voxel grid (binary occupancy, SDF values, or particle cloud) in formats such as OBJ, BINVOX, PLY, or custom binary. Data Structures: Mesh: List of triangles, each defined by three 3D vertices (V1, V2, V3). Voxel Grid: 3D array indexed by (i, j, k). Ray: Defined by origin O and direction D. Intersection Data: List of hit coordinates or distances. Parameters: resolution: Voxel grid spacing (e.g., 0.5 units). Must be finite and > 10^{-6}. samples: Number of random ray directions per voxel for open meshes. Default -1 implies 1 sample/direction. doublethick: Boolean flag. If true, handles double-sided geometry by checking (intersections / 2) % 2 == 1. narrowband: Optional distance threshold. Expands evaluation bounds and filters voxels where |SDF| \le band. surfaceonly: Boolean. If true, retains only voxels intersecting the surface, ignoring interior filling. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Load mesh vertices and indices. Validate that position and index array lengths are multiples of 3. Compute the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of the mesh: bb{min}, bb{max}. Apply optional transforms: scale, center, translate, rotate, or crop. If narrowband is provided, expand bounds: bb{min} -= band, bb{max} += band. Calculate grid dimensions: Nx = \lceil (bb{max}.x - bb{min}.x) / resolution \rceil, similarly for y, z. Calculate spacing if using fixed dimension dim: spacing = \max(bb{max} - bb{min}) / (dim - 2). 2. Voxel Center Calculation: For each voxel index (i, j, k), compute the center coordinate: x = bb{min}.x + (i + 0.5) \times resolution y = bb{min}.y + (j + 0.5) \times resolution z = bb{min}.z + (k + 0.5) \times resolution Ensure coordinates are within the expanded bounds if narrowband is active. 3. Ray Casting and Intersection: Single Ray (Closed Mesh): Cast a ray from the voxel center along a fixed axis (typically +X). Origin: O = (bb{min}.x - 1.0, y, z). Direction: D = (1, 0, 0). Max Distance: max\dist = (bb{max}.x - O.x) + 1.0. Multiple Rays (Open/Incomplete Mesh): If samples > 1, generate random directions on a unit sphere for each sample. Generate uniform random \theta \in [0, 2\pi) and z \in [-1, 1]. Compute direction components: Dx = \sqrt{1 - z^2} \cos(\theta) Dy = \sqrt{1 - z^2} \sin(\theta) Dz = \sqrt{1 - z^2} \cos(\theta) Note: Some implementations use \cos(\theta) for both x and z components. Intersection Test: For each ray, iterate over all mesh triangles and perform the Möller–Trumbore intersection test. Let triangle edges be E1 = V2 - V1, E2 = V3 - V1. Compute determinant: det = \text{dot}(E1, \text{cross}(D, E2)). If |det| < \epsilon, no intersection. Compute inverse: inv\det = 1 / det. Compute barycentric coordinates: u = \text{dot}(O - V1, \text{cross}(D, E2)) \times inv\det v = \text{dot}(D, \text{cross}(O - V1, E1)) \times inv\det t = \text{dot}(E2, \text{cross}(O - V1, E1)) \times inv\det Intersection if 0 \le u \le 1, 0 \le v \le 1, u + v \le 1, and t > \epsilon. Precision Handling: Collect all intersection distances t (or hit coordinates). Sort intersections to correct floating-point ordering errors. Advance ray origin by a small epsilon (e.g., 10^{-4}) after each hit to prevent re-hitting the same face. Limit hits to a maximum count (e.g., 100,000) to prevent infinite loops on degenerate geometry. 4. Occupancy Determination: Parity Rule: Count the number of intersections N{int} to the right of the voxel center (or along the ray). If doublethick is false: is\inside = (N{int} \pmod 2) \neq 0. If doublethick is true: is\inside = ((N{int} / 2) \pmod 2) \neq 0. Voting (Multiple Samples): If samples > 1, vote on the majority result of all sampled rays. If the majority indicates "inside", mark as inside. 5. SDF and Filtering (Optional): Compute the distance from the voxel center to the mesh surface: d = \text{mesh.distance}(center). Assign SDF value: SDF = -d if inside, SDF = d if outside. Apply narrowband filter: Keep voxel only if |SDF| \le band. Apply surfaceonly filter: Keep voxel only if it intersects the surface (often determined by proximity or direct intersection). 6. Output Generation: Save the resulting voxel data to the specified format (OBJ, BINVOX, PLY, etc.). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def voxelizemesh(meshvertices, meshindices, resolution, samples=1, doublethick=False, narrowband=None, surfaceonly=False): # 1. Preprocessing bbmin = [min(v[i] for v in meshvertices) for i in range(3)] bbmax = [max(v[i] for v in meshvertices) for i in range(3)] if narrowband is not None: bbmin = [bbmin[i] - narrowband for i in range(3)] bbmax = [bbmax[i] + narrowband for i in range(3)] dimx = math.ceil((bbmax[0] - bbmin[0]) / resolution) dimy = math.ceil((bbmax[1] - bbmin[1]) / resolution) dimz = math.ceil((bbmax[2] - bbmin[2]) / resolution) grid = {} for j in range(dimy): for k in range(dimz): cy = bbmin[1] + (j + 0.5) resolution cz = bbmin[2] + (k + 0.5) resolution for i in range(dimx): cx = bbmin[0] + (i + 0.5) resolution insidevotes = 0 totalsamples = samples if samples > 1 else 1 for s in range(totalsamples): if totalsamples == 1: rayorigin = [bbmin[0] - 1.0, cy, cz] raydir = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] else: theta = random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) z = random.uniform(-1, 1) rxy = math.sqrt(1 - zz) raydir = [rxy math.cos(theta), rxy math.sin(theta), rxy math.cos(theta)] rayorigin = [cx, cy, cz] intersections = [] currentorigin = rayorigin[:] maxdist = (bbmax[0] - currentorigin[0]) + 1.0 for in range(100000): hitt = float('inf') hitfound = False for triidx in range(0, len(meshindices), 3): v1 = meshvertices[meshindices[triidx]] v2 = meshvertices[meshindices[triidx+1]] v3 = meshvertices[meshindices[triidx+2]] e1 = [v2[0]-v1[0], v2[1]-v1[1], v2[2]-v1[2]] e2 = [v3[0]-v1[0], v3[1]-v1[1], v3[2]-v1[2]] p = cross(raydir, e2) det = dot(e1, p) if abs(det) < 1e-6: continue invdet = 1.0 / det T = [currentorigin[0]-v1[0], currentorigin[1]-v1[1], currentorigin[2]-v1[2]] u = dot(T, cross(raydir, e2)) invdet v = dot(raydir, cross(T, e1)) invdet t = dot(e2, cross(T, e1)) invdet if 0 <= u <= 1 and 0 <= v <= 1 and u + v <= 1 and t > 1e-6 and t < maxdist: if t < hitt: hitt = t hitfound = True if not hitfound: break intersections.append(hitt) currentorigin = [rayorigin[0] + raydir[0](hitt + 1e-4), rayorigin[1] + raydir[1](hitt + 1e-4), rayorigin[2] + raydir[2](hitt + 1e-4)] maxdist -= (hitt + 1e-4) if maxdist <= 0: break intersections.sort() nintersections = len(intersections) if doublethick: isinside = (nintersections // 2) % 2 != 0 else: isinside = nintersections % 2 != 0 if isinside: insidevotes += 1 if totalsamples > 1: isinside = insidevotes > totalsamples / 2 if surfaceonly: dist = pointtomeshdistance(meshvertices, meshindices, [cx, cy, cz]) if dist > resolution 0.5: continue grid[(i, j, k)] = 1.0 else: dist = pointtomeshdistance(meshvertices, meshindices, [cx, cy, cz]) sdfval = -dist if isinside else dist if narrowband is not None: if abs(sdfval) <= narrowband: grid[(i, j, k)] = sdfval else: grid[(i, j, k)] = 0.0 else: grid[(i, j, k)] = 1.0 if isinside else 0.0 return grid def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]] def pointtomeshdistance(vertices, indices, point): mindist = float('inf') for triidx in range(0, len(indices), 3): v1 = vertices[indices[triidx]] v2 = vertices[indices[triidx+1]] v3 = vertices[indices[triidx+2]] e1 = [v2[0]-v1[0], v2[1]-v1[1], v2[2]-v1[2]] e2 = [v3[0]-v1[0], v3[1]-v1[1], v3[2]-v1[2]] p = [point[0]-v1[0], point[1]-v1[1], point[2]-v1[2]] a = dot(e1, e1); b = dot(e1, e2); c = dot(e2, e2) d = dot(e1, p); e = dot(e2, p) denom = ac - bb u = (bc - eb) / denom if denom != 0 else 0.0 v = (ae - db) / denom if denom != 0 else 0.0 u = max(0.0, min(1.0, u)) v = max(0.0, min(1.0, v)) closest = [v1[0] + ue1[0] + ve2[0], v1[1] + ue1[1] + ve2[1], v1[2] + ue1[2] + ve2[2]] distsq = (point[0]-closest[0])2 + (point[1]-closest[1])2 + (point[2]-closest[2])2 if distsq < mindist: mindist = distsq return math.sqrt(mindist) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Double-thick meshes: Standard parity fails for double-sided surfaces. Use (intersections / 2) % 2 logic. Open meshes: Single-ray parity is unreliable. Use multiple random samples and voting. Precision errors: Ray re-hitting the same face causes infinite loops or incorrect counts. Advance origin by 10^{-4}. Sort intersection points to handle precision-induced ordering errors. Malformed input: OBJ/STL files with non-multiple-of-3 vertex/index arrays must be rejected or handled with explicit checks. Memory: High resolutions (e.g., 256^3) can generate multi-gigabyte files. Use binary formats (BINVOX) instead of ASCII OBJ for large grids. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(Nv) for the output grid. Input mesh storage is O(Nt). Performance: GPU acceleration (CUDA) provides significant speedups (400x–2750x) over CPU. Example: Teapot (2464 triangles) at 512^3 resolution with 3 samples took 15.64 seconds on an NVIDIA GTX 970. Example: Bunny (69664 triangles) at 512^3 took 417.62 seconds. Strengths: Robust for closed meshes; generates solid volumes; supports SDF output; parallelizable. Limitations: Slow for high resolutions and complex meshes without acceleration structures; sensitive to floating-point precision; large file sizes for ASCII output. When to use: When solid voxelization or SDF generation is required from a mesh, and performance is not the primary constraint or GPU acceleration is available. When not to use: For real-time applications with very high-resolution grids without GPU support; for open meshes without sufficient sampling. The method originates from computational fabrication and voxelization research. The CUDA implementation was developed for MIT's 6.807 Computational Fabrication course, leveraging the Möller–Trumbore intersection algorithm for GPU acceleration. The Rust implementation (voxelizer-rs) extends this with multi-threading (Rayon), SDF support, and various export formats, addressing robustness issues like precision errors and open mesh handling. It is used in 3D printing pipelines, volume rendering preprocessing, and geometric modeling. differentiablevolumetricrendering, https://github.com/autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) voxelizer, https://github.com/kctess5/voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) voxelizer-rs, https://github.com/lhemerly/voxelizer-rs, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

body: 3D Grid Rasterization converts a triangular mesh into a discrete 3D occupancy grid (voxel array) by mapping mesh geometry to a fixed-resolution integer lattice. It solves the problem of representing continuous surface geometry as a volume suitable for ray marching or other volume rendering techniques. Builds on Voxelization. The method typically follows one of two primary implementations: a Triangle-AABB Sampling approach (common in C++ libraries like voxelizer) or a Slice-and-Rasterize approach (common in Python libraries like meshvox). Both produce a 3D grid where each cell indicates occupancy and optionally color. Inputs: A triangular mesh defined by vertices V and indices I. Target grid dimensions: width W, height H, depth D (or a single resolution R for the largest dimension). Optional: Vertex colors (RGB or RGBA). Optional: STL file path (for direct reading). Outputs: A 3D array voxels of shape (D, W, H) or (Z, X, Y). Data type: Boolean (occupancy) or 32-bit integer (packed ABGR color). 1. AABB (Axis-Aligned Bounding Box) Used to cull triangles. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class AABB: min: Vector3 # Minimum coordinates (x, y, z) max: Vector3 # Maximum coordinates (x, y, z) 2. Triangle Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Triangle: p1: Vector3 p2: Vector3 p3: Vector3 color: Optional[Vector4] # RGBA, if present 3. Voxel Grid (C++ Style) Flat array of unsigned integers (ABGR packed). Layout: index = x + y W + z (W H). Size: W \times H \times D. 4. Voxel Grid (Python Style) Boolean array. Shape: (Z, X, Y). Addressed as voxels[z][x][y]. 5. STL Binary Record (for input parsing) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. stlrecorddtype = [ ('normals', np.float32, (3,)), ('Vertex1', np.float32, (3,)), ('Vertex2', np.float32, (3,)), ('Vertex3', np.float32, (3,)), ('atttr', np.int16, (1,)) ] This method slices the mesh at each height z, computes 2D intersection lines, and rasterizes them into a 2D grid. Steps: 1. Read Mesh: Load STL file (binary or ASCII). 2. Scale and Shift: Find min/max coordinates of all vertices. Compute xyscale = (resolution - 1) / max(width, depth). shift = -min. scale = [xyscale, xyscale, xyscale]. Transform vertices: v' = (v + shift) \times scale. Filter degenerate triangles (fewer than 3 unique points after transformation). 3. Initialize Voxel Array: Boolean array voxels of shape (boundingbox[2], boundingbox[0], boundingbox[1]). 4. Iterate Height z: a. Find Intersecting Triangles: Filter triangles that cross the plane z. A triangle crosses if: It has vertices both above (zv > z) and below (zv < z). OR it has 2 or 3 vertices exactly on the plane (zv == z). Exclude triangles lying entirely on the plane. b. Compute Intersection Lines: For each valid triangle, compute the intersection line segment with the plane z. Cases: 2 vertices on plane: Return those 2 vertices. 1 vertex on plane: Compute intersection point on the edge between the above/below vertex and the on-plane vertex. Return (intersection, on-plane vertex). 0 vertices on plane: Compute intersection points on the two edges crossing the plane. Return those 2 points. Intersection point calculation: Ensure p1.z < p2.z. If p1.z == p2.z, distance = 0. Else, t = \frac{z - p1.z}{p2.z - p1.z}. point = p1 + t \times (p2 - p1). c. Rasterize Lines to 2D Grid: Initialize prepixel grid of size (boundingbox[0], boundingbox[1]) to False. For each x column: Find relevant lines crossing this x. A line is relevant if it spans across x (vertices on both sides) or one vertex is on x and another is above. Compute target y coordinates for each line at this x: If vertical (x0 == x1), return -1 (skip). Else, ratio = \frac{x - x0}{x1 - x0}. y{new} = y0 + ratio \times (y1 - y0). For each y row: If isBlack is True, set prepixel[x][y] = True. If y matches a target y coordinate AND the point lies on the line segment (checked by integer comparison and range checks), toggle isBlack and set prepixel[x][y] = True. Assign prepixel to voxels[z]. 5. Padding (Optional): If padding is enabled, expand dimensions by 2 in each axis and shift data by 1. Pseudocode (Slice-and-Rasterize): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def voxelizesliceandrasterize(meshtriangles, resolution): # 1. Scale and Shift allpoints = [pt for tri in meshtriangles for pt in tri] mins = np.min(allpoints, axis=0) maxs = np.max(allpoints, axis=0) maxdim = max(maxs[0] - mins[0], maxs[1] - mins[1]) if maxdim == 0: maxdim = 1e-9 xyscale = (resolution - 1) / maxdim shift = -mins scale = np.array([xyscale, xyscale, xyscale]) scaledtriangles = [] for tri in meshtriangles: newtri = [(np.array(pt) + shift) scale for pt in tri] if len(set(map(tuple, newtri))) == 3: # Filter degenerate scaledtriangles.append(newtri) zmax = int(np.ceil((maxs[2] - mins[2]) xyscale)) xmax, ymax = resolution, resolution voxels = np.zeros((zmax, xmax, ymax), dtype=bool) # 2. Iterate Height for z in range(zmax): # Find crossing triangles crossingtris = [] for tri in scaledtriangles: zs = [pt[2] for pt in tri] hasabove = any(zv > z for zv in zs) hasbelow = any(zv < z for zv in zs) onplane = sum(1 for zv in zs if abs(zv - z) < 1e-9) if (hasabove and hasbelow) or onplane >= 2: crossingtris.append(tri) # Compute intersection lines lines = [] for tri in crossingtris: p1, p2, p3 = tri pts = [p1, p2, p3] above = [p for p in pts if p[2] > z] below = [p for p in pts if p[2] < z] same = [p for p in pts if abs(p[2] - z) < 1e-9] if len(same) == 2: lines.append((same[0], same[1])) elif len(same) == 1: if above and below: side = wherelinecrossesz(above[0], below[0], z) lines.append((side, same[0])) else: for i in range(3): pa, pb = pts[i], pts[(i+1)%3] if (pa[2] > z) != (pb[2] > z): inter = wherelinecrossesz(pa, pb, z) lines.append(inter) # Rasterize to 2D grid prepixel = np.zeros((xmax, ymax), dtype=bool) for x in range(xmax): isblack = False for y in range(ymax): if isblack: prepixel[x, y] = True for line in lines: if onlineatx(line, x, y): isblack = not isblack prepixel[x, y] = True if isblack: raise ValueError(f"Unbalanced edge crossings at z={z}, x={x}") voxels[z] = prepixel return voxels def wherelinecrossesz(p1, p2, z): if p1[2] > p2[2]: p1, p2 = p2, p1 dist = 0 if abs(p2[2] - p1[2]) < 1e-9 else (z - p1[2]) / (p2[2] - p1[2]) return (p1[0] - dist (p1[0] - p2[0]), p1[1] - dist (p1[1] - p2[1])) def onlineatx(line, x, y): p1, p2 = line if p1[0] == p2[0]: return False # Vertical lines skip ratio = (x - p1[0]) / (p2[0] - p1[0]) newy = p1[1] + ratio (p2[1] - p1[1]) return int(newy) == y and min(p1[0],p2[0]) <= x <= max(p1[0],p2[0]) and min(p1[1],p2[1]) <= y <= max(p1[1],p2[1]) This method iterates over triangles, computes their bounding box in voxel space, and tests each voxel in that box for intersection. Steps: 1. Initialize Grid: Allocate a flat array data of size W \times H \times D, initialized to 0. 2. Compute Mesh AABB: Iterate over all triangles to compute the global bounding box meshaabb of the mesh. 3. Compute Resolution per Axis: resx = \frac{meshaabb.max.x - meshaabb.min.x}{W} resy = \frac{meshaabb.max.y - meshaabb.min.y}{H} resz = \frac{meshaabb.max.z - meshaabb.min.z}{D} 4. Voxelize Points (Optional Pre-step): Some implementations first convert the mesh to a point cloud using vxvoxelizepc with the computed resolutions, then map points to the grid. 5. Iterate Triangles: For each triangle T with vertices v1, v2, v3: a. Compute T's AABB in world space. b. Map the AABB min/max to voxel grid indices. Compute offset: ox = \text{tri\min}.x + \text{fabs}(aabb.min.x). Index: ix = \frac{ox}{ax} \times (W - 1) where ax = aabb.max.x - aabb.min.x. Clamp indices to [0, W-1]. c. Iterate over voxel indices (x, y, z) within the mapped AABB range. d. Intersection Test: For each voxel, construct its AABB (centered at grid point, size resx, resy, resz). Test for intersection with triangle T using vxtriangleboxoverlap. e. Color Interpolation (if colors present): If intersecting, compute the color at the voxel center C{voxel} using barycentric interpolation. Create sub-triangles t1(v1, v2, C{voxel}), t2(v2, v3, C{voxel}), t3(v3, v1, C{voxel}). Compute areas A1, A2, A3. Total Area A = A1 + A2 + A3. Weighted Color C = \frac{C1 A2 + C2 A3 + C3 A1}{A}. f. Insertion: Compute flat index idx = x + y \cdot W + z \cdot (W \cdot H). If data[idx] is 0, set data[idx] = Color. If data[idx] is non-zero, blend: data[idx] = mix(data[idx], Color) (average of existing and new color). Pseudocode (Triangle-AABB Sampling): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def voxelizeaabbsampling(vertices, indices, width, height, depth, colors=None): grid = np.zeros((width, height, depth), dtype=np.uint32) # Compute mesh AABB minv = np.min(vertices, axis=0) maxv = np.max(vertices, axis=0) ax, ay, az = maxv - minv # Handle zero dimensions resx = ax[0] / width if ax[0] > 0 else 1e-9 resy = ax[1] / height if ax[1] > 0 else 1e-9 resz = ax[2] / depth if ax[2] > 0 else 1e-9 for i in range(0, len(indices), 3): i1, i2, i3 = indices[i], indices[i+1], indices[i+2] p1, p2, p3 = vertices[i1], vertices[i2], vertices[i3] trimin = np.minimum(np.minimum(p1, p2), p3) trimax = np.maximum(np.maximum(p1, p2), p3) # Map to voxel indices (S2 formula) ox = trimin[0] + abs(minv[0]) ixmin = int((ox / ax[0]) (width - 1)) if ax[0] > 0 else 0 ixmax = int(((trimax[0] + abs(minv[0])) / ax[0]) (width - 1)) if ax[0] > 0 else 0 # Clamp ixmin = max(0, min(ixmin, width - 1)) ixmax = max(0, min(ixmax, width - 1)) # Similar for y, z... for z in range(zmin, zmax + 1): for y in range(ymin, ymax + 1): for x in range(xmin, xmax + 1): # Intersection test placeholder intersects = True if intersects: # Color interpolation (S4) if colors is not None: c1, c2, c3 = colors[i1], colors[i2], colors[i3] center = np.array([x, y, z]) np.array([resx, resy, resz]) + minv a1 = triarea(p1, p2, center) a2 = triarea(p2, p3, center) a3 = triarea(p3, p1, center) total = a1 + a2 + a3 if total > 0: r = (c1[0]a2 + c2[0]a3 + c3[0]a1) / total g = (c1[1]a2 + c2[1]a3 + c3[1]a1) / total b = (c1[2]a2 + c2[2]a3 + c3[2]a1) / total else: r,g,b = 0,0,0 else: r,g,b = 1,1,1 colorint = ((int(255)&0xff)<<24) | ((int(b255)&0xff)<<16) | ((int(g255)&0xff)<<8) | ((int(r255)&0xff)<<0) idx = x + y width + z (width height) if grid[idx] == 0: grid[idx] = colorint else: # Blend old = grid[idx] newr = ((old>>0)&0xff + int(r255))//2 newg = ((old>>8)&0xff + int(g255))//2 newb = ((old>>16)&0xff + int(b255))//2 grid[idx] = (255<<24) | (newb<<16) | (newg<<8) | newr return grid Resolution: Number of voxels for the largest dimension. Typical value: 100. Width, Height, Depth: Explicit grid dimensions. Padding: Boolean flag (default True). Adds a 1-voxel border of empty space by expanding dimensions by 2 in each axis. Degenerate Triangles: Triangles with collinear or duplicate vertices are filtered out during scaling. Division by Zero: Grid dimensions of zero are handled by ternary checks (e.g., ax == 0.0 ? 0:...). Vertical Lines: In slice rasterization, vertical lines (x0 == x1) return Y=-1, which skips them in scanline fill. Unbalanced Edges: If isBlack is still True after processing all y rows, an error is printed, indicating unbalanced edge crossings. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for "on plane" or "on line" should use a small epsilon to avoid missing intersections due to precision errors. A GPU-based solid voxelization technique that outputs a linked list of starting and ending voxels for each row and column in the voxel grid. It uses an A-buffer approach to handle multiple fragments per pixel by building and sorting linked lists of fragment data. Choose this when you need depth-sorted solid voxels for accurate interior rendering. Not given in the sources. 3D Grid Rasterization is a fundamental technique in voxelization, originating from early computer graphics research on converting polygonal models to volume data. It is widely used in volume rendering pipelines, particularly in differentiable rendering and medical imaging. name: A-Buffer Solid Voxelization
body: A-Buffer Solid Voxelization is a GPU-based technique that voxelize a watertight mesh by rasterizing it into a fixed-width, height, and depth 3D grid and resolving multiple depth intersections per pixel using an A-buffer linked list structure. It differs from standard depth-buffer rasterization by retaining all fragment depth information rather than discarding occluded fragments, allowing it to output a linked list of starting and ending voxels for each row and column in the grid. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A watertight triangle mesh with vertex positions in the interval [-1, 1]. Output: A VoxelizerABufferLinkedList struct containing the grid dimensions, fragment count, and three arrays (headPointers, nodePointers, nodeData) representing a linked list of voxel intersections. Data Structures: The implementation relies on specific C structs and OpenGL resources: 1. Voxelizer: The main context. algorithm: Enum VOXELIZERABUFFER. width, height, depth: Grid dimensions. framebuffer: OpenGL framebuffer object ID. framebufferColor: OpenGL texture ID (GLRGBA, GLUNSIGNEDBYTE, size width x height). meshVertCount: Number of vertices. meshVertPositions: Pointer to vertex data. meshVertBuffer: OpenGL buffer object ID. data: Pointer to VoxelizerABufferData. 2. VoxelizerABufferData: Algorithm-specific state. voxelizer: Pointer to parent Voxelizer. fragCountProgram: Shader program ID for counting fragments. makeFragListProgram: Shader program ID for building the linked list. sortFragListProgram: Shader program ID for sorting the linked list. screenQuadBuffer: OpenGL buffer ID for the screen quad. atomicCounter: OpenGL buffer ID for the atomic counter. headPtrSSBO: Shader Storage Buffer Object (SSBO) ID, size width height 4 bytes. nodePtrSSBO: SSBO ID, size fragmentCount 4 bytes. nodeDataSSBO: SSBO ID, size fragmentCount 4 bytes. fragmentCount: Integer count of fragments. 3. VoxelizerABufferLinkedList: Final output. width, height, depth: Grid dimensions. fragmentCount: Total number of fragments. headPointers: Array of GLint (size width height). nodePointers: Array of GLint (size fragmentCount). nodeData: Array of GLint (size fragmentCount). Steps: 1. Initialization: If voxelizerCount is 0, create an OpenGL window and context, then increment voxelizerCount. Allocate Voxelizer struct. Set width, height, depth. Create a framebuffer with a GLRGBA GLUNSIGNEDBYTE texture of size width x height. Allocate VoxelizerABufferData and initialize algorithm-specific data. 2. Mesh Setup: Upload meshVertPositions to a GLARRAYBUFFER (meshVertBuffer). Enable vertex attribute 0 with 3 floats per vertex. 3. Fragment Counting: Disable GLCULLFACE and GLDEPTHTEST. Bind the framebuffer and set viewport to width x height. Bind meshVertBuffer and use fragCountProgram. Reset the atomic counter to 0. Set modelTransformMatrix uniform. Draw triangles. Retrieve fragmentCount from the atomic counter. 4. Linked List Memory Setup: Map headPtrSSBO (size width height 4 bytes) with GLMAPWRITEBIT | GLMAPINVALIDATEBUFFERBIT. Initialize all entries to -1. Unmap headPtrSSBO. Allocate nodePtrSSBO and nodeDataSSBO (size fragmentCount 4 bytes each). Bind nodePtrSSBO and nodeDataSSBO to binding points 2 and 3 respectively. 5. Create Linked List: Reset atomic counter to 0. Use makeFragListProgram. Set framebufferWidth and modelTransformMatrix uniforms. Draw triangles. Issue GLSHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT memory barrier. 6. Sort Linked List: Bind screenQuadBuffer. Use sortFragListProgram. Set framebufferWidth uniform. Draw 6 vertices (one triangle). Issue GLSHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT memory barrier. 7. Retrieve Results: Allocate VoxelizerABufferLinkedList. Copy width, height, depth, fragmentCount. Allocate headPointers (size width height 4 bytes), nodePointers (size fragmentCount 4 bytes), and nodeData (size fragmentCount 4 bytes). Copy data from headPtrSSBO, nodePtrSSBO, and nodeDataSSBO using glGetBufferSubData. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Create Linked List buffersubdata(data.atomicCounter, 0, 4, b'\x00\x00\x00\x00') useprogram(data.makeFragListProgram) setuniformmatrix4fv('framebufferWidth', 1, False, voxelizer.width) setuniformmatrix4fv('modelTransformMatrix', 1, False, voxelizer.modelTransformMatrix) drawarrays('TRIANGLES', 0, voxelizer.meshVertCount) memorybarrier('SHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT') # 4. Sort Linked List bindarraybuffer(data.screenQuadBuffer) useprogram(data.sortFragListProgram) setuniformmatrix4fv('framebufferWidth', 1, False, voxelizer.width) drawarrays('TRIANGLES', 0, 6) memorybarrier('SHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT') # 5. Retrieve Results linkedlist = allocateintarray(voxelizer.width voxelizer.height) linkedlist.width = voxelizer.width linkedlist.height = voxelizer.height linkedlist.depth = voxelizer.depth linkedlist.fragmentCount = data.fragmentCount headsize = voxelizer.width voxelizer.height 4 nodesize = data.fragmentCount 4 linkedlist.headPointers = allocateintarray(voxelizer.width voxelizer.height) linkedlist.nodePointers = allocateintarray(data.fragmentCount) linkedlist.nodeData = allocateintarray(data.fragmentCount) getbuffersubdata(data.headPtrSSBO, 0, headsize, linkedlist.headPointers) getbuffersubdata(data.nodePtrSSBO, 0, nodesize, linkedlist.nodePointers) getbuffersubdata(data.nodeDataSSBO, 0, nodesize, linkedlist.nodeData) return linkedlist Parameters: Grid Size: Defined by width, height, depth at creation. Vertex Range: Input mesh vertices must be in [-1, 1]. Mesh Type: Input triangle meshes must be watertight. Requirements: OpenGL 4.2 with GLARBshaderstoragebufferobject extension. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Z-axis Clipping: The algorithm does not clip the depth component in the voxel grid. If the mesh extends beyond the grid bounds, it can output an infinite number of voxels along the z-axis. Platform Support: Only Windows is supported at the time of writing. What it is: A method that uses geometry shaders to project mesh triangles directly into voxels. Difference: It avoids the fragment-based A-buffer overhead by generating voxels in the geometry shader stage. When to choose: When hardware supports geometry shaders and you prefer a different pipeline stage for voxel generation. Link: Geometry Shader Voxelization What it is: A sparse voxelization technique that adapts voxel size based on mesh complexity and bounding box thickness. Difference: It produces a sparse representation rather than a dense 3D grid linked list. When to choose: When memory efficiency is critical and the scene has varying levels of detail. Link: Adaptive Sparse Voxelization with Bounding Box Thickness Cases Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles multiple intersections per pixel accurately via the A-buffer linked list. Limitations: Requires OpenGL 4.2 and SSBO support. Does not clip depth, potentially leading to infinite voxel lists if bounds are exceeded. Only supports Windows. When to use: When accurate solid voxelization of watertight meshes is required on modern GPUs with OpenGL 4.2+. When not: When cross-platform support is needed or when the mesh is not watertight. The A-Buffer Solid Voxelization method is part of the "Voxelizer" library, a fast GPU-based solid voxelization library written in C by Kelsey Kurzeja (khkurzeja). The library was released under the MIT license. The author notes that while the library aims for cross-platform support, only Windows was supported at the time of writing. The method was designed to output a linked list of starting and ending voxels for each row and column in the voxel grid. khkurzeja/Voxelizer, https://github.com/khkurzeja/Voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: GPU Mesh Voxelization via Axis-Aligned Projection
head: Axis-Aligned Projection, Axis-aligned voxelization, Dominant Axis Projection, Dominant Axis Selection, Dominant Axis Voxelization, Single-Pass Voxelization via Axis Rotation, Voxelization with Dominant Axis Projection
body: GPU Mesh Voxelization via Axis-Aligned Projection is a rasterization-based technique that converts polygonal triangle meshes into a 3D voxel grid by projecting each triangle onto a 2D plane aligned with its dominant normal axis. It solves the problem of efficiently filling a 3D occupancy or color grid using standard GPU hardware rasterizers, which are optimized for 2D screens. Unlike Geometry Shader Voxelization which may use generic 3D rasterization logic, this method explicitly selects the optimal projection axis per triangle to maximize fragment coverage and minimize holes. It differs from GPU Mesh Voxelization via AABB-Triangle Intersection by relying on hardware rasterization rather than analytical intersection tests, and from GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics by typically using a single draw call with axis-specific view matrices rather than multiple passes or pure atomic accumulation without depth-based projection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Triangle mesh (vertices, indices), voxel grid dimensions (W \times H \times D), world-to-voxel transformation parameters. Output: 3D voxel grid (either RWTexture3D or RWStructuredBuffer) containing occupancy flags, positions, and colors. Data Structures: 1. Constant Buffer (cbuffer): Matrices: World, ViewX, ViewY, ViewZ, Projection. Integers: width, height, depth, bcount (flag for depth/occlusion handling). 2. Voxel Buffer (u1): RWTexture3D<float4> voxels or RWStructuredBuffer<Voxel> voxels where struct Voxel { int3 pos; int4 color; }. 3. Pixel Shader Input (PSINPUT): float4 pos: SVPOSITION, unsigned int axis: COLOR1 (Dominant axis index: 0=X, 1=Y, 2=Z), float4 color: COLOR0 (Optional vertex/texture color), float2 uv: TEXCOORD0 (Optional). Steps: 1. CPU Setup: Compute the voxel grid position, extents, and three view-projection matrices: VPX, VPY, and VPZ. These matrices project 3D world coordinates onto the 2D planes perpendicular to the X, Y, and Z axes respectively, mapping them into the voxel grid space. Configure the GPU pipeline: disable depth testing and face culling to ensure all triangles are processed regardless of occlusion or orientation. Disable color writes to the default render target if using a structured buffer output. 2. Geometry Shader (Dominant Axis Selection): For each input triangle, calculate the face normal \mathbf{n} using the cross product of edge vectors: \mathbf{n} = (\mathbf{v}2 - \mathbf{v}1) \times (\mathbf{v}3 - \mathbf{v}1). Determine the dominant axis index ind by finding the component with the maximum absolute value: \text{maxComponent} = \max(|nx|, |ny|, |nz|) and ind = 0 if |nx| = \text{maxComponent}, 1 if |ny| = \text{maxComponent}, else 2. Select the corresponding view matrix (ViewX, ViewY, or ViewZ). Transform the triangle vertices using the World matrix and the selected View matrix. 3. Reprojection: Reorder the components of the clip-space position to project along the dominant axis. This ensures the rasterizer generates fragments for the most visible projection of the triangle, maximizing coverage: If ind == 0 (X-axis dominant): glPosition = vec4(glin[i].glPosition.zyx, 1.0) If ind == 1 (Y-axis dominant): glPosition = vec4(glin[i].glPosition.xzy, 1.0) If ind == 2 (Z-axis dominant): glPosition = vec4(glin[i].glPosition.xyz, 1.0). Emit the vertex using EmitVertex(). 4. Pixel Shader (Voxel Writing): Receive the projected fragment, the dominant axis index, and color data. Apply conservative rasterization (e.g., "bloated" vertices or NVconservativeraster extension) to guarantee all partially covered voxels are filled and avoid holes. If bcount is non-zero, increment an atomic counter and discard the fragment to handle depth buffering or occlusion culling logic. Calculate the 3D voxel coordinates (x, y, z) from the 2D rasterized position and the dominant axis. Using viewport dimensions W, H and depth D: If axis is 0 (X): x = \text{depth} - \text{input.pos.x}, y = \text{input.pos.z} \times W, z = H - \text{input.pos.y}. If axis is 1 (Y): y = \text{input.pos.x} \times H, z = \text{input.pos.z} \times D, x = W - \text{input.pos.y}. If axis is 2 (Z): z = \text{input.pos.x} \times D, x = \text{input.pos.z} \times W, y = H - \text{input.pos.y}. Write the voxel data (position and color) to the output buffer. If using a RWStructuredBuffer, use an atomic counter (IncrementCounter()) to append voxels, as the order is not guaranteed. If using RWTexture3D, write directly to the calculated 3D index. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometryshader(trianglevertices): # 1. Calculate Normal v0, v1, v2 = trianglevertices edge1 = v1 - v0 edge2 = v2 - v0 normal = cross(edge1, edge2) # 2. Find Dominant Axis absnormal = abs(normal) maxcomp = max(absnormal.x, absnormal.y, absnormal.z) axis = 0 if absnormal.y == maxcomp: axis = 1 elif absnormal.z == maxcomp: axis = 2 # 3. Select View Matrix viewmat = ViewX if axis == 0 else (ViewY if axis == 1 else ViewZ) # 4. Process Vertices outputvertices = [] for i in range(3): worldpos = World vec4(trianglevertices[i], 1.0) viewpos = viewmat worldpos # 5. Reproject for Dominant Axis if axis == 0: reprojected = vec4(viewpos.z, viewpos.y, viewpos.x, 1.0) elif axis == 1: reprojected = vec4(viewpos.x, viewpos.z, viewpos.y, 1.0) else: reprojected = vec4(viewpos.x, viewpos.y, viewpos.z, 1.0) outputvertices.append({ 'pos': reprojected, 'axis': axis, 'color': vertexcolors[i] }) return outputvertices def pixelshader(fragment): # 1. Calculate Voxel Coordinates xndc = fragment.pos.x yndc = fragment.pos.y zndc = fragment.pos.z voxelpos = [0, 0, 0] if fragment.axis == 0: voxelpos[0] = int((depth - zndc) width) voxelpos[1] = int(yndc width) voxelpos[2] = int((height - xndc) height) elif fragment.axis == 1: voxelpos[1] = int((height - zndc) height) voxelpos[0] = int(xndc width) voxelpos[2] = int((depth - yndc) depth) else: voxelpos[2] = int((depth - zndc) depth) voxelpos[0] = int(yndc width) voxelpos[1] = int((height - xndc) height) # 2. Write to Buffer if usestructuredbuffer: index = voxels.IncrementCounter() voxels[index] = Voxel(pos=voxelpos, color=fragment.color) else: voxels[voxelpos] = fragment.color Parameters: Grid Resolution: Commonly tested at 32^3, 128^3, 256^3, 512^3. bcount: Integer flag. If non-zero, triggers atomic counter increment and fragment discard for depth/occlusion management. viewport: Integer flag (0, 1, or 2) to select projection plane in some implementations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes: Standard rasterization only covers pixels where the triangle center lies. This creates holes in the voxel grid. Mitigation requires "bloated" vertices or the NVconservativeraster extension. Overwriting: Using atomic counters for structured buffers means write order is undefined. Without proper depth handling (e.g., bcount logic), voxels may be overwritten incorrectly. Lighting Normal: The Phong lighting calculation must use the surface normal before the dominant axis rotation, because the rotation changes the normal's orientation relative to the light source, leading to incorrect lighting if the rotated normal is used. Precision: Floating-point atomic operations are not universally supported; manual averaging or integer formats may be required for color accumulation. A two-pass GPU algorithm that converts 3D triangle meshes into a list of voxels using conservative rasterization, followed by an octree construction step. It uses atomic counters to determine voxel count for buffer allocation. Choose this when memory efficiency (sparse storage) is critical and you need guaranteed hole-free voxelization. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of triangles, as each triangle is processed once in a single draw call. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H \times D) for the voxel grid storage. Performance: Voxelizing a whole scene at 512 \times 512 \times 512 resolution took 11.70 ms on an NVIDIA GTX 770 without LOD or optimizations. The 128^3 grid is significantly faster. Strengths: Single-pass rendering (efficient), leverages highly optimized hardware rasterizer, simple implementation. Limitations: Requires conservative rasterization to avoid holes, fixed-resolution grid can be memory-intensive for high resolutions, order-independent writing requires careful handling of overwrites. When to use: Real-time global illumination, voxel cone tracing, volumetric effects where speed is prioritized over perfect geometric accuracy. When not to use: When sparse storage is strictly required (use octree variants), or when analytical precision is needed without rasterization artifacts. This method originated as a practical implementation of the first step of Voxel Cone Tracing, a technique for real-time global illumination. It was popularized by blog posts and source code from developers like Alexandre Pestana, Simon Yeung, and Alex Nankervis, who adapted hardware rasterization for 3D grids. The core insight is that the GPU rasterizer can be "tricked" into filling a 3D volume by projecting triangles along their dominant axis, effectively treating the 3D grid as a series of 2D layers. It is widely used in modern real-time rendering pipelines for GI and volumetric effects. name: GPU Mesh Voxelization (Schwarz & Seidel 2010)
head: GPU Mesh Voxelization via AABB-Triangle Intersection, GPU Surface Voxelization, GPU Voxelizer Part 3, GPU-based Mesh Voxelization via Triangle-AABB Intersection, VoxelizeMesh
body: A GPU-accelerated algorithm that converts a triangle mesh into a set of occupied voxel coordinates within a 3D grid by testing each voxel in a triangle's bounding box against the triangle's plane and its three orthogonal projections. It differs from rasterization-based voxelization (which projects triangles into the grid) and ray-casting methods by using explicit geometric containment tests per voxel, providing exact surface occupancy. It builds on GPU Voxelization via Compute Shaders by parallelizing the voxel-triangle intersection logic across threads, one per triangle. Inputs: Triangle mesh defined by vertex positions and face indices. Voxel grid resolution (typically cubic, N \times N \times N) or voxel half-size \delta. Mesh bounding box (often normalized to [0,1]^3 for the kernel). Outputs: A list of occupied voxel coordinates (x, y, z). Data Structures: 1. Triangle Data Buffer: Flat array of floats. Each triangle occupies 9 floats: (v{0x}, v{0y}, v{0z}, v{1x}, v{1y}, v{1z}, v{2x}, v{2y}, v{2z}). 2. Voxel Table (vtable): 1D array of 32-bit unsigned integers. Each bit represents one voxel. Bit index i corresponds to voxel linear index i. Total size is \lceil N^3 / 32 \rceil integers. 3. Output Coordinates: 1D array of integers, 3 per occupied voxel. 4. Grid Info (voxinfo): Struct containing: bbox: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (min/max float3). gridsize: uint3 (Nx, Ny, Nz). ntriangles: sizet. unit: float3, computed as (bbox.max - bbox.min) / gridsize. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Construct the flat triangle data array from vertices and face indices. Compute grid dimensions based on mesh bounds and voxel size: Nx = \lceil bounds.extents.x / \delta \rceil, etc.. Allocate vtable and initialize to zero. 2. Voxelization Kernel Launch: Launch voxelizekernel with one thread block per triangle (or stride-based iteration over triangles). Each thread processes one or more triangles. 3. Per-Triangle Processing (inside voxelizekernel): For each triangle T with vertices v0, v1, v2: a. Normalize Vertices: Transform vertices to local coordinates relative to the mesh bounding box minimum: vi = vi^{world} - bbox.min. If the mesh is normalized to [0,1], vi are already in this range. b. Compute Edges and Normal: e0 = v1 - v0 e1 = v2 - v1 e2 = v0 - v2 n = e0 \times e1 If |n| > 10^{-20}, normalize n = n / |n|. Else, n = (0,0,0). c. Compute Bounding Box in Grid Coordinates: Compute world AABB of the triangle: t{world}.min = \min(v0, v1, v2), t{world}.max = \max(v0, v1, v2). Convert to grid indices: t{grid}.min = \text{clamp}(\lfloor t{world}.min / unit \rfloor, 0, gridsize - 1) t{grid}.max = \text{clamp}(\lfloor t{world}.max / unit \rfloor, 0, gridsize - 1). d. Precompute Plane Test Constants: Define corner point c based on normal signs: c.x = unit.x if n.x > 0, else 0 c.y = unit.y if n.y > 0, else 0 c.z = unit.z if n.z > 0, else 0 Let \deltap = unit (voxel size vector). d1 = n \cdot (c - v0) d2 = n \cdot (\deltap - c - v0). e. Precompute Projection Test Constants: For each of the three orthogonal planes (XY, YZ, ZX), compute 2D edge normals and constants. XY Plane (project to x,y): n{xy\e0} = (-e0.y, e0.x) n{xy\e1} = (-e1.y, e1.x) n{xy\e2} = (-e2.y, e2.x) If n.z < 0, negate all n{xy\ei}. d{xy\e0} = -(n{xy\e0} \cdot (v0.x, v0.y)) + \max(0, unit.x \cdot n{xy\e0}.x) + \max(0, unit.y \cdot n{xy\e0}.y) d{xy\e1} = -(n{xy\e1} \cdot (v1.x, v1.y)) + \max(0, unit.x \cdot n{xy\e1}.x) + \max(0, unit.y \cdot n{xy\e1}.y) d{xy\e2} = -(n{xy\e2} \cdot (v2.x, v2.y)) + \max(0, unit.x \cdot n{xy\e2}.x) + \max(0, unit.y \cdot n{xy\e2}.y). YZ Plane (project to y,z): n{yz\e0} = (-e0.z, e0.y) n{yz\e1} = (-e1.z, e1.y) n{yz\e2} = (-e2.z, e2.y) If n.x < 0, negate all n{yz\ei}. d{yz\e0} = -(n{yz\e0} \cdot (v0.y, v0.z)) + \max(0, unit.y \cdot n{yz\e0}.x) + \max(0, unit.z \cdot n{yz\e0}.y) d{yz\e1} = -(n{yz\e1} \cdot (v1.y, v1.z)) + \max(0, unit.y \cdot n{yz\e1}.x) + \max(0, unit.z \cdot n{yz\e1}.y) d{yz\e2} = -(n{yz\e2} \cdot (v2.y, v2.z)) + \max(0, unit.y \cdot n{yz\e2}.x) + \max(0, unit.z \cdot n{yz\e2}.y). ZX Plane (project to z,x): n{zx\e0} = (-e0.x, e0.z) n{zx\e1} = (-e1.x, e1.z) n{zx\e2} = (-e2.x, e2.z) If n.y < 0, negate all n{zx\ei}. d{zx\e0} = -(n{zx\e0} \cdot (v0.z, v0.x)) + \max(0, unit.x \cdot n{zx\e0}.x) + \max(0, unit.z \cdot n{zx\e0}.y) d{zx\e1} = -(n{zx\e1} \cdot (v1.z, v1.x)) + \max(0, unit.x \cdot n{zx\e1}.x) + \max(0, unit.z \cdot n{zx\e1}.y) d{zx\e2} = -(n{zx\e2} \cdot (v2.z, v2.x)) + \max(0, unit.x \cdot n{zx\e2}.x) + \max(0, unit.z \cdot n{zx\e2}.y). f. Voxel Iteration and Containment Test: Loop z from t{grid}.min.z to t{grid}.max.z: Loop y from t{grid}.min.y to t{grid}.max.y: Loop x from t{grid}.min.x to t{grid}.max.x: 1. Voxel Center: p = (x \cdot unit.x, y \cdot unit.y, z \cdot unit.z). 2. Plane Test: nDOTp = n \cdot p If (nDOTp + d1) \cdot (nDOTp + d2) > 0, the voxel is outside the triangle slab. Continue to next voxel. 3. XY Projection Test: p{xy} = (p.x, p.y) If (n{xy\e0} \cdot p{xy} + d{xy\e0}) < 0 OR (n{xy\e1} \cdot p{xy} + d{xy\e1}) < 0 OR (n{xy\e2} \cdot p{xy} + d{xy\e2}) < 0, the voxel is outside the XY projection. Continue. 4. YZ Projection Test: p{yz} = (p.y, p.z) If (n{yz\e0} \cdot p{yz} + d{yz\e0}) < 0 OR (n{yz\e1} \cdot p{yz} + d{yz\e1}) < 0 OR (n{yz\e2} \cdot p{yz} + d{yz\e2}) < 0, the voxel is outside the YZ projection. Continue. 5. ZX Projection Test: p{zx} = (p.z, p.x) If (n{zx\e0} \cdot p{zx} + d{zx\e0}) < 0 OR (n{zx\e1} \cdot p{zx} + d{zx\e1}) < 0 OR (n{zx\e2} \cdot p{zx} + d{zx\e2}) < 0, the voxel is outside the ZX projection. Continue. 6. Mark Voxel: If all tests pass, compute linear index: loc = x + y \cdot Nx + z \cdot Nx \cdot Ny Set bit in vtable at loc using atomic OR. 4. Sparse Extraction: Launch extractkernel to iterate over all bits in vtable. If bit i is set, atomically increment a counter and store (x, y, z) in the output array. x = i \pmod{Nx} y = (i / Nx) \pmod{Ny} z = i / (Nx \cdot Ny). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def setbit(vtable, index): """Set bit at index in vtable using atomic operation.""" intloc = index // 32 bitpos = 31 - (index % 32) # In CUDA, this would be atomicOr. Here we simulate the logic. vtable[intloc] |= (1 << bitpos) def getbit(vtable, index): """Check if bit at index is set.""" intloc = index // 32 bitpos = 31 - (index % 32) return (vtable[intloc] >> bitpos) & 1 def voxelizemeshgpu(vertices, faces, resolution): """ vertices: list of (x, y, z) floats faces: list of (i0, i1, i2) ints resolution: int, N """ nfaces = len(faces) # Build triangle data buffer (9 floats per triangle) # Assume vertices are normalized to [0,1] or bbox is [0,1] # For this implementation, we assume bbox is [0,1] and vertices are in [0,1] # If not, transform them. # Voxel table: ceil(N^3 / 32) unsigned ints gridbits = resolution resolution resolution gridwords = (gridbits + 31) // 32 vtable = [0] gridwords # Unit size unit = 1.0 / resolution # Launch kernel: one thread per triangle (simplified for CPU simulation) # In GPU, this is parallelized. for tidx in range(nfaces): i0, i1, i2 = faces[tidx] v0 = vertices[i0] v1 = vertices[i1] v2 = vertices[i2] # Edges e0 = (v1[0]-v0[0], v1[1]-v0[1], v1[2]-v0[2]) e1 = (v2[0]-v1[0], v2[1]-v1[1], v2[2]-v1[2]) e2 = (v0[0]-v2[0], v0[1]-v2[1], v0[2]-v2[2]) # Normal n = ( e0[1]e1[2] - e0[2]e1[1], e0[2]e1[0] - e0[0]e1[2], e0[0]e1[1] - e0[1]e1[0]) lenn = math.sqrt(n[0]2 + n[1]2 + n[2]2) if lenn > 1e-20: n = (n[0]/lenn, n[1]/lenn, n[2]/lenn) else: n = (0, 0, 0) # Bounding Box minv = (min(v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]), min(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]), min(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2])) maxv = (max(v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]), max(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]), max(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2])) # Grid coordinates tmin = ( max(0, min(resolution-1, int(minv[0] / unit))), max(0, min(resolution-1, int(minv[1] / unit))), max(0, min(resolution-1, int(minv[2] / unit)))) tmax = ( max(0, min(resolution-1, int(maxv[0] / unit))), max(0, min(resolution-1, int(maxv[1] / unit))), max(0, min(resolution-1, int(maxv[2] / unit)))) # Plane Test Constants c = ( unit if n[0] > 0 else 0.0, unit if n[1] > 0 else 0.0, unit if n[2] > 0 else 0.0) d1 = n[0](c[0]-v0[0]) + n[1](c[1]-v0[1]) + n[2](c[2]-v0[2]) d2 = n[0](unit-c[0]-v0[0]) + n[1](unit-c[1]-v0[1]) + n[2](unit-c[2]-v0[2]) # Projection Tests Constants # XY nxye0 = (-e0[1], e0[0]) nxye1 = (-e1[1], e1[0]) nxye2 = (-e2[1], e2[0]) if n[2] < 0: nxye0 = (-nxye0[0], -nxye0[1]) nxye1 = (-nxye1[0], -nxye1[1]) nxye2 = (-nxye2[0], -nxye2[1]) dxye0 = -(nxye0[0]v0[0] + nxye0[1]v0[1]) + max(0, unitnxye0[0]) + max(0, unitnxye0[1]) dxye1 = -(nxye1[0]v1[0] + nxye1[1]v1[1]) + max(0, unitnxye1[0]) + max(0, unitnxye1[1]) dxye2 = -(nxye2[0]v2[0] + nxye2[1]v2[1]) + max(0, unitnxye2[0]) + max(0, unitnxye2[1]) # YZ nyze0 = (-e0[2], e0[1]) nyze1 = (-e1[2], e1[1]) nyze2 = (-e2[2], e2[1]) if n[0] < 0: nyze0 = (-nyze0[0], -nyze0[1]) nyze1 = (-nyze1[0], -nyze1[1]) nyze2 = (-nyze2[0], -nyze2[1]) dyze0 = -(nyze0[0]v0[1] + nyze0[1]v0[2]) + max(0, unitnyze0[0]) + max(0, unitnyze0[1]) dyze1 = -(nyze1[0]v1[1] + nyze1[1]v1[2]) + max(0, unitnyze1[0]) + max(0, unitnyze1[1]) dyze2 = -(nyze2[0]v2[1] + nyze2[1]v2[2]) + max(0, unitnyze2[0]) + max(0, unitnyze2[1]) # ZX nzxe0 = (-e0[0], e0[2]) nzxe1 = (-e1[0], e1[2]) nzxe2 = (-e2[0], e2[2]) if n[1] < 0: nzxe0 = (-nzxe0[0], -nzxe0[1]) nzxe1 = (-nzxe1[0], -nzxe1[1]) nzxe2 = (-nzxe2[0], -nzxe2[1]) dzxe0 = -(nzxe0[0]v0[2] + nzxe0[1]v0[0]) + max(0, unitnzxe0[0]) + max(0, unitnzxe0[1]) dzxe1 = -(nzxe1[0]v1[2] + nzxe1[1]v1[0]) + max(0, unitnzxe1[0]) + max(0, unitnzxe1[1]) dzxe2 = -(nzxe2[0]v2[2] + nzxe2[1]v2[0]) + max(0, unitnzxe2[0]) + max(0, unitnzxe2[1]) # Iterate Voxels for z in range(tmin[2], tmax[2] + 1): for y in range(tmin[1], tmax[1] + 1): for x in range(tmin[0], tmax[0] + 1): p = (xunit, yunit, zunit) # Plane Test ndotp = n[0]p[0] + n[1]p[1] + n[2]p[2] if (ndotp + d1) (ndotp + d2) > 0: continue # XY Test pxy = (p[0], p[1]) if (nxye0[0]pxy[0] + nxye0[1]pxy[1] + dxye0) < 0: continue if (nxye1[0]pxy[0] + nxye1[1]pxy[1] + dxye1) < 0: continue if (nxye2[0]pxy[0] + nxye2[1]pxy[1] + dxye2) < 0: continue # YZ Test pyz = (p[1], p[2]) if (nyze0[0]pyz[0] + nyze0[1]pyz[1] + dyze0) < 0: continue if (nyze1[0]pyz[0] + nyze1[1]pyz[1] + dyze1) < 0: continue if (nyze2[0]pyz[0] + nyze2[1]pyz[1] + dyze2) < 0: continue # ZX Test pzx = (p[2], p[0]) if (nzxe0[0]pzx[0] + nzxe0[1]pzx[1] + dzxe0) < 0: continue if (nzxe1[0]pzx[0] + nzxe1[1]pzx[1] + dzxe1) < 0: continue if (nzxe2[0]pzx[0] + nzxe2[1]pzx[1] + dzxe2) < 0: continue # Mark Voxel loc = x + yresolution + zresolutionresolution setbit(vtable, loc) # Sparse Extraction occupiedvoxels = [] for i in range(gridbits): if getbit(vtable, i): x = i % resolution y = (i // resolution) % resolution z = i // (resolution resolution) occupiedvoxels.append((x, y, z)) return occupiedvoxels Uses Morton codes and iterative 2D grid traversal within bounding boxes, filling only voxels passing containment tests in projections. Choose for sparse, hierarchical storage. Determines intersected voxels per triangle, supporting non-watertight meshes. Choose for general surface representation without specific sparse structure requirements. Time Complexity: O(N{tri} \cdot N{vox\per\tri}), where N{tri} is the number of triangles and N{vox\per\tri} is the number of voxels in the triangle's bounding box. In the worst case, O(N{tri} \cdot N^3) if triangles span the entire grid, but typically much less due to bounding box culling. Memory Complexity: O(N^3 / 32) for the voxel table, plus O(N{tri}) for triangle data. Performance: Real-time performance (~60 FPS) at high voxel densities (~1M voxels) on modern GPUs. Exact results, but computationally expensive for high triangle counts due to per-voxel-triangle intersection tests. Strengths: Exact geometric tests, parallelizable, no rasterization artifacts. Limitations: Memory intensive for high resolutions due to dense bit grid (unless sparse extraction is used immediately), slow for very high triangle counts. When to use: When exact surface occupancy is required and the mesh is not excessively large. When not to use: For extremely high triangle counts without spatial acceleration, as it performs brute-force triangle-by-voxel testing. Originated from the paper "Fast parallel surface and solid voxelization on GPUs" by Schwarz & Seidel (2010). The algorithm was implemented in CUDA/C++ and demonstrated on NVIDIA GPUs. It is used in real-time applications requiring mesh-to-voxel conversion, such as gameplay systems and rendering. yuyujunjun/mesh-voxelize, https://github.com/yuyujunjun/mesh-voxelize, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bzgeb/UnityGPUMeshVoxelizerPart3, https://github.com/bzgeb/UnityGPUMeshVoxelizerPart3, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) NotABottle/Voxel-Shader, https://github.com/NotABottle/Voxel-Shader, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ivandrodri/gpu-voxelizer, https://github.com/ivandrodri/gpu-voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Cloud Raymarching
head: Cloud Raymarching, Cloud Volume Rendering, Ray Marching with Exponential Attenuation, Real-Time Volumetric Cloud Rendering, Volumetric Cloud Rendering
body: Volumetric cloud raymarching is a technique for rendering volumetric clouds by tracing a ray through a 3D density field, accumulating color based on density, light scattering, and transmittance. It differs from solid geometry ray marching by accumulating color and transmittance over a fixed number of steps or until transmittance drops below a threshold, rather than breaking on the first hit. Unlike billboard or particle clouds, it represents true 3D density fields that interact with light realistically. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position, camera ray direction, cloud volume bounds (min/max), light direction, 3D noise textures (base shape, Worley/cell noise, erosion), and rendering parameters (step size, extinction, scattering coefficients). Outputs: Final pixel color (RGB) and alpha/transmittance. Data Structures: Cloud Volume Bounds: boundsMin (float3), boundsMax (float3) defining the axis-aligned box containing the clouds. Noise Textures: 3D textures (Texture3D) storing density values. Common formats include ARGBFloat with dimensions like 128x128x128. Textures typically include base shape noise, Worley noise, and erosion noise. Uniforms/Constants: Parameters vary by implementation. Source uses uCloudExtinction, uCloudLightStep, uCloudLightAtt, uCloudScatterMin, uCloudScatterMax, uCloudBrightness, uCloudStepMult, cloudCenter, cloudRadius. Source uses boundsMin, boundsMax, clouddensityThr, clouddensityMul, cloudoffset, offsetSpeed, volumemarchsteps, lightmarchsteps, detailscale, detailoffset, detailweight, frwrdscatter, backscatter, basebrightness, phasefactor, randomsample, optimizedmarch, lightAbsorptionThroughCloud, darknessThreshold. Source uses fixed values like stepSize = 100.0, maxDistance = 30000.0, Density Threshold for Lighting = 0.01, Transmittance Attenuation Factor = 0.02, Transmittance Early Exit Threshold = 0.01. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray-Volume Intersection (Optional): Calculate the intersection of the camera ray with the cloud volume. Sphere Intersection: If the volume is spherical, calculate oc = ro - cloudCenter, b = dot(oc, rd), c = dot(oc, oc) - cloudRadius cloudRadius, disc = bb - c. If disc < 0, return transparent. Entry t0 = max(0.0, -b - sqrt(disc)), Exit t1 = min(maxDist, -b + sqrt(disc)). Box Intersection: Compute t0 = (boundsMin - rayOrigin) / rayDir and t1 = (boundsMax - rayOrigin) / rayDir. Determine dstToBox = max(0.0f, max(max(tmin.x, tmin.y), tmin.z)) and dstInsideObj = max(0.0f, min(tmax.x, min(tmax.y, tmax.z)) - dstToBox). If dstInsideObj <= 0, the ray misses or starts inside; proceed with camera-origin marching. 2. Initialization: Initialize step size, loop variable t (or dstTravelled), accumulated color col (or result), and transmittance trans (or transmittance). Step Size: step = (t1 - t0) / (96.0 uCloudStepMult) or stepSize = aDistance / volumemarchsteps or fixed 100.0. Entry Point: entryPoint = rayOrigin + rayDir dstToObj or start at rayOrigin. Transmittance: Initialize to 1.0. 3. Marching Loop: Iterate for a fixed number of steps (e.g., 96, volumemarchsteps, or 128) or until transmittance < 0.01. Position: p = ro + rd t or rayPos = anEntryPoint + aRayDir dstTravelled. Density Sampling: Sample the density field at p. Simple Method: density = SampleCloudDensity(p). Advanced Method: Sample low-res shape noise, apply threshold and multiplier, sample high-res detail noise (fBm), trim cloud using erosion and falloff functions. uvw = (size 0.5f + aPos) baseScale baseScale. shapeNoise = shapeNoiseTex.Sample(uvw + cloudoffset offsetSpeed).r. density = (shapeNoise - clouddensityThr) clouddensityMul. detailFBM = SampleHighRes(uvw). trimmedCloud = TrimCloud(aPos, density, detailFBM). density = trimmedCloud EdgeFallof(aPos) HeightFallof(aPos). Lighting Calculation: If density > 0 (or threshold like 0.001, 0.01): Shadow Ray: Trace towards the light source to compute light attenuation. Simple: Loop 6 times, sampling density along light direction L, accumulating lightSample += cloudDensityField(lp). lightAtt = exp(-lightSample uCloudLightAtt). Advanced: Call LightMarch(rayPos, cosAngle) which performs a box intersection with the cloud volume and accumulates optical depth using MultipleOctaveScattering. Scatter Factor: Implementations vary: scatter = mix(uCloudScatterMin, uCloudScatterMax, lightAtt), compute phase function using Henyey-Greenstein, or use a direct light factor. Color Accumulation: cloudColor = vec3(uCloudBrightness) scatter or lightEnergy += density stepSize transmittance lightTransmittance phaseVal or result += density light transmittance. Transmittance Update: trans = exp(-d uCloudExtinction) or transmittance = exp(-density stepSize 0.02) or transmittance = BeersLaw(density stepSize lightAbsorptionThroughCloud). Early Exit: If transmittance < 0.01, break loop. Advance: t += step or dstTravelled += stepSize. 4. Final Output: Return vec4(col, 1.0 - trans) or float4(col, transmittance). Formulas: Density Field: shape = smoothstep(1.2, 0.6, sphere) flatBottom, where sphere = length(vec3(q.x, q.y 0.55, q.z)), flatBottom = smoothstep(-0.2, 0.0, q.y), q = (p - cloudCenter) / cloudRadius. Beer's Law: T = e^{-aDist}, where aDist is the optical depth. Powder Function: P = 1 - e^{-2 \times aDist}. Henyey-Greenstein Phase Function: P(g, \cos\theta) = \frac{1 - g^2}{4 \pi (1 + g^2 - 2 g \cos\theta)^{1.5}}. Remap: v{new} = minNew + (v{old} - minOld) \times \frac{maxNew - minNew}{maxOld - minOld}. Density Composition: density = BaseNoise - Erosion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendervolumetricclouds(rayorigin, raydir, sundir, boundsmin, boundsmax, maxdistance, stepsize, noisetextures): transmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) pos = rayorigin for in range(int(maxdistance / stepsize)): # Check if inside cloud volume bounds if not (boundsmin.x <= pos.x <= boundsmax.x and boundsmin.y <= pos.y <= boundsmax.y and boundsmin.z <= pos.z <= boundsmax.z): break density = sampleclouddensity(pos, noisetextures) if density > 0.01: light = computesunlight(pos, sundir, noisetextures) accumulatedcolor = ( accumulatedcolor[0] + density light transmittance, accumulatedcolor[1] + density light transmittance, accumulatedcolor[2] + density light transmittance) transmittance = math.exp(-density stepsize 0.02) if transmittance < 0.01: break pos = pos + raydir stepsize return (accumulatedcolor[0], accumulatedcolor[1], accumulatedcolor[2], 1.0 - transmittance) def sampleclouddensity(pos, textures): uvw = pos 0.0005 basenoise = textures['base'].sample(uvw)[0] erosion = textures['erosion'].sample(uvw 0.5)[0] density = basenoise - erosion 0.6 return max(0.0, min(1.0, density)) def computesunlight(pos, sundir, textures): light = 1.0 step = 300.0 currentpos = pos for in range(6): currentpos = currentpos + tuple(s step for s in sundir) d = sampleclouddensity(currentpos, textures) light = math.exp(-d 0.1) return light Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Light Marching Vector Bug: In some implementations, adding a vector (dirToLight stepSize) to a scalar (dstTravelled) and a scalar to a vector (aPos) is a logic error. Edge Falloff Bug: Using dstFromEdgeX twice in the min function for edge weight ignores the Z-axis falloff. Precision: Floating point precision issues may arise in large coordinate spaces; using local coordinates or normalized UVs helps. Degenerate Input: If the ray does not intersect the volume, return transparent immediately. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of raymarch steps (O(N) where N is volumemarchsteps or fixed iterations like 96/128). Lighting calculations add a secondary loop (O(M) where M is lightmarchsteps or 6). Memory Usage: Requires storage for 3D noise textures. A typical implementation uses a 128x128x128 ARGBFloat texture. Measured Performance: Rendering at quarter resolution with TAA upscale is common in AAA games to mitigate performance costs. Typical step counts range from 64 to 128. Strengths: Realistic light interaction (volumetric shadows, subsurface scattering approximation), true 3D structure, smooth transitions. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to multiple texture samples and lighting calculations per pixel. When to Use: When realistic volumetric lighting and 3D cloud structure are required. When Not to Use: When performance is critical and simple billboards or sprites are sufficient. Volumetric cloud rendering has evolved from simple billboards to complex raymarched density fields. Modern real-time implementations often use 3D noise textures (Perlin, Worley) combined with raymarching to approximate atmospheric scattering.
