name: Point Location
head: Octree Point Location, Integer coordinate point location
body:
Point location maps a continuous 3D coordinate vector to a specific leaf node or voxel within a canonical octree. It solves the problem of efficiently retrieving data associated with a spatial position by traversing the tree from a given starting node to the target leaf. What sets this method apart from generic tree traversal is its reliance on precomputed bit masks to determine child indices using constant-time bitwise operations, avoiding the computational cost of arbitrary bit shifts. It builds on Octree Child Index Computation to derive the 0-7 octant offset. Inputs and Outputs: Input: dest: A 3D integer coordinate vector representing the target location. depth: The current depth level in the octree, starting from the root or an intermediate node. index: The index of the current node in the flat node array. maxdepth: The maximum depth of the octree. Output: The scalar value stored in the leaf node containing dest. Data Structures: The method assumes the following data structures, typically stored in an OctreeData container: nodes: A 2D array nodes[depth][index] of type OctNode. caps: An array caps[index] of type OctCap, used for leaf voxels at the deepest level. childbitdepth: A precomputed 1D array childbitdepth[maxdepth]. OctNode layout: childscalars[8]: Array of scalar values for leaf children. childstart: Unsigned integer base pointer or index to the children of this node. childoffset[8]: Array of 8 signed chars representing the offset from childstart to the child node. A value of -1 indicates the child is a leaf (scalar). OctCap layout: childscalars[8]: Array of scalar values for the 8 voxels in the cap. Precomputation: Before traversal, the childbitdepth array is computed for each depth level d from 0 to maxdepth: 	ext{child it\depth}[d] = 1 \ll (	ext{max\depth} - d - 1) This precomputation avoids expensive arbitrary left-shift operations during traversal. Algorithm Steps: 1. Cast Coordinates: Convert continuous input coordinates to integers and ensure they fall within the canonical interval [0, 2^{	ext{max\depth}}). 2. Initialize: Start with the given depth and index. 3. Retrieve Node: Access the current node: node = nodes[depth][index]. 4. Get Mask: Retrieve the precomputed bit mask for the current depth: childbit = childbitdepth[depth]. 5. Compute Child Index: Determine the 0-7 octant index of the child containing dest by testing bits against childbit, shifting results, and combining them: 	ext{child} = ((	ext{dest}.x \ \& \ 	ext{child it}) 
eq 0) \ll 2 \ | \ ((	ext{dest}.y \ \& \ 	ext{child it}) 
eq 0) \ll 1 \ | \ ((	ext{dest}.z \ \& \ 	ext{child it}) 
eq 0) This yields the 0-7 octant offset of the child, and hence its index. 6. Check for Leaf in Interior Node: If node.childoffset[child] == -1, the child is a scalar leaf. Return node.childscalars[child]. 7. Check for Cap Node (Deepest Level): If depth == maxdepth - 2, the node is a cap node containing voxels. Calculate the final child index using the lowest bit (bit 0) of the coordinates: 	ext{child} = (	ext{dest}.x \ \& \ 1) \ll 2 \ | \ (	ext{dest}.y \ \& \ 1) \ll 1 \ | \ (	ext{dest}.z \ \& \ 1) Update index = node.childstart + node.childoffset[child] and return caps[index].childscalars[child]. 8. Traverse Down: If not a leaf and not a cap: Update index to point to the child's start location: index = node.childstart + node.childoffset[child]. Increment depth: depth += 1. Repeat from Step 3. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointlocate(dest: Vec3i, depth: int, index: int, maxdepth: int, nodes: List[List[OctNode]], caps: List[OctCap], childbitdepth: List[int]) -> T: while True: node = nodes[depth][index] childbit = childbitdepth[depth] # Compute child index (0-7) based on bits in dest coordinates child = ((dest.x & childbit) != 0) << 2 | \ ((dest.y & childbit) != 0) << 1 | \ ((dest.z & childbit) != 0) # Check if child is a scalar leaf in an interior node if node.childoffset[child] == -1: return node.childscalars[child] # Check if we are at the cap level (maxdepth - 2) elif depth == maxdepth - 2: # Use the lowest bit for cap nodes index = node.childstart + node.childoffset[child] child = (dest.x & 1) << 2 | (dest.y & 1) << 1 | (dest.z & 1) return caps[index].childscalars[child] # Traverse to the child node index = node.childstart + node.childoffset[child] depth += 1 return 0 # Fallback return, though the loop always returns for valid inputs Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate Range: Coordinates must be within the canonical interval [0, 2^{	ext{max\depth}}] and cast to integers. Cap Nodes: The algorithm explicitly handles the deepest level (maxdepth - 2) as a special case using the lowest bit, implying the octree structure uses "caps" for the finest resolution. Parent Pointers: Parent pointers are omitted to save memory. Neighbor finding (which may call point location) relies on a separate parenttrace array provided by the ray traversal algorithm. An algorithm to traverse and insert a voxel into an Octree using a pre-computed bitstream to determine child indices. Definition: It uses a bitstream b encoding the voxel's position to guide insertion. Steps: 1. If depth d is 0, return a new node containing the voxel v. 2. Extract the child index from the bitstream b using group(b, d, 3) and get the corresponding child n' from node n. 3. If child n' is null, create a new empty node. 4. Recursively insert the voxel into the child node with depth d-1, and set the result as the child at the index derived from the bitstream. Parameters: b: The bitstream encoding the voxel's position. When to choose: Used for dynamic insertion into an octree where a bitstream representation of coordinates is available. Time Complexity: O(d), where d is the depth of the octree, as each iteration performs constant-time bitwise operations and array lookups. Memory Complexity: O(	ext{max\depth}) for the precomputed childbitdepth array. The node structure itself is compact, using childoffset as signed chars to save space. Performance: Precomputing bit masks avoids expensive arbitrary left-shift operations, providing noticeably better performance than the original Frisken and Perry method. Strengths: Fast lookup, low memory overhead (no parent pointers), simple bitwise logic. Limitations: Requires canonical coordinate system [0, 2^{	ext{max\depth}}]. Neighbor finding requires additional infrastructure (parenttrace). Originating from the work of Frisken and Perry, this method was adapted for interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. The original proposal involved creating a single-bit mask corresponding to the current depth and applying it to coordinates. The optimized version, caching childbitdepth to avoid arbitrary shifts, was introduced in subsequent implementations for performance. name: Ray-Octree Traversal (Gargantini and Atkinson variant)
head: Atkinson traversal, Gargantini and Atkinson Octree Ray Traversal, Gargantini and Atkinson Octree Traversal, Gargantini and Atkinson Ray-Octree Traversal, Gargantini and Atkinson variant, Gargantini traversal
body: A single-ray octree traversal algorithm that determines the exact order of child octant intersection by sorting the ray's crossings with the X, Y, and Z mid-planes of the current node. It builds on Ray Traversal of Octree Nodes by fully sorting these mid-plane intersections to march through children sequentially, exploiting binary arithmetic on integer coordinates for efficient child index updates. Unlike coherent techniques (SIMD, packets, frustum-based traversal), it avoids unnecessary work in highly variant scenes where a pixel covers multiple voxels. Inputs: rayorig: Ray origin coordinates (list of 3 floats). raydir: Ray direction coordinates (list of 3 floats). depth: Current octree depth (integer). nodeindex: Index of the current node in the nodes array (integer). parenttrace: Array storing the traversal path (list of integers). cell: Current node's base coordinate in octree space (list of 3 integers). tenter: Ray entry parameter for the current node (float). texit: Ray exit parameter for the current node (float). isovalue: Target isovalue for scalar comparison (float). nodes: Octree node storage nodes[depth][nodeindex]. childbitdepth: Precomputed bitmask array for each depth. maxdepth: Maximum octree depth (integer). Outputs: Returns true if an isosurface intersection is found within the current node's volume; false otherwise. Data Structures: nodes[depth][nodeindex]: Accesses the current OctNode containing childmins, childmaxs, childoffset, and childstart fields. childbitdepth[depth]: Precomputed bitmask for the current depth (e.g., 2^{d{max}-depth}). axistable: Constant array {4, 2, 1} mapping sorted axis indices to bit positions. Steps: 1. Ray-Bounding Box Test: Generate rays in canonical octree space [0, 2^{d{max}}]. Perform a standard ray-bounding box test on the root to discard non-intersecting rays, yielding tenter and texit. 2. Retrieve Node: Access node = nodes[depth][nodeindex] and store nodeindex in parenttrace[depth]. 3. Compute Mid-Planes: Calculate childbit = childbitdepth[depth]. Compute the center of the current cell as floats: center = (cell.x | childbit, cell.y | childbit, cell.z | childbit). Compute intersection distances to the mid-planes: tcenter = (center - rayorig) / raydir. Compute the entry point: penter = rayorig + raydir tenter. 4. Determine First Child: Compare penter coordinates to center to determine the entry octant bits: tc.x = (penter.x \ge center.x) tc.y = (penter.y \ge center.y) tc.z = (penter.z \ge center.z) Compute the first child index: child = (tc.x << 2) | (tc.y << 1) | tc.z. Update childcell: childcell = cell | (tc.x ? childbit: 0, tc.y ? childbit: 0, tc.z ? childbit: 0). 5. Sort Mid-Plane Intersections: Create axisisects array containing the sorted indices of tcenter such that tcenter[axisisects[0]] < tcenter[axisisects[1]] < tcenter[axisisects[2]]. This represents the order of crossing the X, Y, and Z mid-planes. 6. Traverse Children: Initialize childtenter = tenter. Iterate through the sorted axisisects array while tcenter[axisisects[i]] < texit: a. Calculate Exit: childtexit = min(tcenter[axisisects[i]], texit). b. Scalar Check: If isovalue >= node.childmins[child] OR isovalue <= node.childmaxs[child]: i. If node.childoffset == -1: Traverse scalar leaf (see Subtopics). ii. Else if depth == maxdepth - 2: Traverse cap node (see Subtopics). iii. Else: Recursively call traverse(rayorig, raydir, depth+1, node.childstart + node.childoffset[child], parenttrace, childcell, childtenter, childtexit, isovalue, nodes, childbitdepth, maxdepth). c. Exit Check: If childtexit == texit, return false (ray has exited the volume). d. Update Entry: childtenter = childtexit. e. Move to Next Child: i. Get axisbit = axistable[axisisects[i]]. ii. If child & axisbit is true: child &= ~axisbit and childcell[axisisects[i]] &= ~childbit. iii. Else: child |= axisbit and childcell[axisisects[i]] |= childbit. Return false if the loop completes without finding an intersection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverse(rayorig, raydir, depth, nodeindex, parenttrace, cell, tenter, texit, isovalue, nodes, childbitdepth, maxdepth): node = nodes[depth][nodeindex] parenttrace[depth] = nodeindex childbit = childbitdepth[depth] # Compute center (float) and mid-plane intersections center = [float(cell[0] | childbit), float(cell[1] | childbit), float(cell[2] | childbit)] tcenter = [(center[i] - rayorig[i]) / raydir[i] for i in range(3)] penter = [rayorig[i] + raydir[i] tenter for i in range(3)] # Determine first child octant tc = [1 if penter[i] >= center[i] else 0 for i in range(3)] child = (tc[0] << 2) | (tc[1] << 1) | tc[2] childcell = [cell[i] | (childbit if tc[i] else 0) for i in range(3)] # Sort mid-plane intersections: axisisects contains indices 0,1,2 sorted by tcenter value axisisects = sorted(range(3), key=lambda i: tcenter[i]) axistable = [4, 2, 1] childtenter = tenter for i in range(3): axisidx = axisisects[i] if tcenter[axisidx] >= texit: break childtexit = min(tcenter[axisidx], texit) # Check if isovalue is within child's range if isovalue >= node.childmins[child] or isovalue <= node.childmaxs[child]: if node.childoffset == -1: # Sources do not provide full implementation; handles 8-voxel neighborhood and isosurface intersection if traversescalarleaf(childcell, childtenter, childtexit, isovalue): return True elif depth == maxdepth - 2: # Sources do not provide full implementation; handles cap node scalar retrieval if traversecap(childcell, childtenter, childtexit, isovalue): return True else: childnodeindex = node.childstart + node.childoffset[child] if traverse(rayorig, raydir, depth + 1, childnodeindex, parenttrace, childcell, childtenter, childtexit, isovalue, nodes, childbitdepth, maxdepth): return True if childtexit == texit: return False childtenter = childtexit # Move to next child by flipping the bit corresponding to the traversed axis axisbit = axistable[axisidx] if child & axisbit: child &= ~axisbit childcell[axisidx] &= ~childbit else: child |= axisbit childcell[axisidx] |= childbit return False def traversescalarleaf(childcell, childtenter, childtexit, isovalue): # Sources do not provide full implementation; handles 8-voxel neighborhood and isosurface intersection return False def traversecap(childcell, childtenter, childtexit, isovalue): # Sources do not provide full implementation; handles cap node scalar retrieval return False A specialized traversal routine for cap nodes, which are leaf-like structures containing scalar values, differing from interior nodes in how child values are retrieved. Cap intersection is identical to interior nodes, except the isovalue check and recursive call are replaced by determining the values of the eight voxels composing the cell. To optimize neighbor retrieval, given a child octant child (0-7) and a neighbor direction dir (0-7), check if (child & dir) is false; if so, the neighbor value is cap.scalars[dir]. If true, proceed with standard neighbor-finding. A scalar leaf is traversed recursively to the same depth as caps, despite having no children and a homogeneous value. When traversal reaches cap depth, if the neighborhood of identical voxels within the scalar leaf is encountered, no isosurface is present. At the borders of the scalar leaf node, neighbor-finding is performed as for cap nodes to obtain eight voxel values. If the isovalue lies within the minimum and maximum of these eight values, an isosurface intersection is computed using trilinear interpolation. Time Complexity: Moderate initial cost for computing and sorting mid-plane intersections; subsequent child traversal is trivial via bitmask inversion. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for nodes, childbitdepth, and parenttrace. Performance: Avoids SIMD/packet/frustum techniques because highly variant scenes and pixels covering multiple voxels cause unnecessary work and performance decreases compared to single-ray techniques. Wald et al. reported little performance gain from coherent techniques on large data. Strengths: Efficient single-ray traversal using binary arithmetic; no additional transform required for canonical space. Limitations: Scalar leaves and cap nodes require special handling routines. Originated from the technique of Gargantini and Atkinson [5, 6], adapted for octree structures and hashing schemes by Wald et al. in "Interactive Isosurface Ray Tracing of Large Octree Volumes" (2006). It was chosen over Sung [19, 22, 23] and Samet [17, 19, 20] methods as the fastest traversal for their implementation. Used for interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes, such as LLNL Richtmyer-Meshkov instability and Utah CSAFE heptane fire simulations. name: Amanatides–Woo Voxel Traversal
head: 3D DDA, Amanatides-Woo 3D DDA, Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm
body: The Amanatides–Woo algorithm efficiently enumerates the uniform grid cells intersected by a ray in front-to-back order by jumping exactly from one grid boundary to the next, avoiding the pitfalls of naïve ray marching such as missing thin cells, redundant work, and arbitrary step sizes. It serves as the foundational traversal method for image-order volume rendering and voxel-based ray casting, building on Ray-grid traversal by providing an output-sensitive O(K) approach where K is the number of visited cells. Inputs: Ray origin O = (Ox, Oy, Oz), ray direction D = (Dx, Dy, Dz) (non-zero magnitude), voxel grid index bounds [x{min}, x{max}) \times [y{min}, y{max}) \times [z{min}, z{max}), and voxel size V (typically V=1 for unit grids). Outputs: A sequence of voxel indices (i, j, k) visited in front-to-back order. Optionally, the hit voxel position and the normalized face normal of the crossed boundary. Data Structures: voxel: Integer tuple (i, j, k) representing the current cell index. step: Integer tuple (sx, sy, sz) where sa \in \{-1, 0, 1\}. tdelta: Float tuple (\Delta tx, \Delta ty, \Delta tz) representing the t-distance between successive grid plane crossings on each axis. tmax: Float tuple (Tx, Ty, Tz) representing the ray parameter t at which the ray crosses the next grid boundary on each axis. Parameters: Voxel size V: Not given in the sources. Ray bounds: t{enter} (entry into grid) and t{exit} (exit or max ray length). Step-by-Step Method: 1. Clip ray to grid AABB: For each axis, compute entry and exit parameters. If the ray misses the grid, terminate. If the ray origin is inside the grid, t{enter} may be negative; start traversal at t = \max(t{enter}, 0.0). 2. Initialize Direction and Step Signs: For each axis a \in \{x, y, z\}: if Da > 0, set sa = 1; if Da < 0, set sa = -1; if Da = 0, set sa = 0. 3. Calculate \Delta t (Step Size in t): For each axis a where Da \neq 0, compute \Delta ta = V / |Da|. If Da = 0, set \Delta ta = \infty. 4. Determine Starting Voxel and Initial t{max}: Calculate the starting voxel index: i = \lfloor Px / V \rfloor, j = \lfloor Py / V \rfloor, k = \lfloor Pz / V \rfloor, where P = O + t{enter} D. Clamp indices to [x{min}, x{max}), etc.. Calculate the fractional distance into the current voxel: fa = (Pa \bmod V) / V. Calculate the distance to the next boundary in t: Ta = \begin{cases} (1.0 - fa) \cdot \Delta ta & \text{if } Da > 0 \\ fa \cdot \Delta ta & \text{if } Da < 0 \\ \infty & \text{if } Da = 0 \end{cases} Note: If the origin is exactly on a boundary, floating-point conventions must be handled carefully to avoid ambiguity. 5. Traverse: While the current voxel (i, j, k) is within the grid bounds and current t \le t{exit}: 1. Visit voxel (i, j, k). 2. Identify the axis with the smallest Ta. 3. Update the voxel index for that axis: idx{axis} += s{axis}. 4. Update the t{max} for that axis: T{axis} += \Delta t{axis}. 5. Update current t \leftarrow T{axis}. 6. (Optional) Track the last moved axis to determine the surface normal of the hit voxel if a collision is detected. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def amanatideswoo(origin, direction, gridmin, gridmax, voxelsize=1.0, maxt=float('inf')): """ Traverses a uniform voxel grid along a ray in front-to-back order. Assumes origin is already clipped to the grid's AABB if outside. gridmin and gridmax are exclusive index bounds for each axis. """ # 1. Clip ray to grid AABB tenter = -float('inf') texit = float('inf') for axis in range(3): if abs(direction[axis]) < 1e-6: if not (gridmin[axis] <= origin[axis] < gridmax[axis]): return # Ray misses grid else: inv = 1.0 / direction[axis] ta = (gridmin[axis] - origin[axis]) inv tb = (gridmax[axis] - origin[axis]) inv if ta > tb: ta, tb = tb, ta tenter = max(tenter, ta) texit = min(texit, tb) if texit < max(tenter, 0.0): return # Ray misses grid # 2. Start at entry point t = max(tenter, 0.0) pos = [origin[i] + t direction[i] for i in range(3)] # 3. Initial voxel indices voxel = [int(math.floor(pos[i] / voxelsize)) for i in range(3)] for i in range(3): voxel[i] = max(gridmin[i], min(voxel[i], gridmax[i] - 1)) # 4. Step signs step = [0, 0, 0] for i in range(3): if direction[i] > 0: step[i] = 1 elif direction[i] < 0: step[i] = -1 # 5. tdelta and tmax tdelta = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): if abs(direction[i]) > 1e-6: tdelta[i] = voxelsize / abs(direction[i]) fract = (pos[i] / voxelsize) - voxel[i] if direction[i] > 0: tmax[i] = (1.0 - fract) tdelta[i] else: tmax[i] = fract tdelta[i] else: tdelta[i] = float('inf') tmax[i] = float('inf') # 6. Traverse loop while True: if not (gridmin[0] <= voxel[0] < gridmax[0] and gridmin[1] <= voxel[1] < gridmax[1] and gridmin[2] <= voxel[2] < gridmax[2]): break if t > texit: break yield tuple(voxel) # Find axis with smallest tmax minaxis = 0 if tmax[1] < tmax[minaxis]: minaxis = 1 if tmax[2] < tmax[minaxis]: minaxis = 2 voxel[minaxis] += step[minaxis] tmax[minaxis] += tdelta[minaxis] t = tmax[minaxis] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ties: If two or three t{max} values are equal, the ray hits an edge or corner. A strict if/else chain may skip cells. Solutions include stepping all tied axes simultaneously, emitting all "supercover" cells, or using a deterministic half-open convention. Zero Direction Components: If Da = 0, the ray never crosses planes on that axis. Set \Delta ta and Ta to \infty to avoid branching in the loop. Avoid 0 \times \infty NaNs by initializing these axes separately. Boundary Conventions: Origins exactly on voxel planes can cause floor operations to place the origin in a neighboring cell. Define a clear half-open interval convention and test points just below, on, and above boundaries. Numerical Robustness: Large world coordinates, small direction components, and negative zero can cause precision issues. Avoid adding random epsilons; use explicit conventions and targeted tolerance. Time Complexity: O(K), where K is the number of visited cells. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, storing only a few vectors per ray. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Extremely fast per-voxel update (a few comparisons and one addition); output-sensitive; robust for uniform grids. Limitations: Only suitable for uniform grids; performance degrades if the ray traverses many empty cells (though better than marching); requires careful handling of ties and boundaries. When to use: Volume rendering, voxel-based collision detection, and any scenario requiring efficient traversal of a uniform spatial grid. When not to use: Non-uniform grids (the algorithm assumes uniform voxel sizes). The algorithm was introduced by John Amanatides and Andrew Woo in the paper "A Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing," published at Eurographics in 1987. It is a classic example of transforming continuous ray geometry into a discrete event sequence, optimizing the inner loop for ray tracing performance. It is widely used in voxel engines and real-time graphics. CPU-based implementations are simpler for learning but less efficient than GPU compute shaders for large scenes. tacf/cpu-voxel-raytracer-raylib, https://github.com/tacf/cpu-voxel-raytracer-raylib, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal | 3D DDA Learning Guide, https://edukatesengkang.com/2026/08/30/how-to-learn-amanatides-woo-fast-voxel-traversal-3d-dda-tmax-tdelta-grid-crossings-and-robust-ray-marching/, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Make yourself a Voxel Engine THIS weekend, https://daymare.net/blogs/voxel-engine-in-a-weekend/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) viljanvr/VisualNifty, https://github.com/viljanvr/VisualNifty, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ApaarRaina/DiffTomo, https://github.com/ApaarRaina/DiffTomo, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical Volume Traversal with Adaptive Termination
head: Pyramidal Volume Traversal, TraceRay2
body: Hierarchical Volume Traversal with Adaptive Termination is a ray tracing algorithm that uses a pyramidal data structure of binary volumes to skip empty regions and an adaptive termination criterion to stop tracing when opacity changes become negligible. Unlike geometric ray tracing, which uses bounding volumes or spatial subdivision with lists of primitives, this method uses a hierarchical binary volume structure, which is more efficient for volume data because volume datasets have tens of millions of spatially ordered cells with single samples, whereas geometric scenes have hundreds of cells with many primitives. The method traverses a ray through a hierarchy of binary volumes (a pyramid) to determine which regions contain data. It adapts the traversal depth based on the content and terminates early if the accumulated opacity is sufficiently high. Input: Ray parameter \mathbf{u} (defining the ray direction and origin), the pyramidal binary volume structure \{Vm\}, the volume data (color and opacity fields), and parameters \epsilon, m{max}, m{min}, and M (total levels). Output: Final ray color \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}) and accumulated opacity \alpha(\mathbf{u}). The core data structure is a pyramid of binary volumes. Binary Volumes Vm: For each level m \in \{0, \dots, M\}, Vm is a 3D grid of bits. V0 is the base level, and Vm for m > 0 is derived from V{m-1}. Memory layout: (2^{M+1} - 1)/7 bits total for the pyramid. Volume Data: Monochrome color and opacity fields. Memory layout: 2N^3 bytes for color and opacity per voxel. Output Image: Memory layout: P^2 bytes. The binary volumes are defined recursively to indicate the presence of non-zero opacity in their spatial extent. Base Level (V0): V0(\mathbf{i}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \alpha(\mathbf{i} + \Delta\mathbf{i}) = 1 \\ 0 & \text{for } \mathbf{i} \in \{1, 2, \dots, N-1\}^3 \text{ and any } \Delta\mathbf{i} \in \{0, 1\}^3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \alpha is the opacity field, \mathbf{i} is the index, and the condition checks if any of the eight voxels at the vertices of the cell have opacity equal to 1. Higher Levels (Vm, m > 0): Vm(\mathbf{i}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } V{m-1}(2\mathbf{i} - \Delta\mathbf{i}) = 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} for \mathbf{i} \in \{1, 2, \dots, \frac{N-1}{m+1}\}^3 and any \Delta\mathbf{i} \in \{0, 1\}^3. This means a cell at level m is 1 if any of the eight cells at level m-1 that form its octants are 1. \epsilon: Threshold for significant color change. Default value 0.05. Higher values reduce rendering time, lower values reduce artifacts. m{max}: Starting level for traversal. Set to M - 2 for all values of M to minimize traversal costs. m{min}: Lowest level to descend to before rendering. Set to 2 for the current implementation to avoid the high cost of ray-cell intersections at level zero. M: Total number of levels in the pyramid. The algorithm processes each ray \mathbf{u} as follows: 1. Initialize ray color \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}) and opacity \alpha(\mathbf{u}) to 0. 2. Set ray position \mathbf{x} to the entry point of the ray into the volume using First(u). 3. Set current level m to m{max}. 4. Loop while the ray position \mathbf{x} is in bounds (InBounds(x)) and accumulated opacity \alpha(\mathbf{u}) is less than or equal to 1 - \epsilon: a. Calculate the cell index \mathbf{i} at current level m containing point \mathbf{x} using the Index(m, x) procedure. b. If the cell value Vm(\mathbf{i}) is 1 and m > m{min}: i. Decrement level m by 1 to descend into the hierarchy (m:= m - 1). ii. Continue to the next iteration of the loop to re-evaluate the cell at the new level. c. Else (if cell is 1 and at min level, or cell is 0): i. If the cell value Vm(\mathbf{i}) is 1: 1. Determine the exit point of the current cell along the ray using Next(m, x, u). 2. Call RenderCell(u, x, Next(m, x, u)) to render the interval from current \mathbf{x} to the next cell entry point. ii. Advance to the next cell on the same level. iii. While the parent of the new cell differs from the parent of the old cell and m < M: 1. Move up to the parent cell (\mathbf{i}:= \text{Parent}(m, \mathbf{i})). 2. Increment level m (m:= m + 1). iv. Update ray position \mathbf{x} to the entry point of the next cell at the current level m (\mathbf{x}:= \text{Next}(m, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u})). The RenderCell procedure handles the resampling and compositing for a specific interval along the ray defined by entry \mathbf{x}1 and exit \mathbf{x}2. 1. Define image bounds \mathbf{U}1 and \mathbf{U}2 for the cell interval using Image(x1) and Image(x2). 2. Loop through evenly spaced sample locations \mathbf{U} within this interval from \mathbf{U}1 to \mathbf{U}2. Evenly spaced locations are superimposed to avoid noise artifacts caused by resampling at non-uniformly spaced points determined by ray-cell intersections. 3. For each sample \mathbf{U}: a. Get object space coordinates \mathbf{x} using Object(U). b. Check if the base level binary volume V0 at the index of \mathbf{x} is 1 (V0(Index(0, x))). c. If 1: i. Resample color \hat{C}(\mathbf{U}) and opacity \alpha(\mathbf{U}) from the volume data using Sample. ii. Composite the sample into the ray: \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}):= \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}) + \hat{C}(\mathbf{U})(1 - \alpha(\mathbf{u})) \alpha(\mathbf{u}):= \alpha(\mathbf{u}) + \alpha(\mathbf{U})(1 - \alpha(\mathbf{u})). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def TraceRay2(u, epsilon, mmax, mmin, M, V, InBounds, First, Index, Next, Parent, RenderCell): Cray = 0.0 alpharay = 0.0 x = First(u) m = mmax while InBounds(x) and alpharay <= 1.0 - epsilon: i = Index(m, x) if V[m][i] == 1 and m > mmin: m -= 1 continue else: if V[m][i] == 1: xnext = Next(m, x, u) RenderCell(u, x, xnext, Cray, alpharay, V) xnext = Next(m, x, u) while m < M and Parent(m, Index(m, xnext)) != Parent(m, i): i = Parent(m, i) m += 1 x = xnext return Cray, alpharay def RenderCell(u, x1, x2, Cray, alpharay, V): U1 = Image(x1) U2 = Image(x2) for U in range(U1, U2 + 1): x = Object(U) if V[0][Index(0, x)] == 1: Csample = Sample(V.color, x) alphasample = Sample(V.opacity, x) Cray = Cray + Csample (1.0 - alpharay) alpharay = alpharay + alphasample (1.0 - alpharay) return Cray, alpharay Note: Image, Object, and Sample are standard projection and resampling functions. Resampling Artifacts: Resampling at non-uniformly spaced points (determined by ray-cell intersections) adds noise artifacts to the image. The solution is to superimpose evenly spaced sample locations and only resample at those specific points. Level Zero Descent: Descending to level zero is inefficient for orthographic projections because ray-cell intersection costs exceed simple differencing. The solution is to stop descent at m{min}=2 and render level-zero cells within that higher-level cell. Time Complexity: The traversal skips empty regions, reducing the number of samples taken. The adaptive termination stops tracing when opacity is high, further reducing work. The cost of traversal is minimized by starting at m{max} = M - 2. Memory Complexity: The memory required is 2N^3 bytes for the volume data, (2^{M+1} - 1)/7 bits for the pyramid, and P^2 bytes for the output image. Strengths: Efficient for volume data with large empty regions. The hierarchical structure allows skipping large empty areas. The adaptive termination reduces work for opaque regions. Limitations: Inefficient if the volume is mostly opaque or has no empty regions, as the hierarchy may not provide significant skipping. The need for evenly spaced sampling adds complexity. When to Use: Suitable for volume datasets with significant empty space and where ray-cell intersection costs are high (e.g., orthographic projections). When Not to Use: Not suitable for geometric scenes with many primitives per cell, as the method is optimized for volume data with single samples per cell. The method was introduced in the paper "Efficient ray tracing of volume data". It is based on the observation that volume datasets contain coherent regions of uninteresting voxels (opacity zero) and can be encoded as a hierarchical spatial enumeration represented by a pyramid of binary volumes. The method is also known as Pyramidal Volume Traversal or TraceRay2. Efficient ray tracing of volume data, https://doi.org/10.1145/78964.78965, fetched 2026-10-25

name: Empty-space skipping
head: Block Empty Space Skipping, Chebyshev Empty Space Skipping, Empty Region Skipping, Occupancy Grid Pruning
body: Empty-space skipping (ESS) is a ray marching optimization that accelerates volume rendering by skipping regions of the scene that are empty or occluded, thereby reducing the number of samples required to evaluate the radiance field. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like GL-NeRF or VoISDF by explicitly maintaining auxiliary data structures (occupancy grids or distance maps) to prune traversal, whereas other siblings may rely on hierarchical tree structures or adaptive sampling rates without explicit empty-region culling. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, volume dimensions, sampling factor, and precomputed occupancy/distance maps. Outputs: Accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: Occupancy Grid / Distance Map: A 3D texture (texOccupancyMap or texDistanceMap) storing precomputed values, accessed via texelFetch. texOccupancyMap: Stores binary occupancy (1 if occupied, 0 if empty). texDistanceMap: Stores distance to the nearest occupied voxel. Parameters: essType: Integer flag. 1 = Block Empty Space Skipping; 2 = Chebyshev Empty Space Skipping. alphathre: Opacity threshold for empty regions. Typical value: 10^{-2}. earlystopeps: Transmittance threshold for early termination. Typical value: 10^{-4}. samplingfactor: Controls step count relative to volume dimensions. ditheringMode: Integer flag for ray dithering. 1 = procedural noise; 2 = sampled from texNoise texture. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Calculate the number of steps and the step vector. n{\text{steps}} = \lceil \text{dim}{\max} \times \text{ray\length} \times \text{sampling\factor} \rceil \text{step\vector} = \frac{\mathbf{d}}{\|\mathbf{d}\|} \times \frac{\text{ray\length}}{n{\text{steps}} - 1} Handle degenerate rays (infinite, NaN, or length > \sqrt{3}) by terminating immediately. 2. name: Object-Order Empty Space Skipping
head: Block min-max culling, Front-to-back ray-casting with bounding box culling, GPU-based Ray-Casting with Object-Order Empty Space Skipping
body: Object-Order Empty Space Skipping is a GPU-based ray-casting acceleration technique that reduces the computational overhead of traversing transparent regions in a volume by culling entire blocks of voxels before sample evaluation. It differs from image-order methods by using view-dependent bounding geometry to determine ray entry and exit depths per pixel, thereby skipping large portions of empty space with minimal per-pixel overhead. Unlike macrocell or BSP-tree approaches that require complex tree traversal logic, this method relies on simple rasterization of block boundaries to establish search ranges, making it highly efficient for real-time isosurface rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D texture storing the volume data, camera parameters (position c, screen coordinates (x, y)), and a block min-max structure storing the minimum and maximum scalar values for each block in the volume. Output: A rendered image with isosurface shading, where rays are terminated early if they traverse inactive (transparent) blocks. Data Structures: Block Min-Max Structure: For a regular subdivision of the volume into blocks of size B^3 (e.g., 4^3 or 8^3 voxels), this structure stores two values per block: min and max. These represent the minimum and maximum scalar values present in the block's voxel data. Bounding Geometry: A set of 3D primitives representing the bounding boxes of active blocks. This geometry is kept in GPU memory and updated when the isovalue changes. Steps: 1. Ray Direction Computation: For each pixel (x, y), compute the ray direction vector d(x, y) in volume coordinates based on the camera position c: p(t, x, y) = c + t \cdot d(x, y) where t is the distance along the ray. 2. Ray Depth Range Initialization: Determine the initial search range [t{start}(x, y), t{exit}(x, y)] for each ray by rasterizing the block bounding geometry: t{start}: Rasterize the front faces of the active block bounding geometry. Use a depth test (e.g., GLLESS) to retain the closest intersection point, which corresponds to the entry point into the first active block. t{exit}: Rasterize the back faces of the active block bounding geometry. Use an inverted depth test (e.g., GLGREATER) to retain the farthest intersection point, which corresponds to the exit point from the last active block. 3. Ray Casting Loop: Iterate through the volume in front-to-back order within the fragment shader: Sample the volume at the current ray position. Object-Order Skip: If the current ray segment falls within a region covered by inactive blocks (blocks where the isovalue is outside [min, max]), skip the sampling process for that segment. This is handled by the depth range computed in Step 2, which excludes inactive blocks from the initial search range unless they are enclosed by active blocks. Image-Order Skip: For samples within active blocks but in transparent regions, use adaptive sampling or early termination based on accumulated opacity. Refine the isosurface intersection position using iterative bisection if the ray crosses the isovalue. Parameters: Block Size: The volume is subdivided into blocks of size 4^3 or 8^3 voxels. Smaller blocks increase culling precision but increase memory overhead for the min-max structure. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Enclosed Inactive Blocks: Inactive blocks enclosed by active blocks are not excluded from the search range by the bounding geometry because the rasterization only captures the outer boundary of active regions. Samples in these enclosed inactive blocks are skipped on a per-sample basis early in the ray-casting loop, incurring a small overhead. Precision: Depth values for t{start} and t{exit} must be computed with sufficient precision to avoid gaps or overlaps in the bounding geometry, which could lead to incorrect ray ranges. A variant of block min-max culling designed for pre-integrated volume rendering. It modifies the region covered by each block so that each block covers a region of thickness at least the sampling distance, creating overlaps between adjacent blocks. This allows a line segment formed by two sampling points to be tested for transparency using only one block, avoiding the overhead of determining which of multiple intersecting blocks are transparent. Unlike previous methods where a line segment may intersect at most three blocks and requires testing all intersecting blocks, this method tests only one block due to the overlapping region design. Time Complexity: The culling overhead is minimal, as it relies on rasterization of bounding geometry, which is highly optimized on GPUs. The main cost is the ray casting loop, which is reduced by skipping inactive blocks. Memory Complexity: Requires additional memory for the block min-max structure, proportional to the number of blocks in the volume. For large volumes that do not fit in GPU memory, a second level of coarser bricks is maintained, increasing memory usage. Performance: In empty regions, this approach results in a considerable speed-up because only one texture fetch is needed to check the mean value of the block. However, in complex scenes with many active blocks, the overhead of maintaining the bounding geometry and min-max structure may reduce performance gains. Strengths: Simple implementation, low per-pixel overhead, effective for real-time isosurface rendering. Limitations: Enclosed inactive blocks are not fully excluded, leading to per-sample overhead in those regions. Performance may degrade with complex shaders and texture indirections. Object-Order Empty Space Skipping was introduced in the context of GPU-based ray-casting for real-time volume rendering. It builds on earlier approaches that used multiple rendering passes for ray casting, replacing them with a single pass and front-to-back looping in the fragment shader. The technique was developed to overcome limitations of earlier empty space skipping methods, such as high overhead and poor performance with complex shaders. It is widely used in real-time volume rendering applications, particularly for isosurface visualization. name: Early Shader Termination
head: Early End of Computation, Early z-test optimization, Two-pass empty space culling
body: Early Shader Termination is an optimization technique that discards the execution of complex decoding shaders for fragments likely to represent empty space by using an early z-test in a two-pass rendering approach. It builds on Object-Order Empty Space Skipping by adding a lightweight pre-check to avoid expensive shader execution in empty regions. Compared to rendering uncompressed data, this approach initially perceives a loss in performance of a factor of 2-3 due to complex shaders and texture indirections; however, in empty regions, it results in a considerable speed-up because only one texture fetch is needed to check the mean. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A compressed volume dataset where each block (macro-cell) has an associated index texture I storing metadata (specifically the mean value in the R-component) and dependent data textures C1, C2. A slicing polygon representing the current view frustum or volume boundary. Output: A rendered image where empty space fragments are skipped, and depth values are correctly updated to allow subsequent fragments to pass depth tests. Data Structures: Index Texture I: Stores block metadata. The R-component holds the mean value of the block. Dependent Textures C1, C2: Store difference information or raw data, addressed using components of I. Steps: 1. First Pass (Empty Space Detection): Render the slicing polygon twice. In the first pass, issue a simple pixel shader program. In the shader, access index texture I and check the mean value stored in the R-component. If the mean value is zero, render the fragment with color and opacity set to zero. This does not affect the color buffer but sets the depth value in the depth buffer. If the mean value is not zero, discard the fragment using a kill instruction. This prevents the fragment from affecting the color or depth buffer. 2. Second Pass (Complex Rendering): Render the slicing polygon again with the complex shader. Set the depth test to GLGREATER in the second pass. The early z-test only lets fragments pass that were discarded in the first pass (where mean \neq 0). All other fragments (where mean = 0) are discarded before entering the complex shader. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def earlyshadertermination(fragments, indextextureI, complexdecodefunc): """ Simulates the two-pass early shader termination optimization. fragments: list of objects with.coords,.blockid,.z (depth) indextextureI: dict mapping blockid to objects with.R (mean value) complexdecodefunc: callable that returns decoded color for non-empty blocks """ depthbuffer = {} # Maps fragment coordinates to depth from pass 1 pass1discarded = [] # Pass 1: Simple pixel shader for frag in fragments: meanval = indextextureI[frag.blockid].R if meanval == 0: # Empty space: write depth, zero color/opacity depthbuffer[frag.coords] = frag.z pass1discarded.append(False) else: # Non-empty space: discard via kill instruction # Depth buffer retains the last valid depth for this coordinate pass1discarded.append(True) # Pass 2: Complex shader with GLGREATER depth test finaloutput = [] for i, frag in enumerate(fragments): if not pass1discarded[i]: # Early z-test fails: GLGREATER requires frag.z > depthbuffer[frag.coords] # Since pass 1 wrote frag.z, frag.z > frag.z is false. Fragment discarded. continue # Early z-test passes for discarded fragments (mean != 0) lastdepth = depthbuffer.get(frag.coords, -float('inf')) if frag.z > lastdepth: # GLGREATER decoded = complexdecodefunc(frag, indextextureI) finaloutput.append(decoded) return finaloutput Parameters: Depth Test Function: Must be set to GLGREATER in the second pass to leverage the early z-test correctly. Mean Threshold: Zero is used as the threshold for empty space. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Buffer Consistency: If a fragment is discarded in the shader (via kill), the depth value of the fragment rendered last is still valid in the depth buffer. This must be accounted for when using depth tests, as the discarded fragment does not update the depth buffer. Performance Overhead: The two-pass approach introduces overhead. The initial performance loss compared to uncompressed rendering is a factor of 2-3 due to the complexity of the shaders and texture indirections. Adds spatial coherence checks along the scanline direction to skip entire segments of empty space within a macro-cell projection. It builds on Early Shader Termination by optimizing the scope of the termination check. Time Complexity: In empty regions, the complexity is reduced to one texture fetch per block to check the mean. In non-empty regions, the full complex shader is executed. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the index texture I and dependent textures C1, C2. Measured Performance: On an Intel P4 1900 MHz machine, this approach saves another 5 percent of overall rendering time on average when combined with other optimizations like Early End of Computation. Strengths: Considerable speed-up in empty regions, which are frequent in numerical simulation results. Limitations: Initial performance loss of 2-3x compared to uncompressed rendering due to shader complexity and indirections. Requires hardware support for early z-test. The technique was proposed in the context of compression domain volume rendering to address performance losses caused by complex shader programs and texture indirections. It leverages the early z-test feature available on target graphics architectures to avoid executing pixel shaders for fragments that are likely to decode empty space. The concept of terminating computation early is also discussed in the context of cell-based first-hit ray casting, where rendering ends as soon as all pixels are covered, saving approximately 5 percent of overall rendering time. name: Early Scanline Termination
body: Early Scanline Termination is an optimization that stops processing a scanline as soon as a local ray through a pixel does not intersect any iso-surfaces, reducing the number of local rays cast per pixel. It builds on Early Shader Termination by adding a spatial coherence check along the scanline direction, allowing the renderer to skip entire segments of empty space within a macro-cell projection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projected macro-cell, set of surface cells within the macro-cell, current scanline (row or column of pixels), and the image buffer. Output: Updated image buffer with colors for intersected pixels; identification of erroneous blank pixels (holes) for post-processing. Data Structures: Image Buffer: Stores color values for each pixel. Sequence Flags: Two flags per pixel indicating whether the pixel was recently dropped due to horizontal or vertical early scanline termination. Flags are set to 1 for all empty dropped pixels. The bounds of each new sequence of dropped pixels are marked by setting the sequence flag of the pixel immediately preceding the sequence and the pixel immediately following the sequence to 0. A pixel through which a regular local ray has been cast has its sequence flags reset to 0. Steps: 1. Identify all scanlines intersecting the macro-cell projection. 2. Check for problem cases by calculating a representative surface normal for each surface cell and checking dot products with two reference vectors. If a boundary cell prohibits termination, project its center point. The collection of these projections forms a critical region. 3. Iterate through pixels of a scanline from one boundary to the other. If a local ray does not intersect any iso-surface and the pixel is outside the critical region, stop processing the scanline. Mark all remaining empty pixels as dropped, setting the appropriate sequence flag (horizontal or vertical) to 1. Set the sequence flag of the pixel immediately preceding the first dropped pixel and the pixel immediately following the last dropped pixel to 0 to mark the sequence bounds. If a regular local ray is cast through a pixel, reset its sequence flags to 0. 4. After frame completion, identify sequences of blank pixels with sequence flags set, bounded on both sides by non-blank pixels with unset flags. Cast rays from these pixels through the complete volume to fill the holes. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Left-facing surface normals: If projected surface normals point towards the left, early termination is disallowed for scanlines intersecting those parts until all such intersections are processed. Dangerous faces: Certain surface orientations can cause errors if termination is applied. Errors: Early scanline termination can lead to errors in about 0.017 percent of pixels on average, resulting in visible holes. These holes must be identified and filled after frame completion. Sequence Flag Management: Flags must be carefully managed to correctly identify erroneous sequences. Pixels erroneously dropped will never be part of a dropped sequence again. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def earlyscanlinetermination(macrocell, scanlinepixels, imagebuffer, sequenceflags, ishorizontal): # Standard projection of 3D cell centers to 2D image coordinates criticalpoints = [projecttoimage(cell.center) for cell in macrocell.surfacecells if cell.prohibitstermination] terminated = False firstdroppedidx = None lastdroppedidx = None for i, pixel in enumerate(scanlinepixels): if terminated: break # Standard local ray intersection with macro-cell iso-surfaces intersection = castlocalray(pixel) if intersection is not None: # Standard shading and color computation imagebuffer[pixel] = computecolor(intersection) sequenceflags[pixel] = (0, 0) else: # Standard spatial query to check if pixel is outside the critical region if isoutsidecriticalregion(pixel, criticalpoints): terminated = True firstdroppedidx = i for j in range(i, len(scanlinepixels)): p = scanlinepixels[j] imagebuffer[p] = BLANK if ishorizontal: sequenceflags[p] = (1, sequenceflags[p][1]) else: sequenceflags[p] = (sequenceflags[p][0], 1) lastdroppedidx = j # Mark sequence bounds by setting preceding/following flags to 0 if firstdroppedidx > 0: sequenceflags[scanlinepixels[firstdroppedidx - 1]] = (0, 0) if lastdroppedidx + 1 < len(scanlinepixels): sequenceflags[scanlinepixels[lastdroppedidx + 1]] = (0, 0) def fillholes(imagebuffer, sequenceflags, imageheight, imagewidth): for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): if imagebuffer[y, x] == BLANK and sequenceflags[y, x] != (0, 0): # Verify bounds: preceding and following pixels must be non-blank with flags (0,0) # to confirm it is an erroneously dropped sequence imagebuffer[y, x] = castlocalray((x, y)) Performance: Saves another 17 percent of overall rendering time on average. Reduces rays per pixel from 2.483 to 1.285 in the tested scenario. Memory Complexity: Requires two sequence flags per pixel for tracking. Limitations: Errors occur in about 0.017 percent of pixels on average, resulting in visible holes that require post-processing. Performance is dependent on the data set and the position of the view point. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. head: Macrocell Acceleration, Macrocell Zero-Density Skipping, Macrocell rendering with zero-density skip, Ray marcher with macrocell, Skipping macrocells with zero density
body: This method accelerates volume rendering by dividing the volume into coarse grid elements (macrocells) and precomputing a boolean or aggregate value for each to identify and skip regions containing only zero-density cells during ray marching. It builds on the parent Empty-space skipping by applying the concept to a fixed coarse grid hierarchy rather than dynamic traversal structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A structured volume dataset, a transfer function mapping density to opacity/color, and a set of camera rays. Output: Rendered image with reduced computational load in empty regions. Data Structures: Macrocell Grid: A 3D array aligned with the volume, where each element corresponds to a macrocell. Macrocell Values: Each macrocell stores a precomputed boolean indicating if the surface passes through it, or an aggregate density value computed from its constituent fine cells. If the value indicates zero density, the macrocell is considered empty. Steps: 1. Precomputation: For each macrocell in the coarse grid, compute the aggregate density value or boolean skip flag from its constituent fine cells based on the transfer function densities. 2. Ray Traversal: For each pixel, generate a ray and use a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (3DDDA) to traverse the macrocell grid. 3. Macrocell Check: At each macrocell intersection, fetch the precomputed boolean or aggregate value. 4. Skip Decision: If the macrocell contains only zero-density cells (boolean is false or aggregate is zero), skip processing the entire macrocell and advance the ray to the next macrocell boundary. 5. Marching: If the macrocell is not empty, perform standard ray marching within the macrocell, sampling fine cells and accumulating opacity/color. 6. Termination: Stop when the ray exits the volume. Formulas: Let M{ijk} be the aggregate density or boolean flag of macrocell at indices (i,j,k). Let C{lmn} be the density of fine cell at indices (l,m,n). Skip condition: If M{ijk} = 0 (or boolean is false), skip macrocell. Aggregation method: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Macrocell Size: The number of voxels per macrocell dimension. 23 voxels per macrocell is recommended for best performance; 13, 43, and 83 are also tested. Threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overhead Dominance: Performance degrades if the fraction of skippable macrocells is small, because the extra memory access for retrieving macrocell values and condition checks per coarse element adds overhead without sufficient savings. Transfer Function Dependency: Performance gains depend heavily on the transfer function, as macrocell values are computed from transfer function densities. Dataset Variability: On datasets with very few zero-density macrocells (e.g., Engine dataset with 12) or high overhead per check (e.g., Agulhas dataset with 1,395,619 skipped), macrocell skipping can be slower than standard ray marching. accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor[0] += color[0] alpha accumulatedcolor[1] += color[1] alpha accumulatedcolor[2] += color[2] alpha accumulatedopacity += alpha if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break t += stepsize if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity def samplevolume(volume, x, y, z): ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) ix = max(0, min(ix, len(volume)-1)) iy = max(0, min(iy, len(volume[0])-1)) iz = max(0, min(iz, len(volume[0][0])-1)) return volume[ix][iy][iz] def applytransferfunction(density): return [density, density, density], density A GPU-accelerated space-skipping technique for structured volumes that replaces clustered proxy boxes with a triangle mesh bounding the surface between active and inactive macrocells. It solves the host-GPU transfer bottleneck and high depth complexity of prior proxy-box methods by generating the boundary geometry entirely on the GPU and using native RTX hardware for ray-triangle intersection. Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA is a ray traversal technique that accelerates volume rendering by combining a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) for coarse macrocell traversal with adaptive step sizing based on opacity upper bounds. It solves the problem of inefficient sampling in sparse or low-opacity regions by skipping empty macrocells entirely and reducing sample counts in low-opacity ones. Unlike its parent Ray Marcher with Macrocell Empty Space Skipping, which primarily focuses on binary empty-space skipping, this method introduces granularity by adapting the step size within non-empty cells. It differs from Triangulated Active Brick Boundary Mesh for Space Skipping by using a regular grid structure rather than a mesh. An optimization that reduces the number of local rays by trimming each macro-cell to the smallest cuboid containing its portions of the iso-surfaces, rather than projecting the entire macro-cell. It works by initializing a cuboid to size zero and iterating through all cells of the macro-cell; whenever a surface cell is encountered, the cuboid is extended to the smallest necessary size so that it contains this cell. The resulting cuboid is then projected instead of the macro-cell. This saves about 28 percent of overall rendering time on average, though this gain is dependent on the data set and viewpoint position. Time Complexity: Precomputation is O(N) where N is the number of fine cells. Ray marching time is reduced proportionally to the fraction of skipped macrocells. Memory Complexity: O(M) where M is the number of macrocells. Measured Performance: MRI Dataset: Increasing skipped macrocells from 0 to 1,190 reduces rendering time from 44.83 ms to 26.05 ms. Heptane Dataset: Improves time from 51.92 ms to 46.3 ms. Advection Dataset: Improves time from 58.14 ms to 46.29 ms. Engine Dataset: Only 12 macrocells have zero density, leading to worse performance (43.61 ms with macrocell vs 41.46 ms without). Agulhas Dataset: 1,395,619 skipped macrocells, but performance is worse (55.34 ms with macrocell vs 41.53 ms without) due to overhead. Fiber Surface Dataset: Performance without macrocells is 4x-8x slower than with 23-voxel macrocells. Strengths: Simple implementation, effective for sparse volumes with large empty regions. Limitations: Overhead can dominate if skipping fraction is low. Performance is transfer-function dependent. When to Use: Sparse volumes with significant empty space. When Not to Use: Dense volumes or when the transfer function results in few zero-density macrocells. The method originates from research on direct multifield volume ray casting of fiber surfaces and direct volume rendering of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement data. It was developed as an optimization to handle sparse data and improve rendering performance by avoiding unnecessary computations in transparent regions. It is used in interactive fiber surface exploration and tree-based AMR volume rendering pipelines. name: Triangulated Active Brick Boundary Mesh for Space Skipping
head: Active Brick Boundary Mesh, Active Region Boundary Geometry, Boundary Mesh Space Skipping, RTX-Accelerated Empty Space Skipping using Triangulated Active Region Boundary Geometry
body: A GPU-accelerated space-skipping technique for structured volumes that replaces clustered proxy boxes with a triangle mesh bounding the surface between active and inactive macrocells. It solves the host-GPU transfer bottleneck and high depth complexity of prior proxy-box methods by generating the boundary geometry entirely on the GPU and using native RTX hardware for ray-triangle intersection. Inputs: Input volume dimensions Vx \times Vy \times Vz. Brick size K (default 16), defining macrocell resolution. Transfer function (TF) defining active scalar ranges. Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Outputs: Volume integration intervals [t0, t1] for active regions. Final pixel color. Data Structures: 1. Macrocell Grid: Size Mx \times My \times Mz, where Mx = \lfloor Vx/K \rfloor, etc. Each cell stores the minimum and maximum scalar values of input voxels mapping to it. 2. Active Bricks Mask: Boolean grid Mx \times My \times Mz on GPU. true if macrocell has non-zero alpha for current TF. 3. Vertex Array: Pre-allocated float3 array of size N{vtxMax} = (Mx+1)(My+1)(Mz+1). Contains all possible macrocell grid vertices. 4. Triangle Index Array: Pre-allocated int3 array of size N{triMax} (upper bound based on boundary geometry on macrocell faces). Stores indices referencing the Vertex Array. 5. numTriangles: Device-side integer counter, initialized to 0, used as an atomic offset for writing triangles. 6. OptiX BVH: Built over the generated triangle mesh using OptiX 7.2. Steps: 1. Initial Setup: Build Macrocell Grid on host, upload to GPU. Allocate GPU memory for Active Bricks Mask, Vertex Array, and Triangle Index Array. Initialize numTriangles = 0. 2. Active Cell Classification (Per TF Change): Launch CUDA kernel. Each thread maps to one macrocell (i,j,k). Check if macrocell's scalar range maps to non-zero alpha in TF. Write result to ActiveBricksMask[i][j][k]. 3. Boundary Triangle Generation (Per TF Change): Clear numTriangles = 0. Run three templated CUDA kernels for X, Y, Z orientations. For orientation D \in \{0,1,2\} (X,Y,Z): Thread maps to face perpendicular to axis D. Let curr be macrocell index on positive side of face, prev on negative side. If prev is out-of-bounds, treat as inactive. If ActiveBricksMask[prev] == ActiveBricksMask[curr], return. Get 4 vertex indices \{v0, v1, v2, v3\} spanning the face. triID = atomicAdd(&numTriangles, 2). If ActiveBricksMask[prev] is true (prev active, curr inactive): Triangles[triID] = {v0, v1, v2}, Triangles[triID+1] = {v0, v2, v3}. Else (curr active, prev inactive): Triangles[triID] = {v1, v0, v2}, Triangles[triID+1] = {v2, v0, v3}. Winding order points away from active towards inactive. Download numTriangles to host. 4. BVH Rebuild: Update OptiX geometry to reference generated mesh. Rebuild BVH with "optimize for traversal" flag. Compact BVH. 5. Ray Tracing & Integration: Initialize ray with t{min}=0, t{max}=\infty. Trace ray against BVH with DISABLEANYHIT flag. No Hit: Terminate ray. Hit: Get hit distance t{hit} and hit kind (front/back). Back-Facing Hit: Ray is inside volume. Integration interval [t0, t1] = [0, t{hit}]. Front-Facing Hit: Ray enters volume at t0 = t{hit}. Trace same ray with t{min}=t0 to find exit t1. Volume Integration: Sample volume texture at fixed rate dt=0.5 (interleaved) over [t0, t1]. Apply gradient shading and early ray termination. If ray terminated early, return. Else, trace new ray from t1 to find next segment. Repeat. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateboundarymesh(Mx, My, Mz, activecells, numtriangles, triangles): # activecells: 3D boolean array of shape (Mx+1, My+1, Mz+1) # numtriangles: mutable counter [0] # triangles: pre-allocated list of tuples (int3) # Dimensions for faces perpendicular to X, Y, Z dims = [ (range(Mx + 1), range(My), range(Mz)), # X-perpendicular faces (range(Mx), range(My + 1), range(Mz)), # Y-perpendicular faces (range(Mx), range(My), range(Mz + 1)) # Z-perpendicular faces ] for dimidx, (rangei, rangej, rangek) in enumerate(dims): for i in rangei: for j in rangej: for k in rangek: curr = (i, j, k) # prev is on the negative side of the face if dimidx == 0: prev = (i - 1, j, k) elif dimidx == 1: prev = (i, j - 1, k) else: prev = (i, j, k - 1) # Out-of-bounds treated as inactive prevactive = activecells[prev] if isinside(prev, Mx, My, Mz) else False curractive = activecells[curr] if prevactive == curractive: continue # Get 4 vertex indices spanning the face vi = getfacevertexindices(curr, dimidx, Mx, My, Mz) triid = numtriangles[0] numtriangles[0] += 2 if prevactive: triangles[triid] = (vi[0], vi[1], vi[2]) triangles[triid + 1] = (vi[0], vi[2], vi[3]) else: triangles[triid] = (vi[1], vi[0], vi[2]) triangles[triid + 1] = (vi[2], vi[0], vi[3]) def isinside(idx, Mx, My, Mz): return 0 <= idx[0] <= Mx and 0 <= idx[1] <= My and 0 <= idx[2] <= Mz def getfacevertexindices(curr, dimidx, Mx, My, Mz): # Returns 4 vertex indices into the flat vertex array of size (Mx+1)(My+1)(Mz+1) # Vertex index formula: i (My+1)(Mz+1) + j (Mz+1) + k strideyz = (My + 1) (Mz + 1) stridez = Mz + 1 i, j, k = curr if dimidx == 0: # X-perpendicular face at i # Vertices are at (i, j, k), (i, j+1, k), (i, j+1, k+1), (i, j, k+1) return (istrideyz + jstridez + k, istrideyz + (j+1)stridez + k, istrideyz + (j+1)stridez + (k+1), istrideyz + jstridez + (k+1)) elif dimidx == 1: # Y-perpendicular face at j return (istrideyz + jstridez + k, (i+1)strideyz + jstridez + k, (i+1)strideyz + jstridez + (k+1), istrideyz + jstridez + (k+1)) else: # Z-perpendicular face at k return (istrideyz + jstridez + k, (i+1)strideyz + jstridez + k, (i+1)strideyz + (j+1)stridez + k, istrideyz + (j+1)stridez + k) Pitfalls: Warp divergence: Reduced by lowering depth complexity to transitions between active/inactive regions. Host-GPU transfer bottleneck: Avoided by generating geometry on GPU, enabling interactive TF edits. Boundary Faces: Faces on the outside of the volume may have indices mapping outside the macrocell grid; treated as inactive macrocells. Unused Vertices: Pre-allocating all possible vertices results in unused vertices; accepted as a memory cost to avoid tracking usage. Time Complexity: Mesh generation is O(Mx My Mz) per TF change, taking low milliseconds. BVH rebuild is hardware-accelerated. Memory Complexity: Vertex array is fixed size (Mx+1)(My+1)(Mz+1). Triangle array is pre-allocated to upper bound. Performance: Significantly faster than Ganter and Manzke [GM19] due to no host-GPU transfer and no CPU clustering. Strengths: No host-GPU bottleneck. Lower depth complexity than proxy boxes. Hardware-accelerated intersection. Limitations: BVH must be rebuilt on TF change. Pre-allocated vertex array wastes memory. When to use: Interactive TF editing on GPU. Structured volumes. When not to use: Unstructured data. Origin: Ganter and Manzke [GM19] introduced RTX-accelerated space skipping using proxy boxes. This method extends it by replacing boxes with a boundary mesh. History: Inspired by unstructured volume rendering techniques using boundary tetrahedra [BKS97]. Implemented using OptiX 7.2. Usage: Used in interactive volume rendering systems supporting TF editing. name: Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA
head: Adaptive Macrocell Ray Marching
body: Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA is a ray marching algorithm that uses a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) to traverse macrocells of a volume. It adapts the sampling step size based on an opacity upper bound estimate for the current macrocell to skip empty or low-opacity regions. It solves the problem of inefficient sampling in sparse or low-opacity regions by skipping empty macrocells entirely and reducing sample counts in low-opacity ones. Unlike its parent Ray Marcher with Macrocell Empty Space Skipping, which primarily focuses on binary empty-space skipping, this method introduces granularity by adapting the step size within non-empty cells. It differs from Triangulated Active Brick Boundary Mesh for Space Skipping by using a regular grid structure rather than a mesh. The method traverses a volume using a hierarchical approach: a coarse macrocell grid guides the ray, and within each active macrocell, samples are taken at adaptive intervals. Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, near plane t{min}, far plane t{max}. Input: Volume data structure containing macrocell metadata (dimensions, spacing reciprocals, opacity upper bounds). Output: Accumulated color and opacity for the ray. The core data structure is the DeviceVolume (or equivalent), which must contain: macrocelldims: A 3D vector representing the number of macrocells in x, y, and z dimensions. macrocellspacingsrcp: A 3D vector storing the reciprocal of the macrocell spacing in world units, used to transform ray origin and direction into macrocell index space via multiplication. opacityupperbounds: A 3D array (or flattened 1D array) mapping macrocell indices to a scalar value representing the maximum possible opacity contribution of that cell. step: The base sampling step size in world units. floatepsilon: A small constant used to determine if a cell is effectively empty. ADAPTIVESAMPLING: A preprocessor macro that enables or disables the macrocell-based adaptive sampling logic; if defined, the adaptive path is taken, otherwise fixed-step marching is used. 1. Transform Ray to Macrocell Space: Calculate the ray origin and direction in macrocell index space: \mathbf{m}{org} = \mathbf{o} \times \text{macrocell\spacings\rcp} and \mathbf{m}{dir} = \mathbf{d} \times \text{macrocell\spacings\rcp}. 2. Initialize DDA: Initialize a 3D DDA iterator with \mathbf{m}{org}, \mathbf{m}{dir}, t{min}, t{max}, and macrocelldims. 3. Iterate Macrocells: For each macrocell (cell, t0, t1) returned by the DDA, retrieve the opacity upper bound r = \text{opacityUpperBound}(cell). 4. Skip Empty Cells: If |r| \le \text{float\epsilon}, the cell is considered empty and skipped. 5. Determine Step Size: Estimate the adaptive step size: ss = \text{sample\size\scaler}(\text{adaptiveSamplingRate}(step, r), t0, t1). 6. Initialize Interval: Set t = (tx, ty) = (t0, \min(t1, t0 + ss)). 7. Sample Within Macrocell: Loop while ty > tx: evaluate volume at tx, accumulate color/opacity, update tx = ty, update ty = \min(tx + ss, t1). 8. Non-Adaptive Fallback: If ADAPTIVESAMPLING is false, initialize t = (t{min}, \min(t{max}, t{min} + step)) and loop while (ty > tx) \land \text{body}(t), updating tx = ty and ty = \min(tx + step, t{max}). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveraymarchwithmacrocelldda(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, volume): # 1. Transform to macrocell space morg = rayorigin volume.macrocellspacingsrcp mdir = raydirection volume.macrocellspacingsrcp # 2. Initialize DDA iterator # Yields tuples of (cellindex, tenter, texit) dda = dda3(morg, mdir, tmin, tmax, volume.macrocelldims) accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # 3. Traverse macrocells for cellindex, tenter, texit in dda: # 4. Get opacity upper bound r = volume.opacityupperbounds[cellindex] # 5. Skip empty cells if abs(r) <= floatepsilon: continue # 6. Calculate adaptive step size # Standard heuristic: increases step size for lower opacity bounds basestep = adaptivesamplingrate(volume.basestep, r) # Clamps step to fit within [tenter, texit] stepsize = samplesizescaler(basestep, tenter, texit) # 7. Initialize sampling interval tcurr = tenter tnext = min(texit, tcurr + stepsize) # 8. Loop while interval is valid while tnext > tcurr: # Evaluate volume density and transfer function at tcurr density = samplevolume(volume, rayorigin + raydirection tcurr) color, alpha = transferfunction(density) # Standard front-to-back volume compositing accumulatedcolor += color alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedopacity += alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: return accumulatedcolor # Update interval tcurr = tnext tnext = min(tcurr + stepsize, texit) return accumulatedcolor floatepsilon = 1e-6 def dda3(org, dir, tmin, tmax, dims): # Standard 3D DDA traversal yielding (cell, tenter, texit) pass def adaptivesamplingrate(step, r): # Implementation-specific rate adjustment based on opacity bound return step (1.0 + r) def samplesizescaler(step, tenter, texit): # Ensures step does not exceed cell exit boundary return min(step, texit - tenter) def samplevolume(vol, pos): # Trilinear interpolation or hash lookup at pos pass def transferfunction(density): # Maps density to (color, alpha) pass Precision: When t{enter} and t{exit} are very close, floating-point errors may cause the loop condition ty > tx to fail prematurely or infinitely; a small epsilon should be used for comparisons. Zero Direction Components: If raydirection has a zero component, mdir will have a zero component, requiring the DDA implementation to handle degenerate traversal correctly. Opacity Upper Bound Accuracy: If opacityupperbounds are inaccurate (too high), adaptive sampling may not skip enough samples; if too low, empty cells might be sampled unnecessarily. The Resumable Ray Marching Iterator is a GPU-based ray traversal method designed to handle out-of-core volume rendering by pausing ray execution when data is missing from GPU memory and resuming it in subsequent passes. It builds on Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by adding state persistence via Multiple Render Targets (MRTs) and Z-buffer culling to ensure only active rays are processed during data loading. Unlike Network Ray Marching Iterator which may rely on different streaming heuristics, or Macrocell Grid Traversal with Majorant Densities which focuses on density bounds, this method explicitly manages the CPU-GPU synchronization required for dynamic data loading. The Network Ray Marching Iterator is a ray marching algorithm designed for distributed or networked rendering environments, typically leveraging GPU ray tracing APIs such as NVIDIA OptiX. It extends the parent Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by introducing block-level divergence control via blockany to manage thread synchronization across macrocell boundaries. This method is distinct from its siblings because it explicitly handles the "alive" status of rays in a distributed context, ensuring that inactive threads do not waste computation while maintaining adaptive sampling rates based on opacity upper bounds. This method accelerates volumetric path tracing by combining a coarse spatial partition (macrocells) with Delta Tracking (Woodcock tracking) to skip empty or low-opacity regions more efficiently than fixed-step marching. It sets itself apart from its parent Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by explicitly using the alpha component of the transfer function as a majorant extinction coefficient to determine probabilistic free-flight distances, allowing larger steps in homogeneous cells while maintaining unbiased Monte Carlo estimation. Space Skipping with 3DDDA is a mechanism to skip empty regions in sparse volume data using a uniform grid and 3DDDA algorithm. The fragment shader traverses the macrocell grid using 3DDDA in an outer loop. If a macrocell is nonempty, it enters the volume rendering loop with peak finding tests between samples. To begin sampling, it finds the first t to sample when entering a macrocell by solving for the maximum x after T{enter}: x^2/2 + bx = T{enter} \implies x{tenter} = \frac{-b + \sqrt{b^2 + 2aT{enter}}}{a}. It then computes the floor values \lfloor b x{tenter} \rfloor, T(\lfloor b x{tenter} \rfloor) and \frac{\partial T}{\partial x}(\lfloor b x{tenter} \rfloor), then samples and increments as in Equation 17 of the source. To avoid duplicate samples, it stores the greatest t at which it already sampled, and uses the maximum of that and T{enter}. The uniform grid stores min-max values of enclosed voxels, and coarse grids (e.g., 64^3 cells) work best on the GPU. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples taken, with a significantly reduced constant factor by skipping empty macrocells and reducing samples in low-opacity regions. Memory Complexity: O(M) where M is the number of macrocells, as the macrocell grid is much smaller than the full volume grid. Performance: Performance gains are most significant in sparse volumes or volumes with large empty regions. Fairly coarse grids (e.g., 64^3 cells) work best on the GPU. Strengths: Simple uniform grid structure that works well on GPUs. Limitations: Requires precomputed opacity upper bounds. When to Use: Sparse volumes, interactive rendering, and out-of-core rendering (with resumable variant). Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA originates from the instantvnr project, an interactive volume visualization tool based on multi-resolution hash encoding based neural representation. The method was developed by Qi Wu, Michael J. Doyle, and Kwan-Liu Ma, and published in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics in 2023. The use of 3DDDA for space skipping in volume rendering has earlier roots, as seen in work by Knoll et al. on volume ray casting with peak finding. The integration of adaptive sampling based on opacity bounds is a key innovation in instantvnr to handle the sparsity of neural volume representations efficiently. instantvnr, https://github.com/VIDILabs/instantvnr, fetched 2026-10-26 Volume Ray Casting with Peak Finding and Differential..., https://www.sci.utah.edu/~knolla/avrc.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27
