name: Resumable Ray Marching Iterator
head: OptiX7 Adaptive Ray Marching, Resumable Ray Marching
body: The Resumable Ray Marching Iterator is a GPU-based ray traversal method designed to handle out-of-core volume rendering by pausing ray execution when data is missing from GPU memory and resuming it in subsequent passes. It builds on Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by adding state persistence via Multiple Render Targets (MRTs) and Z-buffer culling to ensure only active rays are processed during data loading. Unlike Network Ray Marching Iterator which may rely on different streaming heuristics, or Macrocell Grid Traversal with Majorant Densities which focuses on density bounds, this method explicitly manages the CPU-GPU synchronization required for dynamic data loading. Inputs: Ray origin org and direction dir. Volume bounds tMin, tMax. Volume dimensions dims. Macrocell spacing (via macrocellspacingsrcp). Base sample step step. Adaptive sampling rate parameter adaptiveSamplingRate. Missing data identifiers (node IDs) communicated from GPU to CPU. Outputs: Accumulated color and alpha for the pixel. Updated ray state (position, accumulated color) for resumption. Missing node IDs for CPU-side data loading. The method relies on specific payload structures to store ray state and traversal context. SampleStreamingPayload Stores the state of a ray for resumption and output. pixelindex: Integer identifying the pixel. jitter: Floating point jitter value. alpha: Accumulated alpha (float). color: Accumulated color (vec3f). iter.cell: Current macrocell coordinates (vec3i, present if ADAPTIVESAMPLING is defined). iter.tnext: Next traversal position (vec2f, present if ADAPTIVESAMPLING is defined). iter.nextcellbegin: Offset from tMin to the next cell boundary (float, always present). RadiancePayload Used for primary ray tracing. alpha: Initialized to 0.f. color: Initialized to 0.f. rng: Pointer to random number generator state, initialized to nullptr. ShadowPayload Used for shadow ray tracing. alpha: Initialized to 0.f. rng: Pointer to random number generator state, initialized to nullptr. 1. Initialization: If ADAPTIVESAMPLING is defined, initialize the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) iterator: DDAIter::init(morg, mdir, tMin, tMax, dims). If ADAPTIVESAMPLING is not defined, initialize t.x = max(tMin + nextcellbegin, tMin) and t.y = min(t.x + step, tMax). 2. Ray Marching Loop: Adaptive Mode (ADAPTIVESAMPLING defined): 1. Compute macrocell coordinates: morg = org macrocellspacingsrcp, mdir = dir macrocellspacingsrcp. 2. Perform DDA traversal over macrocells using dda::dda3. 3. For each macrocell interval [t0, t1]: Calculate opacity upper bound r = opacityUpperBound(self, cell). If fabsf(r) <= floatepsilon, the cell is empty; return true to continue DDA to the next cell. Calculate adaptive step size ss using samplesizescaler(adaptiveSamplingRate(step, r), t0, t1). Initialize t = vec2f(t0, min(t1, t0 + ss)). Loop while t.y > t.x: Set DDAIter::nextcellbegin = t.y - tMin. Call body(t) to accumulate color/alpha for the segment [t.x, t.y]. Update t.x = t.y and t.y = min(t.x + ss, t1). Non-Adaptive Mode (ADAPTIVESAMPLING not defined): 1. Loop while t.y > t.x: Set nextcellbegin = t.y - tMin. Call body(t) for the segment [t.x, t.y]. Update t.x = t.y and t.y = min(t.x + step, tMax). 2. Set nextcellbegin = floatlarge and return. 3. Resumability Check: If ADAPTIVESAMPLING is defined, the ray is resumable if DDAIter::resumable(mdir, tMin, tMax, dims) returns true. If ADAPTIVESAMPLING is not defined, the ray is resumable if tMin + nextcellbegin < tMax. 4. Handling Missing Data: If data is missing during traversal, stop the ray and communicate the missing node ID to the CPU. Maintain ray status (preliminary color, missing node ID, current position) in two MRTs. Download missing IDs to the CPU to initiate data loading. 5. Resumption: In the next rendering pass, use a proxy surface to initiate rendering. Use the MRTs as input textures. Use Z-buffer culling (early-Z) to ensure only active pixels (where rays were paused) execute the fragment shader. Resume ray tracing at the last stored position. 6. Shadow Ray Tracing: Create ShadowPayload with a new RNG. Pack pointer to shadow into u0, u1 using packPointer. Call optixTrace with: Traversable from optixLaunchParams. Origin org, direction dir. tmin=0.f, tmax=floatlarge. time=0.0f, mask=255. flag=OPTIXRAYFLAGDISABLEANYHIT. rayType=SHADOWRAYTYPE. sbtStride=RAYTYPECOUNT. missIndex=SHADOWRAYTYPE. u0, u1. Return 1.f - shadow.alpha. Sample Size Scaler Calculates the effective step size to fit an integer number of steps within an interval [t0, t1]: N = \lfloor (t1 - t0) / ss \rfloor + 1 \text{effective\step} = (t1 - t0) / N where ss is the initial adaptive step size estimate. Resumability Condition (Non-Adaptive) \text{resumable} = (tMin + next\cell\begin < tMax) ADAPTIVESAMPLING: A preprocessor macro. Must be defined to enable adaptive sampling logic. If not defined, compilation fails with error "ADAPTIVESAMPLING is not defined". nextcellbegin: Member variable tracking the offset from tMin to the next cell boundary, used for resuming the march. adaptiveSamplingRate: Function/parameter controlling the base adaptive step size based on opacity. step: Base sample step size for non-adaptive mode. Precision: The use of floatepsilon for empty cell detection (fabsf(r) <= floatepsilon) requires careful consideration of floating-point precision in opacity bounds. Boundary Conditions: The loop condition t.y > t.x and the clamping min(t.y, t1) or min(t.y, tMax) must handle cases where the interval is smaller than the step size. Data Loading Latency: The method assumes the CPU can load data fast enough to keep up with rendering; otherwise, frames may be delayed or require multiple passes per frame. Z-Buffer Culling: Relies on early-Z features; if early-Z is disabled or fails, inactive pixels may still execute, wasting resources. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of macrocells traversed and the adaptive step size. Adaptive sampling reduces steps in empty regions, improving performance. Memory Complexity: Requires additional memory for MRTs to store ray state (color, alpha, position, missing ID) for all active pixels. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of active rays and the complexity of the volume data. More missing data leads to more passes, increasing total time. Strengths: Handles out-of-core data efficiently; only loads data within the frustum; adaptive sampling reduces computation in empty regions. Limitations: Requires multiple rendering passes for complete frames if data is missing; relies on CPU-GPU synchronization; complexity in managing ray state. When to use: When volume data exceeds GPU memory capacity and dynamic loading is required. When not to use: When all data fits in GPU memory and low latency is critical, as the overhead of state management and multiple passes may not be justified. The method originates from research on ray-guided streaming for efficient and detailed voxel rendering. It was implemented in the context of OptiX7-based volume renderers, as indicated by the alias "OptiX7 Adaptive Ray Marching" and the use of OptiX-specific features like optixTrace and SBT (Shader Binding Table) configuration. The approach addresses the challenge of rendering large volumetric datasets that cannot fit entirely in GPU memory by streaming data on-demand. name: Network Ray Marching Iterator
head: Distributed Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA, Networked Ray Marching
body: The Network Ray Marching Iterator is a ray marching algorithm designed for distributed or networked rendering environments, typically leveraging GPU ray tracing APIs such as NVIDIA OptiX. It extends the parent Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by introducing block-level divergence control via blockany to manage thread synchronization across macrocell boundaries. This method is distinct from its siblings because it explicitly tracks the "alive" status of rays in a distributed context, ensuring that inactive threads do not waste computation while maintaining adaptive sampling rates based on opacity upper bounds. The algorithm traverses a volume using a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) over macrocells. It adapts the step size within each macrocell based on an estimated opacity upper bound and uses a device function blockany to synchronize thread divergence across the block. Inputs: Ray origin org, ray direction dir, ray segment [tMin, tMax], volume dimensions dims, macrocell spacing inverse macrocellspacingsrcp, and a lambda function defining the per-sample body logic. Outputs: The final "alive" status of the ray after traversal, and accumulated color/opacity if the body function modifies state. Macrocell Coordinates: morg and mdir are floating-point vectors representing the ray origin and direction scaled by the inverse macrocell spacing. DDA State: The DDA yields a tuple (cell, t0, t1, alive) for each macrocell intersection, where cell is the macrocell index, t0 and t1 are the entry and exit distances, and alive is the boolean status of the ray. blockany: A device function that returns true if any thread in the current block satisfies a given condition. floatepsilon: A small constant used to determine if the opacity upper bound is effectively zero. Value not given in the sources. step: The base sampling step size. Value not given in the sources. 1. Calculate Macrocell Coordinates: Compute the ray origin and direction in macrocell space: m\org = org \times macrocell\spacings\rcp, m\dir = dir \times macrocell\spacings\rcp. 2. Invoke DDA: Call the DDA traversal with morg, mdir, tMin, tMax, dims, and a lambda callback. 3. Initialize Loop Variables: Inside the lambda, initialize ss = 100.f (adaptive step size) and nonempty = true. 4. Check Opacity Upper Bound: If alive is true, calculate r = opacityUpperBound(self, cell). If fabsf(r) <= floatepsilon, set nonempty = false. 5. Calculate Adaptive Step: If alive is true, set ss = adaptiveSamplingRate(step, r). 6. Divergence Control: Evaluate blockany(nonempty && alive). If this returns false, return alive (terminate the ray for this block). 7. Initialize Sample Interval: Set t = vec2f(t0, min(t1, t0 + ss)). 8. Sample Loop: Loop while blockany(alive && (t.y > t.x)): update alive = body(t, alive), t.x = t.y, t.y = min(t.x + ss, t1). 9. Return Status: Return the final alive status. If adaptive sampling is not used, initialize t = vec2f(tMin, min(tMax, tMin + step)) and alive = (t.y > t.x). Loop while blockany(alive && (t.y > t.x)): update alive = body(t, alive), t.x = t.y, t.y = min(t.x + step, tMax). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blockany(conditionlist): """Device function: returns True if any element in the list is True.""" return any(conditionlist) def networkraymarchingiterator(org, dir, tmin, tmax, dims, macrocellspacingsrcp, step, floatepsilon, opacityupperbound, adaptivesamplingrate, body): # 1. Calculate macrocell coordinates morg = [org[i] macrocellspacingsrcp for i in range(3)] mdir = [dir[i] macrocellspacingsrcp for i in range(3)] # 2. Call DDA def lambdafunc(cell, t0, t1, alive): # 3. Initialize loop variables ss = 100.0 nonempty = True # 4. Check opacity upper bound if alive: r = opacityupperbound(cell) if abs(r) <= floatepsilon: nonempty = False # 5. Calculate adaptive step if alive: ss = adaptivesamplingrate(step, r) # 6. Divergence control if not blockany([nonempty and alive]): return False # 7. Initialize sample interval tx = t0 ty = min(t1, t0 + ss) # 8. Sample loop while blockany([alive and (ty > tx)]): alive = body(tx, ty, alive) tx = ty ty = min(tx + ss, t1) # 9. Return status return True # Standard 3D DDA implementation (replaces networkdda3) # Fixes initialization bug where cell/tmaxedge were incorrectly sized/initialized cell = [int(morg[i]) if morg[i] >= 0 else int(morg[i]) - 1 for i in range(3)] cell = [max(0, min(dims[i] - 1, cell[i])) for i in range(3)] stepdir = [1 if mdir[i] > 0 else -1 for i in range(3)] tdelta = [1.0 / abs(mdir[i]) if mdir[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] tmaxedge = [ (cell[i] + 1.0 - morg[i]) if mdir[i] > 0 else (cell[i] - morg[i]) for i in range(3) ] t0 = max(tmin, min(tmaxedge)) while t0 < tmax: minidx = 0 minval = tmaxedge[0] for i in range(1, 3): if tmaxedge[i] < minval: minval = tmaxedge[i] minidx = i t1 = min(minval, tmax) alive = True if not lambdafunc(cell, t0, t1, alive): return False tmaxedge[minidx] += tdelta[minidx] cell[minidx] += stepdir[minidx] cell[minidx] = max(0, min(dims[minidx] - 1, cell[minidx])) t0 = t1 return False Precision: The use of floatepsilon for opacity checks determines when a macrocell is considered empty. Boundaries: The min(t1, t0 + ss) logic ensures that the last sample does not exceed the macrocell exit distance t1. Zero Direction Components: The DDA handles rays parallel to grid axes by using infinite deltas for those dimensions. A variant that allows ray traversal to be paused and resumed, useful for progressive rendering. Choose when memory bandwidth is limited or when integrating with progressive refinement techniques. Uses majorant densities for more accurate opacity bounds. Choose when higher accuracy in empty-space skipping is required, at the cost of increased computation per macrocell. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Optimized for distributed rendering on GPUs using ray tracing APIs like OptiX. Strengths: Efficient handling of thread divergence in distributed contexts; adaptive sampling reduces unnecessary computations. Limitations: Requires support for blockany and custom DDA implementations; may not be suitable for non-GPU or non-ray-tracing environments. The Network Ray Marching Iterator was introduced as part of the instantvnr project, a neural volume rendering framework. It builds on the principles of adaptive ray marching and macrocell traversal, extending them to support distributed rendering scenarios. The method is designed to leverage the parallelism of modern GPUs and the synchronization primitives provided by ray tracing APIs. name: Macrocell Grid Traversal with Majorant Densities
head: 3D-DDA with Woodcock tracking, Majorant-based free-flight tracking, Single-Level Macrocell + DDA Space Partitioning
body: This method accelerates volumetric path tracing by combining a coarse spatial partition (macrocells) with Delta Tracking (Woodcock tracking) to skip empty or low-opacity regions more efficiently than fixed-step marching. It sets itself apart from its parent Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by explicitly using the alpha component of the transfer function as a majorant extinction coefficient to determine probabilistic free-flight distances, allowing larger steps in homogeneous cells while maintaining unbiased Monte Carlo estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} in world space; a transfer function TF mapping density to RGBA; a macrocell grid storing min/max density ranges for each cell. Output: Accumulated radiance contribution from the volume along the ray, or a termination signal if the ray exits the volume or is canceled. Data Structures: The spatial partition is defined by DeviceSpacePartitonSingleMC: valueranges: Pointer to range1f, storing min/max density values for each macrocell. majorants: Pointer to float, storing the precomputed majorant extinction coefficient for each macrocell. dims: vec3i, dimensions of the macrocell grid in cells. spac: vec3f, spatial scaling factor (world units per macrocell). spacrcp: vec3f, reciprocal of spac, used to convert world coordinates to macrocell grid coordinates. Macrocell size is fixed at 16 (1 \ll 4), where 4 is MACROCELLSIZEMIP. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Transform the ray origin and direction into macrocell space using the reciprocal scaling factor: \mathbf{m\org} = \mathbf{o} \cdot \mathbf{spac\rcp} and \mathbf{m\dir} = \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{spac\rcp}. Initialize the 3D-DDA iterator with \mathbf{m\org}, \mathbf{m\dir}, and the ray's near/far bounds [t{near}, t{far}] in macrocell space. 2. Majorant Computation: For each macrocell, retrieve the stored min/max density range [d{min}, d{max}]. Look up these values in the transfer function TF to obtain the alpha components \alpha{min} = TF(d{min}).a and \alpha{max} = TF(d{max}).a. The majorant extinction coefficient \sigmat for the cell is derived from these values. In the reference implementation, fixed constants are used for demonstration: \sigmat = 1.0 and density scale = 1.0. Majorants must be recomputed whenever the transfer function changes. 3. Traversal Loop: While the ray has not exited the grid (t < t{far}): a. Cell Access: Determine the current macrocell index idx from the DDA iterator's current cell coordinates (x, y, z): idx = x + y \cdot dims.x + z \cdot dims.x \cdot dims.y. Retrieve the majorant \sigmat = majorants[idx]. b. Empty Cell Skip: If the cell is empty (e.g., d{max} = 0 or \sigmat = 0), advance the DDA iterator to the next intersected cell and continue to step 3a. c. Woodcock Tracking: If the cell is non-empty, perform Delta Tracking within the current cell: i. Compute the distance to the next cell boundary t{cell\end} using the DDA state. ii. Sample a free-flight distance t{ff} from the exponential distribution with rate \sigmat: t{ff} = -\frac{\ln(1 - \xi)}{\sigmat}, where \xi is a uniform random number in [0, 1). iii. Determine the step size t{step} = \min(t{ff}, t{cell\end} - t{current}). iv. Advance the ray position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + (t{current} + t{step}) \mathbf{d}. v. Interaction Check: If t{step} == t{ff}, an interaction occurred. Sample the scattering event (absorption/scattering) based on the actual density at \mathbf{p} and the majorant \sigmat. If scattering occurs, contribute radiance and potentially spawn a new ray. If absorbed, terminate the path. If the interaction is virtual (density < majorant), continue tracking. vi. If t{step} == t{cell\end}, the ray reached the cell boundary. Update t{current} and advance the DDA iterator to the next cell. 4. Termination: If the ray exits the grid (t \ge t{far}) or is canceled by Russian Roulette during scattering, return the accumulated radiance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def macrocelltraversalwithmajorants(rayo, rayd, tnear, tfar, macrocellgrid, transferfunction): """ rayo: list of 3 floats, ray origin in world space rayd: list of 3 floats, ray direction in world space tnear: float, near bound in world space tfar: float, far bound in world space macrocellgrid: dict with keys 'dims', 'spacrcp', 'majorants' transferfunction: callable mapping density to RGBA tuple Returns: accumulated radiance (list of 3 floats) """ import math import random # 1. Transform to macrocell space morg = [rayo[i] macrocellgrid['spacrcp'][i] for i in range(3)] mdir = [rayd[i] macrocellgrid['spacrcp'][i] for i in range(3)] # Initialize 3D-DDA state dims = macrocellgrid['dims'] ddax, dday, ddaz = int(morg[0]), int(morg[1]), int(morg[2]) ddadx = 1 if mdir[0] > 0 else -1 ddady = 1 if mdir[1] > 0 else -1 ddadz = 1 if mdir[2] > 0 else -1 tmaxx = (ddax + (1.0 if ddadx > 0 else 0.0) - morg[0]) / mdir[0] if mdir[0] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxy = (dday + (1.0 if ddady > 0 else 0.0) - morg[1]) / mdir[1] if mdir[1] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxz = (ddaz + (1.0 if ddadz > 0 else 0.0) - morg[2]) / mdir[2] if mdir[2] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltax = ddadx / mdir[0] if mdir[0] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltay = ddady / mdir[1] if mdir[1] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltaz = ddadz / mdir[2] if mdir[2] != 0 else float('inf') accumulatedradiance = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tcurrent = tnear while tcurrent < tfar: # 2. Get current cell info idx = ddax + dday dims[0] + ddaz dims[0] dims[1] sigmat = macrocellgrid['majorants'][idx] # Skip empty cells if sigmat == 0.0: # Advance DDA to next cell if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: ddax += ddadx tmaxx += tdeltax else: ddaz += ddadz tmaxz += tdeltaz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: dday += ddady tmaxy += tdeltay else: ddaz += ddadz tmaxz += tdeltaz continue # 3. Woodcock Tracking within the cell # Get distance to next cell boundary in macrocell space tcellend = min(tmaxx, tmaxy, tmaxz) # Sample free-flight distance xi = random.random() tff = -math.log(1.0 - xi) / sigmat # Determine step size tstep = min(tff, tcellend - tcurrent) # Advance ray tcurrent += tstep pworld = [rayo[i] + tcurrent rayd[i] for i in range(3)] # Check if interaction occurred (virtual or real) if abs(tstep - tff) < 1e-6: # Interaction happened # Sample actual density at pworld (requires random access sampling) density = sampledensity(pworld, macrocellgrid) # Compute actual extinction coefficient from transfer function alphaactual = transferfunction(density)[3] # RGBA index 3 is alpha sigmaa = alphaactual # Simplified: assuming alpha represents extinction # Russian Roulette for scattering vs absorption # Probability of scattering is sigmaa / sigmat if random.random() < sigmaa / sigmat: # Scattering event # Contribute radiance (simplified) pass else: # Absorption break else: # Reached cell boundary, no interaction # Advance DDA if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: ddax += ddadx tmaxx += tdeltax else: ddaz += ddadz tmaxz += tdeltaz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: dday += ddady tmaxy += tdeltay else: ddaz += ddadz tmaxz += tdeltaz return accumulatedradiance def sampledensity(pworld, macrocellgrid): # Not given in the sources. In practice, this queries the underlying VDB or texture. return 0.0 Parameters: MACROCELLSIZEMIP: Log2 of macrocell dimension, typically 4 (size 16). densityscale: Scaling factor for density values, typically 1.0. sigmat: Majorant extinction coefficient, typically 1.0 in basic implementations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transfer Function Changes: Majorants must be recomputed whenever the transfer function changes, as they depend on the min/max density ranges. Homogeneity Assumption: Woodcock tracking is most efficient in homogeneous cells where the majorant closely approximates the actual density. Hierarchical Diminishing Returns: Experiments with hierarchical space skipping showed diminishing returns compared to uniform grids when using RGBA transfer functions, likely due to the overhead of managing multiple levels of majorants. A ray-marching technique for volume rendering that combines a Discrete Differential Analyzer (DDA) for traversing a coarse spatial partition (macrocells) with Delta Tracking (Russian Roulette) for sampling absorption and scattering events within those cells. It sets itself apart from standard DDA by replacing uniform step sizes with probabilistic free-flight distances derived from the majorant, allowing it to skip non-interacting regions within a macrocell more efficiently than fixed-step marching, while avoiding the overhead of full per-voxel traversal. It is chosen when the volume is sparse or heterogeneous, and the transfer function allows for effective majorant estimation. See Delta Tracking with DDA Iteration (Macrocell-based). A renderer using the ANARI API that integrates VDB optimization. It sets itself apart by hiding compression details behind an ANSI-C API, converting ANARI structured-regular fields to NanoVDB grids internally, making the optimization transparent to the user. It is chosen when interoperability with standard visualization tools like ParaView is required. See ANARI Renderer Integration. Time Complexity: O(N{cells} + N{interactions}), where N{cells} is the number of macrocells traversed and N{interactions} is the number of scattering events. The DDA traversal is linear in the number of cells, and Woodcock tracking is efficient in sparse regions. Memory Complexity: O(N{macrocells}) for storing the majorant grid and min/max ranges. This is significantly smaller than a full voxel grid for sparse volumes. Measured Performance: In the reference implementation (Barney renderer), this method reduces sample count in homogeneous regions by allowing larger steps via Woodcock tracking. Performance gains are most significant in sparse volumes where empty cells can be skipped entirely. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty regions; adapts step size to local homogeneity; unbiased Monte Carlo estimation; simple uniform grid structure avoids hierarchical overhead. Limitations: Requires recomputation of majorants if transfer function changes. When to Use: Sparse or heterogeneous volumes with well-defined transfer functions; when unbiased path tracing is required. When Not to Use: Dense volumes where the overhead of macrocell traversal outweighs benefits; when hierarchical structures are preferred (though diminishing returns were observed). This method originates from the integration of VDB optimization into the Barney renderer, a multi-GPU wavefront path tracer. It was developed to leverage the structured-regular fields supported by the ANARI standard while providing efficient volume rendering. The approach builds on earlier work in 3D-DDA for volume rendering [SKTM11] and combines it with Woodcock tracking for free-flight distance sampling. The use of a uniform grid instead of hierarchical structures was chosen due to diminishing returns observed with hierarchical space skipping in the presence of RGBA transfer functions. name: Delta Tracking with DDA Iteration (Macrocell-based)
head: DDAIter-based Delta Tracking, SpacePartition_SingleMC Delta Tracking
body: A ray-marching technique for volume rendering that combines a Discrete Differential Analyzer (DDA) for traversing a coarse spatial partition (macrocells) with Delta Tracking (Russian Roulette) for sampling absorption and scattering events within those cells. It handles sparse or heterogeneous media by skipping empty macrocells and using a majorant density. It sets itself apart from standard DDA by replacing uniform step sizes with probabilistic free-flight distances derived from the majorant, allowing it to skip non-interacting regions within a macrocell more efficiently than fixed-step marching, while avoiding the overhead of full per-voxel traversal. It builds on Macrocell Grid Traversal with Majorant Densities. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin rayorg, ray direction raydir, ray near/far bounds raytnear, raytfar, macrocell grid dimensions dims, spatial inverse scale spacrcp, majorant density accessor accessmajorant, density scale constant, total extinction coefficient sigmat, and an initial optical depth budget tau. Outputs: Boolean foundhit indicating if an interaction occurred, and the hit distance rayt. Data Structures Macrocell Iterator (DDAIter): A stateful iterator that computes the sequence of macrocells intersected by a ray. It maintains current cell coordinates and exit distances. Spatial Parameters (sp): Contains spacrcp (reciprocal of spatial scale) for normalizing coordinates to grid space. Numbered Steps 1. Initialize Macrocell Iterator: Convert ray origin and direction to macrocell grid space. Compute normalized origin: m{org} = ray{org} \times sp.spac\rcp. Compute normalized direction: m{dir} = ray{dir} \times sp.spac\rcp. Call DDAIter::init(morg, mdir, raytnear, raytfar, dims) to set up the traversal state. 2. Initialize Loop State: Set foundhit = false. Determine the starting t for the first cell segment: t = next\cell\begin + ray{tnear}. Initialize tau (optical depth budget) externally. 3. Loop over Macrocells: While DDAIter::next() returns a valid cell c with entry t0 and exit t1: a. Retrieve Majorant: Get the majorant density for cell c: majorant = sp.access\majorant(c) \times density\scale. b. Skip Empty Cells: If |majorant| \le \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small float epsilon), the cell is empty. Return true from the current lambda/function to advance to the next macrocell without processing interaction logic. c. Update Optical Depth Budget: Subtract the optical thickness of the current cell segment from tau. The segment length is (t1 - t). The optical thickness is (t1 - t) \times (majorant \times \sigmat). \tau \leftarrow \tau - (t1 - t) \times (majorant \times \sigmat) d. Check for Event: If \tau > 0.f, an interaction (scattering or absorption) occurred within the previous segment or the budget was exhausted. Return true to advance to the next macrocell. e. Calculate Hit Position: If \tau \le 0.f, the interaction occurs within the current cell segment. Calculate the exact hit position t{hit}: t{hit} = t + \frac{\tau}{majorant \times \sigmat} Warning: This division can cause a division by zero error if majorant is zero but passed the epsilon check, or if sigmat is zero. f. Record Hit: Set foundhit = true. Update nextcellbegin = t{hit} - ray{tnear}. Set output rayt = t{hit}. Return false to terminate the loop. 4. Return Result: After the loop completes (ray exits all macrocells or tau budget remains positive without hitting), return foundhit. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deltatrackingddaiter(rayorg, raydir, raytnear, raytfar, dims, spacrcp, accessmajorant, densityscale, sigmat, tau): # Step 1: Initialize Macrocell Iterator morg = [rayorg[i] spacrcp for i in range(3)] mdir = [raydir[i] spacrcp for i in range(3)] dda = DDAIter(morg, mdir, raytnear, raytfar, dims) # Step 2: Initialize Loop State foundhit = False nextcellbegin = 0.0 t = nextcellbegin + raytnear # Step 3: Loop over Macrocells while dda.next(): c = dda.currentcell t0 = dda.entryt t1 = dda.exitt # Retrieve majorant density majorant = accessmajorant(c) densityscale # Skip empty cells if abs(majorant) <= 1e-6: # floatepsilon t = t1 nextcellbegin = t1 - raytnear continue # Update optical depth budget tau -= (t1 - t) (majorant sigmat) # Check for scattering/absorption event if tau > 0.0: t = t1 nextcellbegin = t1 - raytnear continue # Calculate exact hit position within the current cell # Warning: Division by zero if majorant sigmat is zero t = t + tau / (majorant sigmat) # Record hit foundhit = True nextcellbegin = t - raytnear rayt = t return foundhit, rayt return foundhit, None class DDAIter: """Standard 3D DDA iterator for macrocell traversal.""" def init(self, org, dir, tnear, tfar, dims): self.org = org self.dir = dir self.tnear = tnear self.tfar = tfar self.dims = dims self.t = tnear self.cell = [0, 0, 0] self.step = [0, 0, 0] self.tmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.initdda() def initdda(self): for i in range(3): if self.dir[i] > 0: self.step[i] = 1 self.tmax[i] = (self.cell[i] + 1 - self.org[i]) / self.dir[i] elif self.dir[i] < 0: self.step[i] = -1 self.tmax[i] = (self.cell[i] - self.org[i]) / self.dir[i] else: self.step[i] = 0 self.tmax[i] = float('inf') def next(self): if self.t > self.tfar: return False # entryt is the current t (start of this cell segment) self.entryt = self.t # Find the next boundary self.t = min(self.tmax[0], self.tmax[1], self.tmax[2]) if self.t > self.tfar: self.t = self.tfar self.exitt = self.t # Advance to next cell if self.tmax[0] <= self.tmax[1] and self.tmax[0] <= self.tmax[2]: self.cell[0] += self.step[0] self.tmax[0] += self.step[0] / self.dir[0] elif self.tmax[1] <= self.tmax[2]: self.cell[1] += self.step[1] self.tmax[1] += self.step[1] / self.dir[1] else: self.cell[2] += self.step[2] self.tmax[2] += self.step[2] / self.dir[2] return True @property def currentcell(self): return tuple(self.cell) @property def entryt(self): return self.entryt @property def exitt(self): return self.exitt Parameters densityscale: Constant multiplier for the majorant density. Typically hardcoded to 1.0. sigmat: Total extinction coefficient. Typically hardcoded to 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: The calculation tau / (majorant sigmat) is performed after checking fabsf(majorant) <= floatepsilon. If majorant is exactly zero but passes the epsilon check (or if epsilon is too large), division by zero occurs. The source code explicitly warns: // can have division by zero error. Epsilon Sensitivity: The choice of floatepsilon for skipping empty cells must be small enough to avoid skipping cells with very low but non-zero density, but large enough to handle numerical noise. Time Complexity: O(N{cells}) in the worst case, where N{cells} is the number of macrocells intersected by the ray. However, empty cells are skipped in O(1), making it efficient for sparse media. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray, assuming the macrocell grid is pre-computed and accessible. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of macrocells intersected. Performance improves with larger macrocells (fewer cells to traverse) but may lose precision in heterogeneous media. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty space; handles heterogeneous media via majorants; simple implementation. Limitations: Potential for division by zero; requires pre-computed majorants; may overshoot interactions if majorant is loose. When to use: Sparse or heterogeneous volumetric data where empty space skipping is beneficial. When not to use: Dense, homogeneous media where fixed-step marching might be simpler and faster. This method is part of the Open Volume Renderer project by VIDILabs. It is an implementation detail within a larger modular volume rendering framework. The specific implementation is found in the ovr/renderermacro.h and related source files. name: Orthogonal BSP Tree Construction
head: BSP tree conversion, Orthogonal BSP
body: This method converts a set of arbitrarily positioned and sized grown boxes into an orthogonal Binary Space Partitioning (BSP) tree where every splitting plane is object-aligned. It solves the problem that arbitrary box layouts prevent trivial visibility sorting, which is required for efficient empty-space skipping and occlusion clipping in texture-based volume rendering. Unlike uniform partitioning, this method ensures that the resulting tree structure allows for deterministic front-to-back or back-to-front traversal without complex geometric intersection tests. Inputs: A list of grown boxes generated by Growing Boxes Partitioning. Each box has a defined bounding box and a type (uniform, gradient, or other) based on enclosed voxel properties. Outputs: An orthogonal BSP tree where leaf nodes contain exactly one box (either an original grown box or a child box generated from splitting). Data Structures: BSP Node: Contains a list of boxes and a bounding box of their union, referred to as the "room". Box: Defined by its spatial bounds, type, and an optional parent reference. Hierarchy Constraint: There is only one level of parent-child hierarchy. Parent boxes reside on non-leaf nodes; rendering uses only leaf nodes. No box can be both a child and a parent simultaneously. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a root BSP node. Assign the list of all input grown boxes to the root. Calculate the root's room as the bounding box of the union of all these boxes. 2. Node Splitting: Split nodes until each leaf node contains exactly one box. To split a node: a. Create two child nodes: front and back. b. Choose Partitioning Plane: Select an object-aligned plane that coincides with the faces of at least two boxes in the current node's list to minimize the number of boxes that need to be split. The plane splits the current node's room into two new boxes, which become the rooms of the front and back children. c. Distribute Boxes: Iterate through each box in the current node's list: i. If the box is completely enclosed in the front room, move it to the front child's box list. ii. If the box is completely enclosed in the back room, move it to the back child's box list. iii. If the box is cut by the partitioning plane: 1. Create two new boxes by splitting the original box along the plane. 2. Place one new box in the front child's list and the other in the back child's list. 3. Manage parentage: If the original box is an original grown box (has no parent), set the original box as the parent of the two new boxes. If the original box already has a parent, set that parent as the parent of the two new boxes. Delete the original box from the current node's list. d. Repeat the splitting procedure for child nodes until every leaf node contains exactly one box. 3. Bottom-Up Merging: After the initial split phase, the number of leaf boxes may be significantly greater than the original count. Reduce the tree by merging child nodes if the following conditions are met: a. Both children are uniform, and the merged box (union of their rooms) is still uniform. b. Both children are "other" boxes or both are "gradient" boxes. c. One of the boxes is tiny or very thin (size along one axis is smaller than a threshold). d. If two child nodes being merged have different parent boxes, delete those parent boxes and make all their children parentless (i.e., they become candidates for merging at the next level up). e. The type of the resulting merged box is redetermined based on the enclosed voxel properties. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isenclosed(boxbounds, roombounds): return all(boxbounds.min[i] >= roombounds.min[i] and boxbounds.max[i] <= roombounds.max[i] for i in range(3)) def iscutbyplane(boxbounds, plane): # plane is defined by axis a and coordinate c return boxbounds.min[plane.axis] < plane.c and boxbounds.max[plane.axis] > plane.c def splitbox(boxbounds, plane): # Returns two new bounds split along plane.axis at plane.c b1min = boxbounds.min.copy() b1max = boxbounds.max.copy() b2min = boxbounds.min.copy() b2max = boxbounds.max.copy() b1max[plane.axis] = plane.c b2min[plane.axis] = plane.c return BoxBounds(b1min, b1max), BoxBounds(b2min, b2max) def unionbounds(b1, b2): return BoxBounds( min(b1.min[i], b2.min[i]) for i in range(3), max(b1.max[i], b2.max[i]) for i in range(3)) def isuniform(box): return box.type == 'uniform' def istinyorthin(box, threshold): return any(box.max[i] - box.min[i] < threshold for i in range(3)) def determinemergedtype(b1, b2): # Simplified type determination based on evidence if b1.type == 'uniform' and b2.type == 'uniform': return 'uniform' if b1.type == 'gradient' or b2.type == 'gradient': return 'gradient' return 'other' class BoxBounds: def init(self, minv, maxv): self.min = list(minv) self.max = list(maxv) class Box: def init(self, bounds, boxtype, parent=None): self.bounds = bounds self.type = boxtype self.parent = parent class BSPNode: def init(self, room, boxes): self.room = room self.boxes = boxes self.front = None self.back = None self.parent = None def splitnode(node, threshold): if len(node.boxes) <= 1: return front = BSPNode(None, []) back = BSPNode(None, []) node.front = front node.back = back # Choose plane coinciding with faces of at least two boxes to minimize splits plane = choosepartitioningplane(node.boxes, node.room) # Split room into two boxes for children front.room, back.room = splitroom(node.room, plane) boxestoprocess = list(node.boxes) for box in boxestoprocess: if isenclosed(box.bounds, front.room): front.boxes.append(box) node.boxes.remove(box) elif isenclosed(box.bounds, back.room): back.boxes.append(box) node.boxes.remove(box) elif iscutbyplane(box.bounds, plane): boxfrontbounds, boxbackbounds = splitbox(box.bounds, plane) boxfront = Box(boxfrontbounds, box.type) boxback = Box(boxbackbounds, box.type) front.boxes.append(boxfront) back.boxes.append(boxback) if box.parent is None: boxfront.parent = box boxback.parent = box else: boxfront.parent = box.parent boxback.parent = box.parent node.boxes.remove(box) if len(front.boxes) > 1: splitnode(front, threshold) if len(back.boxes) > 1: splitnode(back, threshold) def mergenodes(node, threshold): if node.front is None or node.back is None: return mergenodes(node.front, threshold) mergenodes(node.back, threshold) frontbox = node.front.boxes[0] if len(node.front.boxes) == 1 else None backbox = node.back.boxes[0] if len(node.back.boxes) == 1 else None if frontbox and backbox: shouldmerge = False if isuniform(frontbox) and isuniform(backbox): mergedbounds = unionbounds(frontbox.bounds, backbox.bounds) if isuniform(Box(mergedbounds, 'uniform')): shouldmerge = True elif frontbox.type == 'other' and backbox.type == 'other': shouldmerge = True elif frontbox.type == 'gradient' and backbox.type == 'gradient': shouldmerge = True elif istinyorthin(frontbox, threshold) or istinyorthin(backbox, threshold): shouldmerge = True if shouldmerge: mergedbox = Box(unionbounds(frontbox.bounds, backbox.bounds), determinemergedtype(frontbox, backbox)) if frontbox.parent != backbox.parent: if frontbox.parent: frontbox.parent.boxes.remove(frontbox) if backbox.parent: backbox.parent.boxes.remove(backbox) mergedbox.parent = None else: mergedbox.parent = frontbox.parent parentnode = node.parent if parentnode: if parentnode.front == node: parentnode.front = BSPNode(mergedbox.bounds, [mergedbox]) else: parentnode.back = BSPNode(mergedbox.bounds, [mergedbox]) node.front = None node.back = None node.boxes = [] def choosepartitioningplane(boxes, room): # Standard implementation: evaluate planes aligned with box faces to minimize cuts # Returns plane with axis and coordinate minimizing split count pass def splitroom(room, plane): # Splits room bounds along plane.axis at plane.c r1min = room.min.copy() r1max = room.max.copy() r2min = room.min.copy() r2max = room.max.copy() r1max[plane.axis] = plane.c r2min[plane.axis] = plane.c return BoxBounds(r1min, r1max), BoxBounds(r2min, r2max) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hierarchy Constraint: Ensure no box is both a child and a parent. The algorithm enforces this by retaining original grown boxes as parents of split children, while deleting intermediate split boxes from their parent lists. Texture Sharing: Child boxes share the texture of their parent with siblings to avoid replicating texels along boundaries. This prevents increased memory requirements that would result from dividing textures and replicating texels for interpolation. Plane Selection: The partitioning plane must coincide with the faces of at least two boxes to minimize splits. Failure to do so may result in excessive box fragmentation. Merging Threshold: The threshold for "tiny or very thin" boxes must be defined to prevent merging boxes that are structurally distinct but small. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The splitting phase depends on the number of boxes and the efficiency of plane selection. The merging phase is bottom-up. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method aims to keep the total number of boxes comparable to the original set before conversion. Texture sharing reduces memory overhead compared to replicating textures. Strengths: Enables trivial visibility sorting for 3D texture rendering by ensuring object-aligned splitting planes. Handles arbitrary box sizes and positions from adaptive partitioning. Limitations: The initial split phase may generate significantly more leaf boxes than the original input, requiring a merging phase to reduce complexity. When to use: When using adaptive partitioning (like Growing Boxes Partitioning) where boxes are not aligned to a uniform grid, and efficient visibility sorting is required for empty-space skipping. This method was introduced by Mueller et al. in the context of empty-space skipping and occlusion clipping for texture-based volume rendering. It addresses the limitation of uniform partitioning, where visibility sorting is trivial, by converting arbitrary grown boxes into a BSP tree structure that supports similar efficient traversal. name: Ray Casting with Depth/Alpha Test for Empty Space Skipping
head: Westermann & Sevenich method, Ray Casting using Alpha and Depth Tests, Empty Space Skipping via OpenGL Tests, Westermann & Sevenich Empty Space Skipping
body: This method accelerates direct volume rendering by skipping empty space intervals in the volume integral, using 2D textures and OpenGL alpha/depth tests to discard non-contributing intervals. It determines the near and far intersection points of rays with the volume by leveraging the GPU's depth buffer, allowing samples to be taken only between these points. Unlike sibling methods that may use complex data structures like octrees or BSP trees, this technique relies on standard OpenGL pipeline tests to bound the ray segment, reducing the number of samples and framebuffer writes. It is particularly effective when the volume has significant external empty space, though its benefit diminishes with high internal data dispersion. Inputs: 3D volume data (scalar field). Camera parameters (projection matrix P, modelview matrix V). Rendering context supporting OpenGL alpha and depth tests. Outputs: Final color image in the framebuffer. Data Structures: 2D Textures: The volume is sliced into 2D planes parallel to the X, Y, and Z axes. For each axis, a set of 2D textures is created, one for each slice. Display Lists: Created for each set of textures (front-to-back and back-to-front) to optimize rendering order. Depth Buffer: Used to store normalized device coordinates (NDC) of the nearest and farthest visible fragments. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (CPU): Calculate the gradient of each volume element using central differences. Perform illumination and shading based on the lighting model variables. Store the resulting color and opacity data in main memory. This step is performed once on the CPU, unlike methods that compute shading dynamically on the GPU. 2. Texture Preparation (CPU/GPU): For each axis (X, Y, Z): For each plane parallel to the axis: Create a 2D texture from the slice data. Load the texture into GPU memory. Create a display list for the set of textures, ordered front-to-back and back-to-front. 3. Determine Ray Bounds (GPU Passes): The goal is to find the entry (P) and exit (Q) points of the ray through the volume. Pass 1 (Near Point): Initialize the depth buffer to 1.0 (maximum NDC depth). Enable the Alpha Test with GLGREATER and a reference value > 0. This discards fragments with zero opacity (empty space). Set the Depth Test criterion to GLLESS. Render the volume slices. The depth buffer will store the distance of the closest significant fragment to the projection plane for each pixel. Pass 2 (Far Point): Initialize the depth buffer to 0.0 (minimum NDC depth). Keep the Alpha Test enabled (GLGREATER, ref > 0). Set the Depth Test criterion to GLGREATER. Render the volume slices. The depth buffer will store the distance of the farthest significant fragment from the projection plane for each pixel. 4. Coordinate Transformation: Read the depth values from the depth buffer for each pixel (xs, ys, zs) in NDC. Transform these NDC coordinates to world coordinates to obtain the ray origin P and ray end Q. The transformation uses the inverse of the projection and modelview matrices: \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ w \end{bmatrix} = (P M)^{-1} V \begin{bmatrix} xs \\ ys \\ zs \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where P is the projection matrix, M is the model matrix, and V is the view matrix. Note: The source notation (PM)^{-1}V implies the combined inverse projection-model matrix applied to the view-transformed NDC point. In standard OpenGL, NDC is derived from clip coordinates, which are derived from eye coordinates via V and P. To go from NDC to World, one typically inverts P and V and applies them in reverse order. The source formula is interpreted as transforming the NDC point back to world space using the inverse of the modelview-projection chain. 5. Ray Casting and Compositing: For each pixel, cast a ray between P (near) and Q (far). Sample the volume along the ray segment defined by t \in [0, 1]: X(t) = Px + (Qx - Px)t Y(t) = Py + (Qy - Py)t Z(t) = Pz + (Qz - Pz)t The increment in t is determined by the number of samples n per ray (e.g., \Delta t = 1/n). Composite the samples using the volume rendering integral. Since empty space outside [P, Q] is skipped, the integral is reduced: L(x) = \int{xA'}^{xB'} \left[ e^{-\int{xA'}^{x0'} \phit(x'')dx''} \epsilon(x0') dx0' \right] where xA' and xB' correspond to points P and Q, \phit is the extinction coefficient, and \epsilon is the color. Draw the final composed color to the framebuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def westermannsevenichrender(volumedata, cameraparams): """ volumedata: 3D array of scalar values cameraparams: dict with 'projectionmatrix', 'modelviewmatrix', 'viewmatrix' """ # Step 1: Preprocessing on CPU gradients = calculatecentraldifferences(volumedata) shadedvolume = applylighting(volumedata, gradients, lightingmodel) # Step 2: Create 2D textures for slices # Determine optimal axis based on camera angle axis = determineoptimalaxis(volumedata, cameraparams) textures = create2dtexturesfromslices(shadedvolume, axis) # Step 3: Pass 1 - Find Near Point (P) glinitdepthbuffer(1.0) glenablealphatest() glalphafunc(GLGREATER, 0.0) # Discard zero opacity gldepthfunc(GLLESS) renderslices(textures, fronttobackorder) neardepthbuffer = glreaddepthbuffer() # Step 4: Pass 2 - Find Far Point (Q) glinitdepthbuffer(0.0) glenablealphatest() glalphafunc(GLGREATER, 0.0) gldepthfunc(GLGREATER) renderslices(textures, backtofrontorder) fardepthbuffer = glreaddepthbuffer() # Step 5: Transform NDC to World Coordinates invprojmodel = invertmatrix(multiplymatrices(cameraparams['projectionmatrix'], cameraparams['modelmatrix'])) # Note: Source formula uses (PM)^-1 V. Standard OpenGL pipeline: World -> Model -> View -> Projection. # NDC is after Projection. To get World from NDC: NDC -> Clip -> Eye -> World. # The source formula is specific to the implementation context. We follow the source's variable mapping. # Pworld and Qworld are computed for each pixel (xs, ys) using neardepthbuffer and fardepthbuffer. # Step 6: Ray Casting for each pixel (xs, ys): znearndc = neardepthbuffer[xs, ys] zfarndc = fardepthbuffer[xs, ys] # Convert NDC to World Pworld = ndctoworld(xs, ys, znearndc, invprojmodel, cameraparams['viewmatrix']) Qworld = ndctoworld(xs, ys, zfarndc, invprojmodel, cameraparams['viewmatrix']) # Ray Casting between P and Q color = compositeray(Pworld, Qworld, volumedata, numsamples) glsetframebuffercolor(xs, ys, color) def ndctoworld(xndc, yndc, zndc, invpm, viewmatrix): """ Transforms NDC coordinates to World coordinates. Follows the source's implication of using inverse projection-model and view matrix. """ # Homogeneous NDC point ndcpoint = [xndc, yndc, zndc, 1.0] # Apply inverse projection-model matrix # Note: In standard OpenGL, we invert Projection then ModelView. # The source formula: [x,y,z,w] = (PM)^-1 V [xs,ys,zs,1] # This suggests V is applied to the NDC point? No, V is part of the forward transform. # Let's stick to the source's explicit formula structure for fidelity, # interpreting V as the view matrix and PM as projectionmodel. # However, mathematically, to go from NDC to World: # 1. NDC to Clip: w=1 (after perspective divide) # 2. Clip to Eye: Inv(P) Clip # 3. Eye to World: Inv(V) Eye # The source formula seems to conflate or simplify. # We will implement the standard inverse chain which achieves the goal described. clippoint = [xndc, yndc, zndc, 1.0] eyepoint = multiplymatrixvector(invert(cameraparams['projectionmatrix']), clippoint) worldpoint = multiplymatrixvector(invert(cameraparams['viewmatrix']), eyepoint) # Perspective divide if necessary (though NDC is already divided) # NDC is [x/w, y/w, z/w]. The input to the inverse is the NDC coordinates. # If the depth buffer stores zndc, we reconstruct the clip z. # This is a simplification for the purpose of the article based on source. return worldpoint def compositeray(P, Q, volume, nsamples): """ Standard front-to-back compositing along the ray segment P to Q. """ tstep = 1.0 / nsamples alphaaccum = 0.0 coloraccum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(nsamples): t = i tstep # Interpolate position pos = P + (Q - P) t # Sample volume (trilinear interpolation) density = samplevolume(pos, volume) # Get color and opacity from transfer function color, opacity = transferfunction(density) # Composite # Cout = Cin + (1 - alphain) Csample alphasample # Aout = Ain + (1 - Ain) alphasample weight = (1.0 - alphaaccum) opacity coloraccum += weight color alphaaccum += weight if alphaaccum >= 1.0: break return coloraccum An optimization for primary rays in volumetric ray tracing that creates a polygonal representation of all objects and projects them into two Z-buffers (nearest and farthest distances). It ensures polygonal models completely contain the actual volumetric objects to bound the ray segment. If no Z-buffer information exists for a pixel, intersection calculations are skipped. It typically reduces primary ray computation by a factor of four. It can also be extended to shadow rays by creating Z-buffer projections from light locations. Time Complexity: Reduces ray casting time to approximately one-quarter of a naive ray caster that samples the entire ray extension. Performance improvements of 3 to 4 times faster are observed when using alpha and depth tests compared to not using them. Memory Complexity: Requires storing 2D textures for all slices along the optimal axis, plus display lists. This is generally less memory-intensive than 3D textures or complex tree structures but requires multiple passes over the data. Strengths: Simple to implement using standard OpenGL features; effective for volumes with large empty regions outside the object; avoids complex data structure traversal. Limitations: Only skips external empty spaces; high internal data dispersion reduces effectiveness as the ray length with skipping becomes similar to the unoptimized length. Illumination is calculated on the CPU in a single pass, preventing dynamic lighting updates without recomputation. When to use: When the volume has significant transparent regions outside the object and dynamic lighting is not required. When not to use: When the volume has high internal dispersion (many small opaque regions throughout) or when dynamic lighting is needed (consider Engel, Kraus & Ertl instead). The method was introduced by Westermann and Sevenich in their work [WS01]. It is a hybrid volume rendering technique that leverages the GPU's depth buffer to skip empty spaces, allowing ray casting to sample only non-transparent material. It differs from Engel, Kraus & Ertl's method by performing illumination calculation uniquely and in the initial phase on the CPU, whereas Engel's method computes it on the GPU. The technique is part of the broader family of empty-space skipping methods aimed at accelerating volume rendering by avoiding regions in the volume that are completely transparent [Parent]. name: Octree Traversal with Min/Max Pruning
head: Knoll et al. Min/Max Tree, Min/Max Hierarchy Ray Traversal, Min/Max Tree, Min/Max Tree Space Skipping, Min/Max Tree Traversal, Octree Ray Tracing with Min/Max Acceleration, Scalar Octree Traversal
body: Octree Traversal with Min/Max Pruning is an acceleration technique for ray tracing isosurfaces in scalar volumes stored in an octree. It solves the problem of efficiently skipping transparent or irrelevant regions during rendering by storing the minimum and maximum scalar values of each node's children. Unlike standard empty-space skipping which may rely on coarse bricks, this method uses the hierarchical min/max ranges to prune nodes that do not contain the target isovalue, allowing for interactive transfer function changes without rebuilding the entire geometry. It sets itself apart by embedding the acceleration structure and scalar data in a single octree, leveraging the duality between voxels and cells to define cell primitives for ray intersection. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Ray entry time t{\text{enter}} and exit time t{\text{exit}} for the volume bounding box. Target isovalue I. Octree structure containing scalar data and min/max metadata. Maximum octree depth D{\text{max}}. Outputs: Boolean indicating if the ray intersects the isosurface within the volume. The octree is stored as a single structure serving as both data container and acceleration tree. Node Layout: Each node contains: childmins: Array of size 8, storing the minimum scalar value present in each of the 8 children. childmaxs: Array of size 8, storing the maximum scalar value present in each of the 8 children. childoffset: Integer. If childoffset == -1, the node is a leaf (scalar data). Otherwise, it is an internal node. Implicit state during traversal: child: Current child index (0-7). childcell: 3D integer coordinate of the current cell within the octree level. Cell Primitive: The algorithm traces rays through cells composed of 8 voxels. A duality exists between voxels and cells: each voxel is mapped to the lower-left corner of a cell by shifting the scalar field backward by half a unit of voxel width. Values outside the octree data are defined as zero. This allows the ray to intersect well-defined cell primitives at each step. 1. Initialization: Start traversal at the root of the octree with the global ray parameters (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}, t{\text{enter}}, t{\text{exit}}). 2. Axis Intersection Calculation: For the current node, calculate the intersection times with the X, Y, and Z octant mid-planes. Store the corresponding axis indices (0, 1, 2) sorted by increasing intersection time in axisisects. 3. Child Traversal Loop: Initialize childtenter = t{\text{enter}}. Iterate through the valid axis intersections in axisisects while the center time t{\text{center}} < t{\text{exit}}: a. Calculate Exit Time: Compute childtexit as the minimum of the intersection time on the current axis (tcenter) and the global texit. b. Min/Max Pruning Check: Check if the isovalue I lies within the child node's scalar range: I \geq \text{node.child\mins[child]} \quad \text{AND} \quad I \leq \text{node.child\maxs[child]} If this condition is false, the node does not contain the isosurface; skip to the next iteration (update childtenter and child index). c. Node Type Handling: Leaf: If node.childoffset == -1, traverse the scalar leaf. If it returns true, the ray hit and the function returns true. Max Depth Cap: If the current depth == octdata.maxdepth and the node is not a leaf, traverse the cap geometry. If it returns true, return true. Internal Node: Recursively traverse it with updated tenter/texit bounds. If it returns true, return true. d. Early Exit: If childtexit == t{\text{exit}}, the ray has exited the volume or the current bounding region without hitting anything relevant; return false. e. Update Entry Time: Set childtenter = childtexit for the next iteration. f. Update Child Index: Determine the axis bit from axistable (e.g., {4, 2, 1} for X, Y, Z) using the current axis index. If the current child index has the axis bit set, clear the bit in child and the corresponding bit in childcell. Otherwise, set the bit in child and the corresponding bit in childcell. 4. Return: If the loop completes without a hit, return false. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseminmax(ray, node, depth, tenter, texit, isovalue, maxdepth): """ Traverses an octree using min/max pruning for isosurface rendering. """ # Compute intersection times with X, Y, Z mid-planes of the current cell. # Returns axis indices (0, 1, 2) sorted by increasing intersection time. axisorder = computeaxisorder(ray, node.cellcoord, tenter, texit) childtenter = tenter child = 0 # Initial child index childcell = node.cellcoord axistable = [4, 2, 1] # Maps axis index to bit mask for axisidx in axisorder: # Intersection time with the current axis mid-plane tcenter = computeintersectiontime(ray, node.cellcoord, axisidx, tenter, texit) if tcenter >= texit: break childtexit = min(tcenter, texit) # Min/Max Pruning Check if isovalue >= node.childmins[child] and isovalue <= node.childmaxs[child]: if node.childoffset == -1: # Traverse scalar leaf (standard ray-march/isosurface check on 8 voxels) if traversescalarleaf(ray, node, childtenter, childtexit, isovalue): return True elif depth == maxdepth: # Traverse cap geometry at max depth if traversecap(ray, node, childtenter, childtexit, isovalue): return True else: # Recursive internal node traversal if traverseminmax(ray, node.children[child], depth + 1, childtenter, childtexit, isovalue, maxdepth): return True if childtexit == texit: return False childtenter = childtexit axisbit = axistable[axisidx] childbit = 1 << axisidx if child & axisbit: child &= ~axisbit childcell[axisidx] &= ~childbit else: child |= axisbit childcell[axisidx] |= childbit return False def computeaxisorder(ray, cellcoord, tenter, texit): """Returns axis indices [0, 1, 2] sorted by intersection time with cell mid-planes.""" times = [] for axis in range(3): t = computeintersectiontime(ray, cellcoord, axis, tenter, texit) times.append((t, axis)) times.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) return [axis for, axis in times] def computeintersectiontime(ray, cellcoord, axis, tenter, texit): """Standard ray-plane intersection with the mid-plane of the current cell along the given axis.""" mid = cellcoord[axis] + 0.5 denom = ray.d[axis] if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return float('inf') t = (mid - ray.o[axis]) / denom if tenter <= t <= texit: return t return float('inf') def traversescalarleaf(ray, node, tenter, texit, isovalue): # Sources do not specify the exact scalar leaf traversal routine. # Standard implementation: ray-march through the 8 voxels of the cell primitive # and check for isosurface intersection within [tenter, texit]. pass def traversecap(ray, node, tenter, texit, isovalue): # Sources do not specify the exact cap traversal routine. # Standard implementation: intersect ray with the cap geometry bounding the cell. pass node.childmins[child]: Minimum scalar value in the child node. node.childmaxs[child]: Maximum scalar value in the child node. octdata.maxdepth: Maximum depth of the octree. Transfer Function (RGB\alpha map): Used to classify regions interactively. Max Depth Cap: At the maximum octree depth, the algorithm does not traverse further into children but instead calls traversecap, implying leaf nodes at max depth represent cap geometry rather than volumetric data. Transfer Function Changes: When the transfer function changes, the min/max ranges are used to reclassify regions. Empty Adaptive Block Refinement (ABR) regions can be deactivated, requiring an interactive rebuild of the BVH if used in conjunction. Precision: The min/max pruning relies on the scalar range. Boundary cases where the isovalue exactly matches a stored min or max value are handled by the inclusive range check, ensuring safe traversal at the cost of potentially reduced pruning efficiency. Memory: The octree stores min/max values for each node, adding overhead to the scalar data. The structure is lossless compressed, occupying a fraction of the original memory footprint. Time: Traversal is front-to-back, allowing early termination. Pruning efficiency depends on the variance of scalar values within nodes. Competitive frame rates on common multicore architectures for large time-variant data. Superior to using bricks' min/max values for space-skipping classification, which is reported to be of much lower quality. Strengths: Allows interactive transfer function changes by recomputing majorants from stored ranges. Efficient memory usage due to compression and single structure for data and acceleration. Limitations: Indirection of the transfer function prevents direct computation of local majorants, requiring subdivision and min/max range storage. Requires pre-processing to store min/max ranges. Use for interactive isosurface rendering of large scalar volumes where transfer function changes are frequent. Use when memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and compression is beneficial. Not suitable for direct volume rendering with complex transfer functions that cannot be approximated by min/max ranges. Not suitable if the volume data is not structured or cannot be converted to an octree. The method was introduced by Knoll et al. in 2006. It is described in "Interactive Isosurface Ray Tracing of Large Octree Volumes". The technique builds on the concept of min/max trees for empty space skipping. It embeds the acceleration tree and scalar data in a single structure, employing optimized octree hash schemes. Large-scale volume visualization. Interactive isosurface rendering. name: Octree Empty Block Culling
head: Octree Leaf Culling, Recursive Status Check
body: Octree Empty Block Culling recursively traverses an octree to determine if a node contains any non-empty data blocks, returning a status of EMPTY or NONEMPTY to enable early ray termination or skipping of empty regions. Inputs: An octree structure where each node has a depth field and a status field. A memory management unit (MMU) or similar accessor providing a getBlock function that returns a pointer to the data block associated with a leaf node, or nullptr if the block is not loaded or does not exist. Outputs: A boolean indicating whether the node (and its subtree) contains non-empty data (true for NONEMPTY, false for EMPTY). Data Structures: Node: depth: Integer, the depth of the node in the octree. status: Enum or integer, EMPTY or NONEMPTY. children: Array of 8 pointers to child nodes (for internal nodes). MMU: getBlock(nodeindex): Returns a pointer to the data block for the leaf node identified by nodeindex, or nullptr. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the current node's status to EMPTY. 2. Check if the current node is a leaf. A node is a leaf if node->depth equals the maximum tree depth. If it is a leaf: Attempt to load the block using mmu->getBlock(nodeindex). If the returned block is nullptr, set node->status = EMPTY and return false. Otherwise, set node->status = NONEMPTY and return true. If it is an internal node: Recursively call the status check function on all 8 children. Children are accessed using linear indexing: childindex = (index << 3) + i + 1 for i from 0 to 7, where index is the index of the current node in a flat array representation. If any child returns true (indicating NONEMPTY), set node->status = NONEMPTY. Return node->status == NONEMPTY. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EMPTY = 0 NONEMPTY = 1 def checkstatus(node, mmu, maxdepth, nodeindex): """ Recursively checks if a node or its subtree contains non-empty data. """ node.status = EMPTY if node.depth == maxdepth: block = mmu.getBlock(nodeindex) if block is None: node.status = EMPTY return False else: node.status = NONEMPTY return True else: baseindex = (nodeindex << 3) + 1 for i in range(8): childindex = baseindex + i if checkstatus(node.children[i], mmu, maxdepth, childindex): node.status = NONEMPTY return node.status == NONEMPTY Parameters: maxdepth: The maximum depth of the octree. This must be set correctly during initialization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Incorrect Depth Initialization: If the tree depth is not set correctly during initialization, the leaf check node->depth == depth may fail, causing all nodes to be treated as internal or leaf incorrectly. Empty Blocks: A leaf node may exist in the octree structure but have no associated data block (e.g., not loaded into memory). The getBlock function must return nullptr in this case, and the node should be marked as EMPTY. Octree Range Culling is a variant where shells' ranges over a node are computed once per pass for up to 4 tiles of 64 functions (each lane owns a function of every tile) instead of once per tile, only for shells reaching the node. A dropped shell has every AO below 10^{-10} over the node; fntail (2 \times 10^{-10} times the column sum of |C|) is added to every function's bound for them. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is described in the context of parallel volume rendering systems, specifically in the VolumeRenderingParallel project. It is used to optimize ray traversal by skipping empty regions of the volume, thereby reducing the number of samples taken and improving rendering performance. hopexn/VolumeRenderingParallel, https://github.com/hopexn/VolumeRenderingParallel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) mdgtoisogpu: optimized GPU isosurface extraction (non-blocking jobs, flood, one measured path), https://github.com/scanberg/mdlib/pull/15, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Direct volume ray casting
body: Direct volume ray casting is an image-order rendering technique that casts a ray through a 3D volume for every pixel, sampling scalar values, mapping them to RGBA via a transfer function, and compositing samples front-to-back using alpha blending to produce the final image. It differs from Isosurface and first-hit ray casting by allowing all voxels to contribute to the final image rather than stopping at the first opaque surface, and from Distance-field ray marching by using uniform step sizes rather than distance-field-guided steps. It replaces slice-stack methods by providing a solid volume appearance from any angle without edge-on gaps. The method relies on the volume rendering integral, discretized into a summation over sample points along a ray. The ray r is parameterized by r(t) = O + tD, entering the volume at t{start} and exiting at t{end} Volume Raycasting Discretization. The data model is sampled using s(t) Volume Raycasting Discretization. The compositing is performed front-to-back. Let C'i be the accumulated color and \alpha'i be the accumulated opacity after sample i, with initial conditions C'0 = 0 and \alpha'0 = 0. For each sample i along the ray: 1. Sample the volume at the current ray position to get a scalar value di. 2. Apply a transfer function to map the scalar value to color Ci and opacity \alphai. 3. Update accumulated color: C'i = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Ci 4. Update accumulated opacity: \alpha'i = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai 5. If \alpha' \ge 1 or a threshold (typically 0.99), terminate the ray (early ray termination). Rays are cast from the eyepoint, one for each pixel. The volume is typically represented as a 3D texture. Gradients for shading are calculated using a central difference operator. To avoid normal discontinuities that cause visible rings on smooth surfaces, the gradient is computed using a two-voxel offset rather than a one-voxel offset. Sampling is performed using trilinear interpolation. A fixed random offset is applied to each ray's start position to prevent sample layers from appearing as bands. The final accumulated color is typically corrected with gamma 2.2. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math def vec3(x, y, z): return [x, y, z] def powvec3(v, exponent): return [v[0]exponent, v[1]exponent, v[2]exponent] def computerayexit(origin, direction, bounds): # Slab intersection for axis-aligned box t0 = max((bounds[0][i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if direction[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)) t1 = min((bounds[1][i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if direction[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)) return max(t0, t1) def trilinearinterpolate(volume, pos, dims): # Standard trilinear interpolation vx = pos[0] (dims[0] - 1) vy = pos[1] (dims[1] - 1) vz = pos[2] (dims[2] - 1) x0, y0, z0 = int(math.floor(vx)), int(math.floor(vy)), int(math.floor(vz)) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 x0 = max(0, min(x0, dims[0]-1)) x1 = max(0, min(x1, dims[0]-1)) y0 = max(0, min(y0, dims[1]-1)) y1 = max(0, min(y1, dims[1]-1)) z0 = max(0, min(z0, dims[2]-1)) z1 = max(0, min(z1, dims[2]-1)) wx = vx - x0 wy = vy - y0 wz = vz - z0 c00 = volume[x0][y0][z0] (1-wx) + volume[x1][y0][z0] wx c01 = volume[x0][y0][z1] (1-wx) + volume[x1][y0][z1] wx c10 = volume[x0][y1][z0] (1-wx) + volume[x1][y1][z0] wx c11 = volume[x0][y1][z1] (1-wx) + volume[x1][y1][z1] wx r0 = c00 (1-wy) + c10 wy r1 = c01 (1-wy) + c11 wy return r0 (1-wz) + r1 wz def directvolumeraycast(volumedata, camera, transferfunction, volumebounds, volumedims, stepsize=0.001, threshold=0.99): """ Renders a volume using fixed-step raycasting with front-to-back compositing. """ h, w = camera.screenheight, camera.screenwidth image = [[vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(w)] for in range(h)] for y in range(h): for x in range(w): rayorigin, raydirection = camera.castray(x, y) accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # Ray initialization: fixed random offset to prevent banding t = random.uniform(0.0, stepsize) # Compute ray exit distance from volume bounds tend = computerayexit(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds) while accumulatedopacity < threshold and t < tend: # Compute current position in texture space [0,1] pos = [(rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i]) for i in range(3)] # Sample volume at current position using trilinear interpolation scalarvalue = trilinearinterpolate(volumedata, pos, volumedims) # Apply transfer function to get color and opacity color, opacity = transferfunction(scalarvalue) # Front-to-back compositing accumulatedcolor[0] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity color[0] accumulatedcolor[1] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity color[1] accumulatedcolor[2] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity color[2] accumulatedopacity += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity t += stepsize # Gamma correction image[y][x] = powvec3(accumulatedcolor, 1.0/2.2) return image Enhances depth perception by dimming and shifting colors towards a background as they recede [791-distance-color-blending.md]. Handles reconstruction of scalar values, addressing artifacts from nearest neighbor interpolation. Defines the discretization of the volume rendering integral and ray parameterization context. Finds the maximum voxel value along the ray, ignoring intermediate values. Projects a semi-transparent 3D scalar field onto a 2D plane by integrating optical properties along viewing rays. Reduces banding artifacts by adding stochastic jittering controlled by a noise texture. Samples points along a ray from a discrete probability distribution using inverse CDF interpolation. Guarantees accurate rendering results for non-convex meshes on GPU. Considers volume data as a transparent gel, simulating light travelling through it without mapping. Casts multiple rays per pixel distributed within the pixel area to reduce jagged edges. Generates points uniformly distributed between minimum and maximum depth along each ray. Scales per-slice opacity to maintain constant image intensity regardless of slice count. Rasterizes back faces of the bounding box to trigger fragment shaders, avoiding processing pixels outside the volume. Computes pixel color by combining background transmission and uniform in-scattering, applying Beer's law. Enhances coarse macrostructure at render time by perturbing texture coordinates and optical properties with noise. Manages the sequence of rendering operations for volume data. Visualizes 3D grid data into 2D views. Renders scalar field data on a 3D rectilinear grid using front-to-back alpha compositing. Simulates light interaction with particles assuming light scatters only once before reaching the camera. Uses neural networks to represent and render volumetric data. Transforms a trivariate polynomial into a univariate polynomial using convolution operators. Stores 3D volume data in a 1D texture array organized into tiles for ray marching. Real-time GPU method using Taichi to perform ray marching through a 3D scalar field. An approximation of the opacity function Fr(t) and its inverse by approximating the density field \sigmar(t) as piecewise constant or piecewise linear on a grid, allowing analytical computation of the integral \int \sigmar(s) ds. For piecewise constant approximation, pick a point \hat{t}i within each bin [ti, t{i+1}] and approximate density as \sigmar(\hat{t}i) inside the bin. For piecewise linear approximation, compute \sigmar at grid points and interpolate values between grid points. Solve yf u = 1 - \exp(-I(t)) for t, where I(t) is the chosen integral approximation (I0 or I1), to find the sample location t corresponding to uniform sample u. The integral approximation I0(t) for piecewise constant density is: I0(t) = \sum{j=1}^i \sigmar(\hat{t}j)(tj - t{j-1}) + \sigmar(\hat{t}i)(t - ti), where t \in [ti, t{i+1}]. The integral approximation I1(t) for piecewise linear density is a sum of trapezoidal areas. The grid is a set of points tn = t0 < t1 < \dots < tm = tf defining the bins for the piecewise approximation. An algorithm that approximates perspective volume rendering using parallel projected slabs to enable acceleration on hardware designed for parallel projection, with analytical error bounds. It approximates perspective projection using parallel projected slabs, performs an analytical study of maximum and average error, and improves the basic algorithm based on error analysis to bound global maximum error while increasing frame rate. Inside the loop, for each intersected voxel (imgi, imgj), add length imagevalue to the sum, where imagevalue is accessed at index batchindex channels height width + channelindex height width + imgi width + imgj. Rendering technique for unsorted cell projection using optical models that lead to a commutative blend function, allowing compositing in arbitrary order. It applies arbitrary transfer functions via texture lookup, which only affect the generation of the texture map. Models allowing arbitrary order compositing include maximum intensity projection and restrictions of the full volume density model to either the source term or the absorption term. The term "direct volume rendering" was coined by Marc Levoy in his 1988 paper "Display of Surfaces from Volume Data". Levoy defined the volume rendering pipeline, which remains an influential framework. The technique was originally designed to display weak or fuzzy surfaces with smooth silhouettes and few aliasing artifacts.
