name: NeRF Volumetric Rendering (Coarse/Fine Sampling)
head: NeRF Volume Rendering, Volume Rendering (NeRF), NeRF Ray Marching, Standard NeRF Rendering, NeRF Two-Stage Sampling, NeRF Coarse-to-Fine Rendering, NeRF Rendering (Coarse and Fine), NeRF Fine Sampling and Rendering
body: NeRF Volumetric Rendering synthesizes novel views by querying a neural radiance field (a coordinate MLP) along camera rays and accumulating outputs using differentiable volume rendering. It solves the view synthesis problem by optimizing a continuous 5D function (spatial location and viewing direction) to predict volume density and view-dependent color. Unlike single-stage uniform sampling, this method employs a two-stage hierarchical sampling strategy: a coarse network estimates density to guide finer sampling in high-density regions, reducing aliasing and improving geometric detail. It operates on a flat batch of rays rather than a spatial grid, enabling efficient training on randomly sampled rays. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, tensor of shape [R, 3]. raysd: Unnormalized ray directions (Blender convention: camera looks down -z), tensor of shape [R, 3]. near, far: Near and far clipping plane distances along the ray, scalars or tensors of shape [R, 1]. coarsemodel, finemodel: Two neural networks with identical architecture but independent weights. nsamples: Number of coarse samples per ray (default 64). Nimportance: Number of additional fine samples to add (default 0 or 128 depending on implementation). perturb: Boolean flag to enable stratified sampling jittering (default True). whitebackground: Boolean flag to composite over white background (default True for Blender dataset). Outputs: rgb: Rendered color, shape [R, 3]. depth: Weighted average depth, shape [R]. acc: Total accumulated opacity, shape [R]. Data Structures: The neural field maps 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma, using positional encoding. Samples are stored as z-values along the ray parameter t. Steps: 1. Ray Initialization and Coarse Sampling: Generate linearly spaced depths t{vals} \in [0, 1] of size n{samples}. Map to world space near/far bounds: z{vals} = \text{near} \cdot (1 - t{vals}) + \text{far} \cdot t{vals} Shape: [R, n{samples}]. If perturb is True, apply stratified sampling: Compute midpoints: mids = 0.5 \cdot (z{vals}[:, 1:] + z{vals}[:,:-1]). Define intervals: lower = [z{vals}[:, 0], mids], upper = [mids, z{vals}[:, -1]]. Jitter: z{vals} = lower + (upper - lower) \cdot \text{rand}(R, n{samples}). 2. Coarse Network Query: Compute 3D points: \mathbf{pts} = \text{rays\o} + \text{rays\d} \cdot z{vals}. Flatten points to [-1, 3] and query coarsemodel to get raw RGB \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. Reshape outputs to [R, n{samples}, 3] and [R, n{samples}]. 3. Coarse Rendering (Alpha Compositing): Compute segment distances \delta: \deltai = (z{vals, i+1} - z{vals, i}) \cdot \|\text{rays\d}\| Append a large value (10^{10}) for the last segment to ensure termination. Compute alpha using softplus activation on density: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\text{softplus}(\sigmai) \cdot \deltai). Add epsilon (10^{-10}) to (1-\alpha) before cumulative product for stability. Compute transmittance T (exclusive cumulative product): Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj + \epsilon). Compute weights: wi = Ti \cdot \alphai. Render coarse maps: C{coarse} = \sum wi \mathbf{c}i, \quad D{coarse} = \sum wi z{i}, \quad A{coarse} = \sum wi. 4. Fine Sampling (Hierarchical): Use coarse weights to guide finer sampling. Exclude the first weight (index 0) as it corresponds to the start of the ray. Add epsilon (10^{-5}) to weights and normalize to form a probability distribution. Compute CDF from weights, prepend zero. Sample N{importance} values from a uniform distribution and use inverse CDF sampling to draw from the coarse weight distribution. Detach z{fine} from the computation graph to prevent gradient flow to the coarse network. 5. Interleaving and Fine Network Query: Concatenate coarse z{vals} and fine z{fine}, then sort them to interleave samples. Compute new 3D points \mathbf{pts}{all} from sorted z-values. Flatten and query finemodel to get \mathbf{c}{fine} and \sigma{fine}. 6. Fine Rendering: Recompute distances \delta and alphas \alpha for the sorted samples using the fine network outputs. Compute new weights wi and transmittance Ti. Render final maps: C{final} = \sum wi \mathbf{c}i. Args: rayso: [R, 3] Ray origins raysd: [R, 3] Ray directions (unnormalized) near: [R, 1] Near plane distances far: [R, 1] Far plane distances coarsemodel: Neural network returning (color, density) finemodel: Neural network returning (color, density) nsamples: int Number of coarse samples Nimportance: int Number of fine samples perturb: bool Enable stratified sampling whitebackground: bool Composite over white epsilonalpha: float Epsilon for alpha stability epsilonweight: float Epsilon for weight normalization Returns: rgb: [R, 3] depth: [R] acc: [R] """ R = rayso.shape[0] # 1. Coarse Sampling tvals = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, nsamples, device=rayso.device) zvals = near (1.0 - tvals) + far tvals # [R, nsamples] if perturb: mids = 0.5 (zvals[:, 1:] + zvals[:,:-1]) upper = torch.cat([mids, zvals[:, -1:]], dim=-1) lower = torch.cat([zvals[:,:1], mids], dim=-1) randomvals = torch.randlike(zvals) zvals = lower + (upper - lower) randomvals # 2. Coarse Network Query ptscoarse = rayso[:, None,:] + raysd[:, None,:] zvals[:,:, None] # [R, nsamples, 3] ptsflat = ptscoarse.reshape(-1, 3) dirsflat = raysd[:, None,:].expand(ptscoarse.shape).reshape(-1, 3) coarseout = coarsemodel(ptsflat, dirsflat) ccoarse = coarseout[0].reshape(R, nsamples, 3) sigmacoarse = coarseout[1].reshape(R, nsamples) # 3. Interleave and Fine Query zall = torch.cat([zvals, zfine], dim=-1) zall, = torch.sort(zall, dim=-1) ptsall = rayso[:, None,:] + raysd[:, None,:] zall[:,:, None] ptsflatall = ptsall.reshape(-1, 3) dirsflatall = raysd[:, None,:].expand(ptsall.shape).reshape(-1, 3) fineout = finemodel(ptsflatall, dirsflatall) cfine = fineout[0].reshape(R, zall.shape[-1], 3) sigmafine = fineout[1].reshape(R, zall.shape[-1]) # 6. Fine Rendering distsall = zall[:, 1:] - zall[:,:-1] distsall = torch.cat([distsall, torch.full((R, 1), 1e10, device=rayso.device)], dim=-1) distsall = distsall torch.norm(raysd, dim=-1, keepdim=True) alphafine = 1.0 - torch.exp(-softplus(sigmafine) distsall) onesall = torch.oneslike(alphafine[:,:1]) Tfine = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([onesall, 1.0 - alphafine + epsilonalpha], dim=-1), dim=-1)[:,:-1] weightsfinefinal = Tfine alphafine rgbfinal = torch.sum(weightsfinefinal[:,:, None] cfine, dim=1) accfinal = torch.sum(weightsfinefinal, dim=1) depthfinal = torch.sum(weightsfinefinal zall, dim=1) if whitebackground: rgbfinal = rgbfinal + (1.0 - accfinal[:, None]) return rgbfinal, depthfinal, accfinal A standalone PyTorch library providing efficient sampling for volumetric rendering, decoupled from radiance field representation, supporting Occupancy Grid and Proposal Network. A technique to refine the sampling distribution along rays by using the weights from a coarse model to generate additional sample points, improving rendering quality with minimal overhead. It calculates midpoints between coarse samples, calls samplepdf with the coarse weights (excluding first and last samples), the number of importance samples N{importance}, and a deterministic flag based on perturb. The sampled positions are detached from the computation graph, concatenated with coarse z-values, sorted, and the fine network is evaluated at the new points. Performance: Hierarchical sampling uses the coarse model's density to guide finer sampling, reducing aliasing and improving detail compared to single-stage uniform sampling. Strengths: Differentiable end-to-end, allowing optimization from images alone; handles view-dependent appearance via directional encoding; hierarchical sampling efficiently allocates samples to dense regions. Limitations: The basic implementation is inefficient and does not converge to a sufficiently high-resolution representation for complex scenes without hierarchical refinement. NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It represents a scene as a continuous 5D function mapping spatial coordinates and viewing directions to volume density and emitted color. The method is trained by minimizing the difference between rendered images and ground truth images using gradient descent, leveraging the differentiability of the volume rendering integral. The coarse-to-fine sampling strategy was introduced to address the inefficiency and aliasing artifacts of uniform sampling, allowing the model to focus computational resources on regions with high density. name: Alpha Compositing Ray Casting
head: Alpha Compositing with White Background, Front-to-back compositing, Front-to-back ray casting, Volume Compositing, Volumetric Compositing, White Background Compositing
body: Alpha Compositing Ray Casting projects a semi-transparent 3D scalar field onto a 2D image plane by integrating optical properties along viewing rays, eliminating the need for binary classification of the data. It differs from Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) by preserving internal texture and visibility through opacity-weighted accumulation rather than selecting only the highest intensity value. The method discretizes the volume rendering integral into a summation over sample points along a ray, performing front-to-back compositing. Inputs: volumetexture: 3D array or texture storing scalar voxel values. camera: Defines ray origins and directions for each pixel. transferfunction: Maps scalar values to RGB color; opacity is often derived directly from the sampled scalar value rather than a separate alpha channel. Implemented as a 2D texture in WebGL contexts. stepsize: Fixed distance between samples, or derived from volume dimensions. threshold: Opacity threshold for early ray termination (typically 0.95–0.99). Outputs: image: 2D array of RGB values representing the final rendered frame. Volume Texture: 3D array of scalar values. Sampled using trilinear interpolation or nearest neighbor. Transfer Function: 2D texture where the x-coordinate is the scalar value and y-coordinate is fixed (e.g., 0.5). Output is RGB. Accumulators: accumulatedcolor (C'): vec3, initialized to (0, 0, 0). accumulatedopacity (\alpha'): float, initialized to 0.0. 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, compute ray origin \bar{o} and direction \bar{d}. 2. Bounding Box Intersection: Intersect the ray with the volume bounds [0,1]^3 to find entry t0 and exit t1. If t0 > t1, discard the pixel. If the eye is inside the volume, clamp t0 to 0.0. 3. Step Size Calculation: Compute step size dt based on volume dimensions V{dim} and ray direction \bar{d}: dt = \min \left( \frac{1}{V{dim,x} |dx|}, \frac{1}{V{dim,y} |dy|}, \frac{1}{V{dim,z} |dz|} \right). 4. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate from t = t0 to t < t1 with increment dt: a. Sample: Evaluate scalar value s at position \bar{p} = \bar{o} + t\bar{d}. b. Transfer Function: Map s to color \bar{c}i; opacity \alphai is typically the sampled scalar value itself. c. Compositing: Update accumulators: C'i = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai \bar{c}i \alpha'i = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai. d. Early Termination: If \alpha' \ge \text{threshold} (typically 0.95 or 0.99), break the loop. 5. Gamma Correction: Apply gamma correction (typically 2.2) to the final accumulated color: \bar{C}{final} = \bar{C}'{last}^{1/2.2}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def alphacompositingraycast(volumetexture, camera, transferfunction, volumedims, stepsize=None, threshold=0.99): """ Renders a volume using front-to-back alpha compositing. Args: volumetexture: 3D array or texture object supporting trilinear sampling. camera: Object with method castray(x, y) returning (origin, direction). transferfunction: Function or 2D texture mapping scalar value -> (color, opacity). volumedims: Tuple (dimx, dimy, dimz) of the volume grid. stepsize: Fixed marching distance. If None, derived from volumedims. threshold: Opacity threshold for early ray termination. Returns: image: 2D list of RGB values. """ import math H, W = camera.height, camera.width image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): rayorigin, raydirection = camera.castray(x, y) # Normalize ray direction length = math.sqrt(sum(dd for d in raydirection)) raydirection = [d/length for d in raydirection] accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 if stepsize is None: dirabs = [max(abs(d), 1e-6) for d in raydirection] dtvec = [1.0 / (volumedims[i] dirabs[i]) for i in range(3)] stepsize = min(dtvec) invdir = [1.0 / d if abs(d) > 1e-6 else 1e6 for d in raydirection] boxmin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] boxmax = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] tmintmp = [(boxmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)] tmaxtmp = [(boxmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)] tmin = [min(tmintmp[i], tmaxtmp[i]) for i in range(3)] tmax = [max(tmintmp[i], tmaxtmp[i]) for i in range(3)] t0 = max(tmin) t1 = min(tmax) if t0 > t1: continue t0 = max(t0, 0.0) t = t0 while t < t1 and accumulatedopacity < threshold: pos = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] scalarvalue = volumetexture.sampletrilinear(pos) color, opacity = transferfunction(scalarvalue) accumulatedcolor[0] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity color[0] accumulatedcolor[1] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity color[1] accumulatedcolor[2] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity color[2] accumulatedopacity += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity t += stepsize image[y][x] = [c (1.0/2.2) for c in accumulatedcolor] return image Threshold: Typically 0.95 or 0.99. Higher thresholds improve accuracy but increase computation. Numerical Stability: In some variants, a small epsilon (\epsilon = 10^{-10}) is added to the product term to prevent instability. Zero Direction Components: If a ray direction component is zero, the step size calculation must clamp it to a small positive value to avoid division by zero. Transfer Function Alpha: Some implementations ignore the transfer function's alpha channel and use the sampled scalar value directly as opacity. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of samples per ray. M depends on volume depth and step size. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume texture, where V is the number of voxels. Performance: Real-time rendering is achievable with hardware acceleration (e.g., WebGL fragment shaders). Software implementations may be slow without optimization. Strengths: Preserves internal structure and texture better than MIP. No binary classification required, reducing false positives/negatives. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large volumes or high resolutions. Sensitive to transfer function design. The technique was popularized by Drebin et al., who introduced volumetric compositing to eliminate binary classification artifacts. Early software implementations were slow, taking several seconds per frame, but later hardware frameworks enabled real-time rendering. It is widely used in medical imaging and scientific visualization. name: Frequency Domain Depth Cueing via Impulse Shifting
head: Analytic signal depth cueing, Cosine Delta Method, Frequency Domain Depth Cueing, Shifted H depth cueing, Shifted spectrum depth cueing
body: Frequency Domain Depth Cueing via Impulse Shifting is a technique for applying distance-based attenuation (depth cueing) to volume rendering entirely within the frequency domain, avoiding expensive spatial-domain convolution or repeated 3D FFTs per view. It modifies the interpolation filter H to a shifted filter H' by convolving it with the Fourier transform of the depth cueing function, allowing the cueing to be applied as a simple 2D operation on the slice plane during extraction. Unlike naive spatial approaches or hybrid methods that require multiple volume copies and per-view 3D transforms, this method leverages the precomputed 3D spectrum and small filter support to make the depth cueing cost negligible compared to interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The 3D Fourier transform of the volume data F(s), the original interpolation filter H(s), the view direction vector V, and depth cueing parameters (strength, offset, period). Output: The modified interpolation filter H'(s) and the final projected image values computed by interpolating F(s) with H'(s). Data Structures: F(s): 3D spectrum of the volume data. H(s): 3D interpolation kernel. Support is small, typically 3^3 to 5^3. H'(s): 2D complex array on the slice plane, representing the modified filter. D(s): 2D complex array representing the Fourier transform of the depth cueing function d(x) evaluated on the slice plane. Method Steps: 1. Define Depth Cueing Function: Choose a depth cueing function d(x) that weights voxels by their distance from the observer. Linear Cueing: dl(x) = C{cue}(V \cdot x) + C{avg}, where V is the view vector, x is the position, C{cue} is the strength, and C{avg} is a constant offset. Sine Wave Cueing: Model d(x) as a half-period sine wave to simplify its transform. Adjust the origin, amplitude, and period such that the value is zero at the farthest voxel and unity at the closest voxel to eliminate the need for a DC term. The period is typically made long enough so the cueing appears almost linear. 2. Compute Fourier Transform of Cueing Function D(s): For Linear Cueing: The transform Dl(s) is computed using a precomputed differential operator convolution VH(s). For Sine Wave Cueing: The transform consists of two impulses: D(s) = C1 \delta(s - sw) + C2 \delta(s + sw) where C1 and C2 are complex constants determined by amplitude and shift, and sw is determined by the period. 3. Compute Modified Filter H'(s): Convolve the original filter with the cueing transform: H'(s) = H(s) D(s) Implementation via Impulse Shifting: Since D(s) consists of impulses (for sine wave cueing), the convolution becomes a sum of shifted copies of H(s) with complex weights: H'(s) = C1 H(s - sw) + C2 H(s + sw). Optimization: To reduce kernel size, one of the impulses can be removed by doubling the weight of the remaining impulse, utilizing the analytic signal property. 4. Interpolate and Project: Use H'(s) instead of H(s) to interpolate F(s) during slice extraction. This operation is 2D, evaluated only on the plane of the slice being extracted. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeshiftedfilter(H, sw, C1, C2, removenegative=False): """ Computes the modified interpolation filter H' for depth cueing. Args: H: 3D complex array, the original interpolation filter on a grid. sw: 3D float array, frequency shift vector. C1, C2: complex numbers, impulse weights. removenegative: bool, if True, removes the negative frequency impulse. Returns: Hprime: 2D complex array on the slice plane, the modified filter. """ # Standard trilinear interpolation of 3D grid H at shifted coordinates (sw and -sw), # extracting the 2D slice plane. Returns 2D complex arrays. Hpos = interpolate3dto2d(H, sw) Hneg = interpolate3dto2d(H, -sw) if removenegative: return 2.0 C1 Hpos return C1 Hpos + C2 Hneg def interpolate3dto2d(grid3d, shiftvec): # Standard trilinear interpolation of 3D grid at shifted coordinates, extracting 2D slice. # For each 2D coordinate on the slice plane, compute the weighted sum of the 8 neighboring 3D grid values # based on fractional distances, handling boundaries by zero-padding. Returns 2D complex array. # Sources do not specify the exact interpolation routine. def renderslice(F, Hprime, sliceplane): """ Renders a slice using the modified filter. Args: F: 3D complex array, volume spectrum. Hprime: 2D complex array, modified filter. sliceplane: 2D array of coordinates defining the extraction plane. Returns: projection: 2D complex array, the projected slice. """ # Standard slice extraction: samples F at the given 2D plane coordinates using trilinear interpolation. Fslice = extractslice(F, sliceplane) # Standard 2D convolution: for each output pixel, compute the weighted sum of neighboring input pixels using kernel Hprime. projection = convolve2d(Fslice, Hprime) return projection.real def extractslice(F, planecoords): # Standard slice extraction: samples F at the given 2D plane coordinates. # For each 2D coordinate, compute trilinear interpolation from the 3D spectrum F. Returns 2D complex array. # Sources do not specify the exact interpolation routine. def convolve2d(A, B): # Standard 2D convolution of array A with kernel B. # For each output pixel, compute the weighted sum of neighboring input pixels using kernel B, handling boundaries by zero-padding. # Sources do not specify the exact convolution routine. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex Output: Removing one impulse (to reduce kernel size) or using a sine wave with two impulses makes the projection image complex (non-real). The imaginary part is a cosine wave (analytic signal artifact). However, the real part of the result still contains the correct projection image. Only the real part should be displayed. Kernel Size: Using a sine wave with two impulses increases the filter kernel size. Removing one impulse mitigates this but introduces complex output. Precomputation: VH (differential operator convolution) can be precomputed and stored in a table, making the computation of H' for linear cueing of insignificant cost. DC Term: Adjusting the sine wave parameters (origin, amplitude, period) to be zero at the farthest voxel and unity at the closest eliminates the DC term, simplifying D(s) to just two impulses. Time Complexity: The 3D forward FFT is performed only once. For each view, the modification of H to H' is a 2D operation on the slice plane. The cost of recomputing H' is negligible compared to the cost of interpolation itself, because the support of H is small (3^3 to 5^3) and D(s) is simple. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D spectrum F(s) and the filter H(s). No additional volume copies are needed. Performance: The depth cueing is "practically free" compared to spatial domain convolution. While asymptotically faster than conventional spatial domain volume rendering, implementation considerations make it barely superior in practice. Strengths: Avoids per-view 3D FFTs; avoids multiple volume copies; high quality due to sinc resampling (inherited from parent method); flexible depth cueing functions. Limitations: Produces complex output (requires taking real part); kernel size can increase with complex cueing functions; requires precomputation of differential operators for linear cueing. Origin: Developed as part of the frequency domain volume rendering work in 1993. Development: It extends the frequency domain volume rendering algorithm by incorporating depth cueing and directional shading entirely in the frequency domain, using properties of the Fourier transform (differentiation theorem) to avoid spatial domain multiplication. Usage: Used in fast volume rendering applications where depth cues are important for shape perception. Fast tri-cubic interpolation is a GPU-based higher-order reconstruction scheme that evaluates a tri-cubic B-spline filter by reducing the number of texture fetches required for the convolution sum, leveraging GPU linear filtering capabilities. It solves the performance bottleneck of standard cubic interpolation, which requires 64 texel fetches for a 3D tri-cubic filter, by using separable filter kernels stored in 1D textures and pre-computed weight/offset functions to achieve the same result with only eight tri-linear texture fetches. It differs from Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling by operating in the spatial domain using fixed B-spline kernels rather than windowed sinc functions in the frequency domain. Inputs: Texture coordinate x (float) in the domain of the volume data. Volume texture containing discrete samples fi. Lookup texture containing pre-computed weight functions gi(x) and offset functions hi(x). Kernel storage texture: A single four-channel 1D floating-point RGBA texture where each channel stores one tile of the discretized reconstruction kernel of width four. Outputs: Reconstructed scalar value f(x) at coordinate x. Data Structures: 1. Lookup Texture: Stores functions g0(x), h0(x), g1(x), h1(x). g0(x) = w0(x) + w1(x) h0(x) = 1 - \frac{w1(x)}{w0(x) + w1(x)} g1(x) = w2(x) + w3(x) h1(x) = 1 + \frac{w3(x)}{w2(x) + w3(x)} Where wk(x) are the cubic B-spline weights. 2. Kernel Storage Texture: 1D floating-point RGBA texture. Width: 4 samples (kernel width). Layout: Each channel (R, G, B, A) stores one of the four kernel tiles. A single texture fetch at position X returns 4 weight values. Numbered Steps: 1. Decomposition: The 3D tri-cubic filter evaluation is decomposed into separable 1D passes due to the tensor-product nature of B-splines. The 3D filter with 64 summands is evaluated using 8 tri-linear texture fetches. 2. 1D Reconstruction (Fast Tri-Cubic): For each dimension, the convolution sum f(x) = w0(x)f{i-1} + w1(x)fi + w2(x)f{i+1} + w3(x)f{i+2} is computed efficiently. Let [x] be the integer part of x. Fetch two consecutive samples from the volume texture using linear interpolation: v0 = \text{texel}([x] - h0(x)) v1 = \text{texel}([x] + h1(x)) Compute the result using pre-computed weights: f{1D}(x) = g0(x)v0 + g1(x)v1. The weights g0, g1 and offsets h0, h1 are retrieved from the lookup texture based on the fractional part of x. 3. Kernel Tile Multiplication (Alternative/Extended Approach): In implementations using explicit kernel tiles (e.g., for Frequency Domain Volume Rendering), the filtering is divided into four passes. Each pass computes the contribution of 16 neighboring samples (4 neighbors \times 4 channels/tiles). A single texture fetch from the kernel storage texture provides the 4 weights for the current tile. The weights are multiplied by the corresponding 4 neighboring texels and summed. 4. Blending: Since hardware does not support blending with floating-point precision during intermediate passes, the intermediate results from the four passes are summed in a separate blending pass. 5. 3D Composition: The separable 1D passes are combined via tensor product to produce the final 3D value. name: Cubic Interpolation (Mitchell-Netravali)
head: Mitchell-Netravali, Mitchell-Netravali Cubic Filter
body: Mitchell-Netravali cubic interpolation is a family of C0 and C1 continuous cubic filters defined by parameters B and C, used to reconstruct volume data while preventing high-frequency leakage artifacts. It distinguishes itself from simpler schemes by offering a tunable trade-off between blurring and ringing, and from fixed B-splines by allowing the generation of Catmull-Rom splines. It builds on Fast tri-cubic interpolation by providing the specific kernel weights for the convolution sum. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume texture V, a sampling position P, and tuning parameters B and C. Output: A single interpolated scalar value at P. Parameters: Tuning parameters B and C. Data Structures: The kernel k(x) is a scalar function. The volume V is accessed via integer voxel coordinates. Method: 1. For each sample point P along the ray, compute the fractional offset x from the nearest voxel center. 2. Compute the kernel weight k(x) using the Mitchell-Netravali formula. 3. Fetch the 64 nearest voxel values in 3D (4 samples per dimension). 4. Compute the weighted sum of these 64 samples. 5. Clamp the result to the valid input range to prevent out-of-bounds values. Kernel Formula: The kernel k(x) is defined piecewise based on |x|: k(x) = \frac{1}{6} \begin{cases} (12 - 9B - 6C)|x^3| + (-18 + 12B + 6C)|x^2| + (6 - 2B), & \text{if } |x| < 1; \\ (-B - 6C)|x^3| + (6B + 30C)|x^2| + (-12B - 48C)|x| + (8B + 24C), & \text{if } 1 \le |x| < 2; \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} Symbol Definitions: x: The distance from the sample point to the voxel center, normalized such that voxel centers are at integers. B, C: Tuning parameters that trade off aliasing effects (blurring, ringing, anisotropy). |x|: Absolute value of x. Parameters: B=1.0, C=0.0: Generates Cubic B-splines. B=0.0, C=0.5: Generates Catmull-Rom splines. Typical values trade off aliasing effects (blurring, ringing, anisotropy). Pitfalls: General cubic interpolation can produce values outside the range of the inputs; these must be clamped. The filter satisfies \sum{n=-\infty}^{\infty} h(x-n) = 1 to prevent sample frequency ripple. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mitchellnetravalikernel(x, B, C): absx = abs(x) if absx < 1.0: return ((12.0 - 9.0 B - 6.0 C) absx3 + (-18.0 + 12.0 B + 6.0 C) absx2 + (6.0 - 2.0 B)) / 6.0 elif absx < 2.0: return ((-B - 6.0 C) absx3 + (6.0 B + 30.0 C) absx2 + (-12.0 B - 48.0 C) absx + (8.0 B + 24.0 C)) / 6.0 else: return 0.0 def samplevolumemitchell(V, xfrac, yfrac, zfrac, B, C): # xfrac, yfrac, zfrac are fractional coordinates in [0, 1) relative to base voxel basex = math.floor(xfrac) basey = math.floor(yfrac) basez = math.floor(zfrac) weightedsum = 0.0 totalweight = 0.0 for dx in range(-1, 3): for dy in range(-1, 3): for dz in range(-1, 3): distx = xfrac - dx disty = yfrac - dy distz = zfrac - dz wx = mitchellnetravalikernel(distx, B, C) wy = mitchellnetravalikernel(disty, B, C) wz = mitchellnetravalikernel(distz, B, C) weight = wx wy wz voxelval = V[basex + dx, basey + dy, basez + dz] weightedsum += weight voxelval totalweight += weight result = weightedsum / totalweight if totalweight > 0 else 0.0 return max(0.0, min(1.0, result)) A higher-order polynomial interpolation scheme for smoother results than linear interpolation, requiring more samples. In 3D, it requires sampling 64 voxels (2^4). It produces smoother results than linear interpolation but increases render time. Time and Memory Complexity: In 3D, cubic interpolation requires sampling 64 nearest samples. Spatial extent is 4N samples, where N is the dimension of the input (i.e., 4, 16, or 64 for 1D, 2D, or 3D cases). As complexity increases, quality increases, but so does computation. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: C0 and C1 continuity prevents high-frequency leakage artifacts. Tunable parameters allow trade-offs between blurring, ringing, and anisotropy. Limited spatial extent. Limitations: Higher computational cost than linear or nearest-neighbor. Can produce values outside the input range, requiring clamping. When to Use: Use when smoother results than linear interpolation are needed and computational resources allow for 64 samples per point. Use when specific artifact characteristics (ringing vs. blurring) need to be tuned via B and C parameters. Originated from Mitchell and Netravali's work on reconstruction filters [Mitchell 88], as cited in. The method is designed to provide C0 and C1 continuity to prevent high-frequency leakage artifacts. It is used in volume rendering for publication-quality imagery. body: Bilinear interpolation estimates values at arbitrary 2D coordinates by linearly interpolating across the four nearest grid points. It sets itself apart from nearest neighbor interpolation by eliminating blocky artifacts while maintaining lower computational cost than higher-order schemes like tri-cubic interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D grid of values V with dimensions resX \times resY, and a query coordinate (x, y) where x, y \in \mathbb{R}. Output: The interpolated scalar value V(x, y). Data Structures: The grid is stored as a 1D contiguous array values of size resX \times resY. Fields: int resX: Width of the grid. int resY: Height of the grid. Data values: Pointer to the memory block. Layout: Element at integer coordinates (x, y) is stored at index x \cdot resY + y. Algorithm Steps: 1. Integer Bounds: Compute the integer coordinates of the lower-left corner of the cell containing (x, y). Let x1 = \lfloor x \rfloor and y1 = \lfloor y \rfloor. If the implementation uses integer truncation for negative numbers (e.g., int(x) in C++), special handling is required. If x < 0, x1 must be set to -\lfloor -x \rfloor - 1 to correctly identify the floor. The same logic applies to y1. 2. Fractional Parts: Compute the interpolation weights (blending factors) as the fractional parts of the coordinates: dx = x - x1 dy = y - y1 These values represent the offset from the corner in the range [0, 1). When working with normalized texture coordinates C and resolution R, the blending factor can also be computed as F = C \times R - \lfloor C \times R \rfloor. 3. Neighbor Fetch: Retrieve the four surrounding grid values: V{00} = Grid(x1, y1) V{10} = Grid(x1 + 1, y1) V{01} = Grid(x1, y1 + 1) V{11} = Grid(x1 + 1, y1 + 1). 4. Interpolation: Compute the final value using the bilinear formula: V(x, y) = V{00}(1 - dx)(1 - dy) + V{10}dx(1 - dy) + V{01}(1 - dx)dy + V{11}dx dy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bilinearinterpolate(values, resX, resY, x, y): # Handle negative coordinates for floor calculation if x < 0: x1 = -int(-x) - 1 else: x1 = int(x) if y < 0: y1 = -int(-y) - 1 else: y1 = int(y) # Compute fractional parts (weights) dx = x - x1 dy = y - y1 # Corrected wrapping logic (fixes the resY/resX bug in) def wrap(idx, dim): if idx < 0: idx = dim - ((-idx) % dim) return idx % dim x0 = wrap(x1, resX) x1next = wrap(x1 + 1, resX) y0 = wrap(y1, resY) y1next = wrap(y1 + 1, resY) v00 = values[x0 resY + y0] v10 = values[x1next resY + y0] v01 = values[x0 resY + y1next] v11 = values[x1next resY + y1next] # Bilinear formula result = (v00 (1 - dx) (1 - dy) + v10 dx (1 - dy) + v01 (1 - dx) dy + v11 dx dy) return result PyTorch Implementation Note: When using torch.nn.functional.gridsample, the input grid coordinates must be negated and reshaped to [batchsize, -1, 1, 2] to match the expected format, and aligncorners=True should be used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Index Wrapping Bug: A common implementation error in wrapping negative indices is using the wrong dimension for the modulo operation. Specifically, if(x<0){x = resX - ((-x) % resY);} is incorrect because it uses resY instead of resX for the x-axis modulo, causing incorrect wrapping along the x-axis. Boundary Conditions: The sources do not specify behavior for coordinates outside the [0, resX-1] \times [0, resY-1] range other than the wrapping bug example. Standard implementations typically clamp or wrap coordinates to the grid boundaries. It typically uses 16-bit unsigned integers for color and opacity values. It is chosen because reconstruction for non-uniform sampling on unstructured meshes is not well understood and is significantly more complex than uniform sampling. It exhibits C1 discontinuities common to linear interpolation. This method uses linear interpolation between two sampled flow vectors of different time steps to handle dynamic vector fields. The interpolated vector is calculated as MR(v, t) = (1 - t)Si(v) + tSj(v), where Si(v) and Sj(v) are vector field slices. A pitfall occurs if the interpolation index k is not in [i, j], as the equation yields extrapolation instead of interpolation. name: Multi-Dimensional Interpolation Extension
head: 3D Kernel Extension Methods, Separable and Radial Kernel Extension
body: This method extends one-dimensional reconstruction kernels to three dimensions for volume rendering. It constructs a 3D filter from a 1D base kernel h' to correctly reconstruct signals on a regular 3D mesh, setting itself apart from radial extension methods by avoiding sample frequency ripple artifacts that occur with rotationally-symmetric kernels on regular grids. Input: A 1D reconstruction kernel function h'(u), where u is the distance from the kernel center. Output: A 3D kernel function h(x, y, z) evaluated at offset coordinates (x, y, z) relative to the sample center. Not given in the sources. Method 1: Separable Extension (Recommended) This method treats each coordinate as an independent variable. It is the correct way to extend filters to higher dimensions for regular meshes. 1. Evaluate the 1D kernel for each coordinate offset: h'(x), h'(y), and h'(z). 2. Multiply the results to form the 3D kernel: h(x, y, z) = h'(x) \times h'(y) \times h'(z). Method 2: Radial Extension This method uses the Euclidean radius from the kernel center as the free variable. This produces rotationally-symmetric kernels. 1. Calculate the radius r from the kernel center: r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}. 2. Evaluate the 1D kernel at the radius: h(x, y, z) = h'(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}). Not given in the sources. Sample Frequency Ripple: Method 2 suffers from sample frequency ripple on regular meshes. Even if input samples have equal amplitude, the output field will not be flat; it will differ from the constant amplitude at points between the equal-valued input samples. Reconstruction Accuracy: Rotationally-symmetric kernels (except for the Gaussian, which is also separable) do not correctly reconstruct a regular mesh. Therefore, Method 2 should generally not be used for standard volume rendering on structured grids. This variant applies the separable extension principle to image warping and affine transformations in volume rendering. Definition: Uses separable kernels to enable two-pass and three-pass image warping. It is much less sensitive to kernel extent sizes because the computational complexity is O(n) for a kernel extent of n, compared to O(n^3) for standard ray-casting methods. Procedure: When using three-pass approaches, the order of passes is critical. All magnification steps must be performed before any minification steps. If minification precedes magnification, multiple samples are collapsed into a single sample during minification, and this information cannot be separated during subsequent passes, leading to signal loss. Usage: Typically employs high-quality reconstruction kernels for all image generation to retain maximum signal information. Complexity: For standard ray-casting, the complexity is O(n^3) for a kernel extent of n. For affine transformation methods using separable kernels, the complexity reduces to O(n). Strengths: Method 1 (Separable) correctly reconstructs regular meshes and avoids the ripple artifacts inherent in Method 2. Limitations: Standard ray-casting methods are sensitive to kernel extent due to O(n^3) complexity. Affine methods mitigate this but require careful pass ordering to avoid information loss. When to use: Use Method 1 for all regular mesh reconstructions. Use Affine Transformation Interpolation when performing image warping or non-axis-aligned rendering where computational efficiency is prioritized and high-quality kernels are required. The distinction between separable and radial extensions was formalized in the context of parallel, feed-forward volume rendering algorithms. The analysis highlights that volume renderers seldom generate images that are axis-aligned with identical sampling rates for input data and the image, necessitating resampling and careful filter design. Hanrahan [Hanrahan 90] is cited as a key contributor who considered these signal processing concerns, specifically regarding the ordering of magnification and minification in affine transformations. name: Hardware Interpolation Approximation
head: Piecewise Bilinear/Trilinear Interpolation via Polygon Subdivision
body: This method approximates volume rendering integration by leveraging standard graphics hardware rasterization, assuming linear interpolation along ray segments. It sets itself apart from analytical integration schemes by relying on the implicit interpolation of the GPU's rasterizer, resulting in view-dependent piecewise bilinear or trilinear interpolation depending on how the hardware subdivides polygons. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset represented as a polygonal mesh (typically quadrilateral faces) and a view direction. Output: A rendered image where color and opacity are accumulated based on the hardware-interpolated scalar field values along rays. Data Structures: The volume is represented as a polygonal mesh with quadrilateral faces. Exact field layouts, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. No explicit lookup tables or pre-computed integrals are required for the interpolation itself. Steps: 1. Polygon Subdivision: The graphics hardware subdivides the input quadrilateral faces into primitives suitable for rasterization. The specific subdivision strategy determines the interpolation order: Case 1 (Triangles): The hardware divides the quadrilateral into two triangles, and linear interpolation is performed across each triangle. Case 2 (Trapezoids): The hardware divides the quadrilateral into trapezoids using horizontal lines through the vertices, and bilinear interpolation is performed within each trapezoid. If a trapezoid degenerates into a triangle, linear interpolation is used. 2. Ray Segment Interpolation: Along each ray segment passing through a rasterized primitive, the scalar field value is assumed to vary linearly. 3. Integration Approximation: The accumulation of color and opacity along the ray is computed based on these linearly interpolated values. The resulting interpolation is piecewise bilinear (if triangles are used) or piecewise trilinear (if trapezoids are used). Formulas: Let V(x) be the scalar field. The hardware approximation assumes V(x) is linear within each rasterized primitive. For a ray segment parameterized by t, the value is interpolated as: V(t) = V0 + t(V1 - V0) where V0 and V1 are the values at the endpoints of the segment within the primitive. The exact functional form depends on the primitive type and the hardware's specific rasterization rules. Parameters: Subdivision Strategy: Determined by the graphics API/hardware. Primitive Type: Triangle or Trapezoid. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View Dependence: The interpolation is view-dependent because the subdivision into pieces depends on the subdivision of the view plane into polygons and any further subdivision produced by the hardware. Specification Ambiguity: The exact interpolation produced by the hardware scheme is hard to determine because interpolation across polygons is not completely determined in the OpenGL specifications. Non-Planar Faces: The method's behavior with non-planar faces is not fully determined by OpenGL specifications. name: First Order Integration (Trapezoid Rule)
head: Linear Interpolation Approximation, Linear approximation, Linear interpolation integration, Standard pre-integrated volume rendering
body: First Order Integration approximates the volume rendering integral by assuming a linear interpolation of the scalar field between two discrete sample points, corresponding to the trapezoid rule. Unlike the piecewise-constant Riemann sum used in zero-order integration, this method captures higher frequencies of the transfer function, reducing visual artifacts caused by discontinuities between consecutive samples. It sets itself apart by requiring pre-computation of integrals into a lookup table indexed by segment endpoints and length, rather than evaluating the transfer function per sample. Inputs: Scalar field values at the front endpoint (sf) and back endpoint (sb) of a ray segment. Length of the ray segment (l). Transfer function mapping scalar values to chromaticity (q) and extinction coefficient (\kappa). Outputs: Pre-computed transparency (T) and color contribution (c) for the segment. Data Structures: 3D Lookup Table (LUT): A 3D array indexed by (sf, sb, l). Dimensions: Determined by the quantization of sf, sb, and l. Content: Each entry stores the pre-integrated transparency and color contribution for the segment defined by those parameters. Steps: 1. Define Linear Interpolation: Approximate the scalar field s(x) within a ray segment of length l as a linear interpolation between the front sample sf and back sample sb. Let x be the distance from the front endpoint (0 \le x \le l). The scalar value at position x is: s(x) = sf + \frac{sb - sf}{l} x 2. Compose with Transfer Function: The extinction coefficient \kappa(x) and chromaticity q(x) are obtained by applying the transfer function to the interpolated scalar field: \kappa(x) = \kappa(s(x)) q(x) = q(s(x)) 3. Integrate over Segment: Compute the transparency T and color contribution c for the segment by integrating the composed functions over the segment length l: T = \exp\left( -\int0^l \kappa(s(x)) \, dx \right) c = \int0^l q(s(x)) \exp\left( -\int0^x \kappa(s(u)) \, du \right) \, dx These integrals are computed numerically during pre-processing. 4. Store in LUT: Store the computed T and c in the 3D lookup table at the index corresponding to (sf, sb, l). Parameters: sf: Scalar value at the front endpoint of the ray segment. sb: Scalar value at the back endpoint of the ray segment. l: Length of the ray segment. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Continuity: The reconstructed signal is C^0 continuous globally but not C^1 continuous inside a dual voxel (between two sample points). Pre-computation Requirement: Unlike zero-order integration, first-order integration requires pre-integration because the scalar field is not constant. Sampling Distance: The sampling distance l affects the computation of color and opacity values, making it a necessary index for the LUT. Time Complexity: Pre-computation is performed offline. Runtime rendering involves 3D texture lookups. Memory Complexity: Requires a 3D lookup table indexed by (sf, sb, l). The size depends on the resolution of each dimension. Performance: Better convergence than zero-order approximation, capturing higher frequencies of the transfer function. Strengths: Reduces visual artifacts from discontinuities between samples; captures high frequencies of the transfer function. Limitations: Requires pre-computation; not C^1 continuous. When to use: When higher visual quality is needed than zero-order integration provides. When not to use: Not given in the sources. First Order Integration, also known as the trapezoid rule approximation in volume rendering, was proposed to improve rendering quality by capturing high frequencies of the transfer function. It addresses the approximation error and visual artifacts associated with zero-order (piecewise-constant) integration by using linear interpolation between samples. The method builds on the concept of pre-integrated volume rendering, where integrals are pre-computed and stored in lookup tables. name: Trilinear Interpolation
head: Trilinear Interpolant, 3D Linear Interpolation, Trilinear Interpolation for Rectilinear Grids
body: Trilinear interpolation estimates the scalar field value at an arbitrary point within a voxel grid by computing a weighted average of the eight surrounding voxel corner values. It solves the problem of sampling continuous volume data at non-integer coordinates, which occurs because ray casting sample points rarely align exactly with voxel centers. Compared to nearest-neighbor interpolation, trilinear interpolation produces significantly smoother images with fewer aliasing artifacts, though it requires approximately five times more computation time. It serves as the foundational reconstruction scheme for direct volume ray casting on regular grids. Inputs: A 3D scalar field defined on a regular grid with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz. A query point P = (x, y, z) in voxel space. Outputs: A single scalar value V representing the interpolated density or intensity at P. Data Structures: The volume data is stored in a 3D array (or flattened 1D array with row-major indexing). Voxel values are accessed via integer indices (i, j, k) where 0 \le i < Dx, 0 \le j < Dy, 0 \le k < Dz. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate Normalization and Offset: If the input coordinates are in world space, convert them to voxel space. Let P{voxel} be the position in voxel coordinates. To ensure that a sample point located exactly at the center of a voxel returns that voxel's value (and not an average of neighbors), shift the coordinate by -0.5 along each axis. P{lattice} = P{voxel} - 0.5 If the grid uses a rectilinear structure with non-uniform spacing, the offset and interpolation weights must be computed using the specific coordinate arrays X, Y, Z rather than simple integer arithmetic. For this article, we assume a regular grid with unit cell sizes as is standard for the basic definition. 2. Determine Containing Voxel: Compute the integer indices of the lower-left-front corner of the voxel containing P{lattice} using the floor function: i0 = \lfloor P{lattice}.x \rfloor j0 = \lfloor P{lattice}.y \rfloor k0 = \lfloor P{lattice}.z \rfloor Clamp these indices to valid bounds. Specifically, if i0 \ge Dx - 1, set i0 = Dx - 2 (and similarly for j, k) to ensure the upper neighbor index i0+1 does not exceed the grid boundary. 3. Compute Fractional Weights: Calculate the fractional distance from the lower-left corner to the query point within the voxel. These fractions serve as interpolation weights. wx = P{lattice}.x - i0 wy = P{lattice}.y - j0 wz = P{lattice}.z - k0 Note that wx, wy, wz \in [0, 1). 4. Retrieve Corner Values: Fetch the scalar values from the eight corners of the containing voxel. Let V{ijk} denote the value at grid index (i, j, k). The eight values are: V{000} = V{i0, j0, k0} V{100} = V{i0+1, j0, k0} V{010} = V{i0, j0+1, k0} V{110} = V{i0+1, j0+1, k0} V{001} = V{i0, j0, k0+1} V{101} = V{i0+1, j0, k0+1} V{011} = V{i0, j0+1, k0+1} V{111} = V{i0+1, j0+1, k0+1} 5. Perform Trilinear Interpolation: The final value is the sum of the corner values weighted by the product of their respective distances to the query point. The weight for a corner is the product of the "closeness" factors (1-w) or w for each dimension. Using the expanded form: \begin{aligned} V = \;& V{000}(1-wx)(1-wy)(1-wz) + V{100}wx(1-wy)(1-wz) \\ + \;& V{010}(1-wx)wy(1-wz) + V{110}wx wy (1-wz) \\ + \;& V{001}(1-wx)(1-wy)wz + V{101}wx(1-wy)wz \\ + \;& V{011}(1-wx)wy wz + V{111}wx wy wz \end{aligned} Alternatively, this can be computed sequentially using three linear interpolations (lerp): 1. Interpolate along X for the bottom face (k=k0) and top face (k=k0+1): C{00} = \text{lerp}(V{000}, V{100}, wx) C{10} = \text{lerp}(V{010}, V{110}, wx) C{01} = \text{lerp}(V{001}, V{101}, wx) C{11} = \text{lerp}(V{011}, V{111}, wx) 2. Interpolate along Y for the resulting pairs: C0 = \text{lerp}(C{00}, C{10}, wy) C1 = \text{lerp}(C{01}, C{11}, wy) 3. Interpolate along Z: V = \text{lerp}(C0, C1, wz) Where \text{lerp}(a, b, t) = a(1-t) + bt. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinearinterpolation(volume, dims, pvoxel): """ volume: 3D array of scalar values, shape (Dx, Dy, Dz) dims: tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) pvoxel: tuple (x, y, z) in voxel space (center-aligned) """ # 1. Shift by -0.5 to align voxel centers with integer grid plattice = (pvoxel[0] - 0.5, pvoxel[1] - 0.5, pvoxel[2] - 0.5) # 2. Compute lower-left indices i0 = int(plattice[0]) j0 = int(plattice[1]) k0 = int(plattice[2]) # 3. Clamp indices to ensure upper neighbors are within bounds # If plattice is exactly at the boundary, floor might give index == dim-1 # We need i0 < Dx-1, so clamp i0 to Dx-2 max i0 = max(0, min(i0, dims[0] - 2)) j0 = max(0, min(j0, dims[1] - 2)) k0 = max(0, min(k0, dims[2] - 2)) # 4. Compute fractional weights wx = plattice[0] - i0 wy = plattice[1] - j0 wz = plattice[2] - k0 # 5. Fetch 8 corner values # Indices: (i0+i, j0+j, k0+k) for i,j,k in {0,1} v000 = volume[i0][j0][k0] v100 = volume[i0+1][j0][k0] v010 = volume[i0][j0+1][k0] v110 = volume[i0+1][j0+1][k0] v001 = volume[i0][j0][k0+1] v101 = volume[i0+1][j0][k0+1] v011 = volume[i0][j0+1][k0+1] v111 = volume[i0+1][j0+1][k0+1] # 6. Interpolate along X c00 = v000 (1 - wx) + v100 wx c10 = v010 (1 - wx) + v110 wx c01 = v001 (1 - wx) + v101 wx c11 = v011 (1 - wx) + v111 wx # 7. Interpolate along Y c0 = c00 (1 - wy) + c10 wy c1 = c01 (1 - wy) + c11 wy # 8. Interpolate along Z result = c0 (1 - wz) + c1 wz return result Parameters: Grid Assumption: Regular grid with unit lengths in all three cell dimensions. If the grid is rectilinear (non-uniform spacing), the weights wx, wy, wz must be calculated as normalized distances between the coordinate arrays X, Y, Z. Precision: Standard single-precision floating point is typically sufficient, but care must be taken with boundary conditions to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: If the query point lies outside the volume bounds, the algorithm must handle out-of-bounds access. Common strategies include clamping the indices to the nearest valid voxel or returning a default value (e.g., 0). Center Alignment: Without the -0.5 offset, a sample point at the exact center of a voxel would incorrectly average all 8 neighbors instead of returning the voxel's own value. Cache Coherence: Naive access patterns to voxel buffers can lead to poor cache coherence, significantly impacting performance. Tiled storage schemes are recommended for production. Artifacts: Trilinear interpolation introduces C^1 discontinuities (false edges or "star patterns") because the triangular pulse reconstruction kernel has infinite extent in the frequency domain. This manifests as apparent sharpness not present in the data. Samples voxel values using nearest neighbor, trilinear, or tricubic interpolation to reconstruct the continuous radiance field from discrete voxel grids. An algorithm that substitutes trilinear interpolation with two bilinear interpolations and one linear interpolation to improve image quality over basic 2D texture rendering. Semi-analytical volume rendering with trilinear interpolation is a direct volume ray casting technique for hexahedral cells that eliminates topological artifacts (discontinuities, holes) in isosurfaces by analytically determining optimal sampling points along the ray. It sets itself apart from standard trilinear interpolation [1531-trilinear-interpolation.md] by replacing uniform sampling with a piecewise-linear approximation over monotonic intervals defined by the analytical extrema of the reconstructed signal, ensuring no isovalue is missed. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, requiring exactly 8 memory fetches and 7 linear interpolations (or equivalent arithmetic operations). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. The data structure is the volume grid itself, O(Nx Ny Nz). Performance: Trilinear interpolation takes approximately 5 times longer to compute than nearest-neighbor lookup. It is significantly faster than higher-order methods like tri-cubic interpolation but provides lower image quality. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally efficient, produces smoother results than nearest-neighbor, widely supported by hardware texture units (often via bilinear + linear approximation) [S1027-hardware-interpolation-approximation.md]. Limitations: Introduces blurring and C^1 discontinuities (false edges). Not suitable for high-fidelity reconstruction where sharp features must be preserved without aliasing. When to use: General-purpose volume rendering where performance is critical and high-frequency artifacts are acceptable or mitigated by other means (e.g., supersampling). When not to use: When high-frequency accuracy is required (use Fast tri-cubic interpolation or Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling), or when rendering rectilinear grids with significant non-uniformity without proper weight calculation. Trilinear interpolation is a standard technique in computer graphics and scientific visualization for sampling 3D scalar fields. It is derived from the tensor product of 1D linear interpolation kernels. The method is fundamental to direct volume ray casting on regular grids. It is implemented in various libraries, including OpenVDB, which uses a nested interpolation structure for sparse voxel grids. The mathematical properties of the trilinear interpolant, including the existence of saddle points, have been analyzed in the context of Marching Cubes and isosurface extraction. name: Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering with Trilinear Interpolation
head: Analytical Integration with Trilinear Reconstruction, Semi-Analytical Preintegration for Hexahedral Cells, Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering, Trilinear Preintegration
body: Semi-analytical volume rendering with trilinear interpolation is a direct volume ray casting technique for hexahedral cells that eliminates topological artifacts such as discontinuities and holes in isosurfaces by analytically determining optimal sampling points along the ray. It sets itself apart from standard trilinear interpolation [1531-trilinear-interpolation.md] by replacing uniform sampling with a piecewise-linear approximation over monotonic intervals defined by the analytical extrema of the reconstructed signal, ensuring no isovalue is missed. Inputs: Scalar field values s{ijk} at the 8 corners (i,j,k) \in \{0,1\}^3 of a hexahedral cell. Ray entry point (x0, y0, z0) and exit point (x1, y1, z1) in normalized cell coordinates [0,1]^3. Transfer functions: color c(s) and opacity \tau(s). Outputs: Accumulated color intensity I for the ray segment traversing the cell. Data Structures: Coefficients a, b, c, d of the cubic polynomial s(t). List of valid extrema R = \{r1, r2, \dots\} within [0,1]. Monotonic intervals defined by sorted sampling points T = \{0, r1, r2, 1\}. Steps: 1. Ray Parametrization: Compute the direction vector components as differences between exit and entry coordinates: vx = x1 - x0, \quad vy = y1 - y0, \quad vz = z1 - z0 The ray is parametrized as x(t) = x0 + t vx, y(t) = y0 + t vy, z(t) = z0 + t vz for t \in [0,1]. 2. Signal Reconstruction (Cubic Polynomial): Substitute the ray parametrization into the trilinear interpolation formula to obtain s(t) = a t^3 + b t^2 + c t + d. The coefficients are linear combinations of the corner values s{ijk} and ray parameters: a = (s{100} - s{000} + s{010} + s{001} + s{111} - s{110} - s{011} - s{101}) vx vy vz b = (-x0 vy vz - vx y0 vz - vx vy z0 + vx vz) s{101} + (x0 vy vz + vx y0 vz + vx vy z0) s{111} + (vy vz - x0 vy vz - vx y0 vz - vx vy z0) s{011} + (-vx vz + vx vy z0 - vy vz + x0 vy vz + vx y0 vz) s{001} + (-vx vz + vx y0 vz + vx vy z0 - vx vy + x0 vy vz) s{100} + (-vx y0 vz - x0 vy vz + vx vy z0) s{110} + (-x0 y0 vz - vx y0 z0 - x0 vy z0 + vx vy z0) s{010} + (-y0 z0 - x0 y0 + y0 + x0 y0 z0) s{010} + (-y0 - z0 - x0 y0 z0 + x0 z0 + y0 z0) s{001} Coefficients c and d are derived similarly by collecting terms of t^1 and t^0 respectively, resulting in sums of 8 terms each involving s{ijk} multiplied by products of x0, y0, z0 and vx, vy, vz. 3. Extrema Calculation: Compute the derivative s'(t) = 3a t^2 + 2b t + c. Find the roots of this quadratic equation: t = \frac{-2b \pm \sqrt{4b^2 - 12ac}}{6a} If a=0, solve the linear equation 2b t + c = 0. If a=0 and b=0, the function is constant and has no extrema. 4. Pruning and Sorting: Discard any roots t such that t < 0 or t > 1. Sort the remaining valid extrema ri in ascending order. Define the sampling points T = [0, r1, r2, \dots, 1]. 5. Interval Approximation: For each consecutive pair of sampling points ti, t{i+1} in T, approximate the signal s(t) as a linear interpolation between the values at the endpoints: s{lin}(t') = (1-t') s(ti) + t' s(t{i+1}), \quad t' \in [0,1] where t' is the local parameter within the interval [ti, t{i+1}]. Let Li = t{i+1} - ti be the length of the interval. 6. Preintegration: Compute the contribution of each interval using preintegration functions C and \alpha. The total intensity is accumulated using front-to-back alpha compositing: I \approx C(s(0), s(r1), L0) + (1 - \alpha(s(0), s(r1), L0)) C(s(r1), s(r2), L1) + \dots where C(a, b, L) = \int0^1 c((1-t') a + t' b) L e^{-\int0^{t'} \tau((1-u) a + u b) L du} dt' \alpha(a, b, L) = 1 - e^{-\int0^1 \tau((1-t') a + t' b) L dt'} In practice, these integrals are evaluated via numerical quadrature or lookup tables. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def semianalyticaltrilinearrender(scorners, x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1, cfunc, taufunc): """ scorners: list of 8 floats [s000, s100, s010, s001, s101, s011, s110, s111] x0,y0,z0: entry point in [0,1]^3 x1,y1,z1: exit point in [0,1]^3 cfunc: color transfer function (returns RGB tuple) taufunc: opacity transfer function (returns float) """ vx, vy, vz = x1 - x0, y1 - y0, z1 - z0 a, b, c, d = computecubiccoefficients(scorners, x0, y0, z0, vx, vy, vz) roots = solvequadratic(3a, 2b, c) validextrema = sorted([r for r in roots if 0.0 <= r <= 1.0]) samplingpoints = [0.0] + validextrema + [1.0] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(len(samplingpoints) - 1): tstart, tend = samplingpoints[i], samplingpoints[i+1] L = tend - tstart sstart, send = evalcubic(a, b, c, d, tstart), evalcubic(a, b, c, d, tend) intervalcolor, intervalalpha = preintegrateinterval(sstart, send, L, cfunc, taufunc) accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[k] + (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) intervalcolor[k] for k in range(3)] accumulatedalpha += (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) intervalalpha return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha def computecubiccoefficients(scorners, x0, y0, z0, vx, vy, vz): a, b, c, d = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): sval = scorners[i4 + j2 + k] cx = [1-x0, -vx, 0.0, 0.0] if i == 0 else [x0, vx, 0.0, 0.0] cy = [1-y0, -vy, 0.0, 0.0] if j == 0 else [y0, vy, 0.0, 0.0] cz = [1-z0, -vz, 0.0, 0.0] if k == 0 else [z0, vz, 0.0, 0.0] pc = [0.0]4 for m in range(4): for n in range(4): if m+n < 4: pc[m+n] += cx[m]cy[n] p = [0.0]4 for m in range(4): for n in range(4): if m+n < 4: p[m+n] += pc[m]cz[n] a += sval p[3]; b += sval p[2]; c += sval p[1]; d += sval p[0] return a, b, c, d def evalcubic(a, b, c, d, t): return ((at + b)t + c)t + d def solvequadratic(A, B, C): if abs(A) < 1e-9: return [-C/B] if abs(B) > 1e-9 else [] disc = BB - 4AC if disc < 0: return [] sqrtdisc = disc0.5 return [(-B - sqrtdisc)/(2A), (-B + sqrtdisc)/(2A)] def preintegrateinterval(sstart, send, L, cfunc, taufunc, steps=16): colorintegral = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tauintegral = 0.0 dt = 1.0 / steps for i in range(steps): tprime = (i + 0.5) dt sval = (1.0 - tprime)sstart + tprimesend cval = cfunc(sval) tauval = taufunc(sval) tauintegral += tauval dt accumulatedopacity = sum(taufunc((1.0 - (j+0.5)dt)sstart + (j+0.5)dtsend) dt for j in range(i+1)) weight = L (1.0 - tprime) colorintegral = [colorintegral[k] + weight cval[k] math.exp(-accumulatedopacity L) for k in range(3)] alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-tauintegral L) return colorintegral, alpha This method extends semi-analytical volume rendering by incorporating local Phong diffuse shading into the integration process. It solves the problem of accurate lighting in volume rendering by reconstructing the shading function as a quadratic polynomial along the ray, allowing for analytical integration of the light contribution. It sets itself apart from scalar-only semi-analytical methods by requiring at most one additional sampling point per cell to capture the shading extremum, while maintaining the topological accuracy of the underlying trilinear interpolation. A technique to handle hybrid cells in Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) by propagating cell splits from the lower level cell to the higher level cell to ensure continuity across cell faces. It identifies hybrid cells (sharing an edge/face with a different level cell) and propagates splits by adding 'source split points' (using the higher-level cell's value) and 'destination split points' (using bilinearly interpolated values from a shared face) to the lower-level cell. This ensures continuity across cell faces either by using the neighbor's value or by matching the interpolation scheme of the neighbor cell, avoiding artifacts. Time Complexity: The method requires solving a quadratic equation and evaluating preintegration functions for each monotonic interval. The number of intervals is small (at most 3), making it faster than high-frequency uniform sampling for preserving topology. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for preintegration tables or numerical quadrature routines. Performance: Efficient on current graphics hardware when combined with a hybrid CPU-GPU mesh traversal technique. Strengths: Guarantees topological accuracy of isosurfaces; avoids missing isovalues; handles arbitrary transfer functions. Limitations: As the topology is consistent from one frame to another, the only remaining kind of artifacts is wobbling of the surfaces and structures inside the cells as the viewpoint changes. Complex coefficient calculation for the cubic polynomial. When to use: High-quality visualization of AMR datasets with hexahedral cells where topological accuracy is critical. Originated in a 2009 paper by titled "High-Quality, Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering for AMR...", this method was developed to address the challenges of visualizing Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) datasets. It builds on the need for view-order cell traversal and high-quality rendering of hexahedral cells in AMR meshes, which often suffer from discontinuities in isosurfaces due to piecewise linear approximations. The method extends standard trilinear interpolation by leveraging the analytical properties of the reconstructed signal to determine sampling points. High-Quality, Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering for AMR..., https://people.freedesktop.org/~marcheu/vis09-amr.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Local Phong Shading with Semi-Analytical Integration
head: Quadratic Shading Integration, Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering with Shading
body:
This method extends semi-analytical volume rendering by incorporating local Phong diffuse shading into the integration process. It solves the problem of accurate lighting in volume rendering by reconstructing the shading function as a quadratic polynomial along the ray, allowing for analytical integration of the light contribution. It sets itself apart from scalar-only semi-analytical methods by requiring at most one additional sampling point per cell to capture the shading extremum, while maintaining the topological accuracy of the underlying trilinear interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Trilinear interpolation coefficients for the scalar field s(x,y,z) within a hexahedral cell; light direction vector \vec{L} = (lx, ly, lz); preintegration tables C{front}, C{back}, and \alpha; ray segment parameters t{start}, t{end} within the cell. Outputs: Integrated color contribution I for the ray segment, accounting for shading. Data Structures: The method relies on the trilinear coefficients s{ijk} (where i,j,k \in \{0,1\}) defining the scalar field s(x,y,z) in the unit cube. The shading function is represented by quadratic coefficients e, f, g for d(t) = e t^2 + f t + g. Steps: 1. Compute the analytical gradient 
abla s(x,y,z) from the trilinear coefficients. Compute the diffuse shading function d(x,y,z) = 
abla s(x,y,z) \cdot \vec{L}. 2. Parametrize the ray as x(t), y(t), z(t) for t \in [0, L] (local cell coordinates). Substitute into d(x,y,z) to obtain the quadratic form d(t) = e \cdot t^2 + f \cdot t + g, where e, f, g are computed from the gradient coefficients and ray parameters. For a parametrized ray inside a cell, the gradient variation over this ray is thus a quadratic form in t. 3. Find the local extremum r of d(t) by setting the derivative to zero: r = -f / (2e). Since d(t) is a quadratic polynomial, there is at most a single local extremum r. 4. Sample the shading function at the cell entry (t=0), cell exit (t=L), and the local extremum r (if 0 < r < L). This requires at most one additional sampling point per cell compared to the scalar-only method. 5. Split the ray segment [0, L] at the extremum r into [0, r] and [r, L] (if r is within the interval). The integral becomes: I = \int0^r c(s(t))d(t)e^{-\int0^t 	au(s(u))du} dt + \intr^L c(s(t))d(t)e^{-\int0^t 	au(s(u))du} dt. 6. Approximate the scalar field s(t) as linear between sample points. For the full cell with extremum r, the total integral is approximated using preintegration functions: I \approx d(s(0)) C{front}(s(0), s(r), r) + d(s(r)) C{back}(s(0), s(r), r) + (1 - \alpha(s(0), s(r), r)) [ d(s(r)) C{front}(s(r), s(L), L-r) + d(s(L)) C{back}(s(r), s(L), L-r) ]. 7. Preintegration functions are defined as: C{back}(a, b, l) = \int0^1 c((1-t') a + t' b) t' e^{-\int0^{t'} 	au((1-t') a + t' b) l du} dt' C{front}(a, b, l) = \int0^1 c((1-t') a + t' b) (1-t') e^{-\int0^{t'} 	au((1-t') a + t' b) l du} dt' \alpha(a, b, l) = 1 - e^{-\int0^1 	au((1-t') b + t' a) l dt'} where a, b are scalar values at interval endpoints, l is the interval length, and c(\cdot), 	au(\cdot) are the color and absorption transfer functions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def integratelocalphongshading(scoeffs, Lvec, tstart, tend, Cfront, Cback, alpha, cfunc, taufunc): # 1. Compute quadratic coefficients e, f, g for d(t) from gradient and ray e, f, g = computeshadingquadratic(scoeffs, Lvec) # 2. Find local extremum r of d(t) = et^2 + ft + g if abs(e) > 1e-9: r = -f / (2.0 e) else: r = None # Linear case, no internal extremum # 3. Determine integration intervals based on extremum if r is not None and tstart < r < tend: t1, t2, t3 = tstart, r, tend else: t1, t2, t3 = tstart, tend, tend # 4. Sample shading function d(t) at interval boundaries d1 = et1t1 + ft1 + g d2 = et2t2 + ft2 + g d3 = et3t3 + ft3 + g # 5. Compute scalar values s(t) at boundaries (linear interpolation assumed) s1 = samplescalar(scoeffs, t1) s2 = samplescalar(scoeffs, t2) s3 = samplescalar(scoeffs, t3) # 6. Compute interval lengths l1 = t2 - t1 l2 = t3 - t2 # 7. Evaluate preintegration functions cf1 = Cfront(s1, s2, l1) cb1 = Cback(s1, s2, l1) a1 = alpha(s1, s2, l1) cf2 = Cfront(s2, s3, l2) cb2 = Cback(s2, s3, l2) # 8. Apply split-interval approximation formula I = d1 cf1 + d2 cb1 if l2 > 0: I += (1.0 - a1) (d2 cf2 + d3 cb2) return I Pitfalls: Discontinuity: The reconstructed scalar field is only C^0 continuous across cell faces. Consequently, the gradient 
abla s is discontinuous, causing shading discontinuities across cell boundaries. Extremum Handling: If the extremum r lies outside the cell interval [0, L], the shading function is monotonic within the cell, and no split is needed. Complexity: Adds at most one additional sample per cell compared to scalar-only semi-analytical rendering. Performance: Not given in the sources for specific hardware performance metrics. Strengths: Captures local lighting variations within cells. Limitations: Shading discontinuities at cell faces may be visible due to C^0 continuity of the scalar field. This method is an extension of the semi-analytical volume rendering approach for AMR (Adaptive Mesh Refinement) data, presented by Marchesin et al. in 2009. It builds on the trilinear interpolation-based semi-analytical integration described in the parent article. High-Quality, Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering for AMR..., https://people.freedesktop.org/~marcheu/vis09-amr.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Stochastic Jittering
head: Jittering Sample Positions, Stochastic Noise, Stochastic Sampling
body: Stochastic Jittering is a sampling technique in direct volume ray casting that replaces regularly spaced sample positions with random offsets within each segment to eliminate banding and "wood-grain" artifacts. Unlike Uniform Ray Sampling, which produces visible structural artifacts due to aliasing, Stochastic Jittering transforms these artifacts into high-frequency noise that is visually less noticeable. It differs from Monte Carlo Volume Rendering in that it typically applies jitter only to the sample positions along the ray rather than using complex importance sampling or stratification for the entire integral, though it is fundamentally a Monte Carlo approach. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin (ray\orig), ray direction (ray\dir), entry point t0 (isect.t0), step size (step\size), sample index (n). Output: Sample position (sample\pos). Data Structures: Noise: A boolean flag to enable or disable the technique. MaxNoiseFactor: A scalar controlling the maximum magnitude of the jitter. NoiseTexture: A 2D texture of size NoiseTextureSize × NoiseTextureSize used to generate spatially coherent jitter values. Steps: 1. Generate a random value r uniformly distributed in [0, 1]. In GPU implementations, this is typically sampled from a noise texture using screen coordinates. 2. Calculate the sample position t along the ray: t = isect.t0 + step\size \times (n + r) where n is the integer sample index (0, 1, 2, \dots). 3. Compute the 3D sample position: sample\pos = ray\orig + t \times ray\dir. Parameters: MaxNoiseFactor: Typical value 0.75. This scales the random offset r to bound the maximum inserted jitter magnitude. Standard stochastic sampling uses r \in [0,1] directly, while VTK implementations scale the noise factor. NoiseTextureSize: Typical value 64. Determines the resolution of the pre-generated noise texture. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: isectt0: Entry point t0 of the ray into the volume. stepsize: Distance between regular sample intervals. n: Integer sample index (0, 1, 2...). rayorig: Ray origin vector. raydir: Ray direction vector. usenoise: Boolean flag to enable jittering. maxnoisefactor: Maximum magnitude of the jitter offset. fragcoord: Screen-space coordinates (x, y) for texture lookup. """ if usenoise: # Sample noise texture at screen coordinates, scaled by texture size r = hash2d(fragcoord[0], fragcoord[1]) # Scale by maximum noise factor if the implementation requires bounded jitter r = r maxnoisefactor t = isectt0 + stepsize (n + r) else: # Standard uniform sampling at the center of the segment t = isectt0 + stepsize (n + 0.5) samplepos = rayorig + t raydir return samplepos Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Without refinement, isosurface rendering errors are inevitable if the sample distance is not reduced; jittering only makes these artifacts less visible. Replaces banding artifacts with noise. The noise can be reduced using quasi-Monte Carlo methods, but this is not implemented in the basic version. Precision issues may arise if stepsize is very small and isectt0 is large, potentially causing loss of precision in the addition isectt0 + stepsize (n + r). It jitters the ray start position along the view direction by adding stepVector texture(Noise, glFragCoord.xy / 256).r. Inside the raycasting loop, if the voxel value V exceeds a threshold, it performs a solidity check: it moves back by half-step (s = -stepVector \times 0.5), samples V. If V > Threshold, it moves forward by quarter-step (s = 0.5), else backward (s = -0.5), and samples again. Lighting proceeds only if the re-sampled V is still > Threshold. This method is chosen when high-frequency slice boundaries are visible despite adequate sample density. It applies depth jittering each frame using a sub-voxel offset derived from a pseudo-random sequence (such as blue noise or Halton sequence) to offset ray positions. A temporal reprojection compute pass then blends the current frame’s 3D texture with the previous frame's 3D texture using camera motion vectors. This is chosen for real-time applications where spatial resolution is limited but temporal coherence can be exploited. Strengths: Eliminates banding artifacts; simple to implement; visually superior to uniform sampling for coarse steps. Limitations: Introduces high-frequency noise; does not reduce isosurface errors without refinement; noise may be distracting in some contexts.
