name: Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling)
head: Inverse CDF Sampling, Fine Sampling, Inverse Opacity Sampling
body: Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling) is a method for generating importance samples along a ray in volume rendering by inverting the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the rendering contribution. It solves the problem of finding the ray parameter t corresponding to a target cumulative density value y, allowing samples to be drawn directly from transmittance estimates rather than computing expensive integrals. Unlike standard NeRF hierarchical sampling, which interpolates exponentiated densities (probabilities) and requires auxiliary losses, this method interpolates the density field directly (piecewise linear or constant), offering better numerical stability for end-to-end optimization. It enables Monte Carlo estimates with fewer ray points and allows gradients to back-propagate through the sampling process to the density field parameters. Inputs: coarsezvals: 1D tensor of depth coordinates for coarse samples, shape (Nc,) or (batch, Nc). coarseweights: 1D tensor of unnormalized importance weights (typically derived from volume density or opacity) corresponding to the coarse samples, shape (Nc,) or (batch, Nc). Nsamples: Integer specifying the number of fine samples to generate per ray. deterministic: Boolean flag. If True, uses deterministic uniform spacing; otherwise uses random jitter. Outputs: finezvals: 1D tensor of interpolated depth coordinates for the fine samples, shape (Nsamples,) or (batch, Nsamples). Data Structures: The method operates on 1D tensors representing the ray's depth interval. For batched operations, dimensions are broadcasted or processed in parallel. Intermediate structures include the Probability Density Function (PDF) and Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) tensors. Steps: 1. Compute PDF: Normalize the coarse weights to form a probability density function. To prevent division by zero or NaNs, add a small epsilon (\epsilon = 10^{-5}) to all weights before normalization. \text{pdf}i = \frac{\text{weights}i + \epsilon}{\sum{j} (\text{weights}j + \epsilon)} where \text{weights} are the coarseweights. 2. Compute CDF: Calculate the cumulative distribution function by taking the cumulative sum of the PDF. Prepend a zero tensor to the CDF to represent the start of the first bin (index 0). \text{cdf}0 = 0 \text{cdf}i = \text{cdf}{i-1} + \text{pdf}{i-1} \quad \text{for } i > 0 In code, this is often implemented as cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[...,:1]), torch.cumsum(pdf, -1)], -1). 3. Generate Query Values: Generate uniform random numbers u in the interval [0, 1] with size Nsamples. If deterministic is True, use linearly spaced values: ui = \frac{i}{N{\text{samples}}} for i \in [0, N{\text{samples}}-1]. If deterministic is False, use random uniform samples: ui \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1). 4. Find Bin Indices: Determine which bin in the CDF each query value u falls into using binary search (searchsorted). \text{inds} = \text{searchsorted}(\text{cdf}, u, \text{side}=\text{'right'}) This returns the index k such that \text{cdf}{k-1} \le u < \text{cdf}k. 5. Determine Bin Boundaries: Identify the lower (below) and upper (above) bin indices for interpolation. Clamp these indices to valid ranges [0, \text{len}(\text{cdf})-1]. \text{below} = \max(0, \text{inds} - 1) \text{above} = \min(\text{len}(\text{cdf}) - 1, \text{inds}) 6. Gather CDF and Depth Values: Retrieve the CDF values and depth coordinates (bins, which are coarsezvals) for the lower and upper bins. \text{cdf}{\text{below}} = \text{cdf}[\text{below}] \text{cdf}{\text{above}} = \text{cdf}[\text{above}] \text{z}{\text{below}} = \text{bins}[\text{below}] \text{z}{\text{above}} = \text{bins}[\text{above}] 7. Interpolate Sample Positions: Perform linear interpolation within the identified bin to find the final sample depth z{\text{sample}}. \text{denom} = \text{cdf}{\text{above}} - \text{cdf}{\text{below}} Handle division by zero by clamping denom to a small value (e.g., 10^{-5}) if it is below the threshold. t = \frac{u - \text{cdf}{\text{below}}}{\max(\text{denom}, 10^{-5})} z{\text{sample}} = \text{z}{\text{below}} + t \cdot (\text{z}{\text{above}} - \text{z}{\text{below}}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def hierarchicalsampling(coarsezvals, coarseweights, Nsamples, deterministic=True): """ Perform hierarchical sampling using inverse CDF. Args: coarsezvals: Tensor of shape (Nc,) or (batch, Nc) containing coarse depth samples. coarseweights: Tensor of shape (Nc,) or (batch, Nc) containing unnormalized weights. Nsamples: int, number of fine samples to generate. deterministic: bool, if True uses linspace, else random uniform. Returns: finezvals: Tensor of shape (Nsamples,) or (batch, Nsamples). """ # Step 1: Compute PDF with epsilon to prevent NaNs eps = 1e-5 weights = coarseweights + eps pdf = weights / torch.sum(weights, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Step 2: Compute CDF and prepend zero cdf = torch.cumsum(pdf, dim=-1) cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[...,:1]), cdf], dim=-1) # Step 3: Generate query values u if deterministic: u = torch.linspace(0., 1., steps=Nsamples).to(cdf.device) # Handle batch dimension if present if cdf.dim() > 1: u = u.unsqueeze(0).expand(cdf.shape[0], -1) else: u = torch.randlike(cdf[...,:1]).expandas(cdf[...,:1]).reshape(cdf.shape[:-1] + (Nsamples,)) # Note: In batched case, u shape should be (batch, Nsamples) # Simplified for single ray or assuming batch dim is handled by broadcasting in torch.rand if cdf.dim() > 1: u = torch.rand(cdf.shape[0], Nsamples).to(cdf.device) # Step 4: Find bin indices inds = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, right=True) # Step 5: Determine bin boundaries below = torch.clamp(inds - 1, min=0) above = torch.clamp(inds, max=cdf.shape[-1] - 1) # Step 6: Gather CDF and bin values # Expand indices for gathering indsg = torch.stack([below, above], dim=-1) # Gather CDF values cdfg = torch.gather(cdf.unsqueeze(1).expandas(indsg), 2, indsg).squeeze(1) # Gather depth values (bins) # Assuming coarsezvals has shape (Nc,) or (batch, Nc) # We need to gather from coarsezvals using below and above indices binsg = torch.gather(coarsezvals.unsqueeze(1).expandas(indsg), 2, indsg).squeeze(1) # Step 7: Interpolate denom = cdfg[..., 1] - cdfg[..., 0] denom = torch.where(denom < 1e-5, torch.oneslike(denom), denom) t = (u - cdfg[..., 0]) / denom finezvals = binsg[..., 0] + t (binsg[..., 1] - binsg[..., 0]) return finezvals Parameters: Nsamples: Integer specifying the number of fine samples to generate per ray. Typical values are 128 or 64. deterministic: Boolean flag. If True, uses deterministic linspace samples instead of random uniform samples for reproducibility. perturb: Float controlling jittering. 0 disables jittering (deterministic midpoints), 1 enables full stratified jittering. This parameter is often used in the coarse pass, but the fine pass here is strictly inverse CDF. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Weights: Zero weights cause division by zero during PDF normalization. Handled by adding \epsilon = 10^{-5} to all weights before normalization. Zero-Width Bins: Zero-width bins (where cdfabove == cdfbelow) cause division by zero during interpolation. Handled by clamping the denominator denom to 10^{-5} if it falls below that threshold. Boundary Conditions: Indices must be clamped to valid ranges [0, \text{len}(\text{cdf})-1] to prevent out-of-bounds access. Inverse Opacity Calculation is a differentiable method for generating importance samples along a ray in volume rendering by inverting the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the rendering contribution. It solves the problem of finding the ray parameter t corresponding to a target cumulative density value y, allowing samples to be drawn directly from transmittance estimates rather than computing expensive integrals. Unlike standard NeRF hierarchical sampling, which interpolates exponentiated densities (probabilities) and requires auxiliary losses, this method interpolates the density field directly (piecewise linear or constant), offering better numerical stability for end-to-end optimization. It enables Monte Carlo estimates with fewer ray points and allows gradients to back-propagate through the sampling process to the density field parameters. Proposal Network Sampling is a method for importance sampling in volume rendering that directly estimates the Probability Density Function (PDF) along a ray using a coarse neural network, known as the proposal network. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform sampling by concentrating samples on high-contribution areas (such as surfaces) while spreading them in empty or occluded regions, providing more accurate transmittance estimation than spatial skipping methods. It builds on Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling) by learning the sampling distribution dynamically rather than relying on static weights. RangeFineSampler is a hierarchical sampling technique for direct volume ray casting that refines coarse samples by generating a dense uniform grid around the coarse sample with the highest weight, supplemented by random samples across the full ray extent. It addresses the problem of missing high-frequency details between coarse samples by concentrating computational effort near the most significant signal while maintaining global coverage through random jittering. Unlike Inverse Opacity Calculation which derives samples from opacity gradients, or Proposal Network Sampling which uses learned neural networks to predict sample locations, RangeFineSampler relies on a deterministic geometric expansion around the peak weight index combined with stochastic uniform sampling. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The method involves computing the PDF and CDF (O(Nc)), generating random numbers (O(Nf)), binary search (O(Nf \log Nc)), and interpolation (O(Nf)). Overall complexity is dominated by O(Nf \log Nc), where Nc is the number of coarse samples and Nf is the number of fine samples. Memory: Requires storage for the CDF and intermediate tensors, proportional to O(Nc + Nf). Measured Performance: Performance depends on the hardware and resolution. On a single 2080 Ti, training a NeRF on a low-res scene (e.g., fern) takes approximately 8 hours for 200k iterations. The method allows for fewer ray points while maintaining accuracy, reducing the computational load compared to uniform sampling. Scaling: The method scales linearly with the number of rays and samples. It is suitable for large-scale volume rendering due to its efficiency in concentrating samples in high-density regions. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Differentiable, allowing gradients to back-propagate through the sampling process. Numerically stable with proper epsilon handling. Efficient importance sampling. Limitations: Requires coarse samples and weights as input. Performance may degrade if coarse weights are inaccurate. When to Use: Use when importance sampling is needed to reduce variance in volume rendering. Use when differentiable sampling is required for end-to-end optimization. When Not to Use: Avoid when computational resources are extremely limited and coarse weights are not available. Avoid when the scene has very low density variations, making importance sampling less beneficial. Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling) originates from the NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) paper by Mildenhall et al.. It was introduced to improve the efficiency of volume rendering by concentrating samples in regions of high density. The method has been widely adopted in subsequent works, including. It is a key component in many modern neural rendering pipelines. name: Inverse Opacity Calculation
head: inverse opacity sampling
body: Inverse Opacity Calculation is a differentiable method for generating importance samples along a ray in volume rendering by inverting the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the rendering contribution. It solves the problem of finding the ray parameter t corresponding to a target cumulative density value y, allowing samples to be drawn directly from transmittance estimates rather than computing expensive integrals. Unlike standard NeRF hierarchical sampling, which interpolates exponentiated densities (probabilities) and requires auxiliary losses, this method interpolates the density field directly (piecewise linear or constant), offering better numerical stability for end-to-end optimization. It enables Monte Carlo estimates with fewer ray points and allows gradients to back-propagate through the sampling process to the density field parameters. Inputs: Ray grid points t1, \dots, t{m+1} (where t1=tn, t{m+1}=tf) and corresponding density values \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(tj) predicted by a neural network. A target cumulative opacity value y \in [0, yf], where yf = 1 - \exp(-\int{tn}^{tf} \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(s) ds) is the total pixel opacity. Outputs: A sample position t along the ray such that the cumulative opacity up to t equals y. Data Structures: Grid Points: Array t of size m+1, sorted t1 < t2 < \dots < t{m+1}. Densities: Array \sigma of size m+1, where \sigmaj = \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(tj) \ge 0. Cumulative Integrals: Precomputed array I of size m+1, where Ij is the integral of density from tn to tj. Steps: 1. Compute Total Opacity (yf): Calculate the total integral I{total} = \int{tn}^{tf} \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(s) ds using the chosen approximation (piecewise constant or linear). Compute yf = 1 - \exp(-I{total}). 2. Generate Target Values: Generate k i.i.d. uniform random samples ui \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1]. Compute target cumulative opacity values: y{fu, i} = yf \cdot ui. Optional Stratification: For lower variance, use stratified sampling: ui \sim \mathcal{U}[\frac{i-1}{k+1}, \frac{i}{k+1}]. 3. Identify Bin: For each y{fu}, find the index i such that the cumulative integral up to ti is less than or equal to the target integral value I{target} = -\ln(1 - y{fu}). Specifically, find i such that Ii \le I{target} < I{i+1}. Note: I{target} is derived from y{fu} via the inverse of the opacity function Fr(t) = 1 - \exp(-\int \sigma). The equation to solve is -\ln(1 - y{fu}) = \int{tn}^t \sigmar(s) ds. 4. Solve for t within Bin: Depending on the density approximation, solve for \Delta t = t - ti: Case A: Piecewise Constant Approximation Assume density is constant \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}i) within bin [ti, t{i+1}]. The integral equation is linear: I{target} = Ii + \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}i)(t - ti) Solve for t: t = ti + \frac{I{target} - Ii}{\sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}i)} Pitfall: If \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}i) \approx 0, add a small epsilon \epsilon to the denominator for stability. Case B: Piecewise Linear Approximation Assume density varies linearly between \sigmai = \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(ti) and \sigma{i+1} = \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(t{i+1}). The integral is quadratic in t. Let \Delta t = t - ti. Formulate the quadratic equation 0 = a\Delta t^2 + b\Delta t + c: a = \frac{\sigma{i+1} - \sigmai}{2} b = \sigmai \times (t{i+1} - ti) c = \left( Ii - I{target} \right) \times (t{i+1} - ti) Here I{target} is the target integral. Solve for \Delta t: \Delta t = \frac{-b + \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} Since the integral is monotonically increasing, we take the positive root. Then t = ti + \Delta t. 5. Back-propagation: The solution t is a differentiable function of the densities \sigma{\mathbf{r}}. Gradients flow from the loss through t to the density network parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def inverseopacitycalculation(tvals, sigmavals, ytargets, approxtype='linear'): """ tvals: Tensor of shape (M+1,), ray grid points t1... t{M+1} sigmavals: Tensor of shape (M+1,), density values at grid points ytargets: Tensor of shape (K,), target cumulative opacity values yfu approxtype: 'constant' or 'linear' Returns: Tensor of shape (K,), sample positions t """ M = len(tvals) - 1 # 1. Compute Cumulative Integrals I I = torch.zeroslike(tvals) if approxtype == 'constant': binwidths = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] binintegrals = sigmavals[:-1] binwidths I[1:] = torch.cumsum(binintegrals, dim=0) elif approxtype == 'linear': binwidths = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] avgsigma = (sigmavals[:-1] + sigmavals[1:]) / 2.0 binintegrals = avgsigma binwidths I[1:] = torch.cumsum(binintegrals, dim=0) else: raise ValueError("Unknown approximation type") # 2. Convert ytargets to target integrals Itargets # y = 1 - exp(-I) => I = -ln(1 - y) # Clamp y to avoid log(0) yclamped = torch.clamp(ytargets, max=1.0 - 1e-6) Itargets = -torch.log(1.0 - yclamped) # 3. Find bins # Find index i such that I[i] <= Itarget < I[i+1] indices = torch.searchsorted(I, Itargets, side='right') indices = torch.clamp(indices - 1, min=0, max=M - 1) ti = tvals[indices] tip1 = tvals[indices + 1] Ii = I[indices] sigmai = sigmavals[indices] sigmaip1 = sigmavals[indices + 1] dtbin = tip1 - ti if approxtype == 'constant': # t = ti + (Itarget - Ii) / sigmai # Add epsilon for stability eps = 1e-6 deltat = (Itargets - Ii) / (sigmai + eps) tsamples = ti + deltat elif approxtype == 'linear': # Quadratic: 0 = adeltat^2 + bdeltat + c a = (sigmaip1 - sigmai) / 2.0 b = sigmai dtbin c = (Ii - Itargets) dtbin discriminant = b2 - 4ac discriminant = torch.clamp(discriminant, min=0.0) sqrtdisc = torch.sqrt(discriminant) # Numerical stability for quadratic root # If a is near zero, use linear approximation: deltat = -c/b zeroa = torch.abs(a) < 1e-6 deltatlinear = torch.where(zeroa, -c / (b + 1e-6), (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a + 1e-6)) # If b is near zero, use deltat = sqrt(c/a) zerob = torch.abs(b) < 1e-6 deltatlinear = torch.where(zerob, torch.sqrt(c / (a + 1e-6)), deltatlinear) tsamples = ti + deltatlinear return tsamples Parameters: k: Number of samples per ray. Typical value is 8 for visible quality without artifacts. Learning rate for proposal density network: Starts at 5 \times 10^{-5} and decays to 5 \times 10^{-6}. Learning rate for fine density network: Starts at 5 \times 10^{-4} and decays to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Density output activation: Softplus (ensures non-negative density). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Density: When \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}i) \approx 0, the denominator in the piecewise constant inverse formula becomes unstable. Add a small epsilon \epsilon to the denominator. Analytic Inversion: The opacity function Fr(t) cannot be computed analytically in practice because it requires integrating the density field. It must be approximated using piecewise constant or linear approximations. Boundary Conditions: Ensure y{target} is clamped to [0, 1-\epsilon] to avoid numerical issues with \ln(1-y). A differentiable method that interpolates the density field directly, offering better numerical stability for end-to-end optimization compared to NeRF's hierarchical sampling. Choose this when optimizing neural radiance fields end-to-end without auxiliary losses. An explicit formula to solve for time t given a target integral value y, assuming density \sigmar varies linearly within each sample interval. The integral approximation is I1(t) = \sum{j=1}^{i} \frac{\sigmar(tj) + \sigmar(t{j-1})}{2} (tj - t{j-1}) + \frac{(\sigmar(ti) + \bar{\sigma}r(t))}{2} (t - ti), where \bar{\sigma}r(t) is the linearly interpolated density at t. Solving y = I1(t) yields the quadratic 0 = a\Delta t^2 + b\Delta t + c with a = \frac{\sigmar(t{i+1}) - \sigmar(ti)}{2}, b = \sigmar(ti) \times (t{i+1} - ti), and c = \left( \sum{j=1}^i \frac{\sigmar(tj) + \sigmar(t{j-1})}{2} (tj - t{j-1}) - y \right) \times (t{i+1} - ti). The root is \Delta t = \frac{-b + \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}. For computational stability, the standard formula is rewritten as \Delta t = \frac{2c}{b + \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}} when a \approx 0, and small epsilon is added to square roots and denominators. If b \approx 0, use \Delta t = \sqrt{c/a}; if a \approx 0, use \Delta t = -c/b. A stable computation method for inverse opacity input y, which combines a uniform sample u and ray opacity yf = 1 - \exp(-\int{tn}^{tf} \sigmar(s)ds). The input is computed as y = -\log(1 - yf u). To avoid precision loss, it is rewritten using logsumexp: y = -\log \left( \exp(\log(1-u)) + \exp(\log u - \int{tn}^{tf} \sigmar(s) ds) \right). For opaque rays where \int{tn}^{tf} \sigmar(s)ds \approx 0, the logsumexp implementation becomes computationally unstable, so y is replaced with u as they are almost identical. An explicit formula to solve for time t given a target integral value y, assuming density \sigmar is constant within each sample interval [t{j-1}, tj]. The integral approximation is I0(t) = \sum{j=1}^i \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}j)(tj - t{j-1}) + \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}i)(t - ti), where \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}j) is the density at sample j and tj are sample positions. Solving y = I0(t) yields t = ti + \frac{y - \sum{j=1}^i \sigmar(\hat{t}j)(tj - t{j-1})}{\sigmar(\hat{t}i)}. When density \sigmar(\hat{t}i) \approx 0, the denominator becomes unstable, so a small epsilon value is added to the denominator to improve stability. Time and Memory Complexity: The method requires computing cumulative integrals O(M) and solving a quadratic/linear equation per sample O(1). It avoids redundant radiance queries compared to dense uniform grids, potentially reducing computation during training and inference. Measured Performance: On the Lego scene (Blender dataset) with (Np=16, Nf=32), RVS achieves PSNR 29.18 vs NeRF 27.09, SSIM 0.928 vs 0.913, and LPIPS 0.112 vs 0.121, with relative training time 0.37 vs 0.39. On the Lego scene with (Np=64, Nf=192), RVS achieves PSNR 33.03 vs NeRF 32.69, SSIM 0.964 vs 0.962, and LPIPS 0.047 vs 0.048, with relative training time 0.98 vs 1.0. On the Blender dataset (average) with (Np=32, Nf=64), RVS achieves PSNR 30.26 vs NeRF 29.49, SSIM 0.939 vs 0.934, and LPIPS 0.082 vs 0.085. On the LLFF dataset (average) with (Np=32, Nf=64), RVS achieves PSNR 26.01 vs NeRF 26.01 (tie), SSIM 0.796 vs 0.796 (tie), and LPIPS 0.273 vs 0.273 (tie). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Fully differentiable, allows end-to-end training without auxiliary reconstruction losses, improves reconstruction quality for hierarchical models, reduces variance with stratified sampling. Limitations: Requires careful handling of zero-density bins. The proposal density learned via RVS is significantly different from NeRF's, suggesting that mimicking the fine density is not optimal for the proposal. When to Use: Use when training neural radiance fields end-to-end and wanting to avoid auxiliary losses. Use when higher quality is needed with fewer samples (e.g., real-time or constrained compute). Do not use if the scene has large regions of zero density without proper epsilon handling, as it may cause instability in the constant approximation. Inverse Opacity Calculation, often referred to as Reparameterized Volume Sampling (RVS), was introduced by Khrulkhov et al. in 2023. It builds on the concept of inverse transform sampling used in NeRF but derives the sampling distribution from the density field directly rather than from a separate proposal network with auxiliary losses. The method leverages the mathematical equivalence between the CDF of the rendering contribution and the transmittance function. It is used in novel view synthesis and neural radiance field optimization. name: Inverse Transform Sampling with Piecewise Linear Density
head: RVS Inverse CDF Sampling, RVS Sampling
body: Inverse Transform Sampling with Piecewise Linear Density is a differentiable method for generating samples along a ray according to a distribution induced by linearly interpolating the volume density \sigma{\mathbf{r}}. It solves the problem of finding the ray parameter t corresponding to a target cumulative density value y, ensuring that samples strictly follow the Beer-Lambert law within each bin. Unlike NeRF's hierarchical sampling, which interpolates exponentiated densities (probabilities), this method interpolates the density field directly, offering better numerical stability for end-to-end optimization. Inputs: u: Uniform random variable, u \in [0, 1). \sigma{\mathbf{r}}: Array of density values at grid knots, size N. ts, te: Start and end parameters of the ray segment. t: Array of grid knots, size N, where t0 = ts and t{N-1} = te. Outputs: t{\text{sample}}: The sampled ray parameter. Data Structures: prefixintegrals: Array of size N, storing the cumulative integral of density from t0 to ti. binintegrals: Array of size N-1, storing the integral of density within each interval [ti, t{i+1}]. Steps: 1. Compute Bin Integrals and Prefix Sums: Calculate the integral of density over each interval using linear interpolation, as required by the quadratic derivation. \text{bin\integrals}i = \frac{\sigma{\mathbf{r}}(ti) + \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(t{i+1})}{2} (t{i+1} - ti) \text{prefix\integrals}0 = 0 \text{prefix\integrals}{i+1} = \text{prefix\integrals}i + \text{bin\integrals}i 2. Compute Inverse Opacity Input y: Calculate the target cumulative density value y from the uniform sample u and the total ray optical depth \tau = \text{prefix\integrals}{N-1}. Using the numerically stable logsumexp operator: y = -\log \left( \exp(\log(1-u)) + \exp(\log u - \tau) \right) Edge Case: When the integral is approximately zero, the logsumexp implementation becomes computationally unstable, and y is replaced with a first-order approximation u \cdot \tau. 3. Find the Interval: Find the index i such that \text{prefix\integrals}i \le y < \text{prefix\integrals}{i+1}. If y \ge \text{prefix\integrals}{N-1}, set t{\text{sample}} = te. 4. Solve for \Delta t: Within the interval [ti, t{i+1}], assume linear density interpolation. We solve for \Delta t = t - ti in the quadratic equation: 0 = a \Delta t^2 + b \Delta t + c Where: a = \frac{\sigma{\mathbf{r}}(t{i+1}) - \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(ti)}{2} b = \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(ti) \cdot (t{i+1} - ti) c = \left( \text{prefix\integrals}i - y \right) \cdot (t{i+1} - ti) Compute the root using the stable formula to avoid cancellation when a \approx 0: \Delta t = \frac{-2c}{b + \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}} Pitfall: If b^2 - 4ac < 0, clamp the discriminant to 0. If the denominator is 0, set \Delta t = 0. 5. Return Result: t{\text{sample}} = ti + \Delta t Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def inversecdfpiecewiselinear(u, sigmas, ts): """ Inverse Transform Sampling with Piecewise Linear Density. Args: u: Uniform random sample [0, 1). sigmas: Density values at knots, shape (N,). ts: Knot positions, shape (N,). Returns: tsample: Sampled position along the ray. """ N = len(ts) if N < 2: return ts[0] # 1. Compute Prefix Integrals (linear interpolation per source derivation) binintegrals = (sigmas[:-1] + sigmas[1:]) / 2.0 np.diff(ts) prefixintegrals = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(binintegrals)]) totaltau = prefixintegrals[-1] # 2. Compute y (Inverse Opacity Input) # Handle numerical stability for small optical depth (transparent rays) if totaltau < 1e-5: y = u totaltau else: term1 = np.log(1.0 - u) term2 = np.log(u) - totaltau maxval = np.maximum(term1, term2) y = - (maxval + np.log(np.exp(term1 - maxval) + np.exp(term2 - maxval))) # 3. Find interval i = np.searchsorted(prefixintegrals, y, side='right') - 1 i = np.clip(i, 0, N - 2) ti = ts[i] tip1 = ts[i+1] sigmai = sigmas[i] sigmaip1 = sigmas[i+1] dtinterval = tip1 - ti # 4. Solve Quadratic a = (sigmaip1 - sigmai) / 2.0 b = sigmai dtinterval c = (prefixintegrals[i] - y) dtinterval discriminant = bb - 4ac if discriminant < 0: discriminant = 0.0 denom = b + np.sqrt(discriminant) if denom == 0: deltat = 0.0 else: # Corrected stable formula: original source had sign error for c < 0 deltat = (-2.0 c) / denom # Clamp deltat to interval bounds deltat = np.clip(deltat, 0.0, dtinterval) return ti + deltat Time Complexity: O(N) to compute prefix integrals; O(\log N) or O(1) to find the interval and solve the quadratic. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store prefix integrals. Strengths: Differentiable; samples follow the Beer-Lambert law within bins; numerically stable for end-to-end optimization compared to exponentiated density interpolation. Limitations: Requires computing prefix integrals; quadratic solution has edge cases for a \approx 0 handled by the stable formula. When to use: When differentiable sampling from a linearly interpolated density field is required, particularly in neural volume rendering contexts like RVS. This method was introduced in "Differentiable Rendering with Reparameterized Volume Sampling" (2023). It contrasts with the original NeRF hierarchical sampling, which uses piecewise constant density interpolation and exponentiates densities. The RVS method interpolates the density field directly, leading to samples that adhere to the Beer-Lambert law within each bin, which is argued to be more suitable for end-to-end optimization due to better numerical stability. name: Proposal Network Sampling
head: Mip-NeRF 360 Sampling, PDF Approaches, Proposal Network
body: Proposal Network Sampling is a method for importance sampling in volume rendering that directly estimates the Probability Density Function (PDF) along a ray using a coarse neural network, known as the proposal network. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform sampling by concentrating samples on high-contribution areas (such as surfaces) while spreading them in empty or occluded regions, providing more accurate transmittance estimation than spatial skipping methods. It builds on Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling) by learning the sampling distribution dynamically rather than relying on static weights. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, near and far clipping distances tn, tf, number of coarse samples Nc, and a proposal network (coarse MLP) \mathcal{M}c. Outputs: A set of fine sample distances \{tj\} drawn from the estimated PDF. Data Structures: Proposal Network: A standard MLP taking 3D position \mathbf{x} as input and outputting scalar volume density \sigma. Sample Points: A sorted array of distances t1, t2, \dots, t{Nc} along the ray. Densities: An array \sigmai = \mathcal{M}c(\mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{d}). Steps: 1. Initialize Nc sample distances ti uniformly along the ray segment [tn, tf]. 2. Evaluate the proposal network at each sample position to obtain densities \sigma(ti). 3. Compute the transmittance estimator T(ti) = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma(tj) \Delta tj), where \Delta tj is the distance between consecutive samples. 4. Compute the discrete PDF estimator p(ti) = \sigma(ti) \exp(-\sigma(ti) \Delta ti). 5. Update the transmittance estimator through gradient descent using the volumetric rendering loss. 6. Draw Nf uniform random numbers uk \in [0, 1] and use inverse CDF sampling to find fine sample distances \{t'k\}. Formulas: Transmittance estimator: T(ti) = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma(tj) \Delta tj), where T(t1) = 1.0. PDF estimator: p(ti) = \sigma(ti) \exp(-\sigma(ti) \Delta ti). Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF): CDF(ti) = \sum{j=1}^{i} p(tj). Inverse CDF interpolation: t'k = t{i} + (t{i+1} - t{i}) \frac{uk - CDF(ti)}{CDF(t{i+1}) - CDF(ti)} for the interval i where CDF(ti) \leq uk < CDF(t{i+1}). Parameters: Dilation factor \epsilonk for resampling level k: \epsilonk = \frac{a}{\prod{k'=1}^{k-1} n{k'}} + b, where n{k'} is the sample count at level k'. Hyperparameter a = 0.5 determines dilation relative to expected bin size. Hyperparameter b = 0.0025 determines dilation in absolute terms. Typical values for Nc and Nf: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: The piece-wise linearity assumption for estimating transmittance along the ray introduces aliasing effects (z-aliasing). No Skipping: Samples are always spread out throughout the entire space without any skipping, which can be inefficient in large empty regions. Rotationally Aliased Proposal: The proposal MLP is supervised only on rays corresponding to input pixels, leading to rotational aliasing artifacts that can be mitigated by histogram dilation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def proposalnetworksampling(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, ncoarse, proposalmlp, nfine): """ Performs proposal network sampling. Args: rayorigin: (3,) array, origin of the ray. raydirection: (3,) array, normalized direction of the ray. tnear: float, near clipping plane. tfar: float, far clipping plane. ncoarse: int, number of coarse samples. proposalmlp: function, takes (N, 3) positions, returns (N,) densities. nfine: int, number of fine samples to draw. Returns: finesamples: (nfine,) array of sampled distances along the ray. """ # Step 1: Initialize coarse sample distances uniformly along the ray dt = (tfar - tnear) / ncoarse tcoarse = [tnear + i dt for i in range(ncoarse)] # Step 2: Evaluate proposal network to get densities positions = [(rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) for t in tcoarse] sigma = [proposalmlp(pos) for pos in positions] # Step 3: Compute transmittance estimator T(ti) # T(ti) = exp(- sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigma(tj) dt) T = [1.0] ncoarse cumulative = 0.0 for i in range(1, ncoarse): cumulative += sigma[i-1] dt T[i] = math.exp(-cumulative) # Step 4: Compute PDF estimator p(ti) # p(ti) = sigma(ti) exp(-sigma(ti) dt) pdf = [sigma[i] math.exp(-sigma[i] dt) for i in range(ncoarse)] # Normalize PDF to form a valid probability mass function pdfsum = sum(pdf) if pdfsum > 0: pdf = [p / pdfsum for p in pdf] else: pdf = [1.0 / ncoarse] ncoarse # Step 5: Update transmittance estimator through gradient descent # (Handled externally by the training loop using volumetric rendering loss) # Step 6: Compute CDF cdf = [0.0] ncoarse cdf[0] = pdf[0] for i in range(1, ncoarse): cdf[i] = cdf[i-1] + pdf[i] # Step 7: Inverse CDF sampling for fine samples finesamples = [] for in range(nfine): u = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) # Find interval i such that cdf[i] <= u < cdf[i+1] idx = 0 while idx < ncoarse - 1 and cdf[idx] < u: idx += 1 idx = min(idx, ncoarse - 2) # Linear interpolation within the interval tprev = tcoarse[idx] tnext = tcoarse[idx + 1] cdfprev = cdf[idx] cdfnext = cdf[idx + 1] denom = cdfnext - cdfprev if denom == 0: tsample = tprev else: tsample = tprev + (tnext - tprev) (u - cdfprev) / denom finesamples.append(tsample) return finesamples A technique to dilate proposal histograms to reduce aliasing artifacts caused by the proposal MLP being supervised only on rays corresponding to input pixels. It widens the intervals of the proposal MLP to counteract rotational aliasing. Definition: Dilates the probability density function derived from the proposal histogram. Method: 1. Compute probability density \hat{p}i = \hat{w}i / (\hat{s}{i+1} - \hat{s}i) from histogram (\hat{s}, \hat{w}). 2. Dilate by computing \max{s-\epsilon \leq s' < s+\epsilon} \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}{\hat{\mathbf{s}}}(s'), where \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}{\hat{\mathbf{s}}}(s) is the interpolation into the step function defined by \hat{s}, \hat{p}. 3. Construct new intervals with endpoints \text{sort}(\hat{s} \cup \hat{s} - \epsilon \cup \hat{s} + \epsilon). 4. Compute max of all intervals in the expanded set. 5. Convert dilated \hat{p} back to histogram by multiplying by interval size. 6. Normalize histogram to sum to 1. Formula: Dilation factor \epsilonk for level k: \epsilonk = \frac{a}{\prod{k'=1}^{k-1} n{k'}} + b, where n{k'} is the sample count at level k'. Parameters: Hyperparameter a = 0.5 determines dilation relative to expected bin size. Hyperparameter b = 0.0025 determines dilation in absolute terms. When to choose: Use when training early stages or when the proposal network shows rotational aliasing artifacts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Provides more accurate transmittance estimation than spatial skipping, concentrating samples on high-contribution areas. However, it is less efficient in large empty regions because it does not skip empty space. Strengths: Accurate transmittance estimation; adapts to scene content via learned PDF; compatible with hierarchical sampling. Limitations: Introduces aliasing due to piece-wise linearity assumption; samples are always spread out, leading to higher sample counts in empty space compared to spatial skipping. When to use: When high-quality rendering is required and the scene has complex geometry or varying density, and computational budget allows for denser sampling in empty regions. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and the scene has large empty volumes, where spatial skipping (e.g., Occupancy Grid) would be more efficient. Proposal Network Sampling originated with the Mip-NeRF 360 paper. It was introduced as a way to improve the efficiency of importance sampling in NeRF by using a coarse MLP to estimate the PDF directly. The method is part of a broader class of "PDF Approaches" that view importance sampling through the lens of transmittance estimation. It addresses the limitations of uniform sampling and simple spatial skipping by learning a distribution that matches the actual contribution of different parts of the ray. name: RangeFineSampler
head: Range-based Fine Sampling
body: RangeFineSampler is a hierarchical sampling technique for direct volume ray casting that refines coarse samples by generating a dense uniform grid around the coarse sample with the highest weight, supplemented by random samples across the full ray extent. It addresses the problem of missing high-frequency details between coarse samples by concentrating computational effort near the most significant signal while maintaining global coverage through random jittering. Unlike Inverse Opacity Calculation which derives samples from opacity gradients, or Proposal Network Sampling which uses learned neural networks to predict sample locations, RangeFineSampler relies on a deterministic geometric expansion around the peak weight index combined with stochastic uniform sampling. The method takes coarse sample positions and weights as input and outputs a refined set of sample positions along the ray. It operates on batches of rays, where each ray has a set of coarse z-values (depths) and corresponding weights. Inputs: coarsezvals: Tensor of shape (numrays, numcoarsesamples) containing the depth positions of coarse samples. coarseweights: Tensor of shape (numrays, numcoarsesamples) containing the importance weights (e.g., density or opacity contribution) for each coarse sample. near: Float, the near plane distance of the ray. far: Float, the far plane distance of the ray. maxsamples: Integer, the maximum total number of samples allowed per ray. Nsamples: Integer, the number of fine samples to generate around the peak. range: Float, the total width of the interval around the max weight z-value where uniform samples are placed. Default is 0.5. deterministic: Boolean, whether to use stratified sampling or pure random jittering. Outputs: zvalsret: Tensor of shape (numrays, numtotalsamples) containing the sorted, refined sample positions. Data Structures: The implementation assumes PyTorch tensors for batched operations. The core logic involves tensor indexing and sorting. Steps: 1. Determine Effective Sample Count: Calculate the number of fine samples to generate around the peak. This is bounded by maxsamples and Nsamples. N{fine} = \min(\text{max\samples}, N{samples}) 2. Find Peak Weight Index: Identify the index of the coarse sample with the maximum weight for each ray. \text{max\indices} = \text{argmax}{dim=-1}(\text{coarse\weights}) 3. Retrieve Peak Z-Value: Get the depth value corresponding to the peak weight for each ray. \text{max\z\vals} = \text{coarse\z\vals}[\text{arange}(\text{num\rays}), \text{max\indices}] 4. Generate Uniform Samples Around Peak: Create a uniform grid of N{fine} samples centered around maxzvals. The grid spans an interval of width range. The formula distributes points evenly across this interval. z{fine} = \text{max\z\vals}[:, \text{None}] - \text{range} + \frac{2 \cdot \text{range}}{N{fine} - 1} \cdot \text{arange}(N{fine}) Note: If N{fine} = 1, this formula divides by zero. In practice, if N{fine}=1, z{fine} is simply maxzvals. 5. Apply Stratified Sampling (Optional): If deterministic is False, apply stratified jittering to the uniform samples to reduce aliasing. Compute midpoints between adjacent uniform samples: \text{mids} = 0.5 \cdot (z{fine}[:, 1:] + z{fine}[:,:-1]) Define intervals: \text{lower} = \text{concat}([z{fine}[:,:1], \text{mids}], \text{dim}=-1) \text{upper} = \text{concat}([\text{mids}, z{fine}[:, -1:]], \text{dim}=-1) Generate random jitter: t{rand} = \text{rand}(z{fine}.shape) Jitter the samples: z{fine} = \text{lower} + (\text{upper} - \text{lower}) \cdot t{rand} If deterministic is True, z{fine} remains the uniform grid from Step 4. 6. Generate Random Samples Across Full Range: Generate N{fine} random samples uniformly distributed between near and far for each ray. z{add} = \text{rand}((\text{num\rays}, N{fine})) \cdot (\text{far} - \text{near}) + \text{near} 7. Combine and Sort (Global): Concatenate the original coarse samples with the random samples z{add} and sort them. This forms the base set of samples for all rays. z{base} = \text{sort}(\text{concat}([\text{coarse\z\vals}, z{add}], \text{dim}=-1), \text{dim}=-1) 8. Inject Fine Samples for Non-Edge Rays: For rays where the peak index is not at the very beginning (index > 0), concatenate the structured fine samples z{fine} with the coarse samples and sort. This ensures the high-density region around the peak is preserved and sorted correctly relative to coarse samples. \text{mask} = \text{max\indices} > 0 z{ret}[\text{mask}] = \text{sort}(\text{concat}([\text{coarse\z\vals}[\text{mask}], z{fine}[\text{mask}]], \text{dim}=-1), \text{dim}=-1) For rays where maxindices == 0, the sorted combination of coarse and random samples (z{base}) is used, as the peak is at the start and the structured fine samples might not be necessary or might overlap significantly with the coarse start. Note: The source logic implies that for maxindices == 0, the fine samples are not injected in the same way, or the mask logic handles the exclusion. The source explicitly states: "For rays where maxindices > 0...". It does not specify the behavior for maxindices == 0 other than implying the previous step's result (z{base}) is used or that the concatenation is skipped. Given the sorting step 7 creates z{base}, and step 8 overwrites for mask, the default for ~mask is z{base}. 9. Return Result: The final tensor z{ret} contains the sorted sample positions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def rangefinesampler(coarsezvals, coarseweights, near, far, maxsamples, Nsamples, rangeval, deterministic=True): """ RangeFineSampler implementation. Args: coarsezvals: (numrays, numcoarse) Tensor of coarse sample depths. coarseweights: (numrays, numcoarse) Tensor of coarse sample weights. near: Float, near plane. far: Float, far plane. maxsamples: Int, max total samples. Nsamples: Int, number of fine samples to generate around peak. rangeval: Float, width of interval around peak. deterministic: Bool, use stratified sampling. Returns: zvalsret: (numrays, numtotal) Tensor of sorted sample depths. """ numrays, numcoarse = coarsezvals.shape # Step 1: Determine effective sample count Nfine = min(maxsamples, Nsamples) # Step 2: Find peak weight index maxindices = torch.argmax(coarseweights, dim=-1) # Step 3: Retrieve peak z-values # maxindices is (numrays,), need to index correctly arangerays = torch.arange(numrays).to(coarsezvals.device) maxzvals = coarsezvals[arangerays, maxindices] # Step 4: Generate uniform samples around peak # Handle Nfine = 1 case to avoid division by zero if Nfine == 1: zfine = maxzvals.unsqueeze(1) else: arangefine = torch.arange(Nfine).to(coarsezvals.device) zfine = maxzvals.unsqueeze(1) - rangeval + (2 rangeval / (Nfine - 1)) arangefine.unsqueeze(0) # Step 5: Stratified sampling if not deterministic: mids = 0.5 (zfine[:, 1:] + zfine[:,:-1]) lower = torch.cat([zfine[:,:1], mids], dim=-1) upper = torch.cat([mids, zfine[:, -1:]], dim=-1) trand = torch.rand(zfine.shape, device=coarsezvals.device) zfine = lower + (upper - lower) trand # Step 6: Generate random samples across full range zadd = torch.rand((numrays, Nfine), device=coarsezvals.device) (far - near) + near # Step 7: Combine coarse and random, sort zbase = torch.sort(torch.cat([coarsezvals, zadd], dim=-1), dim=-1)[0] # Step 8: Inject fine samples for rays where maxindices > 0 mask = maxindices > 0 zvalsret = zbase.clone() if mask.any(): # Concatenate coarse and fine for these rays zcombined = torch.cat([coarsezvals[mask], zfine[mask]], dim=-1) zvalsret[mask] = torch.sort(zcombined, dim=-1)[0] return zvalsret Parameters: range: Float, default 0.5. The total width of the interval around the max weight z-value. Nsamples: Integer. Number of fine samples to generate. maxsamples: Integer. Global cap on total samples. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If Nfine is 1, the uniform spacing formula divides by zero. The implementation must handle this by returning the single peak value. Boundary Conditions: The random samples zadd are strictly within [near, far]. The uniform samples zfine are centered on maxzvals with width range. If maxzvals is close to near or far, zfine may extend outside the valid ray bounds. The source does not explicitly clamp zfine, which is a potential pitfall. Index 0 Peak: When maxindices == 0, the fine samples are not injected. This may lead to lower resolution near the start of the ray if the peak is at the beginning. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) per ray due to sorting, where N is the total number of samples (coarse + fine + random). The dominant cost is the sort operation. Memory Complexity: O(N) per ray to store the sample positions. Performance: The method is computationally efficient as it avoids neural network inference (unlike Proposal Network Sampling) and complex opacity calculations (unlike Inverse Opacity Calculation). It relies on simple tensor operations. Strengths: Simple to implement; concentrates samples where they are most needed (high weight); reduces aliasing via stratified jittering. Limitations: The fixed range parameter may not adapt well to varying scene densities; the lack of clamping for zfine can lead to out-of-bounds samples; the logic for maxindices == 0 may result in suboptimal sampling at the ray start. RangeFineSampler is an implementation detail found in the vf-nerf repository, an unofficial project by albertgassol1. It is not described in a peer-reviewed paper but is part of a codebase that implements vector field neural radiance fields. The method is a heuristic refinement strategy designed to improve visual quality in volume rendering by focusing samples around high-density regions identified by coarse sampling. albertgassol1/vf-nerf, https://github.com/albertgassol1/vf-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Uniform Ray Sampling
head: Random Sampling, Ray Sampling with Randomization, Uniform Point Sampling, Uniform Point Sampling along Rays, Uniform Random Sampling, Uniform Sampling
body: Uniform Ray Sampling generates a fixed number of sample points along camera rays by uniformly distributing depths between a near and far clipping plane. It assumes every point along the ray contributes equally to the final rendering, implying a constant probability density function (PDF) and linearly decaying transmittance. This method serves as the baseline for volume rendering when no transmittance estimator or spatial skipping structure is available. It is distinguished from its siblings by its simplicity and lack of scene-awareness; unlike Stochastic Jittering which adds noise to break symmetry, or Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling) which concentrates samples in high-density regions, uniform sampling treats all intervals equally. It is computationally efficient to implement but yields the lowest rendering efficiency in most cases compared to spatial skipping or PDF-based methods. Inputs: rayso: Tensor of ray origins, shape (N, 3). raysd: Tensor of ray directions, shape (N, 3), typically unit-norm. near: Scalar or tensor defining the near clipping plane distance. far: Scalar or tensor defining the far clipping plane distance. nptsperray (or N{samples}): Integer number of sample points per ray. perturb (optional): Float controlling the magnitude of random noise added for stratification. lindisp (optional): Boolean flag to switch between linear depth and linear disparity sampling. Outputs: samplepoints: Tensor of 3D coordinates, shape (N, n{pts\per\ray}, 3). samplelengths: Tensor of segment lengths, shape (N, n{pts\per\ray}, 1). Data Structures: The method typically populates a RayBundle object containing: origins: (N, 3) directions: (N, 3) samplepoints: (N, n{pts\per\ray}, 3) samplelengths: (N, n{pts\per\ray}, 1). Steps: 1. Generate Depth Values: Create n{pts\per\ray} linearly spaced values ti in the interval [0, 1] using torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, nptsperray). 2. Map to Depth Range: Map ti to the depth range [near, far]. If lindisp is false (linear depth): zi = near \cdot (1 - ti) + far \cdot ti If lindisp is true (linear disparity): zi = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{near}(1 - ti) + \frac{1}{far}ti} 3. Stratification (Optional): If training or perturb > 0, add uniform random noise to break symmetry and reduce variance. Compute midpoints: z{mid, i} = 0.5 \cdot (zi + z{i+1}) for i=0 \dots n-2, with z{mid, n-1} = z{n-1}. Define intervals: upper = [z{mid, 0}, \dots, z{mid, n-2}, z{n-1}] and lower = [z0, \dots, z{n-2}, z{mid, n-2}]. Generate random noise ri \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1]. Update depths: zi = loweri + (upperi - loweri) \cdot perturb \cdot ri. 4. Broadcast Ray Parameters: Reshape rayso from (N, 3) to (N, 1, 3) and repeat along the second dimension to shape (N, n{pts\per\ray}, 3). Reshape raysd from (N, 3) to (N, 1, 3) and repeat along the second dimension to shape (N, n{pts\per\ray}, 3). Reshape z from (n{pts\per\ray}) to (1, n{pts\per\ray}, 1) and repeat along the first dimension to shape (N, n{pts\per\ray}, 1). 5. Compute Sample Points: Calculate 3D coordinates: P = O + D \cdot z where O is the broadcasted origin, D is the broadcasted direction, and z is the broadcasted depth. \text{sample\points} = \text{rays\o} + \text{rays\d} \cdot z 6. Compute Sample Lengths: Calculate segment lengths. Segment lengths are computed as the difference between consecutive depths, \Delta zi = z{i+1} - zi, with the last segment set to a large value (e.g., 10^{10}) to ensure full transmittance decay. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def uniformraysampling(rayso, raysd, near, far, nptsperray, perturb=0.0, lindisp=False): """ Generate uniform sample points along rays. Args: rayso: Tensor of shape (N, 3), ray origins. raysd: Tensor of shape (N, 3), ray directions. near: Float or Tensor of shape (N,), near clipping plane. far: Float or Tensor of shape (N,), far clipping plane. nptsperray: Int, number of samples per ray. perturb: Float, magnitude of random noise for stratification. lindisp: Bool, if True, sample in disparity space. Returns: samplepoints: Tensor of shape (N, nptsperray, 3). samplelengths: Tensor of shape (N, nptsperray, 1). """ # Step 1: Generate linearly spaced t values in [0, 1] tvals = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, nptsperray, device=rayso.device) # Step 2: Map to depth range [near, far] if lindisp: # Linear disparity sampling zvals = 1.0 / (1.0 / near.unsqueeze(1) (1.0 - tvals.unsqueeze(0)) + 1.0 / far.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(0)) else: # Linear depth sampling zvals = near.unsqueeze(1) (1.0 - tvals.unsqueeze(0)) + far.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(0) # Step 3: Stratification (add noise) if perturb > 0.0: # Compute midpoints zvalsmid = 0.5 (zvals[:,:-1] + zvals[:, 1:]) # Define upper and lower bounds for each interval # upper: [zmid0,..., zmid{n-2}, z{n-1}] # lower: [z0,..., z{n-2}, zmid{n-2}] upper = torch.cat([zvalsmid, zvals[:, -1:]], dim=-1) lower = torch.cat([zvals[:,:1], zvalsmid], dim=-1) # Generate random noise randnoise = perturb torch.rand(zvals.shape, device=rayso.device) # Sample uniformly within intervals zvals = lower + (upper - lower) randnoise # Step 4: Broadcast ray origins and directions # rayso: (N, 3) -> (N, 1, 3) -> (N, nptsperray, 3) raysoexpanded = rayso.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, nptsperray, -1) # raysd: (N, 3) -> (N, 1, 3) -> (N, nptsperray, 3) raysdexpanded = raysd.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, nptsperray, -1) # zvals: (N, nptsperray) -> (N, nptsperray, 1) zvalsexpanded = zvals.unsqueeze(-1) # Step 5: Compute sample points # P = O + D z samplepoints = raysoexpanded + raysdexpanded zvalsexpanded # Step 6: Compute sample lengths (deltas) # Delta z is the distance between consecutive samples # deltas[i] = z[i+1] - z[i] deltas = torch.cat([ zvals[:, 1:] - zvals[:,:-1], torch.full((rayso.shape[0], 1), 1e10, device=rayso.device) ], dim=-1).unsqueeze(-1) return samplepoints, deltas Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Near/Far Equality: If near == far, the interval is zero, leading to division by zero in disparity sampling or zero-length samples. Guard against this by clamping or skipping rays. Zero Direction: If ray direction components are zero, normalization or intersection calculations may fail. Replace zero directions with a small epsilon (e.g., 10^{-6}). Precision: Using torch.linspace and broadcasting requires careful shape management to avoid memory bloat for large batches. Degenerate Input: If nptsperray is 0 or negative, return empty tensors. An unbiased radiance estimate that uses stratified sampling to reduce variance compared to uniform sampling, particularly effective for degenerate distributions. A sampling technique ensuring even spacing along rays within a cell using preprocessed ray data and a 4-bit depth-sampling indicator stored in the pixel opacity. Samples points forward along the ray from a known surface intersection to obtain SDF values inside the object, used when the latent space is not pretrained. Steps: 1. Assert numforwardsampling > 0. 2. Get camera position and rays. 3. Initialize insidesamples tensor with zeros, shape (H \times W, num\forward\sampling). 4. Extract valid camera rays and z-depths. If no valid z-depths, return insidesamples. 5. Compute grid offsets: grid\list = 0.5 \cdot clamp\dist \cdot \frac{\text{arange}(num\forward\sampling) + 1}{num\forward\sampling}. 6. Move gridlist to the same device as camera position. 7. Loop over numforwardsampling indices: Get grid value for current index. Generate point samples at valid\zdepth + grid. Decode SDF at points and add grid offset. Concatenate results and copy to insidesamples at valid mask indices. Parameters: numforwardsampling: Integer, number of forward samples. Default 0. Samples points uniformly along rays in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) space, assuming a fixed number of samples per ray regardless of ray length or bounding box intersection. Steps: 1. For each ray index i{ray} and step index i{step}, compute normalized distance: dist = \frac{i{step}}{N{samples}-1}. 2. Compute 3D point coordinates by linear interpolation: px = ox + dx \cdot dist, py = oy + dy \cdot dist, pz = oz + dz \cdot dist, where (o, d) are ray origin and direction. 3. Determine if the point is outside the bounding box defined by xyz{min} and xyz{max} by checking if any coordinate is less than min or greater than max. Parameters: N{samples}: Fixed number of samples per ray. Samples camera rays that reach translucent material after diffuse interactions with a small number of samples, as low as one per ray. Steps: 1. Compute the exit point for the camera ray to determine the maximum depth along the ray, denoted as d{\max}. 2. Place exactly k{\max} samples along the ray using the derived depth formula. Formula: dk = -\frac{1}{\sigmat} \log \left( 1 - \frac{|k(1 - e^{-\sigmat d{\max}})|}{k{\max}} \right) where \sigmat is the extinction coefficient, k is the sample index, and k{\max} is the total number of samples. Parameters: k{\max}: The total number of sample points to place along the ray. The method ensures exactly k{\max} samples are placed. Pitfall: Small Object Width: The sampling scheme handles small object widths by ensuring k{\max} samples are always placed, preventing undersampling. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot n{pts\per\ray}) for generating sample points, where N is the number of rays. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot n{pts\per\ray} \cdot 3) for storing sample points and O(N \cdot n{pts\per\ray}) for depths/lengths. Performance: Uniform sampling is the easiest to implement but has the lowest efficiency in most cases compared to spatial skipping or PDF-based methods. It wastes samples in empty space and misses high-density regions. Strengths: Simple to implement, deterministic (without perturbation), low overhead. Limitations: Inefficient for scenes with large empty regions or complex geometry; requires many samples to converge. When to Use: Baseline method, coarse sampling in hierarchical schemes, or when no spatial acceleration structure is available. When Not to Use: High-quality rendering of complex scenes with sparse geometry, where spatial skipping or importance sampling is preferred. Uniform sampling was introduced as the baseline sampling method in the original NeRF paper [16] (cited as in the context of NerfAcc). It assumes a constant PDF and linearly decaying transmittance, which is inherent to coarse-level NeRF models. It is widely used in neural radiance field implementations due to its simplicity. name: Volume Raycasting Discretization
head: Volume ray marching, Front-to-Back Blending, Front-to-back Ray Casting, Discrete Volume Rendering Integral
body: Volume Raycasting Discretization is a direct volume rendering technique that approximates the volume rendering integral by sampling a 3D scalar field at fixed intervals along rays cast from the camera. It solves the problem of mapping volumetric data to a 2D image plane by performing front-to-back alpha compositing of sampled color and opacity values. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit discretization of the continuous rendering integral into a fixed-step summation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume texture (scalar field), camera parameters (origin, direction, screen dimensions), a transfer function mapping scalar values to color and opacity, a fixed step size \Delta x, and an early termination threshold \alpha{thresh} (typically 0.95 to 0.99). Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: Volume Data: A 3D scalar field stored as a 1D array or 3D texture, typically accessed via row-major indexing or texture sampling. The layout for dimensions dim.x \times dim.y \times dim.z uses stride x \cdot (dim.y \cdot dim.z) + y \cdot dim.z + z. Ray Structure: Defined by an origin point \bar{O} and a direction vector \bar{D}. Accumulators: Per-pixel variables for accumulated color C' (vector) and accumulated opacity \alpha' (scalar), initialized to zero. Transfer Function: Maps scalar values to color and opacity, often implemented as a 1D texture or lookup table. Step Size (\Delta x): The fixed distance between consecutive samples along the ray. Default is 0.001. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the output image with a black background (color \{0,0,0\}, opacity 0). 2. Ray Casting Loop: Iterate over each pixel (i, j) on the image plane. 3. Ray Generation: Compute the ray origin and direction for the current pixel based on camera parameters. 4. Ray Initialization: Compute the ray's entry and exit parameters (t{start}, t{end}) relative to the volume bounding box. Set accumulated color C' = \{0,0,0\} and accumulated opacity \alpha' = 0. 5. Sampling Loop: While \alpha' < \alpha{thresh} and t \le t{end}: a. Sample Volume: Evaluate the scalar value d at the current ray position \bar{P} = \bar{O} + t \cdot \bar{D} using trilinear interpolation from the 8 surrounding voxels. b. Transfer Function: Map the scalar value d to a color C{sample} and opacity \alpha{sample} using the transfer function. c. Compositing: Update the accumulated color and opacity using the front-to-back alpha compositing equations: C'{new} = C'{old} + (1 - \alpha'{old}) \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot C{sample} \alpha'{new} = \alpha'{old} + (1 - \alpha'{old}) \cdot \alpha{sample} d. Advance Ray: Increment t by the step size \Delta x. 6. Final Color: The final pixel color is the accumulated color C'. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def volumeraycastingdiscretization(volumedata, volumedims, camera, transferfunction, stepsize=0.001, threshold=0.99): """ Renders a volume using fixed-step raycasting with front-to-back compositing. volumedata: list of scalars in row-major order volumedims: (dimx, dimy, dimz) camera: object with.screenheight,.screenwidth, and.castray((x, y)) -> (origin, direction) transferfunction: callable(scalar) -> (colorvec3, opacityfloat) """ h, w = camera.screenheight, camera.screenwidth image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(w)] for in range(h)] dimx, dimy, dimz = volumedims stridey = dimz stridex = dimy dimz def trilinearinterpolation(data, dims, x, y, z): # Clamp coordinates to valid range [0, dim-1] x = max(0.0, min(float(dims[0] - 1), x)) y = max(0.0, min(float(dims[1] - 1), y)) z = max(0.0, min(float(dims[2] - 1), z)) x0, y0, z0 = int(x), int(y), int(z) x1, y1, z1 = min(x0 + 1, dims[0] - 1), min(y0 + 1, dims[1] - 1), min(z0 + 1, dims[2] - 1) fx, fy, fz = x - x0, y - y0, z - z0 def getval(ix, iy, iz): return float(data[ix stridex + iy stridey + iz]) c00 = getval(x0, y0, z0) (1-fx) + getval(x1, y0, z0) fx c10 = getval(x0, y1, z0) (1-fx) + getval(x1, y1, z0) fx c01 = getval(x0, y0, z1) (1-fx) + getval(x1, y0, z1) fx c11 = getval(x0, y1, z1) (1-fx) + getval(x1, y1, z1) fx c0 = c00 (1-fy) + c10 fy c1 = c01 (1-fy) + c11 fy return c0 (1-fz) + c1 fz def rayboxintersection(rayo, rayd, dims): tmin, tmax = 0.0, float('inf') for i in range(3): if rayd[i] == 0.0: if rayo[i] < 0.0 or rayo[i] >= dims[i]: return None, None else: t1 = (0.0 - rayo[i]) / rayd[i] t2 = (dims[i] - 1.0 - rayo[i]) / rayd[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tmin = max(tmin, t1) tmax = min(tmax, t2) if tmin > tmax: return None, None return tmin, tmax for y in range(h): for x in range(w): rayo, rayd = camera.castray((x, y)) tstart, tend = rayboxintersection(rayo, rayd, volumedims) if tstart is None: continue acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accopacity = 0.0 # Fixed random offset to prevent banding t = tstart + random.uniform(0.0, stepsize) while accopacity < threshold and t <= tend: pos = (rayo[0] + t rayd[0], rayo[1] + t rayd[1], rayo[2] + t rayd[2]) scalar = trilinearinterpolation(volumedata, volumedims, pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]) colors, opacitys = transferfunction(scalar) weight = (1.0 - accopacity) opacitys acccolor[0] += weight colors[0] acccolor[1] += weight colors[1] acccolor[2] += weight colors[2] accopacity += weight t += stepsize image[y][x] = acccolor return image Parameters: Step Size (\Delta x): The distance between consecutive samples. Too large causes undersampling (aliasing, missed features); too small causes oversampling (performance loss). Default is 0.001. Threshold (\alpha{thresh}): The opacity value at which the ray terminates. Commonly 0.95 or 0.99. Transfer Function: Maps scalar values to color and opacity. A simple example provided in uses normalized data range to compute RGB and alpha: r = (v - DATA{MIN}) / (DATA{MAX} - DATA{MIN}), \alpha = 0.9 if |r - 0.8| < 0.1 else 0.01, R: (DATA{MAX} - v) / (DATA{MAX} - DATA{MIN}), G: 1 - |(DATA{MAX} + DATA{MIN})/2 - v| \times 2 / (DATA{MAX} - DATA{MIN}), B: (v - DATA{MIN}) / (DATA{MAX} - DATA{MIN}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Artifacts: Incorrect handling of the first and last sample points (entry/exit) can cause stepping artifacts or gaps at the volume boundaries. Strategies must accurately sample corner voxels to avoid missing corner samples, which causes intensities to drop to zero prematurely when the ray length is shorter than the step size. Undersampling/Oversampling: Choosing an inappropriate step size leads to visual artifacts or poor performance. Ray Alignment: If a ray does not hit a voxel center exactly, simple nearest-neighbor selection causes reconstruction errors; trilinear interpolation is required. Gradient Calculation: Not given in the sources for this specific method's core algorithm. A sample placement strategy where the first sample point in the volume is calculated as seen from the eye, creating a sampling pattern across pixels that forms concentric lines. Chosen to align sampling with the view direction, potentially reducing aliasing in specific geometries. A technique to improve ray integration approximation by using a 2D ψ table independent of the transfer function, allowing interactive transfer function changes without recomputing the table. A fully CPU-based direct volume rendering technique that uses volume raycasting with multithreaded pixel processing, supporting RGB+transparency transfer functions and Phong lighting (ambient + diffuse), without pixel interpolation or gradient smoothing. A volume rendering technique that casts rays from the camera through the volume and accumulates voxel values along the ray path. Unlike standard front-to-back compositing, this method computes the arithmetic mean of the sampled values (weighted by opacity) to produce an Average Intensity Projection. A sampling method that respects the Nyquist frequency of the image plane by using ray distance as a sampling metric, addressing the fact that transformations from world-space to image-space convolve the volume rendering integral. A technique to approximate the continuous influx of light energy scattered toward the eye (in-scattering) along a camera ray segment by discretizing the integral into a sum of small rectangular areas. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot W), where P is the number of pixels and W is the number of evenly spaced sample locations along a ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, where V is the number of voxels. Performance: Performance is highly dependent on the step size and volume density. Fixed step sizes do not adapt to density variations, risking aliasing or inefficiency. Strengths: Simple to implement and serves as a baseline for more complex methods. Limitations: Fixed step size does not adapt to density variations, risking aliasing or inefficiency. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method is derived from the continuous volume rendering integral by Lacroute using the rectangle rule for numerical integration. The concepts were developed and evaluated in the Inviwo visualization framework, supported by grants from ELLIIT, SeRC, and VINNOVA. name: Hybrid Volume and Isosurface Rendering with Partial Pre-Integration
head: PT with partial preintegration, PTINT
body: Hybrid Volume and Isosurface Rendering with Partial Pre-Integration (PTINT) is a GPU-accelerated cell projection method that combines direct volume rendering with multiple isosurfaces to achieve interactive frame rates. It builds on Partial Pre-Integration by eliminating bus transfer overhead and allowing the simultaneous rendering of opaque or semi-transparent isosurfaces within the same fragment shader passes. Unlike pure ray casting, PTINT uses a tetrahedral discretization that requires no cell connectivity, offering significantly lower memory usage than hardware-accelerated ray casting (HARC) variants. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field defined on a set of n vertices and m tetrahedra. Output: A 2D image with combined volume shading and isosurface geometry. Data Structures and Memory Layout: The method requires no explicit cell connectivity, storing data in textures to optimize GPU access. Texture Element Size: 16 bytes per element. Total Storage: 16(2n + m) bytes for n vertices and m tetrahedra. Storage per Tetrahedron: Assuming an average of 4 tetrahedra per vertex, the storage is 24 bytes per tetrahedron. Memory Usage: Approximately 24 MB for one million cells (20 MB without illumination data). Operational Variants: The algorithm supports three operational variants: 1. Basic Average Scalar Method: Standard volume rendering without pre-integration. 2. Partial Pre-Integration Technique: Uses the \psi table for improved integration accuracy. 3. Partial Pre-Integration with Isosurface Rendering: A hybrid mode combining direct volume rendering with multiple isosurfaces to achieve interactive frame rates by eliminating bus transfer overhead. Algorithm Steps: The rendering is performed in two main passes, with all isosurface computation handled in the second fragment shader to avoid additional rendering passes. 1. First Pass (Volume/Pre-integration): Render the tetrahedra to intermediate framebuffers 2 and 3. Compute gradient vectors gf and gb if lighting or isosurfaces are enabled. If isosurfaces/lighting are not desired, skip gradient computations and skip rendering to framebuffers 2 and 3. 2. Intermediate CPU Pass: Update gradient arrays if they were computed in the first pass. If gradients were skipped, this step is omitted. 3. Second Pass (Hybrid Rendering): Interpolate gradients and compute normals. If gradients were skipped, skip interpolation and normal computation. Perform isosurface detection and shading in the second fragment shader. Apply Phong shading model with controllable diffuse, specular, and ambient coefficients for isosurfaces. Render isosurfaces as fully opaque or semi-transparent fragments. Optimizations and Pitfalls: Early Tetrahedral Discard: An early discard test is applied to improve performance by skipping tetrahedra that do not contribute to the final image. Small Pixel Area Degradation: On datasets like "Liquid Oxygen Post," PTINT may lose performance compared to ray casting at viewpoints where the model occupies a small pixel area, as cell projection approaches are unaffected by pixel area size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderptint(vertices, tetrahedra, isosurfacethresholds, enablelighting, enableisosurfaces): # 1. First Pass: Volume and Gradient Computation if enablelighting or enableisosurfaces: # Compute forward and backward gradients gf and gb # Standard gradient estimation per tetrahedron gradients = estimategradients(vertices, tetrahedra) # Render volume data to intermediate framebuffers 2 and 3 rasterizevolume(vertices, tetrahedra, gradients) else: # Skip gradient computation and framebuffer 2/3 rendering rasterizevolume(vertices, tetrahedra, None) # 2. Intermediate CPU Pass if enablelighting or enableisosurfaces: # Update gradient arrays on CPU # Synchronize gradient data between GPU passes syncgradients(gradients) else: # Skip updating gradient arrays pass # 3. Second Pass: Hybrid Isosurface and Volume Shading if enablelighting or enableisosurfaces: # Interpolate gradients and compute normals # Barycentric interpolation of gradients to fragment positions normals = interpolategradients(vertices, tetrahedra, gradients) else: # Skip interpolation and normal computation normals = None # Apply early tetrahedral discard test # Cull tetrahedra outside view frustum or with zero screen projection visibletets = culltetrahedra(tetrahedra) # Render final image for tet in visibletets: if enableisosurfaces: for threshold in isosurfacethresholds: # Find intersection of scalar field with threshold inside tetrahedron if findisosurfaceintersection(tet, threshold): # Phong shading for isosurface with controllable coefficients # Standard Phong model: ambient + diffuse + specular color = applyphongshading(tet, normals, diffuse=0.8, specular=0.5, ambient=0.2) outputfragment(color, opaque=True) # Or semi-transparent # Render volume contribution # Accumulate color and opacity using partial pre-integration volumecolor = accumulatevolumeshading(tet, normals) outputfragment(volumecolor, alpha=0.5) # Blending with isosurface Time Complexity: Not explicitly defined in sources, but achieves interactive frame rates on tested hardware. Memory Complexity: O(n + m) with a constant factor of 16 bytes per vertex/tet element. Total memory is 16(2n + m) bytes. Measured Performance: Hardware: Intel Pentium IV 3.6 GHz, 2 GB RAM, nVidia GeForce 6800 256 MB, PCI Express 16x. Viewport: 512 \times 512 pixels, constantly rotating model. Blunt Fin Dataset: PTINT outperforms all compared algorithms (GATOR, VICP, VICP Balanced, HARC, HARC INT, HAVIS, HAVS). Oxygen Post Dataset: PTINT loses to ray casting algorithms at certain viewpoints where the model has a small pixel area. Strengths: Low memory footprint (24 bytes/tet vs. 96-144 bytes/tet for HARC variants). No cell connectivity required, freeing GPU memory. Interactive frame rates via elimination of bus transfer overhead. Hybrid visualization allows underlying volumes to be hidden by opaque isosurfaces or enhanced by semi-transparent layers. Limitations: Performance degradation on small pixel area views compared to ray casting. Considerable performance loss if Phong shading is used for isosurfaces due to gradient computation overhead. When to Use: When interactive frame rates are required for large tetrahedral datasets and hybrid volume/isosurface visualization is desired, particularly on hardware with limited GPU memory. When Not to Use: When rendering datasets with small pixel area coverage where ray casting might be more efficient. Origin: Proposed by R. Marroquim et al. in the paper "Volume and Isosurface Rendering with GPU-Accelerated Cell Projection" (CGF 2008). Development: The method extends previous cell projection techniques (GATOR, VICP) and hardware-accelerated ray casting (HARC) by integrating partial pre-integration and isosurface rendering into a unified GPU pipeline. Usage: Tested on datasets including Blunt Fin, Combustion Chamber, Liquid Oxygen Post, Super Phoenix, Fuel Injection, and Electron Distribution Probability. Implemented in C++ with OpenGL 2.0 and GLSL under Linux. name: Average Intensity Projection
head: Additive Reprojection, Average Intensity, Mean Density, Mean Density Projection, Simple Additive Projections, X-ray projection (average)
body: Average Intensity Projection (AIP) is a volume rendering technique that computes the image by averaging the scalar intensities of voxels along rays through the volume onto the image plane. It serves as a simplified alternative to front-to-back compositing, producing an image equivalent to an X-ray projection through the data. Unlike standard ray casting which accounts for opacity and absorption, AIP treats the volume as a transparent medium where every sample contributes equally to the final pixel value, making it computationally inexpensive but prone to low contrast. Inputs: Volume Data: A 3D grid of scalar values. Sources describe two common layouts: 1. 3D Texture: Dimensions X \times Y \times Z (e.g., 256 \times 256 \times 109), stored in a GLTEXTURE3D with GLRGBA internal format but GLRED base format, using GLUNSIGNEDBYTE type. 2. Raw Array: 1D array of unsigned char values with dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz, stored in row-major order. Camera/View: Defined by a view position (viewPos) and a bounding box for the volume (e.g., min vec3(-1.0), max vec3(1.0) or centered at volume origin). Parameters: numsteps: Fixed number of sampling steps along the ray (e.g., 256). scale: Scaling factor for output image dimensions (ImageWidth = VolumeWidth \times scale). isoSurf: Optional uniform float for isosurface extraction mode, processed as iso = isoSurf - floor(isoSurf). Outputs: Image: A 2D grid of pixel values. Format: unsigned char (0-255 range). Dimensions: Scaled width and height. Value: The arithmetic mean of the sampled voxel intensities along the ray. Ray: Defined by origin or and direction dir. Transfer Function (Optional): A 1D texture (GLTEXTURE1D) mapping scalar values to color/opacity. In pure AIP, this is often bypassed or used only for final color mapping. Accumulators: totalVoxelValue or meanSum: Accumulates the sum of sampled intensities. cnt or validSamples: Counts the number of valid samples taken. 1. Initialize: For each pixel, initialize totalVoxelValue = 0.0 and cnt = 1 (to avoid division by zero). 2. Ray Setup: Compute ray origin fpos (fragment position) and direction direction = normalize(fpos - viewPos). Alternatively, for orthographic projections, map pixel coordinates to volume space: originalX = pixelX / scale, originalY = pixelY / scale, with ray origin at (originalX, originalY, 0) and direction (0, 0, 1). 3. Intersection (Perspective): Intersect the ray with the volume bounding box to find entry (tenter) and exit (texit) distances using the slab method. 4. Step Calculation: Calculate ray length dist = distance(entry, exit) and step size stepsize = dist / numsteps. 5. Sampling Loop: Iterate i from 0 to numsteps - 1: Increment counter cnt++. Determine sample position curPos along the ray. Coordinate Transformation: Scale Z-coordinate if necessary: tmp.z = curPos.z 2.3486238532110093 (to handle non-isotropic data or texture normalization). Map to texture coordinates: texPos = (1 + tmp) / 2. Invert Y-axis: texPos.y = 1 - texPos.y (due to image data inversion). Sampling: Fetch value val = texture(texVol, texPos).x. Accumulation: If using raw array indexing (orthographic case): Translate sample to volume center, apply rotation matrix, translate back, check bounds, compute linear index, and fetch voxelIntensity = vol.data[index] / 255.0f. Add to sum: totalVoxelValue += val (or voxelIntensity). Advance: curPos = curPos + direction stepsize. 6. Finalize: Compute the average: meanValue = totalVoxelValue / cnt. 7. Color Mapping (Optional): Map meanValue to a final color using a transfer function or color map. If lighting is enabled, calculate normals from the mean position and apply lighting. Unverified code.
