Args: volumetexture: 3D texture object or array of shape (Z, Y, X) viewpos: Camera position (vec3) imagewidth: Output image width imageheight: Output image height numsteps: Number of samples per ray scale: Scaling factor for image dimensions relative to volume Returns: imagedata: 2D array of floats (0.0 to 1.0) representing average intensity """ imagedata = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) # Define bounding box for intersection (example: unit cube centered at origin) # Note: Specific bounds depend on volume coordinate system. # Source uses min=(-1,-1,-1), max=(1,1,1). Source uses volume indices. bboxmin = np.array([-1.0, -1.0, -1.0]) bboxmax = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Map pixel to world space # Source uses orthographic mapping: originalX = pixelX / scale # Source uses perspective: fpos derived from fragment position on cube # Implementing perspective ray casting as per # Calculate fragment position on the bounding box face # Assuming a standard projection matrix inverse is applied to get fpos # For simplicity, assuming fpos is provided or calculated from screen coords fpos = calculatefragmentposition(x, y, imagewidth, imageheight, bboxmin, bboxmax) direction = normalize(fpos - viewpos) # Ray-Bbox Intersection (Slab Method) tenter, texit = intersectbox(viewpos, direction, bboxmin, bboxmax) if tenter > texit: continue # Ray misses volume dist = texit - tenter stepsize = dist / numsteps totalvalue = 0.0 count = 1 # Avoid division by zero currentpos = viewpos + direction tenter for i in range(numsteps): count += 1 # Coordinate transformation specific to source # Scale Z to fit texture coordinate space [-1, 1] after mapping tmp = np.array([currentpos[0], currentpos[1], currentpos[2] 2.3486238532110093]) # Map to [0, 1] texture coordinates texpos = (1.0 + tmp) / 2.0 # Invert Y axis texpos[1] = 1.0 - texpos[1] # Sample volume # Clamp texpos to [0, 1] to handle boundary conditions texposclamped = np.clip(texpos, 0.0, 1.0) val = samplevolume(volumetexture, texposclamped) totalvalue += val # Advance position currentpos = currentpos + direction stepsize # Compute average meanvalue = totalvalue / count imagedata[y, x] = meanvalue return imagedata def samplevolume(texture, texcoords): """ Samples a 3D texture using trilinear interpolation. """ # Implementation depends on specific texture API. # Assuming standard GLSL-like texture3d behavior return texture3d(texture, texcoords) def intersectbox(origin, direction, minb, maxb): """ Slab method for ray-box intersection. Returns (tenter, texit). Returns None if no intersection. """ tmin = (minb - origin) / direction tmax = (maxb - origin) / direction t1 = np.minimum(tmin, tmax) t2 = np.maximum(tmin, tmax) tenter = np.maximum(np.maximum(t1[0], t1[1]), t1[2]) texit = np.minimum(np.minimum(t2[0], t2[1]), t2[2]) if tenter > texit: return None # Ensure we start inside or at the entry point if tenter < 0: tenter = 0 return tenter, texit Division by Zero: The sample counter cnt is initialized to 1 and incremented before sampling to ensure color /= cnt never divides by zero. Coordinate Inversion: The texture Y-coordinate must be inverted (1 - texPos.y) because image data is often inverted on the Y-axis. Non-Isotropic Data: The Z-coordinate may require scaling by a specific constant (e.g., 2.3486238532110093) before mapping to texture space to handle non-isotropic voxels or specific normalization requirements. Low Contrast: Additive projection techniques suffer from a confused or unclear appearance because all information is projected, resulting in very little contrast to distinguish gradual variations or small abrupt changes. Occlusion: Unlike front-to-back compositing, AIP does not handle obscuration, which can hide structural details. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, where V is the number of voxels. Performance: Very fast due to the lack of complex compositing (opacity/alpha blending) and lighting calculations. Strengths: Simple implementation, fast rendering, useful for quick overviews or X-ray-like visualizations. Limitations: Low contrast, no depth cues from occlusion, sensitive to noise and background clutter. When to Use: When speed is critical and depth perception is not required, or for initial data exploration. When Not to Use: When detailed structural visualization, depth cues, or high contrast is needed. Average Intensity Projection, also known as additive reprojection, was developed by Hohne et al. for medical imaging applications, specifically stereotactic neurosurgery planning. It is one of their generalized projection images, designed to directly image the volume of data without surface shading. The technique is equivalent to an X-ray projection through the volume. It is often contrasted with techniques that use partial volume effects for surface shading or segmentation. name: Differential Sampling
head: Differential construction of T, quadratic ray sampling, Nyquist-respecting ray sampling
body: Differential sampling is a ray discretization strategy for volume raycasting that adapts the sampling density along a ray based on the view-dependent frequency of the image plane, ensuring the sampling rate respects the Nyquist limit. Unlike uniform sampling methods, it uses a quadratic sampling function T(t) derived from ray differentials, allowing variable step sizes that are finer near the viewpoint and coarser further away, which prevents aliasing for features close to the camera. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera parameters (origin \vec{o}, central view direction \vec{w}, right vector \vec{u}, up vector \vec{v}), image plane resolution (\Delta x, \Delta y), a scaling factor sk, and the volume data structure. Outputs: A sequence of sample positions \vec{P}i along the ray and their corresponding transfer function evaluations. Data Structures: The method maintains the following state variables per ray during iteration: \vec{P}: Current 3D sample position. \vec{D}: Unitized ray direction vector. t: Current distance along the ray from the origin. \Delta t: Current step size (derivative of T with respect to t). x: Current image-space coordinate index (integer). T(x): Cumulative distance along the ray corresponding to image coordinate x. Parameters: sk: Scaling factor for the step size multiplier k. Typical value: 4. Theoretical Nyquist limit requires sk < 0.5, but this is excessive in practice. k: Step size multiplier, defined as k = sk |\vec{u}\Delta x + \vec{v}\Delta y|. k0: Constant combining k and geometric factors. If k is arbitrarily chosen, k0 = k. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Generate the ray direction vector \vec{d} for pixel coordinates (x, y) using the pinhole camera model: \vec{d}(x, y) = \vec{w} + x\vec{u} + y\vec{v} where \vec{w} is the central view direction, and \vec{u}, \vec{v} are the right and up vectors. 2. Ray Unitization: Compute the unitized ray direction \vec{D}: \vec{D}(x, y) = \frac{\vec{d}}{\sqrt{\vec{d} \cdot \vec{d}}} 3. Compute Ray Differential Magnitude: Calculate the magnitude of the partial derivative of \vec{D} with respect to the image-space coordinate x. First, compute the vector derivative: \frac{\partial \vec{D}}{\partial x} = \frac{(\vec{d} \cdot \vec{d})\vec{u} - (\vec{d} \cdot \vec{u})\vec{d}}{(\vec{d} \cdot \vec{d})^{3/2}} Then, take its magnitude: \left| \frac{\partial \vec{D}}{\partial x} \right| 4. Compute Coefficients: Compute k using the pixel footprint: k = sk |\vec{u}\Delta x + \vec{v}\Delta y|. Set k0 = k (or k \tan(\theta) if explicit geometric correction is desired, but sources indicate k0=k is sufficient if k is chosen appropriately). Compute coefficient a: a = k0 \left| \frac{\partial \vec{D}}{\partial x} \right| Compute coefficient b: b = k0 5. Initialization: Initialize image coordinate x = 0. Initialize cumulative distance T = 0. Initialize step size \Delta t = b. Initialize position \vec{P} = \vec{o}. Initialize a variable maxtsampled to -\infty to handle macrocell entry duplicates. 6. Sampling Loop: While T < D{exit} (exit distance of the volume): Sample: Evaluate the volume at \vec{P}. Update Max Sampled: maxtsampled = max(maxtsampled, T). Increment Step Size: \Delta t{new} = \Delta t + a Increment Position: \vec{P}{new} = \vec{P} + \Delta t \cdot \vec{D} Update State: \Delta t = \Delta t{new} \vec{P} = \vec{P}{new} T = T + \Delta t{old} \quad \text{(Note: The source implies T accumulates the previous step size or is derived from x. The recurrence in Eq 17 updates P and dt. T is implicitly } \sum \Delta ti \text{ or computed via } T(x) = \frac{a}{2}x^2 + bx \text{ if x is tracked. The source Eq 17 updates P and dt directly. We track T for exit condition.)} Correction based on Eq 15 and 17: The source states "sample at \vec{P} = \vec{P}(T(x))" and then increments. The increment \Delta t in Eq 17 is the current step size used to move from \vec{P}0 to \vec{P}1. The next step size is \Delta t1 = \Delta t0 + a. So, in the loop: 1. Use current \Delta t to move: \vec{P} \leftarrow \vec{P} + \Delta t \cdot \vec{D}. 2. Update \Delta t \leftarrow \Delta t + a. 3. Update T \leftarrow T + \Delta t{previous}. Simpler Implementation: Since T(x) = \frac{a}{2}x^2 + bx, we can just increment x by 1 and compute T(x) directly, then compute \vec{P} from T. However, the source explicitly gives the incremental update in Eq 17. We follow Eq 17. Refined Loop based on Eq 17: The source says: "sample at \vec{P} = \vec{P}(T(x)), and perform the following increments... \vec{P}1 = \vec{P}0 + \Delta t0 \vec{D} and \Delta t1 = \Delta t0 + a". This implies \Delta t0 is the step taken to get to \vec{P}0? No, \Delta t is the derivative \partial T / \partial t. Let's trace: Start: x=0, T=0, \Delta t = b. Sample at T=0 (\vec{P}=\vec{o}). Increment: \vec{P} \leftarrow \vec{P} + b \vec{D}. \Delta t \leftarrow b + a. Next T is b. Sample at T=b. Increment: \vec{P} \leftarrow \vec{P} + (b+a) \vec{D}. \Delta t \leftarrow (b+a) + a. Next T is b + (b+a) = 2b + a. Check against T(x) = \frac{a}{2}x^2 + bx. x=0, T=0. x=1, T = a/2 + b. The incremental sum b + (b+a) = 2b+a does not match a/2+b. Re-reading Source carefully: "The sampling function T has a derivative varying linearly with distance: \Delta T = \partial T / \partial t = at + b". Wait, Eq 6 says \Delta T = \partial T / \partial t = at + b. This is derivative with respect to ray distance t, not image coordinate x. But Eq 15 says \partial^2 T / \partial x^2 = a. There is a confusion in the source text between t and x. Eq 11: \Delta t = kx. Eq 14: \partial T / \partial x = \Delta t. So \partial T / \partial x = k' |\partial D / \partial x| x + k''. This means T is a function of x. The increment in Eq 17: \vec{P}1 = \vec{P}0 + \Delta t0 \vec{D}. Here \Delta t0 is the step size in world space distance. The source states: "incrementing the position... consists only of an extra vector multiplication... on top of the vector addition for uniform sampling." Let's look at Eq 17 again. \Delta t1 = \Delta t0 + a. If \Delta t is the world-space step size, and it increases linearly by a, then \Delta t(x) = \Delta t(0) + x \cdot a. We know \Delta t(0) = b (from Eq 16, \partial T / \partial x = b at x=0, and \partial T / \partial x = \Delta t). So \Delta t(x) = b + a x. The position update is \vec{P}{x+1} = \vec{P}x + \Delta t(x) \vec{D}. The cumulative distance T(x) is \sum{i=0}^{x-1} \Delta t(i) = \sum{i=0}^{x-1} (b + a i) = bx + a \frac{(x-1)x}{2}. This is approximately \frac{a}{2}x^2 + bx. So the implementation should track x (integer) and compute \Delta t based on x. Revised Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Generation: \vec{d} = \vec{w} + x\vec{u} + y\vec{v}. 2. Unitize: \vec{D} = \vec{d} / |\vec{d}|. 3. Compute |\partial \vec{D} / \partial x|: \frac{\partial \vec{D}}{\partial x} = \frac{(\vec{d} \cdot \vec{d})\vec{u} - (\vec{d} \cdot \vec{u})\vec{d}}{(\vec{d} \cdot \vec{d})^{3/2}} \text{mag} = \left| \frac{\partial \vec{D}}{\partial x} \right| 4. Compute Coefficients: k = sk |\vec{u}\Delta x + \vec{v}\Delta y| a = k \cdot \text{mag} b = k 5. Initialization: x = 0 \vec{P} = \vec{o} \Delta t = b 6. Loop: While \vec{P} is inside the volume: Sample volume at \vec{P}. Check for macrocell entry. If entering a new macrocell at T{enter}, compute x{enter} such that T(x{enter}) \approx T{enter}. Set x = \lceil x{enter} \rceil. Recompute \Delta t = b + a \cdot x. Set \vec{P} = \vec{o} + T(x) \vec{D}. Increment: \vec{P} \leftarrow \vec{P} + \Delta t \cdot \vec{D} \Delta t \leftarrow \Delta t + a x \leftarrow x + 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Duplicate Samples at Macrocell Boundaries: When entering a new macrocell, the sampling sequence might restart or overlap. To avoid duplicate samples, store the greatest t already sampled. If the computed T(x) for the new macrocell entry is less than the stored max t, skip or adjust x. Precision: The quadratic growth of step size can lead to large steps far from the camera. Ensure the volume exit condition is robust. Nyquist Limit: Using sk < 0.5 satisfies the Nyquist limit theoretically but is computationally expensive. sk=4 is a practical default. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray. The number of samples is generally higher than uniform sampling for near-field features but lower for far-field features, balancing accuracy and performance. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray for state variables. Strengths: Respects the Nyquist frequency of the image plane, reducing aliasing artifacts for structures close to the viewpoint. Simple incremental update makes it efficient on GPUs. Limitations: Requires computation of ray differentials (\partial \vec{D} / \partial x) per pixel. Adaptive sampling based on local gradients is not used directly due to poor thread coherence on GPUs, though macrocell-based adaptation is possible. When to Use: High-quality volume rendering where aliasing is a concern, particularly for large volumes viewed from varying distances. When Not to Use: Real-time applications with strict performance constraints where uniform sampling is sufficient, or when the volume has no high-frequency features near the camera. Differential sampling was introduced in the context of volume ray casting with peak finding, building on the concept of ray differentials originally formulated by Igehy. The method addresses the issue that regular sampling in world-space undersamples features close to the viewpoint relative to those further away, due to the convolution of the volume rendering integral during the transformation from world-space to image-space. It was implemented in a GLSL fragment shader framework for OpenGL. Volume Ray Casting with Peak Finding and Differential..., https://www.sci.utah.edu/~knolla/avrc.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Classical Ray Tracing Integration
head: Kajiya and Von Herzen
body: Classical Ray Tracing Integration is a volume rendering technique that computes pixel color by combining background transmission (attenuated by absorption) and uniform in-scattering. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric objects with defined boundaries or integrating geometric visibility directly into volume pipelines. Unlike standard direct volume ray casting which samples uniformly along the entire ray, this method explicitly calculates entry and exit points to limit sampling to the volume interior and applies Beer's law for transmission. It is distinguished from Alpha Compositing Ray Casting by its handling of homogeneous spheres via analytical integration, and from Single Scattering Volume Rendering with Ray Marching by its assumption of uniform scattering color. The method operates in two primary modes: analytical integration for homogeneous spheres and ray marching with shading heuristics for general volume data. Both modes rely on the volume rendering integral discretized into a summation over sample points along a ray [Parent principles]. Inputs: Camera ray (origin O, direction D), volume data (3D grid or sphere parameters), transfer function, shading parameters. Outputs: Final pixel color C{final}. 1. Sphere Object (analytical mode): center: vec3 (e.g., [0, 0, -4]). radius: float (e.g., 1.0). sigmaa: float (absorption coefficient, e.g., 0.1). scatter: vec3 (uniform scatter color, e.g., [0.8, 0.1, 0.5]). 2. Volume Context (marching mode): volume: 3D texture or grid. tfn: Transfer function mapping scalar value to (C, \alpha). params: Shading mode (GRADIENTSHADING or SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC), shadingScale, gradientStep, lighting parameters. 1. Intersection Test: Compute parametric distances t0 and t1 where the ray enters and leaves the sphere. If no intersection, return backgroundcolor. 2. Distance Calculation: Compute the distance traveled through the sphere as d = t1 - t0. 3. Transmission: Apply Beer's law to compute the transmission factor T: T = e^{-\sigmaa \cdot d} where \sigmaa is the absorption coefficient. 4. Color Composition: Compute the final color as the sum of the attenuated background and the uniform scatter: C{final} = C{background} \cdot T + C{scatter} \cdot (1 - T). 1. Initialization: Initialize alpha = 0, color = 0. For SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC: Initialize highestOrg = 0, highestColor = 0, highestAlpha = 0. 2. Intersection Check: If the ray intersects the volume bounds [t{start}, t{end}], proceed. Otherwise, return background. 3. Jitter: Generate a random jitter value j \in [0, 1) to offset the first sample position along the ray direction. 4. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate t from t{start} to t{end} with step size marchingStep. Position: Calculate position p = O + t \cdot D. Sample: Get scalar value d using trilinear interpolation [Parent principles]. Transfer Function: Map d to sample color Cs and opacity \alphas. Opacity Correction: Apply opacity correction based on step size to ensure slice-count invariance. Gradient Calculation: Compute gradient No = -\nabla d using a central difference operator with gradientStep. Transform to world space Nw. Transmittance: Calculate current transmittance tr = 1 - \alpha. Shading Mode: If GRADIENTSHADING: Transform ray direction to world space. Compute shaded color C{shade} using lighting model (ambient + directional) with normal Nw. Blend sample color: Cs = \text{lerp}(\text{shadingScale}, Cs, C{shade}). If SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC: Check if current sample density is highest: if \alphas \cdot (1 - \alpha) > \text{highestAlpha}, update highestOrg, highestColor, and highestAlpha. Use unshaded Cs for accumulation. Accumulation: Update color: C{new} = C{old} + (1 - \alpha{old}) \cdot Cs \cdot \alphas. Update alpha: \alpha{new} = \alpha{old} + (1 - \alpha{old}) \cdot \alphas. Termination: If \alpha \ge 0.99 (nearly one), break loop. 5. Final Shading (Heuristic Only): If highestAlpha > 0, compute shadow ray transmittance T{shadow} from highestOrg to light direction. Compute final color: C{final} = \text{lerp}(C{accumulated}, C{highest} \cdot \alpha{highest} \cdot T{shadow}, \text{shadingScale}). 6. Gamma Correction: Apply gamma 2.2 correction to the final color [Parent principles]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def vec3add(a, b): return (a[0] + b[0], a[1] + b[1], a[2] + b[2]) def vec3scale(v, s): return (v[0] s, v[1] s, v[2] s) def vec3pow(v, p): return (v[0] p, v[1] p, v[2] p) def computerayexit(origin, direction, bounds): # Slab intersection for axis-aligned box t0 = max((bounds[0][i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if direction[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)) t1 = min((bounds[1][i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if direction[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)) return max(t0, t1) def trilinearinterpolate(volume, pos, dims): # Standard trilinear interpolation vx = pos[0] (dims[0] - 1) vy = pos[1] (dims[1] - 1) vz = pos[2] (dims[2] - 1) x0, y0, z0 = int(math.floor(vx)), int(math.floor(vy)), int(math.floor(vz)) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 x0 = max(0, min(x0, dims[0]-1)) x1 = max(0, min(x1, dims[0]-1)) y0 = max(0, min(y0, dims[1]-1)) y1 = max(0, min(y1, dims[1]-1)) z0 = max(0, min(z0, dims[2]-1)) z1 = max(0, min(z1, dims[2]-1)) wx = vx - x0 wy = vy - y0 wz = vz - z0 c00 = volume[x0][y0][z0] (1-wx) + volume[x1][y0][z0] wx c01 = volume[x0][y0][z1] (1-wx) + volume[x1][y0][z1] wx c10 = volume[x0][y1][z0] (1-wx) + volume[x1][y1][z0] wx c11 = volume[x0][y1][z1] (1-wx) + volume[x1][y1][z1] wx r0 = c00 (1-wy) + c10 wy r1 = c01 (1-wy) + c11 wy return r0 (1-wz) + r1 wz def classicalraytracingintegration(rayorigin, raydirection, sphere, backgroundcolor, volume=None, params=None): """ Renders a pixel using classical ray tracing integration. Supports homogeneous spheres (analytical) and general volumes (marching). """ def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) # --- Mode 1: Homogeneous Sphere (Analytical) --- if sphere is not None and volume is None: t0, t1 = sphere.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if t0 is None: return backgroundcolor distance = t1 - t0 transmission = math.exp(-sphere.sigmaa distance) finalcolor = vec3add( vec3scale(backgroundcolor, transmission), vec3scale(sphere.scatter, 1.0 - transmission)) return vec3pow(finalcolor, 1.0 / 2.2) # --- Mode 2: General Volume (Ray Marching) --- if volume is not None: tstart, tend = volume.intersectbounds(rayorigin, raydirection) if tstart is None: return backgroundcolor alpha = 0.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) highestorg = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) highestcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) highestalpha = 0.0 jitter = random.random() stepsize = params.marchingStep if params else 0.01 tcurr = tstart + jitter stepsize while alpha < 0.99 and tcurr < tend: p = vec3add(rayorigin, vec3scale(raydirection, tcurr)) scalar = trilinearinterpolate(volume.data, p, volume.dims) samplecolor, samplealpha = volume.tfn(scalar) # Opacity correction for slice-count invariance samplealpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-samplealpha stepsize) grad = volume.samplegradient(p, scalar, params.gradientStep) normalworld = volume.transformnormal(grad) transmittance = 1.0 - alpha if params.mode == "GRADIENTSHADING": dirworld = volume.transformvector(raydirection) shadedcolor = volume.shadescivislight(dirworld, normalworld, samplecolor, params.matgradientshading, params.lightambient, params.lightdirectionalrgb, params.lightdirectionaldir) samplecolor = vec3add(vec3scale(samplecolor, 1.0 - params.shadingScale), vec3scale(shadedcolor, params.shadingScale)) elif params.mode == "SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC": currentdensity = transmittance samplealpha if currentdensity > highestalpha: highestorg = p highestcolor = samplecolor highestalpha = currentdensity contrib = vec3scale(samplecolor, transmittance samplealpha) color = vec3add(color, contrib) alpha += transmittance samplealpha tcurr += stepsize if params.mode == "SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC" and highestalpha > 0.0: # Shadow ray transmittance computation not provided in sources [Comment] shadowtransmittance = 1.0 finalshadedcolor = vec3scale(highestcolor, highestalpha shadowtransmittance) color = vec3add(vec3scale(color, 1.0 - params.shadingScale), vec3scale(finalshadedcolor, params.shadingScale)) return vec3pow(color, 1.0 / 2.2) return backgroundcolor sigmaa: Absorption coefficient. Typical value: 0.1. scatter: Uniform scatter color. Typical value: [0.8, 0.1, 0.5]. backgroundcolor: Color returned if no intersection. Typical value: [0.572, 0.772, 0.921]. shadingScale: Scalar blending unshaded and shaded colors. gradientStep: Step size for gradient estimation. marchingStep: Step size for ray marching. Redundant Distance Calculation: Computing the Euclidean distance between entry and exit points (\|\bar{p}1 - \bar{p}2\|) is correct but computationally redundant if t0 and t1 are known; use t1 - t0. Uniform Scattering Assumption: The analytical mode assumes uniform scattering color regardless of position or direction; it does not account for directional lighting or varying scattering properties. Heuristic Gradient: In SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC, gradients are not accumulated; only the highest density point is stored for deferred shading. Shadow Ray Cost: Computing shadow transmittance from the highest density point adds significant cost for the heuristic mode. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples along the ray. For analytical spheres, it is O(1) per pixel. For marching, it depends on volume density and step size. Memory Complexity: O(1) for analytical mode. O(V) for volume data storage in marching mode. Performance: Analytical integration is extremely fast and exact for homogeneous spheres. Ray marching handles complex scalar fields and supports deferred shading heuristics. Strengths: Exact solution for homogeneous volumes; integrates geometric visibility; supports shading heuristics for complex data. Limitations: Analytical mode is limited to simple shapes; uniform scattering assumption is unrealistic for many volumes; heuristic shading may produce artifacts if the highest density point is not representative. When to use: Ideal for rendering simple volumetric objects (e.g., clouds, smoke balls) or when integrating geometric surfaces with volume data. Avoid for highly anisotropic or spatially varying scattering volumes. The method originates from early volume rendering techniques that combined ray tracing with volume data. The integration of classical ray tracing into volume rendering pipelines was proposed to handle visibility and geometric merging, such as superimposing radiation treatment planning isodose surfaces over CT data. The heuristic shading approach was developed to balance performance and visual quality in scientific visualization. Recent applications include integrating ray tracing for interreflections in 3D Gaussian Splatting. name: Isosurface and first-hit ray casting
body: Isosurface and first-hit ray casting is an image-order rendering technique that determines the visible surface of a volumetric scalar field by tracing rays from the eye and stopping at the nearest point where the scalar value meets a user-defined isovalue C{iso}. It solves the problem of visualizing implicit surfaces embedded within 3D data without requiring explicit mesh extraction or hidden-surface removal. Unlike Direct volume ray casting, which accumulates color and opacity along the entire ray path, this method performs a boolean decision: it returns the first sample C{src} such that C{iso} = C{src} (or C{src} \ge C{iso}), ignoring all subsequent samples. This distinguishes it from Distance-field ray marching, which interpolates signed distance fields for smooth geometry, and Ray-grid traversal, which focuses on efficient voxel access patterns rather than the specific surface-detection logic. The family shares a common mathematical framework for detecting the intersection of a viewing ray with an implicit surface defined by f(\mathbf{x}) = C{iso}. Ray Representation and Bounds: Each pixel generates a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). The ray is parameterized as \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} for t \ge 0. The volume is enclosed in an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) defined by \mathbf{u}{min} and \mathbf{u}{max}. Rays are clipped to this volume. The intersection of the ray with the AABB yields entry t{min} and exit t{max} distances: t0 = (\mathbf{u}{min} - \mathbf{o}) \odot \mathbf{invD}, \quad t1 = (\mathbf{u}{max} - \mathbf{o}) \odot \mathbf{invD} t{min} = \max(\min(t{0x}, t{1x}), \min(t{0y}, t{1y}), \min(t{0z}, t{1z})) t{max} = \min(\max(t{0x}, t{1x}), \max(t{0y}, t{1y}), \max(t{0z}, t{1z})) where \mathbf{invD} = 1.0 / \mathbf{d}. If t{max} \le t{min}, the ray misses the volume entirely. Traversal and Surface Detection: The algorithm traverses the ray from near to far (t{min} to t{max}) to ensure the first hit is found, implementing the "painters algorithm" visibility sorting for implicit surfaces. At each sample point \mathbf{x}(t), a boolean check determines if the surface is found: C = \begin{cases} true & \text{if } C{iso} = C{src} \\ false & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where C{src} is the sampled scalar value f(\mathbf{x}(t)). In discrete implementations, this is often simplified to checking if the sampled value meets or exceeds the threshold (C{src} \ge C{iso}). Hit Processing and Shading: Upon finding a hit at parameter t{hit}, the algorithm computes the 3D position \mathbf{p}{hit} = \mathbf{o} + t{hit}\mathbf{d} and the surface normal \mathbf{n} (typically via the gradient \nabla f) to apply shading models. If no hit is found within t{max}, the pixel is colored with the background color. Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode implements a fixed-step marching variant with sign-change detection and bisection refinement, as described in the literature: def samplescalarfield(p): # Performs 3D texture lookup for scalar field f(p) return texturelookup3d(p) def sampleiso(p, uIsovalue): return samplescalarfield(p) - uIsovalue def hassignchange(dprev, dcurr): return dprev dcurr <= 0.0 def refineisohitbisection(origin, dir, ta, tb, da, db, urefinementiterations): for in range(urefinementiterations): tmid = 0.5 (ta + tb) dmid = sampleiso(origin + tmid dir, uIsovalue) if hassignchange(da, dmid): tb = tmid db = dmid else: ta = tmid da = dmid return 0.5 (ta + tb) def computenormal(p, ustepsize, uIsovalue): h = ustepsize gx = samplescalarfield(p + vec3(h, 0.0, 0.0)) - samplescalarfield(p - vec3(h, 0.0, 0.0)) gy = samplescalarfield(p + vec3(0.0, h, 0.0)) - samplescalarfield(p - vec3(0.0, h, 0.0)) gz = samplescalarfield(p + vec3(0.0, 0.0, h)) - samplescalarfield(p - vec3(0.0, h, 0.0)) grad = vec3(gx, gy, gz) norm = max(length(grad), 1e-12) return -grad / norm def traceshadowray(origin, dir, stepsize, udomainmin, udomainmax, uIsovalue): t = 2.0 stepsize while True: p = origin + t dir if p.x < udomainmin.x or p.y < udomainmin.y or p.z < udomainmin.z or \ p.x > udomainmax.x or p.y > udomainmax.y or p.z > udomainmax.z: break if samplescalarfield(p) >= uIsovalue: return 0.0 t += stepsize return 1.0 def shadeisopoint(phit, lightdirworld, uenableshadows, ustepsize, udomainmin, udomainmax, uIsovalue): normal = computenormal(phit, ustepsize, uIsovalue) diffuse = max(0.0, dot(normal, lightdirworld)) shadow = 1.0 if uenableshadows != 0: shadow = traceshadowray(phit, lightdirworld, ustepsize, udomainmin, udomainmax, uIsovalue) basecolor = vec3(1.0) return basecolor diffuse shadow def integrateisorayworld(origin, dir, tstart, tend, ustepsize, urefinementiterations, uIsovalue, uLightAngle, uenableshadows, udomainmin, udomainmax): rescolor = vec3(0.0) reshit = False # Guard against invalid bounds if tstart >= tend: return rescolor, reshit # Initialize with the first sample inside the volume bounds tprev = tstart dprev = sampleiso(origin + tprev dir, uIsovalue) # Handle case where ray starts exactly on the surface if abs(dprev) < 1e-6: phit = origin + tprev dir lightdirworld = normalize(vec3(cos(uLightAngle 2.0 3.141592653589793), sin(uLightAngle 2.0 3.141592653589793), -1.0)) rescolor = shadeisopoint(phit, lightdirworld, uenableshadows, ustepsize, udomainmin, udomainmax, uIsovalue) reshit = True return rescolor, reshit lightdirworld = normalize(vec3(cos(uLightAngle 2.0 3.141592653589793), sin(uLightAngle 2.0 3.141592653589793), -1.0)) tcurr = tstart + ustepsize while tcurr <= tend: dcurr = sampleiso(origin + tcurr dir, uIsovalue) if hassignchange(dprev, dcurr): thit = refineisohitbisection(origin, dir, tprev, tcurr, dprev, dcurr, urefinementiterations) phit = origin + thit dir rescolor = shadeisopoint(phit, lightdirworld, uenableshadows, ustepsize, udomainmin, udomainmax, uIsovalue) reshit = True break tprev = tcurr dprev = dcurr tcurr += ustepsize return rescolor, reshit A zero-order interpolation ray casting algorithm for generating images of surfaces in binary volumetric data without explicit boundary detection or hidden-surface removal. It distinguishes itself by operating on binary occupancy grids (voxels are either inside or outside) rather than continuous scalar fields, relying on discrete occupancy checks rather than sign-change detection or interpolation. It is chosen when data is already binarized and high-performance, low-complexity rendering is required. Iso-surface Bisection Tracing renders implicit surfaces directly from volumetric scalar fields by tracing rays and locating the zero-crossing of the signed function g(t) = f(\mathbf{x}(t)) - c without extracting polygon meshes. It distinguishes itself from standard ray marching by using interval arithmetic to bound the function over continuous intervals, guaranteeing that no surface features (such as thin shells, cusps, or near-tangent intersections) are missed regardless of sampling density. Unlike Binary Ray Casting, which relies on discrete occupancy grids, and 1-Pass Isosurface Raycaster Adaptive, which uses adaptive step sizes, this method uses fixed-step traversal to detect sign changes followed by deterministic bisection refinement, or interval-arithmetic bisection for robust black-box functions. A single-pass compute shader raycasting method that performs isosurface extraction with adaptive step sizing. It uses a scalar field texture to find the isosurface and a gradient texture for Phong shading. It is chosen when computational resources are limited but higher accuracy than fixed-step marching is needed, adapting the step size based on local field gradients. A minor variant that visualizes the Euclidean distance between pixel coordinates and surface coordinates using a log-scale gamma correction. Definition: It computes the distance d between the pixel's projected surface coordinate \mathbf{s} and the pixel center \mathbf{p}, then applies a logarithmic transformation and gamma correction to produce a depth-aware visualization. Formula: d = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}\|2, \quad l = \log(\max(d, 10^{-2})), \quad v = \left(\frac{l - l{\min}}{l{\max} - l{\min}}\right)^{1/2.33} where l{\min} and l{\max} are the minimum and maximum log-distances across the batch. Parameters: The lower bound for the log argument is clamped to 10^{-2} to prevent \log(0), and the gamma exponent is fixed at 1/2.33 \approx 0.429. Implementation: logdists = ( pxcoords.sub(surfacecoords).norm(dim=-1, p=2, keepdim=True).clamp(1e-2, float('inf')).log()) return ( logdists.sub(logdists.min()).div(logdists.max().sub(logdists.min())).pow(1 / 2.33)) The technique originates from the foundational work on ray tracing by Appel (1968) and Whitted (1980), who established the image-order approach of shooting rays from the eye to determine visibility. Engel et al. (2006) specifically applied these principles to volume graphics, noting that iso-surface rendering in volumes is a special case of transfer function evaluation where only one non-zero solution exists. It is widely used in medical imaging for virtual endoscopy, where visualizing the interior of hollow organs (like the colon or blood vessels) requires precise surface extraction from CT or MRI scalar data. The method contrasts with rasterization by processing pixels in image order, which simplifies visibility handling but can be slower for large screen-space objects. name: Volumetric Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement
head: Volumetric isosurface rendering, Iso Ray Casting, Isosurface Ray Casting, Iso-Surface Rendering, Isosurface mode
body:
Volumetric isosurface rendering with intersection refinement is a real-time technique that extracts an isosurface directly from a 3D volumetric scalar field during ray traversal, avoiding explicit polygon mesh extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes). It detects the surface by checking if the sampled scalar value equals or crosses the target isovalue, stops traversal at the first hit, and refines the intersection position to reduce discretization artifacts. Unlike Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR), which composites the entire volume, this method stops at the first hit, offering higher performance for opaque surfaces. It differs from Real-Time Ray-Casting and Advanced Shading of Discrete Isosurfaces by operating on implicit continuous data rather than discrete extracted meshes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric scalar field texture (f), camera parameters (view/projection matrices, position), an isovalue (uIsovalue), a ray marching step size (uStepSize), and rendering parameters (refinement iterations, shadow enablement). Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the color of the first isosurface intersection, shaded with lighting and shadows. Data Structures: The method relies on Uniform Buffer Objects (UBOs) and a 3D texture sampler. 1. CameraUBO (std140, binding=0): mat4 uView: View matrix. mat4 uProj: Projection matrix. vec3 uCameraPos: Camera position in world space. float pad0: Padding to align to 16 bytes. 2. VolumeUBO (std140, binding=1): vec3 uDomainMin: Minimum bounds of the volume domain. float uStepSize: Step size for ray marching and normal computation. vec3 uDomainMax: Maximum bounds of the volume domain. float uIsovalue: The scalar threshold defining the isosurface. float uLightAngle: Angle for light direction calculation (mapped to 2\pi). int uEnableShadows: Boolean flag (0 or 1) to enable/disable shadow rays. int uRefinementIterations: Number of bisection/refinement iterations. float pad1: Padding. 3. Volume Texture: sampler3D volumeTex at binding=0. Sampled using standard trilinear interpolation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Construction and Box Intersection: For each fragment covered by the volume, construct a ray origin O and direction D from the camera. Compute the intersection parameters t{min} and t{max} for the ray with the volume domain [uDomainMin, uDomainMax]. If t{max} \le t{min}, the ray misses the volume; return empty/no hit. Set t{start} = \max(t{min}, 0.0) and t{end} = t{max}. 2. Ray Marching and Surface Detection: Initialize t{prev} = t{start}. Sample the scalar field at the start position: d{prev} = f(O + t{prev} D) - uIsovalue. Iterate t{curr} from t{start} + uStepSize to t{end} with step uStepSize. At each step, sample the field: d{curr} = f(O + t{curr} D) - uIsovalue. Check for a sign change between d{prev} and d{curr}. A sign change indicates the isosurface lies within the interval [t{prev}, t{curr}]. (Note: Some implementations simply stop when the sampled value exceeds the isovalue). 3. Intersection Refinement: If a sign change is detected, refine the hit position t{hit} using one of two methods described in the sources: Method A: Bisection Refinement Given interval [ta, tb] (initially t{prev}, t{curr}) with signs da, db: 1. Compute midpoint tm = (ta + tb) / 2. 2. Evaluate dm = f(O + tm D) - uIsovalue. 3. If da \cdot dm \le 0, set tb = tm, db = dm; else set ta = tm, da = dm. 4. Repeat for uRefinementIterations (typical range 0–10). 5. Final hit: t{hit} = (ta + tb) / 2. Method B: Linear Interpolation Refinement Let X{prev} = O + t{prev} D and X{next} = O + t{curr} D. Let f{prev} and f{next} be the raw scalar values at these points. 1. Calculate new point: X{new} = (X{next} - X{prev})  rac{uIsovalue - f{prev}}{f{next} - f{prev}} + X{prev} 2. Read volume value f{new} at X{new}. 3. If f{new} > uIsovalue, assign X{new} to X{prev} and f{new} to f{prev}. Otherwise, assign to X{next} and f{next}. 4. Iterate until convergence or a fixed iteration count (typically ~10). 4. Hit Position and Normal Computation: Compute the hit position: P{hit} = O + t{hit} D. Estimate the surface normal using central differences with step size h = uStepSize: gx = f(P{hit} + (h,0,0)) - f(P{hit} - (h,0,0)) gy = f(P{hit} + (0,h,0)) - f(P{hit} - (0,h,0)) gz = f(P{hit} + (0,0,h)) - f(P{hit} - (0,0,h)) The gradient is 
abla f = (gx, gy, gz). The normal is the normalized negative gradient: n = - rac{
abla f}{|
abla f|} The negative gradient ensures the normal points outward toward the lighter medium. Note: In some implementations (e.g., Met.3D), the gradient computation may vary based on grid type (pressure, hybrid, auxiliary). 5. Shading and Shadows: Calculate the light direction vector \ell from uLightAngle (mapped to 2\pi). Compute Lambertian diffuse term: L = \max(0, n \cdot \ell). Shadow Ray Traversal: If uEnableShadows is true, cast a shadow ray from P{hit} in direction \ell. 1. Start at t = 2 \cdot uStepSize to avoid self-intersection due to precision errors. 2. March with step uStepSize. 3. If f(O{shadow} + t \ell) \ge uIsovalue before leaving the volume, return shadow factor S = 0. 4. If the ray exits the volume without hitting, return S = 1. Color Assignment: The final color is computed as: Color = BaseColor \cdot L \cdot S BaseColor can be a fixed color, a color mapped from the isovalue via a transfer function, or a color derived from a secondary scalar field (e.g., coloring wind speed by temperature). Using the isovalue to fetch color avoids artifacts caused by transfer function interpolation at the surface. 6. Multiple Isosurfaces (Optional): If the surface is transparent or multiple isosurfaces are supported, the ray traversal continues after the first hit to composite nested surfaces. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderfragment(origin, direction, domainmin, domainmax, stepsize, isovalue, refinementiterations, enableshadows, lightangle, volumedata): # 1. Ray-box intersection tmin = float('inf') tmax = float('-inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0.0: if origin[i] < domainmin[i] or origin[i] > domainmax[i]: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) else: t1 = (domainmin[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (domainmax[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tenter = min(t1, t2) texit = max(t1, t2) tmin = max(tmin, tenter) tmax = min(tmax, texit) if tmax <= tmin: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) tstart = max(tmin, 0.0) tend = tmax # 2. Ray marching and sign change detection tprev = tstart posprev = origin + tprev direction dprev = samplevolume(posprev, volumedata) - isovalue hit = False finalcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) tcurr = tstart + stepsize while tcurr <= tend: poscurr = origin + tcurr direction dcurr = samplevolume(poscurr, volumedata) - isovalue if dprev dcurr <= 0.0: # Sign change detected, refine intersection ta, tb = tprev, tcurr da, db = dprev, dcurr for in range(refinementiterations): tm = (ta + tb) / 2.0 posm = origin + tm direction dm = samplevolume(posm, volumedata) - isovalue if da dm <= 0.0: tb, db = tm, dm else: ta, da = tm, dm thit = (ta + tb) / 2.0 phit = origin + thit direction # 3. Normal computation h = stepsize gx = samplevolume(phit + (h, 0.0, 0.0), volumedata) - samplevolume(phit - (h, 0.0, 0.0), volumedata) gy = samplevolume(phit + (0.0, h, 0.0), volumedata) - samplevolume(phit - (0.0, h, 0.0), volumedata) gz = samplevolume(phit + (0.0, 0.0, h), volumedata) - samplevolume(phit - (0.0, 0.0, h), volumedata) grad = (gx, gy, gz) normlen = sqrt(gxgx + gygy + gzgz) normal = (-gx/normlen, -gy/normlen, -gz/normlen) # 4. Lighting and shadows angle = lightangle 6.28318530718 lightdir = normalize((cos(angle), sin(angle), -1.0)) diffuse = max(0.0, dot(normal, lightdir)) shadow = 1.0 if enableshadows == 1: tshadow = 2.0 stepsize while True: pshadow = phit + tshadow lightdir if pshadow.x < domainmin.x or pshadow.y < domainmin.y or pshadow.z < domainmin.z or \ pshadow.x > domainmax.x or pshadow.y > domainmax.y or pshadow.z > domainmax.z: break if samplevolume(pshadow, volumedata) >= isovalue: shadow = 0.0 break tshadow += stepsize basecolor = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Fixed color; can be mapped from isovalue or secondary field finalcolor = (basecolor[0]diffuseshadow, basecolor[1]diffuseshadow, basecolor[2]diffuseshadow) hit = True break tprev, dprev = tcurr, dcurr tcurr += stepsize return (finalcolor[0], finalcolor[1], finalcolor[2], 1.0) def samplevolume(pos, volumedata): # Performs trilinear interpolation of the 3D volume texture at pos # Implementation depends on hardware/software backend pass Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray. Refinement adds a constant factor (k iterations) only when a hit is found. Shadow rays add another traversal pass. Memory Complexity: Low. Requires storage for the 3D volume texture and small UBOs. No explicit mesh geometry is stored. Performance: Real-time on modern GPUs. Performance scales with step size and number of samples. Smaller step sizes increase accuracy but reduce frame rate. Optimizations: Empty-space skipping: Using a 32x32x32 brick min/max acceleration structure allows rays to jump over regions that cannot contain the isovalue. Interaction Step Size: A coarser step size can be used during camera interaction to maintain frame rate, with refinement restoring quality. Grid Type: Performance varies by grid type; hybrid or auxiliary pressure grids are significantly more expensive than simple pressure level grids due to complex sampling requirements. Strengths: No preprocessing/mesh extraction required. Dynamic isovalue changes are instantaneous without CPU geometry rebuilds. Avoids the high computational cost of full volume rendering (DVR) for opaque surfaces. High-quality intersection refinement reduces stair-stepping artifacts. Limitations: Discretization artifacts if refinement is insufficient or step size is too large. Self-intersection in shadow rays if not handled (requires offset start). This method was developed as a real-time GPU-based implementation for scientific visualization, notably in the SciVisLab framework. It is also implemented in Met.3D for meteorological data visualization and has been integrated into the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) as vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper2 with features like refined isosurface rendering and shadow mapping. The technique addresses the limitations of traditional isosurface extraction (marching cubes) by providing a direct, flexible, and performant way to visualize scalar fields in real-time. name: Distance-field ray marching
head: Sphere tracing
body: Distance-field ray marching (commonly known as sphere tracing) is a rendering method that finds surfaces by moving along a ray in repeated steps, using a signed distance field (SDF) to choose each step size adaptively, avoiding the tradeoff of fixed-step marching. Unlike naive fixed-step marching which uses a constant increment, sphere tracing uses the SDF value as the step size, ensuring the step is as large as possible without risk of overshooting. Unlike traditional rasterization, the visible shape is defined mathematically by a scene function, not by a triangle mesh. The method renders geometry by shooting a ray through each pixel and repeatedly querying a Signed Distance Function (SDF). An SDF is a formula that, given any point p in space, returns the distance from p to the nearest surface. The sign indicates position: negative inside, positive outside, zero exactly on the surface. The core loop initializes a ray with an origin point ro and a normalized direction vector v. It maintains a current position p (initially ro). In each iteration: 1. The SDF is evaluated at p to get the distance d to the nearest surface. 2. If d < 0, the ray has penetrated the surface; the algorithm returns a hit. 3. If d \le \text{HIT\THRESHOLD} (a small value such as 0.001), the ray has hit the surface. The loop terminates. 4. Otherwise, the position is advanced: p \leftarrow p + d \cdot v. This step size is guaranteed not to overshoot the surface because d is the distance to the nearest surface. 5. The loop continues while the step count is less than \text{MAX\STEPS}. If the loop terminates without a hit (e.g., t exceeds a maximum range or \text{MAX\STEPS} is reached), the ray misses. The scene is defined by combining primitive SDFs. For a sphere of radius r centered at c, the distance function is d(p) = \|p - c\| - r. Union of two objects with distance fields d1 and d2 is iso(p) = \min(d1(p), d2(p)). Intersection is iso(p) = \max(d1(p), d2(p)). Subtraction of object d2 from d1 is iso(p) = \max(d1(p), -d2(p)). Parameters include \text{MAX\STEPS} (a safety cap, typically 32 to 128 depending on implementation) and \text{HIT\THRESHOLD} (epsilon). A maximum range or accumulated travel distance limit can also bound rays that miss. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarch(ro, v, scene, maxsteps=40, hitthreshold=0.001, maxrange=100.0): p = ro for i in range(maxsteps): d = scene(p) if d < 0: return p, True, dot(p - ro, v) if d <= hitthreshold: return p, True, dot(p - ro, v) p += v d if dot(p - ro, v) > maxrange: break return p, False, dot(p - ro, v) Estimates surface normals at an SDF isosurface by numerically computing the gradient using central finite differences along the coordinate axes. Chosen when shading requires accurate normals without explicit mesh data. Uses precomputed gradient, occupancy, and distance maps for efficient empty space skipping. Chosen when rendering large voxel-based volumes where traversal overhead dominates. Applies stochastic Woodcock tracking using macrocell majorants to handle density variations. Chosen for volumetric rendering with highly heterogeneous media. Determines occlusion by sphere tracing a ray towards a light source. Chosen when accurate hard shadows are needed for implicit surfaces. Uses a 3D distance texture with dual bounding boxes to handle boundary conditions and invalid values at texture edges. Chosen when rendering implicit surfaces stored in GPU textures. Refines coarse ray-marched hits using bisection and Newton's method for precise surface intersection. Chosen when high-precision hit locations are required. Adapts step sizes to guarantee safety against overshooting, often using Lipschitz bounds or conservative scaling. Chosen when rendering non-Lipschitz or noisy distance fields. Approximates the intersection of a viewing cone with an implicit surface for antialiasing at grazing angles. Chosen when rendering smooth, alias-free edges without supersampling. Provides mathematical formulas for basic shapes (spheres, boxes, tori) and CSG operations. Chosen as the foundational building blocks for scene construction. The core technique that varies step sizes along a ray using SDF values to guarantee safe progression without penetration. Chosen as the standard baseline for implicit surface rendering. Extends sphere tracing for Fractal Brownian Motion noise using a BVH to compute valid distance bounds and adaptive steps. Chosen for rendering complex procedural fractals efficiently. Performs real-time GPU volume rendering by marching through a 3D scalar field (e.g., smoke density) to compute color and transparency. Chosen for volumetric effects like fog, clouds, or medical data. The technique was introduced as 'Sphere Tracing' by John C. Hart in 1994 in 'Sphere tracing: a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces'. It became widely used in 4k intros released in 2009, specifically in productions like 'Frequency' by xt95 and 'Potatro'. name: SDF Normal Estimation via Finite Differences
head: SDF Normal Estimation, SDF Normal Calculation, Surface Normals from SDF, Central Difference Normal, Finite Difference Normals, Gradient Normal Estimation, Numerical Normal Computation, Gradient-Based Normal Estimation, Finite Difference Normal Estimation, Central Difference Normal Estimation, Finite Difference Normal Computation, Normal Approximation from Scalar Field, Central Differencing for Normal Estimation, Gradient Estimation via Finite Differences, Central finite difference normal estimation
body:
This method estimates the surface normal at a point on a Signed Distance Field (SDF) isosurface by numerically computing the gradient of the distance function using central finite differences along the three coordinate axes. Unlike mesh-based rendering which stores explicit vertex normals, SDF ray marching Distance-field ray marching relies on the field itself to provide shading information. The gradient vector 
abla f is perpendicular to the isosurface; normalizing this vector yields the surface normal \mathbf{n}. Inputs: Query point p = (px, py, pz) on or near the isosurface, typically the hit point from ray marching. SDF evaluation function f(p) returning the signed distance. Outputs: Surface normal vector \mathbf{n}. Data Structures: No complex data structures required; the method requires access to the SDF function f and a scalar \epsilon. Parameters: \epsilon: The perturbation step size. Sources cite specific values: 0.0005 and 0.0007, 0.01, 0.05, 0.05	ext{f} and 0.000001, and 0.0015. The magnitude of \epsilon directly affects the correctness of the normal calculation. Smaller spacing causes noisy gradients, while larger spacing causes over-smoothed directions, requiring a trade-off. Algorithm Steps: 1. Define the perturbation step size \epsilon. 2. Evaluate the SDF at the six neighbors of p along the coordinate axes: fx^+ = f(px + \epsilon, py, pz) fx^- = f(px - \epsilon, py, pz) fy^+ = f(px, py + \epsilon, pz) fy^- = f(px, py - \epsilon, pz) fz^+ = f(px, py, pz + \epsilon) fz^- = f(px, py, pz - \epsilon). 3. Compute the gradient components using central differences: 
abla fx =  rac{fx^+ - fx^-}{2\epsilon} 
abla fy =  rac{fy^+ - fy^-}{2\epsilon} 
abla fz =  rac{fz^+ - fz^-}{2\epsilon} The gradient vector is \mathbf{g} = (
abla fx, 
abla fy, 
abla fz). 4. Normalize the gradient vector to obtain the surface normal: \mathbf{n} =  rac{\mathbf{g}}{\|\mathbf{g}\|}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def estimatesdfnormal(p, scenesdf, epsilon=0.001): """ Estimate the surface normal at point p using central finite differences. Args: p: tuple or list of 3 floats (x, y, z) scenesdf: callable function f(p) -> float epsilon: step size for finite differences Returns: tuple: normalized normal vector (nx, ny, nz) """ x, y, z = p # Evaluate SDF at neighbors along X axis fxplus = scenesdf((x + epsilon, y, z)) fxminus = scenesdf((x - epsilon, y, z)) # Evaluate SDF at neighbors along Y axis fyplus = scenesdf((x, y + epsilon, z)) fyminus = scenesdf((x, y - epsilon, z)) # Evaluate SDF at neighbors along Z axis fzplus = scenesdf((x, y, z + epsilon)) fzminus = scenesdf((x, y, z - epsilon)) # Compute gradient components gradx = (fxplus - fxminus) / (2.0 epsilon) grady = (fyplus - fyminus) / (2.0 epsilon) gradz = (fzplus - fzminus) / (2.0 epsilon) # Normalize the gradient vector magnitude = math.sqrt(gradx2 + grady2 + gradz2) # Guard against zero magnitude (degenerate case) if magnitude < 1e-10: return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) return (gradx / magnitude, grady / magnitude, gradz / magnitude) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Smaller spacing causes noisy gradients, while larger spacing causes over-smoothed directions, requiring a trade-off. Loosely Spaced Voxel Grids: In voxel-based SDF representations with large voxel sizes, the 6-sample central difference method may produce inaccurate normals. In such cases, using 18 or 26 samples provides a better estimate. Estimates mesh vertex normals by computing the negative gradient of the occupancy output with respect to the vertex positions using automatic differentiation. This method requires a differentiable model. It involves converting vertices to tensors, passing them through the model to get occupancy logits, summing the output, and calling backward to extract the gradient. The normal is the negative gradient, normalized. Time Complexity: Requires 6 additional SDF evaluations per normal estimation. For N points, this is 6N function evaluations. Accuracy: Central differences provide a more accurate gradient estimate than forward or backward differences. Strengths: Simple to implement, works with any SDF. Limitations: Requires 6 extra samples, which can be costly in high-performance rendering if SDF evaluation is expensive. Accuracy degrades with poor choice of \epsilon or in loosely spaced voxel grids. When to Use: Standard SDF ray marching where analytical normals are unavailable and performance allows for 6 extra SDF queries. When Not to Use: When performance is critical and SDF evaluation is expensive, or when using voxel-based SDFs with large voxels where 18/26-sample methods are needed. The technique of estimating surface normals via the gradient of a distance field is a fundamental concept in ray marching and implicit surface rendering. It leverages the mathematical property that the gradient of a scalar field is perpendicular to its level sets (isosurfaces). The use of central finite differences for this purpose is a standard numerical analysis technique applied to SDFs. Variants using more samples (18 or 26) are discussed in the context of voxel-based SDFs. name: Spin Shader
head: Spin Shading
body: The Spin Shader visualizes surface geometry by mapping surface normals and camera orientation to a cyclic color field, mimicking spin-1/2 behavior where a 360-degree rotation reverses the texture orientation. Inputs and Outputs: surfacenormals: A tensor of shape (N, 3) containing unit surface normal vectors \mathbf{n} = (x, y, z). cameraorientationconj: A tensor of shape (N, 4) containing the conjugate of the camera orientation quaternion \overline{q}. cycliccolourmap: A lookup table or function mapping points on the unit circle \mathbb{S}^1 to RGB values. degree: An integer parameter (typically 1) passed to the domain colouring function. Output: color: A tensor of shape (N, 3) containing RGB pixel values. Data Structures: Quaternions are represented as 4-element vectors (w, x, y, z). Surface normals are treated as pure-imaginary quaternions 0 + xi + yj + zk. Steps: 1. Embed Normal as Pure Quaternion: Convert the surface normal \mathbf{n} = (x, y, z) into a pure-imaginary quaternion Np by setting the real part to zero: Np = 0 + xi + yj + zk 2. Rotate by Camera Conjugate: Compute the product of the conjugate camera orientation quaternion \overline{q} and the normal quaternion Np to rotate the normal into the camera's local coordinate frame: q' = \overline{q} Np = a + bi + cj + dk \in \mathbb{S}^3 3. Map to \mathbb{S}^1: Transform the resulting quaternion q' into a point on the unit circle \mathbb{S}^1 by computing the real and imaginary parts of the squared quaternion mapping: \text{real} = a^2 - |\mathbf{v}|^2 \text{imag} = 2a|\mathbf{v}| where \mathbf{v} = (b, c, d) and |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{b^2 + c^2 + d^2}. The sequence of mappings is \mathbb{S}^3 \times \mathbb{S}^2 \to \mathbb{S}^3 \to \mathbb{S}^1 \to \mathbb{R}^3{\geq 0}. 4. Domain Colouring: Map the point (\text{imag}, \text{real}) from \mathbb{S}^1 to an RGB color using a cyclic colormap. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def spinshader(surfacenormals: torch.Tensor, cameraorientationconj: torch.Tensor, cycliccolourmap: torch.Tensor, degree: int = 1) -> torch.Tensor: # Step 1: Embed normal as pure-imaginary quaternion (0, x, y, z) npure = F.pad(surfacenormals, [1, 0], value=0.0) # Step 2: Multiply conjugate camera quaternion with pure normal quaternion value = quaternionmultiply(npure, cameraorientationconj) # Unpack result q' = a + bi + cj + dk a = value[..., 0] bcd = value[..., 1:] # Step 3: Map to S^1 normbcd = torch.norm(bcd, dim=-1, p=2) realpart = a.pow(2) - normbcd.pow(2) imagpart = normbcd.mul(a).mul(2) # Step 4: Domain colouring return domaincolouring(imagpart, realpart, cycliccolourmap, degree) def quaternionmultiply(q1: torch.Tensor, q2: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: w1, x1, y1, z1 = q1[..., 0], q1[..., 1], q1[..., 2], q1[..., 3] w2, x2, y2, z2 = q2[..., 0], q2[..., 1], q2[..., 2], q2[..., 3] w = w1w2 - x1x2 - y1y2 - z1z2 x = w1x2 + x1w2 + y1z2 - z1y2 y = w1y2 - x1z2 + y1w2 + z1x2 z = w1z2 + x1y2 - y1x2 + z1w2 return torch.stack([w, x, y, z], dim=-1) def domaincolouring(imag: torch.Tensor, real: torch.Tensor, cmap: torch.Tensor, degree: int) -> torch.Tensor: # Standard cyclic colormap lookup angle = torch.atan2(imag, real) t = (angle / (2 torch.pi) + 1) % 1 idx = (t (cmap.shape[0] - 1)).long() return cmap[idx] Parameters: degree: Typically 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. The Spin Shader originates from ray marching and signed distance function (SDF) rendering, specifically within the context of visualizing quaternion-based transformations. The method draws inspiration from the mathematical concept of spinors in physics, where a 360-degree rotation results in a sign change, effectively reversing the "texture" or phase of the object. kyle-rosa/raymarching, https://github.com/kyle-rosa/raymarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians
body: Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians is a volumetric rendering method that evaluates the full Gaussian mixture along camera rays to accurately handle primitive overlap and compute the volumetric integral, contrasting with the rasterization-based splatting approach of Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of approximations in standard 3DGS, such as ignoring spatial overlap and incorrect self-attenuation, by performing adaptive sampling and integration. Unlike splatting, which projects Gaussians to screen space and blends them, this method traverses the 3D scene directly, ensuring that overlapping primitives are resolved with precision governed by the sample count rather than relying on rasterization approximations. Inputs: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Scene representation: A set of M 3D Gaussians, each defined by mean position \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i (or scale \mathbf{s}i and rotation \mathbf{q}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color coefficients (e.g., spherical harmonics) \mathbf{c}i. Ray marching parameters: Maximum depth, minimum step size, and convergence threshold. Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{C} and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}. Data Structures: Gaussian Tensor: A tensor of shape (M, D) where D includes fields for position (3), scale (3 or 1), rotation (4 for quaternion), opacity (1), and color coefficients (variable, e.g., 4 \times 3 for SH order 1). Ray Buffer: Stores current ray position, accumulated transmittance T, and accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc}. Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Initialize ray position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o}, accumulated transmittance T = 1.0, and accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc} = \mathbf{0}. 2. Adaptive Sampling Loop: While T > \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small threshold, e.g., 10^{-5}) and step count < N{max}: a. Step Selection: Determine the next step size \Delta t using adaptive sampling along the ray. b. Ray Advance: Update ray position: \mathbf{p}{new} = \mathbf{p} + \Delta t \cdot \mathbf{d}. c. Gaussian Evaluation: For each Gaussian i in the scene (or within a spatially accelerated bounding volume): i. Distance Calculation: Compute the squared Mahalanobis distance from the ray point \mathbf{p}{new} to the Gaussian center \boldsymbol{\mu}i: di^2 = (\mathbf{p}{new} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)^T \mathbf{\Sigma}i^{-1} (\mathbf{p}{new} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i) \mathbf{\Sigma}i is the 3D covariance matrix derived from scale and rotation. ii. Density/Opacity Contribution: Compute the Gaussian value at the sample point: gi = \alphai \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} di^2\right) Note that 3DGS typically uses an opacity model, while OTS uses an extinction-based model. The difference lies in how gi is integrated into the transmittance equation. iii. Color Contribution: Compute the view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\mathbf{v}) for the viewing direction \mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{d} using spherical harmonics if applicable. d. Integration: Update accumulated transmittance and color. For 3DGS Marcher (Opacity Model): The contribution is blended based on the Gaussian's opacity relative to the accumulated transmittance. \alpha{contrib} = gi \mathbf{C}{acc} = \mathbf{C}{acc} + T \cdot \alpha{contrib} \cdot \mathbf{c}i T = T \cdot (1 - \alpha{contrib}) This approximates the volumetric integral using the 3DGS opacity formulation. For OTS Marcher (Extinction Model): The contribution is integrated using an extinction-based model, which more accurately handles overlap. \Delta Ti = \exp\left(-\int{t}^{t+\Delta t} \sigmai(\tau) d\tau\right) The integration is performed via adaptive sampling along each ray to compute the transmittance drop. e. Update: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}{new}. 3. Final Color: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{C}{acc} + T \cdot \mathbf{C}{background} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchgaussians(rayo, rayd, gaussians, maxsteps=1000, epsilon=1e-5): # Initialize ray buffer p = rayo.clone() T = torch.tensor(1.0) Cacc = torch.zeros(3) backgroundcolor = torch.zeros(3) # for step in range(maxsteps): if T < epsilon: break # Adaptive step selection along the ray deltat = 0.1 # Sources specify adaptive sampling; exact step logic is implementation-dependent # Advance ray pnew = p + deltat rayd # Evaluate Gaussian mixture for i in range(len(gaussians)): mu, sigmainv, alpha, shcoeffs = gaussians[i] v = -rayd # Viewing direction # Mahalanobis distance diff = pnew - mu dsq = diff @ sigmainv @ diff # Gaussian value gi = alpha torch.exp(-0.5 dsq) # View-dependent color ci = evaluatesphericalharmonics(shcoeffs, v) # Integration model if useextinctionmodel: # OTS Marcher # Extinction-based integration via adaptive sampling transmittancedrop = torch.exp(-gi deltat) # Approximation Cacc += T (1 - transmittancedrop) ci T = transmittancedrop else: # 3DGS Marcher # Opacity-based blending alphacontrib = gi Cacc += T alphacontrib ci T = (1 - alphacontrib) p = pnew # Final color composition C = Cacc + T backgroundcolor return C Parameters: Sample Count: Governs precision. The ray marcher performs adaptive sampling along each ray to accurately resolve Gaussian overlap to compute the volumetric integral with a precision governed by the sample count. Threshold \epsilon: Controls when to stop marching. Typical value: 10^{-5}. Max Steps: Prevents infinite loops. Typical value: 100-1000 depending on scene depth. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Popping artifacts result from approximations made based only on Gaussian centers and ignoring spatial overlap, not floating-point errors. Boundaries: Ray clipping against scene bounds is required. Degenerate Input: Gaussians with zero scale or invalid rotations must be filtered out. Overlap: Standard 3DGS splatting ignores overlap; ray marching resolves it, but at higher computational cost. The OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm is a volumetric rendering method for 3D Gaussians that evaluates the full Gaussian mixture to accurately handle primitive overlap and compute the volumetric integral using an extinction-based model. It distinguishes itself from splatting-based approaches by performing adaptive binning and analytical integration along rays, ensuring that overlapping Gaussians are resolved with precision governed by sample count rather than relying on rasterization approximations. Unlike raytracing solutions for Gaussians, this method explicitly accounts for primitive overlap in the integration process. A ray marching-based renderer that follows the 3DGS model of opacity, reusing the data structures (tensors with weights, positions, scales, and rotations), activation functions, and learning rates of 3DGS. It differs from OTS Marcher in the model of opacity/extinction used, but shares the same ray marching pipeline structure (per-primitive pass, tiling, sorting, per-pixel kernel). A technique to model view-dependent appearance (e.g., reflections) in 3D Gaussian Splatting by representing the color of each Gaussian as a function of the viewing direction using spherical harmonics coefficients, rather than a single static color value. The color is computed by evaluating the spherical harmonics basis functions at the viewing direction vector associated with that Gaussian, using the pre-trained spherical harmonic coefficients stored for that Gaussian. The implementation uses all available spherical harmonic components from pre-trained models, with the baseline comparison using only the 0th order (DC) coefficient, which represents view-independent color. Using all spherical harmonic components produces renderings with view-dependent effects (shiny surfaces, reflections), whereas using only the DC (0th order) component results in view-independent, lower-quality renderings that lack these specular details. The core logic is implemented in the function coloursfromsphericalharmonics in model.py, which must be vectorized. A method that integrates physics-based continuum mechanics directly within 3DGS, treating each Gaussian as a discrete physical particle with volume. It allows direct simulation of the Gaussians, enabling physically accurate dynamics. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(M) to store Gaussian parameters. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance degrades with the number of Gaussians and sample count. Strengths: Accurate handling of overlap and self-attenuation; no rasterization artifacts; consistent with volumetric rendering theory. Limitations: High computational cost due to per-ray evaluation and adaptive sampling. When to use: When accuracy is critical, such as in scientific visualization or offline rendering; when studying the impact of approximations in 3DGS. When not to use: For real-time applications where speed is paramount; standard splatting is preferred for interactive applications. Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians was introduced to systematically analyze and assess the approximations made in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), such as spatial overlap and sorting. The method was developed to clarify the differences between 3DGS and accurate volumetric rendering, specifically regarding opacity vs. extinction-based rendering. It builds on the 3DGS model but replaces the rasterization pipeline with a ray-marching one, allowing for the reuse of learned Gaussian parameters. The approach has been used to demonstrate that approximations like overlap and sorting have negligible impact on still images, especially with a large number of Gaussians.
