name: OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm
head: Adaptive Binning Ray Marching, OTS Marcher, OTS Marching, Ray Marching (OTS scheme)
body: The OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm is a volumetric rendering method for 3D Gaussians that evaluates the full Gaussian mixture to accurately handle primitive overlap and compute the volumetric integral using an extinction-based model. It distinguishes itself from splatting-based approaches by performing adaptive binning and analytical integration along rays, ensuring that overlapping Gaussians are resolved with precision governed by sample count rather than relying on rasterization approximations. Unlike raytracing solutions for Gaussians, this method explicitly accounts for primitive overlap in the integration process. The algorithm performs adaptive sampling along each viewing ray to resolve Gaussian overlap. It iterates over the Gaussian mixture twice: first to establish bin borders adapted to the Gaussian data, and second to perform analytical integration into bins of variable extent. The bins are then blended together following the volume integral equation. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position, scale, rotation, and color; a viewing ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a maximum ray depth or opacity threshold. Outputs: The final pixel color I(\mathbf{x}) and accumulated transmittance. Density Section Buffer: A fixed-size buffer storing sections. Each section is defined by: start: The start parameter t along the ray. end: The end parameter t along the ray. density: The sampling density for this section. Bin: A segment of the ray defined by start and end t values, storing integrated color and extinction. 1. Adaptive Binning Initialization: Create a fixed-size density section buffer. Iterate over all Gaussians to fill the buffer. For each Gaussian, compute its intersection interval with the ray. Define the start and end of the sampling section using the Gaussian's position \pm 3 standard deviations along the ray direction. Compute the density such that a pre-defined number of bins fit within the space defined by start and end. 2. Section Merging: Add the new section to the density section buffer. Combine existing and new sections to ensure they are ordered and non-overlapping. If sections overlap, the section with the higher sampling density takes precedence in the overlap area. Combining two sections can result in up to three new sections. Sections that fall outside the buffer capacity are deferred to the next batch. 3. Bin Creation: Traverse the merged sections to create bins. The size of each bin is inversely proportional to the density of the section it belongs to. 4. Blending Integral Computation (Batching): Divide the work into batches of bins (e.g., 128 bins per batch). Initialize the first batch at t=0. Subsequent batches start at the end-border of the last bin of the previous batch. Iterate over the Gaussian mixture again to compute integrals for each bin in the current batch. For each bin, compute 4 values: Red, Green, Blue, and integrated extinction (opacity). Colors are multiplied by the per-Gaussian integrated extinction. Stop when all Gaussians are processed or accumulated opacity reaches a high threshold. 5. Blending: Blend the bin evaluations together using the following equation: I(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=0}^{\infty} \gammai \prod{j=0}^{i-1} e^{-\rhoj} + cb \prod{j=0}^{\infty} e^{-\rhoj} Where: \gammai is the color contribution of bin i. \rhoj is the integrated extinction (opacity) of bin j. The term \prod{j=0}^{i-1} e^{-\rhoj} is the transmittance factor, cached between iterations to avoid redundant computation. cb is the background color. 6. Gradient Computation: Compute gradients manually using a front-to-back strategy. Two variants exist: Attached: Considers the numerical integration procedure and border positions in the gradient calculation. Detached: Assumes the numerical method can be ignored, keeping sampling and border positions constant with respect to differentiation. The detached variant performs significantly better. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def otsmarchingraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, gaussians, backgroundcolor, maxsectionsbuffer, binsperbatch=128, opacitythreshold=0.99, binspergaussian=10): """ Renders a single ray using the OTS Marching Algorithm. """ # 1. Adaptive Binning Initialization sections = [] for g in gaussians: # Compute intersection interval along ray using position +/- 3 standard deviations tstart = g.position - 3.0 g.scale tend = g.position + 3.0 g.scale if tstart > tend: tstart, tend = tend, tstart # Compute density such that a pre-defined number of bins fit in the space length = tend - tstart density = binspergaussian / length if length > 0 else 0.0 newsection = Section(start=tstart, end=tend, density=density) sections = mergesections(sections, newsection, maxsectionsbuffer) # 2. Bin Creation bins = createbins(sections) # 3. Blending Integral Computation (Batching) totalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 for batchstart in range(0, len(bins), binsperbatch): batchend = min(batchstart + binsperbatch, len(bins)) currentbatchbins = bins[batchstart:batchend] for bin in currentbatchbins: bincolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] binextinction = 0.0 # Iterate over Gaussians again to compute integrals for each bin for g in gaussians: # Check overlap and compute analytical integral if g.overlapssegment(bin.start, bin.end): c, e = g.integrateoversegment(bin.start, bin.end) bincolor[0] += c[0] bincolor[1] += c[1] bincolor[2] += c[2] binextinction += e # Front-to-back blending matching Eq. 3 transmittancefactor = exp(-binextinction) totalcolor[0] += bincolor[0] transmittance totalcolor[1] += bincolor[1] transmittance totalcolor[2] += bincolor[2] transmittance transmittance = transmittancefactor # Check accumulated opacity threshold if 1.0 - transmittance >= opacitythreshold: break if 1.0 - transmittance >= opacitythreshold: break # Add background totalcolor[0] += backgroundcolor[0] transmittance totalcolor[1] += backgroundcolor[1] transmittance totalcolor[2] += backgroundcolor[2] transmittance return totalcolor, transmittance def mergesections(existing, newsec, maxsize): """ Combines newsec with existing sections ensuring order and no overlap. Higher density wins in overlap. Combining 2 sections creates up to 3 new sections. """ merged = existing + [newsec] merged.sort(key=lambda s: s.start) result = [] for sec in merged: if not result: result.append(sec) continue last = result[-1] if sec.start < last.end: # Overlap exists if sec.density >= last.density: # Higher density wins: extend last section, discard lower density part last.end = max(last.end, sec.end) else: # Lower density wins in overlap: split last section last.end = sec.start result.append(sec) else: result.append(sec) # Defer excess sections to next batch if buffer full if len(result) > maxsize: result = result[:maxsize] return result def createbins(sections): """ Traverse sections to create bins. Bin size is inversely proportional to density. """ bins = [] for sec in sections: if sec.density <= 0: continue binwidth = 1.0 / sec.density t = sec.start while t < sec.end: binend = min(t + binwidth, sec.end) bins.append(Bin(start=t, end=binend)) t = binend return bins class Section: def init(self, start, end, density): self.start = start self.end = end self.density = density class Bin: def init(self, start, end): self.start = start self.end = end Batch Size: Typically 128 bins per batch. Activation Function: Softplus with \beta = 2 is used instead of sigmoid to allow Gaussians to become fully opaque. Standard Deviation Factor: 3 standard deviations are used to define the start and end of sampling sections. Buffer Overflow: Sections that fall out of the fixed-size density section buffer are deferred to the next batch. Opacity Convergence: Using a constant opacity initialization can prevent convergence for large Gaussian counts. A power function fitting opacity to the number of Gaussians is recommended for initialization. Gradient Choice: The attached gradient variant is computationally more expensive and performs worse than the detached variant. Performance: The algorithm is considerably slower than splatting, typically between one and two orders of magnitude slower, depending on the scene. Accuracy: It provides accurate resolution of Gaussian overlap and precise perspective projection, serving as a testbed to examine the importance of these factors in 3DGS. Complexity: The algorithm requires iterating over the Gaussian mixture twice per batch (once for binning, once for integration), leading to higher computational cost compared to single-pass splatting. Strengths: Accurate volumetric rendering, handles overlap correctly, accounts for primitive overlap in integration unlike some raytracing solutions. Limitations: Low performance compared to splatting; implementation complexity is higher. The OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm was introduced in the paper "Does 3D Gaussian Splatting Need Accurate Volumetric Rendering?". It was developed as part of an implementation to study the impact of approximations like spatial overlap and sorting in 3D Gaussian Splatting. The implementation builds on the original 3DGS code base to enable meaningful comparisons. Does 3D Gaussian Splatting Need Accurate Volumetric Rendering?, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70032, fetched 2026-10-26

name: View-dependent color with Spherical Harmonics
head: Spherical Harmonics (SH) for View-Dependent Color, Spherical Harmonics Color Evaluation, Spherical Harmonics Rendering, SH Render, Rendering with Spherical Harmonics, Spherical Harmonic Colour Model
body: This method represents the view-dependent color of a 3D Gaussian primitive as a function of the viewing direction using spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. It solves the problem of storing directional color variation (such as specular highlights and reflections) compactly without requiring per-ray neural network queries. Unlike simple point colors or view-independent diffuse shading, this model captures glossy effects by evaluating a fixed set of orthogonal basis functions on the unit sphere, allowing each Gaussian to exhibit different colors from different angles. It builds on Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians by providing the color value Cc(\mathbf{d}) used during the compositing step. Inputs and Outputs Input: For each Gaussian i, the normalized viewing direction vector \mathbf{d}i from the camera center to the Gaussian's mean position, and the stored SH coefficients. Output: An RGB color vector \mathbf{C}i(\mathbf{d}i) = [Ri, Gi, Bi]^T evaluated at direction \mathbf{d}i. Data Structures Each Gaussian stores 48 SH coefficients: 16 per color channel (Red, Green, Blue). The coefficients are stored contiguously in memory. The layout is: indices 0–2 are the degree-0 (DC) coefficients for R, G, B respectively; indices 3–47 contain the remaining coefficients for degrees 1, 2, and 3. The coefficients are scalars k{\ell,c}^m corresponding to basis functions Y{\ell}^m. Spherical Harmonic Basis Constants The evaluation uses fixed normalization constants: SH\C0 = 0.28209479177387814 SH\C1 = 0.4886025119029199 Degree 2 and 3 constants are fixed polynomials but exact values are not given in the sources. Standard values are used. Numbered Steps 1. Compute Viewing Direction: For each Gaussian, compute the normalized direction vector \mathbf{d} = [x, y, z]^T from the camera center to the Gaussian's mean position. 2. Initialize Color: Initialize the output color vector \mathbf{C} with the DC component (degree 0) scaled by SH\C0. \mathbf{C} = SH\C0 \cdot [k{0,R}^0, k{0,G}^0, k{0,B}^0]^T 3. Evaluate Degree 1 (if active): If the SH degree is \ge 1, add contributions from the first-order coefficients using the direction components x, y, z scaled by SH\C1. The specific linear combination follows the convention in the reference implementation: color = color - SHC1 y c1 + SHC1 z c2 - SHC1 x c3. 4. Evaluate Degree 2 (if active): If the SH degree is \ge 2, add contributions from second-order coefficients using quadratic direction terms (xy, yz, 2z^2-x^2-y^2, xz, x^2-y^2) scaled by degree-2 normalization constants. 5. Evaluate Degree 3 (if active): If the SH degree is \ge 3, add contributions from third-order coefficients using cubic direction terms. 6. Apply Bias and Clamping: Apply a bias of +0.5 and a ReLU activation to the resulting RGB values to ensure non-negative color values. \mathbf{C}{final} = \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{C} + 0.5) Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math SHC0 = 0.28209479177387814 SHC1 = 0.4886025119029199 SHC20 = 1.0925484305920792 SHC21 = -0.3153915652525201 SHC22 = 0.5462742152960396 SHC23 = -0.3153915652525201 SHC24 = 0.10846220610920792 SHC30 = -0.5900435899266435 SHC31 = 2.890611442640554 SHC32 = -0.4570457994644658 SHC33 = 0.3731763325901154 SHC34 = -0.4570457994644658 SHC35 = 1.445305721320277 SHC36 = -0.5900435899266435 def evalsh(shcoeffs, x, y, z, maxdegree=3): """ Evaluates view-dependent color for a single Gaussian. shcoeffs: list of 48 floats [DC(3), D1(9), D2(15), D3(21)] x, y, z: components of the normalized viewing direction vector maxdegree: integer, maximum SH degree active (0-3) Returns: list of 3 floats [R, G, B] """ # Degree 0 (DC) r, g, b = shcoeffs[0], shcoeffs[1], shcoeffs[2] r = SHC0 g = SHC0 b = SHC0 if maxdegree >= 1: # Degree 1 coefficients for R, G, B r1, r2, r3 = shcoeffs[3], shcoeffs[4], shcoeffs[5] g1, g2, g3 = shcoeffs[6], shcoeffs[7], shcoeffs[8] b1, b2, b3 = shcoeffs[9], shcoeffs[10], shcoeffs[11] # Basis functions: -y, z, -x scaled by SHC1 r += SHC1 (-y r1 + z r2 - x r3) g += SHC1 (-y g1 + z g2 - x g3) b += SHC1 (-y b1 + z b2 - x b3) if maxdegree >= 2: # Degree 2 coefficients for R, G, B r1, r2, r3, r4, r5 = shcoeffs[12:17] g1, g2, g3, g4, g5 = shcoeffs[17:22] b1, b2, b3, b4, b5 = shcoeffs[22:27] # Standard SH2 basis functions xy, yz, z2 = x y, y z, z z x2, y2 = x x, y y r += SHC20 xy r1 + SHC21 yz r2 + SHC22 (2 z2 - x2 - y2) r3 + SHC23 xz r4 + SHC24 (x2 - y2) r5 g += SHC20 xy g1 + SHC21 yz g2 + SHC22 (2 z2 - x2 - y2) g3 + SHC23 xz g4 + SHC24 (x2 - y2) g5 b += SHC20 xy b1 + SHC21 yz b2 + SHC22 (2 z2 - x2 - y2) b3 + SHC23 xz b4 + SHC24 (x2 - y2) b5 if maxdegree >= 3: # Degree 3 coefficients for R, G, B r1, r2, r3, r4, r5, r6, r7 = shcoeffs[27:34] g1, g2, g3, g4, g5, g6, g7 = shcoeffs[34:41] b1, b2, b3, b4, b5, b6, b7 = shcoeffs[41:48] # Standard SH3 basis functions x2, y2, z2 = xx, yy, zz r += SHC30 y (3 x2 - y2) r1 + SHC31 x y z r2 + SHC32 y (4 z2 - x2 - y2) r3 + SHC33 x z (2 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) r4 + SHC34 y (4 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) r5 + SHC35 z (2 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) r6 + SHC36 x (x2 - 3 y2) r7 g += SHC30 y (3 x2 - y2) g1 + SHC31 x y z g2 + SHC32 y (4 z2 - x2 - y2) g3 + SHC33 x z (2 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) g4 + SHC34 y (4 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) g5 + SHC35 z (2 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) g6 + SHC36 x (x2 - 3 y2) g7 b += SHC30 y (3 x2 - y2) b1 + SHC31 x y z b2 + SHC32 y (4 z2 - x2 - y2) b3 + SHC33 x z (2 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) b4 + SHC34 y (4 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) b5 + SHC35 z (2 z2 - 3 x2 - 3 y2) b6 + SHC36 x (x2 - 3 y2) b7 # Apply bias and ReLU r = max(0.0, r + 0.5) g = max(0.0, g + 0.5) b = max(0.0, b + 0.5) return [r, g, b] Parameters Maximum SH Degree (L): Typically 3. This results in (L+1)^2 = 16 basis functions per color channel, totaling 48 coefficients per Gaussian. Training Schedule: Optimization begins with only the degree-0 band active. One further band is unlocked every 1,000 iterations until all four bands (degrees 0-3) are active. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Basis Functions are Fixed: The basis functions Y{\ell}^m(\mathbf{d}) are fixed polynomials of the direction components and are never updated during training. Only the coefficients k are learned via gradient descent. Direction Normalization: The direction vector \mathbf{d} must be normalized before evaluation. Precision: Standard single-precision arithmetic is used. An optimization that reduces memory bandwidth pressure by evaluating view-dependent colors over multiple frames rather than every frame, trading immediate visual fidelity for rendering performance. Time Complexity: The evaluation of SH coefficients is O(1) per Gaussian per frame, involving a fixed number of multiplications and additions. It is significantly faster than querying a neural network. Memory Complexity: Each Gaussian stores 48 additional float values (48 \times 4 bytes = 192 bytes) for the SH coefficients. This is a constant overhead per primitive. Measured Performance: The method contributes to the overall rendering speed of 3DGS, which reaches 134 fps on the Mip-NeRF360 benchmark. The SH evaluation itself is described as costing "almost nothing at display time". Strengths: Captures view-dependent effects like highlights and reflections, which simple point colors cannot. It is differentiable and can be optimized via gradient descent. Limitations: High-degree SH (degree 3) increases memory usage significantly (48 coefficients vs 3 for DC). It may struggle with very sharp, high-frequency specularities compared to other representations, though degree 3 is generally sufficient for many scenes. When to Use: When view-dependent appearance (specularities, reflections) is important for photorealism. When Not to Use: When memory bandwidth is extremely constrained and view-dependent effects are not critical (use DC only). Origin: The method was introduced in the 3D Gaussian Splatting paper (Kerbl et al., 2023). It repurposes spherical harmonics from irradiance environment maps to represent the color leaving a Gaussian. History: Spherical harmonics are a well-known orthogonal basis for functions on the unit sphere, analogous to Fourier series. The specific application to 3DGS involves truncating the series at degree 3 and learning the coefficients via gradient descent. Usage: It is a core component of the 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline, enabling photorealistic novel view synthesis. An Architectural Review of the 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21739653, fetched 2026-10-26 learning3d/assignment3, https://github.com/learning3d/assignment3, fetched 2026-10-26 thomasantony/splat, https://github.com/thomasantony/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) https://github.com/ZhenyangLiu/Collaborative-Neural-Radiance-Fields-for-Novel-View-Synthesis, https://github.com/ZhenyangLiu/Collaborative-Neural-Radiance-Fields-for-Novel-View-Synthesis, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking
head: Baked view-dependent color buffer, Progressive SH evaluation, Progressive Spherical Harmonics
body: Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking is an optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces memory bandwidth pressure caused by high-degree spherical harmonics (SH) by evaluating view-dependent colors over multiple frames rather than every frame. It alleviates the bottleneck where loading high-degree SH coefficients consumes more memory than the splat's geometric attributes, storing the evaluated results in a "baked" color buffer. Unlike standard per-frame SH evaluation, this method trades immediate visual fidelity for rendering performance, converging to the correct view-dependent color within a short, fixed number of frames. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D Gaussian splats with stored SH coefficients (e.g., Degree 3), camera view direction, and a convergence parameter N (number of frames to fully update all visible splats). Output: A "baked" view-dependent color buffer containing the evaluated RGB color for each visible splat. Data Structures: Splat Attributes: Position, scale, orientation, base color, and flags, consuming 52 bytes per splat. SH Coefficients: For Degree 3, 45 additional floating-point values (16 coefficients times three for RGB, minus three since the base color is handled separately). Baked Color Buffer: Stores the evaluated RGB color for each splat. Size depends on the number of visible splats. For Degree 3, the SH data adds 180 bytes per splat (45 \times 4 bytes) to the staging memory load, which is more than triple the 52 bytes of geometric data. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Create a baked color buffer for all visible splats and initialize it with the base color or the previous frame's baked color. 2. Progressive Update Loop: For each frame f (where f=1, 2, \dots, N): a. Determine the subset of splats to update, targeting a fraction of 1/N of the total visible splats per frame. b. Select a subset of splats (e.g., sequential or random) comprising 1/N of the total visible splats. c. For each selected splat i: i. Evaluate the spherical harmonics function C(\mathbf{v}i) using the splat's SH coefficients and the view direction \mathbf{v}i. ii. Write the resulting RGB color to the baked color buffer for splat i. d. For splats not selected in this frame, retain their previously baked color value. 3. VR Handling: In Virtual Reality, account for different camera directions for left and right eyes. It is sufficient to progressively bake color values for only one eye and reuse them for the other, or evaluate based on the direction to the center of both eyes. 4. Rendering: Use the baked color buffer for shading during the current frame's rasterization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressiveshbaking(splats, viewdirections, numframestoconverge=10): """ splats: List of splat objects with.shcoeffs (45 floats for Degree 3) and.basecolor viewdirections: List of 3D view direction vectors numframestoconverge: N, frames to fully update all visible splats """ numsplats = len(splats) bakedcolors = [splat.basecolor for splat in splats] # Initialize with base color splatsperframe = max(1, numsplats // numframestoconverge) currentsplatidx = 0 for frame in range(numframestoconverge): for in range(splatsperframe): if currentsplatidx >= numsplats: break # Evaluate spherical harmonics: C(v) = sum{l=0}^{L} sum{m=-l}^{l} c{lm} Y{lm}(v) # Standard SH evaluation routine bakedcolors[currentsplatidx] = splats[currentsplatidx].basecolor currentsplatidx += 1 if currentsplatidx >= numsplats: break return bakedcolors Parameters: Convergence Frames (N): Number of frames to fully update all visible splats. Typical value: 10. SH Degree: Degree 3 is used, requiring 45 additional coefficients per splat (16 coefficients times three for RGB, minus three since the base color is handled separately). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: VR Eye Discrepancy: Left and right eyes have different view directions. Reusing baked colors from one eye for the other may cause slight inaccuracies, but is deemed sufficient. Motion Artifacts: Under sufficiently high frame rates, progressive updates cause little to no apparent lag even under motion. Memory Bandwidth: High-degree SH (e.g., Degree 3) adds 180 bytes per splat to staging memory, which is a significant bottleneck compared to 52 bytes of geometric data. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Storing Degree 3 SH coefficients adds 180 bytes per splat (45 \times 4 bytes) to the staging pass memory load. This is more than triple the 52 bytes used for position, scale, orientation, color, and flags. Time: Updating all harmonics per frame is expensive. On the Kinuta scene, updating all harmonics takes 1.6 ms, while updating 1/10th takes 0.6 ms and 1/30th takes 0.5 ms. On the Campus scene, updating all harmonics takes 4.4 ms, while updating 1/10th takes 1.5 ms and 1/30th takes 1.1 ms. Measured Performance: Kinuta Scene: All: 1.6 ms, 1/10th: 0.6 ms, 1/30th: 0.5 ms. Campus Scene: All: 4.4 ms, 1/10th: 1.5 ms, 1/30th: 1.1 ms. Berlin Scene: All: 0.4 ms, 1/10th: 0.2 ms, 1/30th: 0.1 ms. Garden Scene: All: 2.6 ms, 1/10th: 1.9 ms, 1/30th: 1.8 ms. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly reduces memory bandwidth pressure and staging time for high-degree SH. Convergence is typically fast enough (e.g., 10 frames) to cause barely noticeable artifacts. Limitations: Progressive updates introduce a temporary lag in view-dependent color updates, but under sufficiently high frame rates, this causes little to no apparent lag even under motion. Requires additional memory for the baked color buffer. When to Use: Use when rendering high-degree SH (e.g., Degree 3) and memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. Use in VR where per-eye evaluation is expensive. When Not to Use: Use when SH degree is low (e.g., Degree 0 or 1) and bandwidth is not a concern. Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking was introduced in the context of optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting for large models and VR rendering. It addresses the performance bottleneck caused by the large memory footprint of high-degree spherical harmonics coefficients. The technique was developed as part of the Splatshop project, which focuses on efficiently editing large Gaussian Splat models. Splatshop: Efficiently Editing Large Gaussian Splat Models, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70214, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Standard Constant Step Ray Marching
head: Basic Raymarching Loop, Fixed Step Ray Marching, Raymarch, SDF Ray Marching
body: Standard Constant Step Ray Marching is an iterative algorithm for finding the intersection of a ray with an implicit surface or sampling a volume by advancing the ray position at fixed intervals. It mitigates the drawback of root-finding methods that may identify multiple intersection points by focusing on determining the first root (or accumulating volume data). Unlike Spheretracing, which uses the distance field value to determine the step size, this method uses a predefined constant step size, allowing it to work with any function that returns a boolean (inside/outside) or a scalar field, rather than requiring a strict Signed Distance Field (SDF). It builds on Ray-primitive intersection. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{r}0 (e.g., camera position). Ray direction \mathbf{r}d (normalized unit vector). Fixed step size \Delta t. Maximum step count k{\max} (or maximum distance). Implicit surface function f(\mathbf{x}) or scalar field map. (Optional) Bounding box limits t{\min}, t{\max}. Outputs: Intersection distance t (if surface hit). Accumulated radiance/color (if volume rendering). Boolean indicating hit/miss. Data Structures: Scalar variables for position, distance, and counters. No complex structures required. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize step counter k = 0 and current distance t = 0. 2. (Optional) Compute bounding box intersection parameters t{\min} and t{\max} for the ray. 3. Loop while k < k{\max} and (if bounding box is used) t \le t{\max}: a. Calculate current sample point: \mathbf{r}(k) = \mathbf{r}0 + \Delta t \cdot k \cdot \mathbf{r}d. b. Evaluate the field function at \mathbf{r}(k): d = f(\mathbf{r}(k)). c. Surface Intersection Variant: i. If d \le 0 (or d < \epsilon), the ray has hit or passed inside the surface. Return intersection distance t = k \cdot \Delta t. ii. If d > 0 and a maximum distance check is used, break if t > \text{MAX\DIST}. d. Volume Rendering Variant: i. Sample density \rho from d. ii. Evaluate transfer function to get attenuation \alpha and color contribution. iii. Update accumulated radiance: L{\text{new}} = L{\text{old}} \cdot \exp(-\rho \cdot \Delta t \cdot \alpha). iv. Advance t by \Delta t. e. Increment k. 4. If loop completes without hit (surface) or termination (volume), return miss/no intersection. Pseudocode (Surface Intersection): import math def raymarchsurface(r0, rd, stepsize, maxsteps, surfacefunc): """ r0: vec3, ray origin rd: vec3, normalized ray direction stepsize: float, fixed delta t maxsteps: int, maximum iterations surfacefunc: function, returns distance (negative if inside) """ k = 0 t = 0.0 while k < maxsteps: # Calculate current position using fixed step formula pos = r0 + rd (stepsize k) # Sample the implicit surface dist = surfacefunc(pos) # Check for intersection: d <= 0 indicates inside or on surface if dist <= 0.0: return t, True k += 1 t = stepsize k return 0.0, False Pseudocode (Volume Rendering): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raymarchvolume(r0, rd, stepsize, maxsteps, volumefunc, transferfunc): """ volumefunc: returns scalar density transferfunc: returns (density, attenuation) tuple """ t = 0.0 L = 1.0 # Incoming radiance # Optional: Compute tmin, tmax for bounding box # tmin, tmax = computeboxintersection(r0, rd, box) k = 0 while k < maxsteps: pos = r0 + rd t # Sample volume density = volumefunc(pos) # Apply transfer function tfval = transferfunc(density) densityval = tfval.density attenuation = tfval.attenuation # Accumulate radiance L = L math.exp(-densityval stepsize attenuation) t += stepsize k += 1 return L Parameters: \Delta t (Step Size): Critical parameter. Typical values range from 0.001 (high precision/volume) to 0.1 (coarse/surface). k{\max} (Max Steps): Typical value 10–64 depending on scene complexity and step size. \epsilon (Epsilon): Threshold for intersection detection. Often 0.001 or similar small value. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tunneling: If \Delta t is too large, the ray may jump over thin geometry between samples. Performance: If \Delta t is too small, excessive samples are taken in empty space, causing performance loss. Surface Definition: The algorithm assumes f(x) < 0 is inside and f(x) = 0 is the surface boundary. Precision: Fixed steps do not adapt to local geometry, potentially missing details that Spheretracing (adaptive step) would catch. A rendering technique where the pixel color is determined by the number of raymarching steps taken before hitting a surface or reaching the maximum step count, visualizing computational intensity. It serves as a debug or artistic tool rather than a physically accurate method. Time Complexity: O(k{\max}), linear with respect to the maximum number of steps. Memory Complexity: O(1), constant space per ray. Strengths: Simple to implement; works with any implicit function (boolean or scalar), not just SDFs. Limitations: Prone to tunneling if step size is not carefully chosen; inefficient in empty space if step size is small; does not guarantee finding the exact first intersection point as accurately as adaptive methods (like Spheretracing). When to use: Simple shapes, boolean volumes, or when SDF evaluation is expensive/impossible. When not to use: Complex scenes with thin geometry requiring high precision, or when SDFs are available (use Spheretracing instead). The method was indicated by [PH89] and used for rendering Hypertexture volumes. It is similar to volumetric ray-casting techniques. The ray equation \mathbf{r}(k) = \mathbf{r}0 + \Delta t k \mathbf{r}d is a standard formulation for fixed-step traversal. name: CSG Difference
head: SDF Difference, Subtraction of SDFs
body: CSG Difference is a Constructive Solid Geometry operator that subtracts the first implicit function from the second, producing a shape that is solid where the second function is solid, except where the first is solid. It combines two Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) into a single field to represent the volume of the second object minus the first. The method takes two SDF functions, Sa (the subtractor) and Sb (the base), and a query point p. It outputs a new SDF value S(p) representing the distance to the nearest surface of the combined shape, and optionally the gradient for shading. Inputs: Sa(p): Scalar distance to object A at point p. Sb(p): Scalar distance to object B at point p. Va(p): Vector gradient (normal) of Sa at p. Vb(p): Vector gradient (normal) of Sb at p. Data Structures: Scalar fields: Single floating-point values per point. Vector fields: 3D vectors (x, y, z) representing the gradient. Steps: 1. Evaluate the scalar distance for both objects at the query point p: da = Sa(p) db = Sb(p) 2. Compute the combined scalar distance using the maximum function: S(p) = \max(db, -da) 3. Compute the combined vector gradient (normal): V(p) = \max(Vb(p), -Va(p)) Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Smooth Subtraction
head: S-Subtraction
body: Smooth Subtraction provides a smooth approximation of the boolean difference operation (A \setminus B) for two Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). It blends the subtraction of one shape from another using a smoothing parameter k. Inputs: d1: SDF value of the subtracted volume. d2: SDF value of the base volume. k: Smoothing factor or blending radius (k > 0). Output: d: Smoothed SDF value for the difference. The operation is point-wise and scalar, requiring no auxiliary data structures. 1. Compute the blending factor h by clamping a linear function of the distance sum: h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 - 0.5 \frac{d2 + d1}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) 2. Compute the linear interpolation between d2 and -d1 using h: \text{mix}(d2, -d1, h) = d2 \cdot (1 - h) + (-d1) \cdot h 3. Add the smoothstep correction term to the interpolation: d = \text{mix}(d2, -d1, h) + k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 - 0.5 \frac{d2 + d1}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) d = \text{mix}(d2, -d1, h) + k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) \text{mix}(a, b, t) = a \cdot (1 - t) + b \cdot t where \text{clamp}(v, \text{min}, \text{max}) restricts v to [\text{min}, \text{max}]. k: The smoothing factor or blending radius. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Division by Zero: k must be strictly positive to prevent division by zero in the h calculation. Precision: When d1 and d2 are large with opposite signs, cancellation errors may occur in d1 + d2. Unverified code. name: Object Combination Operators
head: SDF boolean operators, smooth minimum alternatives
body: Object Combination Operators are a family of functions that combine two signed distance functions (SDFs), a and b, to produce specific geometric features such as rounded edges, chamfers, stairs, or pipes, rather than the sharp edges produced by standard boolean operations. Unlike the standard min operator used in Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination) or the blending-focused SDF Smooth Union, these operators aim to produce correct distance values or tight distance bounds that preserve Lipschitz continuity when the gradients of the input SDFs are orthogonal. All operators in this family take two scalar distance values, a and b, and a radius parameter r (and occasionally n) as inputs, and return a single scalar distance value. The parameter r specifies the radius of the resulting feature (e.g., the fillet radius) and must be significantly smaller than the size of the objects to maintain validity. The core mathematical property distinguishing these operators from generic smooth minimums is their preservation of Lipschitz continuity. Standard smooth minimums can violate the Lipschitz condition (where the gradient magnitude exceeds 1) when combining SDFs, leading to ray marching artifacts. These operators are designed such that Lipschitz continuity is preserved provided the gradients of the two SDFs are at right angles (orthogonal). If the gradients are off by more than 30 degrees, or if the surfaces are parallel and close to each other, the Lipschitz condition may no longer hold, causing artifacts. The family includes operators for various intersection features: Chamfer: fOpUnionChamfer(a, b, r) = min(min(a, b), (a - r + b) sqrt(0.5)) Intersection Chamfer: fOpIntersectionChamfer(a, b, r) = max(max(a, b), (a + r + b) sqrt(0.5)) Difference Chamfer: fOpDifferenceChamfer(a, b, r) = fOpIntersectionChamfer(a, -b, r) Round: u = max(vec2(r - a, r - b), vec2(0)); fOpUnionRound(a, b, r) = max(r, min(a, b)) - length(u) Intersection Round: u = max(vec2(r + a, r + b), vec2(0)); fOpIntersectionRound(a, b, r) = min(-r, max(a, b)) + length(u) Difference Round: fOpDifferenceRound(a, b, r) = fOpIntersectionRound(a, -b, r) Stairs: s = r/n; u = b - r; fOpUnionStairs(a, b, r, n) = min(min(a, b), 0.5 (u + a + abs(mod(u - a + s, 2 s) - s))) Intersection Stairs: fOpIntersectionStairs(a, b, r, n) = -fOpUnionStairs(-a, -b, r, n) Difference Stairs: fOpDifferenceStairs(a, b, r, n) = -fOpUnionStairs(-a, b, r, n) Soft Union: e = max(r - abs(a - b), 0); fOpUnionSoft(a, b, r) = min(a, b) - e e 0.25 / r Pipe: fOpPipe(a, b, r) = length(vec2(a, b)) - r Engrave: fOpEngrave(a, b, r) = max(a, (a + r - abs(b)) sqrt(0.5)) Groove: fOpGroove(a, b, ra, rb) = max(a, min(a + ra, rb - abs(b))) Tongue: fOpTongue(a, b, ra, rb) = min(a, max(a - ra, abs(b) - rb)) Columns: fOpUnionColumns and fOpDifferenceColumns produce a series of columns or pillars at the intersection, controlled by n. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fOpUnionColumns(a: float, b: float, r: float, n: float) -> float: if a < r and b < r: px = a py = b sqrt2 = math.sqrt(2.0) px = (a - b) / sqrt2 py = (a + b) / sqrt2 px = px - (sqrt2 / 2.0) r columnradius = (r sqrt2) / ((n - 1) 2 + sqrt2) px = px + columnradius sqrt2 if n % 2 == 1: py = py + columnradius period = columnradius 2 py = py - math.floor(py / period) period result = math.sqrt(px2 + py2) - columnradius result = min(result, px) result = min(result, a) return min(result, b) else: return min(a, b) def fOpDifferenceColumns(a: float, b: float, r: float, n: float) -> float: aneg = -a m = min(aneg, b) if aneg < r and b < r: px = aneg py = b sqrt2 = math.sqrt(2.0) px = (aneg - b) / sqrt2 py = (aneg + b) / sqrt2 columnradius = (r sqrt2) / ((n - 1) 2 + sqrt2) py = py + columnradius px = px - (sqrt2 / 2.0) r px = px - (columnradius sqrt2) / 2.0 if n % 2 == 1: py = py + columnradius period = columnradius 2 py = py - math.floor(py / period) period result = -math.sqrt(px2 + py2) + columnradius result = max(result, px) result = min(result, aneg) return -min(result, b) else: return -m Combines two SDFs into a single smooth field using polynomial or LogSumExp approximations, avoiding sharp edges. It is chosen when organic, metaball-like merges are desired without branching or trigonometry. Approximates the boolean intersection of two shapes by blending their overlap region with a radius parameter. It is chosen when a smooth transition is needed instead of the sharp corner of the standard min operator. Extends standard SDFs by associating material properties with primitives, returning a vector of distance and material ID for shading. It is chosen when distinct visual identification of objects within a combined scene is required. These operators were developed to address the limitations of standard boolean SDF operations, which produce sharp, non-smooth edges that can cause artifacts in ray marching if not handled with complex logic. The specific formulations are documented in community resources and shader libraries for real-time ray marching, such as the RayMarching repository and the TD-Raymarching-System. The preservation of Lipschitz continuity for orthogonal gradients is a key theoretical contribution allowing these operators to be used safely in sphere tracing without the gradient blow-up associated with generic smooth minimums. kushchevd/RayMarching, https://github.com/kushchevd/RayMarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) yeataro/TD-Raymarching-System, https://github.com/yeataro/TD-Raymarching-System, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SDF Smooth Union
head: LogSumExp SDF Union, S-Union, Smooth Minimum, Smooth Union, Smooth Union SDF Operator
body: SDF Smooth Union is a constructive operator that blends two Signed Distance Function (SDF) values, a and b, into a single smooth distance field, replacing the sharp edge of a boolean union with a rounded transition controlled by a parameter k. It sets itself apart from the standard min operator by providing a continuous, differentiable transition between shapes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two scalar SDF values a and b (distances from the query point to two primitives), and a smoothing parameter k > 0. Output: A single scalar smooth union distance d{union}. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the operation is element-wise on scalar distances. If material information is carried (as in), the operator may also blend material attributes, but the core distance calculation is scalar. Steps: 1. Compute the interpolation weight h based on the difference between b and a, scaled by k, and clamp it to [0, 1]. 2. Interpolate between b and a using h. 3. Subtract a cubic correction term k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) from the interpolated value. Formulas: There are two primary implementations found in the sources: the Cubic Smooth Minimum and the LogSumExp (Log-Sum-Exp) Smooth Minimum. 1. Cubic Smooth Minimum: h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 + 0.5 \frac{b - a}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) d{union} = \text{mix}(b, a, h) - k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) Where \text{mix}(x, y, t) = x(1-t) + y \cdot t. 2. LogSumExp Smooth Minimum: d{union} = -\frac{1}{k} \ln \left( e^{-k \cdot a} + e^{-k \cdot b} \right) Or equivalently using the log-sum-exp function: d{union} = \frac{1}{-k} \text{logsumexp}(-k \cdot a, -k \cdot b). Parameters: k: The smoothing factor or blend radius. Larger values create a smoother, wider blend between the shapes. Typical values range from 0.1 to 1.0 depending on scene scale, with 1.0f cited as a typical value in and 0.5 or 0.33 used for primitive vs scene blending in. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parameter k Scale: The parameter k must be significantly smaller than the size of the objects to maintain validity. Numerical Stability: In the LogSumExp implementation, direct computation of e^{-k \cdot i} can overflow if -k \cdot i is large positive. Subtracting the maximum value before exponentiation is required for stability. Pseudocode (Cubic Implementation): The cubic implementation is explicitly provided in and. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def smoothunioncubic(a: float, b: float, k: float) -> float: """ Computes the smooth union of two SDF values using the cubic approximation. """ if k <= 0: # Fallback to standard min if k is invalid return min(a, b) h = 0.5 + 0.5 (b - a) / k if h < 0.0: h = 0.0 elif h > 1.0: h = 1.0 mixedval = b (1.0 - h) + a h correction = k h (1.0 - h) return mixedval - correction Pseudocode (LogSumExp Implementation): The LogSumExp implementation is provided in. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def smoothunionlogsumexp(a: float, b: float, k: float) -> float: """ Computes the smooth union of two SDF values using the LogSumExp approximation. """ if k <= 0: return min(a, b) vala = -k a valb = -k b maxval = max(vala, valb) logsum = math.log(math.exp(vala - maxval) + math.exp(valb - maxval)) + maxval return -logsum / k A blending function for combining two SDFs to create organic, metaball-like merges using a cubic smoothing function, controlled by a blend radius parameter k. It sets itself apart by providing a continuous, differentiable transition without branching or trigonometry, suitable for organic shapes. Time Complexity: O(1) per pair of SDFs. The cubic method involves basic arithmetic operations (add, multiply, clamp). The LogSumExp method involves exponentials and logarithms, which are more expensive but still constant time. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional storage is required beyond the input scalars and the output scalar. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales linearly with the number of SDFs to be combined if applied recursively or in a tree structure. Strengths: Produces visually smooth, organic transitions between primitives; differentiable (enabling gradient-based optimization in some contexts). Limitations: Does not preserve exact distance properties (the result is an approximation, not a true SDF in the strict sense everywhere); artifacts can occur if k is too large relative to object size. When to use: When creating organic merges, metaballs, or soft intersections where sharp boolean edges are undesirable. When not to use: When exact distance preservation is critical for ray marching stability in complex non-orthogonal configurations, or when sharp edges are desired (use standard min). The concept of smooth union in SDFs originated from the need to create organic shapes and avoid the visual artifacts of sharp boolean operations in ray marching. The cubic smooth minimum operator was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his online articles on SDFs. The LogSumExp approximation is derived from the soft-minimum function used in machine learning and optimization. These operators are widely used in real-time ray marching for creating metaballs, fluid-like interactions, and smooth architectural details. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) skmhrk1209/Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) kyle-rosa/raymarching, https://github.com/kyle-rosa/raymarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) An Introduction to Raymarching - Maxime Garcia, https://typhomnt.github.io/teaching/raytracing/raymarchingintro/, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) cahekp/Raymarching, https://github.com/cahekp/Raymarching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Polynomial Smooth Minimum
head: Quilez smin, Quilez smooth min, smoothMin
body: Polynomial Smooth Minimum is a blending function for combining two Signed Distance Function (SDF) values to create organic, metaball-like merges between primitives without branching or trigonometry. It sets itself apart from the standard min operator by providing a continuous, differentiable transition controlled by a smoothing radius parameter k, allowing for smooth union operations in Constructive SDF Modeling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two scalar SDF values a and b, and a non-negative smoothing radius k. Output: A single scalar value representing the smooth minimum of a and b. Data Structures: Operates on scalar floating-point values with no auxiliary data structures. Algorithm: The method computes an intermediate blend factor h based on the distance between a and b relative to k, then adjusts the minimum value by a quadratic term. 1. Edge Case Handling: If k \le 10^{-6}, return \min(a, b) to avoid division by zero or numerical instability. 2. Compute Blend Factor: Calculate h = \max(k - |a - b|, 0.0) / k. This value ranges from 0.0 (when |a - b| \ge k) to 1.0 (when a = b). 3. Compute Result: Return \min(a, b) - h^2 \cdot k \cdot 0.25. Note: Source provides an equivalent formulation using h = \text{clamp}(0.5 + 0.5(b - a)/k, 0.0, 1.0) and \text{result} = \text{mix}(b, a, h) - k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h). Both yield identical results for the same inputs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def polynomialsmoothminimum(a: float, b: float, k: float) -> float: if k <= 1e-6: return min(a, b) diff = abs(a - b) h = max(k - diff, 0.0) / k return min(a, b) - (h h k 0.25) Parameters: k: The blend radius parameter, exposed as a UI slider. Typical values are 0.2 or 0.3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: When |a - b| \ge k, h = 0 and the result equals \min(a, b), preserving the hard union outside the blending region. Floating-point precision may cause artifacts when subtracting close values for large k. The dual operator for smooth intersection, combining two SDF values using a smoothing factor k. It computes h = \max(k - |a - b|, 0.0) / k and returns \max(a, b) + h^2 \cdot k \cdot 0.25. Choose this when carving out material smoothly or implementing smooth subtraction, as it is implemented as smax(-d1, d2, k) for smooth subtraction and smax(d1, d2, k) for smooth intersection. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive pair. Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is attributed to Inigo Quilez, a prominent graphics programmer known for his work on ray marching and SDFs. It is widely known in the procedural geometry community as "Quilez smin". The technique is used in real-time ray marching shaders for creating complex organic shapes from simple primitives. name: Smooth Intersection
head: S-Intersection
body: Smooth Intersection is a constructive SDF operator that blends the overlap of two shapes to produce a rounded interior corner, serving as the smooth counterpart to the boolean intersection. Unlike standard smooth minimums which approximate unions, this operator approximates intersections by mixing the input distances based on their relative positions within the blending radius. It is distinguished from its sibling SDF Smooth Union by its focus on the interior region where both distances are negative, whereas the union focuses on the exterior where at least one distance is positive. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two scalar signed distance values d1 and d2, and a smoothing parameter k (radius). Output: A single scalar signed distance value d. Data Structures: None required; the operation is scalar. Parameters: k: The blending radius or smoothness parameter. It controls the width of the transition zone between the sharp intersection and the smooth blend. Formulas: The operator computes an intermediate blend factor h and then mixes the distances: h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 - 0.5 \frac{d2 - d1}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) d = \text{mix}(d2, d1, h) + k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) Where \text{mix}(a, b, t) = a \cdot (1 - t) + b \cdot t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def smoothintersection(d1: float, d2: float, k: float) -> float: # Calculate the blend factor h diff = d2 - d1 h = 0.5 - 0.5 diff / k if h < 0.0: h = 0.0 elif h > 1.0: h = 1.0 # Calculate the mixed distance mixed = d2 (1.0 - h) + d1 h # Add the smoothing term smoothterm = k h (1.0 - h) return mixed + smoothterm Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Approximates the boolean union with rounded edges. Choose when combining objects where the exterior shape is the primary concern. SDF Smooth Union Extends SDFs to handle multiple materials with smooth transitions. Choose when rendering complex scenes with distinct material boundaries. Strengths: Produces smooth, continuous transitions for interior corners; differentiable, making it suitable for gradient-based optimization. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When a smooth, rounded interior corner is desired between two intersecting volumes. When not to use: When sharp, precise boolean intersections are required, or when the intersecting surfaces are nearly parallel. The method originates from PyTorch-based sphere tracing implementations that provide differentiable SDF operations for neural rendering and optimization. It is part of the broader family of smooth CSG operators designed to maintain gradient continuity for training implicit surfaces. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) skmhrk1209/Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Multi-Material Distance Fields
head: Color-Coded SDFs, SDF with Material Data
body: Multi-Material Distance Fields associate material properties with geometric primitives by returning a vector containing both the distance value and the material identifier from the scene's map() function. This extends standard ray marching to enable distinct visual identification of objects within a combined scene without altering the underlying distance field logic. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin ro, ray direction rd, maximum march steps, and a Color Ramp texture. Output: A final pixel color determined by the material ID of the closest hit surface. Data Structures: Multi-Material Point: A 2D vector where the x component is the signed distance value d and the y component is the material identifier m (e.g., a normalized color index). Algorithm Steps: 1. Define Primitive Mappers: Each geometric primitive returns a 2D vector where x is the standard SDF distance and y is a constant material ID. 2. Combine Fields: Use the Union operator to merge primitives. The operator compares only the x components to determine the closest surface, but returns the entire 2D vector of the winning primitive. 3. Ray Marching: Initialize ray distance t = 0. For each step, calculate world position p = ro + rd \cdot t, sample the combined scene d = \text{map}(p), check for intersection if d.x < \epsilon (e.g., 0.001), and advance t \leftarrow t + d.x otherwise. 4. Shading: Upon hit, extract the material ID from d.y, sample a Color Ramp texture using d.y as the coordinate to retrieve the final color, and compute lighting based on the surface normal and retrieved color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec2: def init(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def sdbox(p, h): q = Vec3(abs(p.x)-h.x, abs(p.y)-h.y, abs(p.z)-h.z) return math.sqrt(max(q.x,0)2 + max(q.y,0)2 + max(q.z,0)2) + min(max(q.x, max(q.y, q.z)), 0) def sdsphere(p, r): return math.sqrt(p.x2 + p.y2 + p.z2) - r def sdtorus(p, r): q = math.sqrt(p.x2 + p.z2) - r.x return math.sqrt(q2 + p.y2) - r.y def opU(d1, d2): return d1 if d1.x < d2.x else d2 def maptorus(p): return Vec2(sdtorus(p, Vec2(1.0, 0.2)), 0.5) def mapbox(p): return Vec2(sdbox(Vec3(p.x+3, p.y, p.z), Vec3(0.75, 0.5, 0.5)), 0.25) def mapsphere(p): return Vec2(sdsphere(Vec3(p.x-3, p.y, p.z), 1.0), 0.75) def mapscene(p): ret = opU(maptorus(p), mapbox(p)) return opU(ret, mapsphere(p)) def samplecolorramp(matid): # Simplified texture lookup mapping material ID to RGB return (matid, 1.0 - matid, 0.5) def computelighting(p, rd, color): # Simplified diffuse lighting calculation return (color[0]0.8, color[1]0.8, color[2]0.8) def raymarch(ro, rd): t = 0.0 maxsteps = 64 hitmat = -1.0 for in range(maxsteps): p = Vec3(ro.x + rd.xt, ro.y + rd.yt, ro.z + rd.zt) d = mapscene(p) if d.x < 0.001: hitmat = d.y break t += d.x if hitmat >= 0: color = samplecolorramp(hitmat) return computelighting(p, rd, color) return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) Parameters: ColorRamp: A uniform sampler2D texture mapping material IDs to colors. Threshold: A small epsilon value (e.g., 0.001) for determining intersection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Material ID Precision: Material IDs are discrete, causing sharp visual changes at boundaries between materials. Using integer IDs mapped to discrete texture coordinates is often more robust than continuous floats. Normal Calculation: Normals must be computed carefully to avoid blending across material boundaries if physically based rendering is desired. A data structure that holds surface shading information, including color, physical properties, and texture descriptors, accessible from both host and device code. It distinguishes itself by explicitly separating geometric displacement (via heightmapTex) from shading calculations and by managing texture projection modes and normal deflection scaling. Time Complexity: Identical to standard SDF ray marching, O(N) where N is the number of march steps. The overhead of returning and comparing 2D vectors is negligible. Memory Complexity: Minimal increase; only the material ID needs to be stored per primitive. Strengths: Enables complex, multi-colored scenes with smooth boolean operations without requiring explicit mesh generation or texture mapping on the geometry itself. Limitations: Limited to a finite number of materials determined by the precision of the material ID storage and the resolution of the Color Ramp. Cannot represent continuous material variation across a single object's surface unless the SDF itself encodes that variation. This technique was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his articles on distance functions and raymarching, specifically demonstrating how to extend the map() function to return material data alongside distance. It is widely used in GLSL raymarching demos and shader art to create visually rich scenes from simple geometric primitives. name: Material Object Format
body: The Material Object Format is a data structure that holds surface shading information, including color, physical properties, and texture descriptors, accessible from both host and device code. It distinguishes itself by explicitly separating geometric displacement (via heightmapTex) from shading calculations and by managing texture projection modes and normal deflection scaling. Input: Material parameters (albedo, metalness, roughness, F0) and optional texture descriptors. Output: A Material instance containing shading and texture metadata. The Material object consists of the following fields: | Field | Type | Description | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | albedo | vec3 (linear float) | Surface color in linear RGB. | | metalness | float | Range [0, 1]. Controls specular vs. diffuse shading contribution. | | roughness | float | Range [0, 1]. Controls smoothness of reflections and light scattering. | | F0 | vec3 (linear float) | Base reflectivity when metalness is 0. | | triplar | bool | Texture projection mode. false for XZ planar mapping, true for triplanar mapping. | | normalStrength | float | Linear scaling factor for normal deflection from normal maps. | | albedoTex | int | Texture descriptor for sRGB albedo map. Value -1 if unused. Multiplied with albedo. | | normalTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear detail normal map. Value -1 if unused. | | roughnessTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear roughness map. Value -1 if unused. Multiplied with roughness. | | metalnessTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear metalness map. Value -1 if unused. Multiplied with metalness. | | heightmapTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear displacement heightmap. Value -1 if unused. Used for geometric displacement by the object SDF, not for shading. | | ambietTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear ambient occlusion map. Value -1 if unused. | Texture descriptors are integers referencing texture objects or mipmap arrays, and only the descriptor value is needed to read a texture from device code. Two constructors initialize the Material object: 1. Full Constructor: Takes albedo, metalness, roughness, and F0 as arguments. Sets all texture descriptors (albedoTex, normalTex, roughnessTex, metalnessTex, heightmapTex, ambietTex) to -1. Sets triplar to false (planar mapping). Sets normalStrength to 1.0. 2. Simplified Constructor: Takes albedo, roughness, and metalness. Calls the Full Constructor with these values and a default F0 of [0.04, 0.04, 0.04]. The default F0 is considered the standard base reflectance for most non-metal dielectrics (e.g., plastics, organic materials). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Material: def init(self, albedo, metalness, roughness, F0=None): """ Implements both constructors: Constructor 1 (Full): F0 is provided. Constructor 2 (Simplified): F0 is None, defaults to [0.04, 0.04, 0.04]. """ if F0 is None: F0 = [0.04, 0.04, 0.04] self.albedo = albedo self.metalness = metalness self.roughness = roughness self.F0 = F0 self.triplar = False self.normalStrength = 1.0 self.albedoTex = -1 self.normalTex = -1 self.roughnessTex = -1 self.metalnessTex = -1 self.heightmapTex = -1 self.ambietTex = -1 Texture Descriptors: All texture fields default to -1 to specify the material as textureless. Heightmap vs. Shading: heightmapTex is explicitly excluded from shading calculations and is used solely by the object SDF for geometric displacement. Normal Strength: normalStrength scales normal deflection from normal map textures, which is useful when displacing a surface at a less steep angle than the normal map is designed for. name: SDF Primitives & Operations
head: Basic Shapes, Boolean operations on implicit surfaces, CSG Intersection, Implicit Function CSG, SDF Operations, Subtraction, Union
body: SDF Primitives & Operations define the fundamental geometric building blocks and Boolean compositing rules for Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). This method solves the problem of representing complex 3D geometry as a single continuous scalar field by combining simple analytic shapes (primitives) using arithmetic operators. It is distinguished from mesh-based rendering by replacing explicit topology with implicit distance evaluations, allowing complex scenes to be constructed via simple arithmetic on scalar values. Unlike sibling SDF Transformation which modifies the input coordinate space, this method operates on the output distance values to define the final surface. Inputs: Point \mathbf{p} in 3D space. Primitive parameters (e.g., radius r, box size \mathbf{b}, normal \mathbf{n}). For composite operations: two or more SDF functions fA, fB and their respective parameters. Outputs: A scalar float representing the signed distance from \mathbf{p} to the nearest surface. Positive values indicate outside, zero on the surface, negative inside. No complex data structures are required for basic primitives. The state is defined by the function parameters. For CSG operations, the scene graph is typically a tree of function pointers or lambda expressions evaluating child SDFs. The following analytic primitives are defined by and. All vectors are 3D. 1. Sphere: Centered at origin, radius r. f{sphere}(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p}\| - r 2. Box: Axis-aligned, centered at origin, half-extents \mathbf{b} = (bx, by, bz) where bi > 0. q = |\mathbf{p}| - \mathbf{b} q{max} = \max(q, 0) f{box}(\mathbf{p}) = \|q{max}\| + \min(\max(qx, \max(qy, qz)), 0) 3. Round Box: Box with rounded edges of radius r{round}. f{roundbox}(\mathbf{p}) = f{box}(\mathbf{p}) - r{round} 4. Cylinder: Axis-aligned along Y, height h, radius r. d = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - r h{half} = h / 2 f{cyl}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(\max(d, |py| - h{half}), 0) 5. Round Cylinder: Cylinder with rounded edges. f{roundcyl}(\mathbf{p}) = f{cyl}(\mathbf{p}) - r{round} 6. Plane: Defined by unit normal \mathbf{n} and distance h from origin along \mathbf{n}. f{plane}(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n} - h 7. Torus: Centered at origin, major radius R, minor radius r. q = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - R f{torus}(\mathbf{p}) = \sqrt{q^2 + py^2} - r 8. Ellipsoid: Axis-aligned, radii \mathbf{r} = (rx, ry, rz). \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{p} / \mathbf{r} f{ellipsoid}(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p}'\| - 1 9. Cone: Axis-aligned along Y, height h, radius r at base. d = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} h{half} = h / 2 f{cone}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(\max(d, |py| - h{half}), 0) 10. Pyramid: Height h. Note: Exact formula not provided in sources. 11. Link: Half of a chain-link. Note: Parametrized by position, major/minor radii, and link length. Exact formula not provided. 12. Elongated Torus: Torus extended in x, y, z. Note: Exact formula not provided. Boolean operations combine SDFs fA and fB to create new surfaces. 1. Union (A \cup B): The surface is the boundary of the combined volume. f{union}(\mathbf{p}) = \min(fA(\mathbf{p}), fB(\mathbf{p})) This is the most common operation for combining disjoint or overlapping objects. 2. Intersection (A \cap B): The surface is the boundary of the overlapping volume. f{intersect}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(fA(\mathbf{p}), fB(\mathbf{p})) Source states d(\mathbf{x}, A \cap B) \geq \max(fA, fB). 3. Subtraction (A \ B): The surface is A minus B. f{sub}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(fA(\mathbf{p}), -fB(\mathbf{p})) Normals are required for lighting and are computed via central differences. \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{p}) = \text{normalize}\left( \begin{bmatrix} f(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon \mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \epsilon \mathbf{x}) \\ f(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon \mathbf{y}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \epsilon \mathbf{y}) \\ f(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon \mathbf{z}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \epsilon \mathbf{z}) \end{bmatrix} \right) Where \epsilon is a small epsilon value. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def length(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def maxvec(a, b): return [max(a[0], b[0]), max(a[1], b[1]), max(a[2], b[2])] def minvec(a, b): return [min(a[0], b[0]), min(a[1], b[1]), min(a[2], b[2])] def absvec(v): return [abs(v[0]), abs(v[1]), abs(v[2])] def sphere(p, r): return length(p) - r def box(p, b): q = absvec(p) - b qmax = maxvec(q, [0, 0, 0]) return length(qmax) + min(max(q[0], max(q[1], q[2])), 0) def union(afunc, aparams, bfunc, bparams, p): return min(afunc(p, aparams), bfunc(p, bparams)) def intersection(afunc, aparams, bfunc, bparams, p): return max(afunc(p, aparams), bfunc(p, bparams)) def subtraction(afunc, aparams, bfunc, bparams, p): return max(afunc(p, aparams), -bfunc(p, bparams)) def plane(p, n, h): return sum(p[i] n[i] for i in range(3)) - h def normalat(func, params, p, eps=1e-4): dx = func([p[0]+eps, p[1], p[2]], params) - func([p[0]-eps, p[1], p[2]], params) dy = func([p[0], p[1]+eps, p[2]], params) - func([p[0], p[1]-eps, p[2]], params) dz = func([p[0], p[1], p[2]+eps], params) - func([p[0], p[1], p[2]-eps], params) vec = [dx, dy, dz] l = length(vec) if l == 0: return [0, 1, 0] # Fallback return [vec[0]/l, vec[1]/l, vec[2]/l] Epsilon: For normal calculation, a small value. Radius/Size: Primitive-specific. Precision: Near the surface (f(\mathbf{p}) \approx 0), floating-point errors can cause jitter in ray marching steps. Subtraction Artifacts: Subtracting a large object from a small one can result in inverted normals if not handled correctly by the CSG logic. Smooth Union: Not covered in basic operations, but standard min/max creates sharp edges. Smooth unions require additional blending functions. Operators: |\cdot| is absolute value, \|\cdot\| is length of vector, \max/\min are maximum/minimum operators. \max(di, 0) applies the maximum operator to each component of vector di with 0. This primitive is the basis for axis-aligned bounding boxes and is computationally efficient due to the absence of square roots in the intermediate steps [1092-signed-box-distance-function.md]. A signed distance function for a sphere centered at the origin, returning the distance from a point to the sphere surface. It is the simplest analytic primitive and serves as a building block for more complex shapes like ellipsoids and solid noise [1237-sphere-signed-distance-function.md]. Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) on implicit functions composites multiple primitive shapes into a single implicit surface by applying Boolean logic to their distance fields. This method allows the rendering of complex geometries composed of multiple primitives using a single field evaluation, which is essential for ray marching and bisection tracers. Unlike explicit mesh operations, CSG on implicit functions reduces geometric composition to arithmetic operations on scalar values, enabling normals and shadows derived from the resulting field's gradient. It is distinguished from sibling primitives by its role as a compositing layer that combines the outputs of Sphere Signed Distance Function, Signed Box Distance Function, and other primitives into a unified scene representation. A set of functions that modify the input position vector p in place to create periodic, mirrored, or reflected spatial structures for Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). They partition space into cells and return a cell index for optional use as a random seed. These operators allow for the creation of infinite repeating patterns (e.g., grids, tiles) without increasing geometric complexity [1730-sdf-domain-manipulation-operators.md]. Basic Signed Distance Functions for common geometric shapes: Sphere, Box, Torus. These are the atomic elements from which all other SDF scenes are constructed [1731-sdf-primitives.md]. Rounding an SDF by subtracting a constant distance value from the SDF result. This operation effectively thickens or thins the surface uniformly and is used to create rounded edges on boxes or to adjust collision boundaries [1829-sdf-rounding.md]. Definition: Signed distance function for a plane P defined by unit normal \mathbf{n} and height h. Formula: f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{n} - h, where \mathbf{n} is the unit normal and h defines the relative placement of the plane. Parameter: h: Defines the relative placement of the plane with respect to the plane perpendicular to normal \mathbf{n} intersecting the origin. Definition: Creating complex geometry by subtracting domain-repeated smaller objects from a non-repeated larger object (e.g., domain repeated cubes subtracted from a larger sphere). Step: Combine domain repetition with subtracting distance fields from each other to create complex objects. Definition: A sphere-based primitive that uses the location and radius to 'window' a noise function, where density is the sum of a windowing function and a fractal function. Formula: noiseDensity(P) = m(P) + (1 - |P/radius|), where P is in the local space of the primitive and m(P) is the fractal function. Parameter: A: The maximal amplitude of the fractal function fbm. Code: Implementation of getSample for SolidNoisePoint: transforms to local space, evaluates fractal function with gamma and amplitude, computes distance function, and returns \max(0, distance + fractal) \times density. Pitfall: Due to the fractal function, density may be positive outside the sphere's radius. The function has non-negative values at most A units away from the radius, requiring bounds padding. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive evaluation. CSG operations add a constant factor proportional to the number of children in the scene graph. Memory Complexity: O(1) for primitives. Scene graph size depends on the number of primitives. Measured Performance: Highly efficient on GPUs due to lack of branching and simple arithmetic. Strengths: Infinite resolution (analytic). Easy to implement and debug. Compact memory footprint. Natural support for smooth blending and morphing. Limitations: Cannot represent arbitrary topology (e.g., self-intersections in complex ways without CSG). Normals are approximate if computed via finite differences. When to use: Ideal for real-time rendering of stylized, geometric, or procedural scenes. When not to use: When photorealistic detail from scanned meshes is required, or when the geometry is too complex for efficient CSG evaluation. The concept of Signed Distance Fields for rendering was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his blog posts and books on ray marching. The mathematical foundations of CSG with distance fields were established by Hart. The technique has become a staple in real-time graphics for creating procedural geometry, VFX, and stylized rendering.
