name: CSG Operations on Implicit Functions
head: CSG implicit surfaces, SDF Boolean Operations, Union/Intersection via min/max
body: Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) on implicit functions composites multiple primitive shapes into a single implicit surface by applying Boolean logic to their distance fields. This method allows the rendering of complex geometries composed of multiple primitives using a single field evaluation, which is essential for ray marching and bisection tracers. Unlike explicit mesh operations, CSG on implicit functions reduces geometric composition to arithmetic operations on scalar values, enabling normals and shadows derived from the resulting field's gradient. It is distinguished from sibling primitives by its role as a compositing layer that combines the outputs of Sphere Signed Distance Function, Signed Box Distance Function, and other primitives into a unified scene representation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two or more signed distance functions (SDFs), denoted f1(\mathbf{p}) and f2(\mathbf{p}), evaluated at a point \mathbf{p} in 3D space. Each fi returns a scalar representing the signed distance to the surface of the i-th primitive. Outputs: A new signed distance function f{result}(\mathbf{p}) that represents the Boolean combination of the input shapes. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values during ray marching. In voxel-based implementations, it operates on 3D grids of floating-point values. Core Formulas: The fundamental CSG operations on SDFs are defined as follows: 1. Union: The distance to the union is the minimum of the individual distances. A point is inside the union if it is inside at least one component. f{union}(\mathbf{p}) = \min(f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})) 2. Intersection: The distance to the intersection is bounded by the maximum of the individual distances. A point is inside the intersection only if it is inside all components. f{intersection}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})) 3. Difference (Subtraction): Subtracting shape B from shape A is equivalent to intersecting A with the complement of B. The complement of an SDF is its negation. f{diff}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(f1(\mathbf{p}), -f2(\mathbf{p})) Proof of Correctness for Intersection (Signed Distance Bounds): While Union preserves the exact signed distance property, Intersection and Difference yield signed distance bounds rather than exact distances. This is because DeMorgan’s theorem does not hold directly with min/max operators for distance bounds (the minimum operator is not complemented properly). The correctness of the intersection bound \max(dA, dB) is verified by four cases: Case I (dA < 0, dB < 0): Both points are inside. The distance to the intersection edge is the larger (less negative) of the two distances. Case II (dA < 0, dB > 0): Point is inside A but outside B. The closest point on A to \mathbf{p} may not be in the intersection, but no point in the intersection can be closer than dB. Thus, the bound is dB (which is > dA). Case III (dA > 0, dB < 0): Symmetric to Case II. Case IV (dA > 0, dB > 0): Both points are outside. The closest point in the intersection is no closer than the farther of the two distances. Pseudocode (Ray Marching Context): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchcsg(scenefunc, rayorigin, raydirection, maxsteps=64, maxdist=100.0, epsilon=0.001): """ Standard sphere tracing loop using a composite CSG scene function. scenefunc(p) must internally call the appropriate min/max operations. """ t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): pos = rayorigin + t raydirection dist = scenefunc(pos) if dist < epsilon: return t, pos if t > maxdist: return float('inf'), None t += dist return float('inf'), None Pseudocode (Voxel Grid Context): For voxel-based level set operations, the operations are applied element-wise across the grid. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelunion(buffera, bufferb): """In-place union of two voxel buffers.""" dims = buffera.dims() for k in range(dims.min.z, dims.max.z + 1): for j in range(dims.min.y, dims.max.y + 1): for i in range(dims.min.x, dims.max.x + 1): buffera[i, j, k] = min(buffera[i, j, k], bufferb[i, j, k]) def voxeldifference(buffera, bufferb): """In-place difference (A minus B) of two voxel buffers.""" dims = buffera.dims() for k in range(dims.min.z, dims.max.z + 1): for j in range(dims.min.y, dims.max.y + 1): for i in range(dims.min.x, dims.max.x + 1): buffera[i, j, k] = max(buffera[i, j, k], -bufferb[i, j, k]) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Material/Color Changes: Polygonizers generating meshes from CSG level sets do not inherently consider material properties. This can lead to drastic color changes between vertices at CSG boundaries if materials are not treated as surface boundaries (inside/outside changes). Signed Distance Bound Accuracy: Intersection and Difference operations do not preserve the exact signed distance property. The resulting field is a bound, which may cause sphere tracing to step conservatively compared to an exact SDF, though it remains valid for rendering. An alternative to the standard Union operation that creates a smooth transition (rounded fillets) between the edges of two shapes rather than a sharp crease. It takes an additional float parameter k (typically 0 to 2) determining the degree of smoothness. It uses a polynomial blend function smin(a, b, k) instead of min(a, b). Similar to Smooth Union, this operation creates a smooth transition for the intersection of two shapes. It retains the common part but blends the boundary smoothly using a smooth blend function with a smoothness parameter k. Similar to Smooth Union, this operation subtracts the second shape from the first with a smooth transition at the boundary. It applies the smooth blend function combined with negation logic. A binary operation that takes the union of two shapes and creates a set of steps between the edges where they connect. Union Stairs takes two additional float parameters: r (step width) and n (number of steps). Behaves like Union Stairs but performs subtraction (A minus B) instead of union, creating stepped boundaries for the difference operation. Behaves like Union Stairs but performs intersection, creating stepped boundaries for the intersection operation. A unary operation that adds Perlin noise to the signed distance of a shape. It takes a float parameter noiseProp (0 to 0.5) determining the intensity of the noise. It uses a GLSL mix function to blend the noise into the distance value: mix(f, f + noise, noiseProp). A unary operation that creates a hole inside a shape, resulting in a hollow object. It takes a float parameter thickness (smaller values result in larger holes). A voxel-based implementation of CSG operations that applies Boolean logic directly to discrete 3D grids. Union is implemented as Anew(i,j,k) = min(A(i,j,k), B(i,j,k)), intersection as Anew(i,j,k) = max(A(i,j,k), B(i,j,k)), and difference as Anew(i,j,k) = max(A(i,j,k), -B(i,j,k)). In user interface terms, intersection corresponds to a copy operation, union to a paste operation, and difference to a cut operation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simplicity: Complex geometry is defined by simple arithmetic expressions. Normals and Shadows: Surface normals are derived analytically from the gradient of the composite SDF, and soft shadows can be computed using the same field, requiring no additional data structures. Exact Bounds: Union preserves the exact signed distance property, allowing for optimal sphere tracing step sizes. Limitations: Intersection Bounds: Intersection and Difference operations yield signed distance bounds, not exact distances. Material Handling: Standard CSG does not handle material changes at boundaries automatically; explicit handling is required for correct shading across different materials. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. CSG on implicit surfaces was formalized following Ricci's work in 1974, which established that minimum and maximum operations on functions result in union and intersection operations on their implicit surfaces. The method is a cornerstone of ray-marched rendering, enabling the creation of complex fractals and composite objects with minimal code overhead. The specific arithmetic formulations for SDFs (min for union, max for intersection) were further detailed in subsequent literature on geometric methods for ray tracing. name: Stack-Based SDF Editor
head: Post-order SDF construction, RPN-style SDF editor
body: An interactive editor that constructs Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) from primitives and operations using a stack-based interface similar to Reverse Polish Notation (RPN), implicitly representing a tree with postorder traversal. It differs from explicit tree editors by deferring structure resolution until compilation, allowing users to build complex scenes by pushing operations onto a linear stack where only the top item is visible until combined. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of operations pushed onto a stack, categorized as Shapes, Transformations, or CSG Operations. Output: A compiled GLSL shader string containing the SDF evaluation function. Data Structures: Operation Stack: A list of operation objects representing the postorder traversal of the scene graph. AST Tree: A recursive structure built from the stack where nodes are either leaves (primitive shapes annotated with domain-modifying transformations) or internal nodes (CSG operations acting on range values). Numbered Steps: 1. Push Operation: Operations are pushed onto the stack. The editor only considers the first item by default; subsequent items are not visible until joined via union or other operations. 2. Invalidate Cache: Modifying any parameter calls #invalidate, which clears the cached shader program to trigger recompilation on the next access. 3. Build SDF (Tree Reconstruction): The buildSDF function iterates over the stack, popping off previous operations according to the arity of the current operation to reconstruct the tree structure. 4. Generate GLSL: The system recursively traverses the AST, transforming nodes to appropriate calls. At leaves, it composes domain-modifying functions in the opposite order of application. Internal nodes generate range operations (e.g., min for union). 5. Compile: The generated GLSL string is spliced into a template and compiled. Formulas: Union: S{union}(p) = \min(SA(p), SB(p)). Domain Transformation Composition: If transformations T1, T2, \dots are applied to a shape, the input position p is transformed by composing them in the opposite order: Tn(\dots T2(T1(p)) \dots). Parameters: Primitive Types: Box and Sphere (e.g., radius 1.0). Transformations: Translate (vec3 offset) and Rotate (float angle). CSG Operations: Union and Intersection. Configuration: Uses lazy evaluation and caching via getter/setter methods that call #invalidate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility: Subsequent stack items remain invisible until a union or similar operation combines them with the top item. AST vs Conceptual Tree: The generated AST differs from the conceptual operation tree because domain modifications (transformations) are attached to leaves, while range modifications (CSG operations) form internal nodes. Performance: Without #invalidate caching, the shader would be reassembled and compiled on every frame, causing severe inefficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildsdf(stack): aststack = [] for op in stack: if op['type'] == 'Shape': aststack.append({'type': 'Leaf', 'shape': op['shape'], 'transforms': [], 'params': op.get('params', {})}) elif op['type'] == 'Transform': if aststack: aststack[-1]['transforms'].append(op['transform']) elif op['type'] == 'CSG': if len(aststack) >= 2: right = aststack.pop() left = aststack.pop() aststack.append({'type': 'CSG', 'op': op['op'], 'left': left, 'right': right}) return aststack[0] if aststack else None def generateglsl(node): if node['type'] == 'Leaf': p = "p" for t in reversed(node['transforms']): if t['type'] == 'Translate': p = f"opTx({p}, vec3({t['x']}, {t['y']}, {t['z']}))" elif t['type'] == 'Rotate': p = f"opRotX({p}, {t['angle']})" radius = node['params'].get('radius', '1.0') return f"sd{node['shape'].upper()}({p}, {radius})" elif node['type'] == 'CSG': leftcode = generateglsl(node['left']) rightcode = generateglsl(node['right']) if node['op'] == 'Union': return f"min({leftcode}, {rightcode})" elif node['op'] == 'Intersection': return f"max({leftcode}, {rightcode})" return f"min({leftcode}, {rightcode})" return "" Caching via #invalidate prevents recompilation on every frame, making runtime evaluation efficient. The Config class uses lazy evaluation and caching to avoid unnecessary shader recompilation. The interface is described as intuitive once the input model is understood. name: Signed Box Distance Function
head: Box SDF, SDF Box, Rectangular (Axis-Aligned Box) SDF, SDF Cube, SDF Half-space Intersection
body: The Signed Box Distance Function computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of an axis-aligned box, returning a negative value if the point is inside and a positive value if it is outside. It distinguishes itself from sibling primitives like the Sphere SDF by handling the distinct geometric regions of a box (faces, edges, and corners) using component-wise absolute values and max/min operations, ensuring the distance estimate is never an underestimation. This property is critical for sphere tracing, as underestimating the distance can cause the ray to overshoot the surface or produce incorrect ambient occlusion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point p \in \mathbb{R}^3 and box parameters: center c \in \mathbb{R}^3 and side lengths s \in \mathbb{R}^3 (where si > 0). Alternatively, the box can be defined by half-extents e = s/2. Output: A scalar signed distance d \in \mathbb{R}. d < 0 indicates the point is inside the box; d > 0 indicates the point is outside; d = 0 indicates the point is on the surface. Data Structures: The box is defined by two vectors: center (3 floats) and sidelengths (3 floats). In some implementations, these are learnable parameters. Algorithm: The standard robust implementation (Algorithm 3.6 in) proceeds as follows: 1. Translate and Scale: Compute the vector from the box center to the point, then subtract the half-extents. q = |p - c| - \frac{s}{2} Here, | \cdot | is the component-wise absolute value. Let q = (qx, qy, qz). 2. Determine Inside/Outside: Calculate the maximum component of q. m = \max(qx, \max(qy, qz)) This value represents the distance to the closest face if the point is inside. 3. Compute Distance: The outside distance is the Euclidean norm of the positive components of q (clamping negative components to zero): d{\text{out}} = \| \max(q, 0) \|2 = \sqrt{\max(qx, 0)^2 + \max(qy, 0)^2 + \max(qz, 0)^2} The inside distance is the minimum of m and zero: d{\text{in}} = \min(m, 0) The final signed distance is the sum: d = d{\text{out}} + d{\text{in}} This branchless formulation is mathematically equivalent to the conditional version but avoids branching in shader execution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def signedboxdistance(p, center, sidelengths): """ Computes the exact signed distance from point p to an axis-aligned box. Args: p: vec3, query point coordinates. center: vec3, center of the box. sidelengths: vec3, lengths of the box sides (x, y, z). Returns: float: Signed distance. Negative if inside, positive if outside. """ # Step 1: Translate point to box-local space and subtract half-extents # q = |p - center| - sidelengths / 2 qx = abs(p.x - center.x) - sidelengths.x / 2.0 qy = abs(p.y - center.y) - sidelengths.y / 2.0 qz = abs(p.z - center.z) - sidelengths.z / 2.0 # Step 2: Determine inside/outside boundary via max component # m = max(qx, max(qy, qz)) m = qx if qy > m: m = qy if qz > m: m = qz # Step 3: Compute outside distance (L2 norm of positive components) qxpos = qx if qx > 0.0 else 0.0 qypos = qy if qy > 0.0 else 0.0 qzpos = qz if qz > 0.0 else 0.0 dout = sqrt(qxpos qxpos + qypos qypos + qzpos qzpos) # Step 4: Compute inside distance (min of max component and 0) din = m if m < 0.0 else 0.0 # Step 5: Return combined signed distance return dout + din Parameters: center: The 3D coordinates of the box center. Default: (0, 0, 0). sidelengths: The width, height, and depth of the box. Must be positive. Half-extents e = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) yield a 1 \times 1 \times 1 box. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Underestimation: An incorrect implementation (e.g., Algorithm 3.5 in) may underestimate the distance in corner regions. This leads to smaller ray steps, slower convergence, and incorrect ambient occlusion (artifacts like black dots or banding). Overestimation: Overestimating the distance can cause the ray to pass through the surface or inaccurately estimate the surface position, also negatively impacting ambient occlusion. Precision: The use of absolute values and max/min operations is numerically stable. However, floating-point precision issues near the surface (d \approx 0) are common to all SDFs and may require epsilon clamping in downstream shading logic. Computes distance to a sphere. Simpler than the box, as it relies solely on radial distance. Choose when rotational symmetry is sufficient. Generalizes the sphere to non-uniform scaling. More complex than the box, requiring iterative or approximate methods for exact distance. Choose when anisotropic scaling is needed. Computes distance to a line segment with rounded caps. More complex than the box, involving projection onto a line. Choose for organic or limb-like shapes. Computes distance to an infinite plane. The simplest primitive. Choose for ground planes or infinite boundaries. Time Complexity: O(1). The computation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations (subtractions, absolute values, max/min, and one square root). Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are required. Strengths: Exact distance calculation; robust for sphere tracing; efficient; handles all octants uniformly via symmetry. Limitations: Only applies to axis-aligned boxes. For rotated boxes, the point must be transformed into the box's local coordinate system first. When to use: When rendering axis-aligned rectangular volumes or bounding boxes in ray marching. When not to use: For rotated boxes (use transformation) or when approximate distance is acceptable and simpler primitives suffice (though box SDF is already very simple). The Signed Box Distance Function is a fundamental primitive in Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering, popularized by Inigo Quilez in his online resources on distance functions. It is used in ray marching for rendering implicit surfaces and in neural rendering pipelines where it serves as a learnable primitive. The correct formulation (Algorithm 3.6) was highlighted in academic work on GPU ray marching to avoid artifacts in ambient occlusion computation. name: Sphere Signed Distance Function
head: Sphere SDF, SDF Sphere, Signed Distance Function Sphere, Signed Distance Function (SDF) for Sphere, Sphere Implicit Function, Sphere Distance Estimator, sdSphere, Sphere distance, implicit sphere
body: The Sphere Signed Distance Function (SDF) computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point in 3D space to the surface of a sphere, providing a signed value that indicates whether the point lies inside (negative), outside (positive), or on (zero) the surface. It serves as a fundamental implicit primitive in distance-field ray marching, enabling efficient step-size estimation. Unlike the Ellipsoid Signed Distance Function, which requires solving higher-degree polynomials, the sphere SDF is analytically closed-form and computationally minimal. Inputs: p: The query point in 3D space, represented as a vector (x, y, z) or vec3. c: The center of the sphere, represented as a 3D vector (cx, cy, cz). Default is the origin (0, 0, 0). r: The physical radius of the sphere, a scalar value r \ge 0. Output: d: A scalar representing the signed distance. d = 0 on the surface, d < 0 inside, d > 0 outside. No complex data structures are required. In neural implicit representations, c and r may be stored as learnable parameters (tensors). The signed distance d(p) from a point p to a sphere with center c and radius r is defined as: d(p) = \| p - c \| - r Where: \| \cdot \| denotes the Euclidean norm (L2 norm). \| p - c \| = \sqrt{(px - cx)^2 + (py - cy)^2 + (pz - cz)^2}. If the sphere is centered at the origin (c = 0), the formula simplifies to: d(p) = \| p \| - r Radius (r): The physical radius of the sphere. In some implementations, this is a hardcoded constant (e.g., 0.5 or 1.0), while in others (particularly neural implicit fields), it is a learnable parameter initialized from configuration. Center (c): The 3D coordinates of the sphere's center. Like the radius, this can be fixed or learnable. Default is (0, 0, 0). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def spheresdf(p, c, r): dx = p[0] - c[0] dy = p[1] - c[1] dz = p[2] - c[2] disttocenter = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) return disttocenter - r 1. Definition Order: In some scripting environments (e.g., Fennel/Lua), the SDF function must be defined before any object constructor or scene graph that references it, due to top-down evaluation order. The 2D analog of the sphere SDF. It computes the signed distance from a 2D point p to a circle of radius r centered at the origin. Formula: d(p) = \|p\| - r, where \|p\| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}. Usage: Used in 2D ray marching or as a cross-section primitive. Code: pub fn circle(p: Vec2, r: f32) -> f32 { p.length() - r }. Time Complexity: O(1). The computation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations (subtractions, multiplications, one addition, one square root). Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Exactness: Provides the exact Euclidean distance, unlike voxel-based approximations. Limitations: Shape Limitation: Only represents perfect spheres. Cannot represent complex organic shapes without composition (e.g., blending with other SDFs). When to use: Ideal for simple geometric primitives and as building blocks for complex scenes via Boolean operations (union, intersection). When not to use: When the object is not spherical or when high-frequency geometric detail is required without composition. The Sphere SDF is one of the most basic implicit surface representations, originating from the field of constructive solid geometry (CSG) and ray marching. It was popularized in the context of real-time graphics by Inigo Quilez, who compiled a list of distance functions for common shapes. The mathematical foundation relies on the definition of a sphere as the locus of points equidistant from a center. The use of signed distances for ray marching (spheretracing) was formalized by John C. Hart in 1994, who demonstrated that the sphere SDF allows for efficient antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces. The simplicity of the sphere SDF makes it a standard example in tutorials on distance field rendering. name: SDF Transformation
head: Domain Distortion, Domain Transformations, SDF Affine Transformation, SDF Inverse Transformation, SDF Spatial Transformations, Transforming SDF Geometry, Transforming implicit surfaces
body: SDF Transformation is a technique for applying geometric transformations (rotation, translation, scaling, bending, twisting, tiling) to implicit surfaces defined by Signed Distance Fields. It operates in the domain of the distance function: instead of transforming the object's vertices or the camera's view matrix, it transforms the query point \mathbf{x} before evaluating the distance function f. This builds on Signed Distance Field (SDF) Primitive Definition by allowing primitives to be manipulated spatially. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query position \mathbf{x} in world space, and a transformation T (defined by parameters such as rotation quaternion, translation vector, scale factor, or bend/twist coefficients). Output: A signed distance value d representing the distance from \mathbf{x} to the transformed surface. Data Structures: Transformation parameters are stored as scalars (scale s, angle \theta), vectors (translation \mathbf{d}, bend axis), or quaternions (orientation \mathbf{q}). Method: The core principle is that to transform a surface by T, one must evaluate the original distance function f at the inverse-transformed point T^{-1}(\mathbf{x}). 1. Compute Inverse Transform: Calculate \mathbf{x}' = T^{-1}(\mathbf{x}). 2. Evaluate Distance: Query the base SDF primitive: d' = f(\mathbf{x}'). 3. Adjust Distance (if necessary): If T is an isometry (rotation, translation, reflection), the distance is preserved: d = d'. If T involves non-isometric scaling or deformation, the distance must be scaled by the appropriate factor (typically the scale factor s or the Lipschitz constant) to maintain metric correctness. Formulas: General Principle: The transformed surface is defined by the zero-level set of the composed function: f(T^{-1}(\mathbf{x})) = 0 \quad Isometries (Translation, Rotation): For isometries, the distance value returned by the SDF does not need adjustment: d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{I} \circ f^{-1}(0)) = d(\mathbf{I}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}), f^{-1}(0)) \quad Where \mathbf{I} is the isometry transformation. Uniform Scale: A uniform scale S(x) = s\mathbf{x} has inverse S^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{s}\mathbf{x}. The distance must be multiplied by s to preserve accuracy: d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{S}(f^{-1}(0))) = s \cdot d(\mathbf{S}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}), f^{-1}(0)) \quad Step-by-step: 1. \mathbf{x}' = \frac{1}{s} \mathbf{x}. 2. d' = f(\mathbf{x}'). 3. Return s \cdot d'. Translation: Shifts the shape by vector \mathbf{d}. The inverse translation subtracts \mathbf{d} from the position: \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{d} Example: To move a sphere by \mathbf{d}, evaluate sphere(p - d). Rotation: Rotates the point by the inverse of the desired rotation. Axis-Aligned: Rotate around axis k by angle \theta. Apply the inverse rotation to the query point. Quaternion: Given orientation quaternion \mathbf{q}, apply the conjugate \mathbf{q}^ to the vector part of the query position. Combined: For combined Scale (S), Rotation (R), and Translation (T), apply the inverse of the product matrix to the query point in homogeneous coordinates: \mathbf{p}{transformed} = ( \mathbf{p}{query} \cdot (S \cdot R \cdot T)^{-1}).xyz \quad Twist: Rotates the x-z plane around the y-axis by an angle proportional to y. Let k be the twist factor. The angle is \theta = k \cdot y. \mathbf{x}' = \text{rotateY}(\mathbf{x}, k \cdot y) \quad Note: The source uses 0.5 \times py as the angle. Bend: Bends the shape about the x-axis. Rotates the x-y plane around the z-axis by an angle proportional to x. Let k be the bend factor. \mathbf{x}' = \text{rotateZ}(\mathbf{x}, k \cdot x) \quad Infinite Tiling (Repetition): Reproduces the shape infinitely. Takes period c. Requires position in the positive quadrant for standard modulo implementations, or uses a centered modulo. \mathbf{x}' = \text{mod}(\mathbf{x} + 0.5c, c) - 0.5c \quad Example for x and z axes with period 1: glsl p.x = mod(p.x, 1.0) - 0.5; p.z = mod(p.z, 1.0) - 0.5; Finite Tiling: Variant of Infinite Tile with a bounding box defined by corner vector \mathbf{l}. The additional vector \mathbf{l} is used to limit the number of repetitions of the shape. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rotatey(p, angle): """Rotate vector p around Y axis by angle (radians).""" c = math.cos(angle) s = math.sin(angle) x, y, z = p return (x c + z s, y, -x s + z c) def rotatez(p, angle): """Rotate vector p around Z axis by angle (radians).""" c = math.cos(angle) s = math.sin(angle) x, y, z = p return (x c - y s, x s + y c, z) def transformsdf(p, transformtype, params, basesdf): """ Apply transformation to SDF query point. Args: p: Input query position (tuple of 3 floats) transformtype: String identifier ('translate', 'scale', 'twist', 'bend', 'tile') params: Dictionary of transformation parameters basesdf: Function f(x) returning distance to untransformed primitive Returns: Signed distance value """ x, y, z = p if transformtype == 'translate': # Inverse translation: subtract translation vector d = params['translation'] # tuple of 3 floats pprime = (x - d[0], y - d[1], z - d[2]) elif transformtype == 'scale': # Inverse scale: divide by scale factor s = params['scale'] # float pprime = (x / s, y / s, z / s) # Scale distance output d = basesdf(pprime) return s d elif transformtype == 'twist': # Twist around Y axis. Angle proportional to y. k = params['twistfactor'] # float angle = k y pprime = rotatey(p, angle) elif transformtype == 'bend': # Bend around X axis (rotates X-Y plane around Z). # Angle proportional to x. k = params['bendfactor'] # float angle = k x pprime = rotatez(p, angle) elif transformtype == 'tile': # Infinite tiling c = params['period'] # float # Centered modulo applied to all components pprime = ( (x + 0.5 c) % c - 0.5 c, (y + 0.5 c) % c - 0.5 c, (z + 0.5 c) % c - 0.5 c) else: # Identity or unsupported pprime = p return basesdf(pprime) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When combining multiple transformations (e.g., Scale Rotation Translation), matrix inversion order matters. The combined transformation matrix is inverted as a whole before application. Tiling Boundaries: Infinite tiling using modulo can cause discontinuities at the boundaries if the primitive is not symmetric or if the modulo implementation does not center the result correctly. Unbounded Twist: Twisting is not Lipschitz continuous over unbounded domains. It must be constrained to a specific domain (e.g., a cylinder) to ensure the Lipschitz constant remains bounded for ray marching stability. A volume described by a field function d = f(x,y,z), where d represents density/distance. Points inside have d < 0, outside have d > 0, and on the contour d = 0. This is the fundamental evaluation step within the transformed domain. Computes distances to implicitly defined surfaces after applying spatial transformations by adjusting the Lipschitz constant of the inverse transformation. Definition: Ensures the distance function remains valid for root-finding algorithms by bounding the rate of change. Formulas: Isometry: No adjustment needed. Uniform Scale: Distance scaled by 1/s in the inverse domain, but returned distance scaled by s. Taper: Lipschitz constant Lip{taper} = \min \frac{1}{s(z)}. Twist (Bounded): Lip{twist} = \sqrt{4 + \frac{\theta^2}{4}}. Pitfall: Twisting is not Lipschitz on unbounded domains; it must be constrained to a domain like a unit cylinder along the twisting axis. A technique to create a 'blob effect' by perturbing the position p with trigonometric functions before querying the SDF. Definition: Perturbs coordinates using sine/cosine waves. Step: 1. px += 0.02 \cdot \cos(8 py + 3 pz). 2. py += 0.02 \cdot \sin(6 pz + 7 px). 3. pz += 0.02 \cdot \cos(8 px + 9 px) (Note: Source uses px twice in the last term). Pitfall: This is considered "cheating" because it breaks the strict mathematical properties of the SDF (Lipschitz continuity), potentially causing ray marching artifacts if the perturbation amplitude is too large relative to the frequency. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, same as the base SDF evaluation. The cost is dominated by the arithmetic operations of the inverse transform (matrix-vector multiplication or trigonometric functions). Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is required for geometry or transformation matrices beyond the parameters passed to the shader/function. Performance: Highly efficient for instancing and animation. Transformations are computed per-ray-sample, allowing for dynamic animation (e.g., twisting, bending) without CPU-side updates. Strengths: No need to store transformed vertices. Infinite tiling is free. Easy to compose complex shapes from simple primitives. Limitations: Non-isometric transformations (scaling, bending) require careful distance compensation to maintain correct ray marching step sizes. Complex deformations (twist, bend) may violate Lipschitz conditions if not bounded, leading to missed intersections or jitter in ray marching. Normal calculation requires differentiating the inverse transform, which can be complex for non-linear transformations like twist/bend. SDF transformations originated in the context of ray marching and implicit surface rendering. Early work by Hart formalized the use of inverse transformations for isometries and uniform scaling. Barr extended this to general deformations (taper, twist) and introduced the concept of Lipschitz constants to ensure the validity of the sphere tracing algorithm. The technique became popular in shader programming and procedural modeling (e.g., "shadertoy" culture) for its ability to create complex, animated geometry with minimal code. name: Splatting
body: Splatting is an object-order volume rendering technique that computes the contribution of each voxel to the image by convolving the voxel with a filter (kernel) that distributes its value to a neighborhood of pixels on the screen. It differs from feed-backward (image-order/ray-casting) methods by mapping direction: feed-forward spreads input information to output (object-order), while feed-backward queries input from output pixels. It offers rendering quality similar to ray casting, and both ray casting and splatting provided in some cases better image qualities than shear-warp. The core mechanism of splatting involves treating the volume as a continuous function defined by smooth kernels centered at each voxel. The rendering process follows these shared steps: 1. Kernel Definition: Each voxel is represented by a 3D reconstruction kernel, typically a Gaussian distribution with mean \mu = 0.0 and standard deviation \sigma = 1.0, truncated outside a radius of 2.0 with a peak value of 1.0. The contribution of a voxel at position D to a screen point (x,y,z) is given by: \text{contribution}D(x,y,z) = hV(x-Dx, y-Dy, z-Dz) \cdot \rho(D) where hV is the volumetric reconstruction kernel and \rho(D) is the voxel density. 2. Projection (Splatting): The 3D kernel is projected onto the 2D image plane, creating a "footprint" or "splat". The weight of the splat at pixel (x,y) relative to the voxel's projection (Dx, Dy) is: \text{weight}(x,y)D = \text{footprint}(x-Dx, y-Dy) The intensity written to the pixel is modulated by the voxel density: P(x,y) = \text{weight}(x,y) \cdot \rho(D). 3. Footprint Representation: For regular grids, the footprint is typically a circle invariant to rotations. To avoid aliasing, the opacity is convolved with a smoothing kernel (e.g., Gaussian). A splat diameter of 1.6 times the spacing between values is sufficient to avoid aliasing while preventing excessive blurring. For perspective projections, the splat size must be adjusted according to the sample's distance from the viewpoint. Efficient representation often uses a screen-aligned quadrilateral texture-mapped with an opacity-weighted texture. 4. Compositing: Splats are composited using alpha blending. Depending on the optical model, they must be rendered in front-to-back or back-to-front order. Compositing in splatting is performed along sheets (all pixels at once for a set of voxels), whereas ray-casting composites along rays (one sample at a time). 5. Sheet-Based Traversal: A common implementation traverses the volume one sheet of voxels at a time, from front to back. The sheet (x-y, x-z, or y-z) nearest to being parallel with the image plane is selected. Each voxel in the sheet is transformed from grid space to screen space, shaded independently to produce an (R,G,B,\alpha) tuple, and projected into an accumulation sheet. The accumulation sheet is composited with the working image after all voxels in the sheet are processed. 6. Shading: Shading can be performed via pre-shading (classifying/shading voxels before projection) or post-shading. Post-shading maintains three sheet-buffers (previous, current, next), projects 3D kernels into the next buffer, estimates gradients using central differences on the current buffer based on the next and previous buffers, and shades using the normalized gradient. It solves the computational cost of ray-marching by assuming Gaussians do not overlap and are sorted by view-space depth, trading continuous extinction accumulation for efficient, hole-free reconstruction. It differs from standard point rendering by using anisotropic, band-limited elliptical footprints derived from the Gaussian covariance, whereas simplified variants use screen-aligned spherical impostors with isotropic falloff. A technique merging splatting with raycasting principles, where splats are suspended in object space and rays are spawned to intersect them, enabling perspective projection efficiency and acceleration methods. An optimization for volume splatting that skips processing of voxels when the accumulated opacity at the target screen pixels is already full, analogous to early ray termination in ray casting. It works by projecting two volumes: the density volume and an opacity volume. For each projected voxel, a 2D bounding box is computed around the pixels covering the splat. If all pixels inside the bounding box have full opacity (1.0 or near 1.0), the voxel processing is skipped. A rendering solution introduced in that uses extinction (referred to as 'density' in NeRF literature) instead of the learned opacity value used in 3DGS, to analyze the difference between opacity-based and accurate volumetric rendering. For small numbers of primitives, extinction-based splatting performs better than opacity-based splatting. However, with more primitives, opacity splatting performs best. A volume rendering algorithm that performs classification and shading after voxels are projected onto the screen to avoid blurring object edges, which occurs when classification is done prior to projection. It projects voxel densities onto the screen using regular splats (radially symmetric interpolation kernels). It projects gradient volumes onto the screen using gradient splats, OR computes gradients on the projection plane using central differencing on the projected density. It performs per-pixel shading using the computed gradients to classify and color the voxels. An optimization uses lookup tables for shading to handle the added overhead of screen gradients and per-pixel shading. Computing gradients on the projection plane via central differencing reduces the number of footprint rasterizations by a factor of four compared to projecting a separate gradient volume, because only voxel densities need to be projected. A progressive refinement algorithm for volume rendering using a pyramidal volume representation to achieve real-time interactive rendering. It constructs a pyramidal volume representation that stores average values and estimated error for each cell. It fits an octtree to the pyramid based on a user-supplied precision threshold. It draws the octtree using a set of splats (footprints), where each splat is scaled to match the size of the projection of the corresponding volume cell. It approximates the splats with RGBA Gouraud-shaded polygons for efficient rasterization on modern graphics workstations. A method to adjust splat radii to prevent holes between splats when samples are elevated in the normal direction of the base plane, by scaling the radius based on the angle between the splat normal and the base plane normal. The radius r is calculated as: r = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}\mu}{0.1 + 0.9\langle n, nB \rangle} where r is the radius, \mu is the sampling step size of the regular grid, n is the normal vector of the splat, and nB is the normal vector of the base plane. The constant 0.1 in the denominator establishes scaling and prevents division by zero or excessively large radii when the dot product is small. The constant 0.9 in the denominator controls the maximal radius increase; when \langle n, nB \rangle = 1, the denominator is 1.0, and r = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}\mu. If samples are elevated in the normal direction of the plane, holes may occur between splats if radii are not adjusted. A large angle between the splat normal and the plane normal indicates large variance between neighboring elevation values, resulting in increased spatial gaps, necessitating larger radii. A method for modeling dynamic Gaussians for time-varying content. It develops a spatiotemporal structure encoder to capture deformations of both positions and colors over time. A method that mitigates popping artifacts caused by the sorting procedure in volume splatting. A method that enhances robustness by detecting outliers in a richer, pre-trained feature space to ignore transient distractors. Splatting was originally proposed by Lee Westover in 1990. It is based on the idea of treating each voxel as a fuzzy spherical ball (3D Gaussian) projected onto the screen, determining how every pixel might be affected by that voxel, as opposed to ray-casting which determines how every voxel affects a pixel. The continuous volume is defined as a collection of smooth functions (Gaussians) centered at each voxel, with density assigned at the center and dropping off according to the distribution. The term "splat" refers to the footprint left on the image plane, analogous to throwing a cube of gelatinous material onto the plane. Axis-aligned sheet buffered splatting causes 'popping' artifacts when viewing angles change around 45 degrees because kernels in consecutive sheets are composited together while kernels on the same sheet are added together, and addition/compositing are not equivalent. To mitigate this, image-aligned sheet buffered splatting aligns sheet buffers parallel with the image plane regardless of volume orientation, slicing the volume into thin slabs representing portions of the line integral through the entire kernel. Splatting algorithms suffer from time-consuming computations necessary to compute the view-dependent filters with which to convolute the voxels in the volume. Observations showed that overall splatting offers a rendering quality similar to that of ray casting, and both ray casting and splatting provided in some cases better image qualities than shear-warp. This is because in shear-warp, rendered voxels were interpolated without prior opacity and color being incorporated, whereas splatting incorporates these during the footprint projection. name: EWA Splatting
head: Elliptical Weighted Average Splatting
body: EWA Splatting is an object-order rendering technique that approximates the volumetric integration of 3D Gaussian primitives by projecting them into 2D elliptical disks (splats) and rasterizing them as screen-space filters. It solves the computational cost of ray-marching by assuming Gaussians do not overlap and are sorted by view-space depth, trading continuous extinction accumulation for efficient, hole-free reconstruction. It differs from standard point rendering by using anisotropic, band-limited elliptical footprints derived from the Gaussian covariance, whereas simplified variants use screen-aligned spherical impostors with isotropic falloff. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by weight wi, mean position \boldsymbol{\mu}i (in camera space), and 3 \times 3 covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i. Camera projection matrix \mathbf{P} and view matrix \mathbf{W}. Outputs: A 2D image with accumulated color and depth. Data Structures: Surfel vertex buffer layout (stride 64 bytes): Offset 0: center (vec3, 3 floats) Offset 12: tangentu (vec3, 3 floats) Offset 24: tangentv (vec3, 3 floats) Offset 36: clippingplane (vec3, 3 floats) Offset 48: colorrgba (vec4, 4 unsigned bytes) Uniforms: UniformBufferParameter: color (vec3, offset 0), shininess (float, offset 12), radiusscale (float, offset 16), ewaradius (float, offset 20), epsilon (float, offset 24). Total 8 floats. UniformBufferFrustum: 6 frustum planes (vec4). UniformBufferRaycast: projectionmatrixinv (mat4), viewport (vec4). Steps: 1. Frustum Culling: Extract 6 frustum planes from the projection matrix. A splat is visible if its bounding sphere intersects the view frustum. python def extractfrustumplanes(P): frustumplanes = [] for i in range(6): sign = -1.0 if i % 2 == 0 else 1.0 rowidx = i // 2 plane = [P[3][j] + sign P[rowidx][j] for j in range(4)] norm = (plane[0]2 + plane[1]2 + plane[2]2)0.5 plane = [x / norm for x in plane] frustumplanes.append(plane) return frustumplanes 2. 2D Gaussian Projection (EWA): Project the 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space to determine the splat's shape and position. Compute the Jacobian \mathbf{J} of the perspective projection, approximated by first-order Taylor expansion at the Gaussian mean \boldsymbol{\mu}: \mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix} 1/\mu2 & 0 & -\mu0/\mu2^2 \\ 0 & 1/\mu2 & -\mu1/\mu2^2 \\ \mu0/l & \mu1/l & \mu2/l \end{pmatrix} where l = \|\boldsymbol{\mu}\|2 and \boldsymbol{\mu} = (\mu0, \mu1, \mu2) is the mean in camera space. Compute the projected 2D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}': \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{J}^T where \mathbf{W} transforms to camera space. The projected 2D Gaussian is \mathcal{G}2^n(\mathbf{p}, wi, \boldsymbol{\mu}'i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i). The weight w is preserved across projection. 3. Sorting: Sort all visible Gaussians by their view-space depth (z-coordinate of \boldsymbol{\mu}i) from front to back. 4. Rasterization (Soft Z-Buffer Passes): Standard EWA applies a bandlimiting prefilter to avoid frequencies higher than the Nyquist frequency. A common GPU implementation uses a three-pass soft z-buffer approach with spherical impostors. Bandlimiting Prefilter: Generate a 1D filter kernel texture using \sigma = 0.316228 to approximate the prefilter. python def generatefilterkernel(): sigma = 0.316228 kernel = [] for i in range(256): x = i / 255.0 w = (x x) / (2.0 sigma) kernel.append(math.exp(-w)) return kernel Pass 1 (Visibility/Depth): Bind FBO, clear color and depth buffers. Render splats as point sprites. Set glPointSize based on the projected radius r: s = h \cdot \cot\left(\frac{\theta{fov}}{2}\right) \cdot \frac{r}{w{clip}} where h is viewport height, \theta{fov} is FOV, and w{clip} is clip-space w. Compute analytic front-surface depth of the sphere impostor for each fragment: z{surface} = z{center} - \sqrt{r^2 - x^2 - y^2} where x, y are fragment coordinates relative to splat center. Push depth back by \varepsilon before writing to define a thin depth slab. Discard fragments outside the unit disk. Write only depth; mask off color. Pass 2 (Attribute Blending): Disable depth writes and depth testing. Set blending to pure additive (GLONE, GLONE). Rasterize splats again. For each fragment, compare its depth against the depth texture from Pass 1. Discard fragments falling behind the \varepsilon slab. Accumulate attributes with weight w = w{radial} \cdot w{depth}: Radial falloff: w{radial} = 1 - \frac{d}{r}, where d is distance from splat center. Depth falloff: w{depth} = \frac{z{surface} - z{frag}}{\varepsilon}, where z{frag} is current fragment depth. Pass 3 (Normalization/Shading): Render a full-screen quad. Compute weighted average color and normal: \mathbf{c} = \frac{\sumi wi \mathbf{c}i}{\sumi wi}, \quad \mathbf{n} = \frac{\sumi wi \mathbf{n}i}{\lVert \sumi wi \mathbf{n}i \rVert} Apply Phong lighting. Parameters: mepsilon: Epsilon value for numerical stability, default 1.0 \times 10^{-3}. Defines the thickness of the thin depth slab around the visible surface. mradiusscale: Scale factor for splat radius, default 1.0. mewaradius: Radius for EWA filter approximation, default 1.0. sigma: Gaussian filter kernel parameter, 0.316228. mshininess: Shininess value for Phong splatting, default 8.0. msmooth: Boolean flag that enables depth and normal texture attachment on the FBO, and enables blending/smoothing in the finalization pass. mmultisample: Boolean flag that enables multisampling. Pitfalls: Botsch et al.'s approximation of screen-space extents can underestimate splat size, causing chopping artifacts; a safety factor >1 is required. Zwicker et al.'s centralized conics approach is numerically unstable when projection approaches a line. Weyrich et al.'s method yields NDC coordinates, preventing frustum culling, and fails if the projected ellipse becomes a parabola or hyperbola. EWA filter requires soft z-buffer to be active; otherwise, it is disabled. Depth mask is explicitly disabled during splatting when soft z-buffer is enabled to allow alpha blending to accumulate depth correctly. Converts point clouds to continuous shaded surfaces via G-buffers and deferred shading, differing from standard splatting by deferring lighting calculations to a final pass [1072-deferred-surface-splatting.md]. Choose it when surface normals and deferred shading are required [1072-deferred-surface-splatting.md]. A parameterization scheme for EWA-based splatting that scales the learned weight \theta so the projected amplitude equals \theta at the thinnest view, differing from standard EWA by ensuring robust gradient-descent optimization [1155-opacity-thin-side-ots.md]. Choose it when training 3D Gaussians requires stable opacity gradients [1155-opacity-thin-side-ots.md]. Extends EWA to irregular grids using elliptical Radial Basis Functions and sheet buffers, differing from standard EWA by supporting volume rendering on non-uniform structures [1186-gpu-accelerated-volume-splatting-with-elliptical-rbfs.md]. Choose it for GPU-accelerated volume rendering on irregular point distributions [1186-gpu-accelerated-volume-splatting-with-elliptical-rbfs.md]. Represents points as 3D ellipsoids and warps slicing planes to unit sphere coordinates for efficient GPU rasterization, differing from standard EWA by avoiding expensive square roots and conditional statements during ellipsoid slicing [1290-ellipsoidal-kernel-splatting-with-warped-slicing.md]. Choose it when rendering dense 3D ellipsoidal kernels with hard-wired GPU texture mapping [1290-ellipsoidal-kernel-splatting-with-warped-slicing.md]. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Hole-free reconstruction, efficient rasterization, avoids expensive volume integration. Limitations: Assumes no overlap; continuous extinction is ignored. Numerical instability when projection approaches a line, or failure if projected ellipse becomes a parabola or hyperbola. When to use: Real-time rendering of point clouds or Gaussian splats where efficient rasterization and hole-free reconstruction are prioritized over physical accuracy of attenuation. EWA Splatting originated from the need to render point-sampled surfaces without aliasing or holes. It was formalized by Zwicker et al. (2001) as "Surface Splatting," using Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) filters to project object-space reconstruction filters to screen space. It builds on Gaussian Splatting by providing the rasterization backend for 3D Gaussian primitives, approximating the volumetric integral via 2D projections. name: Post-rasterization Smearing
head: Accumulated Motion Blur, Post-Rasterization Velocity Smearing, Velocity Buffer Smear, Velocity buffer smearing
body: Post-rasterization smearing is a technique to approximate motion blur in voxel buffers by deferring the blurring operation until after the rasterization/splatting phase is complete. Unlike methods that smear individual samples during rasterization, this approach accumulates velocity information in a separate buffer and applies a single, global smear pass. It is chosen when performance is prioritized over handling complex overlapping primitives with divergent motion vectors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel buffer containing density/intensity values, and a separate velocity buffer storing accumulated motion vectors for each voxel. Output: A motion-blurred voxel buffer. Data Structures: 1. Density Buffer: Standard voxel grid storing scalar values (e.g., density, color). 2. Velocity Buffer: A voxel grid of the same dimensions as the density buffer. Each voxel stores a 3D vector (\vec{v}) representing the accumulated motion. Layout: Typically stored as three floating-point values (x, y, z) per voxel. Initialization: Zeroed before the frame begins. Steps: 1. Rasterization/Splatting with Velocity Accumulation: For each primitive (or sample) being rasterized: Determine its motion vector \vec{m} for the current frame. Rasterize the primitive into the density buffer as usual. Add \vec{m} to the corresponding voxels in the velocity buffer. Note: If multiple primitives overlap in a voxel, their velocity vectors are summed (accumulated). 2. Velocity Normalization/Averaging (Optional Variant): To resolve direction ambiguity when multiple primitives overlap, calculate the average motion vector per voxel: \vec{v}{avg} = \frac{\sum \vec{m}i}{N} where N is the number of primitives contributing to that voxel. Pitfall: This averaging can cause visual artifacts if primitives have drastically different velocities. 3. Global Smear Pass: Iterate through every voxel in the density buffer. Retrieve the accumulated velocity \vec{v} from the velocity buffer for that voxel. Smear the voxel's value along \vec{v}. This distributes the value evenly across the voxels touched by the motion vector, preserving the sum of values. Implementation Note: The smear direction is derived directly from the accumulated velocity. If \vec{v} is zero, no smear occurs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def postrasterizationsmearing(densitybuffer, velocitybuffer, primitives): """ densitybuffer: 3D array of floats, initialized to 0 velocitybuffer: 3D array of vec3, initialized to (0,0,0) primitives: list of objects, each with a method getmotionvector() and a rasterizeinto() method """ # Step 1: Accumulate velocities during rasterization for primitive in primitives: motionvec = primitive.getmotionvector() primitive.rasterizeinto(densitybuffer) # Accumulate motion vector into the velocity buffer for affected voxels affectedvoxels = primitive.getaffectedvoxelindices() for voxelidx in affectedvoxels: velocitybuffer[voxelidx] += motionvec # Step 2: Global smear pass blurredbuffer = copy(densitybuffer) for voxelidx in allvoxelsinbuffer: v = velocitybuffer[voxelidx] # If no motion, skip if length(v) == 0: continue # Smear the density value along the velocity vector # This distributes the value evenly across the path defined by v smearvalue = blurredbuffer[voxelidx] clearaffectedvoxels(blurredbuffer, voxelidx, v) distributeevenly(blurredbuffer, voxelidx, v, smearvalue) return blurredbuffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overlapping Primitives with Divergent Velocities: If input primitives overlap and have drastically different motion vectors, it becomes impossible to calculate a valid single direction to smear in. Visual Artifacts: Keeping track of the average motion vector in overlapping voxels can cause visual artifacts in the final render. Camera Motion Cancellation: If the camera moves at the same speed as the primitives, motion should cancel out, resulting in a sharp image. However, because motion blur is baked into the voxel buffer via accumulated velocity, this cancellation is not possible, leading to incorrect blur. Retains both density and velocity buffers and calculates motion blur during rendering. This avoids reduced shading detail in motion-blurred areas but still suffers from the overlapping primitive problem. If the lit volume is voxelized, motion blur can be applied after lighting. This solves the problem of lighting a voxel buffer with motion blur baked in, but still shows artifacts where overlapping primitives have different velocity vectors. Performance: Often faster than smearing each sample as it is written to the buffer, as it requires only a single global smear pass after rasterization. Memory: Requires an additional velocity buffer of the same size as the density buffer, increasing memory usage. Limitations: Poor handling of complex scenes with overlapping primitives having divergent motion vectors. Cannot correctly handle camera motion cancellation. Use Cases: Suitable for simple scenes or when performance is critical and visual artifacts from overlapping divergent motions are acceptable. Microvoxel-based volume renderers may benefit from the variant that retains separate buffers. This method is described in the context of production volume rendering fundamentals, specifically as an alternative to per-sample smearing during rasterization. It is part of a broader discussion on motion blur techniques in voxel-based rendering pipelines. name: Gaussian Splatting
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting, 3DGS, 3DGS representation, EWA Volume Splatting, Elliptical Weighted Average splatting, Gaussian Splat, Volume Splatting, 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization, 3D Gaussian Splat Representation & Band-0 SH Decoding
body: Gaussian Splatting is an object-order direct volume rendering algorithm that represents a scene as a collection of overlapping 3D Gaussian primitives, projecting them onto the image plane and alpha-compositing them to generate the final image. It serves as a fast, high-quality alternative to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by leveraging volumetric rendering principles to preserve differentiability while employing point-based rasterization for efficient training and rendering. Unlike traditional opacity-based splatting, 3DGS assigns a single opacity value per primitive, allowing for constant transparency regardless of viewing direction and enabling the optimization of a well-behaved, bounded scalar. It builds on EWA Splatting but simplifies the formulation by ignoring self-attenuation and approximating perspective projection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of M 3D Gaussians \{gi\}{i=1}^M, where each gi is defined by center \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity \sigmai, and color ci; a camera with intrinsics K and extrinsics W; and image dimensions H \times W. Output: A 2D image I of size H \times W. Data Structures: Each Gaussian splat stores the following fields: pos: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, center position in world space. scale: s \in \mathbb{R}^3, size along each local axis (stored in log space). rot: q \in \mathbb{R}^4, orientation as a unit quaternion. color: ci \in \mathbb{R}^3, RGB color. In the standard format, this is decoded from spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. Band-0 SH coefficients f{dc} \in \mathbb{R}^3 are converted to RGB using C0 = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}} \approx 0.282: \text{color} = \text{clamp}(0.5 + C0 \cdot f{dc}, 0, 1) opacity: \sigmai \in \mathbb{R}, opacity in [0, 1] (stored as a logit). The 3D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i is parameterized via diagonalization \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i = V S V^T, where S = \text{diag}(e^{s1}, e^{s2}, e^{s3}) and V is the rotation matrix derived from the quaternion q. Rendering Pipeline: The rendering process follows these steps: 1. Projection: For each Gaussian i, compute the 2D screen-space covariance matrix \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i. First, transform the 3D covariance to camera coordinates: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i = W \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i W^T. Then, approximate the perspective projection PK around the Gaussian center \boldsymbol{\mu}i using its Jacobian \mathbf{J} \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times3}: PK(\mathbf{x}) \approx PK(\boldsymbol{\mu}i) + \mathbf{J}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i) The projected 2D covariance is: \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i = \mathbf{J} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i \mathbf{J}^T The projected mean is \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}i = PK(\boldsymbol{\mu}i). 2. Rasterization (Splatting): For each pixel p in the image, identify the set of K Gaussians whose projected footprints cover p. This is typically done using a tile-based rasterization strategy. For each covering Gaussian, evaluate the 2D Gaussian value at pixel p: \tilde{G}i(p) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(p - \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}i)^T \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i^{-1} (p - \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}i)\right) 3. Sorting: Sort the K Gaussians intersecting the view ray for pixel p by distance from their centers to the camera position (back-to-front order). Note: This sorting is based on centers, which is an approximation. 4. Alpha-Compositing: Compute the final pixel intensity If by alpha-compositing the sorted Gaussians: If = \sum{i=1}^N ci \tilde{\sigma}i \tilde{G}i(p) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \left(1 - \tilde{\sigma}j \tilde{G}j(p)\right) where N is the number of sorted Gaussians, \tilde{\sigma}i = \sigmai, and \tilde{G}i(p) is the Gaussian value at p. Training and Optimization: The scene parameters \theta (the set of Gaussians) are optimized by minimizing the photometric loss between the rendered image I{\theta,i} and the input view Ii: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \| I{\theta,i} - Ii \|^2 Gradients are backpropagated to update Gaussian parameters using Adam. During training, the number of Gaussians is dynamically adjusted: splitting large Gaussians, cloning those that underfit detail, and pruning those with low opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendergaussiansplats(gaussians, camera, imagewidth, imageheight): import math # Initialize output buffers colorbuffer = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageheight)] alphabuffer = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] # Precompute camera matrices Rcam = camera.extrinsics[:3,:3] tcam = camera.extrinsics[:3, 3] K = camera.intrinsics[:3,:3] projected = [] for g in gaussians: # 1. Build 3D covariance from scale and rotation S = [[math.exp(g.scale[0]), 0, 0], [0, math.exp(g.scale[1]), 0], [0, 0, math.exp(g.scale[2])]] V = quaterniontorotationmatrix(g.rot) Sigma3d = matmul(matmul(V, S), transpose(V)) # 2. Transform to camera space Sigmacam = matmul(matmul(Rcam, Sigma3d), transpose(Rcam)) # 3. Project center to camera space mucam = vec3add(matmul(Rcam, g.pos), tcam) z = mucam[2] if z <= 0.0: continue # Behind camera # 4. Compute Jacobian of perspective projection K23 = [K[0][:3], K[1][:3]] J = [[K23[r][c] / z for c in range(3)] for r in range(2)] for r in range(2): J[r][2] -= (K23[r][0]mucam[0] + K23[r][1]mucam[1] + K23[r][2]mucam[2]) / (z z) # 5. Project covariance and stabilize Sigma2d = matmul(matmul(J, Sigmacam), transpose(J)) Sigma2d[0][0] += 0.3 Sigma2d[1][1] += 0.3 # 6. Project center to screen mu2dhom = matmul(K, [mucam[0], mucam[1], mucam[2], 1.0]) mu2d = [mu2dhom[0] / mu2dhom[2], mu2dhom[1] / mu2dhom[2]] # 7. Compute bounding box (3-sigma extent) extentx = 3.0 math.sqrt(Sigma2d[0][0]) extenty = 3.0 math.sqrt(Sigma2d[1][1]) xmin, xmax = int(mu2d[0] - extentx), int(mu2d[0] + extentx) ymin, ymax = int(mu2d[1] - A rendering technique that treats each point as a Gaussian reconstruction kernel on the surface, projects it into screen space, and convolves it with a low-pass filter to produce a resampling filter actually rasterized. This implementation uses a simplified kernel: screen-aligned spherical impostors with isotropic linear falloff, rasterized as plain point sprites, trading anisotropic, correctly band-limited footprint for a formulation needing no per-point normals or radii. A rendering approach that correctly accounts for the attenuation of a Gaussian's own extinction along the ray path (self-attenuation), rather than ignoring it or using a first-order Taylor approximation. An optimization for the inner pixel loop of a Gaussian splatting rasterizer that hoists row-constant terms outside the inner (column) loop to minimize arithmetic operations per pixel. Computes the 2D screen-space covariance matrix and its inverse for a 3D Gaussian splat, ensuring numerical stability by adding a small epsilon to the diagonal to guarantee positive definiteness. A method that separates intrinsic and dynamic appearance attributes per Gaussian point to mitigate transient occlusions and photometric variations. It employs an adaptive sampling strategy, leverages 2D visibility maps, uses depth regularization, and aligns pixel appearance features from image triplanes directly to 3D Gaussians. A method for 'in-the-wild' settings that integrates robust DINO features and a lightweight appearance modeling module within the 3DGS framework. It handles unconstrained photo collections. A method for modeling dynamic Gaussians for time-varying content. It develops a spatiotemporal structure encoder to capture deformations of both positions and colors over time. An extension that introduces 2D and 3D Gaussian filters to improve robustness to aliasing caused by resolution changes. A method that employs an unscented transform for more precise Gaussian projection onto the image plane, improving the affine approximation of the projection operator. A method that extends 3DGS by conditioning Gaussians on learned appearance embeddings and training unsupervised transient Gaussians to ignore occluders. A method that uses a feed-forward network (FFN) for monocular reconstruction, generating 3DGS scenes by estimating depth from a single view. A method that tokenizes two to four images and their camera parameters, concatenates them, and passes them through a transformer block whose output tokens are decoded into Gaussian parameters. A method that incorporates an epipolar transformer to generalize features between two views, paired with a probabilistic prediction of Gaussians aligned along camera-to-pixel rays. A method that improves sparse-view reconstruction by defining two independent reconstructions and comparing them to discard inaccurate Gaussians. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Complex scenes require approximately 200,000–500,000 Gaussians, resulting in significant memory and storage demands. Each Gaussian stores position, scale, rotation, SH coefficients, and opacity. Time: Rendering is O(M \cdot A), where M is the number of Gaussians and A is the average number of splats per pixel. Training uses gradient descent to update Gaussian parameters, but the rasterization pipeline itself is highly optimized for real-time performance. Performance: 3DGS enables real-time rendering capabilities for novel view synthesis. It is significantly faster than NeRFs for rendering, as it avoids the need for volumetric ray marching and MLP evaluation. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High-quality view synthesis, real-time rendering, differentiable optimization. Limitations: High memory footprint. The emission-absorption model limits performance on highly reflective surfaces and prevents relighting. Standard 3DGS uses a dilation-based filter which fails to suppress high-frequency artifacts when varying focal length or camera distance. Approximations in visibility resolution (sorting by centers) can cause popping artifacts. Self-attenuation is not treated correctly. When to Use: Use for real-time novel view synthesis of static scenes with moderate complexity. Avoid for scenes with highly reflective surfaces or when relighting is required. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. It builds on EWA Volume Splatting and other point-based rendering works. The method was developed to overcome the computational cost of evaluating the volume rendering equation via quadrature, which requires querying points outside Gaussian supports. It provides a fast, high-quality alternative to NeRF by using a hybrid, primitive-based rendering method. name: Unnormalized 3D Gaussian Function
head: 3D Gaussian amplitude, Unnormalized Gaussian
body: The Unnormalized 3D Gaussian Function is a Gaussian representation used in 3D Gaussian Splatting where the amplitude a at the mean \boldsymbol{\mu} equals the opacity, representing the peak capacity to block or emit light. It differs from the Normalized 3D Gaussian Function by parameterizing the function via its peak value rather than its integral, making a the intensity at the center rather than the total light capacity. Inputs: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The query point in 3D space. a \in \mathbb{R}: The amplitude (peak value) at the mean. \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The mean position (center) of the Gaussian. \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: The covariance matrix defining the shape and orientation. Outputs: g \in \mathbb{R}: The value of the unnormalized Gaussian function at \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: The function requires the covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} and its inverse \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}. In implementation, \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is often derived from a rotation matrix \mathbf{R} and a scaling vector \mathbf{s} such that \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T, where \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}). Formulas: The unnormalized Gaussian function \mathcal{G}D^\mu is defined as: \mathcal{G}D^\mu(\mathbf{x}, a, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = a \mathcal{I}D(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \mathcal{N}D(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) Where \mathcal{N}D is the standard D-dimensional Gaussian probability density function (PDF): \mathcal{N}D(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{\mathcal{I}D(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})} And \mathcal{I}D(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) is the unbounded integral of the exponential part, ensuring the PDF integrates to one: \mathcal{I}D(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \sqrt{(2\pi)^D \det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})} Substituting the PDF into the unnormalized definition, the \mathcal{I}D(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) terms cancel out, yielding the practical computation formula: \mathcal{G}D^\mu(\mathbf{x}, a, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = a e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})} Conversion to Normalized Weight: To convert between the unnormalized amplitude a and the normalized weight w (where w is the integral of the function over all space), the following relationship holds: a = \frac{w}{\mathcal{I}D(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def unnormalizedgaussian(x, a, mu, Sigmainv): """ Computes the value of the unnormalized 3D Gaussian function. Args: x: Query point (3,) a: Amplitude at the mean (scalar) mu: Mean position (3,) Sigmainv: Inverse covariance matrix (3, 3) Returns: Value of the Gaussian at x """ diff = [x[i] - mu[i] for i in range(3)] exponent = 0.0 for i in range(3): rowsum = 0.0 for j in range(3): rowsum += Sigmainv[i][j] diff[j] exponent += diff[i] rowsum return a math.exp(-0.5 exponent) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: If \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is singular (non-invertible), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} cannot be computed. In practice, \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is constructed from a rotation and scaling, ensuring it remains positive semi-definite. Degenerate scaling (zero scale) leads to infinite amplitude for a fixed weight w, or zero width for a fixed amplitude a. Precision: For points far from \boldsymbol{\mu}, the exponent becomes large and negative, potentially causing underflow to zero. This is standard behavior for Gaussian splatting cutoffs. Uses weight w as the integral rather than peak amplitude. Choose when the total light capacity is the primary physical quantity of interest. Time Complexity: O(1) per evaluation, dominated by the matrix-vector multiplication in the exponent. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary storage per Gaussian for the inverse covariance. Strengths: Directly parameterizes the peak intensity, which aligns with how opacity is often interpreted in rendering (peak blocking/emission). Limitations: The value at the mean depends on the spread of the Gaussian; a wider Gaussian with the same peak amplitude a contributes less total energy than a narrow one. This makes a less intuitive for conservation of energy compared to w. The unnormalized Gaussian function is defined in as a Gaussian representation used in 3D Gaussian Splatting where the amplitude at the mean equals the opacity. It serves as a standard mathematical primitive for spatial distribution modeling in splatting-based rendering pipelines.
