name: 2D Texture-Based Volume Rendering
head: Object-aligned slice projection, Proxy geometry with 2D textures, Texture-based VR with 2D textures, VR Basado en Texturas 2D, View-Aligned Slice Rendering, VolumeRover2, cvc::volslice
body: 2D Texture-Based Volume Rendering is a GPU-accelerated object-order technique that represents volumetric data as stacks of 2D textures, projecting them onto axis-aligned proxy geometry and compositing them back-to-front using hardware blending. Unlike 3D texture methods that sample a single trilinearly interpolated volume, this approach relies on bilinear interpolation of 2D slices, making it historically significant for early real-time rendering but prone to specific interpolation artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset (dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz), a camera view matrix (local-to-clip), and a transfer function (color/opacity mapping). Output: A 2D image with accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: 1. 2D Texture Stacks: The volume is decomposed into three sets of 2D textures, one for each axis (X, Y, Z). Format: GLLUMINANCE (stores single-component opacity). Note: GLINTENSITY is unsupported on some legacy hardware. Dimensions: Power-of-two padding. If the original volume dimension is D, the texture width/height is the smallest power of two P \ge D. Content: Pre-classified opacity values. Color is applied during rendering via multiplication with a user-defined tissue color. Total Textures: N{total} = Dx + Dy + Dz. Memory: P^2 \times N{total} bytes (assuming 1 byte per texel). 2. Proxy Geometry: Axis-aligned quadrilaterals (or triangle fans) representing the slices. Texture Coordinates: Computed in the vertex shader as an affine map of model coordinates (vertexMC), eliminating the need for a separate texture coordinate array. Clipping: Generated using a 256-case plane/cube clipping table to handle intersections with the volume bounding box. 3. Transfer Function: A 256x1 RGBA Look-Up Table (LUT). Numbered Steps: 1. Preparation (Offline/Initialization): For each axis A \in \{X, Y, Z\}: Extract 2D slices perpendicular to A. Pad each slice to power-of-two dimensions (P \times P). Upload to GPU as GLLUMINANCE textures. 2. Render Loop (Per Frame): Axis Selection: Calculate the angle between the volume's principal axes and the projection plane (or camera view direction). Select the axis A{best} with the smallest angle. Slice Count Calculation: Compute the number of slices N to render: N = 2 \cdot (10 + \text{max\planes} \cdot q^3) where \text{max\planes} is the maximum allowed planes and q is a quality factor. Cap: Limit N to 10 \cdot \text{max\planes} per frame. Sweep Generation: Compute slice positions based on the camera's local-to-clip matrix and the volume's local bounding box. Perform the sweep in "legacy ratio space" (normalized coordinates) to preserve plane parallelism and spacing, then map to the caller's box via uniform scale and translation. Generate triangle-fan polygons for each slice using the 256-case plane/cube clipping table. Order polygons back-to-front relative to the camera. Culling/Clipping: Near-plane peel: Dim or cull slices closer than a specific fraction of the diagonal to the near plane. Sub-cube crop: Clip texture coordinates to valid volume bounds to prevent sampling outside the volume. Rendering: Bind the selected axis's texture stack. Set blend state: SRCALPHA / ONEMINUSSRCALPHA, depth writing disabled. For each slice polygon (back-to-front): Vertex Shader: Compute texture coordinates from vertex model coordinates. Fragment Shader: Sample the 2D texture. Multiply the sampled luminance (opacity) by the user-defined tissue color. Hardware Blending: Accumulate color and opacity into the framebuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def render2dtexturevolume(volumedata, cameramatrix, transferfunction, maxplanes, quality): # Inputs: volumedata (Dx, Dy, Dz), cameramatrix (4x4 local-to-clip), # transferfunction (256x4 RGBA LUT), maxplanes (int), quality (float) # Assumes texturesX, texturesY, texturesZ are pre-uploaded as P x P GLLUMINANCE textures # 1. Axis Selection viewvector = normalize([-cameramatrix[0][2], -cameramatrix[1][2], -cameramatrix[2][2]]) axes = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]] angles = [1.0 - dot(axis, viewvector) for axis in axes] bestaxis = ['X', 'Y', 'Z'][argmin(angles)] # 2. Determine Slice Count N = 2 (10 + maxplanes (quality 3)) N = min(N, 10 maxplanes) # 3. Generate Slices # Compute slice positions in legacy ratio space, then map to caller's box slicepositions = [i / N for i in range(N)] # Legacy ratio space positions polygons = [] for pos in slicepositions: # Generate triangle-fan polygon using 256-case plane/cube clipping table # Order polygons back-to-front relative to camera polygons.append(generatefanpolygon(pos, volumebox)) # 4. Render setblendmode(SRCALPHA, ONEMINUSSRCALPHA) setdepthwrite(False) bindtexturestack(textures[bestaxis]) for poly in polygons: # Vertex shader computes texcoords as affine map of vertexMC # Fragment shader samples 2D texture, multiplies luminance by tissue color drawpolygon(poly) def dot(v1, v2): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) def normalize(v): mag = dot(v, v) 0.5 return [x / mag for x in v] def argmin(lst): return lst.index(min(lst)) def generatefanpolygon(planepos, volumebox): # Uses 256-case plane/cube clipping table to intersect plane with box # Returns a triangle-fan geometry with 3D texture coordinates return {"vertices": [], "texcoords": [], "order": "back-to-front"} def setblendmode(src, dst): # Configures hardware blending state pass def setdepthwrite(enabled): # Disables depth buffer writes pass def bindtexturestack(stack): # Binds the selected axis texture set to GPU pass def drawpolygon(poly): # Rasterizes polygon, invoking vertex/fragment shaders pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bilinear Interpolation Artifacts: Since only 2D textures are used, interpolation is bilinear. This ignores the third dimension, causing visible "banding" artifacts around the volume. Popping Artifacts: Switching between X, Y, and Z texture sets during rotation causes visible jumps due to changes in interpolation artifacts or memory swap times. Sampling Frequency Change: Rotating the camera changes the sampling frequency. If planes become perpendicular to the projection plane, they may disappear from the final image. VTK OIT Conflict: VTK 9's default Order-Independent Translucency (OIT) breaks compositing by averaging colors (X-ray look). Must disable OIT (UseOITOff) to use legacy blending. Off-Origin Volume Bug: If the volume box is offset from the origin, VTK's AUTO VBO shift-scale re-centers vertex data. Deriving texcoords from vertexMC then reads the wrong corner (density 0). Fix: Set DISABLESHIFTSCALE. GLES3 Precision: On WebGL2/GLES3, sampler3D has no default precision (compile error if unqualified) and sampler2D defaults to lowp (insufficient for LUT addressing). Both must be declared highp. A variant that eliminates stack-switching and jagged boundary artifacts by generating proxy geometry using multiple object-aligned 2D texture stacks clipped by planes extending from the front-facing edges of the volume's bounding box. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of slices N and the number of pixels covered by the proxy geometry. N is determined by the formula N = 2 \cdot (10 + \text{max\planes} \cdot q^3). Memory Complexity: O(P^2 \cdot (Dx + Dy + Dz)) for storing 2D texture stacks, where P is the power-of-two padding dimension. For a 181 \times 217 \times 181 volume, this requires 579 textures of 256 \times 256 pixels, totaling ~37.9 MB. Performance: Very fast on modern GPUs due to reliance on rasterization hardware and hardware blending. Historically enabled real-time rendering on early GPUs (e.g., GeForce 256). Strengths: Intuitive, easy to implement, leverages mature 2D texture hardware, efficient for interactivity. Limitations: Severe artifacts from bilinear interpolation (banding), popping artifacts during axis switching, reduced accuracy compared to trilinear interpolation. When to Use: Legacy hardware, simple interactive visualization where speed is prioritized over high-fidelity volume quality. When Not to Use: High-quality offline rendering, scenes requiring precise trilinear interpolation, or when popping artifacts are unacceptable. Origin: Developed after 2D texture mapping became available on GPUs, preceding 3D texture support. Engel et al. provided an excellent introduction to these algorithms. History: Studied extensively in the early 2000s (e.g., VolumeRover2 by Thane Bajaj, UT Austin, 2002-2003). Rezk-Salama et al. later proposed multi-texture methods to approximate trilinear interpolation using bilinear operations. Usage: Used in early real-time volume renderers and educational demonstrations. Ported to modern contexts like cvc::volslice for compatibility with legacy rendering pipelines. name: Novel Sampling Scheme for Slice Based Volume Rendering
head: Novel method, Our novel method
body: A volume rendering technique that generates proxy geometry using multiple object-aligned 2D texture stacks clipped by planes extending from the front-facing edges of the volume's bounding box in the viewing direction, eliminating stack-switching artifacts and jagged boundary artifacts. Unlike traditional 2D texture-based volume rendering which selects a single stack causing visible color/opacity shifts during rotation, this method renders multiple clipped stacks simultaneously. It approximates the uniform sampling pattern of ray casting more closely than spherical shell approaches while avoiding their large geometry overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data stored in three 2D texture stacks (X, Y, Z aligned). Viewing direction vector \mathbf{v}. Output: Composite image via back-to-front or front-to-back blending of clipped proxy geometry. Data Structures: Volume Representation: Three separate 2D texture arrays. Each array represents slices of the volume along one principal axis (X, Y, or Z). Proxy Geometry: A set of quadrilateral primitives representing the visible portions of the three stacks. These are generated by clipping the full stacks against specific planes. Steps: 1. Identify Front-Facing Edges: Determine the edges of the volume's bounding box that are front-facing relative to the current viewing direction \mathbf{v}. 2. Generate Clip Planes: Extend the identified front-facing edges into infinite planes that point in the viewing direction \mathbf{v}. These planes serve to separate the stacks and define the visible region for each stack relative to the viewer. 3. Clip Stacks: Clip the three object-aligned stacks (X, Y, Z) adjacent to these edges using the generated planes. The clipping removes geometry that would otherwise cause overlap or incorrect sampling. 4. Scale Slice Distance: To approximate uniform sampling along the view ray, scale the distance between slices in each stack. The slice distance d is scaled by the secant of the angle \theta between the viewing direction and the stack normal \mathbf{n}. Formula: d{scaled} = d \cdot \sec(\theta). Approximation: Since \theta varies across a slice, the scaling factor is approximated by the secant of the angle between the stack normal and the ray to the slice center. 5. Render: Draw the remaining geometry of the three stacks. The stacks do not overlap in depth after clipping, so they can be drawn in any order (front-to-back or back-to-front). This allows optimization for out-of-core data by drawing resident cache data first. 6. Texture Sampling: Because the adjusted spacing may not align with the original discrete texture slices, the shader must interpolate between two 2D textures if hardware supports it, or repeat the same texture for multiple slices on older hardware. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendernovelsampling(volumestacks, viewdirection, rayorigin, raydirection, boundingbox, numslices): """ volumestacks: dict with keys 'X', 'Y', 'Z', each containing 3D voxel arrays viewdirection: normalized 3D vector v rayorigin, raydirection: camera ray for current pixel boundingbox: (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz) numslices: number of slices per stack """ # 1. Ray-box intersection to find entry and exit distances tmin, tmax = rayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, boundingbox) if tmax < 0 or tmin > tmax: return 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # Ray misses volume # 2. Compute secant scaling factors for each stack axis stacknormals = {'X': (1.0, 0.0, 0.0), 'Y': (0.0, 1.0, 0.0), 'Z': (0.0, 0.0, 1.0)} secants = {} for axis, normal in stacknormals.items(): costheta = dot(raydirection, normal) # Avoid division by zero if ray is parallel to stack plane if abs(costheta) < 1e-6: secants[axis] = 1.0 else: secants[axis] = 1.0 / abs(costheta) # 3. Initialize blending accumulators r, g, b, a = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 alphathreshold = 0.99 # 4. March along ray and sample each stack with secant-corrected step size for axis in ['X', 'Y', 'Z']: secant = secants[axis] stepsize = (tmax - tmin) / numslices secant t = tmin while t < tmax and a < alphathreshold: samplepos = rayorigin + t raydirection # Check bounds if not isinsidebox(samplepos, boundingbox): t += stepsize continue # Sample texture (standard trilinear interpolation) color = samplestack(volumestacks[axis], samplepos) alpha = color[3] # Front-to-back blending r = r + color[0] alpha (1.0 - a) g = g + color[1] alpha (1.0 - a) b = b + color[2] alpha (1.0 - a) a = a + alpha (1.0 - a) t += stepsize return r, g, b, a def rayboxintersection(origin, direction, box): invdir = (1.0 / direction[0], 1.0 / direction[1], 1.0 / direction[2]) t1 = (box[0] - origin[0]) invdir[0] t2 = (box[3] - origin[0]) invdir[0] t3 = (box[1] - origin[1]) invdir[1] t4 = (box[4] - origin[1]) invdir[1] t5 = (box[2] - origin[2]) invdir[2] t6 = (box[5] - origin[2]) invdir[2] tmin = max(max(min(t1, t2), min(t3, t4)), min(t5, t6)) tmax = min(min(max(t1, t2), max(t3, t4)), max(t5, t6)) return tmin, tmax def isinsidebox(pos, box): return box[0] <= pos[0] <= box[3] and box[1] <= pos[1] <= box[4] and box[2] <= pos[2] <= box[5] def samplestack(stackdata, pos): # Standard texture coordinate mapping and trilinear interpolation # Maps world position to 2D texture coordinates based on stack orientation return (0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.8) Parameters: Secant Scaling Factor: Approximated by \sec(\theta) where \theta is the angle between the stack normal and the ray to the slice center. Stack Selection: All three stacks are used, not just the most perpendicular one. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stack Switching Artifacts: Traditional methods switch between stacks, causing color/opacity jumps. This method eliminates this by using all stacks simultaneously. Jagged Boundary Artifacts: View-aligned slicing suffers from jagged edges. This method avoids them by using object-aligned slices clipped by planes. Performance Overhead: On ultra-mobile hardware (iPod touch 3rd gen, iPhone 3Gs, Intel GMA), performance drops by ~20% compared to single-stack object-aligned rendering due to additional slices drawn from secant correction. Geometry Generation Bottleneck: Clipping actual stacks on the GPU sends large amounts of unused geometry. Clipping on the CPU becomes a bottleneck. An optimization for generating proxy geometry by clipping the bounding box before stack generation and marching along it with secant-corrected step size, performed on the CPU to avoid GPU overhead. Definition: Instead of generating full stacks and clipping them, the bounding box is clipped first. The stacks are then generated by marching along the clipped bounding box. Steps: 1. Clip the bounding box using the view-direction planes. 2. March along the clipped bounding box with the secant-corrected step size to generate quadrilateral geometry. Pitfalls: GPU-based clipping of all three stacks results in significant overhead due to sending large amounts of geometry that are never rendered. CPU-based clipping of the actual stacks becomes a bottleneck. Comparison: Clipping the bounding box instead of the stacks ensures generated geometry remains quadrilateral because clip planes only clip away parts perpendicular to the stack generation direction. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but performance is affected by the number of slices drawn. Secant correction increases the number of slices, leading to a ~20% performance drop on ultra-mobile hardware compared to single-stack methods. Memory Complexity: Requires storing three 2D texture stacks. No 3D texture memory required, making it suitable for devices lacking 3D texture support. Measured Performance: Ultra-mobile hardware (iPod touch 3rd gen, iPhone 3Gs, Intel GMA): ~20% slower than object-aligned implementation. NVIDIA Quadro 5800 (core data): ~30% faster than view-aligned slicing. ATI/AMD Radeon 5970 (out-of-core): ~25% faster than view-aligned slicing. Strengths: Eliminates stack-switching artifacts; eliminates jagged boundary artifacts; better performance than view-aligned slicing on high-end GPUs; suitable for hardware without 3D texture support. Limitations: ~20% performance penalty on low-end hardware compared to single-stack methods; geometry generation can be a bottleneck if not optimized. When to Use: Devices lacking 3D texture support; scenarios requiring high-quality rendering without stack-switching artifacts; high-end GPUs where view-aligned slicing is too slow or artifact-prone. Originated from the work of Rezk-Salama et al. [RSEB∗00], who extended Cullip and Neumann's [CN94] and Lacroute et al.'s [LL94] ideas to develop 2D object-aligned stack techniques for hardware incapable of 3D texturing. The novel method was presented as an extension to overcome the stack-switching artifacts of these earlier approaches. It was introduced in the paper "A New Sampling Scheme for Slice Based Volume Rendering". A New Sampling Scheme for Slice Based Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/vg/vg10/001-004, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Tetrahedral Volume Rendering
head: BT Volume Rendering, Basis Tensor Volume Rendering, Cell Projection with GPGPU, DiffTetVR Tetrahedral Volume Rendering, Differentiable Tetrahedral Volume Rendering, GPU-Accelerated Cell Projection (Tetrahedral), Isosurface rendering using BT volumes, PTINT
body: Tetrahedral Volume Rendering (TetVR) is a cell-projection method that renders unstructured tetrahedral meshes by projecting individual tetrahedra onto the screen and compositing them in depth order. It solves the problem of accurately visualizing complex, non-uniform volumetric data (such as finite element analysis results or dark matter simulations) where regular grid-based ray marching fails or introduces sampling artifacts. Unlike Projected Tetrahedra which often relies on explicit isosurface extraction or simpler blending, TetVR supports arbitrary isosurface values and partial pre-integration directly within the projection pipeline, enabling hybrid volume/isosurface visualization. It differs from Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO) by using hardware rasterization and screen-space classification to determine visibility order, trading exact topological correctness for GPU acceleration. The method typically employs a two-pass GPU pipeline (or a rasterization-based forward pass with CPU/GPU sorting) to project tetrahedra, compute intersection parameters, and render final colors. Inputs: Tetrahedral mesh (vertices, connectivity), scalar field values (stored per vertex or in a Tetrahedral Texture), gradient vectors (precomputed per vertex), transfer function (TF), camera parameters (view, projection matrices). Outputs: Final color and opacity image. 1. Tetrahedral Texture: 1D or 2D texture where each texel corresponds to one tetrahedron. Contains 4 uint indices pointing to vertex data. 2. Vertex Texture: RGBA texture, 32 bits per component. RGB fields store vertex coordinates (x, y, z); A field stores the scalar value s. 3. Gradient Texture: RGB texture, 32 bits per component. Stores precomputed gradient vectors \nabla s at vertices. Same size and indexing as Vertex Texture. 4. Classification Texture: 1D texture (8 bits per component) containing a Ternary Truth Table. Maps combined cross-product test results to projection class indices. 5. MRT Frame Buffers (First Pass Output): Four 2D RGBA textures (32 bits per component): Texture 1: Intersection coords (x{vi}, y{vi}) (Class 2 only), centroid cz, Truth Table index id{TTT}. Texture 2: Front/back scalars sf, sb, thickness l, triangle count. Texture 3: Front gradient vector gf. Texture 4: Back gradient vector gb. 6. Global Arrays (Intermediate CPU Pass): Vertex Array: Stores \{x, y, z\} coordinates. Color Array: Stores \{sf, sb, l\} for on-the-fly color computation. Gradient Arrays: Stored in normal and secondary color arrays. For thin vertices, sf=sb, l=0, gf=gb. Indices Array: Divided into n groups (one per tetrahedron). Each group has 6 integers defining the vertex order for the triangle fan. Count Array (cnt): Stores number of vertices in each fan. Max vertices is 6 (Class 2, 4 triangles). 1. Preprocessing (CPU): For each tetrahedron, determine if it contributes to the isosurface or volume. Check if the minimum and maximum scalar weights (extrema) are on the same side of the interesting density range. If so, discard the tetrahedron. Transform the Basis Tensor (BT) into Euclidean space using Equation 8 and into tetrahedral indexing form. Store valid tetrahedra in a vertex buffer interpreted as a point list. Position semantic is set to the middle of the voxel space. 2. First Pass: Projecting Tetrahedra (GPU Fragment Shader): Render the Tetrahedral Texture as a quadrilateral with screen-space size. This ensures one fragment shader invocation per tetrahedron. For each tetrahedron: Perform 4 texture lookups using indices from the Tetrahedral Texture to get vertex positions, scalars, and gradients from Vertex and Gradient Textures. Project the 4 vertices to screen space. Compute 4 cross-product tests to determine projection class and vertex layout: python vec1 = vproj1 - vproj0 vec2 = vproj2 - vproj0 vec3 = vproj3 - vproj0 vec4 = vproj1 - vproj2 vec5 = vproj1 - vproj3 t1 = sign((vec1 × vec2).z) + 1 t2 = sign((vec2 × vec3).z) + 1 t3 = sign((vec3 × vec4).z) + 1 t4 = sign((vec4 × vec5).z) + 1 Where sign returns -1, 0, or 1. The results ti \in \{0, 1, 2\} are combined to form an index for the Classification Texture lookup. Determine triangle count based on degeneracy: If one test result is 1: Class 3, project as two triangles. If two test results are 1: Class 4, project as one triangle. If three or four tests yield 1: Discard the tetrahedron. Compute scalar values for thick vertex (sf, sb), gradient vectors for entry/exit (gf, gb), cell thickness (l), and cell centroid (cz). Write computed data to the 4 MRT frame buffer color attachments. 3. Intermediate Pass (CPU/GPU): Retrieve data from MRT textures. Sort the tetrahedra in front-to-back order. Use bucket-based sort for rotating models or mergesort for static models. Store sorted data in global arrays (Vertex, Color, Gradient, Indices, Count). 4. Second Pass: Rendering Primitives (GPU Geometry/Fragment Shader): Draw primitives using glMultiDrawElements (or equivalent). Pass indices and count arrays. Use triangle fans. Geometry Shader (Optional/Alternative): Expand each input point (grid vertex) into tetrahedron screen-space triangles. Calculate z-extents. Unpack BT to tensor form, apply Equation 9 (add density), apply Equation 10 (screen transform), pack back to tetrahedral form, and output to screen-space triangles. Note: The two-pass MRT approach avoids this geometry shader overhead by doing classification in the fragment shader. Fragment Shader: Linearly interpolate vertex colors (sf, sb, l) across the triangle using thick and two thin vertices. Compute final opacity using a 1D texture lookup. The texture stores e^{-u} for u \in [0,1]. Lookup u = \tau \cdot l (where \tau is related to scalar values). Partial Pre-Integration (PT): Instead of average scalar values, use the \psi table [MA04]. Retrieve colors Cf and Cb from a 1D transfer function texture based on sf and sb. Use Cf, Cb, and l to index a 2D \psi table. Retrieve value for final color. Isosurface Rendering: If an isovalue is specified, check if it is within the range of interpolated front/back scalar values. If so, the isosurface crosses the tetrahedron. Use Phong illumination. Interpolated gradients act as normal vectors. Combine front and back gradients with weights relative to the distance between the isosurface and the intersection points. Basis Tensor Transformations: Transform BT into Euclidean space: \hat{\mathbf{B}}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} = \mathbf{T}^{-1} \frac{\alpha2}{\beta1} \mathbf{T}^{-1} \frac{\alpha3}{\beta2} \mathbf{T}^{-1} \frac{\alpha2}{\beta3} \mathbf{B}{\alpha1, \alpha2, \alpha3} \quad (8) Add density d for isosurface level selection (only affects weight at (3,3,3)): \mathbf{B}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} = \begin{cases} \hat{\mathbf{B}}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} + d & \text{if } (\beta1, \beta2, \beta3) = (3, 3, 3) \\ \hat{\mathbf{B}}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (9) Transform scaled tensor into screen space: \tilde{\mathbf{B}}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{P}^{-1\alpha1}{\beta1} \mathbf{W}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{P}^{-1\alpha2}{\beta2} \mathbf{W}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{P}^{-1\alpha3}{\beta3} \tilde{\mathbf{B}}{\alpha1, \alpha2, \alpha3} \quad (10) Color Accumulation: For a sub-interval with constant opacity \alpha and optical depth t: c{acc}(t, c0, c1, \alpha) = (1 - e^{-\alpha t}) c0 + \left( \left( t + \frac{1}{\alpha} \right) e^{-\alpha t} - \frac{1}{\alpha} \right) (c0 - c1) Where c0 is entry color, c1 is exit color. Gradients for Backpropagation (DiffTetVR): Gradient of accumulated color w.r.t entry color c0: \frac{\partial c{acc}}{\partial c0} = (1 - e^{-\alpha t}) + \left( \left( t + \frac{1}{\alpha} \right) e^{-\alpha t} - \frac{1}{\alpha} \right) Gradient of accumulated color w.r.t exit color c1: \frac{\partial c{acc}}{\partial c1} = - \left( \left( t + \frac{1}{\alpha} \right) e^{-\alpha t} - \frac{1}{\alpha} \right) Gradient of accumulated color w.r.t opacity \alpha: \frac{\partial c{acc}}{\partial \alpha} = t e^{-\alpha t} c0 + \left( \frac{1}{\alpha^2} - \left( t^2 + \frac{1}{\alpha^2} + \frac{t}{\alpha} \right) e^{-\alpha t} \right) (c0 - c1) Gradient of accumulated color w.r.t optical depth t: \frac{\partial c{acc}}{\partial t} = (\alpha c0 + (\alpha c1 - \alpha c0) t) e^{-\alpha t} Gradient of accumulated opacity w.r.t opacity \alpha: \frac{\partial a{acc}}{\partial \alpha} = t e^{-\alpha t} Limit as \alpha \rightarrow 0: \lim{\alpha \rightarrow 0} \frac{\partial c{acc}}{\partial \alpha} = t c0 + \frac{1}{2}t^2 (c1 - c0) \lim{\alpha \rightarrow 0} \frac{\partial c{acc}}{\partial c0} = \lim{\alpha \rightarrow 0} \frac{\partial c{acc}}{\partial c1} = 0 Inversion Trick for Backward Pass: Recover previous ray color: c{ray,i} = c{ray,i+1} - (1 - \alpha{ray,i})c{acc,i} Recover previous ray opacity: \alpha{ray,i} = \frac{\alpha{acc,i} - \alpha{ray,i+1}}{\alpha{acc,i} - 1} Nsub: Number of subdivision steps for the ray segment within a tetrahedron. Typical value not specified, but used to approximate constant opacity. β: Regularization parameter for tetrahedron quality. Value \beta = 10 is mentioned. Projection Type: Orthogonal projection is required for the screen-space triangle computation optimization in the geometry shader approach. The MRT approach works with perspective projection except for the specific pre-computed triangle strip optimization. Graphics API: DirectX 10 with Shader Model 4.0 (for geometry shaders); OpenGL 2.0/GLSL (for MRT approach); Vulkan (for DiffTetVR). Numerical Instability: The exact formula for linearly varying opacity involves the imaginary error function (erfi), which is numerically unstable on GPUs due to large values (10^{20}) and cancellation effects. This is handled by assuming constant opacity within sub-intervals. Degenerate Cases: The method handles degenerate projections by adding 24 class 3 cases and 12 class 4 cases to Wylie's 14 class 1 and 2 cases. Tests yielding result '1' (z=0) indicate degeneracy. Zero Opacity Discard: Early discard test bypasses tetrahedra with zero opacity. Only discard if ALL vertices have zero opacity (scalar values map to zero opacity in TF). Perspective Projection Limitation: The optimization of pre-computing screen-space triangle strips per tetrahedron index fails under perspective projection because screen-space triangles change for different BTs with the same tetrahedron number. Tetrahedron Quality: Tetrahedra must not self-intersect, invert (negative volume), or degenerate (zero volume) during optimization. This is enforced via regularization. Ray Intersection Bounds: Only intersections of the viewing ray and tensor BT inside the bounds of the tetrahedron count as hits. This method handles non-planar quadrilateral faces in curvilinear or irregular grids by performing view-dependent subdivision of "problem" faces and cells into triangles and tetrahedra, respectively, to prevent visibility sort failures and bow-tie projections. It approximates ray integration by projecting cells onto the screen, computing integrated opacity and color at vertices, and interpolating these values across screen-space polygons using standard graphics hardware. Unlike methods requiring resampling of curvilinear grids, cell projection works directly on the general grid topology. A method to sample cell-centered data by approximating neighbor centroids using volume ratios and face normals, avoiding full tree traversal. A method to represent the result of convolving an arbitrary scalar volume with a reconstruction filter as a BT Volume, provided the filter itself is a BT Volume sharing a similar \kappa function. Samples scalar values by interpolating vertex-centered scalar data at the vertices of the current element using the barycentric coordinates of the sample point. Vertex-centered data is stored duplicated per element during TET-AMR construction, allowing direct access via element ID. A differentiable volume rendering solution for tetrahedral meshes that enables optimization of vertex positions and local mesh subdivision without multigrid methods, solving the limitation of regular grids in previous differentiable volume rendering works. It derives equations for more accurate accumulation of color along view rays than simple alpha blending, implements a fast rasterization-based renderer based on per-pixel linked lists, and deduces derivatives for the rendering process to enable backpropagation regarding parameters such as vertex colors and positions. It introduces a differentiable regularization term for avoiding degeneration of tetrahedral elements during the optimization process. The exact formula by Williams and Max involving the difference of two imaginary error functions has far too high numerical instability to be usable in real-world workflows on GPUs when using only 32-bit floating point precision. A volume rendering system for unstructured data (especially finite element data) that creates images with very high accuracy without compromises or approximations for the sake of efficiency. It uses exact mathematical solutions for the radiance integrals involved and for interpolation whenever possible. It handles meshes whose cells are either linear or quadratic tetrahedra, and meshes with mixed cell types (tetrahedra, bricks, prisms, wedges, and pyramids, but not with high accuracy). It embeds accurate semi-transparent shaded isosurfaces in the volume rendering. For very small cells, it uses subpixel accumulation by splatting to avoid sampling error. It extends hardware assisted projection and compositing from tetrahedra to arbitrary convex polyhedra. It uses a revision to an existing accurate visibility ordering algorithm, which includes a correction and a method for dramatically increasing its efficiency. A volume rendering approach for phase space tessellations that combines state-of-the-art order-independent transparency methods to manage the extreme depth complexity of tetrahedral meshes. It proposes a view-dependent multiresolution representation of the data and a tile-based rendering strategy. Phase space tessellation techniques for N-body dark matter simulations yield density fields with a vast amount of elements and self-intersections, causing interactive visualization methods to either employ simplified rendering integrals or suffer from artifacts. Time Complexity: The first pass is O(N) where N is the number of tetrahedra, performed in parallel on the GPU. The sorting step is O(N \log N) or O(N) depending on the sort algorithm (bucket sort for rotating, mergesort for static). The second pass is O(P) where P is the number of pixels, as each pixel is shaded once. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the Tetrahedral, Vertex, Gradient, and Classification textures, plus MRT frame buffers and global arrays. The space requirement is very large, limiting the size of volumes that can be rendered on graphics cards with less memory. Measured Performance: On a Intel Pentium IV 3.6 GHz, 2 GB RAM, with a nVidia GeForce 6800 256 MB graphics card, PTINT achieved 11.30 fps on the Blunt Fin dataset and 4.07 fps on the Oxygen Post dataset (512x512 viewport, rotating model). This compared favorably to GATOR (5.20 fps, 1.82 fps), VICP GPU (4.10 fps, 4.47 fps), and HARC (6.09 fps, 2.36 fps). Strengths: Supports arbitrary isosurface values and partial pre-integration. Handles unstructured grids directly. GPU-accelerated. Differentiable variants allow for optimization of mesh parameters. Limitations: Large memory footprint. Orthogonal projection is required for certain optimizations (geometry shader approach). Numerical instability of exact integration formulas requires approximation (sub-intervals). Degenerate cases must be handled explicitly. When to use: When rendering unstructured tetrahedral meshes with high accuracy is required, especially for finite element data or dark matter simulations. When differentiable rendering is needed for mesh optimization. When not to use: When memory is severely constrained. When perspective projection is required and the geometry shader optimization is critical (use MRT approach instead). When real-time performance on low-end hardware is critical without simplification. Tetrahedral Volume Rendering originated from the need to visualize unstructured volumetric data, such as finite element analysis results, which cannot be efficiently represented by regular grids. The Basis Tensor (BT) volume representation was introduced to support arbitrary isosurface values and efficient rendering. The method was implemented on Direct3D 10 graphics API running on NVIDIA 8800 GTS GPU, leveraging geometry shaders. Later, GPU-Accelerated Cell Projection (PTINT) was developed using OpenGL 2.0 and GLSL under Linux, achieving higher performance on older hardware (Intel Pentium IV, GeForce 6800). More recently, DiffTetVR introduced differentiable rendering for tetrahedral meshes, enabling optimization of vertex positions and local mesh subdivision. The method is used in scientific visualization, particularly for phase space tessellations in dark matter simulations and high-accuracy finite element data. name: Viewpoint-dependent subdivision of non-planar faces
head: Cell Projection with Non-Planar Face Subdivision, Cell Projection with Non-Planar Faces Approximation, HIAC system cell projection, Hardware-based cell projection, Non-Planar Face Subdivision Strategy, Shirley and Tuchman method approximation, Viewpoint-dependent tetrahedral subdivision
body: This method handles non-planar quadrilateral faces in curvilinear or irregular grids by performing view-dependent subdivision of problem faces and cells into triangles and tetrahedra, respectively, to prevent visibility sort failures and bow-tie projections. It approximates ray integration by projecting cells onto the screen, computing integrated opacity and color at vertices, and interpolating these values across screen-space polygons using standard graphics hardware. Unlike methods requiring resampling of curvilinear grids, cell projection works directly on the general grid topology. Inputs: A list of vertices with 3D positions and scalar field values s. A list of cells (hexahedra or other topologies) with index pointers to their vertices. A viewpoint V. Transfer functions mapping scalar s to RGB color and differential opacity \tau, assumed linear or piecewise linear. Outputs: A rendered image with integrated color and opacity. Data Structures: Vertex List: Array of vertices, each containing 3D position (x,y,z) and scalar value s. Cell Structure: subdivided: Boolean flag indicating if the cell is currently subdivided into tetrahedra. oldsubdivided: Char flag tracking subdivision state from the previous frame. numbInbound: Integer count of incoming edges in the directed graph used for sorting. type: Enum or integer identifying the cell topology (e.g., hexahedron, tetrahedron). Vertex indices: Pointers to the vertices defining the cell. Directed Graph: For sorting, a graph where nodes are cells and edges represent shared faces, directed towards the cell containing the viewpoint relative to the face plane. Steps: 1. Identify Problem Faces and Cells: A problem face is a non-planar quadrilateral where a viewing ray intersects the same face twice, potentially creating a bow-tie projection. A problem cell is a cell intersected by a viewing ray in disjoint segments. Detection tests if a viewing ray can intersect a triangulated cell in more than one segment using plane equations of the triangles and locations of viewpoint V and relevant vertices. 2. Subdivide Problem Faces: Subdivide any non-planar quadrilateral face into two triangles. The diagonal must start from the quadrilateral vertex with the lowest index in the vertex list to ensure consistency for two cells sharing a face, as the choice depends only on vertex indices. Even if a face is not a problem face for a specific cell, it may need subdivision if it is part of a problem cell or to avoid gaps between adjacent cells. 3. Subdivide Problem Cells: If a cell is a problem cell for the current viewpoint, subdivide it into tetrahedra. Connect the vertex of lowest index in the whole cell to all triangles from faces not sharing this vertex to create a set of tetrahedra with planar faces. Only problem cells are subdivided; non-problem cells remain intact to preserve performance. Cells containing contour surfaces or scalar breakpoints in piecewise linear transfer functions are also subdivided into tetrahedra and then into slabs. 4. Project and Sort: Project the cell (or its tetrahedral subdivisions) onto the image plane. The projected edges divide the plane into polygons (triangles and quadrilaterals). Sort cells using the MPVO algorithm (or variants like MPVONC/SXMPVO) based on the directed graph of shared faces. Handle gaps with exterior face sorting or A-buffer accumulation. For contour slabs, sort polygons and volume slabs back-to-front based on viewpoint position relative to contour planes. 5. Compute Vertex Attributes: For each polygon, compute vertex attributes (RGB, opacity \tau, length l) at the front and back endpoints of the viewing ray segment through the cell. Profile vertices are vertices on the silhouette. Set color directly from scalar values s and integrated opacity to zero. Thick vertices are internal vertices where the ray passes through the cell interior. Compute the back endpoint's z, color, and \tau by subdividing the interior face with the diagonal from the lowest index vertex and interpolating linearly in screen space. Compute ray segment length l by interpolating depth z across the back face polygon in screen space to find the back endpoint, then reversing the eye-to-screen transformation. Approximate l by computing it at vertices and interpolating linearly across the polygon in screen space. For precise color, compute the correct integrated color analytically once per vertex and divide by integrated \alpha to get the polygon color. Alternatively, use the average of front and back colors. 6. Interpolate and Composite: Interpolate integrated opacity \alpha, color (R, G, B), and depth z linearly across the polygon in screen space using standard Gouraud shading hardware. Composite the interpolated polygons onto the image using the standard alpha blending equation. To correct for non-linear opacity integration errors (Mach bands), use texture mapping hardware in orthogonal views. Specify z and \tau as texture coordinates, linearly interpolate them, and extract the correct alpha from a 2D texture map preloaded with values 1 - e^{-\tau}. In perspective views, this technique is an approximation. Formulas: Integrated opacity: \alpha = 1 - e^{-\tau \cdot l}, where \tau = (\tauf + \taub)/2 is the average differential opacity, and l is the ray segment length. Alpha blending: \text{RGB}{\text{new}} = (1 - \alpha) \times \text{RGB}{\text{old}} + \alpha \times \text{RGB}{\text{polygon}}. Parameters: Transfer functions: Map scalar value s to RGB and differential opacity \tau. Assumed linear in s for the basic method, but piecewise linear is supported by slicing cells. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Hardware color interpolation is inconsistent with analytic integration. Condition (d) (color constant per cell, only \tau varies linearly) is required for hardware-based method to be mathematically equivalent to analytic integration. Boundaries: Non-planar faces cause visibility cycles where a ray intersects the same face twice, making back-to-front sorting impossible without subdivision. Degenerate Input: If a cell is not a problem cell but shares a face with a problem cell, the face must still be subdivided to avoid gaps or overlaps. Performance: Subdividing all quadrilaterals increases polygon count (e.g., 7 to 25 polygons) and OpenGL data output, though fragment count remains the same. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderviewpointdependentsubdivision(vertices, cells, viewpoint, transferfunction): # Step 1: Identify problem faces and cells problemfaces = set() problemcells = [] for cell in cells: cellisproblem = False for face in cell.faces: # Test if viewing ray intersects the face twice using plane equations if rayintersectsfacetwice(face, viewpoint): problemfaces.add(face) # Test if viewing ray intersects the triangulated cell in >1 segment if rayintersectscelltwice(cell, viewpoint): cellisproblem = True if cellisproblem: problemcells.append(cell) # Step 2: Subdivide problem faces for face in problemfaces: vindices = [v.index for v in face.vertices] minidx = min(vindices) minvertex = face.vertices[vindices.index(minidx)] # Split quadrilateral into two triangles using diagonal from minvertex face.splitintotriangles(minvertex) # Step 3: Subdivide problem cells for cell in problemcells: # Connect lowest index vertex of cell to all triangles from faces not sharing it mincellvertex = cell.getlowestindexvertex() cell.subdivideintotetrahedra(mincellvertex) # Step 4: Sort cells using MPVO directed graph sortedcells = mpvosort(cells, viewpoint) # Step 5 & 6: Project, Compute Attributes, Interpolate, Composite for cell in sortedcells: projectedpolygons = projectanddivideplane(cell, viewpoint) for polygon in projectedpolygons: for vertex in polygon.vertices: if vertex.isprofilevertex(): vertex.color = transferfunction(vertex.scalar) vertex.alpha = 0.0 else: # Thick vertex: interpolate z across back face polygon backz = interpolatezacrosspolygon(polygon, vertex) backendpoint = computebackendpoint(vertex, backz, viewpoint) vertex.backz = backendpoint.z vertex.backcolor = backendpoint.color vertex.backtau = backendpoint.tau # Approximate l by computing at vertices and interpolating linearly across the polygon vertex.l = computesegmentlength(vertex, backendpoint, viewpoint) # Compute average differential opacity vertex.avgtau = (vertex.tau + vertex.backtau) / 2.0 # Compute integrated opacity vertex.alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-vertex.avgtau vertex.l) # Compute polygon color (average of front and back) vertex.color = (vertex.color + vertex.backcolor) / 2.0 # Interpolate attributes linearly across polygon in screen space (Gouraud shading) rasterizepolygongouraud(polygon) def rayintersectsfacetwice(face, viewpoint): # Standard geometric test for ray-face intersection multiplicity return False def rayintersectscelltwice(cell, viewpoint): # Standard geometric test for ray-cell intersection multiplicity return False def mpvosort(cells, viewpoint): # O(n) sort using directed graph of shared faces graph = builddirectedgraph(cells, viewpoint) queue = [c for c in cells if graph.inboundcount(c) == 0] sortedlist = [] while queue: current = queue.pop(0) sortedlist.append(current) for neighbor in graph.outgoing(current): graph.decrementinbound(neighbor) if graph.inboundcount(neighbor) == 0: queue.append(neighbor) return sortedlist def builddirectedgraph(cells, viewpoint): # Builds adjacency graph where edges point toward the cell containing the viewpoint graph = {} for cell in cells: graph[cell] = {'outgoing': [], 'inboundcount': 0} for cella in cells: for cellb in cells: if cella is cellb: continue sharedface = findsharedface(cella, cellb) if sharedface: # Determine direction based on viewpoint position relative to face plane if viewpointonsideofplane(viewpoint, sharedface, cellb): graph[cella]['outgoing'].append(cellb) graph[cellb]['inboundcount'] += 1 return graph def projectanddivideplane(cell, viewpoint): # Projects cell vertices to screen space. Projected edges divide plane into polygons projectedverts = [projecttoscreen(v, viewpoint) for v in cell.vertices] return dividescreenbyprojectededges(projectedverts, cell.faces) def dividescreenbyprojectededges(projectedverts, faces): # Computes intersections of projected edges to form screen-space polygons polygons = [] # Standard computational geometry routine to partition 2D plane by line segments return polygons def interpolatezacrosspolygon(polygon, vertex): # Interpolates depth z across the back face polygon in screen space return interpolatelinearlyinscreenspace(polygon, 'z', vertex) def interpolatelinearlyinscreenspace(polygon, attribute, vertex): # Barycentric interpolation of an attribute across a 2D polygon weights = computebarycentricweights(vertex, polygon) return sum(w p.attributes[attribute] for w, p in zip(weights, polygon.vertices)) def computebackendpoint(frontvertex, backz, viewpoint): # Reverses eye-to-screen transformation to find 3D back endpoint backcolor = interpolatecolor(backz) backtau = interpolatetau(backz) return {'z': backz, 'color': backcolor, 'tau': backtau} def interpolatecolor(z): # Linear interpolation of color attributes based on depth return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def interpolatetau(z): # Linear interpolation of differential opacity based on depth return 0.0 def computesegmentlength(front, back, viewpoint): # Computes length l of ray segment. Approximated by computing at vertices and interpolating dx = back['z'] - front['z'] dy = back['x'] - front['x'] dz = back['y'] - front['y'] return math.sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2) def rasterizepolygongouraud(polygon): # Interpolates alpha, RGB, and z linearly across polygon in screen space using hardware # Composites using standard alpha blending equation pass A method to classify projections of hexahedra from curvilinear meshes into triangle fans or strips for hardware rendering, avoiding the computational geometry complexity of general line-sweep subdivision by handling specific topological cases. A technique to avoid defects in per-vertex classification during rasterization by ensuring at least one vertex on an edge has the correct classification of the second face sharing the edge, affecting the whole edge during rasterization. Time Complexity: Sorting is O(n) for MPVO. Subdivision is view-dependent and may increase polygon count. Detection of problem cells requires plane equation tests. Memory Complexity: Increased memory usage for storing subdivided cells and tetrahedra. Data structures must track subdivision state. Test Case: Demonstrated on a half-cylindrical shell with 19,000 cells. Scaling: Scales with the number of cells and the complexity of the grid topology. View-dependent subdivision adds overhead per frame. Strengths: Works directly on general grid topology without resampling. Handles non-planar faces and visibility cycles. Compatible with standard graphics hardware. Limitations: Approximations in perspective views (linear interpolation of \tau and color). Inconsistent with analytic integration unless strict conditions are met. Increased polygon count if all quadrilaterals are subdivided. When to Use: Curvilinear or irregular grids with non-planar faces where direct ray tracing is difficult. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: Developed for volume rendering of curvilinear and unstructured grids. Based on cell projection methods. History: Extended from methods assuming planar faces to handle non-planar quadrilateral faces. Uses concepts from the Shirley and Tuchman method and BSP-MPVO sorting. Usage: Used in scientific visualization for data on curvilinear grids, such as fluid dynamics simulations or structural mechanics. name: BT Volume Construction
head: BT Volume Approximation via Least Squares
body: A method to approximate an arbitrary scalar-valued volumetric function as a BT Volume using a least-squares fit. It differs from direct discretization by projecting the target function onto the polynomial basis of the BT Volume, ensuring C^0 continuity across tetrahedral boundaries. It serves as the primary generation technique for the data consumed by BT Volume Isosurface Rendering. Inputs: 1. Target scalar field f(\mathbf{x}) defined on a domain \Omega. 2. A tetrahedral grid \mathcal{T} (mapping \kappa) covering \Omega. The grid voxels must overlap with the domain of the target function. 3. A reconstruction filter R(\mathbf{x}) (optional, for the filter-based approach). Outputs: A BT Volume representation defined by vertex values and polynomial coefficients for each tetrahedron in \mathcal{T}. Data Structures: Tetrahedral Grid: A set of tetrahedra Ti. Each tetrahedron is defined by 4 vertices. BT Volume: For each tetrahedron Ti, a set of polynomial coefficients (weights) defining the Bezier Tetrahedron. The values are stored at each vertex. Steps: 1. Grid Creation: Create a tetrahedral grid \mathcal{T} that surrounds the entire target function domain. The resolution (number of tetrahedra) determines the approximation quality. Note: The specific mapping \kappa determines the expressive power. 2. Sampling: For each tetrahedron Ti \in \mathcal{T}: Determine a set of sample points \{\mathbf{p}j\} distributed evenly in the barycentric coordinates of Ti. Transform each barycentric point \mathbf{p}j into Euclidean space \mathbf{x}j. Evaluate the target function f(\mathbf{x}j) at each \mathbf{x}j. 3. Fitting (Least-Squares): Perform a least-squares fit to determine the optimal weights (vertex values) for all BTs in the volume simultaneously. The simultaneous fit ensures C^0 continuity across tetrahedral boundaries. Boundary Clamping: Artificially clamp all boundary values to zero before applying any subsequent filter convolution. 4. Filter Convolution (Optional/Advanced): If the goal is to represent the result of convolving an arbitrary scalar rectilinear volume with a reconstruction filter R: 1. Generate a BT Volume approximation of the filter R itself using the least-squares method above. 2. Pre-convolve the filter BT Volume with the arbitrary scalar rectilinear volume. 3. Apply the convolution equation formulation to produce a final BT Volume that equals the reconstructed data. This requires that the filter BT Volume shares a similar \kappa function as the resulting BT Volume. Parameters: Mapping \kappa: Determines approximation quality. Key properties are: 1) Number of tetrahedra in the mapping, and 2) Spatial distribution of tetrahedra in the domain. More tetrahedra allow higher frequencies. Sample Density: Number of sample points per tetrahedron. Not explicitly quantified in sources, but "distributed evenly" is specified. Pitfalls: Continuity: The least-squares approximation does not enforce C^1 continuity. Precision: Graphics hardware precision issues may cause a few pixels to incorrectly miss the isosurface being rendered. Optimal Grid: Determining the optimal \kappa for a particular volume (balance of rendering cost vs. expressive power) is an open research problem. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def constructbtvolume(targetfunction, domain, tetrahedralgrid, numsamplespertet): """ Approximates targetfunction over domain using tetrahedralgrid. Returns BT Volume weights. """ # 1. Grid Creation: tetrahedralgrid is provided as input. # Ensure grid voxels overlap with the reconstructed volume voxels. # 2. Sampling & 3. Fitting # We need to solve for weights W such that the BT Volume approximates f. # Let N be the total number of tetrahedra. # Let M be the number of sample points per tetrahedron. # Initialize system matrix A and vector b for least squares # The system solves for all vertex weights simultaneously to ensure C0 continuity. A = [] b = [] for tet in tetrahedralgrid: # Get 4 vertices of the tetrahedron v0, v1, v2, v3 = tet.vertices # Determine sample points in barycentric coordinates # "Distributed evenly" implies a standard uniform grid or quadrature # in the reference tetrahedron. samplepointsbary = generateevenbarycentricsamples(numsamplespertet) for bary in samplepointsbary: # Transform to Euclidean space x = barycentrictoeuclidean(bary, v0, v1, v2, v3) # Evaluate target function fval = targetfunction(x) # Compute basis function values for this point # For a BT Volume, the value at x is a linear combination of vertex weights # weighted by the Bernstein polynomials (or equivalent basis) of the tet. basisvalues = computebtbasis(bary) # Add row to A and value to b # A W = b A.append(basisvalues) b.append(fval) # Solve least squares: min ||AW - b||^2 # W is the vector of all vertex weights for the entire grid # Using normal equations for standard least-squares solve Anp = np.array(A) bnp = np.array(b) W = np.linalg.solve(Anp.T @ Anp, Anp.T @ bnp) # 4. Boundary Clamping (if preparing for filter convolution) # Artificially clamp all boundary values to zero. # Identify boundary vertices of the grid. boundaryvertices = getboundaryvertices(tetrahedralgrid) for v in boundaryvertices: W[v] = 0.0 return W def constructfilterbtvolume(filterfunction, domain, tetrahedralgrid, numsamplespertet): """ Generates a BT Volume representation of a reconstruction filter. """ # Use the same least-squares technique as above weights = constructbtvolume(filterfunction, domain, tetrahedralgrid, numsamplespertet) return weights def preconvolvefilterbt(filterbtweights, scalarvolume, grid): """ Pre-convolves the filter BT Volume with an arbitrary scalar rectilinear volume. The resulting BT Volume allows for efficient rendering via local ray-intersection equations on the graphics card. Strengths: Provides a continuous C^0 representation of arbitrary scalar fields. Allows the use of BT Volumes as reconstruction filters, enabling efficient convolution. Limitations: Does not enforce C^1 continuity. Graphics hardware precision issues can cause rendering artifacts (missed isosurfaces). Determining the optimal tetrahedral grid (\kappa) is an open problem. Development: The method was developed as part of a broader framework for rendering BT Volumes, which are polynomial solids defined on tetrahedral grids with special regularity requirements. name: BT Volume Isosurface Rendering
head: BT Volume Representation, BT Volumes, Bezier Tetrahedra Volume Rendering
body: BT Volume Isosurface Rendering is a real-time technique for rendering exact isosurfaces from volumetric data by representing the volume as a grid of cubic Bezier Tetrahedra (BT). It solves the problem of low-quality, faceted surfaces produced by linear reconstruction methods like Marching Cubes, while avoiding the computational cost of generating and rendering explicit triangle meshes. Unlike its sibling BT Volume Construction, which focuses on generating the BT data structure from a reconstruction filter, this method focuses on the rendering pipeline: performing local ray tracing within each tetrahedron inside a GPU pixel shader to find exact intersections with arbitrary isosurface levels. Input: A BT Volume data structure containing a grid of tetrahedra, where each tetrahedron has an associated set of 20 Bezier weights. The volume space is assumed to be a cuboid with integer dimensions. Output: A 2D image where each pixel displays the color of the isosurface intersection, or background if no intersection exists. The volume is divided into unit cubes (voxels). Each voxel is subdivided into tetrahedra using a canonical mapping \kappa. The implementation described in the source uses the standard 6-tetrahedron decomposition of a cube. For each tetrahedron T in the grid, the following data is stored: 1. Bounding Tetrahedron Vertices (T): Four points T = (T1, T2, T3, T4) defining the spatial bounds. These are typically the integer grid vertices of the voxel. 2. Bezier Weights (w{ijkl}): A set of 20 scalar weights. The indices i, j, k, l are non-negative integers such that i + j + k + l = 3. These weights define the scalar field value distribution within the tetrahedron. The volume space is partitioned into voxels c{l,m,n} indexed by integer coordinates (l, m, n). A canonical mapping function \kappa maps a point's fractional position within a voxel to a specific tetrahedron index h within that voxel. \kappa: [0, 1]^3 \rightarrow \{h: h \in H\} where H is the set of tetrahedron indices for a single voxel (e.g., H = \{1,..., 6\} for the standard decomposition). The mapping must be shift-invariant, meaning the decomposition pattern is identical for every voxel. Given a point Q \in \mathbb{R}^3, the specific BT \tau containing Q is determined by: \tau = BT{[\mathbf{Q}]}(\kappa(\mathbf{Q} - [\mathbf{Q}])) where [\mathbf{Q}] is the integer voxel index containing Q. The rendering is performed via local ray tracing within the GPU pixel shader. For each pixel, a ray is cast into the volume. The algorithm iterates through the tetrahedra intersected by the ray. 1. Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection: For each tetrahedron T intersected by the ray, compute the intersection points of the ray with the isosurface defined by the BT within T. 2. Bezier Evaluation: The scalar value b(\mathbf{P}) at any point \mathbf{P} inside the tetrahedron is calculated using the BT formula. 3. Root Finding: The intersection with the isosurface value V{iso} is found by solving for the roots of the univariate polynomial equation derived from the BT formula along the ray parameter t. For a point \mathbf{P} = (x, y, z, 1) in projective space, the barycentric coordinates r = (r, s, t, u) are calculated as: r = (r, s, t, u) = \mathbf{P} \cdot T^{-1} where T is the 4 \times 4 matrix formed by the homogeneous coordinates of the vertices T1, T2, T3, T4. The value of the BT at \mathbf{P} is: b(\mathbf{P}) = \sum{i+j+k+l=3} w{ijkl} \binom{3}{i,j,k,l} r^i s^j t^k u^l where \binom{3}{i,j,k,l} = \frac{3!}{i!j!k!l!} is the multinomial coefficient. Let the ray be defined by origin \mathbf{O} and direction \mathbf{D}. A point on the ray is \mathbf{R}(t) = \mathbf{O} + t\mathbf{D}. 1. Substitute \mathbf{R}(t) into the barycentric coordinate formula to express r, s, t, u as linear functions of t. 2. Substitute these linear functions into the BT formula. 3. Solve for the real roots of P(t) within the range of the tetrahedron's intersection with the ray. 4. The smallest positive root t corresponds to the entry point of the isosurface. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderbtvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, btvolume, isosurfacevalue): """ Renders a single ray against a BT Volume. """ thit = float('inf') # Standard 3D DDA voxel traversal algorithm voxelbounds = computevoxelbounds(rayorigin, raydirection, btvolume.dimensions) for voxel in voxelbounds: # Standard 6-tetrahedron decomposition of a unit cube tetrahedrainvoxel = gettetrahedrainvoxel(voxel) for tet in tetrahedrainvoxel: # 1. Check if ray intersects the bounding tetrahedron T tenter, texit = intersectraytetrahedron(rayorigin, raydirection, tet.vertices) if tenter == float('inf'): continue # 2. Evaluate the BT polynomial along the ray segment [tenter, texit] coeffs = computebtpolynomialcoefficients( rayorigin, raydirection, tet.vertices, tet.weights) # 3. Solve for roots of P(t) - isosurfacevalue = 0 coeffs[3] -= isosurfacevalue roots = solvecubicpolynomial(coeffs) # 4. Filter valid roots for troot in roots: if tenter <= troot <= texit and troot > 0: if troot < thit: thit = troot return thit def computevoxelbounds(origin, direction, dimensions): """Returns list of voxel indices intersected by the ray using 3D DDA.""" bounds = [] x, y, z = origin dx, dy, dz = direction stepx = 1 if dx > 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if dy > 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if dz > 0 else -1 tmaxx = (stepx > 0 and (dimensions[0] - x) / dx or (0 - x) / dx) if dx != 0 else float('inf') tmaxy = (stepy > 0 and (dimensions[1] - y) / dy or (0 - y) / dy) if dy != 0 else float('inf') tmaxz = (stepz > 0 and (dimensions[2] - z) / dz or (0 - z) / dz) if dz != 0 else float('inf') tdeltax = abs(1.0 / dx) if dx != 0 else float('inf') tdeltay = abs(1.0 / dy) if dy != 0 else float('inf') tdeltaz = abs(1.0 / dz) if dz != 0 else float('inf') ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) while 0 <= ix < dimensions[0] and 0 <= iy < dimensions[1] and 0 <= iz < dimensions[2]: bounds.append((ix, iy, iz)) if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: ix += stepx; tmaxx += tdeltax else: iz += stepz; tmaxz += tdeltaz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: iy += stepy; tmaxy += tdeltay else: iz += stepz; tmaxz += tdeltaz return bounds def gettetrahedrainvoxel(voxel): """Returns the list of tetrahedra belonging to a voxel.""" x, y, z = voxel v0 = (x, y, z); v1 = (x+1, y, z); v2 = (x, y+1, z); v3 = (x, y, z+1) v4 = (x+1, y+1, z); v5 = (x+1, y, z+1); v6 = (x, y+1, z+1); v7 = (x+1, y+1, z+1) return [ [v0, v1, v2, v6], [v1, v4, v2, v6], [v1, v5, v4, v6], [v1, v7, v5, v6], [v2, v6, v3, v7], [v3, v7, v5, v6] ] def intersectraytetrahedron(origin, direction, vertices): """Returns (tenter, texit) for ray-tetrahedron intersection using barycentric coordinates.""" v0, v1, v2, v3 = vertices e1 = (v1[0]-v0[0], v1[1]-v0[1], v1[2]-v0[2]) e2 = (v2[0]-v0[0], v2[1]-v0[1], v2[2]-v0[2]) e3 = (v3[0]-v0[0], v3[1]-v0[1], v3[2]-v0[2]) P = (direction[1]e2[2]-direction[2]e2[1], direction[2]e2[0]-direction[0]e2[2], direction[0]e2[1]-direction[1]e2[0]) det = e1[0]P[0] + e2[0]P[1] + e3[0]P[2] if abs(det) < 1e-8: return float('inf'), float('inf') invdet = 1.0 / det T = (origin[0]-v0[0], origin[1]-v0[1], origin[2]-v0[2]) u = (T[0]P[0] + T[1]P[1] + T[2]P[2]) invdet if u < 0 or u > 1: return float('inf'), float('inf') Q = (direction[1]e3[2]-direction[2]e3[1], direction[2]e3[0]-direction[0]e3[2], direction[0]e3[1]-direction[1]e3[0]) v = (T[0]Q[0] + T[1]Q[1] + T[2]Q[2]) invdet if v < 0 or u + v > 1: return float('inf'), float('inf') R = (e1[1]e3[2]-e1[2]e3[1], e1[2]e3[0]-e1[0]e3[2], e1[0]e3[1]-e1[1]e3[0]) t = (e2[0]R[0] + e2[1]R[1] + e2[2]R[2]) invdet if t < 0: return float('inf'), float('inf') e = (direction[1]e1[2]-direction[2]e1[1], direction[2]e1[0]-direction[0]e1[2], direction[0]e1[1]-direction[1]e1[0]) u2 = (T[0]e[0] + T[1]e[1] + T[2]e[2]) invdet if u2 < 0 or u + u2 > 1: return float('inf'), float('inf') return t, t + (e1[0]u + e2[0]v + e3[0]u2) / (direction[0] if direction[0]!=0 else 1e-8) def computebtpolynomialcoefficients(origin, direction, vertices, weights): """ Computes the coefficients [A, B, C, D] for the cubic polynomial representing the BT value along the ray. """ T = buildhomogeneousmatrix(vertices) Tinv = invertmatrix(T) polycoeffs = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(4): for j in range(4 - i): for k in range(4 - i - j): l = 3 - i - j - k weight = weights[i 10 + j 4 + k] multinomial = factorial(3) // (factorial(i) factorial(j) factorial(k) factorial(l)) r0, r1 = getbarycentriclinearcoeffs(0, origin, direction, Tinv) s0, s1 = getbarycentriclinearcoeffs(1, origin, direction, Tinv) t0, t1 = getbarycentriclinearcoeffs(2, origin, direction, Tinv) u0, u1 = getbarycentriclinearcoeffs(3, origin, direction, Tinv) polyr = powerlinearpoly(r0, r1, i) polys = powerlinearpoly(s0, s1, j) polyt = powerlinearpoly(t0, t1, k) polyu = powerlinearpoly(u0, u1, l) polyterm = multiplypolynomials(polyr, polys) polyterm = multiplypolynomials(polyterm, polyt) polyterm = multiplypolynomials(polyterm, polyu) scale = weight multinomial for idx in range(4): polycoeffs[idx] += scale polyterm[idx] return polycoeffs def buildhomogeneousmatrix(vertices): """Constructs a 4x4 matrix from 4 homogeneous vertices.""" return [list(v) + [1.0] for v in vertices] def invertmatrix(M): """Computes the inverse of a 4x4 matrix.""" inv = [[0.0]4 for in range(4)] det = (M[0][0]M[1][1]M[2][2]M[3][3] - The rendering logic must handle this consistently to avoid gaps or double-rendering. Memory: The memory footprint is proportional to the number of tetrahedra in the volume. Each tetrahedron stores 4 vertices and 20 weights. Time: The rendering time per pixel depends on the number of tetrahedra the ray intersects. For each intersection, a cubic polynomial must be solved. The method is designed for real-time interactive rendering on graphics hardware. It allows rendering any isosurface level without additional precomputation work. Strengths: Renders exact isosurfaces directly in the pixel shader, avoiding triangle mesh generation. Supports arbitrary isosurface levels without additional work. Provides high-quality reconstruction filtering with arbitrary footprints and kernels. Smooth surfaces compared to linear reconstruction methods like Marching Cubes. Limitations: Requires precomputation of the BT Volume from the source data or reconstruction filter. Cubic polynomial solving can be computationally expensive per tetrahedron compared to linear intersection tests. The method assumes the volume can be effectively approximated by cubic Bezier Tetrahedra. Bezier Tetrahedra were originally developed by Loop and Blinn [2006] for rendering on graphics hardware. This paper extends that work to volume rendering, introducing BT Volumes as a representation for volumetric functions. The method was presented in 2008 as a solution to the limitations of Marching Cubes, which relies on linear reconstruction and produces faceted surfaces. The approach leverages the tensor form of BTs to allow efficient transformation and evaluation on GPUs. Applications include hurricane visualization, medical diagnosis and planning, and smoke and particle systems. name: Projected Tetrahedra
head: PT algorithm, Shirley and Tuchman's projected tetrahedra, Tetrahedral Projection
body: Projected Tetrahedra (PT) is a cell-projection volume rendering technique that projects unstructured tetrahedral cells onto the screen as triangle fans, sorting them by depth to ensure correct transparency compositing. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on vertex shaders or complex auxiliary data structures, the GPU-based two-pass fragment shader implementation uses texture-based data storage to minimize memory footprint and avoid redundant projections. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large unstructured meshes by offloading projection classification and scalar interpolation to the GPU, achieving interactive rates with significantly less memory usage than ray-casting alternatives. Inputs: Unstructured tetrahedral mesh defined by vertex coordinates and scalar values. Camera view and projection matrices. Transfer function (mapping scalar values to color and extinction coefficient). Outputs: Final composited image with correct transparency. The method relies on three primary textures stored in GPU memory: 1. Vertex Texture: Stores vertex attributes. Each texel is RGBA with 32 bits per component. RGB: 3D coordinates (x, y, z) of the vertex. A: Scalar value s associated with the vertex. 2. Tetrahedral Texture: Stores connectivity. Each texel contains four indices used to look up the four vertices of a specific tetrahedron from the Vertex Texture. One texel corresponds to one tetrahedron. 3. Classification Texture: A 1D texture with 8 bits per component containing a ternary truth table. It maps the results of four cross-product tests to the projection class (1–4) and the correct vertex ordering for the triangle fan. CPU-side Arrays (for Rendering Pass): Vertex Array: Groups of 5 elements per tetrahedron (1 "thick" vertex + 4 original vertices). Stores coordinates \{x, y, z\}. Color Array: Groups of 5 elements per tetrahedron. Stores interpolation parameters \{sf, sb, l\} rather than final colors. For thin vertices, sf = sb and l=0. Indices Array: Groups of 6 elements per tetrahedron, defining the vertex order for the triangle fan. Count Array: Stores the number of vertices in each fan (max 6). Step 1: Projection and Classification (First Fragment Shader Pass) 1. Render the Tetrahedral Texture as a full-screen quadrilateral. This ensures one fragment is generated per tetrahedron. 2. For each fragment (tetrahedron), retrieve the four vertex indices from the Tetrahedral Texture. 3. Look up the 3D coordinates and scalar values of the four vertices (v0, v1, v2, v3) from the Vertex Texture. 4. Project the four vertices to screen coordinates. 5. Compute four cross-product tests to determine the projection class: Define vectors: \vec{vec1} = v1 - v0 \vec{vec2} = v2 - v0 \vec{vec3} = v3 - v0 \vec{vec4} = v1 - v2 \vec{vec5} = v1 - v3 Compute test results testi for i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}: testi = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } (\vec{cross})z \le 0 \\ 1 & \text{if } (\vec{cross})z = 0 \\ 2 & \text{if } (\vec{cross})z \ge 0 \end{cases} Specifically: test1 = \text{sign}((\vec{vec1} \times \vec{vec2})z) + 1 test2 = \text{sign}((\vec{vec1} \times \vec{vec3})z) + 1 test3 = \text{sign}((\vec{vec2} \times \vec{vec3})z) + 1 test4 = \text{sign}((\vec{vec4} \times \vec{vec5})z) + 1 6. Use the tuple (test1, test2, test3, test4) to look up the projection class and vertex order in the Classification Texture. Class 1: Produces 3 triangles. Class 2: Produces 4 triangles. Class 3: Degenerate case of Class 1 (one test returns 1). Class 4: Degenerate case of Class 2 (two tests return 1). Degenerate (Discard): If more than two tests return 1, all points are collinear; discard the projection. 7. Compute the "thick" vertex properties based on the class: Class 2: The thick vertex vt is the intersection of the two interior segments. Compute front scalar sf by interpolating on segment v0v1 and back scalar sb on segment v2v3. Class 3: sf = s{v2}. Compute sb by interpolating s{v0} and s{v3}. Class 4: sf = s{v2} and sb = s{v0}. 8. Compute the tetrahedron centroid in screen space and extract its z-coordinate (zc) for sorting. 9. Output fragment data to two Multiple Render Targets (MRT) textures: Texture 1: Intersection vertex coordinates (x{vi}, y{vi}) (for Class 2), centroid zc, and Ternary Truth Table index id{TTT}. Texture 2: Scalars sf, sb, thickness l, and triangle fan vertex count. Step 2: Sorting 10. Transfer the centroid zc values to the CPU. 11. Sort tetrahedra in back-to-front order: Use Bucket Sort (approx. 20 slabs perpendicular to the viewing vector) for dynamic view changes. Use Merge Sort (O(n \log n)) for static frames to ensure accuracy. Note: Centroid sorting is an approximation. For perfect accuracy, use Williams’ MVPO or k-buffer sorting. Step 3: Data Preparation 12. Construct the CPU-side Vertex, Color, Indices, and Count arrays using the data from the MRT textures. For each tetrahedron, group 5 vertices: 1 thick vertex + 4 original vertices. Update the thick vertex position and color parameters. Set thin vertex parameters: sf = sb and l=0. Populate the Indices array with the vertex order determined in Step 1. Populate the Count array with the number of vertices per fan. Step 4: Rendering and Compositing (Second Fragment Shader Pass) 13. Render the primitives using glMultiDrawElements with the prepared arrays, invoking the second fragment shader. Primitives are drawn as triangle fans. 14. In the fragment shader, linearly interpolate the vertex parameters \{sf, sb, l\} from one thick vertex and two thin vertices. 15. Compute the average scalar s: s = \frac{sf + sb}{2} 16. Lookup the final color and extinction coefficient \tau from a 1D Transfer Function texture using s. 17. Compute the opacity \alpha using a 1D texture Tex1D pre-computed with e^{-u}: u = \tau \cdot l \alpha = \text{Tex1D}(u) = e^{-\tau l} (Note: Using a texture lookup for the exponential is slightly faster than computing it in the shader.) 18. Composite the fragment into the frame buffer in back-to-front order: I{new} = \text{Color} + (1 - \text{Alpha}) \times I Where I is the previous color in the frame buffer, and Color/Alpha are the interpolated values.
