TetrahedralTexture = [...] # 2D array of 4-tuples of indices VertexTexture = [...] # 2D array of (RGB, A) ClassificationTexture = [...] # 1D array mapping test tuples to class/order TransferFunctionTexture = [...] # 1D array mapping scalar to (Color, tau) ExponentialTexture = [...] # 1D array mapping u to e^-u framebuffercolor = [...] # 2D array storing current pixel colors def project(v): # Applies standard view and projection transformation return applyviewprojection(v) def cross(a, b): return (a.yb.z - a.zb.y, a.zb.x - a.xb.z, a.xb.y - a.yb.x) def sign(x): return 1 if x > 0 else (-1 if x < 0 else 0) def intersectsegments(p1, p2, p3, p4): # Returns 2D intersection point of line p1-p2 and p3-p4 denom = (p1.x - p2.x) (p3.y - p4.y) - (p1.y - p2.y) (p3.x - p4.x) if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return None t = ((p1.x - p3.x) (p3.y - p4.y) - (p1.y - p3.y) (p3.x - p4.x)) / denom return (p1.x + t (p2.x - p1.x), p1.y + t (p2.y - p1.y)) def interpolatescalar(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def fragmentshaderpass1(texelcoord): # 1. Retrieve tetrahedron indices tetindices = TetrahedralTexture[texelcoord] # 2. Retrieve vertex data v0data = VertexTexture[tetindices[0]] v1data = VertexTexture[tetindices[1]] v2data = VertexTexture[tetindices[2]] v3data = VertexTexture[tetindices[3]] v0 = v0data.rgb v1 = v1data.rgb v2 = v2data.rgb v3 = v3data.rgb s0 = v0data.a s1 = v1data.a s2 = v2data.a s3 = v3data.a # 3. Project to screen ps0 = project(v0) ps1 = project(v1) ps2 = project(v2) ps3 = project(v3) # 4. Compute cross products vec1 = ps1 - ps0 vec2 = ps2 - ps0 vec3 = ps3 - ps0 vec4 = ps1 - ps2 vec5 = ps1 - ps3 cross1 = cross(vec1, vec2) cross2 = cross(vec1, vec3) cross3 = cross(vec2, vec3) cross4 = cross(vec4, vec5) # 5. Compute test results (maps to 0, 1, 2) test1 = sign(cross1.z) + 1 test2 = sign(cross2.z) + 1 test3 = sign(cross3.z) + 1 test4 = sign(cross4.z) + 1 # 6. Check for degenerate (collinear) case if (test1 == 1) + (test2 == 1) + (test3 == 1) + (test4 == 1) > 2: return None # discard # 7. Lookup class and order classinfo = ClassificationTexture[(test1, test2, test3, test4)] classid = classinfo.classid vertexorder = classinfo.vertexorder # 8. Compute thick vertex properties if classid == 2: vt = intersectsegments(ps0, ps1, ps2, ps3) tv0v1 = ((vt.x - ps0.x) / (ps1.x - ps0.x)) if abs(ps1.x - ps0.x) > 1e-9 else 0.5 tv2v3 = ((vt.x - ps2.x) / (ps3.x - ps2.x)) if abs(ps3.x - ps2.x) > 1e-9 else 0.5 sf = interpolatescalar(s0, s1, tv0v1) sb = interpolatescalar(s2, s3, tv2v3) elif classid == 3: sf = s2 sb = interpolatescalar(s0, s3, 0.5) elif classid == 4: sf = s2 sb = s0 else: # Class 1 vt = None sf, sb = s0, s1 # 9. Compute centroid z centroid = (v0 + v1 + v2 + v3) / 4.0 centroidscreen = project(centroid) zc = centroidscreen.z # 10. Output to MRTs MRT1 = { 'xvi': vt.x if classid == 2 else 0, 'yvi': vt.y if classid == 2 else 0, 'zc': zc, 'idTTT': (test1, test2, test3, test4) } # l is computed as the ray segment length in the shader MRT2 = { 'sf': sf, 'sb': sb, 'l': 1.0, 'count': vertexorder.count } return MRT1, MRT2 def fragmentshaderpass2(interpolatedsf, interpolatedsb, interpolatedl, screencoords): # 1. Average scalar s = (interpolatedsf + interpolatedsb) / 2.0 # 2. Lookup Color and Tau tfresult = TransferFunctionTexture[s] Color = tfresult.rgb tau = tfresult.a # 3. Compute Opacity u = tau interpolatedl Alpha = ExponentialTexture[u] # Pre-computed e^-u # 4. Composite I = framebuffercolor[screencoords] Inew = Color + (1 - Alpha) I return Inew Bucket Sort Slabs: Approximately 20 slabs perpendicular to the viewing vector. Texture Precision: 32 bits per component for Vertex and Tetrahedral textures; 8 bits for Classification texture. Degenerate Tetrahedra: If more than two cross-product tests return 1, the vertices are projected onto a line. These must be discarded to prevent artifacts. Sorting Accuracy: Sorting by centroid is not 100% accurate. For perfect ordering, use Williams’ MVPO or k-buffer sorting. Perspective Distortion: In perspective views, linear interpolation of extinction coefficient \tau is an approximation because front and back faces have different perspective distortions. Hardware perspective-correct interpolation is insufficient for the average \tau. Mach Bands: Linear interpolation of integrated opacity \alpha across the polygon is not mathematically equivalent to the exponential calculation, potentially causing Mach bands. Using a pre-computed texture for e^{-\tau l} mitigates this. Non-planar Faces: Subdividing quadrilateral faces into triangles can cause gaps or overlaps between adjacent cells due to different z interpolations. A view-dependent sorting algorithm for tetrahedral datasets that uses logical partitioning to enable parallel processing, solving the dependency and sequence limitations of neighboring tetrahedra in parallel performance. A GPU implementation that splits the PT algorithm into an update pass (computing view-dependent data by projecting tetrahedra in screen coordinates) and a rendering pass (drawing projected tetrahedra by interpolating scalar values using a texture-based transfer function), achieving interactive rates by storing the model in texture memory and avoiding redundant projections. A technique using a hardware polygon rendering pipeline with hardware compositing to volume render arbitrary unstructured grids composed of convex polyhedral cells. It requires global sorting for back-to-front compositing. An approach to overcome the data transfer bottleneck between CPU and graphics board by using a view-independent description of the unstructured mesh, building a fixed set of data in preprocessing reused every frame. A flexible and highly efficient hardware-assisted volume renderer grounded on the original PT algorithm. It is exclusively based on the rasterization of simple geometric primitives and takes full advantage of graphics hardware. Volume rendering is performed entirely on the GPU within a single pass through the pipeline. Time Complexity: Sorting is O(n \log n) for merge sort or O(n) for bucket sort (with constant factor for slab assignment). Rendering is linear in the number of tetrahedra. Sorting is identified as a bottleneck that affects visualization efficiency heavily. Memory Complexity: Approximately 20 bytes per tetrahedron (16 bytes for texture elements + overhead for 4 tets/vertex average). This is significantly lower than HARC PPI (96 bytes/tet) or HARC (144 bytes/tet). Performance: Renders over 2.0 M Tet/s on current graphics hardware. Optimized software implementations achieved 15 fps for 12,936 cells and 1 fps for 240,122 cells on older hardware. Strengths: Low memory footprint, interactive rates, view-dependent optimization. Limitations: Requires sorting (bottleneck), approximation in perspective views, degenerate cases must be handled. Projected Tetrahedra was introduced by Shirley and Tuchman as a fast algorithm for unstructured volume visualization. It generates triangles that can be rendered by hardware acceleration, relying on a view-dependent projection and visibility sort. The specific GPU-based two-pass fragment shader implementation described here was developed by Marroquim et al. to leverage programmable graphics cards for interactive rendering. name: Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO)
head: SXMPVO (Scanning Exact MPVO), Scanning Exact MPVO (SXMPVO), Scanning Exact Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering
body: SXMPVO is an image-space visibility ordering algorithm for cell projection volume rendering of unstructured data. It solves the problem that the standard Maximal Polyhedra Visibility Ordering (MPVO) method fails for nonconvex meshes because it ignores ordering relations along viewing rays that cross empty space ("ray-gaps") between non-adjacent cells. SXMPVO achieves "image-space correctness" by combining MPVO's face-based partial ordering with scan-conversion of exterior faces into an A-Buffer to resolve these ray-gaps. Unlike object-precision methods like XMPVO, SXMPVO uses image-precision ray shooting, making it faster and simpler to implement while guaranteeing correct sorting for acyclic meshes. The algorithm computes a global ordering of cells in an unstructured mesh (tetrahedral, hexahedral, or "zoo" meshes) to produce correct segment sorting along viewing rays. It assumes the mesh is acyclic; if a cycle exists, the algorithm reports it. The mesh may have nonconvex boundaries, disconnected components, and cells with nonplanar surfaces, provided the projections of cell edges do not cross ("bow tie" quadrilaterals). Input: An unstructured mesh (cells, faces, vertices), a viewpoint, and an image resolution (w \times h). Output: A total ordering sequence of cells b = c{im} < c{im-1} < \dots < c{i1} < c{i0} = a, where b comes before a in the sorted sequence. The algorithm builds on MPVO data structures. For a tetrahedral mesh, MPVO structures require 4f + 14n words, where f is the number of interior faces and n is the number of cells. This includes the adjacency graph, cell vertices, plane equation coefficients, arrows, and one word per cell for flags. SXMPVO adds the following structures: 1. Exterior Face List: A list holding a record for each exterior face. Each record contains: a pointer to the face, a pointer to the cell to which the face belongs, the face’s centroid, and a next pointer. 2. A-Buffer: Implemented as an array of pixel (PIX) lists, one per pixel in the screen image (w \times h). PIX List Entry (PIX Entry): Contains the distance z from the screen to the point where the ray through pixel p intersects face f, a pointer to f, and a next pointer for the PIX list. 3. PN List: Every cell has a PN list pointer, initially set to NULL. PN List Entry (PN Entry): Contains the cell number of the occluded cell and a next pointer. The PN list for a cell contains all exterior cells it occludes (its dependencies). Phase I: Create Partial Ordering of Interior Cells 1. Traverse all cells to mark arrows on shared interior faces, exactly as in MPVO Phase I. This determines "behind" relations from adjacent cells. 2. Set a sink cell flag in each cell to true or false based on whether it has outbound arrows. 3. Create the Exterior Face List containing all exterior faces. Complexity: O(n). Phase II: Sort Exterior Faces 1. Sort the exterior faces in the Exterior Face List by increasing distance from the screen to the face’s centroid. Complexity: O(b \log b) for Phase II, where b is the number of exterior cells. Phase III: Scan Convert Exterior Faces and Record PN Relations 1. Initialize the A-Buffer (array of PIX lists). 2. Remove exterior faces from the sorted queue one at a time and scan-convert their interiors in 3D. When using hardware rasterization (e.g., OpenGL), sample at pixel centers. For each pixel p of an exterior face f enumerated by scan conversion: Create a new PIX entry containing the distance z from the screen to the intersection point, a pointer to f, and a next pointer. Insert the PIX entry into the PIX list in the A-Buffer for pixel p, ordered by decreasing z. Optimization: Since faces are sorted by centroid distance, insertions occur at or near the beginning of the PIX list. Use an efficient insertion sort. 3. After rasterizing all exterior faces, clean up PIX lists: Discard the first entry of every PIX list (the back-facing face where the ray exits the mesh for the last time, which has no matching front-facing face behind it). If the viewpoint is outside the mesh, the PIX lists have an even number of entries, so also discard the last entry (the face through which the ray enters the mesh for the first time). 4. Traverse each PIX list in the A-Buffer to discover dependencies: For each pair of consecutive entries on a PIX list (after cleanup), identify a Pseudoneighbor (PN) relation. A PN pair consists of a front-facing face of cell c{ij} and a back-facing face of cell c{ij-1}. The cell contributing the back-facing face (c{ij-1}) is the occluding PN. The cell contributing the front-facing face (c{ij}) is the occluded PN. Add a PN entry to the PN list of the occluding PN, containing the cell number of the occluded cell. Set the sink cell flag of the occluded PN to false. Duplicate Handling: Check if the PN relation is already in the occluding PN's PN list. If not, add it to the head of the list. If found, move it to the head if not already there (to exploit coherence). Complexity: O(wh + a) for most data sets, where a is the total area of all exterior faces (pixels scanned). Phase IV: Depth First Search (DFS) for Total Ordering 1. Traverse all cells to find sink cells (those whose sink cell flag is still true). 2. Perform a Depth First Search (DFS) on the directed graph to generate the total ordering of the cells. Traverse each edge in the graph twice. Modification: Occluded neighbors (cells on the PN list of cell c) are now eligible neighbors of c in the DFS. Complexity: O(n + a). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sxmpvo(mesh, viewpoint, imagewidth, imageheight, viewpointoutside): n = mesh.numcells b = mesh.numexteriorfaces w, h = imagewidth, imageheight # Phase I: Create Partial Ordering of Interior Cells exteriorfaces = [] for cell in mesh.cells: cell.sinkflag = True for face in cell.faces: if face.isinterior(): face.arrow = True # Mark arrow for MPVO behind relation else: exteriorfaces.append({'face': face, 'cell': cell, 'centroid': face.centroid, 'next': None}) # Phase II: Sort Exterior Faces exteriorfaces.sort(key=lambda f: distance(viewpoint, f['centroid'])) # Phase III: Scan Convert Exterior Faces and Record PN Relations # A-Buffer: array of head pointers for PIX linked lists abuffer = [None] (w h) pnlists = [None] n # PN list head pointers, initially NULL def insertpixentry(head, entry): # Insertion sort by decreasing z if head is None or entry['z'] >= head['z']: entry['next'] = head return entry curr = head while curr['next'] and curr['next']['z'] > entry['z']: curr = curr['next'] entry['next'] = curr['next'] curr['next'] = entry return head for frecord in exteriorfaces: face = frecord['face'] # Scan-convert face, sampling at pixel centers pixelscovered = scanconvertface(face, viewpoint) for pidx, pcenter in pixelscovered: z = computezdistance(viewpoint, pcenter, face) pixentry = {'z': z, 'face': face, 'next': None} abuffer[pidx] = insertpixentry(abuffer[pidx], pixentry) # Clean up PIX lists for pidx in range(w h): head = abuffer[pidx] if head is None: continue # Discard first entry (back-facing face where ray exits mesh last time) head = head['next'] abuffer[pidx] = head # Discard last entry if viewpoint outside mesh if viewpointoutside: if head is None: continue curr = head while curr['next'] is not None: curr = curr['next'] curr['next'] = None # Traverse PIX list to discover PN dependencies curr = head while curr is not None and curr['next'] is not None: frontentry = curr['next'] backentry = curr occludedcell = frontentry['face'].cell occludingcell = backentry['face'].cell # Add PN relation to occluding PN's list addpnrelation(pnlists, occludingcell.index, occludedcell.index) occludedcell.sinkflag = False # Update sink flag curr = curr['next'] # Phase IV: Depth First Search (DFS) for Total Ordering sinkcells = [c for c in mesh.cells if c.sinkflag] ordering = [] visited = set() def dfs(cell): if cell.index in visited: return visited.add(cell.index) for pnidx in getpnlist(pnlists, cell.index): neighbor = mesh.cells[pnidx] dfs(neighbor) ordering.append(cell) for sink in sinkcells: dfs(sink) return ordering def addpnrelation(pnlists, occludingidx, occludedidx): # Check for duplicates and move to head if found head = pnlists[occludingidx] curr = head while curr is not None: if curr['cellidx'] == occludedidx: # Move to head if not already there if curr != head: pnlists[occludingidx] = curr['next'] curr['next'] = head head = curr pnlists[occludingidx] = head return curr = curr['next'] # Add new entry to head pnlists[occludingidx] = {'cellidx': occludedidx, 'next': head} def getpnlist(pnlists, cellidx): # Standard linked list traversal result = [] curr = pnlists[cellidx] while curr is not None: result.append(curr['cellidx']) curr = curr['next'] return result def scanconvertface(face, viewpoint): # Standard rasterization returning list of (pixelindex, pixelcenter) return [] def computezdistance(viewpoint, pixelcenter, face): # Compute distance from viewpoint to intersection along ray return 0.0 def distance(point1, point2): # Euclidean distance return 0.0 Image Resolution: The visibility ordering is correct if the image resolution used for volume rendering is the same as the one used for computing the visibility ordering relations. Mesh Constraint: The mesh must be acyclic. Geometry Constraint: Cells may have nonplanar surfaces, provided their edges do not have projections that cross each other ("bow tie" quadrilateral projections). Tiny Cells: Tiny cells (those not projecting onto any screen pixels) may be output out of order if they are exterior cells, because the relationship a <{vp} b is only guaranteed if there is a continuous sequence of adjacent intervening cells. Sorting sink cells by increasing distance of their centroid to the viewpoint reduces sorting errors for tiny exterior cells. Splatting: If splatting is used for antialiasing, sorting errors may occur for tiny cells because the relationship a <{vp} b is not guaranteed across regions where ray-gaps may occur. Non-strict Ordering: The sort may not be a strict visibility ordering if overlapping faces are not sampled at points in the region of overlap, though the image space ordering remains correct. An algorithm that improves XMPVO results by building a view-independent BSP tree of the exterior faces to reduce the number of ray shooting queries needed. It augments MPVO ordering using binary space partitions on boundary elements. Runtime is O(n + bp), where p is the size of a small subset of exterior cells. However, building the BSP structure is very slow, and the tree can become deep and unbalanced, leading to O(b) cost per search and O(b^2) overall flavor. Results are orders of magnitude better than previous exact methods, but SXMPVO is faster and easier to implement than BSP-XMPVO. Time Complexity: O(wh + a + n) for most data sets, where w, h are image dimensions, a is the projected area (pixels scanned), and n is the number of cells. Expected cost is O(wh(\hat{d}e + 1) + n), where \hat{d}e is the average depth complexity of exterior faces. Memory Complexity: O(wh + a) for A-Buffer, O(a) for PN lists, O(n) for PN list head pointers, and O(b) for exterior face list. Performance: On an SGI Power Onyx (R10000 250 MHz), for helix3.5 (3.57M cells, 375x450 image), SXMPVO uses 367 MB total vs MPVONC's 347.4 MB. Sorting time for a tetrahedral mesh with 1.5 million cells and 550,000 exterior faces was measured as a linear function of projected exterior face area. On a 2.53 GHz Pentium 4, throughput is 500K-600K tetrahedra per second for a 1,050,000 pixel image. Strengths: Faster than all published exact visibility ordering algorithms in object or image space. Handles nonconvex boundaries, disconnected meshes, and mixed cell types. No extra preprocessing compared to MPVO. Limitations: Slower than MPVONC because it must determine and respect every relationship MPVONC does, plus exterior face relations. Requires acyclic meshes. Tiny exterior cells may be out of order. SXMPVO was introduced by Cook, Max, Williams, and Silva in a manuscript received in 2003 and accepted in 2004. It builds on MPVO and XMPVO. ZSWEEP is a related algorithm by Mitchell, Silva, and Farias (2000) that uses a sweep plane approach. SXMPVO is used for volume rendering systems based on cell projection of unstructured data, specifically tetrahedral and zoo meshes. name: Topological Sort for Cell Projection
head: MPVO, MPVO algorithm, Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering, Maximal Polyhedra Visibility Ordering, Exact Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering, Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection
body: Topological Sort for Cell Projection (MPVO) is an O(n) algorithm for computing a back-to-front visibility ordering of convex polyhedral cells in a convex grid. It solves the occlusion ordering problem required for correct alpha-blending in object-order volume rendering by constructing a directed graph of pairwise occlusion relations between adjacent cells and performing a topological sort. Unlike Tetrahedral Volume Rendering or Projected Tetrahedra which may rely on simpler centroid or distance-based heuristics, MPVO guarantees a correct visibility order for convex meshes by respecting the transitive occlusion chain along viewing rays. It fails on non-convex meshes because it ignores occlusion across empty space between non-adjacent cells. Inputs: A convex grid of convex polyhedral cells; a viewpoint V (for perspective) or a projection direction vector \vec{d} (for orthogonal). Outputs: A list of cells sorted in back-to-front order, where an occluded cell precedes an occluder. Data Structures: 1. Cell Node: Contains incount (integer, number of incoming edges), outgoing (list of cell references it occludes), and incoming (list of cell references that occlude it). 2. Directed Graph: Implicitly defined by adjacency, where nodes are cells and edges represent occlusion relations. 3. Queue: A FIFO queue for cells with incount == 0. Definitions: Relation B <{vp} A: Cell B must be rendered before cell A. This holds if the viewpoint V is on the same side of the shared face F between A and B as cell A is. This implies A occludes B, but B cannot occlude A. Arrow Direction: The direction is calculated using the plane equation for the face and the coordinates of the viewpoint (for perspective views) or a vector along the direction of projection (for orthogonal views). Algorithm Steps: 1. Phase I: Construct Partial Ordering (Graph Construction) Initialize all cells C: set C.incount = 0. For each interior face f shared by cells c1 and c2: Determine the direction of occlusion using the face plane equation and viewpoint/projection vector. Perspective View: If V and c1 are on the same side of the plane of f, then c1 occludes c2. Orthogonal View: If the projection direction \vec{d} aligns with the outward normal of c1 relative to f, c1 is in front of c2. Add a directed edge from the occluded cell to the occluder. Increment the occluder's incount. Identify source cells: Cells with incount == 0. Add these to the queue. 2. Phase II: Topological Sort (Kahn's Algorithm) While queue is not empty: Dequeue a cell C. Add C to the sorted output list. For each neighbor B in C.outgoing: decrement B.incount. If B.incount == 0, enqueue B. If the queue empties before all cells are output, a visibility cycle exists. Note: An alternative Phase II uses Depth-First Search with visited and cycledetection flags to output cells. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mpvosort(cells, interiorfaces, viewpoint, isorthogonal=False, projectiondir=None): # Phase I: Initialize and build graph for cell in cells: cell.incount = 0 cell.outgoing = [] cell.incoming = [] for c1, c2, face in interiorfaces: # Determine occlusion direction if isorthogonal: n = face.normal if dot(projectiondir, n) > 0: occluder, occluded = c1, c2 else: occluder, occluded = c2, c1 else: # Perspective: V and c1 on same side of face plane -> c1 occludes c2 n = face.normal P = face.center dv = dot(n, viewpoint - P) dc1 = dot(n, c1.center - P) if (dv > 0 and dc1 > 0) or (dv < 0 and dc1 < 0): occluder, occluded = c1, c2 else: occluder, occluded = c2, c1 # Add edge: occluded -> occluder occluded.outgoing.append(occluder) occluder.incoming.append(occluded) occluder.incount += 1 # Identify source cells (incount == 0) queue = [c for c in cells if c.incount == 0] # Phase II: Topological Sort (Kahn's algorithm) sortedoutput = [] head = 0 while head < len(queue): currentcell = queue[head] head += 1 sortedoutput.append(currentcell) for neighbor in currentcell.outgoing: neighbor.incount -= 1 if neighbor.incount == 0: queue.append(neighbor) if len(sortedoutput) < len(cells): raise ValueError("Visibility cycle detected") return sortedoutput Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Cycles: If the graph contains a cycle, the topological sort fails. In the queue-based variant, this is detected if the queue empties before all cells are output. Cycles imply no global visibility order exists; cells must be subdivided or per-pixel sorting used. Non-Convex Grids: If the grid is non-convex, viewing rays may leave the volume through an external face, cross empty space, and re-enter another cell. MPVO only considers shared faces, so it misses these cross-gap occlusions. Complexity Accounting: Each cell is treated twice during initialization and once in the loop; each edge is treated once in initialization and once in the loop. Manages pixel-level intersection lists for exterior faces on non-convex grids, avoiding true visibility sort complexities while ensuring correct hardware rendering. Choose when exact ordering is needed but the mesh has concavities. Sorts based on power distance with small constant computations. Choose when the mesh is a Delaunay triangulation, as it is not guaranteed to be accurate otherwise. Sorts all faces projecting onto a pixel at render time. Choose when visibility cycles are expected, as a sort always exists per pixel center even without a global sort. Augments MPVO by discovering exterior face relations using ray shooting queries at edge intersections and vertices of the projection complex. Choose when handling non-convex meshes requires exact ordering without per-pixel overhead. Heuristic extension to nonconvex meshes sorting exterior cells by centroid distance. Choose for fast rendering of large non-convex datasets where real-time interaction is prioritized over exact correctness. Time Complexity: O(n) for convex grids, where n is the number of cells. Memory Complexity: Linear space O(n) for data structures. Measured performance with hardware, resolution, and scene: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear scaling with cell count n. Strengths: Very fast, accurate for convex meshes, low computational overhead, detects visibility cycles. Limitations: Fails for non-convex meshes (requires extra gap relations or approximate methods). Requires convexity of cells and grid. When to use: Convex grids of convex polyhedral cells where exact visibility ordering is required and performance is critical. When not to use: Non-convex meshes, non-planar faces, or when real-time interaction with very large non-convex datasets is needed (use Approximate MPVONC or Per-Pixel Sorting). The MPVO algorithm was described by Williams [27] and similarly by Max et al. [15]. It is based on the observation that for convex meshes, local occlusion relations across shared faces define a partial order that can be topologically sorted to yield a correct global visibility order. It is a foundational method for cell projection volume rendering. It is used in direct volume rendering and scientific visualization. name: Kraus and Ertl Method
body: The Kraus and Ertl method handles visibility cycles in convex meshes during cell projection volume rendering. It addresses cases where a global topological sort of cells is impossible due to cyclic visibility dependencies, while a local sort still exists for each pixel center. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projected images of convex, non-overlapping cells on the screen. Output: A correctly sorted and composited image that resolves visibility cycles. Data Structures: The method relies on the output of the basic MPVO sorting algorithm to identify cycle pixels. Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Apply the basic MPVO sorting algorithm to detect pixels where the cell ordering forms a cycle. 2. Isolate these pixels and their associated cells. 3. Use special hardware compositing methods to scan-convert each isolated cycle. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def krausandertlmethod(mpvosortresults): outputbuffer = {} cyclepixels = [] # Step 1 & 2: Detect and isolate cycles using MPVO output for pixel, sortdata in mpvosortresults.items(): if sortdata.hascycle: cyclepixels.append(pixel) # Step 3: Hardware compositing for each cycle for pixel in cyclepixels: cyclecells = sortdata.cyclecells # The source does not specify the exact hardware compositing # or scan-conversion algorithm used to resolve the cycle. outputbuffer[pixel] = cyclecells return outputbuffer Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Rendering costs per cycle increase quadratically in the number of cells involved in the cycle. The method is designed for convex meshes. Time Complexity: Rendering costs per cycle increase quadratically in the number of cells involved in the cycle. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles visibility cycles gracefully for convex non-overlapping cells. For convex non-overlapping cells, there is always a visibility sort for each pixel center even if there is no global visibility sort of the cells. Limitations: Quadratic cost per cycle. Limited to convex meshes in its original form. When to use: When rendering convex meshes with potential visibility cycles where standard MPVO fails. When not to use: When rendering non-convex meshes without extension. The method was introduced by Kraus and Ertl. The method could be extended to nonconvex meshes using the SXMPVO algorithm. name: Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering
head: Fourier projection rendering, Fourier approach to volume rendering, Attenuation-only rendering via Fourier projection-slice theorem, Frequency Domain Volume Rendering
body: Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering is a method for generating attenuation-only images (X-ray-like projections) by exploiting the Fourier projection-slice theorem to compute projections in O(N^2 \log N) time per view, avoiding the O(N^3) cost of digital compositing. Unlike conventional volume rendering or ray-casting, this method does not exhibit occlusion or hidden surface removal; it computes an order-independent linear projection where voxels on a viewing ray contribute equally regardless of distance. It is distinguished from its sibling Domain-transform methods by its specific reliance on frequency-domain slicing to achieve computational efficiency for parallel projections. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume f(\mathbf{x}) sampled on a 3D integer lattice of size N \times N \times N. Output: A 2D projection image I for a given viewing direction. Data Structures: 3D Spectrum: An array of N^3 complex coefficients (or real coefficients if using a Hartley transform). Requires 32-bit floating point precision for accuracy, increasing memory by a factor of 4 compared to 8-bit input volume. If using standard complex arithmetic, it requires 16 bytes per voxel (pair of 64-bit doubles). 2D Slice: An array of N^2 coefficients extracted from the 3D spectrum. Parameters: N: Side length of the cubical volume. Assumed to be an integer power of two for FFT efficiency. V: Normalized viewing direction vector. Defines the orientation of the slice in frequency space. Note: V points away from the eye. W: Nonzero width of the interpolating filter used during slice extraction. Typical value: 4 (a 4^3 tap filter). k2: Factor by which volume width is increased via zero-padding. Typical value: k2 = 4/3 (16% margin). M: Resolution of the projection slice (M \times M). Must be high enough to prevent aliasing. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Frequency Domain Transformation): Compute the 3D discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of the scalar volume f(\mathbf{x}). For real volumes, a Discrete Hartley Transform (DHT) may be substituted to halve memory and time. Vignetting Correction: To cope with vignetting (attenuation of the periphery due to non-ideal filter response), premultiply the volume data f(\mathbf{x}) by the reciprocal of the filter response Pm(\mathbf{x}) = 1/h(\mathbf{x}) before the forward transformation. Here H(\mathbf{s}) is the interpolation filter in frequency space, and h(\mathbf{x}) is its spatial response. Zero Padding: Surround the data with a margin of zeros to avoid ghosting artifacts. A typical margin is 16% (k2=4/3). 2. Slice Extraction (Per View): For each view defined by direction V: Define an extraction plane passing through the origin of the frequency domain and perpendicular to V. Interpolate the discrete spectrum F(\mathbf{s}) along this plane using a filter H(\mathbf{s}). Since the plane does not typically pass through integer lattice points, interpolation from nearby samples is required. Resample the interpolated spectrum to obtain a 2D spectrum. 3. Inverse Transform: Compute the inverse 2D Fourier transform (or inverse FHT) of the extracted 2D slice to generate the final projection image I. Formulas: The Fourier projection-slice theorem states that the 2D image obtained by taking line integrals of the volume along rays perpendicular to the image plane is a Fourier transform pair with the 2D spectrum obtained by extracting a slice from the Fourier transform of the volume along a plane which includes the origin and is parallel to the image plane. Mathematically, the projection operator \PiV is defined as: I = \PiV(f) = \mathcal{F}2^{-1} \{ \mathcal{F}3 \{ f \} \deltaV \} where \mathcal{F}3 is the 3D Fourier transform, \mathcal{F}2^{-1} is the 2D inverse Fourier transform, and \deltaV restricts the spectrum to a plane passing through the origin and perpendicular to viewing direction V. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fourierprojectionslicerendering(volume, viewingdirection): """ volume: 3D list of lists of lists of floats, shape (N, N, N). viewingdirection: list of 3 floats, normalized vector V pointing away from eye. Returns: 2D list of lists of floats, shape (M, M), the projection image. """ N = len(volume) k2 = 4.0 / 3.0 margin = int(N (k2 - 1) / 2) paddedsize = int(N k2) M = N # 1. Preprocessing: Zero Padding paddedvolume = [[[0.0] paddedsize for in range(paddedsize)] for in range(paddedsize)] for i in range(N): for j in range(N): for k in range(N): paddedvolume[i + margin][j + margin][k + margin] = volume[i][j][k] # 2. Vignetting Correction # Premultiply by reciprocal of filter spatial response h(x) correctedvolume = [[[0.0] paddedsize for in range(paddedsize)] for in range(paddedsize)] for i in range(paddedsize): for j in range(paddedsize): for k in range(paddedsize): x, y, z = i - margin, j - margin, k - margin hval = spatialfilterresponse(x, y, z) correctedvolume[i][j][k] = paddedvolume[i][j][k] / max(hval, 1e-8) # 3. Forward 3D FFT spectrum = fft3d(correctedvolume) # 4. Slice Extraction # Generate orthonormal basis (U, T) for the plane perpendicular to V U, T = generateorthonormalbasis(viewingdirection) center = paddedsize // 2 slice2d = [[[0.0] M for in range(M)] for in range(2)] for i in range(M): for j in range(M): # Map 2D pixel indices to 3D frequency coordinates sx = center + U[0] (i - M / 2) + T[0] (j - M / 2) sy = center + U[1] (i - M / 2) + T[1] (j - M / 2) sz = center + U[2] (i - M / 2) + T[2] (j - M / 2) # Interpolate complex spectrum at (sx, sy, sz) slice2d[0][i][j], slice2d[1][i][j] = interpolate3dcomplex(spectrum, sx, sy, sz) # 5. Inverse 2D FFT projection = ifft2d(slice2d) return projection def spatialfilterresponse(x, y, z): # Returns the spatial response h(x) of the interpolation filter. # Typically a separable kernel (e.g., 4^3 tap tricubic spline). return 1.0 def generateorthonormalbasis(V): # Standard vector math to find two vectors orthogonal to V arbitrary = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] if abs(V[0]) < 0.9 else [0.0, 1.0, 0.0] u = cross(V, arbitrary) u = normalize(u) t = cross(V, u) t = normalize(t) return u, t def interpolate3dcomplex(grid, x, y, z): # Standard 3D grid interpolation (e.g., tricubic spline) for complex values. return 0.0, 0.0 def fft3d(data): # Standard radix-2 3D FFT algorithm pass def ifft2d(data): # Standard radix-2 2D IFFT algorithm pass This variant focuses on practical optimizations for the base algorithm. Slices are extracted using a tricubic interpolating spline. A key optimization is replacing the FFT with a Fast Hartley Transform (FHT), which halves per-view rendering time and memory requirements for real-valued data. Further speedups can be achieved by optimizing the filter and trimming zero padding. A shading model that approximates exponential attenuation with locally varying coefficients by linear attenuation with a constant coefficient, allowing the integrand to be expressed as a Fourier projection. This restores depth perception to the otherwise occlusion-free X-ray projections. Time Complexity: Preprocessing: O(N^3 \log N) operations to compute the 3D spectrum. Per-View Rendering: O(N^2 \log N) operations for the inverse transform, plus O(W^3 N^2) for slice extraction where W is the filter width. The overall cost is dominated by the 2D inverse FFT, O(n^2 \log n). Interpolation Cost: High interpolation cost is a bottleneck. Interpolation is O(n^2) with large constant factors, often taking more time than the FFT for practical data sizes (128^3 or 256^3). Memory Complexity: Requires 16 bytes per voxel (pair of 64-bit doubles) for complex arithmetic, compared to 1 byte in spatial domain algorithms. Zero padding increases memory by a factor of k2^3. Performance: For N=256, digital compositing requires 16M operations, while FVR requires 512K operations (speedup >10x) theoretically. In practice, interpolation overhead reduces this gain. GPU acceleration can achieve highly interactive framerates (factor of 17 speedup reported). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Fast generation of X-ray-like projections; suitable for MR angiography and attenuation-only renderings where speed is prioritized. Limitations: No occlusion or depth cues (unless added via shading models); vignetting artifacts; ghosting artifacts from interpolation; high memory usage; only supports parallel projection. The method is based on the Fourier projection-slice theorem, which states that the inverse transform of a slice extracted from the frequency domain representation of a volume yields a projection of the volume in a direction perpendicular to the slice. It was independently proposed for image synthesis by Dunne and Malzbender. Marc Levoy published the foundational paper "Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem" in 1992. Takashi Totsuka and Marc Levoy extended this in 1993 with "Frequency Domain Volume Rendering," introducing shading models in the frequency domain. Later, Viola et al. accelerated the method using GPU-based pipelines. name: Implementation Details for Fourier Volume Rendering
head: Fourier Volume Rendering Implementation, Fourier Volume Rendering with Zero Padding and Tricubic Interpolation, Implementation Details for Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering
body: This article details the specific algorithmic steps, data structures, and parameter choices required to implement the Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering method Parent. It solves the problem of efficiently generating attenuation-only images (X-ray-like projections) and shaded volume renderings by exploiting the Fourier projection-slice theorem. What sets this implementation apart from standard digital compositing is the use of frequency-domain slicing and inverse transformation, reducing the per-view complexity from O(N^3) to O(N^2 \log N). Input: A 3D voxel volume V of size N \times N \times N (typically 128^3). Output: A 2D image I of size 128 \times 128. 1. Preprocessed Volume (V{pad}): A 3D array of size N{pad} \times N{pad} \times N{pad}, where N{pad} = \lceil 1.16 N \rceil. The original data occupies the center, surrounded by a 16% zero-margin. 2. 3D Spectrum (\hat{V}): The result of the 3D FFT of V{pad}. 3. Slices: 2D arrays extracted from \hat{V} corresponding to specific viewing angles. 1. Edge Enhancement: Apply an edge sharpening operator to the input volume V. 2. Nonlinear Windowing: Apply a nonlinear density range windowing operator to the edge-enhanced data. This step may be skipped for specific attenuation-only visualizations (e.g., X-ray projections). 3. Zero Padding: Surround the processed volume with a margin of zeros equal to 16% of the volume width. The padded dimension is N{pad} = \lceil 1.16 N \rceil. This margin prevents "ghosting" artifacts caused by spectral leakage. 1. Weighting: Apply the desired shading or attenuation weighting function W to the preprocessed volume V{pad} to create a weighted volume Vw. 2. 3D FFT: Compute the 3D Fast Fourier Transform of Vw to obtain the spectrum \hat{V}. \hat{V} = \text{FFT3D}(Vw) For each viewing direction defined by a normal vector \mathbf{n}: 1. Slice Extraction: Extract a 2D slice from the 3D spectrum \hat{V} that corresponds to the projection plane orthogonal to \mathbf{n}. The slice width equals the spectral width of the volume. Use a tricubic interpolating spline to extract the slice values from the discrete 3D spectrum grid. 2. 2D Inverse FFT: Compute the 2D Inverse Fast Fourier Transform of the extracted slice to obtain a 2D projection in the spatial domain. P = \text{IFFT2D}(\text{Slice}(\hat{V}, \mathbf{n})) 3. Weighting: Apply viewing or lighting direction weights to the projection P. 4. Summation: Sum the weighted projections from all necessary angles (or a single projection for attenuation-only) to produce the final 128 \times 128 image I. I = \sum Pi Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def edgeenhance(volume): # Standard edge enhancement applies a spatial filter (e.g., Laplacian) # The exact operator is not specified in the sources. return volume # Placeholder for spatial convolution def nonlinearwindow(volume, alpha=2.0): # Nonlinear windowing remaps intensity (e.g., power law or sigmoid) # The exact function is not specified in the sources. return np.power(volume, alpha) # Placeholder for intensity remapping def applyweighting(volume, weights): # Weights depend on the shading model (attenuation, diffuse, etc.) return volume weights def getslicecoordinates(viewdirection, Npad): # Maps viewdirection to 2D plane coordinates in the frequency grid. # Standard approach computes orthonormal basis vectors u, v orthogonal to viewdirection. # The exact geometric mapping is not detailed in the sources. return np.zeros((Npad, Npad)) # Placeholder for coordinate mapping def tricubicinterpolate(spectrum, coords): # Standard tricubic spline interpolation samples the 3D spectrum at coords. # The exact implementation is not detailed in the sources. return np.zeroslike(coords) # Placeholder for spline interpolation def applyviewweights(projection, viewdirection): # Applies lighting/attenuation weights based on view direction. # Model-specific weighting is not detailed in the sources. return projection 0.5 # Placeholder for directional weighting def fouriervolumerendering(V, views, weights3d, imagesize=128): N = V.shape[0] margin = int(0.16 N) Npad = N + 2 margin # Initialize padded volume with zeros Vpad = np.zeros((Npad, Npad, Npad), dtype=V.dtype) # Place original data in the center start, end = margin, N + margin Vpad[start:end, start:end, start:end] = V # Preprocessing Vpad = edgeenhance(Vpad) Vpad = nonlinearwindow(Vpad) # Precomputation Vweighted = applyweighting(Vpad, weights3d) spectrum = np.fft.fftn(Vweighted) # Per-View Rendering finalimage = np.zeros((imagesize, imagesize)) for view in views: coords = getslicecoordinates(view, Npad) slice2d = tricubicinterpolate(spectrum, coords) projection = np.fft.ifftn(slice2d) projection = applyviewweights(projection, view) finalimage += np.real(projection) return finalimage Zero Padding Margin: 16% of the volume width. Interpolation Method: Tricubic interpolating spline. Input Volume Size: Typically 128^3 voxels. Output Image Size: Typically 128 \times 128 pixels. Ghosting: Failing to add the 16% zero-padding margin results in ghosting artifacts due to spectral leakage. Interactive Segmentation: Preprocessing steps (edge sharpening, nonlinear windowing) are applied before the 3D FFT. Changing these operators requires recomputing the entire 3D spectrum, which hinders interactive data segmentation. Mitigation: If segmentation is linear, it can be handled by precomputing spectra for basis materials (e.g., fat, muscle, bone) and weighting them at image generation time. An optimization technique for frequency domain volume rendering that selects between a large and a small interpolation filter based on the local spectral energy of the 3D spectrum, reducing interpolation cost while maintaining image quality. This variant highlights the preprocessing stage where edge sharpening and nonlinear density range windowing operators are applied directly to the input volume data before computing the forward 3D Fourier transform. The key pitfall is that modifying these operators requires recomputing the entire 3D Fourier spectra, which hinders interactive data segmentation if hardwired into the preprocessing pipeline. Time Complexity: O(N^2 \log N) per view, avoiding the O(N^3) cost of digital compositing. Memory Complexity: Varies by shading model. 48 MB for simple attenuation models (equation 3.1.4) to 256 MB for complex shading models (equation 3.3.2) for a 128^3 volume. Performance: On a 36 MHz Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX with a sequential C implementation: Simple model: ~6 seconds per view (~1.5 seconds per slice). Complex model: >1 minute per view (due to paging). Optimizations: Replacing FFT with Fast Hartley Transform (FHT) halves per-view rendering time and memory requirements. Optimizing the filter and trimming zero padding can provide another factor of two speedup. Parallelization is possible at fine grain (within FFT) or coarse grain (between slices). Hardware acceleration using video coprocessors or DSPs is amenable, especially with fixed-point frequency spectra. Strengths: Asymptotically faster than conventional volume rendering for very large volumes. Limitations: High constant factor makes it slower than conventional methods for small volumes. Preprocessing changes require full spectrum recomputation. Origin: The method is based on the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, as described by Marc Levoy in "Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem". History: The implementation was tested on early 1990s hardware (Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX). The approach was developed to address the high computational cost of traditional volume rendering. Usage: Used for generating attenuation-only projections (X-rays) and shaded volume renderings. name: Linear Depth Cueing via Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem
head: Fourier Projection-Slice Depth Cueing, Linear Attenuation via Fourier Projection-Slice, Linear Depth Cueing
body: A shading model that enhances depth perception in X-ray projections by weighting volume points based on their distance from the viewer, without introducing occlusion. It replaces per-voxel shading followed by projection with projection followed by per-pixel shading, allowing depth cueing (linear attenuation) to be computed efficiently by factoring the viewing direction out of the integral. Unlike opaque volume renderings, this method produces X-ray-like projections with no occlusion, but the linear shading provides sufficient shape cues for spatial understanding, especially in motion. Inputs: Volume density \rho(x,y,z) and emission coefficient C(x,y,z), combined as f(x,y,z) = \rho(x,y,z)C(x,y,z). Normalized viewing direction vector \mathbf{V} = (Vx, Vy, Vz), pointing away from the eye. Constant linear attenuation coefficient \tau. Linear depth function \mathbf{D}(P) = mP + b, where P is position along the ray. Outputs: 2D projection image I. Data Structures: Four 3D spectra (frequency domain representations) of the volume, each of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz (complex values). Two-dimensional slices extracted from these spectra for inverse transformation. Steps: 1. Precomputation: Create four copies of the volume data f(x,y,z). Multiply the first copy by 1. Multiply the second copy by Dx(x,y,z), the x-component of the depth function. Multiply the third copy by Dy(x,y,z), the y-component of the depth function. Multiply the fourth copy by Dz(x,y,z), the z-component of the depth function. Compute the 3D Fourier Transform of each of the four modified volumes to yield four 3D spectra: \mathcal{F}\{f\}, \mathcal{F}\{Dx f\}, \mathcal{F}\{Dy f\}, and \mathcal{F}\{Dz f\}. 2. Per-view Rendering: For the current viewing direction \mathbf{V}, extract 2D slices from each of the four 3D spectra corresponding to the projection plane defined by \mathbf{V}. Compute the 2D Inverse Fourier Transform of each extracted slice to obtain spatial domain images. Weight the inverse-transformed images by the components of \mathbf{V} and the constant terms derived from the attenuation model: Multiply the image from \mathcal{F}\{Dx f\} by Vx. Multiply the image from \mathcal{F}\{Dy f\} by Vy. Multiply the image from \mathcal{F}\{Dz f\} by Vz. Multiply the image from \mathcal{F}\{f\} by the constant c1 = \tau/2 - \tau/2 (Vx + Vy + Vz). Sum the four weighted images to produce the final output image I. Formula: The intensity I at a pixel is given by: I = Vx \Pi{\mathbf{V}} \left[ \left(\frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} Dx \right) \rho C \right] + Vy \Pi{\mathbf{V}} \left[ \left(\frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} Dy \right) \rho C \right] + Vz \Pi{\mathbf{V}} \left[ \left(\frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} Dz \right) \rho C \right] + c1 \Pi{\mathbf{V}} [\rho C] where \Pi{\mathbf{V}} is the projection operator, Dx, Dy, Dz are components of \mathbf{D}, and c1 = \tau/2 - \tau/2 (Vx + Vy + Vz). The underlying integral being approximated is: IP = \inta^b \rho(P(t)) C(P(t)) \left[ \frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} (\mathbf{D}(P(t)) \cdot \mathbf{V}) \right] dt where \mathbf{D} = mP + b is a linear function of position. Parameters: \tau: Constant linear attenuation coefficient. \mathbf{V}: Normalized viewing direction vector. m, b: Constants defining the linear depth function \mathbf{D}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ghosting: To avoid ghosting artifacts caused by spectral leakage, the input volume must be surrounded by a margin of zeros. The margin width is N(k2-1)/2 on each side, where k2 is the factor by which the volume width is increased. Viewing Direction Convention: \mathbf{V} must point away from the eye, not towards it. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputespectra(rho, C, Dx, Dy, Dz): """ Precomputes the four 3D spectra required for linear depth cueing. Args: rho: 3D array of density values. C: 3D array of emission coefficients. Dx, Dy, Dz: 3D arrays of depth function components. Returns: spectra: List of four 3D complex arrays [Sf, SDx, SDy, SDz]. """ f = rho C # Standard 3D FFT implementation Sf = fft3d(f) SDx = fft3d(f Dx) SDy = fft3d(f Dy) SDz = fft3d(f Dz) return [Sf, SDx, SDy, SDz] def renderlineardepthcueing(spectra, V, tau): """ Renders a single view using linear depth cueing via Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem. Args: spectra: List of four 3D complex arrays [Sf, SDx, SDy, SDz]. V: Tuple (Vx, Vy, Vz) normalized vector pointing away from eye. tau: Constant linear attenuation coefficient. Returns: image: 2D array representing the rendered projection. """ Sf, SDx, SDy, SDz = spectra Vx, Vy, Vz = V c1 = tau / 2.0 - (tau / 2.0) (Vx + Vy + Vz) # Extracts a 2D slice from the 3D spectrum along the plane orthogonal to V, per the Fourier slice theorem slicef = extractslice(Sf, V) sliceDx = extractslice(SDx, V) sliceDy = extractslice(SDy, V) sliceDz = extractslice(SDz, V) # Standard 2D IFFT implementation imgf = ifft2d(slicef) imgDx = ifft2d(sliceDx) imgDy = ifft2d(sliceDy) imgDz = ifft2d(sliceDz) # Weight and sum according to the projection formula # The tau/2 factor is applied here to match the exact mathematical formulation termbase = c1 imgf termDx = Vx (tau / 2.0) imgDx termDy = Vy (tau / 2.0) imgDy termDz = Vz (tau / 2.0) imgDz image = termbase + termDx + termDy + termDz return image.real Composite Depth Cueing and Directional Shading is a frequency-domain rendering technique that simultaneously applies linear depth cueing (attenuation) and hemispherical directional shading to volume data. It solves the problem of efficiently computing both effects within the Fourier Projection-Slice framework, where naive spatial-domain computation would be prohibitively expensive. It sets itself apart from its parent method, Linear Depth Cueing via Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, by combining the attenuation model with a hemispherical illumination model that avoids the nonlinear absolute value operator, allowing the lighting direction to be factored out of the integral. This requires 16 precomputed spectra and is slower than individual models due to a high constant factor, though asymptotically less expensive than conventional rendering. Memory: 48 megabytes for the 128^3 voxel cube implementation described. Performance: Rendering time was approximately 6 seconds per view on a 36 MHz Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX for the linear depth cueing equation (approx. 1.5 seconds per extracted slice). Scaling: Per-view processing time increases by a factor of k2^2 if the volume width is increased by a factor of k2 due to zero padding. Memory requirements increase by a factor of k2^3. Strengths: Efficient computation of depth cueing in the frequency domain; produces X-ray-like projections with shape cues. Limitations: No occlusion; requires zero-padding to avoid ghosting artifacts. Originated in the work of Marc Levoy, described in "Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem". The method is part of a family of algorithms for generating realistically shaded renderings of volume data using the Fourier projection-slice theorem. Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/fourier/fourier.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem in Volume Rendering, https://www.scribd.com/document/796298963/Marc-Levoy-Volume-rendering-using-the-Fourier-projection-slice-theorem, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Composite Depth Cueing and Directional Shading
head: Composite Shading Model, Hemispherical Illumination Shading
body: Composite Depth Cueing and Directional Shading is a frequency-domain rendering technique that simultaneously applies linear depth cueing (attenuation) and hemispherical directional shading to volume data. It solves the problem of efficiently computing both effects within the Fourier Projection-Slice framework, where naive spatial-domain computation would be prohibitively expensive. It sets itself apart from its parent method, Linear Depth Cueing via Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, by combining the attenuation model with a hemispherical illumination model that avoids the nonlinear absolute value operator, allowing the lighting direction to be factored out of the integral. This requires 16 precomputed spectra and is slower than individual models due to a high constant factor, though asymptotically less expensive than conventional rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume of albedo \Omega(x,y,z), orientation field N(x,y,z), depth vector field D(x,y,z), viewing direction V, lighting direction L, attenuation parameter \tau, and light intensity Is. Output: Rendered image intensity I. Data Structures: The method relies on 16 precomputed 3D spectra derived from the albedo volume \Omega and the geometric fields N and D. VL Vector: A tuple of 13 elements representing products of viewing direction components V and lighting direction components L. Layout: (Vx Lx, Vx Ly, Vx Lz, Vy Lx, Vy Ly, Vy Lz, Vz Lx, Vz Ly, Vz Lz, Vx, Vy, Vz, Lx, Ly, Lz). Note: The source text refers to it as a 12-element vector, but explicitly lists 13 components in the formula. DN Vector: A tuple of 13 elements representing products of depth vector components D and orientation components N. Layout: (Dx Nx, Dx Ny, Dx Nz, Dy Nx, Dy Ny, Dy Nz, Dz Nx, Dz Ny, Dz Nz, Dx, Dy, Dz, Nx, Ny, Nz). Formulas: The rendered intensity I is calculated as: I = \frac{\tau \pi}{2} VL \cdot \PiV \left[ \left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} DN(x,y,z)\right) Is \Omega(x,y,z) \right] + \frac{\tau \pi}{2} c3 \PiV [Is \Omega(x,y,z)] Where: Is: Intensity of the light source. \tau: Attenuation coefficient parameter. \PiV: Fourier projection operator along viewing direction V. c3: Constant term defined as c3 = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \sumi VLi. VL \cdot \PiV [\dots] denotes the dot product between the VL vector and the corresponding vector of projected spectra. Steps: 1. Precomputation (Offline): 1. Expand the integrand product (\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} N \cdot L)(\frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} D \cdot V) into 16 basis terms: 1, Ni (3 terms), Dj (3 terms), and Ni Dj (9 terms). 2. Create 16 basis volumes by multiplying Is \Omega(x,y,z) by each basis term. 3. Compute the 3D Fourier Transform of each basis volume to yield 16 precomputed spectra. 2. Per-View Rendering (Online): 1. For the current viewing direction V and lighting direction L, extract 2D slices from each of the 16 precomputed 3D spectra along V. 2. Compute the 2D Inverse Fourier Transform of each extracted slice to obtain spatial domain images. 3. Weight each image by coefficients derived from L and V, and sum them according to the expanded formula. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def fft3d(vol): # Standard 3D Fast Fourier Transform return np.fft.fftn(vol) def ifft2d(slice2d): # Standard 2D Inverse Fast Fourier Transform return np.fft.ifft2(slice2d) def slicespectrum(spec3d, dirv): # Extract 2D slice from 3D spectrum along direction dirv # Standard operation in Fourier projection-slice rendering return extractslicealongvector(spec3d, dirv) def compositedepthcueingshading(volume, orientation, depthfield, viewingdir, lightingdir, tau, lightintensity): """ Renders a volume using composite depth cueing and directional shading. Args: volume: 3D array of albedo Omega(x,y,z) orientation: 3D array of orientation field N(x,y,z) depthfield: 3D array of depth vector field D(x,y,z) viewingdir: 3D vector V lightingdir: 3D vector L tau: float, attenuation parameter lightintensity: float, Is Returns: 2D array, rendered image """ # Precomputation (Assumed to be done once or cached) # Basis functions for the 16 spectra based on expansion of (1/2 + 1/2 N.L) (tau/2 + tau/2 D.V) # Terms: 1, Ni (3), Dj (3), NiDj (9) basisvolumes = [] # Base albedo (1) basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume) # N components (3) basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume orientation[:,:,0]) # Nx basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume orientation[:,:,1]) # Ny basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume orientation[:,:,2]) # Nz # D components (3) basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume depthfield[:,:,0]) # Dx basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume depthfield[:,:,1]) # Dy basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume depthfield[:,:,2]) # Dz # Cross terms Ni Dj (9) for i in range(3): for j in range(3): basisvolumes.append(lightintensity volume orientation[:,:,i] depthfield[:,:,j]) # Compute 3D FFT for each basis volume spectra = [fft3d(bv) for bv in basisvolumes] # Per-view rendering V = viewingdir L = lightingdir # Extract slices from spectra along V slices = [slicespectrum(spec, V) for spec in spectra] # Inverse FFT to get spatial images images = [ifft2d(s) for s in slices] # Coefficients from expanded integrand: Is Omega (pitau/4) [1 + sum(Li Ni) + sum(Vj Dj) + sum(Li Vj Ni Dj)] coeffbase = (tau np.pi) / 4 coeffn = [(tau np.pi) / 4 L[i] for i in range(3)] coeffd = [(tau np.pi) / 4 V[i] for i in range(3)] coeffnd = [[(tau np.pi) / 4 L[i] V[j] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] # Map images to coefficients and sum # Image 0: Base # Image 1-3: Ni # Image 4-6: Dj # Image 7-15: Ni Dj imagesum = images[0] coeffbase for i in range(3): imagesum += images[1+i] coeffn[i] for i in range(3): imagesum += images[4+i] coeffd[i] for i in range(3): for j in range(3): imagesum += images[7 + i3 + j] coeffnd[i][j] return imagesum Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Emission: The composite model ignores emission \rho C from the depth cueing equation. In this context, emission can be interpreted as ambient illumination. Memory: The requirement for 16 spectra can lead to significant memory usage, potentially causing paging on older systems. This method combines linear depth cueing and directional shading within the frequency domain to replace O(n^3) spatial domain computations with O(n^2) frequency domain operations. It solves the problem of efficiently applying both attenuation and illumination in Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering [Parent]. It sets itself apart from naive frequency domain combinations by reversing the standard order of operations (applying depth cueing and interpolation first, then shading) to utilize a single composite filter, thereby avoiding the computational cost of multiple convolutions. Time Complexity: Asymptotically less expensive than conventional volume rendering (O(n^2) vs O(n^3)), but with a high constant factor due to the 16 spectra and 16 inverse FFTs per view. Memory Complexity: Requires storing 16 3D spectra. For a 128^3 voxel cube, this amounts to 256 megabytes. Measured Performance: On a 36 MHz Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX, rendering time was over a minute per view for a 128^2 image, mostly due to paging. Strengths: Efficiently combines two shading effects; avoids nonlinear operators; plausible shading for diffuse objects resembling a cloudy day appearance. Limitations: High constant factor makes it slower than conventional rendering for small volumes; sensitive to memory constraints; ignores emission/ambient light. When to Use: Large volumes where asymptotic efficiency outweighs constant overhead; scenes requiring both depth cueing and directional shading. When Not to Use: Small volumes; hardware with limited memory; scenes requiring accurate ambient lighting or emission. The method was developed by Marc Levoy as part of his work on Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering. It appears in the paper "Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem". The technique was demonstrated on a CT scan of a human skull. The approach was implemented in C on a Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX. The paper suggests that replacing the FFT with an FHT (Fast Hartley Transform) could halve the rendering time and memory requirements. PDF Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/fourier/fourier.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem in Volume Rendering, https://www.scribd.com/document/796298963/Marc-Levoy-Volume-rendering-using-the-Fourier-projection-slice-theorem, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Combined Depth Cueing and Shading
head: Directional Shading in Frequency Domain, Frequency Domain Shading and Depth Cueing, Linear Depth Cueing, Reversed order shading and cueing
body:
This method combines linear depth cueing and directional shading within the frequency domain to replace O(n^3) spatial domain computations with O(n^2) frequency domain operations. It solves the problem of efficiently applying both attenuation and illumination in Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering [Parent]. It sets itself apart from naive frequency domain combinations by reversing the standard order of operations (applying depth cueing and interpolation first, then shading) to utilize a single composite filter, thereby avoiding the computational cost of multiple convolutions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volume spectrum \hat{f}(\mathbf{s}), view direction \mathbf{V}, light direction \mathbf{L}, depth cueing function d(x), and interpolation filter H(\mathbf{s}). Output: Rendered image with combined depth cueing and directional shading. Data Structures: Spectrum: 3D complex array \hat{f}(\mathbf{s}) where \mathbf{s} = (sx, sy, sz). Composite Filter: H'(\mathbf{s}) combines interpolation and depth cueing in the frequency domain. Light Coefficients: Constants C{dif}, L{dif} for shading magnitude. Depth Cueing Coefficients: C{cue} for linear depth cueing. Steps: 1. Reverse Order Strategy: Instead of applying shading first (which requires two convolutions: one to recover the pure spectrum for shading, and one to apply depth cueing), reverse the order: apply depth cueing and interpolation simultaneously using the composite filter H', then apply shading. 2. Composite Filtering: Use H'(\mathbf{s}) to perform interpolation and linear depth cueing at once during slice extraction. 3. Shading Application: Apply directional shading to the depth-cued and interpolated data. 4. Adjustment for Non-Perpendicular Light: If the light direction \mathbf{L} is not perpendicular to the view direction \mathbf{V}, an adjustment term must be computed to correct for the distortion of the gradient vector caused by the reversed order. 5. Linear Depth Cueing Adjustment: For linear depth cueing, compute the difference term adjustment during slice extraction without convolution if \mathbf{L} is not perpendicular to \mathbf{V}. Formulas: The shading equation in the spatial domain includes an ambient term and a shading term involving the gradient 
abla f: I = C{amb} +  rac{1}{2} C{dif} L{dif} (
abla f \cdot \mathbf{L}) When depth cueing d(x) is applied, the gradient term becomes 
abla [f(x) d(x)] \cdot \mathbf{L}. Using the product rule: 
abla [f(x) d(x)] \cdot \mathbf{L} = (
abla f(x) \cdot \mathbf{L}) d(x) + f(x) (
abla d(x) \cdot \mathbf{L}) Since d(x) is a function of depth t = \mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{x}, 
abla d(x) = d'{1D}(\mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{x}) \mathbf{V}. The difference term (error introduced by reversed order) is: f(x) d'{1D}(\mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{x}) (\mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{L}) For linear depth cueing, d{1D}(t) is linear, so d'{1D}(t) is constant. The full adjustment term including coefficients is:  rac{1}{2} C{cue} C{dif} L{dif} f(x) (\mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{L}) This term can be computed during slice extraction without convolution. Parameters: Light Direction \mathbf{L}: Often set perpendicular to \mathbf{V} to maximize shading effect (side lighting). Depth Cueing Function: Linear depth cueing is specified. Filter Size: 3 	imes 3 	imes 3 filter used in experiments, consuming 27 input samples per output sample. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendercombineddepthcueingshading(spectrum, viewdir, lightdir, coeffs): """ Renders volume with combined depth cueing and shading using reversed order. Args: spectrum: 3D complex array of volume spectrum. viewdir: 3D vector, view direction V. lightdir: 3D vector, light direction L. coeffs: Dictionary containing Ccue, Cdif, Ldif, Camb. Returns: Rendered image array. """ vdotl = sum(v l for v, l in zip(viewdir, lightdir)) adjustmentfactor = 0.5 coeffs['Ccue'] coeffs['Cdif'] coeffs['Ldif'] vdotl # Step 1 & 2: Extract slices using composite filter H' (interpolation + depth cueing) # In Fourier Projection-Slice rendering, slices are extracted in the frequency domain. # We iterate over slice orientations/positions, apply H', and inverse FFT to spatial domain. depthcuedslices = [] for sliceparams in getsliceparameters(spectrum.shape, viewdir): # Apply composite filter H' in frequency domain filteredspectrum = spectrum Hprime(sliceparams, coeffs) # Inverse FFT to get spatial slice slicedata = ifft2(filteredspectrum) depthcuedslices.append(slicedata) # Step 3 & 4: Apply shading and adjustment shadedslices = [] for slicedata in depthcuedslices: # Compute gradient in spatial domain for shading gradf = computegradient(slicedata) # Apply shading term shaded = coeffs['Camb'] + 0.5 coeffs['Cdif'] coeffs['Ldif'] (gradf lightdir).sum(axis=-1) # Apply adjustment if V is not perpendicular to L if vdotl != 0: # Adjustment = 0.5 Ccue Cdif Ldif f(x) (V. L) # f(x) here is the depth-cued spatial data before shading adjustment = adjustmentfactor slicedata.real shaded = shaded + adjustment shadedslices.append(shaded) # Step 5: Composite slices into final image image = compositeslices(shadedslices) return image def getsliceparameters(volumeshape, viewdir): """Generates slice extraction parameters for the given view direction.""" # Standard Fourier Projection-Slice slice extraction logic return [] # Implementation depends on specific projection-slice grid def Hprime(sliceparams, coeffs): """Composite filter combining interpolation and linear depth cueing.""" # H'(s) = H(s) D(s) where H is interpolation filter and D is depth cueing filter return sliceparams['interpolationfilter'] sliceparams['depthcueingfilter'] def computegradient(data): """Computes spatial gradient using finite differences.""" # Standard 3-point central difference implementation pass def compositeslices(slices): """Projects/accumulates slices into a 2D image based on view direction.""" # Standard projection-slice accumulation pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perpendicular Light: If \mathbf{L} is perpendicular to \mathbf{V}, \mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{L} = 0, and the adjustment term is zero. No correction is needed. Non-Linear Depth Cueing: For complex depth cueing functions, a convolution is necessary for the adjustment term, increasing computational cost. Gradient Distortion: Applying depth cueing before shading distorts the gradient vector, leading to incorrect shading. Reversing the order avoids this but requires the adjustment term. A technique to combine depth cueing and directional shading by reversing the order of operations (applying depth cueing and interpolation first, then shading) to use a single composite filter H' and avoid two convolutions. It is chosen when computational efficiency is prioritized and the light direction is not perpendicular to the view direction, requiring an adjustment term. The adjustment term is f(x) d'{1D}(\mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{x}) (\mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{L}), which is zero if d(x) is linear and \mathbf{L} is perpendicular to \mathbf{V}. Time Complexity: O(n^2 \log n) for the frequency domain computation, replacing O(n^3) spatial domain computations. The interpolation step is O(n^2) and consumes most of the running time. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D spectrum and intermediate slices. Measured Performance: A 128^3 volume can be rendered in a fraction of a second on a conventional workstation. The adaptive filtering scheme reduced the cost of interpolation to about 15% of the non-adaptive case. Strengths: Significant speed advantage over conventional volume rendering; no visible difference compared to conventional spatial domain rendering with identical shading and depth cueing. Limitations: The frequency domain projection operator is non-occluding, resulting in a loss of realism. The reversed order requires an adjustment term if \mathbf{L} is not perpendicular to \mathbf{V}. When to Use: Use when high performance is needed for large volumes and occlusion is not required. When Not to Use: When occlusion is critical for realism or when the light direction is complex and non-perpendicular, requiring expensive convolutions for adjustment. Originated by Takashi Totsuka and Marc Levoy in 1993. The paper "Frequency Domain Volume Rendering" was presented at SIGGRAPH 1993. The method replaces O(n^3) spatial domain computations (specifically shading and depth cueing) with O(n^2) frequency domain methods to reduce computational cost.
