name: Frequency Domain Shear-Warp Volume Rendering
head: FDVR, Fourier Volume Rendering, Resampling in the Frequency Domain
body: Frequency Domain Shear-Warp Volume Rendering is a technique that performs the shear transformation of the shear-warp factorization in the frequency domain using the shifting theorem, allowing for arbitrary, view-independent sampling distances along viewing rays via zero-padding interpolation. Unlike standard shear-warp algorithms where sampling distance is coarse and view-dependent, this method decouples sampling density from the viewing direction by resampling in the frequency domain, thereby avoiding the large spatial zero-padding required by spatial-domain shear methods. The method builds on Frequency Domain Volume Rendering by replacing the spatial shear stage with frequency-domain operations. Inputs and Outputs Input: Volume dataset V of size N \times N \times N (cubiform, power of two), viewing vector \vec{v}{so}, desired sampling distance s', slice distance dk. Output: Rendered image with arbitrary sampling distance s' along viewing rays. Data Structures Volume Data: 3D array of voxel values. Frequency Domain: 3D complex array resulting from FFT. Slices: 2D arrays representing planes perpendicular to the viewing direction. Numbered Steps 1. Permutation: Change the storage order of voxels in memory to maximize cache coherency, such that the (i, j) plane is most perpendicular to the viewing direction. The volume starts in the standard object coordinate system, already permuted such that the (i, j) plane is most perpendicular to the viewing direction. 2. 3D Fourier Transform: Compute the 3D Fourier transform of the permuted volume to reach the frequency domain representation. 3. Calculate Pre-Resampling Sampling Distance (s): Compute the sampling distance along the viewing rays before resampling using the viewing vector and slice distance. Normalize the viewing vector \vec{v}{so} = (v{so,i}, v{so,j}, v{so,k}) in the k direction by dividing each component by v{so,k}, yielding \vec{v}'{so} = (v'{so,i}, v'{so,j}, v'{so,k}) with v'{so,k} = 1.0. Calculate s using the formula: s = dk \sqrt{(v'{so,i})^2 + (v'{so,j})^2 + (v'{so,k})^2} where s is the sampling distance before resampling, dk is the distance between volume slices along the k axis, and v'{so,i}, v'{so,j}, v'{so,k} are the components of the normalized viewing vector. 4. Calculate Post-Resampling Slice Count (K'): Determine the number of slices needed after resampling to achieve the desired sampling distance s' using the ratio of desired to current sampling distance and the current slice count K. The relationship is given by: \frac{s'}{s} = \frac{K}{K'} Solve for K': K' = \frac{sK}{s'} Round K' to the closest integer K0 \in \mathbb{N}. 5. Zero-Padding: Append zeros in the frequency domain along the k direction to increase the number of slices from K to K0, exploiting the packing theorem (zero-padding interpolation property). The difference between K0 and K is the amount of zero-padding necessary for the selected sampling distance s0. Note: For K0 > 50, the deviation from the desired sampling distance s0 is below \pm 1.0\%. 6. Inverse Fourier Transform in k: Apply an inverse Fourier transform in the k direction while keeping the i and j directions in the frequency domain to obtain sheared slices. This stage effectively performs the shear transformation via the shifting theorem in the frequency domain. 7. Inverse Fourier Transform in i and j: Apply 2D inverse Fourier transforms to the sheared slices to bring the i and j dimensions into the spatial domain, preparing them for compositing. 8. Compositing: Perform numeric integration along the viewing rays on the resampled slices. This stage uses the arbitrary sampling distance s' independent of the viewing direction. 9. Warping: Transform the intermediate image of the compositing stage into the final image. The warping in this method remains similar to the standard shear-warp algorithm. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def frequencydomainshearwarprender(volume, origin, direction, step): """ Renders a ray using Frequency Domain Shear-Warp Volume Rendering. Precomputes frequency-domain slices, then composites along the ray. """ N = volume.shape[0] # Step 1 & 2: Permutation & 3D FFT # Permutation aligns (i,j) plane perpendicular to viewing direction. # Standard permutation reorders axes so k aligns with the dominant viewing direction component. permutedvolume = np.transpose(volume, (2, 0, 1)) freqvolume = np.fft.fftn(permutedvolume) # Step 3: Pre-Resampling Sampling Distance (s) vx, vy, vz = direction vprimex = vx / vz vprimey = vy / vz vprimez = 1.0 s = step np.sqrt(vprimex2 + vprimey2 + vprimez2) # Step 4: Post-Resampling Slice Count (K') K = N K0float = (s K) / step K0pad = int(round(K0float)) # Step 5: Zero-Padding in frequency domain along k paddedfreq = np.zeros((K0pad, N, N), dtype=complex) paddedfreq[:N,:,:] = freqvolume # Step 6: Inverse FFT in k shearedslicesfreq = np.fft.ifft(paddedfreq, axis=0) # Step 7: Inverse FFT in i and j spatialslices = np.fft.ifft2(shearedslicesfreq, axes=(1, 2)) # Step 8: Compositing along the ray # Ray: P(t) = origin + t direction # We sample at intervals of 'step' along the ray. # Map ray coordinates to slice indices. # Standard shear-warp warping transforms ray coordinates to the permuted space. # Here we simulate sampling along the k-axis of the spatial slices. numsamples = int(np.ceil(np.linalg.norm(origin) / step)) samples = [] T = 1.0 C = 0.0 for t in np.arange(0, numsamples step, step): kidx = int(round(t)) if 0 <= kidx < spatialslices.shape[0]: # Sample center of slice (scalar volume) val = np.real(spatialslices[kidx, N//2, N//2]) alpha = val step C = C + alpha T T = T (1.0 - alpha) samples.append(C) else: samples.append(C) return samples[:4] Parameters Desired Sampling Distance (s'): The target sampling distance along the viewing rays, which is independent of the view direction. Slice Distance (dk): The distance between volume slices along the k axis in the object coordinate system. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Spatial Domain Zero-Padding: If spatial domain zero-padding is too small in shear-based methods, data passes over the border and re-enters from the other side due to periodicity, an error amplified by consecutive shears. This method avoids this by not requiring large spatial domain zero-padding. Rounding Error: Zero-padding can only be applied in discrete steps, so K0 is rounded to the closest integer. For K0 > 50, the deviation from the desired sampling distance s0 is below \pm 1.0\%. Time Complexity: For a cubiform dataset with edge length N (power of two), the computational complexity is 6 \cdot N^3 \log2 N, consisting of one 3D FFT (3 \cdot N^3 \log2 N), N^2 1D IFFTs (N^3 \log2 N), and N^2 2D IFFTs (N^3 \log2 N). Memory Complexity: The method does not require large spatial domain zero-padding, resulting in significantly lower memory consumption compared to methods like Li et al.'s, which requires memory >5x higher. Performance: Experimental results show that the presented method outperforms established algorithms in the quality of the produced images. If the data is sampled above the Nyquist rate, the method is capable of perfect reconstruction of the original function. Strengths: Allows arbitrary, view-independent sampling distances; avoids periodicity errors from spatial shear; high reconstruction quality. Limitations: Requires FFT computation; rounding of slice count may introduce minor sampling distance deviations (negligible for K0 > 50). Origin: The method was introduced in a paper by researchers from the University of Technology, Austria, and Simon Fraser University, Vancouver, Canada. History: It is conceptually based on the shear-warp factorization, which consists of permutation, shearing, compositing, and warping stages. The method proposes performing the shear transformation in the frequency domain using the shifting theorem. Usage: Used for high-quality volume rendering, particularly where view-independent sampling and high reconstruction quality are required. name: Isosurface extraction
body: Isosurface extraction generates an explicit polygonal mesh representing the surface where a scalar field equals a specific threshold (isovalue) from volumetric data. It solves the problem of visualizing internal structures or boundaries within volumetric data by approximating the implicit surface f(x,y,z) = I. What sets this family apart from direct volume rendering is that it produces an explicit geometric representation (mesh) rather than a rasterized image. Unlike Blocky meshing, which produces voxel-aligned stair-step surfaces, isosurface methods typically interpolate between grid points to create smooth, curved surfaces. All isosurface extraction algorithms operate on a discretized domain, typically a regular grid (Cartesian, octree, or tetrahedral) where each cell contains scalar values at its vertices. The core mechanism involves traversing the grid cells and evaluating the scalar field at cell vertices or edges. For cubic grids, vertex values are compared against the isovalue to determine a topological configuration (e.g., a 256-case index). For tetrahedral or hybrid grids, the method identifies edges where the scalar field changes sign. Intersection points are computed using inverse linear interpolation for the parameter and linear interpolation for 3D coordinates: t = (I - fa) / (fb - fa) and P = Va + t(Vb - Va). The intersection points are then connected to form primitives (triangles, quads, or polygons). Adjacent cell primitives are merged into a coherent mesh, often requiring vertex merging to avoid duplicates. Generates a triangular mesh from a 3D scalar field by processing each voxel independently. It determines the topology of the isosurface intersection with cube boundaries based on vertex values relative to an isolevel. Uses a fixed lookup table to resolve intersections, making it straightforward but complicated to implement due to fifteen distinct special cases. Choose it for general-purpose cubic grid extraction. Places a single vertex inside each grid cell intersected by the surface, optimizing its position by minimizing a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) derived from Hermite data. Unlike Marching Cubes, which places vertices on cell edges, it preserves sharp features and produces manifold, watertight meshes. Choose it when feature preservation and watertightness are critical. Begins with a seed point and grows a triangulation across an implicit surface by advancing the front boundary. Choose it for incremental surface generation or when starting from a known point on the surface. Projects a query point onto a surface defined by input points and normals by fitting a local quadratic function. Choose it for refining vertex positions or projecting points onto implicit surfaces. Provides a standardized interface for invoking various extraction algorithms. Choose it to abstract algorithm selection and manage multiple extraction methods uniformly. Extracts isosurfaces from 3D voxel data by constructing a wire frame of N-cycles (closed loops of voxel faces) enclosing active voxels, which are then triangulated. Choose it for volume-enclosing surfaces from voxel data without topological ambiguities. Constructs a mesh by placing a single vertex per active voxel at the weighted average of grid points on intersected edges. Unlike Marching Cubes, it generates exactly one vertex per voxel, resulting in a sparser mesh. Choose it for performance-critical applications where exact vertex placement is less important than speed and sparsity. Reconstructs a Piecewise Linear Interface Concept (PLIC) plane in Volume of Fluid (VOF) simulations on arbitrary polyhedral grids. Choose it for fluid dynamics simulations requiring accurate interface reconstruction. Generates a 3D mesh from a trained DVR model by querying an implicit occupancy field using adaptive resolution. Choose it for neural implicit surface reconstruction. Precomputed data structures mapping voxel corner signs to intersected edges and triangle indices. Solves topology determination without runtime branching. Choose it for CPU/GPU implementations prioritizing simplicity and topological consistency over geometric optimality. Produces topologically consistent surfaces with a local convexity property, where the polygonal contour inside each cell encloses a convex negative space. Choose it when topological robustness and convexity guarantees are required. GPU-accelerated technique processing a 3D scalar volume grid using a compute shader. Adapts classic Marching Cubes for parallel execution with fixed-size buffers and atomic counters. Choose it for real-time or high-throughput implicit function to mesh conversion on GPUs. Data structure to obtain active cells for a particular isosurface with optimal query complexity O(\log(n) + k). Choose it for accelerating cell extraction in large volumes. Uses an octree as a spatial discretization structure instead of a Cartesian grid. Allows for adaptive resolution but may cause cracks if not adapted to the surface. Choose it for multi-resolution data where adaptive sampling is beneficial. Approximates the isosurface position between two sample points by iteratively halving the interval based on scalar field values. Choose it for high-precision interpolation in sparse or expensive-to-evaluate fields. Generates triangulation tables for isosurface extraction in n-dimensional hypercubes. Choose it for extracting surfaces from higher-dimensional data or hypercubic grids. Smooths a 2D or 3D binary embedding array by assigning negative/positive values to preserve fine details and thin structures. Choose it for post-processing binary embeddings to retain thin features. Extracts intersection-free isosurfaces using intersections with a tetrahedral grid's edges, guaranteeing freedom from self-intersections. Choose it when topological correctness and intersection-free output are mandatory. Triangulates non-convex or complex polygons resulting from extraction into triangles, minimizing total area to reduce visual artifacts. Choose it for post-processing extracted polygons to improve mesh quality. Maps one of the 256 possible cube configurations to one of 23 canonical base cases using precomputed rotation and base case mappings to simplify triangle generation logic. Choose it to reduce lookup table size and simplify implementation. Converts isosurfaces to point clouds by evaluating chunks of voxels and extracting vertices at the center of intersected edges, without generating face data. Choose it for point-based rendering or when surface reconstruction is deferred to the GPU. Detects patch boundaries as groups of rings of linear contours on cell faces for automatic construction of look-up tables. Choose it for automated table generation in custom contouring methods. Sequentially visits all cells in the volume to identify active cells containing the isosurface by checking if the isovalue is contained in the half-open interval [v{min}, v{max}). Requires only storage for the original volume data and yields linear time complexity O(n). Choose it for simple, memory-efficient extraction when acceleration structures are unnecessary. name: Dual Contouring
head: Ju's method, Ju et al. 2002 dual contouring, Dual Contouring of Hermite Data, QEF-based Dual Contouring, Dual Contouring with QEF Vertex Optimization
body: Dual Contouring is an isosurface extraction algorithm that places a single vertex inside each grid cell intersected by the surface, optimizing its position by minimizing a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) derived from Hermite data (intersection points and surface normals). Unlike Marching Cubes, which places vertices on cell edges, Dual Contouring preserves sharp features and produces manifold, watertight meshes. Inputs: A scalar field f(x, y, z) or Signed Distance Field (SDF). Grid dimensions and bounds [x{min}, x{max}) \times [y{min}, y{max}) \times [z{min}, z{max}). Optional: Pre-computed Hermite data (intersection points and normals). Parameters: Regularization weight (reg), SVD tolerance (svd\tol), clamp flag (clamp), iteration counts (outer\iters, inner\iters), SDF weights (\mu, hermite\weight, update\weight), and convergence tolerance (tol). Outputs: A list of vertices and a list of faces (quads or triangles) forming the mesh. Data structures: vertindices mapping cell coordinates (x, y, z) to vertex indices. Intersection Struct: points: NDArray<float3> of intersection points (N, 3). normals: NDArray<float3> of surface normals (N, 3). edges: NDArray<uint2> identifying the edges crossed. cellindices: NDArray<uint> mapping intersections to cells. celloffsets: NDArray<uint> offsets for cell-based iteration. isout: NDArray<bool> status flags. hasnormals: bool indicating if normals are present. QEF Matrix (per cell): Matrix A of size k \times 3, where k is the number of intersection points. Each row i is the normal vector ni. Vector b of size k, where bi = \text{dot}(ni, Pi). 1. Grid Traversal and Intersection Detection: Iterate over all cells (x, y, z) in the grid range. For each cell, evaluate the scalar field at the 8 corners v{dx,dy,dz} = f(x+dx, y+dy, z+dz) where dx, dy, dz \in \{0, 1\}. Identify edges where the sign of the field changes (i.e., v{start} > 0 \neq v{end} > 0). If fewer than 2 sign-changing edges exist, skip the cell (no vertex created). 2. Intersection Point and Normal Computation: For each intersected edge, compute the intersection point P using linear interpolation: P = Va + t(Vb - Va), \quad t = \frac{I - f(Va)}{f(Vb) - f(Va)} where Va, Vb are the edge endpoints, f(Va), f(Vb) are the scalar field values at the endpoints, and I is the isovalue. Normals are typically pre-computed or derived from the gradient of the scalar field. 3. QEF Construction: For each cell, construct the QEF system A V = b. Rows of A are the normals ni at intersection points Pi. Elements of b are bi = \text{dot}(ni, Pi). 4. Vertex Placement (QEF Solution): Solve for vertex position V by minimizing \| A V - b \|^2. Use Jacobi SVD eigendecomposition for the symmetric positive semi-definite system. Use mass-point bias for rank-deficient cases (e.g., coplanar normals). If clamp is true, the vertex position is constrained to the cell bounds. 5. Mesh Generation (Quad/Triangle Creation): For each sign-changing minimal grid edge, identify the 4 cells sharing that edge. Each cell contributes its computed vertex to form a quad. Split quads into triangles. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dualcontouring(grid, level=0.0, reg=1e-2, svdtol=1e-6, clamp=True, biasstrength=0.0): """ Extracts isosurface from grid using Dual Contouring. grid: 3D array of scalar values. level: Iso-value (default 0.0). reg: Regularization weight for QEF. svdtol: SVD tolerance. clamp: Clamp vertex to cell bounds. biasstrength: Weight for mass-point bias to handle rank deficiency. """ vertices = [] faces = [] vertindices = {} shape = grid.shape def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def lerp(p0, p1, t): return [p0[d] + t(p1[d]-p0[d]) for d in range(3)] def clampval(v, minv, maxv): return max(minv, min(maxv, v)) def findedges(corners, level): edges = [] edgepairs = [(0,1), (0,2), (0,4), (1,3), (1,5), (2,3), (2,6), (3,7), (4,5), (4,6), (5,7), (6,7)] for i, j in edgepairs: if (corners[i] - level) (corners[j] - level) < 0: edges.append((i, j)) return edges def computenormal(grid, p, shape): ix = clampval(int(round(p[0])), 1, shape[0]-2) iy = clampval(int(round(p[1])), 1, shape[1]-2) iz = clampval(int(round(p[2])), 1, shape[2]-2) fx = (grid[ix+1, iy, iz] - grid[ix-1, iy, iz]) / 2.0 fy = (grid[ix, iy+1, iz] - grid[ix, iy-1, iz]) / 2.0 fz = (grid[ix, iy, iz+1] - grid[ix, iy, iz-1]) / 2.0 norm = math.sqrt(fx2 + fy2 + fz2) if norm == 0: return [0, 0, 1] return [fx/norm, fy/norm, fz/norm] def solveqef(A, b, reg, tol): # Solve normal equations (A^T A) V = A^T b with regularization AtA = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] Atb = [0.0]3 for k in range(len(A)): for i in range(3): for j in range(3): AtA[i][j] += A[k][i] A[k][j] Atb[i] += A[k][i] b[k] for i in range(3): AtA[i][i] += reg # Gaussian elimination M = [AtA[i] + [Atb[i]] for i in range(3)] for i in range(3): pivot = M[i][i] if abs(pivot) < tol: pivot = tol for j in range(i+1, 3): factor = M[j][i] / pivot for k in range(i, 4): M[j][k] -= factor M[i][k] V = [0.0]3 for i in range(2, -1, -1): V[i] = M[i][3] for j in range(i+1, 3): V[i] -= M[i][j] V[j] V[i] /= M[i][i] return V for x in range(shape[0] - 1): for y in range(shape[1] - 1): for z in range(shape[2] - 1): corners = [ grid[x, y, z], grid[x+1, y, z], grid[x, y+1, z], grid[x+1, y+1, z], grid[x, y, z+1], grid[x+1, y, z+1], grid[x, y+1, z+1], grid[x+1, y+1, z+1] ] edgeindices = findedges(corners, level) if len(edgeindices) < 2: continue intersections = [] for i, j in edgeindices: v0, v1 = corners[i], corners[j] t = (level - v0) / (v1 - v0) if abs(v1 - v0) > 1e-9 else 0.5 p0 = [x + (i&1), y + ((i>>1)&1), z + (i>>2)] p1 = [x + (j&1), y + ((j>>1)&1), z + (j>>2)] P = lerp(p0, p1, t) n = computenormal(grid, P, shape) intersections.append((P, n)) A = [n for, n in intersections] b = [dot(n, P) for P, n in intersections] # Mass-point bias for rank deficiency if biasstrength > 0: centroid = [sum(p[d] for p, in intersections) / len(intersections) for d in range(3)] for d in range(3): axisnormal = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] axisnormal[d] = biasstrength A.append(axisnormal) b.append(dot(axisnormal, centroid)) V = solveqef(A, b, reg, svdtol) if clamp: V = [clampval(V[d], x, x+1) for d in range(3)] cellkey = (x, y, z) vertindices[cellkey] = len(vertices) vertices.append(V) # Face generation: iterate over all grid edges to form quads/triangles edgecells = {} for x in range(shape[0] - 1): for y in range(shape[1] - 1): for z in range(shape[2] - 1): if (x, y, z) not in vertindices: continue for dx, dy, dz in [(1,0,0), (0,1,0), (0,0,1)]: ex, ey, ez = min(x, x+dx), min(y, y+dy), min(z, z+dz) edgekey = (ex, ey, ez, dx, dy, dz) if edgekey not in edgecells: edgecells[edgekey] = [] edgecells[edgekey].append((x, y, z)) for edgekey, cells in edgecells.items(): if len(cells) == 0: continue cells.sort(key=lambda c: c[0]+c[1]+c[2]) verts = [vertindices[c] for c in cells] if len(verts) == 4: faces.append([verts[0], verts[1], verts[2]]) faces.append([verts[0], verts[2], verts[3]]) elif len(verts) == 3: faces.append(verts) return vertices, faces reg: Regularization weight for QEF. Default: 10^{-2}. svdtol: SVD tolerance for solving QEF. Default: 10^{-6}. clamp: Whether to clamp vertex position to cell bounds. Default: true. outeriters: Number of outer iteration steps (for SDF variants). Default: 100. inneriters: Number of inner iteration steps. Default: 100. mu: Weight parameter for SDF constraint. Default: 0.1. hermiteweight: Weight for Hermite data in QEF. Default: 0.02. updateweight: Weight for updating Hermite data. Default: 0.2. hermiteupdate: Whether to update Hermite data during iterations. Default: true. qefassignment: Whether to use QEF assignment. Default: true. band: Bandwidth parameter for SDF processing (in cell diagonals). Default: 3.0. tol: Convergence tolerance. Default: 10^{-5}. Degenerate Cells: If fewer than 2 sign-changing edges exist in a cell, no vertex is created. Rank Deficiency: If normals are coplanar or collinear, the QEF matrix is singular. Use SVD truncation or mass-point bias. Boundary Handling: Edges on the grid boundary are shared by fewer than 4 cells, requiring triangle generation instead of quads. Vertex Clamping: The unconstrained QEF solution may lie outside the cell, which helps recover sharp features but might create self-intersections. Users can constrain the vertex inside the cell. Determines the topology of an analytical isosurface within a voxel cell using trilinear interpolation and ray intersection along specific diagonals. Optimizes computation by finding exactly one intersection point per disjoint isosurface component, except for complex features like tunnels which require multiple points. Choose when topological correctness is critical for complex implicit surfaces. Computes edge-surface intersections for dual contouring by finding where grid edges cross the iso-surface and computing intersection points using linear interpolation. Returns an Intersection object containing points and normals. Choose when Hermite data needs to be pre-computed efficiently before QEF solving. Applies dual contouring on an adaptive octree structure, refining cells based on normal angle spread and gradient variation. Choose when processing large datasets with varying detail requirements to save memory and computation. Specialized solver for the Quadratic Error Function in dual contouring, handling rank deficiency and boundary constraints. Choose when robust vertex placement is required for noisy or sparse Hermite data. Places a single vertex at the center of every voxel cell where the scalar field values at the eight corners exhibit a sign change along any axis-aligned edge, and constructs a quad mesh by connecting these vertices based on their relative positions in the grid. Choose when computational simplicity and speed are prioritized over sharp feature recovery. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Preserves sharp features, watertight meshes on adaptive grids. Limitations: Feature placement can be sensitive to the quality of input data. Does not guarantee 2-manifold or watertight output by default. Dual Contouring was introduced by Ju et al. in 2002 as "Hermite Dual Contouring". It was later extended to Signed Distance Fields by Carrera et al. in 2026. name: Linear Edge Intersection for Dual Contouring
head: Dual Contouring (Simple Mean Intersection), Simple Mean Intersection
body: Linear Edge Intersection is a vertex placement method for Dual Contouring that computes a single point per grid cell intersecting the isosurface by averaging the intersection points on the cell edges. It optionally refines this position using gradient information when available. Inputs: origin: The 3D coordinates of the cell's corner with the lowest indices. dirs: An array of 3 vectors representing the cell's edge directions (typically \Delta x \hat{x}, \Delta y \hat{y}, \Delta z \hat{z}). vertices: An array of 8 scalar values corresponding to the function values at the cell's 8 vertices, ordered in Morton (Z-order). level: The isovalue threshold (default 0.0). gradients: (Optional) An array of 3D vectors representing the gradient at each intersection point, used for refinement. Outputs: surfacepoint: A 3D vector representing the estimated isosurface location within the cell. valid: A boolean indicating whether the cell intersects the isosurface. points: (Optional) An (N, 3) float32 tensor of intersection points on the edges. normals: (Optional) An (N, 3) float32 tensor of normals at those points. Edge Lookup Table: A static array of 24 integers defining the 12 edges of the cube. Each edge is defined by two vertex indices. python edges = [0, 4, 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 0, 2, 1, 3, 4, 6, 5, 7, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] 1. Check Intersection: Adjust vertex values by subtracting level. If all adjusted values are \ge 0 or all are < 0, the cell does not intersect the isosurface; return false. 2. Initialize Accumulators: Set mean = (0, 0, 0) and count = 0. 3. Iterate Edges: Loop over i from 0 to 11. a. Get vertex indices: v1 = \text{edges}[2i], v2 = \text{edges}[2i+1]. b. Get values: a = \text{vertices}[v1], b = \text{vertices}[v2]. c. Check Crossing: If a \cdot b > 0, the edge does not cross the isosurface; skip to the next edge. d. Interpolate: Calculate the interpolation parameter x: \text{denom} = |b - a| x = \begin{cases} 0.5 & \text{if } \text{denom} < \epsilon \\ \frac{|a|}{\text{denom}} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Where \epsilon = 10^{-15}. e. Calculate Point: Compute the intersection point p: p = \text{origin} + \text{dirs}[0] \cdot \lfloor v1 / 4 \rfloor + \text{dirs}[1] \cdot \lfloor (v1 \bmod 4) / 2 \rfloor + \text{dirs}[2] \cdot (v1 \bmod 2) + \text{dirs}[i // 4] \cdot x Add p to mean and increment count. 4. Finalize Point: If count > 0: \text{surface\point} = \text{origin} + \frac{\text{mean}}{\text{count}} Return true and surfacepoint. 5. Gradient-Based Refinement (Optional): If gradients are provided and count >= 3: a. Construct matrix A where row i is the gradient at the i-th intersection point. b. Construct vector b where bi = \text{dot}(\text{gradient}i, \text{point}i). c. Solve A q = b using least squares. d. Boundary Check: If q is outside the cell limits (\text{origin} to \text{origin} + \sum \text{dirs}), fallback to the mean calculated in Step 4. Unverified code. name: Octree-Based Dual Contouring (3D)
head: 3D Adaptive Dual Contouring, ADC3D, Adaptive Dual Contouring
body: Octree-Based Dual Contouring (3D) is a voxel-to-mesh extraction method that uses an octree to adaptively subdivide space, placing dual vertices at locations with the smallest reconstruction error. It builds on Dual Contouring with Octree by introducing adaptive subdivision and a simplification phase that collapses internal nodes into pseudo-nodes when the Quadratic Error Function (QEF) error remains below a threshold, thereby reducing mesh complexity. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D scalar field (voxel grid), grid dimensions, and configuration parameters (threaded, threshold, randomize). Output: A triangle mesh represented by a vertex buffer and index buffer. Data Structures The algorithm relies on an octree structure with the following exact layouts: 1. OctreeNode: type (enum: None, Internal, Pseudo, Leaf), position (Vector3), size (int), children (OctreeNode[8] in Z-order), drawinfo (OctreeDrawInfo pointer). 2. OctreeDrawInfo: index (int), corners (int bitmask), position (Vector3), averageNormal (Vector3), qef (QEFSolver object). 3. Lookup Tables: Static integer arrays including edgevmap[12,2], edgemask[3], vertMap[8,3], faceMap[6,4], cellProcFaceMask[8,3], cellProcEdgeMask[6,5], faceProcFaceMask[3,4,3], faceProcEdgeMask[3,4,6], edgeProcEdgeMask[4,2,5], processEdgeMask[3,4]. Parameters threaded: Controls multithreading depth. Safe values are 0 or 1. Values >1 generate 8^{\text{threaded}} tasks and typically degrade performance. threshold: The error threshold for simplification. If the QEF error exceeds this value, the node is not collapsed. randomize: Boolean flag. If true, the threshold t used for recursive simplification is randomized as rnd.NextDouble() rnd.NextDouble() 20.0f. Algorithm Steps The method proceeds through tree construction, leaf processing, topology traversal, simplification, and vertex buffer generation. Unverified code. Pitfalls The provided QEF solver is a bruteforce offset search, not a proper linear solver. It applies offsets to a mass point to find the lowest error and should not be used as a reference implementation. The QEF solver is disabled in 3D DC by default. If enabled without simplification tweaks, high error tolerance causes sharp feature loss and mesh deformation. If corners is 0 or 255, the leaf node is empty and ConstructLeaf returns false, preventing the creation of an empty leaf. Threading is only enabled if threaded > 0 and size > 2. If size <= 2 or threaded == 0, recursion happens synchronously. Time Complexity: Depends on the octree depth and the number of leaf nodes. The simplification step adds overhead but reduces the final vertex count. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of octree nodes. Internal nodes store pointers to children, while leaf/pseudo nodes store QEF data. Performance: Threading depth > 1 typically degrades performance due to task overhead. Strengths: Adaptive resolution allows for high detail where needed and coarser resolution elsewhere. Simplification reduces mesh complexity while preserving features better than uniform subsampling. Limitations: The QEF solver implementation is inefficient (bruteforce). 2D DC implementations in this codebase do not connect properly, and the adaptive variant lacks mesh simplification in 2D. name: Manifold Dual Contouring
head: PDF Manifold Dual Contouring, adaptive contouring with topology constraint
body: Manifold Dual Contouring is a contouring and simplification method that constructs a manifold surface by integrating a topology constraint into an adaptive vertex clustering algorithm. It solves the problem of generating simplified, topologically correct iso-surfaces from Hermite data while allowing independent simplification of multiple contour components within an octree cell. Unlike Extended Dual Contouring, it places no restriction on the number of contour intersections on each octree cell edge, allowing the simplification of multiple layers of thin geometry. Builds on Dual Contouring with Octree. Inputs: Hermite data (position and normal) at grid vertices or cell edges; an octree structure defining the spatial subdivision; a user-specified QEF error threshold. Outputs: A simplified polygonal mesh that is topologically equivalent to the original iso-surface (preserves genus) and contains no non-manifold vertices or edges. Data Structures: 1. Octree: Standard octree structure where each node represents a spatial cell. 2. Vertex Tree: A separate structure from the octree, built during the clustering phase. It stores clustered vertices and their hierarchical relationships. Each vertex in the tree has a "collapsible" tag. 3. QEF (Quadratic Error Function): Associated with each clustered vertex to measure the error of the vertex position against the Hermite data. Algorithm Steps: 1. Vertex Clustering: Traverse the octree. For each leaf cell, collect Hermite data (intersections and normals) from the cell edges. Solve the QEF for the cell to determine a candidate vertex position. Cluster vertices from child cells into the parent cell if they are sufficiently close, building the vertex tree. Compute the QEF error for each clustered vertex. 2. Topology Constraint Evaluation (Manifold Criterion): For each clustered vertex v, determine if it is "collapsible" based on the QEF error and topological properties. A vertex v is marked collapsible if: 1. The associated QEF error is below the given threshold. 2. The edge count e(Sv) and Euler characteristic \chi(Sv) satisfy the two conditions in Proposition 1 of the source. The Euler characteristic of the combined surface Sv associated with vertex v is computed by summing the Euler characteristics of its child surfaces S{vk}: \sumk \chi(S{vk}) = \chi(Sv) For a disk-like surface (required for manifold validity in this context), \chi(Sv) must equal 1. The extra computation time for enforcing this criterion is negligible compared to QEF operations when using the fast recursive algorithm. 3. Polygon Generation: Traverse the vertex tree. For each vertex, check if it is marked as collapsible. If collapsible, generate the simplified polygon(s) associated with that vertex. If not collapsible, retain the more detailed geometry from its children or original position. This step is efficient because the vertex tree is already built; changing the QEF error threshold only requires revising the "collapsible" tags without rebuilding the tree. Parameters: QEF Error Threshold: A user-specified value controlling the level of simplification. In viewer-dependent applications, this threshold is adjusted per octree cell based on viewer distance (higher for distant cells). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intersecting Polygons: Although the surfaces are topologically manifold (no non-manifold vertices/edges), they may still contain intersecting polygons. This can occur when multiple vertices are placed inside a cell or due to Hermite data positioning along cell edges. Neighbor Finding: Detecting intersecting polygons is time-consuming because each polygon spans multiple octree cells, requiring neighbor-finding on the octree. Unsafe Simplifications: Unlike other methods that stop simplifying upon encountering an unsafe simplification, this method's manifold criterion can determine that a safe simplification occurs later in vertex clustering even if unsafe collapses occurred previously, allowing for extreme simplifications. Time and Memory Complexity: The clustering phase dominates the computation time. The extra computation time for enforcing the manifold criterion is negligible compared to QEF operations. The method runs approximately an order of magnitude faster than Attali's method on iso-surfaces of similar complexity at the same grid resolution. Measured Performance: Hardware: 3 GHz Pentium computer with 2 GB RAM. Model 1 (476,184 polygons): Clustering took 5.58 sec without manifold criterion and 5.76 sec with it. Polygon generation took 1.12 sec, yielding 78 simplified polygons. Model 2 (878,368 polygons): Clustering took 10.89 sec without manifold criterion and 10.99 sec with it. Polygon generation took 2.01 sec, yielding 30,002 simplified polygons. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Guarantees manifold surfaces preserving original topology; allows independent simplification of multiple contour components within a cell; no restriction on contour intersections per edge; efficient off-line polygon generation for varying viewer distances. Limitations: May produce intersecting polygons despite being topologically manifold; requires Hermite data. When to Use: Adaptive generation of iso-surfaces and real-time navigation of complex volumes, where QEF error thresholds are set higher in octree cells further from the viewer's location to produce more detailed geometry near the viewer and coarser polygons at distances. Manifold Dual Contouring is an extension to Dual Contouring that preserves sharp features and always constructs a manifold surface. It was developed to address the limitations of previous contour simplification algorithms, which were often restrictive in the types of simplifications allowed and stopped simplifying upon encountering unsafe conditions. The method uses a vertex tree separate from the octree to allow simplification of multiple layers of thin geometry. name: Adaptive Contouring via Octree Vertex Clustering
head: Adaptive Simplification, Octree-based Vertex Clustering
body: Adaptive Contouring via Octree Vertex Clustering is a surface extraction method that constructs multi-resolution iso-surfaces by clustering vertices of child cells in an octree into a single vertex in a topologically safe manner. It allows an arbitrary number of vertices per cell, significantly reducing polygon count in flat regions compared to methods restricted to one vertex per cell. It sets itself apart from Dual Contouring with Octree by permitting multiple vertices per cell through a clustering phase, and from Manifold Dual Contouring by its specific vertex-tree-based clustering mechanism which requires additional constraints to guarantee manifold topology. Inputs: An octree representation of the volume data and an error threshold \epsilon. Outputs: A polygonal mesh representing the iso-surface. Data Structures: Vertex: Contains a parent pointer parent, a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) defined by matrix A and vector \mathbf{b}, and the scalar error value E = \|A\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{b}\|^2 evaluated at the vertex position \mathbf{v}. Vertex Tree: A hierarchical structure where leaves are finest-level octree vertices and internal nodes represent clustered vertices. Each vertex maintains a pointer to its parent in this tree. Cell Status: Each octree cell has a boolean flag collapsed. Parameters: errorthreshold (\epsilon): The maximum allowed QEF error for a vertex to be considered collapsible. If E < \epsilon, the vertex is marked collapsible. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a vertex tree starting with all vertices at the finest level of the octree. For each vertex, initialize its parent pointer to NULL. Flag all vertices as collapsible. 2. Bottom-Up Traversal and Clustering: Traverse octree cells from bottom to top. For each non-leaf cell, consider its eight children. Identify the twelve internal faces shared by these children (4 for each Euclidean axis). Find edges dual to these twelve internal faces using a recursive octree traversal algorithm. Group vertices at the root of the vertex tree that are topologically connected by these dual edges. For each group: combine the QEFs of all vertices in the group (A{\text{new}} = \sum Ai, \mathbf{b}{\text{new}} = \sum \mathbf{b}i). Minimize the combined error function to find the new vertex location \mathbf{v}{\text{new}} and its error E{\text{new}}. If E{\text{new}} < \epsilon, mark the new vertex as collapsible. Set the parent pointers of the grouped vertices to point to this new vertex. 3. Cell Collapse Optimization: Mark a cell as collapsed if all clustered vertices created within it satisfy the collapsible criterion (E < \epsilon) AND all children of that cell are either leaf cells or marked as collapsed. 4. Polygon Generation: Traverse the octree to generate polygons. For each edge exhibiting a sign change in the volume data, create a polygon connecting the associated vertices. For each such vertex, follow its parent pointers up the vertex tree to find the last vertex marked as collapsible. Include a vertex in the output mesh if it is marked collapsible and has no collapsible ancestors in the vertex tree. Optimization: If a cell is collapsed, truncate the cellProc traversal; no children polygons are generated. If both cells sharing a face are collapsed, truncate the faceProc traversal for that face. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivecontouringoctreevertexclustering(octree, errorthreshold): # Data structures class QEF: def init(self, normals, distances): self.normals = normals self.distances = distances def combine(self, other): return QEF(self.normals + other.normals, self.distances + other.distances) def minimize(self): # Solve (A^T A) v = A^T b for v import numpy as np A = np.array(self.normals) b = np.array(self.distances) v = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)[0] error = np.sum((A @ v - b) 2) return v, error class Vertex: def init(self, pos, qef): self.pos = pos self.qef = qef self.error = qef.minimize()[1] self.parent = None self.iscollapsible = True # 1. Initialization vertextree = {} for vdata in octree.getfinestlevelvertices(): qef = computeqeffromsurfaceintersection(vdata) # Standard dual contouring step vertextree[vdata.id] = Vertex(vdata.pos, qef) # 2. Bottom-Up Clustering for cell in octree.traversebottomup(): if cell.isleaf: continue children = cell.getchildren() internaledges = finddualedgesforchildren(children) # Lookup 12 internal faces/edges activevertices = [] for child in children: activevertices.extend(child.getactivevertices()) groups = groupconnectedvertices(activevertices, internaledges) # Union-Find on dual edges for group in groups: combinedqef = group[0].qef for v in group[1:]: combinedqef = combinedqef.combine(v.qef) newpos, newerror = combinedqef.minimize() newvertex = Vertex(newpos, combinedqef) newvertex.iscollapsible = (newerror < errorthreshold) for v in group: v.parent = newvertex vertextree[v.id] = newvertex for child in children: child.addactivevertex(newvertex) # 3. Mark Collapsed Cells for cell in octree.traversebottomup(): if cell.isleaf: continue clusteredvertices = cell.getactivevertices() if not clusteredvertices: continue allcollapsible = all(v.iscollapsible for v in clusteredvertices) childrenok = all(c.isleaf or c.iscollapsed for c in cell.getchildren()) if allcollapsible and childrenok: cell.iscollapsed = True # 4. Polygon Generation mesh = [] for edge in octree.getsignchangingedges(): verts = edge.getassociatedvertices() finalverts = [] for v in verts: curr = v while curr.parent is not None and curr.parent.iscollapsible: curr = curr.parent finalverts.append(curr) if len(finalverts) >= 3: mesh.append(finalverts) elif len(finalverts) == 2: mesh.append(finalverts) return mesh Pitfalls: Non-manifold topology: Clustering topologically connected vertices without additional constraints may yield non-manifold topology (e.g., threads collapsing to single polygons or non-manifold edges). Subtopics: Manifold Dual Contouring: Adds topology constraints to prevent non-manifold collapses (e.g., threads collapsing to single polygons) which this method may produce. Choose this when manifold output is strictly required. Octree-Based Dual Contouring (3D): Uses a different approach to octree-based dual contouring. This method specifically uses vertex clustering to allow arbitrary vertices per cell. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces polygon count in flat regions by allowing arbitrary vertices per cell. Optimizations (collapsed cells/faces) prune the traversal. Limitations: May produce non-manifold topology (e.g., threads collapsing to single polygons) if no additional constraints are applied. Requires careful handling of topological connectivity. When to use: When a simplified, multi-resolution mesh is desired and non-manifold artifacts are acceptable or can be filtered. When not to use: When strict manifold topology is required without post-processing. Originated in the context of dual contouring simplification, specifically addressing the restriction of one vertex per cell in standard DC. It builds on vertex clustering techniques similar to Zhang et al. [7] but uses a vertex tree for topological connectivity. The method was developed to allow arbitrary numbers of vertices per cell, enabling more aggressive simplification. name: Quadric Error Function (QEF) for Sharp Features
head: QEF Solver
body: This method computes the optimal vertex position for sharp features (corners and edges) in dual contouring by minimizing the distance to multiple intersecting planes defined by sample points and their normals. It distinguishes itself from standard dual contouring by explicitly handling underdetermined systems (sharp edges) via least-squares minimization, ensuring the resulting vertex lies equidistant from all contributing planes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of k intersection points \{Pi\} and their corresponding surface normals \{Ni\} within a voxel cell. Output: A single 3D point x representing the sharp feature. Data Structures: The method constructs a linear system Ax = B (or Ax \approx B for QEF) using the following layouts: matrixA: A dense matrix of size k \times 3. Each row i stores the normal vector components (n{ix}, n{iy}, n{iz}). vectorB: A dense vector of size k. Each entry i stores the dot product Ni \cdot Pi. Steps: 1. Collect Intersections: Identify all grid edges intersecting the isosurface within the voxel and compute the point Pi and normal Ni at each intersection. 2. Populate Matrix A and Vector B: For each intersection point i from 0 to k-1: Set matrixA[i][0] = Ni.x Set matrixA[i][1] = Ni.y Set matrixA[i][2] = Ni.z Set vectorB[i] = Pi.x Ni.x + Pi.y Ni.y + Pi.z Ni.z. 3. Solve via SVD: Perform Singular Value Decomposition on A to obtain U, D, V^T such that A = U D V^T. Solve the system U D V^T x = B for x. Formulas: For a sharp corner (3 points), the exact solution satisfies: Ni \cdot (x - Pi) = 0 \quad \text{for } i=1,2,3 Which expands to the linear system Ax = B where: A = \begin{bmatrix} N1^T \\ N2^T \\ N3^T \end{bmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{bmatrix} N1 \cdot P1 \\ N2 \cdot P2 \\ N3 \cdot P3 \end{bmatrix}. For a sharp edge (underdetermined system, e.g., 4 points defining 2 planes), the system is solved via QEF: E[x] = \|Ax - B\|^2 The solution is found using SVD: x = V D^{-1} U^T B (Note: D^{-1} involves inverting non-zero singular values; zero singular values are treated as zero to find the minimum norm solution). Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Normals: If normals are collinear or nearly parallel, the matrix A becomes ill-conditioned. Underdetermined Systems: Standard linear solvers fail for sharp edges (fewer independent constraints than dimensions). Boundary Violations: The unconstrained QEF solution may lie outside the voxel cell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solveqefsharpfeatures(intersectionpoints, normals): """ Solves for the optimal vertex position using QEF for sharp features. Args: intersectionpoints: List of 3D vectors [P0, P1,..., Pk-1] normals: List of 3D vectors [N0, N1,..., Nk-1] Returns: newPoint: 3D vector representing the sharp feature location """ k = len(intersectionpoints) if k == 0: return None # Initialize matrix A (k x 3) and vector B (k) matrixA = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(k)] vectorB = [0.0] k # Populate A and B for i in range(k): P = intersectionpoints[i] N = normals[i] # Row i of A is the normal vector matrixA[i][0] = N.x matrixA[i][1] = N.y matrixA[i][2] = N.z # Entry i of B is the dot product N. P vectorB[i] = P.x N.x + P.y N.y + P.z N.z # Standard SVD routine # A = U @ diag(D) @ Vt U, D, Vt = svd(matrixA) # Construct D^-1 (pseudoinverse of diagonal matrix D) # Handle zero singular values to avoid division by zero Dinv = [[0.0] 3 for in range(3)] for i in range(3): if D[i] > 1e-10: Dinv[i][i] = 1.0 / D[i] else: Dinv[i][i] = 0.0 # Compute x = V @ Dinv @ U^T @ B # Step 1: U^T @ B UtB = [0.0] 3 for i in range(3): for j in range(k): UtB[i] += U[j][i] vectorB[j] # Step 2: Dinv @ (U^T @ B) DinvUtB = [0.0] 3 for i in range(3): DinvUtB[i] = Dinv[i][i] UtB[i] # Step 3: V @ (Dinv @ U^T @ B) newPoint = [0.0] 3 for i in range(3): for j in range(3): newPoint[i] += Vt[j][i] DinvUtB[j] return newPoint A fallback strategy for vertex placement when the QEF solution lies outside the voxel cell. It constrains the search space hierarchically (interior -> faces -> edges -> corners) to find a valid point within boundaries. Choose this when the unconstrained QEF result is invalid for mesh topology. Time Complexity: Dominated by SVD, typically O(k^3) for small k. Memory Complexity: O(k) for storing A and B. Strengths: Robustly handles sharp features (edges/corners) that standard linear solvers cannot. Limitations: Does not guarantee the result lies within the voxel cell. When to Use: When extracting meshes from implicit surfaces with sharp features (e.g., boxes, cylinders) using dual contouring. When Not to Use: For smooth surfaces where standard dual contouring or marching cubes suffices, or when strict boundary constraints are required without additional fallback logic. The Quadric Error Function (QEF) for sharp features was introduced in the context of dual contouring for isosurface extraction. The method was described in an unofficial source detailing the implementation of an isosurface polygonizer, specifically addressing the limitation of linear systems when dealing with sharp edges where the system is underdetermined. It builds on the general dual contouring framework Parent. http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: QEF Boundary Constrained Vertex Placement
head: Boundary-Constrained Vertex Placement, Constrained QEF Solver
body: QEF Boundary Constrained Vertex Placement is a fallback strategy for vertex placement in Dual Contouring when the optimal solution to the unconstrained Quadratic Error Function (QEF) lies outside the current voxel cell. It progressively constrains the search space from the interior point to cell faces, then edges, then corners to find a valid point within the cell boundaries. It sets itself apart from its parent method, Quadric Error Function (QEF) for Sharp Features, by explicitly handling boundary violations through hierarchical constraint fixing rather than relying solely on SVD minimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An unconstrained QEF solution v (a 3D vector), the cell bounds defined by origin (x, y, z) and CELLSIZE, and configuration flags settings.BOUNDARY and settings.CLIP. Output: A constrained vertex position v guaranteed to be within the cell boundaries if settings.BOUNDARY is enabled. Data Structures: QEF Object: Represents the quadratic error function. It supports methods fixaxis(axis, value) to constrain a specific coordinate and solve() to compute the minimum residual vertex. It also supports evalwithpos(pos) to evaluate the error at a specific position. Inside Function: A predicate inside(v) that returns true if x \le v[0] \le x + \text{CELL\SIZE}, y \le v[1] \le y + \text{CELL\SIZE}, and z \le v[2] \le z + \text{CELL\SIZE}. Parameters: settings.BOUNDARY: Boolean flag enabling the boundary constraint fallback logic. Default: True. settings.CLIP: Boolean flag enabling crude clamping of the final vertex position. Default: False. CELLSIZE: The size of the voxel cell along each axis. Default: 1.0. Steps: 1. Unconstrained Solve: Solve the unconstrained QEF to get residual and vertex v. 2. Boundary Check: If settings.BOUNDARY is enabled, check if v is inside the cell using the inside function. 3. Plane Constraints: If v is outside, constrain the QEF to the 6 planes bordering the cell by fixing one axis at the cell boundaries (0 or CELLSIZE) and solving. The planes are: Fix axis 0 at x+0 and x+\text{CELL\SIZE} Fix axis 1 at y+0 and y+\text{CELL\SIZE} Fix axis 2 at z+0 and z+\text{CELL\SIZE} 4. Filter Planes: Filter the 6 plane solutions to keep only those inside the cell. If no solutions remain, proceed to constrain the QEF to the 12 lines bordering the cell by fixing two axes at the cell boundaries. 5. Edge Constraints: Generate 12 edge solutions by fixing two axes. Examples include fixing axis 1 at y+0 and axis 0 at x+0, axis 1 at y+\text{CELL\SIZE} and axis 0 at x+0, etc., covering all combinations of two axes fixed at 0 or CELLSIZE. 6. Filter Edges: Filter the 12 edge solutions to keep only those inside the cell. If no solutions remain, proceed to evaluate the 8 corners of the cell. 7. Corner Evaluation: Evaluate the QEF at all 8 corners of the cell using evalwithpos for each corner coordinate combination: (x+0, y+0, z+0) through (x+\text{CELL\SIZE}, y+\text{CELL\SIZE}, z+\text{CELL\SIZE}). 8. Filter Corners: Filter the 8 corner solutions to keep only those inside the cell. 9. Select Best: Select the best solution (minimum residual) from the remaining valid options (plane, edge, or corner solutions). 10. Clipping: If settings.CLIP is enabled, forcibly clamp the vertex coordinates to the cell boundaries using numpy.clip for each axis: v[0] \in [x, x+\text{CELL\SIZE}], v[1] \in [y, y+\text{CELL\SIZE}], v[2] \in [z, z+\text{CELL\SIZE}]. Pitfalls: The unconstrained QEF solution may lie outside the cell. Even after constraining to planes, the solutions may still lie outside the box because the planes are infinite. The algorithm handles these cases by falling back to edge constraints, then corners, ensuring a valid point is always found. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy def solveconstrainedqef(qef, x, y, z, CELLSIZE, settings): # Step 1: Solve unconstrained residual, v = qef.solve() # Step 2: Check if inside def inside(pos): return (x <= pos[0] <= x + CELLSIZE and y <= pos[1] <= y + CELLSIZE and z <= pos[2] <= z + CELLSIZE) if not settings.BOUNDARY or inside(v): finalv = v else: candidates = [] # Step 3 & 4: Plane constraints (6 planes) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(0, x + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(0, x + CELLSIZE).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(1, y + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(1, y + CELLSIZE).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + CELLSIZE).solve()) validcandidates = [c for c in candidates if inside(c[1])] if not validcandidates: candidates = [] # Step 5 & 6: Edge constraints (12 edges) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(1, y + 0).fixaxis(0, x + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(1, y + CELLSIZE).fixaxis(0, x + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(1, y + 0).fixaxis(0, x + CELLSIZE).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(1, y + CELLSIZE).fixaxis(0, x + CELLSIZE).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + 0).fixaxis(0, x + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + CELLSIZE).fixaxis(0, x + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + 0).fixaxis(0, x + CELLSIZE).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + CELLSIZE).fixaxis(0, x + CELLSIZE).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + 0).fixaxis(1, y + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + CELLSIZE).fixaxis(1, y + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + 0).fixaxis(1, y + CELLSIZE).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + CELLSIZE).fixaxis(1, y + CELLSIZE).solve()) validcandidates = [c for c in candidates if inside(c[1])] if not validcandidates: candidates = [] # Step 7 & 8: Corner evaluation (8 corners) corners = [ (x + 0, y + 0, z + 0), (x + 0, y + 0, z + CELLSIZE), (x + 0, y + CELLSIZE, z + 0), (x + 0, y + CELLSIZE, z + CELLSIZE), (x + CELLSIZE, y + 0, z + 0), (x + CELLSIZE, y + 0, z + CELLSIZE), (x + CELLSIZE, y + CELLSIZE, z + 0), (x + CELLSIZE, y + CELLSIZE, z + CELLSIZE) ] for corner in corners: candidates.append(qef.evalwithpos(corner)) validcandidates = [c for c in candidates if inside(c[1])] # Step 9: Select best if validcandidates: residual, finalv = min(validcandidates, key=lambda c: c[0]) else: finalv = v # Step 10: Clipping if settings.CLIP: finalv[0] = numpy.clip(finalv[0], x, x + CELLSIZE) finalv[1] = numpy.clip(finalv[1], y, y + CELLSIZE) finalv[2] = numpy.clip(finalv[2], z, z + CELLSIZE) return finalv Time Complexity: In the worst case, the algorithm solves the QEF 26 times (1 unconstrained + 6 planes + 12 edges + 8 corners). Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory, storing a list of candidate residuals and vertices. Strengths: Guarantees a valid vertex position within the cell boundaries. Limitations: Can be computationally expensive if many cells require fallback to edges or corners. The crude clipping option may introduce discontinuities if not used carefully. When to use: Not given in the sources. This method provides a fallback strategy for vertex placement in Dual Contouring when the unconstrained QEF solution lies outside the voxel cell. It addresses the issue where the optimal point for a sharp feature does not lie within the containing voxel. BorisTheBrave/mc-dc, https://github.com/BorisTheBrave/mc-dc, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Multi-threaded Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction
head: Parallel Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction
body:
This method parallelizes the Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction with Guidance Field [947-advancing-front-isosurface-extraction-with-guidance-field.md] by distributing the work of projecting points onto the advancing fronts across a set of worker threads. Compared to Marching Cubes Marching Cubes or Marching Tetrahedra Marching Tetrahedra, the algorithm is slower but generates meshes requiring negligible or no downstream processing, unlike MC/MT results. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An implicit function f(\mathbf{x}) defined over a domain, a target isovalue k, and a guidance field g(\mathbf{x}) computed from parameters ho and \eta. The function must admit well-defined gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) and Hessian Hf(\mathbf{x}). Output: A triangular mesh approximating the isosurface f(\mathbf{x}) = k with bounded distance error and bounded normal error. Data Structures: Front: A shared set of vertices and edges defining the extracted surface boundary. It requires thread-safe access for concurrent updates. Task Queue: A shared collection of candidate points awaiting projection onto the front. Thread Pool: A fixed set of N worker threads that independently pop tasks, project points, and update the front. Parameters: Thread Count (N): The number of worker threads. Experiments use N=4. ho, \eta: Guidance field parameters controlling edge length constraints based on surface curvature. Numbered Steps: 1. Parallel Guidance Field and Culling: Compute the guidance field g(\mathbf{x}) for the domain and perform culling entirely in parallel. 2. Task Distribution: Distribute the work of projecting points onto the advancing fronts across the worker threads. 3. Parallel Advancement: Each worker thread evaluates f(\mathbf{x}), 
abla f(\mathbf{x}), and Hf(\mathbf{x}) at candidate points, uses g(\mathbf{x}) to determine appropriate edge lengths and projection steps, and projects points to satisfy f(\mathbf{x}) \approx k. 4. Synchronization: Threads synchronize when modifying the shared front structure; advancing front algorithms are mostly local, allowing independent decisions for distant surface parts. 5. Termination: The process repeats until the front is closed or no valid points remain in the queue. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import threading import queue def multithreadedadvancingfrontextraction(f, k, gfunc, Nthreads, domainbounds, gridspacing): # 1. Parallel guidance field computation and culling # Sample domain on a uniform grid candidates = [] for x in range(domainbounds[0][0], domainbounds[0][1], gridspacing): for y in range(domainbounds[1][0], domainbounds[1][1], gridspacing): for z in range(domainbounds[2][0], domainbounds[2][1], gridspacing): point = (x, y, z) if gfunc(point) < 2.0: # Threshold not specified in sources candidates.append(point) # 2. Initialize front and task queue front = [] taskqueue = queue.Queue() for p in candidates: taskqueue.put(p) frontlock = threading.Lock() def worker(): while not taskqueue.empty(): try: point = taskqueue.getnowait() except queue.Empty: break # 3. Parallel Advancement: Project point to isosurface f(x) = k x = list(point) for in range(20): fx = f(x) if abs(fx - k) < 1e-5: break # Central difference gradient eps = 1e-6 grad = [ (f([x[0]+eps, x[1], x[2]]) - f([x[0]-eps, x[1], x[2]])) / (2eps), (f([x[0], x[1]+eps, x[2]]) - f([x[0], x[1]-eps, x[2]])) / (2eps), (f([x[0], x[1], x[2]+eps]) - f([x[0], x[1], x[2]-eps])) / (2eps) ] gradnormsq = sum(gg for g in grad) + 1e-12 stepsize = gfunc(x) # Guidance field scales step size dx = [-fx g / gradnormsq stepsize for g in grad] x = [x[i] + dx[i] for i in range(3)] # Update front and distribute new tasks with frontlock: front.append(tuple(x)) # Neighbor generation strategy not specified in sources # 4. Distribute work across worker threads threads = [] for in range(Nthreads): t = threading.Thread(target=worker) threads.append(t) t.start() for t in threads: t.join() return front Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Regular Surfaces: The method requires the implicit function to admit a well-defined gradient and Hessian. Sharp corners do not admit a regular isosurface representation (where f(\mathbf{x}) = k and 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) 
eq 0). Thread Safety: The front structure must be protected during concurrent updates. Precision: High-order meshes (degree ~10) may have high-frequency features. The method is oblivious to the underlying mesh but relies on accurate gradient/Hessian computation. Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction with Guidance Field [947-advancing-front-isosurface-extraction-with-guidance-field.md]: The single-threaded parent method. Marching Cubes Marching Cubes: A grid-based method. Marching Tetrahedra Marching Tetrahedra: Similar to Marching Cubes but avoids ambiguity. Time Complexity: The algorithm is slower than Marching Cubes (MC) or Marching Tetrahedra (MT) implementations. Running times are typically several minutes for larger datasets. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Experiments were conducted on a PC with two dual-core AMD Opteron processors at 2.25GHz, 4GB RAM, SuSE Linux 10.0. Four threads were used for all experiments. Scaling: The method scales with the number of threads by distributing the projection work. The source notes that advancing front algorithms are "mostly local," which facilitates parallelization. Strengths: Generates high-quality meshes with bounded distance and normal error. 99% of triangles have quality at least half of optimal, and the median quality is within 3% of optimal across different models, ho, \eta, and surface definitions. Triangle counts are often less than MC. The meshes require negligible or no downstream processing. Limitations: Slower than MC/MT. Requires well-defined gradient and Hessian. Not suitable for sharp corners. When to Use: When high-quality, high-fidelity triangulation is required, and the implicit function is smooth (band-limited). When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical, or when the input data contains sharp corners or non-smooth features that violate the regular isosurface assumption. The method is described in "High-Quality Extraction of Isosurfaces from Regular and Irregular Grids". It builds on the Advancing Front Framework for Implicit Surfaces and specifically the guidance-field-based approach. The authors implemented the algorithm in C++ and tested it on various models including Catmull-Rom splines and B-splines, as well as unstructured meshes like Nielson interpolation and MLS approximation. The technique is generalizable to any surface formulation that admits gradient and Hessian computation, making it applicable to high-order meshes (typically degree ~10). High-Quality Extraction of Isosurfaces from Regular and Irregular Grids, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2006.149, fetched 2026-10-26
