name: NeRF Training Loop
head: NeRF Training, NeRF Optimization Loop, Neural Radiance Fields Training
body: The NeRF training loop optimizes a coordinate-based neural field (MLP or SIREN) to reconstruct a scene by minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) between rendered RGB values and ground truth images. It iterates over epochs and batches, sampling random pixels, generating ray bundles, performing a forward pass through the network, computing loss, and updating weights via backpropagation. Inputs: Training dataset: Images, camera poses (c2w), and intrinsics (K). Model: A neural network (MLP or SIREN) mapping 3D coordinates (and optionally viewing directions) to color and density. Hyperparameters: Learning rate, batch size, number of epochs, sampling parameters (near/far bounds, number of samples per ray). Outputs: Trained model weights and optimizer state saved as checkpoints. Rendered images/videos for evaluation. Data Structures: raysrgb: Pre-computed array of shape [(N-1)HW, 3, 3] (or [Nrays, 3, 3] in mini-batch). Axis 0 is flattened pixel index. Axis 1 is channel type (0: ray origin, 1: ray direction, 2: observed RGB). Axis 2 is XYZ/RGB components. Data type is float32. camera: Object containing camera-to-world matrix (c2w), intrinsics (K), and image dimensions. Checkpoint dictionary: Keys are model (statedict), optimizer (statedict), and epoch (int). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Parse command-line arguments and initialize summary writers for logging training and validation metrics. Instantiate the neural network model; if using SIREN, apply specific weight initialization (Uniform distribution scaled by \omega0). Initialize the Adam optimizer with learning rate lr. Initialize a learning rate scheduler (LambdaLR with decay factor \gamma and step size s). Load training and validation datasets; compute near/far bounds based on dataset type (LLFF uses bounding depths or NDC with near=0.0 and far=1.0, Blender uses fixed near=2.0 and far=6.0, DeepVoxels uses mean camera distance). Create a DataLoader with batchsize=1, shuffle=True, numworkers=0, and collatefn=trivialcollate. If --rvs is enabled, replace the global render function with the reparameterized volume sampling version. 2. Training Loop (for epoch from startepoch to numepochs): Data Loading: Extract image, camera, and cameraidx from the batch; move tensors to CUDA. Ray Sampling: Sample pixel coordinates (x, y) from the image grid; full-batch implementations cover the entire grid while mini-batch uses a random subset. Generate ray origins and directions using camera intrinsics and poses. Construct ray bundle tensor containing ro, rd, near, far, and optionally viewing directions if useviewdirs is enabled. Forward Pass: Sample points along each ray within [near, far] bounds; perturb sampling times if perturb > 0. Pass sampled 3D coordinates (and viewing directions) through the neural network to predict volume density (\sigma) and color (c). Perform differentiable volume rendering to compute predicted RGB for each ray. Loss Calculation: Compute MSE loss between predicted RGB and ground truth RGB at sampled pixels. If coarse network output exists and --rvs is not enabled, add its MSE loss to the total loss. If using volume SDF rendering, add Eikonal loss term: L{eikonal} = \lambda{eikonal} \|\nabla \phi(x) - 1\|^2. Compute gradients and Laplacian for visualization before the backward pass. Backpropagation: Zero gradients (optimizer.zerograd()), compute gradients (loss.backward()), update weights (optimizer.step()). Scheduler Step: Update learning rate via lr{new} = lr{old} \times \gamma^{(epoch / s)}. Checkpointing: If epoch % checkpointinterval == 0 and epoch > 0, save model state, optimizer state, and epoch number. Evaluation: If epoch % renderinterval == 0 and epoch > 0, render images using test poses and save to disk. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F def trainnerfloop(model, optimizer, scheduler, trainloader, valloader, cfg): startepoch = 0 if cfg.resumepath: checkpoint = torch.load(cfg.resumepath, weightsonly=False) model.loadstatedict(checkpoint['model']) optimizer.loadstatedict(checkpoint['optimizer']) startepoch = checkpoint['epoch'] + 1 for epoch in range(startepoch, cfg.training.numepochs): model.train() totalloss = 0.0 for batch in trainloader: image = batch['image'].cuda().unsqueeze(0) camera = batch['camera'].cuda() xygrid = getrandompixelsfromimage( cfg.training.batchsize, cfg.data.imagesize, camera) rayso, raysd = getraysfrompixels(xygrid, cfg.data.imagesize, camera) raybundle = { 'origins': rayso, 'directions': raysd, 'near': cfg.training.near, 'far': cfg.training.far, 'useviewdirs': cfg.model.useviewdirs } out = model(raybundle) predrgb = out['rgb'] gtrgb = sampleimagesatxy(image, xygrid) loss = F.mseloss(predrgb, gtrgb) if cfg.renderer.type == 'volumesdf': eikonalloss = geteikonalloss( model.implicitfn, cfg.training.batchsize, cfg.training.bounds, gtrgb.device) loss += cfg.training.eikonalweight eikonalloss if epoch % cfg.training.stepstilsummary == 0: grad = gradient(predrgb, raybundle['origins']) laplacian = laplace(predrgb, raybundle['origins']) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() totalloss += loss.item() scheduler.step() if epoch % cfg.training.checkpointinterval == 0 and epoch > 0: savecheckpoint( model.statedict(), optimizer.statedict(), epoch, cfg.training.checkpointpath) if epoch % cfg.training.renderinterval == 0 and epoch > 0: renderevaluation(model, valloader, cfg) def getrandompixelsfromimage(batchsize, imagesize, camera): H, W = imagesize x = torch.randint(0, W, (batchsize,)) y = torch.randint(0, H, (batchsize,)) return torch.stack([x, y], dim=1) def getraysfrompixels(xygrid, imagesize, camera): H, W = imagesize K = camera['K'] c2w = camera['c2w'] Kinv = torch.inverse(K) ones = torch.oneslike(xygrid[...,:1]) pixelcoords = torch.cat([xygrid.float(), ones], dim=-1) dirscam = torch.matmul(Kinv, pixelcoords.t()).t() dirscam = F.normalize(dirscam, dim=-1) dirsworld = torch.matmul(c2w[:3,:3], dirscam.t()).t() originsworld = c2w[:3, 3].unsqueeze(0).expand(xygrid.shape[0], -1) return originsworld, dirsworld def sampleimagesatxy(image, xygrid): H, W = image.shape[1:3] xnorm = (xygrid[:, 0].float() / (W - 1)) 2 - 1 ynorm = (xygrid[:, 1].float() / (H - 1)) 2 - 1 grid = torch.stack([xnorm, ynorm], dim=-1).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(1) img4d = image.permute(0, 3, 1, 2) sampled = F.gridsample(img4d, grid, aligncorners=True) return sampled.squeeze(-1).squeeze(0).permute(1, 0) def gradient(output, input): grad = torch.autograd.grad( output.sum(), input, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0] return grad def laplace(output, input): grad = gradient(output, input) div = torch.autograd.grad( grad.sum(), input, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0] return div def geteikonalloss(implicitfn, batchsize, bounds, device): pts = torch.rand(batchsize, 3, device=device) (bounds[1] - bounds[0]) + bounds[0] pts.requiresgrad(True) phi = implicitfn(pts) grad = torch.autograd.grad( phi.sum(), pts, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0] return torch.mean((torch.norm(grad, dim=1) - 1.0) 2) def savecheckpoint(modelstate, optimizerstate, epoch, path): torch.save({ 'model': modelstate, 'optimizer': optimizerstate, 'epoch': epoch }, path) def renderevaluation(model, valloader, cfg): model.eval() with torch.nograd(): for batch in valloader: pass Parameters: lr (float): Learning rate for Adam optimizer. totalsteps (int): Number of optimization steps. lrschedulergamma (float): Gamma factor for the LambdaLR scheduler. lrschedulerstepsize (int): Step size interval for the LambdaLR scheduler. perturb (float): Jitter amount for sampling; 0.0 for no jitter, 1.0 for jitter. rawnoisestd (float): Standard deviation of noise added to regularize \sigmaa output; default 0.0, 1e0 recommended. multires (int): Log2 of max frequency for positional encoding of 3D location; default 10. multiresviews (int): Log2 of max frequency for positional encoding of 2D direction; default 4. eikonalweight (float): Weight for the Eikonal loss term in volume SDF rendering. checkpointinterval (int): Frequency of checkpoint saving in epochs. renderinterval (int): Frequency of rendering evaluation in epochs. numepochs (int): Total number of training epochs. renderfactor (int): Downsampling factor to speed up rendering; set 4 or 8 for fast preview, default 0. datasettype (str): Dataset options: llff / blender / deepvoxels; default llff. useviewdirs (bool): Use full 5D input instead of 3D. samplesunion (bool): Flag for samples union variant. rvs (bool): Use reparameterized volume sampling version of the algorithm. precropiters (int): Number of steps to train on central crops; default 0. precropfrac (float): Fraction of image taken for central crops; default 0.5. testskip (int): Will load 1/N images from test/val sets; default 8. shape (str): DeepVoxels shape options: armchair / cube / greek / vase; default greek. whitebkgd (bool): Set to render synthetic data on a white background. halfres (bool): Load Blender synthetic data at 400x400 instead of 800x800. factor (int): Downsample factor for LLFF images; default 8. nondc (bool): Do not use normalized device coordinates. lindisp (bool): Sampling linearly in disparity rather than depth. spherify (bool): Set for spherical 360 scenes. llffhold (int): Will take every 1/N images as LLFF test set; default 8. iprint (int): Frequency of console printout and metric logging; default 100. iimg (int): Frequency of TensorBoard image logging; default 500. iweights (int): Frequency of weight checkpoint saving; default 10000. itestset (int): Frequency of testset saving; default 50000. ivideo (int): Frequency of renderposes video saving; default 50000. Nrand (int): Number of random rays to sample per batch; typical value 1024 or 2048. usebatching (bool): Boolean flag determining if random ray batching is enabled. chunk (int): Maximum number of rays processed per forward pass to limit VRAM usage. stepstilsummary (int): Frequency of logging and plotting. nlayersxyz (int): Number of layers for 3D location MLP; default 6. nhiddenneuronsxyz (int): Hidden neurons for 3D location MLP; default 128. nhiddenneuronsdir (int): Hidden neurons for direction MLP; default 64. appendxyz (list): List of layers to append 3D coordinates to; default [3]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Computation Order: Higher-order derivatives (gradient, Laplacian) for logging must be computed before loss.backward() because the backward pass frees the autograd graph. Precision: Use float32 for standard training; float64 may be needed for precise gradient checks but increases memory usage. Boundary Conditions: Ensure ray sampling respects near/far bounds to avoid NaNs in density computation. Degenerate Input: Handle cases where camera intrinsics are missing by initializing with default values based on image dimensions. Loads image data and transform matrices from paths, moving them to the specified device. Generates the initial grid using generategrid with gridsize, pointsdistance, infosize=4, and device. Training requires multiple epochs and iterations. Chunking controls maximum memory usage without affecting final results. Scaling: Memory and compute scale linearly with batch size and ray samples. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The training procedure involves iterative optimization of a neural radiance field by sampling random rays per iteration, rendering predicted colors via volume integration, computing MSE loss against ground truth, and updating network weights via gradient descent. It builds on coordinate-based neural representations. name: Training Ray Batching
head: Random Ray Batching, Random Ray Batching for NeRF Training
body: Training Ray Batching is a data loading strategy for NeRF optimization that pre-computes rays for all training images, concatenates them with target RGB colors, and samples random subsets per iteration. It differs from Single Image Sampling by drawing rays globally across the entire training dataset rather than restricting them to one image per step, ensuring uniform exposure to all views. Inputs: poses: Array of camera poses, shape (numimg, 3, 4). images: Array of training images, shape (numimg, H, W, 3). K: Camera intrinsic matrix, shape (3, 3). itrain: List of indices for training images. Nrand: Number of rays per batch. Data Structures: raysrgb: A flat tensor of shape (Ntotal, 3, 3) where Ntotal = len(itrain) H W. The first dimension indexes the ray, the second dimension has size 3 representing [rayorigin, raydirection, targetrgb], and the third dimension is the vector size 3. Steps: 1. Generate Rays: For each pose p in poses[:,:3,:4], call getraysnp(H, W, K, p) to generate ray origins and directions. Stack these into a tensor rays of shape (numimg, ro+rd, H, W, 3) where ro+rd = 2. 2. Concatenate Targets: Concatenate rays with images[:,None] along axis 1. images is expanded to (numimg, 1, H, W, 3). Result raysrgb has shape (numimg, ro+rd+rgb, H, W, 3) which equals (numimg, 3, H, W, 3). 3. Transpose: Transpose raysrgb from (numimg, 3, H, W, 3) to (numimg, H, W, 3, 3) using np.transpose(raysrgb, [0, 2, 3, 1, 4]). 4. Filter Training Set: Stack only the images in itrain into raysrgb. Result shape is (len(itrain), H, W, 3, 3). 5. Reshape: Flatten the spatial and image dimensions by reshaping to (-1, 3, 3). The first dimension becomes len(itrain) H W. 6. Cast: Convert to np.float32. 7. Shuffle: Randomly shuffle the entire array using np.random.shuffle(raysrgb). 8. Sample Batch: In each iteration, slice raysrgb[ibatch: ibatch + Nrand]. Transpose the batch to shape (3, Nrand, 3) (equivalent to 2+1, Nrand, 3) to separate origins, directions, and targets. 9. Update Index: Increment ibatch by Nrand. If ibatch >= raysrgb.shape[0], shuffle raysrgb again using torch.randperm and reset ibatch to 0. Parameters: Nrand: Default 32 32 4 = 4096. nobatching: Boolean. If True, disables this method in favor of single-image sampling. K: Simplified intrinsic [[f, 0, W/2], [0, f, H/2], [0, 0, 1]]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch def generaterays(H, W, K, pose): """Standard ray generation routine. Returns (2, H, W, 3) for origins and directions.""" # Standard implementation computes camera centers and per-pixel ray directions # from the pose matrix and intrinsic calibration K. origins = np.zeros((H, W, 3), dtype=np.float32) directions = np.zeros((H, W, 3), dtype=np.float32) #... standard ray casting logic... return np.stack([origins, directions], axis=0) def prepareraybatch(poses, images, K, itrain, Nrand=4096): numimg = poses.shape[0] H, W = images.shape[1], images.shape[2] # Step 1: Generate rays for all images rayslist = [generaterays(H, W, K, p) for p in poses[:,:3,:4]] rays = np.stack(rayslist, axis=0) # (numimg, 2, H, W, 3) # Step 2: Concatenate with target RGB raysrgb = np.concatenate([rays, images[:, None]], axis=1) # (numimg, 3, H, W, 3) # Step 3: Transpose to (numimg, H, W, 3, 3) raysrgb = np.transpose(raysrgb, [0, 2, 3, 1, 4]) # Step 4: Filter for training set raysrgb = np.stack([raysrgb[i] for i in itrain], axis=0) # (len(itrain), H, W, 3, 3) # Step 5: Reshape to flat list (-1, 3, 3) raysrgb = np.reshape(raysrgb, [-1, 3, 3]) # Step 6: Cast to float32 raysrgb = raysrgb.astype(np.float32) # Step 7: Shuffle np.random.shuffle(raysrgb) # Move to GPU device = torch.device('cuda') # Standard device selection raysrgb = torch.Tensor(raysrgb).to(device) ibatch = 0 return raysrgb, ibatch def samplebatch(raysrgb, ibatch, Nrand): # Step 8: Slice batch batch = raysrgb[ibatch: ibatch + Nrand] # (Nrand, 3, 3) # Transpose to (3, Nrand, 3) batch = torch.transpose(batch, 0, 1) # Separate rays and targets batchrays = batch[:2] # (2, Nrand, 3) targets = batch[2] # (Nrand, 3) # Step 9: Update index ibatch += Nrand if ibatch >= raysrgb.shape[0]: # Shuffle again if end of dataset reached randidx = torch.randperm(raysrgb.shape[0]) raysrgb = raysrgb[randidx] ibatch = 0 return batchrays, targets, ibatch Edge Cases: If Nrand does not divide the total number of rays evenly, the last batch in an epoch will be smaller unless padding is implemented. The source code simply slices until the end, then shuffles and resets. Precision issues may arise if H and W are large, leading to very large raysrgb tensors. Memory usage is O(numimg H W). Samples Nrand rays from a single randomly chosen training image per iteration. Chosen when memory is constrained or when specific view-dependent effects are studied in isolation. Renders rays in chunks to manage GPU memory during the forward pass. This is a rendering optimization, not a data loading strategy, but often used in conjunction with batching. Time Complexity: Pre-computation is O(numimg H W). Sampling is O(Nrand) per iteration. Shuffling is O(Ntotal) per epoch. Memory Complexity: O(numimg H W) to store the pre-computed raysrgb tensor. Performance: Default Nrand=4096 provides a balance between gradient noise and computational efficiency. Strengths: Ensures all training views are seen uniformly per epoch. Reduces overhead of ray generation during training. Limitations: High memory usage for high-resolution images. Shuffling large tensors can be slow. Originated in the original NeRF implementation by Mildenhall et al.. The method was designed to efficiently train neural radiance fields by leveraging pre-computed ray data to accelerate the training loop. name: NeRF System Data Preparation
head: Blender Dataset Loading, NeRF training data sampling, NeRF validation data sampling, Synthetic NeRF Dataset
body: This method prepares training and validation data for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by loading synthetic scenes (typically Blender datasets), parsing camera metadata, and precomputing ray origins and directions. It differs from general volume rendering by handling specific coordinate conventions (e.g., OpenCV to NeRF's camera space) and background compositing for synthetic data. It builds on Training Ray Batching by providing the structured ray tensors that are subsequently shuffled and sampled. Inputs: Image files and metadata files (transforms{split}.json). Configuration parameters: near, far, WHITEBG, backgroundcolor. Outputs: A tensor of rays with shape (N, 6) where the first 3 dimensions are ray origins (ox, oy, oz) and the next 3 are normalized ray directions (dx, dy, dz). Target RGB values with shape (N, 3). (Optional) Foreground masks with shape (N, 1) or (N, 3). transforms{split}.json: Contains a list of frames. Each frame has filepath, transformmatrix (4x4), and optionally foregroundmask. cameraanglex: Horizontal field of view in radians. 1. Load Metadata and Compute Focal Length: For Blender datasets, load transforms{split}.json. Extract cameraanglex and compute the focal length f: f = \frac{0.5 \cdot W}{\tan(0.5 \cdot \text{camera\angle\x})}. 2. Preprocess Images and Poses: For each frame in the split, load the image and convert to RGBA. Resize to dimensions (W, H). Composite onto a white background if WHITEBG is true: \text{rgb} = \text{rgba}{:3} \cdot \text{rgba}{3:} + (1 - \text{rgba}{3:}). Extract the camera-to-world matrix C2W from the frame's transformmatrix. 3. Generate Ray Origins and Directions: For each camera pose C2W, generate rays for every pixel (i, j) in the image grid. Create pixel coordinate grids i \in [0, W-1] and j \in [0, H-1]. Compute camera-space directions (OpenCV convention: z-forward, y-down, x-right): d{cam} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{i - Cx}{f} \\ -\frac{j - Cy}{f} \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} where Cx = W/2 and Cy = H/2. Transform directions to world space: d{world} = d{cam} \cdot C2W{0:3, 0:3}^T. Set ray origins to the camera center: o{world} = C2W{0:3, 3}. 4. Sample Rays for Training: During training, not all rays are used per iteration to save memory and compute. Determine the number of rays to sample (Nrand). Select random image indices. If batchimagesampling is enabled, sample trainnumrays indices from the dataset; otherwise, sample 1 index. For the selected images, sample random pixel coordinates (x, y). Extract the corresponding ray origins and directions from the precomputed arrays. Normalize the ray directions: d{norm} = \frac{d}{\|d\|2}. Concatenate origins and normalized directions into a tensor of shape (Nrand, 6). 5. Handle Background Color: Set the model's background color based on configuration: if backgroundcolor is 'white', initialize as torch.ones((3,)); if 'random', initialize with random values. name: Ray-box intersection
head: Slab Test, Slab Method, Smits' method, AABB Slab Method, Slab intersection, AABB Ray Intersection, Ray-AABB Intersection, Ray-BBox Intersection, Kay and Kajiya slab test, Smits' Ray-Box Intersection, Ray-Bounding Box Intersection, Ray-Axis-Aligned Bounding Box Intersection
body: The ray-box intersection method determines whether a ray intersects an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) by treating the box as the intersection of three pairs of parallel planes, known as slabs. It computes the entry (t{near}) and exit (t{far}) distances for each slab pair and checks for overlap across all three axes. Unlike general primitive intersection methods, this approach exploits the axis-aligned nature of the box to reduce the problem to simple scalar comparisons and vector operations, making it the dominant technique for bounding volume hierarchy traversal in ray tracing. Inputs: Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} = (ox, oy, oz) and direction \mathbf{v} = (vx, vy, vz), parameterized as \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{v}. AABB: Defined by minimum corner \mathbf{p}0 = (x0, y0, z0) and maximum corner \mathbf{p}1 = (x1, y1, z1). Ray Interval (Optional): A valid hit distance interval [t{min}, t{max}] representing the range of t-values on the ray that count as a hit. Outputs: Boolean indicating intersection. If intersecting, the entry distance t{near} and exit distance t{far}. The method operates on scalar values or 3D vectors. Inverse Ray Direction: \mathbf{invV} = (1/vx, 1/vy, 1/vz). Interval Vectors: Vectors storing the computed t-values for the lower and upper bounds of each axis. The method can be implemented in two primary styles: the iterative scalar approach (Kay and Kajiya original) and the compact vector approach (widely used in modern kernels). This approach processes each axis (X, Y, Z) sequentially, updating global t{near} and t{far} values. 1. Initialize t{near} = -\infty and t{far} = \infty. 2. For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: a. Let oi be the ray origin component, vi be the ray direction component, mini be the box minimum coordinate, and maxi be the box maximum coordinate. b. Check for parallelism: If vi = 0: i. If oi < mini or oi > maxi, the ray is outside the slab. Return false (miss). ii. Otherwise, the ray is inside the slab along this axis; continue to the next axis. c. Compute intersection distances with the near and far planes of the slab: t1 = \frac{mini - oi}{vi} t2 = \frac{maxi - oi}{vi} d. Ensure t1 is the smaller value (entry) and t2 is the larger value (exit). If t1 > t2, swap t1 and t2. e. Update the global intersection interval: t{near} = \max(t{near}, t1) t{far} = \min(t{far}, t2) f. Check for miss: If t{near} > t{far}, the intervals do not overlap. Return false. g. Check if the box is behind the ray: If t{far} < 0, the entire box is behind the ray origin. Return false. 3. If the loop completes without returning false, the ray intersects the box. Return true. This approach computes all intersections in parallel using vector operations, often branchless. 1. Compute the inverse ray direction: \mathbf{invV} = (1/vx, 1/vy, 1/vz). 2. Compute the t-values for the lower and upper bounds of the box: \mathbf{t}{lower} = (\mathbf{p}0 - \mathbf{o}) \odot \mathbf{invV} \mathbf{t}{upper} = (\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{o}) \odot \mathbf{invV} where \odot denotes component-wise multiplication. 3. Determine the entry and exit t-values for each slab by taking the component-wise minimum and maximum of \mathbf{t}{lower} and \mathbf{t}{upper}: \mathbf{t}{min\slabs} = \min(\mathbf{t}{lower}, \mathbf{t}{upper}) \mathbf{t}{max\slabs} = \max(\mathbf{t}{lower}, \mathbf{t}{upper}) 4. Incorporate the ray's valid hit interval [t{min}, t{max}] as a fourth dimension (or separate scalar check). t{box\min} = \max(\mathbf{t}{min\slabs}.x, \mathbf{t}{min\slabs}.y, \mathbf{t}{min\slabs}.z, t{min}) t{box\max} = \min(\mathbf{t}{max\slabs}.x, \mathbf{t}{max\slabs}.y, \mathbf{t}{max\slabs}.z, t{max}) 5. The ray intersects the box if t{box\min} \le t{box\max}. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the robust compact vector approach, handling zero direction components and negative zeros correctly per IEEE 754 standards. def slabsboxtest(p0, p1, rayorigin, raydir, raytmin, raytmax): """ Determines if a ray intersects an AABB. Handles zero direction components and negative zeros robustly. """ tnear = float('-inf') tfar = float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydir[i] == 0.0: if rayorigin[i] < p0[i] or rayorigin[i] > p1[i]: return False, None, None continue invd = 1.0 / raydir[i] t1 = (p0[i] - rayorigin[i]) invd t2 = (p1[i] - rayorigin[i]) invd if invd >= 0.0: tnear = max(tnear, t1) tfar = min(tfar, t2) else: tnear = max(tnear, t2) tfar = min(tfar, t1) if tnear > tfar: return False, None, None if tfar < 0.0: return False, None, None return True, max(tnear, raytmin), min(tfar, raytmax) Ray Direction: Must be normalized in many applications, but the algorithm works with unnormalized directions as long as invraydir is computed correctly. Box Corners: \mathbf{p}0 and \mathbf{p}1 must satisfy p{0,i} \le p{1,i} for all i \in \{x,y,z\}. Ray Interval: The interval [t{min}, t{max}] represents the valid hit distances on the ray. Typical values are not given in the sources. Zero Direction Components: The algorithm produces correct results for rays with zero direction components (parallel to axes) provided the hardware is IEEE floating-point compliant. The division by zero in invraydir results in infinity, which is handled correctly by the min/max logic. Explicit checks for vi = 0 prevent NaN generation when the ray origin lies exactly on a box boundary. Negative Zero Direction: If a direction component is -0.0, testing the sign of the direction itself fails due to IEEE 754 rules. The robust implementation tests the sign of the reciprocal direction component instead. Ray Origin on Box Face: If the ray origin lies exactly on the box surface and the direction points along the face, naive implementations may result in NaN (Not a Number), causing the test to return false. This behavior can be modified if specific handling is required. Branchless Optimization: Removing early exit checks (like if tnear > tfar) creates a branchless implementation. While this performs more arithmetic operations, it significantly increases performance on modern hardware by avoiding branch mispredictions. Converts an inner bounding box to a list of bounds relative to an enclosing box, adding entries for sides where the inner box is strictly contained. It initializes a counter, loops over dimensions to count boundaries, allocates an array of ANNorthHalfSpace structs, and populates them with dimension index, cutting value, and sign (+1 or -1) based on whether the inner box's lower or upper bound is strictly inside the enclosing box. Computes entry and exit points of rays intersecting a bounding box by rendering the box geometry to textures using OpenGL, storing hit positions in 16-bit floating point textures. It creates a Framebuffer Object (FBO) with GLRGBA16F color attachments and a GLDEPTHCOMPONENT16 depth renderbuffer, enables face culling and depth testing, and draws the cube geometry using a hit shader program passing the MVP matrix as a uniform. The depth buffer must be cleared along with the color buffer, and correct depth writing from the geometry shader is required. Time Complexity: The algorithm performs a fixed number of arithmetic operations and comparisons regardless of scene complexity. Performance: The slabs test is the dominant method for AABB intersection due to its simplicity and efficiency. Branchless implementations are preferred in high-performance ray tracing kernels (e.g., Embree) to maximize throughput on SIMD units and GPUs. Strengths: Fast, robust, easy to implement, works well with SIMD/vectorization. Limitations: Only applicable to axis-aligned boxes. Origin: The method was introduced by T. L. Kay and J. T. Kajiya in their 1986 paper "Ray tracing complex scenes" presented at SIGGRAPH. Development: The algorithm has become the standard for AABB intersection in ray tracing. It is widely used in modern ray tracing kernels such as Embree and in astronomical simulation tools like raytheia. Usage: It is used for primary ray-scene intersection testing, shadow ray occlusion testing, frustum culling, and spatial traversal of octree and grid acceleration structures. name: Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement
head: Bisection Refinement, Intersection refined isosurface rendering, Iso Hit Bisection, Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement, Isosurface shader, Linear Interpolation Refinement
body: Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement is an iterative root-finding method used to refine the intersection position after a sign change has been detected during ray marching. It narrows down the interval [t{prev}, t{curr}] containing the isosurface by iteratively applying linear interpolation (bisection) within the segment. This approach solves the problem of geometric inaccuracy inherent in discrete sampling, providing a balance between computational speed and visual fidelity. Unlike closed-form algebraic solutions or higher-order root isolation techniques, it relies on repeated linear approximation. It builds on Linear Edge Intersection by applying similar linear interpolation principles within an iterative refinement loop over a ray segment rather than a single edge. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Interval bounds [t{prev}, t{curr}] (or corresponding spatial points \mathbf{x}{prev}, \mathbf{x}{curr}) where the scalar field values d{prev} and d{curr} have opposite signs relative to the isovalue \rho (i.e., a sign change is detected). Scalar field values d{prev} = f(\mathbf{x}{prev}) and d{curr} = f(\mathbf{x}{curr}). Target isovalue \rho. Number of refinement iterations N (typically 4–10). Outputs: Refined intersection parameter t{hit} or point \mathbf{x}{hit}. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values and 3D vectors, storing only the current interval bounds and field values. Steps: 1. Initialization: Identify the interval [\mathbf{x}{near}, \mathbf{x}{far}] such that f(\mathbf{x}{near}) < \rho and f(\mathbf{x}{far}) \ge \rho (or vice versa, depending on convention). Let f{near} = f(\mathbf{x}{near}) and f{far} = f(\mathbf{x}{far}). 2. Iteration Loop: Repeat N times: a. Calculate the new sample position \mathbf{x}{new} using linear interpolation between \mathbf{x}{near} and \mathbf{x}{far} based on the ratio of the distance from f{near} to \rho over the total interval f{far} - f{near}: \mathbf{x}{new} = (\mathbf{x}{far} - \mathbf{x}{near}) \frac{\rho - f{near}}{f{far} - f{near}} + \mathbf{x}{near} b. Sample the scalar field value at the new position: f{new} = f(\mathbf{x}{new}). c. Update the interval bounds: If f{new} > \rho (the new point is "in front" of the isosurface, assuming higher values are inside), set \mathbf{x}{far} = \mathbf{x}{new} and f{far} = f{new}. Otherwise (f{new} \le \rho), set \mathbf{x}{near} = \mathbf{x}{new} and f{near} = f{new}. 3. Result: After N iterations, the refined intersection point is \mathbf{x}{hit} = \mathbf{x}{new}. Shade this point and return. 4. Edge Cases: If the initial detection does not find a sign change, or if the loop condition fails (e.g., ray leaves volume), advance to the next sampling step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def refineisohitbisection(origin, direction, tprev, tcurr, dprev, dcurr, isovalue, numiterations): """ Refines the intersection position of a ray with an isosurface using iterative bisection. """ # Initialize interval bounds xnear = origin + tprev direction xfar = origin + tcurr direction fnear = dprev ffar = dcurr # Ensure correct ordering: fnear < isovalue <= ffar if fnear >= isovalue: xnear, xfar = xfar, xnear fnear, ffar = ffar, fnear xnew = xnear fnew = fnear for i in range(numiterations): # Guard against division by zero if ffar == fnear if ffar == fnear: break tratio = (isovalue - fnear) / (ffar - fnear) xnew = xnear + (xfar - xnear) tratio # Sample scalar field at xnew (implementation depends on volume data structure) fnew = samplescalarfield(xnew) # Update interval bounds if fnew > isovalue: xfar = xnew ffar = fnew else: xnear = xnew fnear = fnew # Return the refined parameter thit = dot(xnew - origin, direction) return thit Parameters: numiterations: The number of bisection steps to perform. Typical values range from 4 to 10. Source states that a fixed number of 4 steps is sufficient for high-quality positions. Source uses up to 10 iterations. Source mentions a parameter uRefinementIterations with a typical value of 5. More iterations improve accuracy at the cost of additional scalar field evaluations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If f{far} == f{near}, the interpolation ratio is undefined. This can occur if the scalar field is flat or if precision issues cause identical values. A guard should be added to break the loop or return the current estimate. Sign Convention: The method assumes a consistent sign convention (e.g., f < \rho is outside, f \ge \rho is inside). If the sign change detection logic uses a different convention, the update logic for xnear and xfar must be adjusted accordingly. Complex Topologies: In regions with high curvature or complex topology, linear interpolation may not accurately represent the surface, leading to artifacts. Precision: Floating-point precision errors can accumulate, especially if the interval becomes very small. Using double precision for intermediate calculations may be beneficial in critical applications. Neubauer's algorithm is a method for finding the intersection of a viewing ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinearly interpolated scalar data within a voxel. It solves the problem of locating the precise root of the implicit function f(t) = \rho(R(t)) - \rho{iso} by using repeated linear interpolation to refine the intersection position within the ray segment containing the root. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on iterative linear approximation rather than closed-form algebraic solutions (like Schwarze's Analytic Inversion) or root isolation techniques (like Isolation and Iterative Root Finding), offering a balance of speed and moderate accuracy at the cost of potential artifacts in complex topologies. Fast Ray-Surface Intersection is an approximate method for determining the intersection point of a ray with an iso-surface within a volume rendering cell, trading geometric accuracy for computational speed. It solves the problem of finding the first-hit surface location without the high cost of inverting trilinear interpolation. Unlike exact intersection methods which compute all roots of the cubic polynomial derived from trilinear interpolation, this method subdivides the ray segment within the cell and uses linear interpolation to estimate the hit point, producing visually indistinguishable results in final renderings while being significantly faster. The Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement is an iterative root-finding algorithm used to refine the depth value d where a signed distance function (SDF) or occupancy logit crosses a threshold. It estimates the next intersection point using linear interpolation between two bracketing points. The Bisection Method is an iterative root-finding algorithm used to refine the intersection position of a ray with an implicit surface within a specific segment identified by adaptive sampling. It serves as an alternative to the Secant method in ray marching pipelines, guaranteeing convergence by halving the search interval at each step. Unlike the Secant method, which uses linear interpolation between two points, the Bisection method relies solely on the sign of the field function evaluations to narrow the interval. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of refinement iterations. Each iteration requires one scalar field evaluation and basic arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Source reports that 4 iterations are sufficient for high-quality positions, suggesting a low computational overhead. Source uses up to 10 iterations, which may be more conservative. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides significantly better accuracy than simple midpoint detection. Limitations: May produce artifacts in complex topologies due to the assumption of linearity. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement is a technique used in real-time volume graphics and isosurface rendering. It was described in the context of real-time ray-casting and advanced shading of discrete isosurfaces by Sigg et al. in 2005. The method is also referenced in the book "Real-Time Volume Graphics" by Hadwiger et al.. It is used in volume rendering pipelines, such as the VTK vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper2. name: Neubauer's Ray-Voxel Intersection Algorithm
head: Neubauer, Neubauer's Method, Repeated Linear Interpolation
body: Neubauer's algorithm is a method for finding the intersection of a viewing ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinearly interpolated scalar data within a voxel. It solves the problem of locating the precise root of the implicit function f(t) = \rho(R(t)) - \rho{iso} by using repeated linear interpolation to refine the intersection position within the ray segment containing the root. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on iterative linear approximation rather than closed-form algebraic solutions (like Schwarze's Analytic Inversion) or root isolation techniques (like Isolation and Iterative Root Finding), offering a balance of speed and moderate accuracy at the cost of potential artifacts in complex topologies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray R(t) = \mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{b}, where \mathbf{a} is the origin and \mathbf{b} is the direction. The interval [t{in}, t{out}] where the ray overlaps the voxel. The scalar field values \rho{ijk} at the eight vertices of the voxel. The iso-value \rho{iso}. The number of iterations N (typically 2-3). Output: The hit distance t{hit} along the ray, or a "NO HIT" status if no intersection is found within the voxel. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on scalar values representing the ray parameter t and the interpolated density \rho. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Set the search interval boundaries: t0:= t{in} t1:= t{out} Compute the density values at the boundaries: \rho0:= \rho(R(t0)) \rho1:= \rho(R(t1)) where \rho(R(t)) is computed via trilinear interpolation of the voxel's vertex data. 2. Initial Sign Check: If \text{sign}(\rho0 - \rho{iso}) = \text{sign}(\rho1 - \rho{iso}), return NO HIT. This indicates that the iso-surface does not cross the ray segment within the voxel, or crosses an even number of times, which the method cannot detect. 3. Iterative Refinement (Repeated Linear Interpolation): For i = 1 to N: a. Compute the candidate intersection parameter t using linear interpolation (secant step): t:= t0 + (t1 - t0) \frac{\rho{iso} - \rho0}{\rho1 - \rho0} b. Evaluate the density at the candidate point: \rho{new}:= \rho(R(t)) c. Determine which sub-segment contains the root by comparing signs: If \text{sign}(\rho{new} - \rho{iso}) = \text{sign}(\rho0 - \rho{iso}): The root lies in the upper sub-segment [t, t1]. Update: t0:= t \rho0:= \rho{new} Else: The root lies in the lower sub-segment [t0, t]. Update: t1:= t \rho1:= \rho{new} 4. Final Result: After N iterations, compute the final hit distance: t{hit}:= t0 + (t1 - t0) \frac{\rho{iso} - \rho0}{\rho1 - \rho0} Return t{hit}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def NeubauerRayVoxelIntersection(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelbounds, voxeldata, rhoiso, N=3): """ rayorigin: tuple (x, y, z) raydirection: tuple (dx, dy, dz) voxelbounds: tuple (x0, x1, y0, y1, z0, z1) voxeldata: list/tuple of 8 floats representing density at voxel corners rhoiso: float, the iso-surface value N: int, number of interpolation iterations """ # 1. Calculate ray-voxel overlap interval [tin, tout] using slab method x0, x1, y0, y1, z0, z1 = voxelbounds tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for axis in range(3): p = rayorigin[axis] d = raydirection[axis] b0 = [x0, y0, z0][axis] b1 = [x1, y1, z1][axis] if abs(d) < 1e-12: if p < b0 or p > b1: return None else: t1 = (b0 - p) / d t2 = (b1 - p) / d if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tmin = max(tmin, t1) tmax = min(tmax, t2) if tmin > tmax: return None tin, tout = tmin, tmax # Helper to evaluate trilinear interpolation def evaluatedensity(t): px = rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0] py = rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1] pz = rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2] u = (px - x0) / (x1 - x0) v = (py - y0) / (y1 - y0) w = (pz - z0) / (z1 - z0) u = max(0.0, min(1.0, u)) v = max(0.0, min(1.0, v)) w = max(0.0, min(1.0, w)) d000 = voxeldata[0]; d100 = voxeldata[1] d010 = voxeldata[2]; d110 = voxeldata[3] d001 = voxeldata[4]; d101 = voxeldata[5] d011 = voxeldata[6]; d111 = voxeldata[7] d00 = d000 (1 - u) + d100 u d10 = d010 (1 - u) + d110 u d01 = d001 (1 - u) + d101 u d11 = d011 (1 - u) + d111 u d0 = d00 (1 - v) + d10 v d1 = d01 (1 - v) + d11 v return d0 (1 - w) + d1 w # 2. Initialize interval t0 = tin t1 = tout rho0 = evaluatedensity(t0) rho1 = evaluatedensity(t1) # 3. Initial sign check def sign(val): if val > 0: return 1 elif val < 0: return -1 else: return 0 if sign(rho0 - rhoiso) == sign(rho1 - rhoiso): return None # 4. Iterative refinement for i in range(N): if abs(rho1 - rho0) < 1e-12: t = (t0 + t1) / 2.0 else: t = t0 + (t1 - t0) (rhoiso - rho0) / (rho1 - rho0) rhonew = evaluatedensity(t) if sign(rhonew - rhoiso) == sign(rho0 - rhoiso): t0 = t rho0 = rhonew else: t1 = t rho1 = rhonew # 5. Final result if abs(rho1 - rho0) < 1e-12: thit = (t0 + t1) / 2.0 else: thit = t0 + (t1 - t0) (rhoiso - rho0) / (rho1 - rho0) return thit Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Intersections: The algorithm assumes a single root within the segment defined by differing signs. It can falsely return the last intersection point if three intersections are contained within a voxel but two of them are within the first ray segment. Complex Topologies: In cases where the function has two roots, the entry and exit densities may be on the same side of \rho{iso}, causing the initial sign check to return NO HIT incorrectly. SIMD Compatibility: The control flow involves conditional updates to t0, t1, \rho0, \rho1 based on sign comparisons. This inconsistent decision-making on which segment to handle makes the base algorithm less suitable for SIMD than methods with uniform control flow, although it is still functional and faster than Schwarze's method in SIMD contexts. Precision: As an iterative approximation, it is prone to approximation artifacts and image errors for complex voxel configurations compared to exact methods. Schwarze's Analytic Inversion is a method for computing the exact intersection of a ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinearly interpolated scalar data within a voxel. It solves the cubic polynomial resulting from substituting the ray equation into the trilinear interpolation function to find the precise root. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Neubauer's algorithm by its reliance on closed-form algebraic solutions (Cardano's formula) rather than iterative refinement or isolation techniques, offering mathematical exactness at the cost of significant computational expense and numerical instability. Isolation and Iterative Root Finding is a ray-voxel intersection algorithm for iso-surfaces that combines the speed of Neubauer's method with the correctness guarantees of Schwarze's method. It solves the problem of finding the first intersection of a ray with a cubic polynomial within a voxel by first isolating the root interval using the polynomial's extrema, then refining the location via iterative root finding. Unlike Neubauer's method, which can fail or return incorrect intersections when multiple roots exist in a segment, this method guarantees that the final interval contains exactly one root, ensuring the first valid intersection is found. It is roughly three times faster than Schwarze's method while maintaining superior numerical stability. Marmitt's Ray-Cell Intersection computes the point where a ray intersects an isosurface defined by trilinear interpolation within a 3D voxel cell. It solves for the first positive root of the cubic polynomial derived from the cell's corner values using an iterative bisection refinement strategy. Unlike analytical cubic solvers (e.g., Schwarze’s method), this approach is slightly faster and yields single-precision, numerically stable results. It builds on Neubauer's Ray-Voxel Intersection Algorithm by applying iterative root finding specifically to the reconstructed cell geometry. Time and Memory Complexity: The algorithm performs a fixed number of iterations N (typically 2-3). Each iteration requires one trilinear interpolation evaluation. Trilinear interpolation is O(1) with a constant number of arithmetic operations. Thus, the time complexity per ray-voxel intersection is O(N), which is effectively constant. Memory complexity is O(1) as it only stores a few scalar variables. Measured Performance: On a 1.8GHz AMD Opteron CPU, Neubauer achieves an average of 3.04 million ray-voxel intersections per second in synthetic setups (Table 1). In SIMD mode on synthetic setups, Neubauer achieves an average of 3.04 million ray-cell intersections per second (Table 2). On real-world datasets (Bonsai, Aneurism, Engine), Neubauer achieves approximately 2.93-2.94 million intersections per second (Table 3). In SIMD mode on real-world datasets, Neubauer achieves 6.94-7.65 million intersections per second, a speedup of factor 2.3-2.6 over sequential code (Table 4). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Faster than the accurate but slow Schwarze algorithm. Better suited for SIMD implementation than Schwarze due to simpler control flow (though still not ideal). Integrated into the OpenRT realtime ray tracing system. Limitations: Prone to approximation artifacts and image errors for complex voxel configurations. Can fail to locate valid intersections in cases with multiple roots or specific topological configurations. Less numerically stable than isolation-based methods. When to Use: Use when performance is critical and the voxel data topology is relatively simple, or when an approximate intersection is acceptable. It is a good baseline for SIMD-accelerated volume rendering where the overhead of exact solvers is prohibitive. When Not to Use: Avoid when high accuracy is required, especially for complex iso-surfaces with multiple intersections within a single voxel, or when numerical stability is paramount. Neubauer's algorithm was proposed by Neubauer et al. in 2002. It was analyzed and compared with other ray-voxel intersection techniques (including Schwarze's method and linear interpolation) in the context of iso-surface volume rendering by Wald et al. in 2004. The method is integrated into the OpenRT realtime ray tracing system for iso-surface volume rendering, where it serves as a fast, approximate intersection primitive. name: Schwarze's Analytic Inversion
head: Cardano's formula method, Exact Ray-Surface Intersection, Schwarze approach
body: Schwarze's Analytic Inversion is a method for computing the exact intersection of a ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinearly interpolated scalar data within a voxel. It solves the cubic polynomial resulting from substituting the ray equation into the trilinear interpolation function to find the precise root. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Neubauer's algorithm by its reliance on closed-form algebraic solutions (Cardano's formula) rather than iterative refinement or isolation techniques, offering mathematical exactness at the cost of significant computational expense and numerical instability. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, voxel corner values \rho{ijk} for i,j,k \in \{0,1\}, iso-value \rho{iso}, voxel dimensions \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z, and traversal interval [t{in}, t{out}]. Output: The smallest ray parameter t \in [t{in}, t{out}] such that the interpolated density equals \rho{iso}, or None if no intersection exists in the interval. Data Structures: The method operates on the coefficients of the cubic polynomial f(t) = \rho(t) - \rho{iso} = 0. Let the ray be \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. The density \rho(t) is a cubic polynomial in t: \rho(t) = a t^3 + b t^2 + c t + d The coefficients a, b, c, d are computed from the voxel corner densities and ray direction components. The target polynomial is f(t) = a t^3 + b t^2 + c t + (d - \rho{iso}). Steps: 1. Compute Polynomial Coefficients: Calculate a, b, c, d based on the trilinear interpolation model and the ray parameters. 2. Check Special Cases: If |a| is negligible (below a threshold), the polynomial is quadratic or lower. Solve using the quadratic formula or linear equation. Note that even the quadratic case requires a costly square root operation. If |a| and |b| are negligible, solve the linear equation ct + (d - \rho{iso}) = 0. 3. Solve Cubic (Cardano's Formula): For the full cubic case (a \neq 0): Normalize the polynomial to x^3 + px + q = 0 by substituting t = x - \frac{b}{3a}. Calculate the discriminant D = (q/2)^2 + (p/3)^3. Apply Cardano's formula, which involves computing cosines and inverse cosines (arccos) to handle the trigonometric solution for the three real roots case when D \leq 0. Compute all three roots of the polynomial. 4. Filter Roots: Identify roots t that lie within the voxel traversal interval [t{in}, t{out}]. Select the smallest valid t as the intersection point. 5. Return Result: Return the smallest valid t. If no roots are in the interval, return None. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def schwarzeanalyticinversion(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelcorners, rhoiso, tin, tout, voxelsize): # voxelcorners: [rho000, rho100, rho010, rho110, rho001, rho101, rho011, rho111] # voxelsize: [dx, dy, dz] def cbrt(x): return math.copysign(abs(x)(1/3), x) def computetrilinearcoeffs(o, d, corners, vs): dx, dy, dz = vs u0, u1 = o[0]/dx, d[0]/dx v0, v1 = o[1]/dy, d[1]/dy w0, w1 = o[2]/dz, d[2]/dz # Basis coefficients for trilinear interpolation c00 = corners[0] c10 = corners[1] - corners[0] c01 = corners[2] - corners[0] c001 = corners[4] - corners[0] c11 = corners[3] - corners[1] - corners[2] + corners[0] c101 = corners[5] - corners[1] - corners[4] + corners[0] c011 = corners[6] - corners[2] - corners[4] + corners[0] c111 = corners[7] - corners[3] - corners[5] - corners[6] + corners[1] + corners[2] + corners[4] - corners[0] # Taylor expansion coefficients at t=0: rho(t) = d + ct + bt^2 + at^3 a = u1 v1 w1 c111 b = u1 v1 c11 + u1 w1 c101 + v1 w1 c011 c = (u1 (c10 + c11 v0 + c101 w0 + c111 v0 w0) + v1 (c01 + c11 u0 + c011 w0 + c111 u0 w0) + w1 (c001 + c101 u0 + c011 v0 + c111 u0 v0)) dval = (c00 + c10 u0 + c01 v0 + c001 w0 + c11 u0 v0 + c101 u0 w0 + c011 v0 w0 + c111 u0 v0 w0) return a, b, c, dval EPSILON = 1e-8 a, b, c, d = computetrilinearcoeffs(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelcorners, voxelsize) d -= rhoiso # 2. Handle special cases if abs(a) < EPSILON: if abs(b) < EPSILON: # Linear: ct + d = 0 if abs(c) < EPSILON: return None t = -d / c return t if tin <= t <= tout else None else: # Quadratic: bt^2 + ct + d = 0 disc = cc - 4bd if disc < 0: return None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-c + sqrtdisc) / (2b) t2 = (-c - sqrtdisc) / (2b) valid = [t for t in (t1, t2) if tin <= t <= tout] return min(valid) if valid else None # 3. Full Cubic Case: at^3 + bt^2 + ct + d = 0 shift = b / (3a) p = (3ac - bb) / (3aa) q = (2bbb - 9abc + 27aad) / (27aaa) roots = [] D = (q/2)2 + (p/3)3 if D <= 0: # Three real roots using trigonometric formula if p >= 0: sqrtD = math.sqrt(D) u = cbrt(-q/2 + sqrtD) v = cbrt(-q/2 - sqrtD) roots.append(u + v + shift) else: r = math.sqrt(-p3 / 27.0) costheta = -q / (2 r) if abs(r) > EPSILON else 0.0 costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta)) theta = math.acos(costheta) for k in range(3): angle = (theta + 2 math.pi k) / 3.0 x = 2 math.sqrt(-p/3.0) math.cos(angle) roots.append(x + shift) else: # One real root using Cardano's radical formula sqrtD = math.sqrt(D) u = cbrt(-q/2 + sqrtD) v = cbrt(-q/2 - sqrtD) roots.append(u + v + shift) # 4. Filter and return smallest valid t valid = [t for t in roots if tin <= t <= tout] return min(valid) if valid else None Parameters: EPSILON: A small threshold for determining if coefficients a or b are negligible. Value not given in the sources. rhoiso: The iso-surface density value. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Stability: The algebraic solution is prone to numerical problems, especially in single-precision floating point, making it difficult to tune to avoid incorrectly computed intersections. Special Cases: Small coefficients A and/or B indicate the polynomial does not have full degree and must be solved more directly (quadratic or linear). Cost: The method involves costly square root, cosine, and inverse cosine operations. Boundary Handling: Roots must be strictly checked against [t{in}, t{out}] to avoid returning intersections outside the current voxel or behind the ray origin. Time Complexity: High. The method requires computing cube roots, square roots, and trigonometric functions (arccos, cos) for every voxel intersection test. Memory Complexity: Low. It requires storing only the polynomial coefficients and a few temporary variables. Performance: Computationally very expensive. It is considered too slow for interactive volume rendering due to speed and numerical stability issues compared to isolation methods. Strengths: Mathematically the most accurate solution for computing intersection in volume ray tracing. It provides exact intersection points. Limitations: Prone to numerical instability, particularly in single precision. The computational cost is prohibitive for real-time applications. When to use: When exact intersection accuracy is critical and performance is not a constraint. When not to use: For interactive volume rendering or when numerical stability in single precision is required. Origin: Introduced by Lin et al. and Parker et al.. The method is also referred to as the Schwarze approach, citing [Sch90] and [PSL+98]. History: It was developed as a highly accurate alternative to approximate methods like the simple midpoint algorithm or linear interpolation refinements. Usage: It is commonly applied in volume ray tracing where exactness is prioritized over speed, though it has largely been superseded by more stable iterative or isolation-based methods for interactive applications. name: Isolation and Iterative Root Finding
head: Isolation method, New intersection algorithm
body: Isolation and Iterative Root Finding is a ray-voxel intersection algorithm designed to locate the first intersection of a viewing ray with an iso-surface within a voxel. It solves the problem of balancing computational speed with numerical correctness, addressing the inaccuracies of Neubauer's method and the slowness of Schwarze's method. It sets itself apart by first isolating the root interval using polynomial extrema analysis, guaranteeing exactly one root in the final interval, and then applying iterative refinement. This approach is roughly three times faster than Schwarze's method while providing the same correctness guarantees and better numerical stability. The method operates on a cubic polynomial f(t) representing the density along the ray segment [t{in}, t{out}]. The algorithm consists of two phases: root isolation via extrema analysis, followed by iterative root finding. Inputs: Ray segment endpoints t{in} and t{out}. Polynomial coefficients A, B, C, D for f(t) = At^3 + Bt^2 + Ct + D. Outputs: Intersection parameter t{hit} or "NO HIT". Data Structures: Floating-point variables for t, f, e (extrema). Quadratic solver for f'(t). Steps: 1. Initialization: Set t0 = t{in}, t1 = t{out}. Evaluate f0 = f(t0) and f1 = f(t1). 2. Extrema Analysis: Compute the derivative f'(t) = 3At^2 + 2Bt + C. Solve the quadratic equation f'(t) = 0 for real roots. Let the roots be e0 and e1 with e0 \le e1. If no real roots exist, skip to Step 4. 3. Interval Isolation: Iterate through the extrema to narrow the search interval [t0, t1] to a segment containing exactly one root. For each extremum e \in \{e0, e1\}: If e is not in [t0, t1], continue to the next extremum. If e is in [t0, t1]: Evaluate f(e). If \text{sign}(f(e)) == \text{sign}(f0): The extremum is on the same side of the iso-surface as the start of the current segment. Advance the start of the segment: t0:= e f0:= f(e). Else: The extremum is on the opposite side. The root lies between the previous start and this extremum. Set the end of the segment: t1:= e f1:= f(e). Note: The algorithm processes e0 then e1. If e0 splits the interval, the subsequent check for e1 operates on the new [t0, t1]. 4. Hit Check: If \text{sign}(f0) == \text{sign}(f1), return "NO HIT". Otherwise, the interval [t0, t1] contains exactly one root. 5. Iterative Refinement: Use repeated linear interpolation (regula falsi) to find the root within [t0, t1]. Loop i from 1 to N (typically N=2 or 3): Compute candidate t: t = t0 + (t1 - t0) \frac{-f0}{f1 - f0} Evaluate f(t). If \text{sign}(f(t)) == \text{sign}(f0): t0:= t f0:= f(t). Else: t1:= t f1:= f(t). 6. Return Result: Return t{hit} = t0 + (t1 - t0) \frac{-f0}{f1 - f0}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def isolationanditerativerootfinding(tin, tout, A, B, C, D, N=3): def f(t): return A t3 + B t2 + C t + D def sign(x): return 1 if x >= 0 else -1 t0 = tin t1 = tout f0 = f(t0) f1 = f(t1) # Find extrema by solving f'(t) = 3At^2 + 2Bt + C = 0 aquad = 3 A bquad = 2 B cquad = C discriminant = bquad2 - 4 aquad cquad if discriminant >= 0: sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) e0 = (-bquad - sqrtdisc) / (2 aquad) e1 = (-bquad + sqrtdisc) / (2 aquad) extrema = [e0, e1] if e0 <= e1 else [e1, e0] for e in extrema: if t0 <= e <= t1: fe = f(e) if sign(fe) == sign(f0): t0 = e f0 = fe else: t1 = e f1 = fe if sign(f0) == sign(f1): return None # NO HIT # Iterative refinement using repeated linear interpolation for in range(N): denom = f1 - f0 if abs(denom) < 1e-12: # Guard against division by zero break t = t0 + (t1 - t0) (-f0) / denom ft = f(t) if sign(ft) == sign(f0): t0 = t f0 = ft else: t1 = t f1 = ft denom = f1 - f0 if abs(denom) < 1e-12: thit = t0 else: thit = t0 + (t1 - t0) (-f0) / denom return thit Parameters: Number of iterations N: Typically 2 or 3. A fixed number is usually faster than an adaptive termination criterion. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Three Intersections: Neubauer's method can falsely return the last intersection if three intersections are contained within a voxel and two are in the first segment. Isolation and Iterative Root Finding avoids this by explicitly isolating the first root interval using extrema, ensuring the returned root is the first one. Precision: The method relies on evaluating the polynomial. Since coefficients are known, this avoids costly trilinear interpolation during refinement, improving speed and stability. No Real Extrema: If the discriminant is negative, the polynomial is monotonic in the interval, and the initial [t{in}, t{out}] is used directly. Division by Zero: If f1 converges to f0 during refinement, the denominator f1 - f0 becomes zero; the implementation guards against this by checking the denominator magnitude before division. A root finding algorithm for polynomials in Bernstein form that isolates and refines the first intersection of a viewing ray with an isosurface by subdividing the control polygon using the de Casteljau algorithm at its intersection with the zero axis. It sets itself apart from knot insertion methods like [MR07] by offering quadratic convergence speed and constant memory usage without index operations, making it significantly faster for GPU architectures. A root finding approach based on Sturm Series working in power form. A root-finder in power form using the Sturm Series to count multiplicities of roots in a given interval. It uses binary subdivision of the search interval. The algorithm computes the Sturm Series at the beginning, evaluates it once during every iteration step, and subdivides the search interval in a binary manner. Numerical problems natural for power form implementations get more severe for more iterations. It exhibits exponential convergence with constant memory consumption during iteration, but high memory consumption overall as the whole Sturm Series needs to be kept in memory during the entire execution. For degree 9 (tri-cubic), execution time is 0.077 (relative), MSE is 0.003, and max err is 1.0. Time Complexity: Roughly a factor of three faster than Schwarze code while providing same guarantees on correctness and better numerical stability. The cost is dominated by solving the quadratic equation for extrema and evaluating the polynomial. Memory Complexity: Low for the isolation method. High for Sturm Series variant as the whole series is kept in memory. Measured Performance: For degree 9 (tri-cubic) polynomials, the method (referred to as "RF" or Regula Falsi in comparisons) shows relative execution time of 0.062-0.077 compared to Schwarze's 1.0, with low Mean Squared Error (0.003-0.016) and max error (0.66-1.0). Strengths: Correctness guarantees similar to Schwarze's method; better numerical stability than Neubauer's; well-suited for SIMD parallel implementation due to little branching and regular control flow. Limitations: Requires computing polynomial coefficients and extrema upfront. Numerical problems inherent to power form implementations can become more severe with more iterations if using Sturm Series variants. When to use: When high performance is required but correctness cannot be compromised, such as in real-time volume rendering of smooth iso-surfaces. When not to use: If the overhead of computing coefficients is prohibitive and lower precision is acceptable. The method was derived by Wald et al. in 2004 as a response to the trade-offs between existing ray-voxel intersection techniques. It aims to combine the speed of Neubauer's method with the correctness of Schwarze's method. The approach leverages the fact that repeated linear interpolation is fast and reliable if the start interval contains exactly one root, which is guaranteed by the prior extrema analysis. It is particularly effective for SIMD implementations, as demonstrated by Wald et al., who showed that modern SIMD instruction sets can significantly improve performance for this algorithm due to its data-parallel nature and lack of complex control flow. name: de Casteljau-based root finding
head: Root Finding: de Casteljau Subdivision (LR81), de Casteljau Subdivision
body: A root finding algorithm for polynomials in Bernstein form that isolates and refines the first intersection of a viewing ray with an isosurface by subdividing the control polygon using the de Casteljau algorithm at its intersection with the zero axis. It sets itself apart from knot insertion methods like [MR07] by offering quadratic convergence speed and constant memory usage without index operations, making it significantly faster for GPU architectures. Inputs and outputs: The method takes a polynomial P(t) in Bernstein basis of degree n defined by control points \mathbf{b}0, \dots, \mathbf{b}n, and an isovalue c. It solves f(t) = P(t) - c = 0 for t \in [0, 1]. The output is the parameter t corresponding to the first root. Data structures: The algorithm stores the Bernstein control polygon as a list or array of scalar values. It requires no auxiliary index arrays or dynamic memory, maintaining constant memory usage throughout execution. Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute the initial control polygon for f(t) = P(t) - c by subtracting the isovalue from each control point. 2. Iteration: Repeat the following subdivision step for a fixed number of iterations k (typically 3 to 7, depending on the interpolation type): a. Find the intersection of the current control polygon with the zero axis by locating the edge that crosses zero. b. Compute the parameter t{split} at this intersection using linear interpolation between the crossing control points. c. Apply the de Casteljau algorithm to subdivide the control polygon at t{split}. d. Select the left segment of the subdivided polygon to isolate the first root. e. Update the control polygon to this selected segment. 3. Result: After k iterations, the remaining control polygon is sufficiently small to approximate the root. Formulas: The de Casteljau algorithm for a parameter t and control points \mathbf{b}i^{(0)} = \mathbf{b}i computes: \mathbf{b}i^{(r)} = (1-t) \mathbf{b}{i-1}^{(r-1)} + t \mathbf{b}i^{(r-1)} for r=1, \dots, n and i=r, \dots, n. The left control points are \mathbf{b}0^{(r)} and the right control points are \mathbf{b}n^{(r)}. Parameters: Number of iterations k: 3 to 7. Edge cases and pitfalls: The method assumes the root is isolated or that the first root is sought. For isolated roots, simpler methods like regula falsi may be faster in the second phase, but the isolation step can cause branch divergence on GPUs. The Bernstein form offers a control polygon with a variation diminishing property. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decasteljaurootfinding(controlpoints, isovalue, numiterations): """ Find the root of P(t) - isovalue = 0 using de Casteljau subdivision. Args: controlpoints: List of control points for the polynomial P(t). isovalue: The isovalue c. numiterations: Number of subdivision iterations (3-7). Returns: t: Approximate root parameter. """ # Initialize control points for f(t) = P(t) - c cp = [p - isovalue for p in controlpoints] tstart, tend = 0.0, 1.0 n = len(cp) - 1 for in range(numiterations): # Find intersection of control polygon with zero axis tsplit = 0.5 # Fallback if no crossing found for i in range(n): if cp[i] cp[i+1] < 0: # Linear interpolation to find exact crossing parameter tsplit = (i + abs(cp[i]) / (abs(cp[i]) + abs(cp[i+1]))) / n break # Compute de Casteljau triangle to extract left control polygon leftcp = [cp[0]] b = list(cp) for r in range(1, n + 1): newb = [] for i in range(len(b) - 1): newb.append((1 - tsplit) b[i] + tsplit b[i+1]) b = newb leftcp.append(b[0]) # Update to the left segment (first root) cp = leftcp tend = tsplit return (tstart + tend) / 2 A root finding algorithm based on knot insertion with linear convergence speed and linear complexity per step. It requires index operations and memory usage grows with every iteration step, limiting the maximum number of iterations. For degree 9 (tri-cubic), it has a relative execution time of 1.0, MSE of 0.034, and max error of 0.85, making it more than 10 times slower than de Casteljau-based root finding. A root finding method using Regula Falsi combined with De Casteljau subdivision for root isolation. While the second phase (Regula Falsi) can outperform de Casteljau-based root finding for isolated roots, the isolation step is not well suited for CUDA due to diverging branches. Time Complexity: Quadratic complexity per step due to the de Casteljau algorithm. Convergence: Quadratic convergence speed. Memory: Constant memory usage, no index operations required. Performance: For degree 9 (tri-cubic), relative execution time is 0.076 (compared to MR07's 1.0), MSE is 0.003, and max error is 0.66. It is more than 10 times faster than the MR07 knot insertion algorithm. Strengths: Fast, constant memory, suitable for GPU (CUDA) due to lack of diverging branches and index operations. Limitations: Fixed number of iterations required; not optimal for isolated roots where simpler methods like Regula Falsi could be faster in the refinement phase. Originated from the work cited as [LR81] in the context of volume rendering using wavelet-based multiresolution isosurface rendering. It is used as a primary root finding method in GPU-based volume rendering pipelines due to its efficiency and suitability for parallel architectures. name: Marmitt's Ray-Cell Intersection
head: Cell Intersection, Isosurface Intersection (Neubauer iterative root finder), Isosurface Intersection via Neubauer Iterative Root Finder, Marmitt et al. 03 method, Marmitt et al. root finder, Neubauer iterative root finder, Ray-Isosurface Intersection
body: Marmitt's Ray-Cell Intersection computes the intersection point of a ray with an isosurface defined by trilinear interpolation inside a 3D voxel cell. It solves for the first positive root of the cubic polynomial derived from the cell's corner values using an iterative bisection refinement strategy. Compared to analytical cubic solvers like Schwarze’s method, this approach is slightly faster and yields single-precision, numerically stable results. It implements the Neubauer iterative root finder. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Isosurface value I{\text{iso}}. Eight scalar values v0, \dots, v7 at the corners of the 3D cell. Outputs: Intersection parameter t along the ray. If no root exists in [0, \infty), the method reports no intersection. Data Structures: The cell is defined by 8 scalar values. No additional geometric data structures are required beyond the corner values and the ray parameters. Algorithm Steps: 1. Cell Reconstruction: Reconstruct the cell from octree voxel data using forward neighbors. 2. Polynomial Formulation: Compute the cubic polynomial P(t) such that P(t) = 0 corresponds to the trilinear interpolation of the cell values equaling I{\text{iso}} along the ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. The coefficients are derived by substituting the ray equation into the trilinear basis functions. 3. Iterative Root Finding: Iteratively re-parameterize the ray into sub-intervals within the cell until a sign change is detected within the sub-interval and a root is found. 4. Hit Position: Evaluate the ray at the first positive root of the cubic polynomial to obtain the intersection point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def marmittraycellintersection(rayorigin, raydir, cornervalues, isovalue, tolerance=1e-6): """ rayorigin: (ox, oy, oz) raydir: (dx, dy, dz) cornervalues: list of 8 floats [v000, v100, v010, v110, v001, v101, v011, v111] isovalue: float tolerance: float, convergence threshold Returns: t (float) or None """ ox, oy, oz = rayorigin dx, dy, dz = raydir v000, v100, v010, v110, v001, v101, v011, v111 = cornervalues def evaluatetrilinear(t): x = ox + t dx y = oy + t dy z = oz + t dz val = (v000 (1 - x) (1 - y) (1 - z) + v100 x (1 - y) (1 - z) + v010 (1 - x) y (1 - z) + v110 x y (1 - z) + v001 (1 - x) (1 - y) z + v101 x (1 - y) z + v011 (1 - x) y z + v111 x y z) return val - isovalue tmin = 0.0 tmax = float('inf') pmin = evaluatetrilinear(tmin) while tmax - tmin > tolerance: tmid = (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 pmid = evaluatetrilinear(tmid) if pmin pmid < 0: tmax = tmid else: tmin = tmid pmin = pmid if tmax == float('inf'): tmax = tmin 2.0 + 1.0 pmax = evaluatetrilinear(tmax) if pmin pmax > 0: return None return (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Sign Change: If the polynomial does not change sign within the cell, there is no intersection. Precision: Single-precision arithmetic is used, which yields numerically stable results. Gradient Computation: Normals are computed using a forward-difference stencil on the same cell to avoid the high cost of neighbor-finding. Time Complexity: The root finding uses iterative bisection, converging logarithmically with precision. Each iteration evaluates the trilinear polynomial in constant time. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray, as no cell data needs to be stored per ray. Performance: Slightly faster than analytical cubic solvers. Strengths: Numerically stable in single precision. Simple to implement. Limitations: Iterative nature may be slower than a direct analytical solution if the solver is highly optimized, but the source claims it is faster. Requires cell reconstruction (neighbor finding) which is costly if not cached. The method is based on the Neubauer iterative root finder proposed by Marmitt et al.. It is described in the context of isosurface ray tracing of octree volumes. The approach was compared to Schwarze’s cubic solver used by Parker et al. and found to be faster and more stable in single precision.
