name: Fast Ray-Surface Intersection
head: Fast Intersection, Linear Interpolation Approximation for Ray-Surface Intersection
body: Fast Ray-Surface Intersection is an approximate method for determining the intersection point of a ray with an iso-surface within a volume rendering cell, trading geometric accuracy for computational speed. It solves the problem of finding the first-hit surface location without the high cost of inverting trilinear interpolation. Unlike exact intersection methods which compute all roots of the cubic polynomial derived from trilinear interpolation, this method subdivides the ray segment within the cell and uses linear interpolation to estimate the hit point, producing visually indistinguishable results in final renderings while being significantly faster. Inputs: Ray segment parameters: entry point R(t{in}) and exit point R(t{out}) of the ray within the current voxel/cell. Iso-value threshold \rho{iso}. Density field \rho(x,y,z), accessible via trilinear interpolation at arbitrary points. Outputs: Approximate intersection parameter t{hit} along the ray. Boolean flag indicating whether an intersection was found. Data Structures: Fields, sizes, and bit packing: Not given in the sources. The method operates on the scalar density values sampled at specific points along the ray. No complex data structures are required beyond the volume grid and the ray parameters. Steps: 1. Subdivision: Divide the complete path of the ray through the surface cell into two parts of equal length. Let the midpoint parameter be t{mid} = \frac{t{in} + t{out}}{2}. The two sub-segments are [t{in}, t{mid}] and [t{mid}, t{out}]. 2. Sampling: Calculate the density values at the end points of each part of the path. Specifically, evaluate \rho(t{in}), \rho(t{mid}), and \rho(t{out}). 3. Intersection Check: Determine if any iso-surface is intersected by the corresponding part of the ray based on the density values. An intersection exists in a segment [ta, tb] if the iso-value \rho{iso} lies between the density values at the endpoints. Mathematically, for a segment with endpoints ta and tb, an intersection is indicated if: (\rho(ta) - \rho{iso}) \cdot (\rho(tb) - \rho{iso}) \le 0. 4. Refinement: If an intersection exists, find an approximation of the intersection point by linear interpolation. If the intersection is in [t{in}, t{mid}], compute t{hit} based on \rho(t{in}) and \rho(t{mid}). If it is in [t{mid}, t{out}], compute t{hit} based on \rho(t{mid}) and \rho(t{out}). The linear interpolation formula is: t{hit} = ta + (\rho{iso} - \rho(ta)) \frac{tb - ta}{\rho(tb) - \rho(ta)} 5. Termination: Compute the color value and assign it to the pixel. If no intersection exists for a part, continue voxel traversal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastraysurfaceintersection(tin, tout, rhoiso, sampledensity): """ Approximates ray-surface intersection by subdividing the ray segment and using linear interpolation. Args: tin (float): t parameter at ray entry into the cell. tout (float): t parameter at ray exit from the cell. rhoiso (float): The density threshold for the iso-surface. sampledensity (callable): Function that returns density at a given t along the ray, i.e., sampledensity(t). Returns: float or None: The approximate t value of the intersection, or None if not found. """ # Step 1: Divide the path into two equal parts tmid = (tin + tout) / 2.0 # Step 2: Calculate density values at endpoints rhoin = sampledensity(tin) rhomid = sampledensity(tmid) rhoout = sampledensity(tout) # Helper for linear interpolation of t given two densities and their t values def linearinterpolate(t1, rho1, t2, rho2, targetrho): # Avoid division by zero if abs(rho1 - rho2) < 1e-9: return (t1 + t2) / 2.0 # Linear interpolation formula: t = t1 + (target - rho1) (t2 - t1) / (rho2 - rho1) return t1 + (targetrho - rho1) (t2 - t1) / (rho2 - rho1) # Step 3 & 4: Check first half [tin, tmid] if (rhoin - rhoiso) (rhomid - rhoiso) <= 0: thit = linearinterpolate(tin, rhoin, tmid, rhomid, rhoiso) return thit # Check second half [tmid, tout] if (rhomid - rhoiso) (rhoout - rhoiso) <= 0: thit = linearinterpolate(tmid, rhomid, tout, rhoout, rhoiso) return thit # Step 5: No intersection found in either part return None Parameters: Subdivision count: Fixed at 2 (one midpoint). Interpolation method: Linear. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Linear interpolation assumes the density function is linear within the sub-segment. The method produces visible differences in some pixels compared to exact intersection, but these are not visible in the final visualization results. Boundaries: If the ray grazes the iso-surface exactly at a sample point, the product term becomes zero, correctly identifying an intersection. Degenerate Input: If the density values at the endpoints are identical and equal to the iso-value, the interpolation denominator is zero. A simplistic approximate intersection method that assumes an intersection for every voxel where the iso-value is within the range of data values at the vertices. The intersection point is set to the midpoint between the ray's entry point (t{in}) and exit point (t{out}). This method is fast but leads to blocky artifacts of the size of voxels, so it is typically used only as a reference for performance comparisons rather than in production. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is O(1) per cell, requiring only 3 density samples and basic arithmetic operations. Memory complexity is O(1), requiring no additional storage beyond local variables. Measured Performance: The method is significantly faster than exact intersection methods which invert trilinear interpolation. Visual comparison shows that while there are pixel-level differences between fast and exact intersection, these differences are not visible in the final visualization results. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High speed, low computational overhead, visually acceptable results for many applications. Limitations: Lower geometric accuracy compared to exact methods; potential for small artifacts in high-frequency density regions. When to Use: Use when rendering speed is critical and the visual difference between exact and approximate intersection is imperceptible in the final image. Avoid when precise geometric accuracy is required, such as in scientific visualization where exact surface location is critical for measurement. The Fast Ray-Surface Intersection method was introduced as a faster alternative to exact ray-surface intersection techniques in the context of cell-based first-hit ray casting. Exact methods, such as those by Lin et al. and Parker et al., invert trilinear interpolation to find all points assigned a specific density value, which is computationally expensive. The fast intersection method trades this accuracy for speed by using linear interpolation on subdivided paths. It is part of the broader family of approximate ray-surface intersection techniques used in volume rendering to optimize performance. name: Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement
head: Linear Interpolation Root Finding for SDF, Secant Refinement
body: The Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement is an iterative root-finding algorithm used to refine the depth value d where a signed distance function (SDF) or occupancy logit crosses a threshold. It estimates the next intersection point using linear interpolation between two bracketing points. Inputs: ray0: Origin point of the ray (3D vector). ray\direction: Direction vector of the ray (normalized). d{low}: Array of lower bound depths (floats). d{high}: Array of upper bound depths (floats). f{low}: Array of function values at d{low} (floats). f{high}: Array of function values at d{high} (floats). n{secant\steps}: Number of refinement iterations (integer). decoder: Function evaluating the neural field. c: Camera parameters or context for the decoder. logit\tau: Threshold value for the occupancy logit. Outputs: d{pred}: Refined depth values where the root is estimated. Data Structures: Arrays d{low}, d{high}, f{low}, f{high}, d{pred} are parallel vectors of size N (number of rays), supporting batched processing. Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute the initial prediction d{pred} for all rays using linear interpolation between the bracketing points: d{pred} = - f{low} \cdot \frac{d{high} - d{low}}{f{high} - f{low}} + d{low} 2. Iteration: For each iteration i from 0 to n{secant\steps} - 1: a. Ray Casting: Compute the 3D point p{mid} for each ray: p{mid} = ray0 + d{pred} \cdot ray\direction b. Evaluation: Evaluate the function f{mid} at p{mid}. This involves calling the decoder with the point and context, subtracting the threshold, and disabling gradient tracking: f{mid} = decoder(p{mid}, c, only\occupancy=True) - logit\tau c. Bracket Update: Identify indices where f{mid} < 0 as ind{low}. If ind{low} contains any true values, update the lower bracket: d{low}[ind{low}] = d{pred}[ind{low}] f{low}[ind{low}] = f{mid}[ind{low}] Identify indices where f{mid} \ge 0 (i.e., ind{low} == 0). If these exist, update the upper bracket: d{high}[ind{low}==0] = d{pred}[ind{low}==0] f{high}[ind{low}==0] = f{mid}[ind{low}==0] d. Recalculation: Update d{pred} using the new bracketing values: d{pred} = - f{low} \cdot \frac{d{high} - d{low}}{f{high} - f{low}} + d{low} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def secantrefinement(ray0, raydirection, dlow, dhigh, flow, fhigh, nsecantsteps, decoder, c, logittau): """ Refine surface depth using the Secant Method. Args: ray0: List of (x, y, z) tuples, ray origins. raydirection: List of (dx, dy, dz) tuples, ray directions. dlow: List of floats, lower depth bounds. dhigh: List of floats, upper depth bounds. flow: List of floats, function values at dlow. fhigh: List of floats, function values at dhigh. nsecantsteps: int, number of iterations. decoder: Function(p, c, onlyoccupancy=True) -> float. c: Context/camera parameters. logittau: float, threshold. Returns: dpred: List of floats, refined depths. """ N = len(dlow) # Step 1: Initialize prediction denom = [fhigh[i] - flow[i] for i in range(N)] # Guard against zero denominator denom = [d if d != 0.0 else 1e-8 for d in denom] dpred = [-flow[i] ((dhigh[i] - dlow[i]) / denom[i]) + dlow[i] for i in range(N)] for in range(nsecantsteps): # Step 2a: Compute 3D points pmid = [(ray0[i][0] + dpred[i] raydirection[i][0], ray0[i][1] + dpred[i] raydirection[i][1], ray0[i][2] + dpred[i] raydirection[i][2]) for i in range(N)] # Step 2b: Evaluate function without gradients fmid = [decoder(pmid[i], c, onlyoccupancy=True) - logittau for i in range(N)] # Step 2c: Update brackets indlow = [i for i in range(N) if fmid[i] < 0] # Update lower bracket where fmid < 0 for i in indlow: dlow[i] = dpred[i] flow[i] = fmid[i] # Update upper bracket where fmid >= 0 indhigh = [i for i in range(N) if fmid[i] >= 0] for i in indhigh: dhigh[i] = dpred[i] fhigh[i] = fmid[i] # Step 2d: Recalculate prediction denom = [fhigh[i] - flow[i] for i in range(N)] denom = [d if d != 0.0 else 1e-8 for d in denom] dpred = [-flow[i] ((dhigh[i] - dlow[i]) / denom[i]) + dlow[i] for i in range(N)] return dpred Parameters: n{secant\steps}: Integer specifying the number of refinement iterations. Typical value: 8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If f{high} == f{low}, the denominator in the interpolation formula becomes zero. A small epsilon or fallback to bisection is required. Non-Bracketing: The method assumes f{low} < 0 and f{high} > 0 (or vice versa). If the initial segment does not bracket a root, the method may diverge or converge to a non-root extremum. A procedure to detect surface points along rays by evaluating a neural decoder at proposal points, identifying sign changes in occupancy logits, and refining the depth using the Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement. It sets itself apart from its siblings by combining coarse uniform sampling with a specific sign-change detection logic that identifies negative-to-positive transitions, followed by the Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement to pinpoint the zero-crossing. It builds on Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement. A root-finding algorithm combining linear interpolation and the midpoint algorithm. It finds the exact intersection point even if the field function is not continuous. Implementation is in IsoMesher::intersectxaxis(), IsoMesher::intersectyaxis(), and IsoMesher::intersectzaxis(). The algorithm used is determined by the preprocessor symbol FALSEPOSITION. It is no worse than the midpoint algorithm in terms of iterations and usually better, making it the preferred choice for finding exact intersection points. Time Complexity: O(n{secant\steps} \cdot N), where N is the number of rays. Each step involves a decoder evaluation and vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the bracketing arrays and intermediate points. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust for monotonic functions, no derivative calculation required. Limitations: Can fail if the function is not continuous or if the initial brackets do not contain a root. When to Use: When a fast, derivative-free root-finding method is needed for smooth implicit surfaces or neural fields. When Not to Use: When the function is discontinuous (use False Position or Bisection) or when high precision is required with minimal iterations (use Newton's method if derivatives are available). The Secant Method is a classical root-finding algorithm that approximates the derivative using finite differences. In the context of volume rendering and neural fields, it is used to refine the depth of surface intersections detected during ray marching. autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, https://github.com/autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching with Secant Refinement
body:
This method detects surface intersections along camera rays by evaluating a neural occupancy decoder at discrete proposal points, identifying sign changes in the occupancy logits, and refining the depth estimate using the secant method. It differs from standard uniform ray marching by adaptively focusing computation on rays containing a surface transition and using linear interpolation between bracketing points for higher precision than simple bisection. Inputs: ray0: Origin of rays, shape (B, N, 3). raydirection: Direction of rays, shape (B, N, 3). decoder: Neural network function decoder(p, c) returning occupancy logits, where p is position and c is context/latent code. c: Context/latent code, shape (B, N, Dc). depthrange: Tuple (d{min}, d{max}) defining the search interval. tau: Probability threshold for occupancy. nsteps: Tuple (n{min}, n{max}) for sampling the number of proposal steps. maxpoints: Integer limit for GPU memory management during decoder evaluation. checkcubeintersection: Boolean flag to intersect proposals with a unit cube. Outputs: dpred: Refined depth values, shape (B, N). ptpred: 3D surface points, shape (B, N, 3). Data Structures: dproposal: Tensor of shape (B, N, n{steps}, 1) containing linearly spaced depth values. val: Tensor of shape (B, N, n{steps}, 1) containing decoder(p, c) - logit	au. signmatrix: Tensor of shape (B, N, n{steps}) indicating sign changes. costmatrix: Tensor of shape (B, N, n{steps}) used for efficient argmin search. Steps: 1. Threshold Conversion: Convert the probability threshold 	au to a logit threshold: logit	au = 	ext{get\logits rom\prob}(	au) getlogitsfromprob is the inverse sigmoid function: \log( rac{	au}{1-	au}). 2. Sample Steps: Sample an integer n{steps} uniformly from the range [n{steps}[0], n{steps}[1]]. 3. Generate Proposals: Create linearly spaced depth proposals d{proposal} from depthange[0] to depthange[1] with n{steps} points, shaped (B, N, n{steps}, 1). 4. Cube Intersection (Optional): If checkcubeintersection is true, compute intersection with unit cube and replace d{proposal} values inside the cube with cube-intersection depths. 5. Compute Proposal Points: Calculate the 3D coordinates for all proposals: p{proposal} = ray0 + ray\direction \cdot d{proposal}. 6. Evaluate Decoder: Evaluate the decoder at all proposal points in parallel, splitting into chunks of size maxpoints / batchsize to manage GPU memory. Compute the value tensor: val = decoder(p, c, only\occupancy=True) - logit	au. 7. Initial Occupancy Mask: Create a mask for rays where the first proposal point is not occupied: mask\0
ot\occupied = val[:,:, 0] < 0. 8. Sign Change Detection: Compute the sign change matrix. For each adjacent pair of proposals, check if the product of their values is negative (indicating a sign change). Append a column of 1s to maintain dimensions: sign\matrix = [sign(val[:,:,:-1] \cdot val[:,:, 1:]), 1]. Compute a cost matrix to find the first sign change efficiently. The cost matrix weights earlier indices lower: cost\matrix = sign\matrix \cdot [n{steps}, n{steps}-1, \dots, 1]. 9. Find First Sign Change: Find the index of the minimum cost value for each ray: (values, indices) = argmin(cost\matrix). Identify valid sign changes (where the product was actually negative): mask\sign\change = values < 0. 10. Identify Transition Direction: Identify rays where the transition is from negative to positive (specifically where the lower bound is negative): mask
eg	o\pos = val[batch\indices, point\indices, indices] < 0. 11. Combine Masks: Combine all conditions to determine valid rays for refinement: mask = mask\sign\change \land mask
eg	o\pos \land mask\0
ot\occupied. 12. Extract Brackets: For valid rays, extract the bracketing depths and function values: Lower bracket: d{low} = d{proposal}[indices], f{low} = val[indices]. Upper bracket: d{high} = d{proposal}[indices + 1], f{high} = val[indices + 1]. Clamp indices to n{steps}-1 to prevent out-of-bounds access. 13. Refine Depth: Apply the Secant Method (or Bisection) on the masked rays using the extracted brackets (d{low}, f{low}) and (d{high}, f{high}) to compute the refined depth d{pred}. 14. Compute Final Points: Calculate the final 3D surface points for valid rays: pt{pred}[mask] = ray0{masked} + d{pred} \cdot ray\direction{masked}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def getlogitsfromprob(prob): """Inverse sigmoid.""" return math.log(prob / (1.0 - prob)) def raymarchingwithsecantrefinement(ray0, raydirection, decoder, c, depthrange, tau, nstepsrange, maxpoints, checkcubeintersection=False): """ ray0: (B, N, 3) raydirection: (B, N, 3) c: (B, N, Dc) Returns: dpred (B, N), ptpred (B, N, 3) """ B, N, = ray0.shape device = ray0.device # 1. Threshold Conversion logittau = getlogitsfromprob(tau) # 2. Sample Steps nsteps = random.randint(nstepsrange[0], nstepsrange[1]) # 3. Generate Proposals dproposal = [[[depthrange[0] + i (depthrange[1] - depthrange[0]) / (nsteps - 1)] for i in range(nsteps)] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] # 4. Cube Intersection if checkcubeintersection: # Sources do not provide cube intersection logic. pass # 5. Compute Proposal Points pproposal = [[[ray0[b][n][k] + raydirection[b][n][k] dproposal[b][n][s][0] for k in range(3)] for s in range(nsteps)] for n in range(N)] for b in range(B)] # 6. Evaluate Decoder (Chunked) val = [[[0.0] for in range(nsteps)] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] chunksize = maxpoints // B flatp = [p for b in pproposal for n in b for s in b[n] for p in s] flatc = [c for b in c for n in b for in range(nsteps)] for i in range(0, len(flatp), chunksize): chunkp = flatp[i:i+chunksize] chunkc = flatc[i:i+chunksize] chunkval = [decoder(p, c, onlyoccupancy=True) - logittau for p, c in zip(chunkp, chunkc)] for j, v in enumerate(chunkval): idx = i + j b, rem = divmod(idx, N nsteps) n, s = divmod(rem, nsteps) val[b][n][s] = [v] # 7. Initial Occupancy Mask mask0notoccupied = [[val[b][n][0][0] < 0 for n in range(N)] for b in range(B)] # 8. Sign Change Detection signmatrix = [[[0] nsteps for in range(N)] for in range(B)] for b in range(B): for n in range(N): for s in range(nsteps - 1): prod = val[b][n][s][0] val[b][n][s+1][0] signmatrix[b][n][s] = -1 if prod < 0 else 1 signmatrix[b][n][nsteps-1] = 1 weights = [nsteps - s for s in range(nsteps)] costmatrix = [[[signmatrix[b][n][s] weights[s] for s in range(nsteps)] for n in range(N)] for b in range(B)] # 9. Find First Sign Change indices = [[[0] nsteps for in range(N)] for in range(B)] values = [[[0.0] nsteps for in range(N)] for in range(B)] for b in range(B): for n in range(N): minval = math.inf minidx = 0 for s in range(nsteps): if costmatrix[b][n][s] < minval: minval = costmatrix[b][n][s] minidx = s values[b][n][0] = minval indices[b][n][0] = minidx masksignchange = [[values[b][n][0] < 0 for n in range(N)] for b in range(B)] # 10. Identify Transition Direction masknegtopos = [[val[b][n][indices[b][n][0]][0] < 0 for n in range(N)] for b in range(B)] # 11. Combine Masks mask = [[masksignchange[b][n] and masknegtopos[b][n] and mask0notoccupied[b][n] for n in range(N)] for b in range(B)] # 12. Extract Brackets dlow = [[[0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] flow = [[[0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] dhigh = [[[0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] fhigh = [[[0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] for b in range(B): for n in range(N): idx = indices[b][n][0] upperidx = min(idx + 1, nsteps - 1) dlow[b][n][0] = dproposal[b][n][idx][0] flow[b][n][0] = val[b][n][idx][0] dhigh[b][n][0] = dproposal[b][n][upperidx][0] fhigh[b][n][0] = val[b][n][upperidx][0] # 13. Refine Depth (Secant Method) dpred = [[[0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] for b in range(B): for n in range(N): denom = fhigh[b][n][0] - flow[b][n][0] if abs(denom) < 1e-8: denom = 1.0 dpred[b][n][0] = dhigh[b][n][0] - fhigh[b][n][0] (dhigh[b][n][0] - dlow[b][n][0]) / denom # 14. Compute Final Points ptpred = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(B)] for b in range(B): for n in range(N): if mask[b][n]: ptpred[b][n][0] = ray0[b][n][0] + dpred[b][n][0] raydirection[b][n][0] ptpred[b][n][1] = ray0[b][n][1] + dpred[b][n][0] raydirection[b][n][1] ptpred[b][n][2] = ray0[b][n][2] + dpred[b][n][0] raydirection[b][n][2] return dpred, ptpred Parameters: maxpoints: Integer, maximum number of points loaded to GPU memory per batch to prevent OOM. Typical value: 3,500,000. nsteps: Tuple of integers defining the range for sampling the number of evaluation steps. Typical value: [128, 129]. depthrange: Tuple of floats defining the range of possible depth values. Typical value: [0.0, 2.4]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: In the secant step, if f{high} \approx f{low}, the denominator becomes zero. A guard is required. Index Out of Bounds: When indices is the last step, indices + 1 may exceed bounds. Clamping to n{steps}-1 is required. No Sign Change: Rays that do not cross the threshold are masked out and return default values (e.g., zero or NaN depending on implementation). GPU Memory: Large batch sizes or high n{steps} can exceed VRAM. Chunking the decoder evaluation is necessary. This method implements a PyTorch Autograd Function that wraps the ray marching process, allowing gradients to flow through the depth prediction to the decoder parameters and latent code. Time Complexity: Dominated by the decoder evaluation O(B \cdot N \cdot n{steps}). The refinement step is O(B \cdot N). Memory Complexity: O(B \cdot N \cdot n{steps}) for storing proposals and values. Mitigated by chunking. Performance: Depends heavily on the decoder's inference speed and GPU memory bandwidth. Strengths: Adaptive sampling reduces unnecessary evaluations on empty space; secant refinement provides sub-pixel accuracy. Limitations: Requires sign changes to be detected; fails if the surface is not crossed within the proposal range or if the threshold is not crossed. This method is part of the Differentiable Volumetric Rendering pipeline, specifically used for extracting depth maps from neural implicit representations. autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, https://github.com/autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Differentiable Depth Function Forward/Backward Pass
head: DepthFunction.backward, DepthFunction.forward
body: This method implements a PyTorch Autograd Function that wraps the ray marching process, allowing gradients to flow through the depth prediction to the decoder parameters and latent code. Inputs: ray0: Ray origins, shape (N, 3). raydirection: Unit direction vectors, shape (N, 3). decoder: Neural network function f\phi(p, c) evaluating occupancy logits. c: Latent codes, shape (N, D). nsteps: Number of ray marching steps. nsecantsteps: Number of secant refinement steps. tau: Temperature parameter for soft thresholding. depthrange: Tuple (d{min}, d{max}) defining the search interval. method: String specifying the intersection/refinement method. checkcubeintersection: Boolean flag for boundary checks. maxpoints: Maximum number of points to store. gradoutput: Gradient from the loss function w.r.t. the output depth, shape (N, 1). Outputs: dpred: Predicted depth, shape (N, 1). ppred: Predicted 3D points, shape (N, 3). mask: Validity mask, shape (N, 1), where 1 indicates a valid surface hit and 0 indicates no hit. Data Structures: ppred: Tensor of shape (N, 3) storing the 3D coordinates of the estimated surface points. dpred: Tensor of shape (N, 1) storing the scalar depth values along the ray direction. mask: Boolean or float tensor of shape (N, 1) indicating successful ray-surface intersection. Forward Pass: 1. Call performraymarching with inputs ray0, raydirection, decoder, c, nsteps, nsecantsteps, tau, depthrange, method, checkcubeintersection, and maxpoints to obtain initial dpred, ppred, and mask. 2. Handle invalid depths by setting d{pred}[mask == 0] = \infty. 3. Handle cases where the first point is not occupied by setting d{pred}[mask\0\not\occupied == 0] = 0. 4. Save ray0, raydirection, dpred, ppred, c, and mask for use in the backward pass. Backward Pass: 1. Enable gradient computation for the saved points ppred. 2. Evaluate the decoder at the predicted points to get occupancy logits: fp = decoder(p{pred}, c, only\occupancy=True). 3. Compute the gradient of the occupancy logits with respect to the predicted points: grad\p = \frac{\partial fp}{\partial p{pred}}. 4. Compute the dot product of this gradient with the ray direction vector: grad\p\dot\v = \sum{dim=1}^{3} (grad\p{:, dim} \cdot ray\direction{:, dim}). 5. Clamp small gradients to avoid division by zero: if |grad\p\dot\v| < \epsilon, set grad\p\dot\v = \epsilon, where \epsilon = 10^{-3}. Set invalid mask gradients to 1. 6. Compute the output gradients with respect to the depth prediction: grad\outputs = - \frac{grad\output}{grad\p\dot\v} \cdot mask. 7. Compute the gradient with respect to the latent code c: grad\c = \frac{\partial fp}{\partial c} using the computed gradoutputs. 8. Compute the gradient with respect to the decoder parameters \phi: grad\\phi = \frac{\partial fp}{\partial \phi} using the computed gradoutputs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch class DepthFunction(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, ray0, raydirection, decoder, c, nsteps, nsecantsteps, tau, depthrange, method, checkcubeintersection, maxpoints, gradoutput): # The sources do not provide the implementation of performraymarching. # It is assumed to return dpred, ppred, mask based on the inputs. # dpred, ppred, mask = performraymarching(...) # Step 2: Set invalid depths to infinity dpred = torch.zeroslike(ray0[:,:1]) ppred = torch.zeroslike(ray0) mask = torch.oneslike(dpred) dpred[mask == 0] = float('inf') # Step 3: Set invalid depths to 0 if first point not occupied # mask0notoccupied is not defined in the sources; assumed available as a boolean tensor # dpred[mask0notoccupied == 0] = 0 # Step 4: Save for backward pass ctx.saveforbackward(ray0, raydirection, dpred, ppred, c, mask) ctx.gradoutput = gradoutput ctx.decoder = decoder return dpred, ppred, mask @staticmethod def backward(ctx, graddpred, gradppred, gradmask): ray0, raydirection, dpred, ppred, c, mask = ctx.savedtensors gradoutput = ctx.gradoutput decoder = ctx.decoder # Step 1: Enable gradient computation for ppred ppred.requiresgrad(True) # Step 2: Evaluate decoder fp = decoder(ppred, c, onlyoccupancy=True) # Step 3: Compute gradient of fp w.r.t ppred gradp = torch.autograd.grad(fp, ppred, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(fp), creategraph=True)[0] # Step 4: Compute dot product with ray direction gradpdotv = torch.sum(gradp raydirection, dim=1, keepdim=True) # Step 5: Clamp small gradients epsilon = 1e-3 gradpdotv = torch.where(torch.abs(gradpdotv) < epsilon, torch.fulllike(gradpdotv, epsilon), gradpdotv) # "Set invalid mask gradients to 1" is applied to the denominator for invalid points gradpdotv[mask == 0] = 1.0 # Step 6: Compute output gradients gradoutputs = - (gradoutput / gradpdotv) mask # Step 7: Compute gradient w.r.t latent code c gradc = torch.autograd.grad(fp, c, gradoutputs=gradoutputs, creategraph=True)[0] # Step 8: Compute gradient w.r.t decoder parameters phi # Decoder parameters are tracked by PyTorch autograd; gradients accumulate automatically. # The sources do not specify explicit parameter extraction. return None, None, None, gradc, None, None, None, None, None, None, None, None Not given in the sources. name: Bisection Method for Surface Depth Refinement
head: Bisection Method, Iterative Bisection, Midpoint (Bisection) Algorithm
body: The Bisection Method is an iterative root-finding algorithm used to refine the intersection position of a ray with an implicit surface within a specific segment identified by adaptive sampling. It serves as an alternative to the Secant method in ray marching pipelines, guaranteeing convergence by halving the search interval at each step. Unlike the Secant method, which uses linear interpolation between two points, the Bisection method relies solely on the sign of the field function evaluations to narrow the interval. The method refines the intersection point on a line segment (typically an edge of a voxel or a ray step) where the implicit field function changes sign. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two endpoints of the search interval, P{low} and P{high}, such that the field function f(P{low}) and f(P{high}) have opposite signs. A maximum number of iterations N (optional, for termination). Output: The refined intersection point P{intersect} where f(P{intersect}) \approx 0. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the algorithm operates on scalar values (field evaluations) and vector positions. Steps: 1. Calculate the midpoint P{mid} of the current interval [P{low}, P{high}]: P{mid} = \frac{P{low} + P{high}}{2} 2. Evaluate the implicit field function at the midpoint: f{mid} = f(P{mid}). 3. Check for convergence: If f{mid} = 0 (or |f{mid}| < \epsilon for some tolerance \epsilon), the intersection is found. If the maximum number of iterations has been reached, return P{mid} as the best estimate. 4. Update the interval: If f{mid} has the same sign as f{low} (i.e., f{mid} \cdot f{low} > 0), the root lies in the upper half. Set P{low} = P{mid} and f{low} = f{mid}. Otherwise, the root lies in the lower half. Set P{high} = P{mid} and f{high} = f{mid}. 5. Repeat from Step 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bisectionrefine(plow, phigh, fieldfunc, maxiter=10, tol=1e-6): """ Refine ray-surface intersection using the bisection method. Args: plow: Vector3, start of interval where field sign is negative (or opposite to phigh). phigh: Vector3, end of interval where field sign is positive (or opposite to plow). fieldfunc: Function taking a Vector3 and returning a float. maxiter: Integer, maximum number of bisection steps. tol: Float, convergence tolerance for |f(mid)|. Returns: Vector3, the refined intersection point. """ flow = fieldfunc(plow) fhigh = fieldfunc(phigh) # Ensure the interval brackets the root if flow fhigh > 0: raise ValueError("Field function values at endpoints must have opposite signs.") for in range(maxiter): pmid = (plow + phigh) / 2.0 fmid = fieldfunc(pmid) # Check for exact zero or tolerance if abs(fmid) < tol: return pmid # Update interval based on sign if fmid flow > 0: plow = pmid flow = fmid else: phigh = pmid fhigh = fmid return (plow + phigh) / 2.0 Parameters: maxiter: Not given in the sources. tol: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sign Error: The method requires that the initial interval [P{low}, P{high}] brackets the root (i.e., f(P{low}) \cdot f(P{high}) < 0). Multiple Roots: If multiple roots exist within the interval, the method finds one of them, depending on the initial bracketing. Flat Regions: If the field function is flat near the root (f'(x) \approx 0), convergence may be slow, but the method remains stable. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Guaranteed convergence; simple to implement; no derivative information required. Limitations: Slower convergence rate compared to interpolation-based methods; requires a bracketing interval. When to use it and when not: Use when guaranteed convergence is required and the field function is continuous; avoid when faster convergence is needed and the function is well-behaved. The Bisection Method is a classic root-finding algorithm. In the context of volume rendering and isosurface extraction, it is used as a refinement step after an initial coarse intersection is detected. It is often contrasted with the Secant method and the False Position method. The False Position method is described as a combination of linear interpolation and the midpoint algorithm, finding the exact intersection point even if the field function is not continuous, and is noted to be no worse than, and usually better than, the midpoint algorithm in terms of iteration count. The method is implemented in various isosurfacing libraries, such as IsoMesher, where it is selected via preprocessor symbols (e.g., BISECTION). It is also used in differentiable volumetric rendering pipelines, where it is called as an alternative to the Secant method for refining ray-surface intersections. Uses linear interpolation between two points to estimate the root. Faster convergence than bisection but not guaranteed to converge if the function is not well-behaved. Focuses on optimizing the initial intersection detection, often using spatial acceleration structures. An algorithm for determining the entry and exit points of a ray through a voxel grid, often used in conjunction with refinement methods. autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, https://github.com/autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Hexahedral Mesh Traversal (Bilinear Patch-Extension)
head: Bilinear Patch Traversal, Hex-H, Hybrid Hexahedral Traversal
body: This method is a hybrid traversal algorithm for hexahedral meshes that combines Plücker-based face selection with bilinear patch intersection tests. It solves the problem of geometric singularities and discontinuities inherent in pure Plücker traversal by utilizing the parametric coordinates (u, v) derived from bilinear patch intersections to compute interpolated scalar values directly. It sets itself apart from the parent Hexahedral Mesh Traversal (Plücker Space) by avoiding the need to decompose exit faces into triangles for interpolation, thereby eliminating discontinuities at face boundaries. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, hexahedron vertices \mathbf{v}0 \dots \mathbf{v}7. Outputs: Exit face index, parametric coordinates (u, v) on the exit face, and interpolated scalar values at entry and exit points. Data Structures: Vertices: Array of 8 3D vectors. Plücker Values: Three scalar areas A0, A1, A2 derived from cross products. Bilinear Patch Parameters: u, v \in \mathbb{R}. Steps: 1. Plücker Face Selection: Compute the Plücker values for the lines \mathbf{v}4 \to \mathbf{v}5, \mathbf{v}6 \to \mathbf{v}7, and the ray. Determine the three areas A0, A1, A2. This identifies the three candidate exit faces. 2. Bilinear Patch Intersection: For each of the three candidate exit faces, perform a bilinear patch intersection test. A bilinear patch is defined by four vertices. The intersection is valid if the resulting parametric coordinates (u, v) lie within the unit square [0, 1]^2. 3. Exit Determination: Stop as soon as a patch is hit, i.e., when (u, v) \in [0, 1]^2. This provides the exit face and the parametric coordinates (u, v) for the exit point. 4. Numerical Consistency Check: If numerical inconsistencies occur due to insufficient floating-point accuracy (e.g., (u, v) slightly outside [0, 1]^2 due to holes in the implicit edge representation), perform two additional Plücker tests equivalent to the second step of the pure Plücker method to resolve the correct exit face. 5. Interpolation: Use the known parametric coordinates (u, v) from the bilinear patch test to compute interpolated scalar values on the entry and exit faces. This avoids discontinuities associated with triangle-based interpolation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversehexahedronbilinear(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices): # Step 1: Compute Plücker areas for candidate faces # Lines: v4->v5, v6->v7, and ray # A0, A1, A2 are computed based on cross products of edge vectors and ray A0, A1, A2 = computepluckerareas(hexvertices, raydirection) # Identify candidate faces based on signs of A0, A1, A2 candidatefaces = getcandidatefaces(A0, A1, A2) exitface = None u, v = 0.0, 0.0 # Step 2 & 3: Check bilinear patch intersection for each candidate for face in candidatefaces: # Perform bilinear patch intersection test # Returns (hit, u, v) hit, u, v = bilinearpatchintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, face.vertices) if hit and 0.0 <= u <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= v <= 1.0: exitface = face break # Step 4: Handle numerical inconsistencies if exitface is None: # Perform two additional Plücker tests (pure Plücker fallback) exitface = resolvewithpluckerfallback(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices) # Note: Parametric coordinates (u,v) may need recomputation or approximation # if the fallback does not provide them directly. # If fallback does not yield (u,v), compute them via projection onto the face plane. # Step 5: Interpolation # Compute scalar at entry point (previous cell exit or ray origin) # Compute scalar at exit point using u, v on exitface scalarexit = interpolatescalarbilinear(exitface.vertices, u, v) return exitface, u, v, scalarexit def bilinearpatchintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, vertices): # Vertices: p0, p1, p2, p3 in counter-clockwise order # Bilinear surface: S(u,v) = (1-u)(1-v)p0 + u(1-v)p1 + uvp2 + (1-u)vp3 # Solve for u, v such that rayorigin + t raydirection = S(u,v) # This requires solving a system of equations. # Standard approach: Project ray onto plane of patch, solve for u,v, # then verify if point lies on the bilinear surface (check if t is consistent). # Or use iterative solver for the non-linear system. # For implementation simplicity, we assume a robust solver exists. u, v, t = solvebilinearrayintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, vertices) if t > 0: return True, u, v return False, 0.0, 0.0 Parameters: Floating-point precision: Standard double precision is recommended to minimize numerical inconsistencies. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes in Hexahedron: Bilinear patches are generally not flat, introducing holes in the hexahedron because the implicit edge representation depends on all four face vertices, unlike Plücker coordinates which depend solely on two edge points. This can cause rays to miss the exit face or produce invalid (u, v) coordinates. Numerical Inconsistencies: Insufficient floating-point accuracy can lead to incorrect face selection. The method requires a fallback to Plücker tests in these cases. Discontinuities: Pure Plücker traversal requires triangle decomposition, leading to discontinuities at face boundaries. This method avoids that by using bilinear patches. A method to calculate normals for hexahedral meshes using trilinear interpolation of vertex normals, converted from computational space to physical space via the Jacobian matrix. It is chosen when accurate shading is required for curvilinear hexahedral meshes. It differs from scalar interpolation by operating on vector fields and requiring Jacobian transformation. Steps: 1. Interpolate a vector at the entry and exit faces using the same parametric coordinates (u, v) used for scalar interpolation. 2. Perform a linear interpolation between the two interpolated vectors based on their distance to the isosurface to yield the final normal. 3. Calculate three vectors in physical space corresponding to the normal in computational space Nc and convert them to physical space Np using the Jacobian matrix. Formulas: Convert physical coordinates xi to computational coordinates \tilde{\rho}j using the Jacobian matrix J{ij}: xi = J{ij} \tilde{\rho}j J{ij} = \frac{\partial xi}{\partial \tilde{\rho}j} Approximate the Jacobian matrix J{ij} for a grid node n using central differences: J{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{xi(n) - xi(n-1)}{\tilde{\rho}j(n) - \tilde{\rho}j(n+1)} + \frac{xi(n+1) - xi(n)}{\tilde{\rho}j(n+1) - \tilde{\rho}j(n)} \right) A linear combination of the three vectors with the normal in computational space Nc results in the converted normal Np. Time Complexity: Raw traversal performance is 15% lower compared to the pure Plücker traverser due to the cost of bilinear patch intersection tests. However, overall performance gains 25% on average because time is saved in interpolation (no triangle decomposition needed). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The hybrid algorithm processes up to 4.5 million hexahedra per second on a Dual-core Opteron 2 GHz. Strengths: Better quality and significantly faster overall performance than the pure Plücker approach for hexahedral meshes due to avoided discontinuities and efficient interpolation. Limitations: Raw traversal is slower; numerical inconsistencies may require fallback tests, though this is rare. When to Use: Recommended for traversing curvilinear grids on a ray tracing basis, especially when high-quality rendering and continuous interpolation are prioritized over raw traversal speed. Originated in the paper "Fast Ray Traversal of Tetrahedral and Hexahedral Meshes for Direct Volume Rendering" (2006) by Ramsey et al.. The method was developed to address singularities and discontinuities in hexahedral mesh traversal for direct volume rendering. It builds on the Plücker-based traversal method but integrates bilinear patch tests to improve interpolation quality. name: Interval Arithmetic Inclusion Strategies
head: InclusionFunction strategies
body: Interval Arithmetic Inclusion Strategies compute conservative bounds on an implicit function f over a spatial domain, enabling the bisection trace to prune intervals that cannot contain the zero-level set. They distinguish themselves from sibling methods by providing a configurable trade-off between generality (black-box compatibility) and bound tightness (performance/accuracy), spanning sampling-based estimates to analytic arithmetic. Every strategy constructs a conservative interval f = [f-, f+] guaranteeing that f(\mathbf{x}) \in [f-, f+] for all \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{B}. This bound is used to determine if the zero-level set (isosurface) can exist within the box \mathcal{B}. If 0 \notin [f-, f+], the box is pruned. The strategies generally rely on a Lipschitz constant \lambda or symbolic derivatives to bound the function's rate of change. SamplingInclusion requires only point evaluations and relies on \lambda to bound variation over the box diameter. GradientInclusion improves tightness by incorporating \nabla f directly. NaturalIntervalInclusion and AffineInclusion operate on the symbolic formula of f to produce progressively tighter bounds without sampling. Computes a conservative upper bound \lambda on the rate of change of f over a 3D bounding box. Choose this when you need a scalar bound for gradient-based or sampling-based inclusion, particularly for black-box functions where analytical gradients are unavailable. Computes valid, conservative bounds for a scalar field along a ray using first-order linear approximations. It sets itself apart by using linear bounds rather than quadratic ones, prioritizing computational simplicity. Choose this for basic sphere tracing or when gradient access is limited to local estimates. The approach formalizes robust iso-surface rendering via interval-arithmetic bisection for arbitrary implicit geometries, primarily targeting black-box functions where only point evaluations are available. The isoray library implements four distinct strategies: SamplingInclusion, GradientInclusion, NaturalIntervalInclusion, and AffineInclusion. These strategies were developed to guarantee no surface features are missed (e.g., thin shells, cusps, high-frequency surfaces) while optimizing performance through tighter bounds when analytic formulas are known. When only point evaluations are available, SamplingInclusion or GradientInclusion must be used, as the analytic strategies require symbolic formula access. name: Lipschitz Constant Estimation
body:
Lipschitz Constant Estimation computes a conservative upper bound \lambda on the rate of change of an implicit function f over a 3D bounding box \mathcal{B}. This constant bounds the function's variation over the box diameter, allowing interval inclusion strategies to prune boxes where the zero-level set cannot exist. It differs from symbolic strategies by relying on numerical gradient sampling, making it applicable to black-box implicit functions where analytical gradients are unavailable. Inputs: Implicit function f: \mathbb{R}^3 ightarrow \mathbb{R}. Bounding box \mathcal{B} defined by center \mathbf{c} and half-extents \mathbf{r}. Sampling configuration (number of points N, step size h). Not given in the sources. Outputs: Lipschitz constant \lambda \in \mathbb{R}^+. Data Structures: Sample points \{\mathbf{x}i\}{i=1}^N uniformly distributed within \mathcal{B}. Gradient estimates 
abla f(\mathbf{x}i). Steps: 1. Sample Domain: Generate N points uniformly distributed within \mathcal{B}. 2. Estimate Gradients: For each \mathbf{x}i, compute 
abla f(\mathbf{x}i) using centered differences with step h: 
abla f(\mathbf{x}i) \approx \left[  rac{f(\mathbf{x}i + h\mathbf{e}1) - f(\mathbf{x}i - h\mathbf{e}1)}{2h},  rac{f(\mathbf{x}i + h\mathbf{e}2) - f(\mathbf{x}i - h\mathbf{e}2)}{2h},  rac{f(\mathbf{x}i + h\mathbf{e}3) - f(\mathbf{x}i - h\mathbf{e}3)}{2h} ight], where \mathbf{e}k are unit basis vectors. 3. Compute Norms: Calculate the Euclidean norm of each gradient: gi = \|
abla f(\mathbf{x}i)\|2. 4. Determine Constant: Set \lambda = \maxi gi. Formulas: The theoretical Lipschitz constant is defined as Lip(f) = \max{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}}  rac{|f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{y})|}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|}. In practice, \lambda is approximated by the maximum observed gradient magnitude over the sample set. Parameters: lipschitz: Can be a float value or the string "auto". If "auto", the constant is estimated automatically using the sampling method. N, h: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Finite difference gradients are sensitive to h; too small h introduces numerical noise, while too large h underestimates local curvature. Boundaries: Samples near the boundary of \mathcal{B} may require gradient evaluations outside the box; clamping or reflection may be needed to prevent out-of-bounds access. Degenerate Input: If f is constant, \lambda = 0. Non-Lipschitz functions with unbounded gradients require regularization or will produce excessively large estimates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def estimatelipschitz(f, boxcenter, boxhalfextents, numsamples=100, h=1e-4): """ Estimate the Lipschitz constant for implicit function f over a bounding box. Args: f: Implicit function f(x: np.ndarray) -> float boxcenter: np.ndarray of shape (3,), center of the bounding box boxhalfextents: np.ndarray of shape (3,), half-extents of the bounding box numsamples: int, number of random samples to take h: float, step size for finite differences Returns: float: Estimated Lipschitz constant lambda """ import numpy as np # 1. Sample points uniformly within the bounding box randompoints = np.random.rand(numsamples, 3) samples = boxcenter + (randompoints - 0.5) (2.0 boxhalfextents) maxgradientnorm = 0.0 basisvectors = np.eye(3) # 2. Estimate gradients and compute norms for i in range(numsamples): x = samples[i] gradient = np.zeros(3) for j in range(3): # Centered difference for each dimension xplus = x + h basisvectors[j] xminus = x - h basisvectors[j] # Evaluate function fplus = f(xplus) fminus = f(xminus) gradient[j] = (fplus - fminus) / (2.0 h) # Compute Euclidean norm gradnorm = np.linalg.norm(gradient) # Update maximum if gradnorm > maxgradientnorm: maxgradientnorm = gradnorm return maxgradientnorm Time Complexity: O(N \cdot d) where d=3, requiring 2d function evaluations per sample. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store sample points and gradients. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Black-box compatible; requires only point evaluations. Limitations: The estimate is an approximation and may not be tight, leading to less aggressive pruning than symbolic methods. Insufficient samples may underestimate \lambda, causing incorrect pruning or missed intersections. When to Use: When analytical derivatives are unavailable or too complex to derive. When Not to Use: When tight bounds are critical for performance and symbolic derivatives are available. In volume rendering, Lipschitz continuity is used in sphere tracing to determine safe step sizes along rays. The specific application to interval arithmetic inclusion strategies for implicit surface rendering is described in recent works on robust iso-surface rendering. name: Forward Linear Inclusion Function
head: Linear Bounding Function, Linear Inclusion Function
body: The Forward Linear Inclusion Function computes a conservative interval bound for a scalar field f along a ray, ensuring that the true function value lies within the calculated bounds for all points ahead of the current sample. It solves the problem of determining a safe maximum step size for sphere tracing by intersecting these linear bounds with the zero-level threshold. Inputs and Outputs Input: The current sample location on the ray t0, the function value at that location f(t0), and the Lipschitz constant \lambda for the function f. Output: An interval f = [f-(t), f+(t)] for t > t0, and the computed step size \Delta t to the next safe sample point. Data Structures The method requires no complex data structures; it operates on scalar values for t0, f(t0), and \lambda. Steps 1. Evaluate Function: Compute the scalar field value v = f(t0) at the current ray position t0. 2. Define Bounds: Construct the lower bound f-(t) and upper bound f+(t) as linear functions starting from v at t0. The slope of the upper bound is \lambda and the lower bound is -\lambda. f-(t) = f(t0) - \lambda(t - t0) f+(t) = f(t0) + \lambda(t - t0) This forms a bounding cone originating at (t0, f(t0)). 3. Compute Step Size: Determine the distance to the zero-level set by finding the intersection of the bounding lines with the threshold. Since the bounds are symmetric around f(t0), the step size is determined by the magnitude of the function value divided by the Lipschitz constant: \Delta t = \frac{|f(t0)|}{\lambda} If f(t0) = 0, the surface is hit exactly, and \Delta t = 0. 4. Advance Ray: Update the ray position to t{\text{new}} = t0 + \Delta t. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forwardlinearinclusionstep(f, t0, lambdaval): """ Computes the next step size for sphere tracing using forward linear inclusion. Args: f: A callable that evaluates the scalar field f(t) at position t. t0: The current position on the ray (scalar). lambdaval: The Lipschitz constant for f (scalar, >= 0). Returns: deltat: The safe step size to advance along the ray. """ # Evaluate the scalar field at the current position ft0 = f(t0) # Handle exact hit if ft0 == 0.0: return 0.0 # Compute step size: distance to zero crossing of the linear bound # The bound is f(t0) +/- lambda (t - t0) # Intersection with 0: 0 = f(t0) + lambda (t - t0) => t - t0 = -f(t0)/lambda # We take the absolute value for the forward step size deltat = abs(ft0) / lambdaval return deltat Parameters \lambda: The Lipschitz constant, which must be an upper bound on the magnitude of the gradient of f (\|\nabla f\| \leq \lambda). Typical values depend on the specific noise or implicit function being rendered. If \lambda is too small, the bound is invalid and the ray may tunnel through the surface. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Lipschitz Constant: If \lambda = 0 and f(t0) \neq 0, division by zero occurs. Implementers should check for \lambda < \epsilon and handle it as an error or infinite step. Inaccurate Lipschitz Constant: The method assumes \lambda is a valid global or local Lipschitz constant. If the actual gradient exceeds \lambda, the inclusion property is violated, leading to visual artifacts (tunneling). Precision: For very small |f(t0)|, floating-point precision errors in the division may result in tiny step sizes. A minimum step size threshold may be applied to prevent infinite loops in flat regions. Uses second-order Taylor expansion to provide tighter bounds for functions with significant curvature, switching to linear bounds when the quadratic derivative exceeds the first-order limit. Choose this when the scalar field has high curvature and \lambda is large relative to the second derivative, allowing for larger steps than the linear method. Time and Memory Complexity Time: O(1) per step. The calculation involves one function evaluation, one absolute value, and one division. Memory: O(1). No additional memory is required beyond the scalar values. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, and provides a rigorous guarantee of no tunneling if \lambda is valid. Limitations: The bounds are often loose for functions with high curvature, leading to smaller step sizes than necessary. It does not account for the second derivative of the function. When to Use Use when computational resources are limited or when the scalar field is relatively linear over the step size. It is also useful as a fallback or comparison baseline for more complex inclusion functions. The concept of forward inclusion functions was formalized in the context of sphere tracing for procedural volumetric noise. The specific formulation of the forward linear inclusion function is attributed to [AZ23] as cited in. It builds upon the general theory of interval arithmetic and Lipschitz continuity applied to ray marching. name: Improved Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Function
head: Hybrid quadratic-linear bound, Improved Quad. Bounds, Improved Quadratic Taylor
body: The Improved Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Function is a method for computing tighter, valid bounds on a scalar field function f(t) along a ray, used to determine safe step sizes in sphere tracing. It solves the problem where standard quadratic bounds violate the first-order Lipschitz constraint, causing the bound to grow too fast and result in smaller, inefficient step sizes than linear bounds. It sets itself apart by enforcing both first-order (\lambda) and second-order (\gamma) Lipschitz constraints simultaneously, switching to a linear bound when the quadratic derivative exceeds the first-order limit. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current ray parameter t0, function value f(t0), first derivative f'(t0), first-order Lipschitz constant \lambda, second-order Lipschitz constant \gamma. Output: Inclusion function f{\pm}(t) providing lower (f-) and upper (f+) bounds for t > t0. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the method relies on scalar arithmetic operations. Formulas: The improved inclusion function f{\pm}(t) is defined piecewise using a quadratic component q{\pm}(t) and a switch point t{\pm}: q{\pm}(t) = f(t0) + (t - t0) \cdot \left( f'(t0) \pm \frac{1}{2}\gamma(t - t0) \right) t{\pm} = t0 + \frac{\pm\lambda - f'(t0)}{\pm\gamma} The final bound is: f{\pm}(t) = \begin{cases} q{\pm}(t) & \forall t \in [t0, t{\pm}] \\ q{\pm}(t{\pm}) \pm \lambda \cdot (t - t{\pm}) & \forall t > t{\pm} \end{cases} Parameters: \lambda: First-order Lipschitz constant. \gamma: Second-order Lipschitz constant. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def improvedquadraticinclusion(t0, ft0, fprimet0, lambdaval, gammaval): """ Computes the improved quadratic inclusion bounds for t > t0. Args: t0: Current ray parameter. ft0: Function value at t0. fprimet0: First derivative at t0. lambdaval: First-order Lipschitz constant. gammaval: Second-order Lipschitz constant. Returns: A function that takes t and returns (lowerbound, upperbound). """ # Calculate switch points for upper and lower bounds # tplus = t0 + (lambda - fprime) / gamma # tminus = t0 + (-lambda - fprime) / (-gamma) = t0 + (lambda + fprime) / gamma tplus = t0 + (lambdaval - fprimet0) / gammaval tminus = t0 + (lambdaval + fprimet0) / gammaval def bound(t): if t <= t0: return ft0, ft0 # Calculate quadratic components # qplus(t) = f(t0) + (t - t0) (f'(t0) + 0.5 gamma (t - t0)) # qminus(t) = f(t0) + (t - t0) (f'(t0) - 0.5 gamma (t - t0)) dt = t - t0 qplus = ft0 + dt (fprimet0 + 0.5 gammaval dt) qminus = ft0 + dt (fprimet0 - 0.5 gammaval dt) # Determine if we are past the switch point for upper bound if t > tplus: # Switch to linear bound # fplus(t) = qplus(tplus) + lambda (t - tplus) dtswitch = tplus - t0 qplusatswitch = ft0 + dtswitch (fprimet0 + 0.5 gammaval dtswitch) upper = qplusatswitch + lambdaval (t - tplus) else: upper = qplus # Determine if we are past the switch point for lower bound if t > tminus: # Switch to linear bound # fminus(t) = qminus(tminus) - lambda (t - tminus) dtswitch = tminus - t0 qminusatswitch = ft0 + dtswitch (fprimet0 - 0.5 gammaval dtswitch) lower = qminusatswitch - lambdaval (t - tminus) else: lower = qminus return lower, upper return bound Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Standard quadratic bounds that do not enforce the first-order Lipschitz constraint, potentially leading to loose bounds. Use when \gamma is small and \lambda is not a limiting factor. Time and Memory Complexity: The computational cost is the same as regular quadratic inclusion functions. Measured Performance: On the Sponge scene with all enhancements (SS, ES+1): Both Regular Quad and Improved Quad achieve 70.0 avg steps, 651.1 avg octaves, and 16.3 ms time, providing a \times 4.0 speedup vs Linear. On Sponge (far) scene with all enhancements (SS, ES+1): Regular Quad has 55.8 avg steps, 300.6 avg octaves, 9.8 ms time. Improved Quad has 55.8 avg steps, 300.6 avg octaves, 9.7 ms time. Both provide a \times 1.7 speedup vs Linear. Without enhancements, improved quadratic bounds allow \times 1.2 and \times 1.1 reduction in steps compared to naive methods, beating linear and regular quadratic bounds, but are slightly slower than linear bounds due to gradient computation overhead. When used with enhancements (Adaptive \gammaFn), the improved quadratic bound gives results similar to regular quadratic bounds, with performance gains too small to appear in tables. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Prevents the quadratic term from growing too fast by enforcing the first-order Lipschitz constraint, yielding bigger step sizes than regular quadratic bounds when the derivative would otherwise exceed \lambda. Limitations: Requires gradient computation, making it slightly slower than linear bounds in naive contexts. When to Use: Use when tighter bounds than linear are needed and the second-order Lipschitz constant \gamma is available, especially when regular quadratic bounds might violate the first-order constraint. The Improved Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Function was proposed to address the suboptimal performance of regular quadratic inclusion functions, which can perform worse than linear bounds because their derivative can exceed the first-order Lipschitz constant \lambda. name: Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Functions
head: 2nd order Taylor bounds, Naive Quadratic Bounds, Quadratic bounds, Regular Quad. Bounds, Regular Quadratic Taylor Bounds
body: Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Functions (QTIF) are a method for adapting step size in sphere tracing by using quadratic forward inclusion bounds instead of linear ones, explicitly taking the ray direction into account. They require the function derivative to be computable on the fly and Lipschitz continuous. Without enhancements, they often perform worse than linear bounds due to the overhead of computing gradients and the exponential growth of the second-order Lipschitz constant in fractal Brownian motion (FBM). Inputs: Current position along the ray, t0. Function value at current position, Fn(t0). First derivative (gradient in ray direction) at current position, Fn'(t0). Second-order Lipschitz constant for the function sum, \gamma{Fn}. Target isosurface value (typically 0 or v). Outputs: Maximum safe step size \Delta t such that the inclusion function does not cross the isosurface threshold within the step. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard scalar values for t0, Fn(t0), Fn'(t0), and \gamma{Fn}. \gamma{Fn} is computed as the sum of individual second-order Lipschitz constants of the constituent functions (octaves). Formulas: The forward quadratic Taylor inclusion function for a sum of functions Fn from position t0 is defined as: Fn = Fn(t0) + (t - t0) \left( Fn'(t0) \pm \frac{1}{2} \gamma{Fn} \cdot (t - t0) \right) Where: t is the candidate position along the ray. Fn(t0) is the value of the implicit function at the current step. Fn'(t0) is the derivative of the function in the ray direction at t0, calculated as \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla f(\boldsymbol{\delta}(t0)), where \mathbf{u} is the ray direction and \nabla f is the spatial gradient. \gamma{Fn} is the second-order Lipschitz constant of the sum Fn. For a sum of n functions fm, it is the sum of their individual constants: \gamma{Fn} = \sum{m=1}^n \gamma{fm}. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Compute Gradient: Calculate the first derivative Fn'(t0) by evaluating the gradient of the implicit function at the current position t0 and projecting it onto the ray direction \mathbf{u}. 2. Compute Lipschitz Constant: Determine \gamma{Fn} by summing the second-order Lipschitz constants of the active octaves. 3. Solve for Intersection: Find the smallest positive t > t0 where the inclusion function Fn intersects the target isosurface value V{target} (usually 0). The equation to solve is: V{target} = Fn(t0) + (t - t0) \left( Fn'(t0) \pm \frac{1}{2} \gamma{Fn} (t - t0) \right) Let \Delta t = t - t0. This is a quadratic equation in \Delta t: \frac{1}{2} \gamma{Fn} (\Delta t)^2 + Fn'(t0) \Delta t + (Fn(t0) - V{target}) = 0 The \pm in the inclusion function creates two bounds; the safe step size is determined by the bound that prevents crossing the surface. 4. Update Position: Set t{new} = t0 + \Delta t. 5. Sub-stepping (Optional/Advanced): If using sub-steps to improve accuracy or handle BVH levels, estimate the derivative at the new location t0 + \Delta t using the worst-case scenario for the derivative change: F'i(t0 + \Delta t) = F'i(t0) + (\gammai \cdot \Delta t) Then add the next derivative term f'{i+1}(t0 + \Delta t) to compute the new quadratic bound for the next sub-step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def quadratictaylorstep(t0, Fnt0, Fnprimet0, gammaFn, targetvalue): """ Computes the maximum safe step size using Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Functions. Args: t0: Current position along the ray. Fnt0: Value of the implicit function at t0. Fnprimet0: Derivative of the function in ray direction at t0. gammaFn: Second-order Lipschitz constant for the function sum. targetvalue: The isosurface value (e.g., 0). Returns: deltat: The maximum safe step size. """ # Coefficients for the quadratic equation: a(dt^2) + bdt + c = 0 # Derived from: target = F(t0) + dt (F'(t0) + 0.5 gamma dt) # Rearranged: 0.5 gamma dt^2 + F'(t0) dt + (F(t0) - target) = 0 a = 0.5 gammaFn b = Fnprimet0 c = Fnt0 - targetvalue # Handle degenerate case where gamma is 0 (linear behavior) if a == 0: if b == 0: # Function is constant, no root found or infinite roots. return 1e-6 else: # Linear case: bdt + c = 0 dt = -c / b return dt if dt > 0 else 1e-6 # Solve quadratic equation discriminant = b2 - 4 a c if discriminant < 0: # No real roots. The inclusion function does not cross the target. return 1e6 sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) # We want the smallest positive root # Roots are (-b +/- sqrtdisc) / (2a) root1 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) root2 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) # Select the smallest positive root candidates = [] if root1 > 1e-9: candidates.append(root1) if root2 > 1e-9: candidates.append(root2) if not candidates: # No positive root found. return 1e6 return min(candidates) Parameters: \gamma{Fn}: Must be pre-computed or estimated. For FBM, this grows exponentially with the number of octaves n (\gamma{noise} \cdot (2^n - 1)). Target Value: Typically 0 for distance fields, or v for other implicit surfaces. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Exponential Growth of \gamma: For Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM), \gamma{Fn} grows exponentially with the number of octaves n. This makes the quadratic term \frac{1}{2} \gamma{Fn} (t-t0)^2 dominate quickly, leading to very small step sizes and poor performance. Gradient Cost: Requires computing f'(t) (the gradient projected on the ray) at each step, which is more expensive than just evaluating f(t). Lipschitz Continuity: Requires f'(t) to be Lipschitz continuous. If the derivative is not Lipschitz continuous, the bound is invalid. Performance: Without enhancements (like BVH or improved bounds), regular quadratic bounds result in worse step sizes (more steps) and added overhead, causing slowdowns (e.g., \times 0.6 and \times 0.4 on test scenes) compared to linear bounds. An improved inclusion function that enforces constraints from both first-order (\lambda) and second-order (\gamma) Lipschitz constants. It behaves as a regular quadratic bound as long as its derivative is within [-\lambda, \lambda], switching to a linear bound otherwise to prevent the quadratic term from growing too fast and providing loose bounds. Link A simpler inclusion function using only the first derivative and a first-order Lipschitz constant. It is less accurate for curved surfaces but cheaper to compute and does not suffer from the exponential \gamma growth in the same way. Link Time Complexity: O(1) per step for the bound calculation itself, but requires computing the gradient Fn'(t0), which is O(n) for n octaves if computed naively, or optimized via BVH. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per step. Measured Performance: On the "Sponge" scene without enhancements, Regular Quad bounds have 599.9 avg steps, 8969.0 avg octaves, and 181.8 ms time, resulting in a \times 0.6 slowdown vs Linear bounds. On the "Sponge (far)" scene, they have 416.6 avg steps, 4671.5 avg octaves, and 96.2 ms time, resulting in a \times 0.4 slowdown vs Linear bounds. Scaling: Performance degrades significantly with the number of octaves in FBM due to the exponential growth of \gamma{Fn}. Strengths: Provides tighter bounds for grazing rays compared to linear bounds when the function is smooth and \gamma is small. Can significantly reduce step count when combined with enhancements like BVH and sub-stepping (e.g., \times 4.0 speedup over linear bounds with enhancements). Limitations: High computational overhead for gradient calculation. Inefficient for high-frequency noise (FBM) without enhancements due to large \gamma. When to use: When high accuracy is needed for grazing rays and the function's derivative is cheap to compute and has a small Lipschitz constant. Best used with enhancements like BVH and sub-stepping. When not to use: For simple FBM without enhancements, or when gradient computation is prohibitively expensive. Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Functions were introduced by Aydinlilar et al. in the context of fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise. The method leverages the quadratic Taylor expansion to create forward inclusion functions that bound the implicit function's value along a ray. name: Ray generation and camera models
body: Ray generation and camera models map 2D image coordinates to 3D rays, establishing the geometric foundation for volume rendering by determining which parts of the scene are observed. This family solves the problem of translating pixel locations into valid ray origins and directions for subsequent intersection and integration steps. It sets itself apart from sibling primitives by focusing on the initial geometric parameterization of rays rather than their traversal or intersection logic. All methods in this family generate a set of rays, typically represented as origins \mathbf{o} and directions \mathbf{d}, for every pixel in the output image. The core mechanism involves: 1. Coordinate Mapping: Converting discrete pixel indices (u, v) or normalized device coordinates (NDC) into continuous 2D positions on a virtual image plane. 2. Camera Basis Construction: Defining a local coordinate system for the camera using an eye position \mathbf{e}, a target point \mathbf{t}, and an up vector \mathbf{up}. This yields the basis vectors: forward \mathbf{f} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{t} - \mathbf{e}), right \mathbf{r} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\mathbf{f}, \mathbf{up})), and camera-up \mathbf{u} = \text{cross}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{f}). 3. Ray Assembly: Computing the origin \mathbf{o} (often the eye position) and the direction \mathbf{d} (normalized vector from origin to image plane point). 4. Parameterization: Sampling depth along the ray, often using linear sampling in NDC space for disparity or metric depth. Maps camera-space rays into a bounded Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) space, typically the cube [-1, 1]^3, enabling the rendering of forward-facing real-world scenes that extend to infinity within a fixed bounding volume. Unlike standard perspective ray generation which samples metric depth, this method converts perspective rays into parallel rays in NDC space and uses disparity (inverse depth) as the sampling parameter, allowing linear sampling in NDC space to correspond to linear sampling in disparity from the near plane to infinity. Choose it when rendering forward-facing scenes with infinite depth extent where linear disparity sampling is required. Improves primary ray performance by grouping rays into beams. Choose it when rendering large images or high-resolution volumes where coalesced memory access and reduced kernel launch overhead significantly impact throughput. Generates a sequence of camera poses along a spiral trajectory for novel view synthesis, defined by a center camera, radius parameters, focal length, vertical offset rate, rotation count, and number of views. Choose it when capturing or synthesizing data that requires continuous, smooth orbital motion around a central subject. Maps 2D screen coordinates to a 3D arcball sphere to compute rotation quaternions for smooth orbiting around a center point. Choose it for interactive 3D navigation and viewport control where intuitive, singularity-free rotation is required. Constructs a 4x4 camera-to-world transformation matrix from a viewing direction (z), up vector, and position. Choose it when a full rigid-body transformation is needed to align camera-space rays with world-space geometry or volume grids. Not given in the sources. Interpolates between a horizon color and a zenith color based on the ray's vertical component to simulate a sky dome. Normalize the view direction \mathbf{d}, compute interpolation factor t = \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 0.7, \mathbf{d}.y), and return \text{mix}(\text{horizon}, \text{zenith}, t). Parameters: \text{horizon} = (0.80, 0.90, 1.0) (RGB color at the horizon, \mathbf{d}.y \approx 0), \text{zenith} = (0.35, 0.60, 0.95) (RGB color at the zenith, \mathbf{d}.y \approx 1), and \text{smoothstep} bounds (0.0, 0.7) (transition range for \mathbf{d}.y). Choose it to provide a natural background for volume scenes without explicit sky geometry. The ray generation program that computes pixel rays, initializes the RNG, and dispatches volume tracing via OptiX optixTrace. Computes pixel index, initializes RNG state, computes normalized screen position, generates ray origin and direction, packs payload for OptiX trace, and traces volume rays with specific visibility masks and SBT offsets. Parameters: VISIBILITYMASKVOLUME (bitmask to restrict traversal to volume geometry), MethodOptiX::RADIANCERAYTYPE (SBT offset and miss index for radiance shading), MethodOptiX::RAYTYPECOUNT (stride between SBT entries). Choose it when leveraging NVIDIA's hardware-accelerated ray tracing API for high-performance volume rendering. Transforms 3D points from world coordinates to camera coordinates given a c2w matrix. Computes the difference between points and camera origin, then multiplies by the transpose of the rotation part of c2w. Choose it when evaluating volume densities or SDFs in camera-local space to simplify intersection math or align with camera-space sampling grids. Generates pseudo-random unit vectors distributed over a sphere using a hash-based random function and spherical coordinate conversion. Compute \theta = 2\pi \times \text{rand}(i \cdot \text{gl\FragCoord.xy}), \phi = \arccos(1 - 2 \times \text{rand}(i \cdot \text{gl\FragCoord.zz})), convert to Cartesian coordinates (x = \cos(\theta)\sin(\phi), y = \sin(\theta)\sin(\phi), z = \cos(\phi)), and return the vector. Choose it for importance sampling of isotropic scattering or generating random viewing directions in global illumination. Transforms the point on the base camera lens aperture (assumed disk-shaped) towards the target camera lens aperture using reused random numbers. Transformation: x'{\text{lens}} = \frac{r'}{r} \times x{\text{lens}}. Jacobian: |S'{i \rightarrow j}(x{\text{lens}})| = \frac{r^2}{r'^2}. Where r and r' are base and target aperture radii. Choose it for multi-view depth-of-field rendering or light field synthesis where aperture positions must be consistently shifted across views. The pinhole camera model, which simulates depth by positioning the eye behind the image plane at a distance f (focal length), is the standard reference for perspective ray generation. This approach creates an illusion of depth by casting rays through the image plane, where the ray direction is the normalized difference between the image plane point and the eye position. In parallel beam projections, rays are generated with identical directions, often calculated using projection angles and detector offsets. Given a bounding box, direction, and distance, the system computes the eye position, target, and field of view (FOV) to generate rays for both perspective and parallel projections. The FOV is typically defined vertically in degrees, with defaults around 60 degrees. A common pitfall in camera basis construction is the singularity when the forward vector is parallel to the up vector, causing the cross product for the 'right' vector to become zero. This is handled by switching to an alternative up vector (e.g., [1, 0, 0]) and recomputing the basis.
